######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-history-origins | Medicaid's Origins: 1965 to Today
Medicaid's Origins: 1965 to Today
Born in 1965: A Great Society Program
Medicaid was created on July 30, 1965, when President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965 (Public Law 89-97). The same law created Medicare. Medicaid was added as Title XIX of the Social Security Act, and Johnson signed the bill in Independence, Missouri, with former President Harry Truman — who had championed national health insurance two decades earlier — at his side.
Both programs were part of Johnson's "Great Society" agenda, a sweeping set of domestic reforms aimed at reducing poverty and racial injustice. But the two programs were built very differently. Medicare was designed as a uniform federal program for people 65 and older. Medicaid, by contrast, was designed as a federal-state partnership: the federal government would pay a share of the cost, but each state would run its own program within federal rules.
This design choice is the single most important thing to understand about Medicaid. Because states administer their own programs, "Medicaid" is really 56 different programs — one for each state, the District of Columbia, and the territories — each with different eligibility rules, covered benefits, and provider payment rates. Two people with identical incomes can qualify in one state and be turned away in another.
Medicaid is authorized by Title XIX of the Social Security Act. It is jointly financed by the federal and state governments but administered by the states within federal guidelines — which is why eligibility and benefits vary widely from state to state.
From Welfare Add-On to Health Insurer
In its early decades, Medicaid was tightly tied to cash welfare. Eligibility was generally linked to receipt of welfare benefits, meaning that to get Medicaid you usually had to qualify for a cash-assistance program first. This linked health coverage to welfare status rather than treating it as health insurance in its own right.
A key early expansion came in 1972, when Congress created the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program. SSI consolidated cash assistance for low-income aged, blind, and disabled people, and in most states it led to automatic Medicaid eligibility for SSI recipients. This permanently expanded Medicaid's role as a payer for people with disabilities and the low-income elderly — populations that remain among the program's most expensive enrollees today.
Over the following decades, Congress gradually decoupled Medicaid from welfare. A series of laws in the 1980s extended coverage to low-income pregnant women and children regardless of welfare status, transforming Medicaid into a broad health-financing program rather than a welfare appendage.

CHIP and the Coverage of Children
The next major milestone came in 1997, when the Balanced Budget Act created the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), originally known as SCHIP. CHIP was designed to cover children in families that earned too much to qualify for Medicaid but could not afford private insurance — generally children in families below roughly 200 percent of the federal poverty level.
CHIP gave states a new, capped pot of federal money and substantial flexibility: states could run CHIP as an expansion of Medicaid, as a separate program, or as a combination of both. Together, Medicaid and CHIP became the backbone of children's health coverage in the United States, and the two programs are now reported and tracked together in most federal enrollment data.
CHIP was enacted as part of the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which provided roughly $40 billion in federal funding through fiscal year 2007 to cover low-income, uninsured children not eligible for Medicaid.
Unlike Medicaid, which is an open-ended entitlement, CHIP funding is capped — states receive a set federal allotment each year. This structural difference still shapes how the two programs are financed and renewed by Congress today.
The Balanced Budget Act of 1997
The ACA and the Biggest Expansion in 50 Years
The Affordable Care Act (ACA), signed in 2010, called for the single largest expansion in Medicaid's history. Starting January 1, 2014, the ACA extended Medicaid eligibility to nearly all non-elderly adults with incomes up to 138 percent of the federal poverty level — including, for the first time, low-income adults without dependent children, who had historically been excluded in most states.
The ACA also created a single, income-based eligibility standard called Modified Adjusted Gross Income (MAGI), replacing a patchwork of welfare-linked rules with one application and one set of rules aligned with the insurance marketplaces. The federal government agreed to pay an unusually generous share of the cost for the newly eligible adults to encourage states to expand.
But in 2012, the Supreme Court changed the plan. In National Federation of Independent Business v. Sebelius, decided June 28, 2012, the Court ruled that the federal government could not force states to expand Medicaid by threatening to withhold all of their existing Medicaid funding. The practical effect was to make the ACA Medicaid expansion optional for each state.

Medicaid Before and After the ACA Expansion
Because of the 2012 Supreme Court decision, ACA Medicaid expansion is optional. As of mid-2025, 41 states (including the District of Columbia) had adopted expansion while 10 states had not — which is why a low-income adult's eligibility still depends heavily on the state they live in.
Expansion Is a State Choice
Medicaid Today: Scale and Significance
Six decades after its creation, Medicaid is one of the largest sources of health coverage in the United States. In fiscal year 2023, Medicaid provided coverage to roughly 96 million individuals over the course of the year at a total cost of about $894 billion. The federal government paid approximately 69 percent of that total and states paid the rest.
Medicaid represented about 18 percent of all national health spending in 2023, making it comparable in scale to Medicare and one of the dominant payers in the entire health system. It is also the nation's primary payer for long-term care and a major financer of births, behavioral health, and care for people with disabilities.
Enrollment fluctuates with the economy and with policy. It surged during the COVID-19 pandemic when states were temporarily barred from disenrolling people, then fell sharply during the post-pandemic "unwinding." As of June 2026, about 73.2 million people were enrolled in Medicaid and CHIP combined — still slightly above pre-pandemic levels but well below the pandemic peak.

Who Medicaid Covers: Populations & Benefits
Four Major Populations
Medicaid does not cover everyone who is poor. It covers specific groups of low-income people defined by federal law and state choices. The program organizes its enrollees into four major populations: children, non-disabled (often called "non-elderly") adults, people who qualify on the basis of a disability, and adults age 65 and older.
Historically, eligibility was "categorical" — you had to fit into a recognized category (such as a child, a pregnant woman, a parent, an aged person, or a person with a disability) and also have a low income. The 2010 Affordable Care Act added a fifth pathway for low-income adults generally, but the categorical structure still shapes how the program works, how benefits are set, and how spending is distributed.
Understanding these four groups is the key to understanding Medicaid's finances, because the populations that make up most of the enrollment are not the populations that drive most of the spending — a tension that runs through nearly every Medicaid policy debate.
Medicaid enrollees fall into four major groups: children, non-disabled adults, people eligible due to disability, and adults 65 and older. Children are the largest group by enrollment, but older adults and people with disabilities drive the majority of spending.
Children: The Largest Group
Children are the single largest group of Medicaid enrollees. Together with the Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP), Medicaid covers a large share of all American children, financing a substantial fraction of all births and serving as the backbone of pediatric coverage for low-income families.
Children also receive Medicaid's most comprehensive benefit guarantee: Early and Periodic Screening, Diagnostic, and Treatment, known as EPSDT. EPSDT requires states to cover periodic and as-needed medical, vision, hearing, and dental screening for children under 21 — and, crucially, to cover any service needed to "correct or ameliorate" a child's physical or mental condition, even if that service is otherwise optional for adults.
Despite being the largest enrollment group, children are relatively inexpensive to cover because most are healthy. In fiscal year 2023, children represented roughly 35 percent of full-benefit enrollment but only about 15 to 16 percent of Medicaid spending.
EPSDT is the most comprehensive pediatric benefit in American health coverage: states must cover any medically necessary service for an eligible child, even services that are optional for adult enrollees.
The Elderly and People With Disabilities: Where the Money Goes
The populations that drive Medicaid spending are adults 65 and older and people who qualify on the basis of a disability. Together these two groups make up a minority of enrollment but the majority of spending, because they tend to have chronic conditions, complex needs, and high rates of long-term care use.
The per-enrollee numbers make the gap vivid. Spending per enrollee is highest for people with disabilities (around $20,950) and older adults (around $20,194) — roughly six times the per-enrollee spending for children (around $3,321), according to KFF analysis of federal data.
This is also why Medicaid is the nation's primary payer for long-term services and supports (LTSS). Medicare generally does not pay for extended nursing-home stays or ongoing personal care, so Medicaid fills that gap — covering nursing facility care and home-based care for people who have exhausted their resources.

Dual Eligibles: Covered by Both Medicare and Medicaid
A particularly important subgroup is "dual eligibles" — people enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid. These are typically low-income older adults or people with disabilities who qualify for Medicare but also meet Medicaid's income and asset limits. For them, Medicare is the primary payer and Medicaid wraps around it, covering premiums, cost-sharing, and benefits Medicare does not, such as long-term care.
Dual eligibles are a small share of enrollees but a hugely disproportionate share of cost. KFF estimates that roughly 12 million Americans are enrolled in both programs — nearly 9 million with full Medicaid benefits and about 3 million with partial benefits. This high-need population accounts for a disproportionate share — about a third — of combined Medicare and Medicaid spending, which is why aligning and coordinating their care is a major policy priority.
Medicaid and Medicare are the first- and second-largest public payers for long-term services and supports, together accounting for roughly 63.6 percent of all LTSS spending nationwide in 2023.
Because Medicare generally does not cover extended nursing-home or personal-care needs, Medicaid is the de facto national long-term care program — a role most enrollees and families do not anticipate until they need it.
Medicaid as the Payer for Long-Term Care
Mandatory vs. Optional Benefits
Just as eligibility groups are split into mandatory and optional, so are benefits. Federal law requires every state Medicaid program to cover a core set of mandatory benefits. These include inpatient and outpatient hospital services, physician services, laboratory and x-ray services, nursing facility services, family planning, federally qualified health center and rural health clinic services, and EPSDT for children.
Beyond that floor, states may choose to cover a wide range of optional benefits — such as prescription drugs (covered by every state in practice), dental care for adults, physical therapy, and home and community-based services. Because these are optional, the exact benefit package an adult receives depends heavily on which state they live in.
This mandatory-versus-optional structure, layered on top of the mandatory-versus-optional eligibility groups, is what makes Medicaid so variable. Two adults with the same income and the same diagnosis can receive very different coverage simply because they live in different states.

Medicaid Benefits: Required vs. State Choice
Some "optional" benefits are nearly universal in practice — every state Medicaid program covers prescription drugs, for example, even though drug coverage is technically optional under federal law. "Optional" describes the legal category, not how common the benefit actually is.
Optional Does Not Mean Rare

######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-eligibility-magi | How Medicaid Eligibility Works: MAGI & Income Rules
How Medicaid Eligibility Works: MAGI & Income Rules
Two Worlds of Eligibility
Medicaid eligibility is not governed by a single income rule. Since the Affordable Care Act, the program effectively runs on two parallel systems. Most enrollees — children, pregnant women, parents and caretakers, and the ACA adult expansion group — qualify under "MAGI" rules. A separate set of older adults and people with disabilities qualify under "non-MAGI" rules that look very different.
Understanding which world an applicant falls into is the first step in any eligibility determination, because the two systems count income differently, treat assets differently, and use different thresholds. Getting the category wrong leads to the wrong answer.
This lesson walks through the MAGI system first — because it covers the majority of enrollees — and then explains how the non-MAGI pathways for the aged, blind, and disabled differ.
Most Medicaid enrollees qualify under MAGI (Modified Adjusted Gross Income) rules: an income-only test with no asset test. Older adults and people with disabilities typically qualify under separate non-MAGI rules that DO include asset limits.
What MAGI Is
MAGI stands for Modified Adjusted Gross Income. It starts with the adjusted gross income (AGI) reported on a federal tax return and adds back a few items: untaxed foreign income, tax-exempt interest, and the non-taxable portion of Social Security benefits. The result is a single, tax-based measure of income used across Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA marketplace subsidies.
MAGI was introduced by the ACA to replace a chaotic patchwork. Before 2014, states used dozens of different income-counting methods with their own deductions and disregards. MAGI created one standardized methodology, aligning the rules so that a household generally files one application and is routed to the right program automatically.
A Medicaid or CHIP household under MAGI is generally the same as a tax household — the people an applicant claims or is claimed with on a federal tax return. This tax-based definition is what makes the system simpler and more uniform than the old welfare-style rules.
Take the household's adjusted gross income from the federal tax return.

How a MAGI Determination Works
The 138% Threshold and the 5% Disregard
In states that adopted the ACA expansion, adults qualify if their MAGI is at or below 138 percent of the federal poverty level (FPL). This single number — 138 percent — is one of the most cited figures in Medicaid policy, but there is a subtle wrinkle behind it.
The statute actually sets the expansion limit at 133 percent of FPL, but the law also provides a standard "income disregard" equal to 5 percent of FPL. When you subtract that 5 percent disregard, an applicant earning exactly 138 percent of FPL is treated as if they earn 133 percent — which is why the effective threshold everyone refers to is 138 percent. Importantly, the disregard equals 5 percent of the poverty level, not 5 percent of the applicant's income.
Because the federal poverty guidelines are updated annually, the dollar value of "138 percent" changes each year. For 2026, the federal poverty level is roughly $15,960 for an individual and about $33,000 for a family of four in the 48 contiguous states; 138 percent of those figures comes to roughly $22,000 for an individual and about $45,500 for a family of four.

A common mistake is to think the 5% disregard subtracts 5% of the applicant's income. It does not — it subtracts an amount equal to 5% of the federal poverty level. That is what turns the statutory 133% limit into the familiar 138% figure.
The Disregard Is 5% of the Poverty Level, Not 5% of Income
No Asset Test for MAGI Groups
One of the most consequential features of MAGI is what it leaves out: there is no asset or resource test. The ACA prohibits states from counting savings, property, or other assets when determining MAGI-based eligibility. A family qualifies based on income alone.
This was a major simplification. Under the old welfare-linked rules, applicants often had to document and "spend down" savings, prove they did not own disqualifying assets, and navigate state-specific resource limits. Eliminating the asset test for MAGI groups removed a significant administrative barrier and made enrollment faster and more automatic.
Income limits also vary by group. Children and pregnant women frequently qualify at higher income levels than adults — often well above 138 percent of FPL, sometimes up to 200 percent or more depending on the state and the CHIP structure — reflecting a longstanding policy priority of covering kids broadly.
Because MAGI aligns Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace subsidy rules, a family can submit a single application and be sorted automatically: the children might land in CHIP, a parent in expansion Medicaid, and a higher-earning adult relative in a subsidized marketplace plan.
This "no wrong door" design was a core goal of the ACA — replacing separate welfare-style applications with one tax-based pathway into the right coverage.
One Application, Many Programs
The Non-MAGI World: Older Adults and People With Disabilities
People who qualify for Medicaid based on age (65 and older), blindness, or disability are exempt from MAGI rules. They use "non-MAGI" pathways, which more closely resemble the older eligibility system — and, critically, they usually DO include an asset test.
The only mandatory non-MAGI pathway is for people who receive Supplemental Security Income (SSI). SSI limits recipients to a modest monthly income and no more than $2,000 in countable assets for an individual. Most non-MAGI enrollees must document that they have limited savings, which is why this group faces far more paperwork than MAGI enrollees.
These asset rules become especially important for long-term care. People seeking Medicaid coverage of nursing-home or home-based long-term care generally face both income limits and a $2,000 asset limit (with some categories tied to 300 percent of the SSI income standard), which is why Medicaid long-term care eligibility is so much more complex than MAGI eligibility for a working family.

MAGI vs. Non-MAGI Eligibility
Medicaid eligibility runs on two systems: MAGI rules for most enrollees and non-MAGI rules for the aged, blind, and disabled.
MAGI (Modified Adjusted Gross Income) starts from tax-return AGI and adds back untaxed foreign income, tax-exempt interest, and non-taxable Social Security benefits.
The ACA introduced MAGI to replace dozens of inconsistent state income-counting methods with one standardized, tax-based methodology.
The well-known 138% of FPL expansion limit is built from a statutory 133% threshold plus a standard 5%-of-FPL income disregard.
The 5% disregard equals 5% of the federal poverty level, not 5% of the applicant's income — a frequent point of confusion.
MAGI eligibility has no asset or resource test; a family qualifies based on income alone, which greatly simplified enrollment.
Non-MAGI pathways for older adults and people with disabilities still include asset limits — often $2,000 per individual under SSI rules — which is central to Medicaid long-term care eligibility.

######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-unwinding-redeterminations | The Great Unwinding: Post-COVID Redeterminations
The Great Unwinding: Post-COVID Redeterminations
A Three-Year Pause on Disenrollment
In normal times, Medicaid enrollees must renew their eligibility periodically — typically once a year — and states disenroll people who no longer qualify or who fail to complete the paperwork. The COVID-19 pandemic suspended that machinery for three years, creating the conditions for what became the largest coverage disruption in the program's history.
At the start of the pandemic in 2020, Congress passed the Families First Coronavirus Response Act (FFCRA). It offered states enhanced federal Medicaid funding in exchange for a condition: states had to keep nearly everyone continuously enrolled, regardless of whether their circumstances changed. This "continuous enrollment provision" meant that for three years, almost no one was disenrolled from Medicaid.
The result was an unprecedented surge in enrollment. Medicaid and CHIP rolls grew by more than 23 million people, reaching nearly 95 million by the time the provision ended — a historic high driven not by a sudden spike in poverty but by the simple fact that the normal "exit door" had been bolted shut.
The "continuous enrollment provision" of the 2020 Families First Coronavirus Response Act barred states from disenrolling most Medicaid members for three years in exchange for extra federal funding. Enrollment swelled to nearly 95 million.
When and How the Pause Ended
The continuous enrollment provision was originally tied to the COVID-19 public health emergency. But in the Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023, signed December 29, 2022, Congress "delinked" the two — setting a fixed end date of March 31, 2023, rather than letting it ride on the emergency declaration. This gave states a predictable date to plan around.
Starting April 1, 2023, states resumed normal eligibility reviews. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) gave states an "unwinding period" of up to 12 months to initiate renewals for their entire caseload — meaning every enrollee's eligibility had to be re-checked over the following year, a massive administrative undertaking after three years of paused renewals.
The enhanced federal funding that came with continuous enrollment was phased down on a schedule rather than cut off at once: a 6.2 percentage-point boost ran through March 2023, then 5 points through June, 2.5 points through September, and 1.5 points through December 2023. States had to meet certain reporting and procedural requirements to keep the phased-down funding.
FFCRA continuous enrollment begins; disenrollments effectively paused.

The Unwinding Timeline
The Scale of the Disenrollment
As states worked through their backlogs, the numbers were staggering. By the time the unwinding concluded in most states, KFF found that about 25 million people had lost Medicaid coverage through the process. Roughly 56 million renewals were completed with coverage retained — meaning about 31 percent of completed renewals ended in disenrollment.
Yet the program did not shrink below where it started. Because of the pandemic-era growth, total Medicaid/CHIP enrollment after the unwinding remained roughly 10 million higher than pre-pandemic levels — the rolls came down sharply from their peak but settled above February 2020.
Outcomes varied enormously by state, reflecting differences in renewal policies and systems. Disenrollment rates ranged from highs around 57 percent in some states to lows around 12 percent in others — a reminder that, as always in Medicaid, where you live shapes what happens to you.

Procedural Terminations: Losing Coverage Over Paperwork
The most important policy lesson of the unwinding is hidden in why people lost coverage. Among those disenrolled, nearly seven in ten — about 69 percent — were dropped for "procedural" reasons: missing paperwork, an outdated mailing address, an unreturned form. Only about 31 percent were actually determined to be ineligible.
This distinction matters enormously. A procedural termination does not mean a person no longer qualifies for Medicaid — it means the state could not confirm their eligibility through the renewal process. Many of those disenrolled were almost certainly still eligible and simply got caught in administrative churn, losing coverage they were entitled to keep.
States can reduce procedural terminations through "ex parte" (automatic) renewals, in which the state confirms eligibility using data it already has — such as tax and wage records — without requiring the enrollee to fill out anything. States with strong ex parte systems had far lower procedural disenrollment rates.
About 69% of unwinding disenrollments were for paperwork or procedural reasons, not because the person was found ineligible. A "procedural termination" means the state could not verify eligibility — many of those people still qualified and lost coverage they were entitled to.
Procedural Termination Is Not the Same as Ineligibility
Children and the Ex Parte Problem
Children were hit especially hard, and one specific system flaw made it worse. In August 2023, CMS determined that 29 states were running their automatic (ex parte) renewals at the household level instead of the individual level. Because children typically qualify for Medicaid or CHIP at higher income thresholds than adults, this flaw improperly dropped many children who should have kept coverage.
Federal officials sounded the alarm, estimating that potentially millions of children across many states had been improperly disenrolled. CMS directed states to fix their systems and to reinstate affected children — including providing retroactive coverage — illustrating how a technical configuration error can ripple into a large-scale coverage loss for the program's most vulnerable enrollees.
The episode reinforced a broader theme: in a program as large and decentralized as Medicaid, administrative design choices — how renewals are processed, whether data is used automatically, how a household is defined — can matter as much as the underlying eligibility rules in determining who actually stays covered.
In August 2023, CMS found that 29 states were processing automatic renewals at the household level rather than per individual. Because kids qualify at higher income limits than adults, eligible children were dropped when the whole household was evaluated together.
CMS ordered states to correct the error and reinstate improperly disenrolled children with retroactive coverage — a real example of how a single processing rule affected the coverage of large numbers of children.
The Household Ex Parte Error of 2023
The 2020 Families First Coronavirus Response Act required states to keep most Medicaid enrollees continuously enrolled in exchange for enhanced federal funding.
Continuous enrollment pushed Medicaid/CHIP enrollment up by more than 23 million people, to nearly 95 million.
The Consolidated Appropriations Act of 2023 ended continuous enrollment on March 31, 2023, delinking it from the public health emergency.
States got a 12-month "unwinding" period starting April 2023 to redetermine their entire caseload, with enhanced funding phased down on a schedule.
About 25 million people lost coverage during the unwinding, though net enrollment remained roughly 10 million above pre-pandemic levels.

######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-fmap-federal-match | The Federal Match: How FMAP Works
The Federal Match: How FMAP Works
The Engine of Medicaid Financing
Medicaid is jointly financed by the federal and state governments, but the federal government does not simply hand states a fixed grant. Instead, it matches state spending: for every dollar a state spends on covered Medicaid services, the federal government pays a share. That share is called the Federal Medical Assistance Percentage, or FMAP.
FMAP is the single most important number in Medicaid financing. It determines how much a state must put up to "draw down" federal dollars, shapes whether states expand or cut their programs, and drives the budget math behind nearly every Medicaid policy debate in Congress and in state capitals.
Crucially, the federal match is an open-ended entitlement. As long as a state is willing to spend its own money on covered services for eligible people, there is no cap on how much the federal government will match. This open-ended structure is what makes Medicaid behave so differently from a block grant or a capped program.
FMAP (Federal Medical Assistance Percentage) is the share of each state's Medicaid spending paid by the federal government. It is open-ended: there is no fixed limit on the federal match as long as the state keeps spending on eligible enrollees and services.
How the FMAP Formula Works
The regular FMAP is set by a formula in federal law that ties each state's match rate to its per capita income relative to the national average. The formula is designed so that poorer states get a higher federal match and wealthier states get a lower one — a deliberate equalizing mechanism.
The formula squares the ratio of state-to-national per capita income, which gives below-average-income states progressively more generous matches. A state whose per capita income equals the national average lands at an FMAP of about 55 percent (meaning the state pays 45 percent). The per capita income figures used are an average of the three most recent years of data, so the rates lag the economy by a few years.
No matter what the formula produces, federal law caps the match within a band: the regular FMAP can never be lower than 50 percent or higher than 83 percent. In practice this means the federal government pays between half and roughly five-sixths of a state's regular Medicaid costs, depending on the state's wealth.
No state's regular match falls below 50% (Congressional Research Service)

High-income states are floored at the 50% minimum even though the formula alone might assign them less. That is why states like New York and California receive a 50% regular match while lower-income states can receive far more.
Wealthier States Get a Lower Match — But Never Below 50%
Drawing Down Federal Dollars
The match structure means states must spend their own money first to unlock federal money — a process often called "drawing down" federal funds. A state cannot receive the federal share without putting up its required state share.
The leverage this creates is substantial. At a 50 percent match, each state dollar brings one federal dollar. At higher match rates, the multiplier grows: across all states, every $1 of state Medicaid spending draws between roughly $1 and about $3 of federal money. This is why Medicaid is such a powerful budget tool for states — and why cuts to state Medicaid spending also forfeit federal dollars.
Because the entitlement is open-ended, the match also flexes automatically with need. When a recession pushes more people onto Medicaid, federal spending rises automatically to match the additional state spending — there is no appropriation that has to be re-voted to cover more enrollees.

How the Federal Match Flows
Enhanced Match Rates: Expansion and CHIP
Some Medicaid spending is matched at higher "enhanced" rates than the regular FMAP. The most important is the ACA expansion match. For adults made newly eligible by the Affordable Care Act, the federal government paid 100 percent of costs from 2014 through 2016, then phased the match down to 90 percent in 2020 — where it has remained since.
That 90 percent expansion match is far more generous than any state's regular FMAP, which is precisely why it was designed to entice states to expand. A state that expands pays only 10 cents of every expansion dollar, with the federal government covering the other 90 cents.
CHIP also carries an enhanced match. The CHIP "E-FMAP" is calculated by reducing a state's regular state share by 30 percent, producing matches typically in the range of roughly 65 to 85 percent across states. Unlike open-ended Medicaid, however, CHIP funding is capped by federal allotments — a structural difference that shapes how the two programs are budgeted.

Regular vs. Enhanced Federal Match
Why FMAP Drives Policy
Because the federal match is so large, FMAP is at the center of how states make decisions and how Congress thinks about Medicaid reform. A state weighing whether to expand Medicaid, add an optional benefit, or raise provider rates is really weighing how many federal dollars its own spending will unlock.
It is also why proposals to convert Medicaid into a block grant or per-capita cap are so consequential. Those proposals would replace the open-ended match with a fixed federal amount, shifting financial risk to states if enrollment or costs grow faster than the cap — a fundamental change to the program's 1965 financing design.
Conversely, lowering the enhanced expansion match from 90 percent would dramatically raise the cost to states of covering expansion adults, which is why analysts model such changes carefully: small changes in the match rate translate into billions of dollars and can determine whether coverage is sustained or scaled back.
Under the ACA, a state that expands Medicaid pays only about 10% of the cost of covering newly eligible adults, with the federal government paying 90%.
That ratio — far more generous than any regular FMAP — is the core financial reason 41 states (including DC) had adopted expansion by mid-2025, and why debates about reducing the 90% match are treated as existential for those programs.
The 90% Match as an Expansion Incentive

######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-managed-care-organizations | MCOs: Capitation, Networks & Accountability
MCOs: Capitation, Networks & Accountability
How Most People Actually Get Medicaid
When people imagine Medicaid, they often picture the state directly paying a doctor each time an enrollee gets care. But that fee-for-service model is no longer how most Medicaid works. Today the majority of enrollees get their care through private health plans under contract with the state, known as Medicaid managed care organizations, or MCOs.
Under managed care, the state pays an MCO a fixed monthly amount for each enrolled member, and the MCO takes on the responsibility — and the financial risk — of arranging and paying for that member's covered care. This shifts day-to-day operations from the state to private plans and fundamentally changes the incentives in the program.
The scale of this shift is enormous. In 2024, more than 73 million people — about 85 percent of Medicaid enrollees — received some or all of their care through a Medicaid managed care plan, and as of July 2025, 42 states (including DC) contracted with comprehensive, risk-based managed care plans.
A Medicaid managed care organization (MCO) is a private health plan paid a fixed monthly amount per enrollee by the state to arrange and pay for that enrollee's covered care. Most Medicaid enrollees are now in managed care rather than fee-for-service.
Capitation: Paying Per Member, Per Month
The defining feature of MCOs is capitation. Instead of paying for each service after it happens, the state pays the MCO a predetermined, per-member-per-month (PMPM) amount to cover and coordinate all of an enrollee's Medicaid services. The plan keeps the difference if it spends less than the capitation payment and absorbs the loss if it spends more.
This is what makes managed care "risk-based." The financial risk of an enrollee's care moves from the state to the plan. In theory this gives MCOs an incentive to keep members healthy and coordinate care efficiently; in practice it also creates a tension — a plan can profit by spending less, so strong oversight is needed to ensure it does not skimp on necessary care.
Federal rules require that capitation rates be "actuarially sound" — projected to cover all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs under the plan's contract. Rates are set in advance by actuaries based on expected enrollment, the health profile (or "acuity") of members, and projected utilization.
Fee-for-Service (FFS)
State pays providers per service

Managed Care (MCO)

Fee-for-Service vs. Managed Care
The Main Types of Managed Care
Not all "managed care" is the same. State Medicaid programs use three main types of arrangements. The dominant model is comprehensive risk-based managed care, in which an MCO is fully at risk for a broad set of benefits in exchange for capitation — this is what most people mean by "Medicaid managed care."
A second model is primary care case management (PCCM). PCCM is really a managed fee-for-service system: enrollees are linked to a primary care provider who is paid a small monthly fee to coordinate care, but services are still billed fee-for-service. The state, not a plan, keeps the financial risk.
A third category is limited-benefit plans, which manage only a specific slice of care — such as behavioral health, dental, or non-emergency transportation — rather than the full benefit package. A single enrollee might be in a comprehensive MCO for most care and a limited-benefit plan for one carved-out service.

Networks and Access
Because an MCO is responsible for arranging care, it builds a network of contracted providers — primary care doctors, specialists, hospitals, behavioral health clinicians — that its members use. The composition of that network directly determines whether members can actually get the care they are entitled to.
This is why states impose network adequacy standards on MCOs, requiring them to maintain enough providers, within reasonable distances and wait times, to serve their enrollees. A capitation payment is meaningless if members cannot find a doctor who participates, so access standards are a core part of holding plans accountable.
Network adequacy is a recurring challenge in Medicaid because provider payment rates are often lower than commercial or Medicare rates, which can limit how many providers are willing to participate. Ensuring adequate networks is therefore one of the central oversight responsibilities states take on when they contract with MCOs.
Medicaid managed care has grown into one of the largest privatized public programs in the country: a small number of large insurers operate Medicaid plans across many states, collectively covering tens of millions of enrollees.
This scale is why CMS and state Medicaid agencies devote so much attention to contract requirements, network standards, and financial oversight — the day-to-day Medicaid experience of most enrollees now runs through these private plans.
A Large, Privatized Delivery System
Accountability: The Medical Loss Ratio
A key tool for holding MCOs accountable is the medical loss ratio (MLR). The MLR measures how much of the capitation revenue a plan actually spends on health care for members, as opposed to administration and profit. A higher MLR means more of each dollar went to care.
Since 2019, federal rules have required states to set capitation rates so that each MCO can reasonably be expected to achieve an MLR of at least 85 percent. In other words, at least 85 cents of every capitation dollar should go to medical care and quality improvement, leaving no more than 15 cents for administration and profit.
The MLR is a direct response to the central risk of capitation: that a plan paid a fixed amount might pad its margins by underspending on care. By setting a floor on medical spending, the MLR — alongside network adequacy rules, quality reporting, and contract oversight — forms the accountability backbone of Medicaid managed care.
Capitation gives MCOs an incentive to coordinate care efficiently, but also a financial incentive to spend less — which could mean denying or delaying needed care. The 85% medical loss ratio floor, network adequacy standards, and quality reporting exist precisely to counter that risk.
Capitation Cuts Both Ways

######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-1115-waivers | Section 1115 Waivers: Laboratories of Democracy
Section 1115 Waivers: Laboratories of Democracy
How States Bend the Rules
Medicaid is governed by a detailed set of federal requirements in the Social Security Act. But the law also contains a powerful escape hatch: Section 1115. This provision lets the Secretary of Health and Human Services approve experimental, pilot, or demonstration projects that depart from the normal rules, as long as the Secretary finds they are likely to promote the objectives of the Medicaid program.
In practice, Section 1115 lets a state ask the federal government for permission to run its Medicaid program differently than the statute would otherwise allow — covering populations or services that are not normally eligible, testing new payment models, or restructuring delivery. It is the single most flexible tool in Medicaid, and it has made the program a genuine laboratory for policy experimentation.
The breadth of the authority is striking: under Section 1115, the Secretary can waive almost any of the state plan requirements in Section 1902 of the Act to the extent necessary to carry out the demonstration. That is why 1115 waivers can reshape a state's program in ways that look very different from "textbook" Medicaid.
A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary approve state Medicaid projects that depart from normal federal rules, as long as they are found likely to promote the objectives of Medicaid. It is the program's most flexible authority.
The Budget Neutrality Guardrail
The flexibility of Section 1115 is not unlimited. The central guardrail is "budget neutrality": over the life of the demonstration, federal Medicaid spending under the waiver may not exceed what federal spending would have been without it. In other words, a state can rearrange how federal dollars are used, but it generally cannot use a waiver to draw down more federal money than it otherwise would have.
Budget neutrality is a longstanding policy and practice rather than an explicit statutory command, and it is typically calculated on a per-enrollee basis. This lets a state reinvest projected savings from one part of its program into new services elsewhere — funding innovations without increasing net federal cost.
This requirement is why waiver negotiations are so technical. Much of the back-and-forth between a state and CMS is about how to project the "without-waiver" baseline and demonstrate that the proposed demonstration will stay within it over the approval period.
Budget neutrality is the core guardrail of Section 1115: federal spending under the waiver cannot exceed what it would have been without the waiver, usually measured on a per-enrollee basis.
How a Waiver Gets Approved
Getting an 1115 waiver is a deliberate, transparent process. Before a state even submits its application to CMS, federal rules require it to provide public notice and hold a state-level public comment period of at least 30 days, publishing the application, objectives, and estimated impact on enrollment and spending.
Once the state submits a complete application, CMS opens its own 30-day federal public comment period, posting the application and collecting comments online. CMS then reviews each proposed policy case by case to judge whether it aligns with Medicaid's objectives, and negotiates terms with the state — a process that can stretch from several months to a couple of years.
Because 1115 authority is meant for research and demonstration, states must also commit to evaluation. They are required to have an approved, publicly available evaluation strategy and to submit interim and final ("summative") evaluation reports, so that the lessons of each experiment are documented.
The state publishes its proposal and holds a state-level comment period of at least 30 days.

The 1115 Waiver Lifecycle
What States Use Waivers For
Section 1115 waivers have been used for an enormous range of purposes, and the dominant uses shift with each administration's priorities. Some states have used waivers to expand coverage to new populations; others to restructure financing; others to test conditions on eligibility. The same tool can be pointed in very different policy directions.
Three recurring categories illustrate the range. Some administrations approved work and community-engagement requirements, conditioning coverage for some adults on employment or related activities. Many states have used Delivery System Reform Incentive Payment (DSRIP) waivers to fund provider-led delivery system transformation. And more recently, states have used waivers to address health-related social needs (HRSN) such as housing and nutrition.
This flexibility is why people call 1115 waivers "laboratories of democracy" — they let individual states test approaches that, if successful, can inform national policy, and if unsuccessful, are contained to the demonstration rather than imposed everywhere.

Common Uses of Section 1115 Waivers
Real Demonstrations in Action
Concrete examples show how varied these demonstrations are. In 2011, CMS approved Texas's 1115 waiver, which paired an uncompensated-care funding pool with a DSRIP program to fund innovative initiatives for Medicaid beneficiaries. New York launched its own DSRIP program under an 1115 waiver approved in 2014, focused on reducing avoidable hospital use, before it expired in 2020.
More recently, the federal government approved a wave of waivers addressing health-related social needs. As of early 2024, eight states — including Arizona, Arkansas, California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, and Washington — had approved demonstrations authorizing evidence-based housing and nutrition services for specific high-need populations.
Across the country, 1115 demonstrations are now widespread: nearly every state has at least one active Section 1115 waiver, and some have several. That near-universal adoption is why understanding 1115 authority is essential to understanding how Medicaid actually operates state by state — the "rules" in any given state are often shaped as much by its waivers as by the base statute.
Beginning in the 2020s, CMS approved Section 1115 waivers letting states use Medicaid to pay for evidence-based health-related social needs — such as short-term housing supports and medically tailored nutrition — for targeted high-need populations.
States including California, Massachusetts, and others used this authority to test whether addressing social drivers of health can improve outcomes and reduce costly medical care, exactly the kind of experiment Section 1115 was designed to enable.
HRSN Waivers for Housing and Nutrition
Section 1115 of the Social Security Act lets the HHS Secretary approve demonstration projects that depart from normal Medicaid rules if they promote the program's objectives.
Under 1115, the Secretary can waive almost any state plan requirement in Section 1902 to the extent needed to run the demonstration.
The central guardrail is budget neutrality: federal spending under the waiver cannot exceed what it would have been without it, usually measured per enrollee.
Approval requires both state and federal public comment periods (30 days each) and case-by-case CMS review and negotiation, often taking months to years.
Demonstrations are generally approved for an initial five-year period and require an evaluation strategy with interim and final reports.
States use waivers for very different goals — expanding coverage, testing work requirements, DSRIP delivery reform, and health-related social needs like housing and nutrition.
1115 waivers are nearly universal (nearly every state has at least one active waiver), so a state's real Medicaid program is often shaped as much by its waivers as by the base statute.
Budget neutrality means that over the life of the demonstration, federal Medicaid spending under the waiver cannot exceed projected federal spending without it — typically calculated on a per-enrollee basis. It lets states reinvest projected savings into innovations without increasing net federal cost.

######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-hcbs-waivers | HCBS Waivers: Care at Home Instead of in Institutions
HCBS Waivers: Care at Home Instead of in Institutions
The Institutional Bias Problem
Medicaid is the nation's primary payer for long-term services and supports (LTSS) — the help people with disabilities and frail older adults need with daily activities like bathing, dressing, eating, and managing medications. But for much of Medicaid's history, the program was structurally tilted toward providing that help in institutions rather than in people's own homes.
The tilt comes from the statute itself. Under federal Medicaid rules, coverage of nursing facility care is mandatory — every state must cover it — while coverage of most home- and community-based services (HCBS) is optional. This asymmetry is known as Medicaid's "institutional bias."
The bias also appears in eligibility. In many cases, individuals can qualify for Medicaid at a higher income and asset threshold when they receive nursing facility care than when they receive personal care or home health care at home — nudging people toward the very institutional settings that most would prefer to avoid.
Medicaid's "institutional bias" exists because federal law makes nursing facility coverage mandatory but most home- and community-based services (HCBS) optional — historically steering people toward institutions rather than home-based care.
The 1915(c) Waiver Solution
Congress created a fix in 1981: the Section 1915(c) home- and community-based services waiver. This authority lets states offer a broad range of home-based services to people who would otherwise require institutional care — directly countering the institutional bias built into the base program.
The logic of a 1915(c) waiver is a trade. To enroll, a person must have a level of need that would qualify them for an institutional benefit, such as nursing facility care. In exchange, the state can wrap services around them at home — personal care, respite, home modifications, supported employment, day programs, and more — that traditional Medicaid would not otherwise cover.
There is a financial guardrail: the services a person receives under the waiver must, on average, cost no more than the institutional care they would otherwise need. The waiver is meant to be a cost-effective substitute for institutionalization, not an open-ended new benefit.
The person must need a level of care that would qualify for an institutional Medicaid benefit, like nursing facility care.
Establish institutional level of need
The state provides HCBS — personal care, respite, home modifications, supported employment, and more.
Offer home-based alternatives
Average waiver costs must not exceed what institutional care would have cost.
Stay cost-neutral
States may limit the waiver to specific groups, such as people with I/DD or older adults.
Target the population
How a 1915(c) Waiver Works
Olmstead: When the Supreme Court Stepped In
The push toward community-based care got a powerful boost from the courts. In Olmstead v. L.C., decided June 22, 1999, the Supreme Court held that the unjustified institutional segregation of people with disabilities is a form of discrimination prohibited by Title II of the Americans with Disabilities Act.
The case involved two women in Georgia, Lois Curtis and Elaine Wilson, who had been kept confined in a state psychiatric hospital for years after clinicians agreed they were ready for community placement. The Court established a three-part test: community placement is required when treatment professionals deem it appropriate, the individual does not oppose it, and it can be reasonably accommodated given the state's resources and the needs of others.
This principle, known as the ADA's "integration mandate," reframed home- and community-based care as a civil right rather than merely a policy option. It created sustained legal pressure on states to expand HCBS and reduce unnecessary institutionalization.
Unjustified institutional segregation of people with disabilities is a form of discrimination under the Americans with Disabilities Act — the core holding of Olmstead v. L.C. (1999).
The Rebalancing of Long-Term Care
Together, the 1915(c) waiver authority and the Olmstead decision drove a dramatic "rebalancing" of Medicaid long-term care away from institutions and toward the community. The shift over two decades was profound.
In 1999, when Olmstead was decided, about 27 percent of Medicaid LTSS spending went to home- and community-based services and roughly 73 percent went to institutional care. By 2020, those proportions had essentially flipped: 62.5 percent of LTSS spending went to HCBS and 37.5 percent to institutions.
This reversal represents one of the most significant structural changes in the history of American long-term care — moving from a system that assumed institutional placement to one in which most Medicaid long-term care dollars now support people living in their own homes and communities.

Waiting Lists: The Catch
There is a major catch to HCBS waivers. Because most HCBS are optional, states are allowed to cap the number of people they serve under a waiver — limiting the number of "slots." When demand for home-based services exceeds the available slots, the result is a waiting list.
These waiting lists are large and persistent. More than 707,000 people were on HCBS waiver waiting lists in 2017, and more than 710,000 were on waiting or interest lists in 2024 — meaning hundreds of thousands of people who qualify for home-based care must wait, sometimes for years, for a slot to open. People with intellectual and developmental disabilities (I/DD) make up most of those waiting — about two-thirds in 2017 and 73 percent in 2024.
Waiting lists expose the central tension of the HCBS waiver model: institutional care is a mandatory entitlement that no one waits for, while community-based care — the option most people prefer — can be capped and rationed. This is why advocates continue to push for stronger HCBS guarantees, and why waiting-list size is a closely watched measure of how well a state is meeting the spirit of Olmstead.
Because nursing facility care is a mandatory Medicaid benefit but HCBS is optional and can be capped, a person can be entitled to institutional care immediately while waiting years for a home-based waiver slot — the opposite of what most people want.
Nursing Homes Have No Waiting List — Home Care Often Does

To use a 1915(c) waiver, a person must meet an institutional level of need, and average waiver costs must not exceed the cost of institutional care.

######## medicaid-101 | medicaid-quality-measures | Measuring Medicaid Quality: HEDIS, CAHPS & State Reporting
Measuring Medicaid Quality: HEDIS, CAHPS & State Reporting
Why Measure Medicaid Quality?
Covering people is only half of Medicaid's job; the other half is making sure the care they receive is actually good. Because most Medicaid enrollees now get care through private managed care plans paid a fixed amount per member, there is a built-in risk that a plan could cut corners to save money. Quality measurement is how states and the federal government keep watch.
Quality measurement turns vague questions — "Are kids getting their vaccines?" "Can adults get appointments when they need them?" — into standardized numbers that can be compared across plans, across states, and over time. Those numbers feed oversight, public reporting, and increasingly, payment.
Three pillars dominate Medicaid quality measurement: HEDIS (clinical process and outcome measures), CAHPS (patient experience surveys), and the federal Adult and Child Core Sets (a standardized national reporting set). This lesson walks through each and how they fit together.
Medicaid quality measurement converts care into standardized, comparable numbers. The three pillars are HEDIS (clinical measures), CAHPS (patient experience), and the federal Adult and Child Core Sets (national reporting).
HEDIS: The Clinical Yardstick
HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — is the most widely used set of health plan performance measures in the United States. It is developed and maintained by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), a private nonprofit, and used by commercial, Medicare, and Medicaid plans alike.
HEDIS includes more than 90 measures across six domains of care, spanning prevention, acute care, and chronic care. It captures structure, process, and outcomes: things like childhood immunization status, follow-up after a hospitalization for mental illness, controlling high blood pressure, and screening for cancer. Because the specifications are standardized, one plan's diabetes-control rate can be compared directly with another's.
Standardization is the whole point. Without common definitions, every plan could define "well-child visit" or "blood pressure control" differently, making comparison meaningless. HEDIS provides the shared yardstick that lets states benchmark plans against each other and against national norms.

CAHPS: Asking Patients Directly
HEDIS tells you what was done clinically, but it cannot tell you what care felt like to the person receiving it. That is the job of CAHPS — the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems. CAHPS is a family of standardized patient-experience surveys originally developed under the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ).
The CAHPS Health Plan Survey asks members directly about their experiences. It produces four global ratings — overall health care, the health plan, the personal doctor, and the specialist seen most often — plus composite scores in areas like getting care quickly, getting needed care, customer service, and how well doctors communicate.
CAHPS is tightly integrated with HEDIS: NCQA asks plans to submit results from a modified version of the CAHPS Health Plan Survey as part of HEDIS reporting. Together, the two give a fuller picture — HEDIS for clinical performance, CAHPS for the patient's lived experience.

The Adult and Child Core Sets
To make quality comparable across all 50 states, CMS maintains standardized national measure sets specifically for Medicaid and CHIP: the Core Set of Adult Health Care Quality Measures and the Core Set of Children's Health Care Quality Measures. Many of these draw on HEDIS and CAHPS specifications.
For years, state reporting on these Core Sets was voluntary, which meant patchy and inconsistent national data. That changed in 2024: reporting of the Child Core Set and of the behavioral health measures within the Adult Core Set became mandatory for all states, the District of Columbia, and the territories. The first round of mandatory reporting had to be submitted and certified by states by December 31, 2024.
Mandatory reporting is a significant step. It gives CMS and the public a consistent, nationwide view of how Medicaid and CHIP are performing on priorities like children's preventive care and behavioral health — and creates accountability that voluntary reporting never could.
The 2024 mandatory behavioral health measure set drew 7 measures from the Child Core Set and 11 from the Adult Core Set, covering areas such as follow-up after mental health hospitalization and monitoring for people on certain medications.
CMS uses these measures to track and push progress on behavioral health across state Medicaid and CHIP programs — an area of intense need that consistent national reporting can finally illuminate.
Behavioral Health in the Core Sets
Turning Measures Into Accountability: The EQRO
Measures are only useful if the underlying data is trustworthy and someone acts on it. In Medicaid managed care, that role falls to the External Quality Review Organization (EQRO). Federal rules require every state that contracts with managed care plans to hire at least one independent EQRO to conduct an annual external quality review of each plan.
The EQRO evaluates each plan on quality, timeliness, and access to care, and produces an annual technical report. Two of its core activities are validating the performance-measure data plans report and conducting HEDIS Compliance Audits — the industry's gold-standard check that a plan can produce valid, reliable measure data. Under the federal "nonduplication" option, many states let the plan-funded HEDIS Audit satisfy the external review's performance-measure validation requirement.
This is the loop that ties the whole system together: plans report HEDIS and CAHPS results, states fold many of those into the federal Core Sets, and independent EQROs validate the data and hold plans accountable. Quality measurement is not paperwork for its own sake — it is the mechanism that protects enrollees in a program where most care is delivered by private plans paid a fixed amount.

######## clinical-quality-measurement | why-quality-measurement-matters | Why Quality Measurement Matters
Why Quality Measurement Matters
The Problem Hiding in Plain Sight
For most of the 20th century, American medicine assumed that well-trained doctors working in good hospitals delivered good care, and there was little systematic effort to check. Quality was treated as a matter of individual competence and professional reputation, not something you measured, reported, or improved as a system.
That assumption shattered at the turn of the century, when a pair of landmark reports forced the country to confront how often care fell short. The realization was uncomfortable: the gap between the care people should receive and the care they actually received was enormous, and largely invisible because no one was measuring it.
Clinical quality measurement is the response to that problem. It is the discipline of defining what good care looks like, turning it into standardized metrics, and using the resulting data to hold the system accountable and drive improvement. This lesson explains why that discipline exists and why it matters.
Clinical quality measurement is the systematic practice of defining good care, converting it into standardized metrics, and using the data to improve outcomes and hold the health system accountable.
To Err Is Human: The Wake-Up Call
In November 1999, the Institute of Medicine (IOM) released "To Err Is Human: Building a Safer Health System." Its central finding stunned the public and the profession: between 44,000 and 98,000 Americans were dying each year as a result of preventable medical errors in hospitals.
To put that in perspective, even the lower estimate would have made medical error the eighth leading cause of death in the United States — killing more people than motor vehicle accidents, breast cancer, or AIDS. The report estimated that medication errors alone accounted for about 7,000 deaths annually, and that the economic cost of preventable adverse events ran to tens of billions of dollars.
Crucially, the report reframed the problem. It argued that most errors were not the fault of bad individuals but of bad systems — poorly designed processes that set up competent people to fail. The solution, therefore, was not to blame and punish, but to measure, learn, and redesign. That insight launched the modern patient-safety and quality-measurement movements.

Crossing the Quality Chasm: The Six Aims
Two years later, in 2001, the IOM followed up with "Crossing the Quality Chasm: A New Health System for the 21st Century." Where the first report focused on safety, this one widened the lens to the entire quality gap — the chasm between the care we know how to deliver and the care patients actually get.
Its lasting contribution was a definition of quality itself. The report proposed six "Aims for Improvement" that still anchor quality measurement today: care should be safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. These six aims gave the field a shared vocabulary — any quality measure can be mapped to one or more of them.
The inclusion of equity as a core aim was especially consequential. By naming equitable care — care that does not vary in quality based on personal characteristics like race, gender, geography, or income — as a defining feature of quality, the report planted the seed for the equity-focused measurement work that has become central to the field.
Avoiding harm to patients from the care that is meant to help them.
Safe
Providing evidence-based care to those who benefit and avoiding underuse and overuse.
Effective
Respecting and responding to individual patient preferences, needs, and values.
Patient-centered
Reducing waits and harmful delays for patients and caregivers.
Timely
Avoiding waste of equipment, supplies, ideas, and energy.
Efficient
Ensuring care does not vary in quality due to gender, ethnicity, geography, or socioeconomic status.
Equitable
The Six Aims of Quality (IOM, 2001)
How Big Is the Gap? The Evidence
The IOM reports made the case conceptually; a landmark study soon quantified it. In 2003, Elizabeth McGlynn and colleagues published a study in the New England Journal of Medicine examining whether adults actually received recommended care.
The researchers reviewed the medical records of nearly 7,000 adults across 12 metropolitan areas, scoring care against 439 clinical indicators for 30 conditions plus preventive care. The headline result: on average, participants received just 54.9 percent of recommended care — barely more than a coin flip.
The variation was striking. Performance ranged from about 79 percent of recommended care for senile cataracts down to just 10.5 percent for alcohol dependence. The study made the abstract "quality chasm" concrete and measurable, and demonstrated exactly why the field needed standardized measures: you cannot close a gap you cannot see.
McGlynn and colleagues found U.S. adults received only about 55% of recommended care, with wide variation by condition — from ~79% for cataracts to ~10.5% for alcohol dependence.
Published in the New England Journal of Medicine, it became one of the most-cited demonstrations that the quality gap was real, large, and unevenly distributed — strengthening the case for systematic measurement.
The McGlynn "Quality of Health Care" Study (2003)
Why Measurement Drives Improvement
The premise behind quality measurement is often summarized as "what gets measured gets managed." When performance is quantified, problems become visible, comparisons become possible, and attention concentrates where the data points. Measurement creates accountability and transparency that professional good intentions alone cannot.
In practice, measurement now drives improvement through several channels: internal quality improvement teams use it to target their efforts, public reporting lets patients and purchasers compare providers, and value-based payment programs tie reimbursement directly to measured performance. Each channel depends on having trustworthy, standardized measures.
But measurement is a tool, not a guarantee. Measuring the wrong things, or measuring well-intentioned things poorly, can distract clinicians, create administrative burden, and even harm care by encouraging "teaching to the test." The rest of this course is about doing measurement well — choosing meaningful measures, calculating them correctly, and using them to genuinely improve care rather than just generate reports.
"What gets measured gets managed" cuts both ways. Poorly chosen measures can divert attention from what matters, add documentation burden, and incentivize gaming the metric instead of improving care. Good measurement requires choosing the right measures, not just more of them.
Measurement Can Backfire

######## clinical-quality-measurement | structure-process-outcome | Structure, Process, and Outcome Measures
Structure, Process, and Outcome Measures
A Framework for Thinking About Quality
If you want to measure the quality of care, you first need a way to organize what you are measuring. The dominant framework for doing this was created by one physician-scholar, Avedis Donabedian, and it has shaped quality measurement for more than half a century.
Donabedian first laid out his model in a 1966 article, "Evaluating the Quality of Medical Care," which became one of the most-cited public health articles of the 20th century. His insight was deceptively simple: information about quality can be drawn from three categories — structure, process, and outcome — and these three categories are causally linked.
The linkage is the heart of the model. As Donabedian put it, good structure increases the likelihood of good process, and good process increases the likelihood of good outcome. Understanding which kind of measure you are looking at — and how the three relate — is foundational to everything else in quality measurement.
The Donabedian model organizes quality measurement into three categories — structure, process, and outcome — linked by a chain: good structure makes good process more likely, and good process makes good outcomes more likely.
Structure: The Conditions of Care
Structure measures capture the relatively stable characteristics of the providers and the environment in which care is delivered — the context, not the care itself. Donabedian defined structure as the stable attributes of the settings where care happens.
Concrete examples include the physical plant (hospital buildings and equipment), human resources (staffing levels, nurse-to-patient ratios, clinician credentials), and organizational features (financing, governance, whether the hospital uses a certified electronic health record). These are things you can often verify without watching a single patient encounter.
Structure measures are easy to assess and relatively stable over time, which makes them attractive. Their weakness is that they are the furthest removed from the patient. A hospital can have excellent facilities and well-credentialed staff and still deliver poor care — good structure makes good care more likely, but does not guarantee it.
For this reason, structure measures are often treated as necessary preconditions rather than proof of quality. They answer the question "is the capacity for good care in place?" — not "did good care actually happen?"
Process: What Was Actually Done
Process measures capture the transactions between patients and providers — what clinicians actually do during care. They answer the question "are we doing the things we say we should do?" Process measures assess whether evidence-based care was properly applied.
Examples are everywhere in quality programs: the share of diabetic patients who received an eye exam, the percentage of heart-attack patients given aspirin on arrival, whether a patient was screened for depression, or the time between a discharge order and the patient actually leaving. Each captures a specific, controllable step in the care process.
Process measures have a major practical advantage: they are directly actionable and largely within the provider's control. If a process measure is low, the team usually knows exactly what to fix. They also require little or no risk adjustment, because they measure what clinicians did rather than how sick the patients were — which is why many quality programs lean heavily on process measures.
Process Measures
Measure what clinicians actually did
Directly actionable and controllable
Little risk adjustment needed

Outcome Measures
Measure the result for the patient
The "ultimate validator" of quality
Require careful risk adjustment
Harder to attribute and subject to time lags
Process vs. Outcome Measures
Outcome: The Result for the Patient
Outcome measures capture the effects of care on the health status of patients and populations — the results that ultimately matter. Examples include surgical-site infection rates, 30-day mortality, hospital readmissions, functional status, and patient-reported quality of life.
Donabedian called outcomes the "ultimate validators" of the quality of care, and intuitively they are what everyone cares about. But outcome measures carry two serious complications. First, outcomes have time lags and are often influenced by many factors beyond any single provider — a 30-day readmission depends not just on hospital care but on the patient's other conditions, medication adherence, and social circumstances.
Second, because they reflect patient mix, outcome measures usually require risk adjustment — statistical correction for how sick the patients were — to be compared fairly. Without it, a hospital that treats sicker patients looks worse even if its care is excellent. Risk adjustment promotes fair comparison, but it is technically difficult and, done poorly, can itself distort incentives.
Because outcomes are high-stakes, they are more vulnerable to gaming than process or structure measures. A classic example: a measure tracking patient falls led some facilities to confine patients to bed, reducing falls but harming recovery. Measuring the right outcome — and watching for perverse responses — is essential.
Outcome Measures Can Be Gamed
Balancing Measures and Using the Framework
Modern quality improvement adds a fourth practical category that does not fit neatly into Donabedian's triad: balancing measures. A balancing measure watches for unintended consequences — checking that improving one thing did not quietly worsen another.
For example, a team working to reduce hospital length of stay might track 30-day readmissions as a balancing measure, to make sure faster discharges are not simply sending patients home too soon. Balancing measures guard against the "whack-a-mole" risk that optimizing a single metric creates a new problem elsewhere.
In practice, robust quality programs use a mix of all these measure types. Structure confirms the foundation is in place, process shows whether the right care was delivered, outcomes validate whether patients actually benefited, and balancing measures catch side effects. No single type tells the whole story — the art of measurement is combining them into a coherent picture.
Consider sepsis care. A structure measure might be whether the hospital has a 24/7 rapid-response team. A process measure is the share of septic patients who received antibiotics within the first hour. An outcome measure is sepsis mortality.
A balancing measure might track unnecessary antibiotic use, ensuring the drive for speed does not fuel antibiotic overuse. Together they show whether good structure led to good process and ultimately to good outcomes — exactly the chain Donabedian described.
The Donabedian Chain in Action
Avedis Donabedian's 1966 model organizes quality measurement into three linked categories: structure, process, and outcome.
The model's core logic: good structure increases the likelihood of good process, which increases the likelihood of good outcomes.
Structure measures capture the stable context of care (facilities, staffing, equipment) — necessary preconditions but not proof of good care.
Process measures capture what clinicians actually did; they are directly actionable, largely controllable, and need little risk adjustment.
Outcome measures capture results for patients and are the "ultimate validators," but require risk adjustment and are subject to time lags and attribution problems.
Outcome measures are the most vulnerable to gaming, so teams must choose the right outcomes and watch for perverse responses.
Balancing measures track unintended consequences, and strong quality programs combine structure, process, outcome, and balancing measures rather than relying on one type.
This is a process measure: it captures what clinicians actually did during care (administering aspirin) — a controllable, evidence-based step. A structure measure would describe the care environment (e.g., staffing), and an outcome measure would capture the result (e.g., 30-day mortality).
