######## clinical-quality-measurement | measure-stewardship | Measure Stewardship: NCQA, CMS, TJC, NQF
Measure Stewardship: NCQA, CMS, TJC, NQF
Who Owns a Quality Measure?
A quality measure is not a casual statistic. Behind every measure — say, "percentage of adults with diabetes whose blood sugar is controlled" — sits an organization responsible for defining it precisely, keeping it current with the evidence, and deciding when to retire it. That organization is called the measure steward.
Measure stewardship is a formal, ongoing responsibility. Stewards approve a measure's content, update the diagnostic and procedure codes tied to its technical specifications, adjust the measure as clinical evidence changes, and can withdraw it from use when it becomes obsolete. A related role, the measure developer, does the technical work of building and maintaining measures, often under a steward's direction; a single organization can play both roles.
Understanding who stewards which measures matters because it tells you where a measure's authority and accountability live. The U.S. measurement ecosystem is dominated by a handful of organizations, each with a distinct role — and the landscape shifted notably in 2023.
A measure steward is the organization responsible for defining a quality measure, keeping its specifications current with clinical evidence, and retiring it when obsolete. Measure developers build and maintain measures, often under a steward's direction.
NCQA: Steward of HEDIS
The National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) is a private nonprofit and the steward of HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — one of the most widely used performance-measurement tools in health care. When a health plan reports a "HEDIS measure," NCQA wrote and maintains the specification.
NCQA's influence comes from both its measures and its accreditation programs. Health plans seek NCQA accreditation, and HEDIS results feed directly into plan ratings and into many state Medicaid and Medicare Advantage oversight processes. Because NCQA controls the specifications, it effectively defines what "good" looks like for a huge swath of preventive and chronic-care quality.
NCQA is also driving the transition from manual chart-based HEDIS reporting toward fully digital quality measures — a shift covered later in this course — which positions it at the center of the field's technical future as well as its present.
In short, NCQA is the steward most associated with ambulatory, preventive, and chronic-disease measurement across commercial, Medicaid, and Medicare Advantage plans.
CMS and The Joint Commission
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) is the single largest force in U.S. quality measurement. CMS stewards most measures developed under its contracts, and its measure inventory houses over 500 measures used across dozens of federal programs — from hospital reporting to physician payment. Because CMS measures are tied to payment and public reporting for Medicare and Medicaid, they carry enormous weight.
The Joint Commission (TJC) plays a different but complementary role. TJC accredits hospitals and other facilities, and its accredited organizations must meet performance-measurement requirements by submitting data through TJC's ORYX program — including electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) and chart-abstracted measures. For hospitals, TJC accreditation is often a practical prerequisite for participating in Medicare.
The division of labor is roughly this: NCQA dominates health-plan and ambulatory measurement, CMS dominates federal payment and public-reporting programs, and TJC ties measurement to facility accreditation. Many measures flow between them — a single eCQM might be developed for CMS, reported through TJC's ORYX, and overlap with HEDIS.

Major Quality Measurement Organizations
Endorsement and the NQF Transition
Stewards develop and maintain measures, but a separate function determines whether a measure is considered scientifically sound and worthy of national use: endorsement. Section 1890 of the Social Security Act requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to contract with a "consensus-based entity" (CBE) to run a transparent, multi-stakeholder process for endorsing quality and cost measures and keeping them updated.
For most of the field's history, that consensus-based entity was the National Quality Forum (NQF) — a nonprofit whose "NQF-endorsed" stamp became the gold standard signaling a measure had passed rigorous scientific review. The CBE also convenes the Measure Applications Partnership (MAP), a multi-stakeholder group that recommends to HHS which measures to use in CMS programs, as part of an annual "pre-rulemaking" process.
This changed in 2023. Effective March 27, 2023, NQF was no longer the contracted CBE for CMS; CMS instead awarded the contract to the Battelle Memorial Institute, which now runs the consensus-based functions under the banner of the Partnership for Quality Measurement (PQM). Notably, PQM charges no membership dues, opening participation to the public for free. Separately, in August 2023 The Joint Commission acquired NQF, which continues some endorsement activities within TJC.
A common outdated belief is that "NQF endorses measures for CMS." Since March 2023, the contracted consensus-based entity is Battelle, operating as the Partnership for Quality Measurement (PQM). NQF itself was acquired by The Joint Commission later in 2023.
NQF Is No Longer the CMS Consensus-Based Entity
How the Pieces Fit Together
Put together, the lifecycle of a measure crosses several of these organizations. A developer builds a measure; a steward (NCQA, CMS, or another) maintains it; the consensus-based entity endorses it through a transparent process; the Measure Applications Partnership recommends whether it should be used in federal programs; and CMS or accreditors like TJC then put it into payment and reporting.
This layered structure exists to balance two things: rigor and accountability. No single organization should be able to declare a measure "good" and force it into payment unilaterally. By separating stewardship, endorsement, and program selection, the system builds in scientific review and public input before a measure can affect how providers are paid or rated.
For anyone working in quality, the practical lesson is to always know a measure's provenance: who stewards it, whether it is endorsed, and which programs use it. Those facts determine how authoritative the measure is, how stable its specifications are, and how seriously providers must take it.

######## clinical-quality-measurement | hedis-measures-overview | HEDIS Measures: What They Are and How They're Calculated
HEDIS Measures: What They Are and How They're Calculated
The Most Widely Used Measure Set in America
HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — is the most widely used set of health-plan performance measures in the United States. Stewarded by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), it is reported by commercial, Medicaid, and Medicare Advantage plans covering the large majority of insured Americans.
HEDIS matters because its results are everywhere. They feed NCQA health-plan accreditation and ratings, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, and many state Medicaid oversight programs. Because the specifications are standardized and audited, a plan's breast-cancer-screening rate in one state can be compared directly with another plan's across the country.
NCQA updates HEDIS each "measurement year" (MY), adding, revising, and retiring measures as evidence changes. The current set includes more than 90 measures, giving plans and regulators a broad, comparable picture of performance across the spectrum of care.
HEDIS is NCQA's standardized set of 90+ health-plan performance measures, updated annually by measurement year. Its results drive accreditation, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, and Medicaid oversight.
The Domains of Care
HEDIS organizes its measures into domains so that performance can be understood by category rather than as a jumble of individual metrics. The set spans roughly six domains covering the breadth of plan performance.
The domains include Effectiveness of Care (the largest, covering preventive and chronic-disease care like screenings and diabetes control), Access/Availability of Care, Experience of Care, Utilization and Risk-Adjusted Utilization, Health Plan Descriptive Information, and measures collected through electronic clinical data systems. The Effectiveness of Care domain is where most of the familiar clinical measures live.
This organization maps neatly onto the Donabedian framework and the IOM aims: effectiveness and access measures are largely process-oriented, experience measures capture patient-centeredness, and utilization measures help detect underuse and overuse. The domains let a plan see not just whether it is doing well, but in which dimension of quality.
Across the full set (NCQA)

How a HEDIS Measure Is Calculated
At its core, almost every HEDIS measure is a rate: a numerator divided by a denominator. The denominator is the eligible population — the members who could have received the service in question. The numerator is the subset of those members who actually received it (or met the clinical target). The rate is simply numerator ÷ denominator.
Defining the denominator precisely is most of the work. NCQA specifies an "eligible population" using age, gender, diagnosis, and enrollment criteria, then subtracts denominator exclusions — members for whom the service would not be appropriate. HEDIS commonly excludes people in hospice or palliative care, those with advanced illness or frailty, and long-term nursing-home residents, because the measured service may not benefit them.
Two other rules shape the denominator. A continuous enrollment requirement specifies how long a member must have been enrolled (with only small allowable gaps) before they count, so a plan is not judged on members it barely covered. And measures define a precise measurement window for when qualifying events and services must occur.
Apply age, gender, diagnosis, and continuous-enrollment criteria to define who could receive the service.
Identify the eligible population
Remove members for whom the service is inappropriate (e.g., hospice, frailty, advanced illness).

Identify which eligible members received the service or met the clinical target.

Rate = numerator ÷ denominator, reported as a percentage.

Calculating a HEDIS Rate
Where the Data Comes From
A measure is only as good as the data feeding it, and HEDIS uses three collection methods. The administrative method relies entirely on claims and encounter data the plan already has — it is cheap and complete but captures only what was billed. If a service happened but was not coded on a claim, administrative data misses it.
The hybrid method addresses that gap by combining administrative data with manual review of a random sample of medical records — traditionally 411 members — to find services that were delivered but not captured in claims. Hybrid measurement is more accurate but labor-intensive and expensive, requiring trained abstractors to pull data from charts.
The third and increasingly important method is the Electronic Clinical Data Systems (ECDS) method, which draws structured clinical data directly from EHRs, registries, and health information exchanges. NCQA is steadily moving measures to ECDS reporting to capture richer clinical detail without manual chart abstraction — a key step in the broader transition to digital quality measures.

HEDIS Data Collection Methods
A Worked Example: Controlling High Blood Pressure
Consider one of the best-known HEDIS measures, Controlling High Blood Pressure (CBP). It assesses adults 18 to 85 years of age who have a diagnosis of hypertension and whose blood pressure was adequately controlled during the measurement year.
The denominator is members aged 18 to 85 with a hypertension diagnosis (identified on at least two different dates of service within the specified window) who meet enrollment criteria, minus the standard exclusions. The numerator is the subset whose most recent representative blood pressure reading was below 140/90 mm Hg — both systolic under 140 and diastolic under 90. If multiple readings occur on the same day, the lowest systolic and lowest diastolic values are used.
This single measure shows why HEDIS specifications are so detailed: the age range, the two-diagnosis requirement, the exact blood-pressure threshold, and the rule for choosing among same-day readings are all spelled out precisely. That precision is exactly what makes one plan's CBP rate genuinely comparable to another's — and it is why HEDIS measures cannot be calculated casually from rough data.
Denominator: adults 18-85 with a hypertension diagnosis on at least two service dates, meeting enrollment rules, minus exclusions.
Numerator: those whose most recent representative BP reading is <140/90 mm Hg.
A plan that controls blood pressure in 700 of 1,000 eligible hypertensive members reports a CBP rate of 70%. The precise, standardized definition is what makes that 70% comparable across plans nationwide.
Controlling High Blood Pressure (CBP)

######## clinical-quality-measurement | cahps-patient-experience | CAHPS Surveys: Measuring Patient Experience
CAHPS Surveys: Measuring Patient Experience
Measuring Care From the Patient's Seat
Clinical measures like HEDIS tell you what was done to and for a patient. But they cannot tell you what the care felt like from the patient's side — whether their doctor listened, whether they got help quickly, whether anyone explained their medications. Capturing that perspective is the job of CAHPS.
CAHPS — the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems — is a program run by the federal Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ). It began in 1995 to build the scientific understanding of patient experience as part of advancing safe, patient-centered care. CAHPS is not a single survey but a family of rigorously developed, standardized surveys.
Each CAHPS survey is designed for a specific setting — hospitals, health plans, clinician practices, dialysis facilities, and more. To carry the CAHPS name, a survey must be approved by the CAHPS Consortium overseen by AHRQ, which is what guarantees the surveys are scientifically sound and comparable across organizations.
CAHPS is AHRQ's family of standardized surveys, launched in 1995, that measure patient experience. Each survey targets a specific care setting and must be approved by the AHRQ-overseen CAHPS Consortium.
Experience Is Not Satisfaction
The single most important concept in CAHPS is a distinction that is easy to miss: patient experience is not the same as patient satisfaction. The two terms are often used interchangeably, but CAHPS deliberately measures experience, not satisfaction.
A satisfaction question asks how happy a patient was — a subjective rating that depends heavily on expectations. An experience question asks whether something that should happen in care actually happened, and how often. Instead of "How satisfied were you with communication?" CAHPS asks "During this hospital stay, how often did doctors explain things in a way you could understand?"
This framing matters because experience questions are actionable and fair. "How often did nurses treat you with courtesy and respect?" points to a specific, improvable behavior, and it is far less swayed by whether a patient simply liked their food or their room. By anchoring on concrete events rather than feelings, CAHPS produces data that organizations can actually act on.
Satisfaction Questions
Ask how happy or pleased the patient was
Subjective; shaped by expectations
Hard to act on directly
Easily swayed by amenities
Experience Questions (CAHPS)
Ask whether/how often something happened
Anchored on concrete events

More comparable and fair across patients
Satisfaction vs. Experience
HCAHPS: The Hospital Survey
The most consequential member of the CAHPS family is HCAHPS — the Hospital CAHPS survey — the first national, standardized, publicly reported survey of patients' hospital experiences. It exists to let patients and the public compare hospitals on experience using the same questions everywhere.
HCAHPS has a long development pedigree. Beginning in 2002, CMS partnered with AHRQ to develop and test it; it was endorsed by the National Quality Forum in 2005, implemented in October 2006, and its results were first publicly reported in March 2008. That careful, multi-year development is why HCAHPS scores are treated as credible enough to drive payment.
The survey organizes its questions into composite topics that reflect the core of the hospital experience: communication with nurses, communication with doctors, responsiveness of hospital staff, communication about medicines, discharge information, care transition, the hospital environment (cleanliness and quietness), and an overall hospital rating.
How often nurses communicated clearly and respectfully.

HCAHPS Composite Topics
When Experience Affects Payment
HCAHPS is not just informational — it has real financial teeth. Results are publicly reported on Medicare's Care Compare website and feed directly into the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) program, which redistributes a portion of Medicare payments based on performance.
The weight is significant: patient-experience measures from HCAHPS make up a substantial share of a hospital's Value-Based Purchasing score. That means how patients answer questions about communication, responsiveness, and discharge can swing a hospital's Medicare reimbursement by meaningful amounts each year.
Tying payment to patient experience was a deliberate policy choice: it signals that how care is delivered — not just whether the clinical box was checked — is part of quality. It also raised the stakes for getting the measurement right, because money now rides on the numbers.
HCAHPS results are publicly posted on Care Compare and built into Hospital VBP, which redistributes a percentage of Medicare payments based on performance.
Patient-experience scores form a large portion of each hospital's VBP score, so consistent shortfalls in, say, communication or responsiveness can translate into real reductions in Medicare reimbursement — making patient experience a board-level financial issue, not just a satisfaction metric.
HCAHPS in Hospital Value-Based Purchasing
Making the Comparison Fair
Comparing hospitals or plans on patient experience is only fair if the comparison accounts for differences that have nothing to do with quality. CAHPS surveys therefore apply adjustments before results are publicly reported.
Two adjustments are central. Patient-mix adjustment accounts for differences in the kinds of patients each organization serves — factors like age, education, and health status that are known to influence how people answer experience questions, independent of the care's quality. Mode adjustment accounts for the fact that people respond differently depending on whether they were surveyed by mail, phone, or another method.
These adjustments are the experience-survey analog of risk adjustment for clinical outcomes. Without them, a hospital serving an older or sicker population could look worse purely because of who it treats, not how well it treats them. The adjustments are what make a hospital's publicly reported scores a fair basis for comparison — and for payment.
Publicly reported CAHPS scores are patient-mix and mode adjusted precisely because raw responses are influenced by who answered and how they were surveyed. Comparing unadjusted scores across organizations can be misleading — always use the adjusted, reported figures.
Don't Read Raw Scores as Quality

######## clinical-quality-measurement | hedis-quality-improvement | Using HEDIS Data for Quality Improvement
Using HEDIS Data for Quality Improvement
From Scorekeeping to Improvement
Calculating HEDIS rates is only half the job. A breast-cancer-screening rate of 68 percent is a scorecard, not an improvement. The real value of HEDIS comes from using the data to find where care is falling short and then systematically closing those shortfalls — turning measurement into action.
For health plans, HEDIS performance is not optional housekeeping. Results drive NCQA accreditation, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, Medicaid oversight, and performance-based payments. A plan that lets its rates drift loses accreditation standing, Star bonuses, and contract leverage — so improving HEDIS scores is a core operational discipline, not a once-a-year reporting exercise.
This lesson covers how organizations actually move HEDIS numbers: by understanding the data-timing problem, finding and closing "care gaps," enriching their data, and benchmarking against peers to know where to focus.
HEDIS quality improvement means using measure results to find and close gaps in care — not just reporting a score. For plans, HEDIS performance drives accreditation, Star Ratings, Medicaid oversight, and payment.
The Care Gap: The Unit of Improvement
The central concept in HEDIS improvement is the "care gap" (also called a gap in care). A care gap is an eligible member who has not yet met a measure's numerator requirement — for example, a woman due for a mammogram who has not had one, or a diabetic member with no recorded eye exam this year.
Improving a HEDIS rate is, mechanically, the work of closing care gaps: getting each open member the needed service (and getting it documented) before the measurement window ends. Every gap closed moves a member from the denominator-only group into the numerator, raising the rate.
Plans generate "gap-in-care reports" that list, member by member, which measures are still open. These reports are then routed to care managers and to the member's providers, who do the outreach — scheduling the overdue screening, ordering the lab, or confirming a service already happened. The care gap is the actionable unit that connects a statistic to a specific person and a specific next step.
Run gap-in-care reports to find eligible members who have not met each measure.
Identify open gaps
Send gaps to care managers and the member's providers for outreach.
Route to the right actor
Get the member the needed care and ensure it is coded and captured.
Deliver and document the service
Confirm the gap closed and the member moved into the numerator.
Re-check
The Care-Gap Closure Loop
The Data Lag Problem
HEDIS improvement is shaped by an awkward timing problem: HEDIS data collection is largely retrospective. Plans rely heavily on claims, and claims arrive weeks or months after care is delivered. By the time a gap shows up in the data, the measurement year may be nearly over and the window to act is closing.
This creates the classic "year-end chase," where plans scramble in the final months to close gaps and abstract charts before hard deadlines — supplemental data submission and medical-record review both end on fixed dates after the measurement year. Gaps not closed and documented before those deadlines simply count against the plan, even if the member was actually eligible to be compliant.
The better answer is year-round, proactive gap monitoring rather than a reactive year-end sprint. Plans increasingly use near-real-time dashboards and alerts that flag open measures as soon as data arrives, so outreach happens continuously. Effective gap closure, as practitioners put it, starts not with today's data but with yesterday's performance — acting early instead of waiting for the retrospective picture to settle.
Because HEDIS data is retrospective, gaps surface late and plans scramble before fixed deadlines for supplemental data and chart review. Relying on a year-end chase guarantees some genuinely eligible members are missed; year-round monitoring is the fix.
The Year-End Chase Is a Symptom, Not a Strategy
Better Data: Supplemental and Standardized
A huge share of "missed" care is not actually missed — it happened but never made it into the plan's claims data. Closing that visibility gap is where supplemental data comes in: structured clinical data pulled from electronic health records, health information exchanges, and data aggregators to capture services that claims alone do not show.
Supplemental data is especially powerful for measures that need clinical values rather than just a billing code — blood pressure readings for the hypertension measure, A1c results for diabetes control. Those numbers live in the EHR, not on a claim. By ingesting and normalizing this data to national standards and HEDIS value sets, plans can credit care that was genuinely delivered, raising numerator accuracy without chasing a single chart by hand.
This is also why the field is moving from manual hybrid chart abstraction toward electronic clinical data systems (ECDS) reporting. Richer, standardized electronic data both improves measured performance and cuts the administrative burden of the year-end chase — a theme that connects directly to the digital quality measures covered later in this course.
A plan's claims might show a diabetic member had an office visit but not record an A1c result, leaving the diabetes-control measure open. Pulling the actual A1c value from the practice's EHR via a data feed or HIE can close that gap — the care happened, it just was not on a claim.
Normalizing such clinical data to HEDIS value sets lets plans credit real care, improve numerator accuracy, and reduce reliance on labor-intensive manual chart review.
Supplemental Clinical Data Closing Gaps
Benchmarking: Knowing Where to Push
With limited time and staff, a plan cannot work every measure equally hard. Benchmarking tells it where the opportunity is greatest. NCQA's Quality Compass is the standard tool: it provides national, regional, and state benchmarks for each HEDIS and CAHPS measure, plus plan-level results for competitor analysis.
Quality Compass reports performance at percentiles — commonly the 10th, 25th, 50th, 75th, and 90th — so a plan can see not just its own rate but where that rate falls in the distribution. A measure sitting at the 25th percentile is a bigger improvement opportunity (and a bigger accreditation/Star risk) than one already at the 90th.
Used well, benchmarking turns improvement into a focused, data-driven exercise: identify the measures lagging peers, target the care gaps within them, deploy outreach and supplemental data, and re-measure against the benchmark. The formal mechanics of running those improvement cycles — Plan-Do-Study-Act and the Model for Improvement — are covered later in this course; HEDIS data is what feeds them.

######## clinical-quality-measurement | hospital-compare-star-ratings | Hospital Compare and Star Ratings
Hospital Compare and Star Ratings
Putting Quality in Front of the Public
Quality measurement only changes behavior if someone sees the results. For decades, hospital quality data lived inside regulators and the hospitals themselves. The federal government changed that by publishing it — letting patients, families, and purchasers compare hospitals directly. That public-reporting effort is the subject of this lesson.
The story begins with Hospital Compare, a website CMS launched in 2005 through the Hospital Quality Alliance, a public-private collaboration formed in 2002 to promote reporting of hospital quality. The first release was modest: a ten-measure "starter set" of process-of-care measures covering heart attack, heart failure, pneumonia, and surgical care.
In 2020, CMS consolidated its various "Compare" tools (Hospital Compare, Nursing Home Compare, and others) into a single site called Care Compare on Medicare.gov. The underlying idea never changed: make standardized quality data easy for ordinary people to find and understand.
Hospital Compare (launched 2005, now part of Care Compare on Medicare.gov) is CMS's public website for comparing hospitals on standardized quality measures — turning quality data into something patients and purchasers can actually see.
The Problem With Raw Measures
Care Compare publishes a large number of individual measures — readmission rates, infection rates, timely-care percentages, patient-experience scores, and more. For a clinician or analyst, that detail is gold. For a patient choosing where to have surgery, it is overwhelming: dozens of numbers with no obvious way to weigh them against each other.
CMS's answer was the Overall Hospital Quality Star Rating: a single summary score, from one to five stars, designed to roll up many measures into one number ordinary people can grasp at a glance. The goal was explicitly to make hospital comparison easy to comprehend.
This is a recurring tension in quality measurement: detailed measures are accurate but unusable by laypeople, while a single summary score is usable but hides nuance. The star rating is a deliberate trade toward usability — and, as we will see, that trade is also why it is controversial.
Think of a restaurant. A health inspector's full report lists every individual finding — water temperature, glove use, storage dates. Useful to an expert, baffling to a diner. The single letter grade in the window is the star rating: it compresses all of it into one symbol you can read in a second, at the cost of the detail underneath.
Why CMS rolls many measures into one star rating
The Five Measure Groups
The star rating does not treat every measure separately. It sorts the measures into five "measure groups," computes a score for each group, and then combines those group scores into the overall rating. Understanding the five groups is the key to understanding what the star actually reflects.
The five groups are Mortality, Safety of Care, Readmission, Patient Experience, and Timely & Effective Care. The first four are weighted equally at 22 percent each, and Timely & Effective Care is weighted at 12 percent. So mortality, safety, readmissions, and patient experience together drive about 88 percent of a hospital's overall rating.
Patient experience appearing at a full 22 percent — equal to mortality — is striking. It means how patients report their care felt (via the HCAHPS survey) counts as much in the overall star as how many patients died. That is a deliberate statement that experience is a core dimension of quality, not a soft extra.

The Five Star Rating Measure Groups
How a Hospital Earns a Rating
Not every hospital gets a star rating, and the rules for who qualifies matter. The rating uses a subset of the measures already on Care Compare — 46 measures were included in the July 2024 calculation — after excluding measures that are retired, reported by too few hospitals, structural, duplicative, or "non-directional" (where it is unclear whether higher or lower is better).
To receive an overall star, a hospital must have at least three measures in at least three of the five groups, and at least one of those groups must be Mortality or Safety of Care. This threshold ensures the rating rests on enough data to be meaningful and always includes a serious clinical-outcome dimension.
When a hospital lacks enough measures in a group, CMS redistributes that group's weight proportionally across the groups it does have. A hospital must also participate in CMS reporting programs — such as the Hospital Inpatient and Outpatient Quality Reporting programs — to be eligible at all. The ratings are recalculated and refreshed annually.

How the Overall Star Is Built
Strengths, Limits, and Controversy
The star rating succeeds at its core purpose: it gives the public a single, comparable, easy-to-read signal of hospital quality, and it pressures hospitals to improve on the dimensions it measures. Because it is public and tied to a hospital's reputation, it has real influence on behavior.
But it draws persistent criticism. Hospitals and researchers argue that rolling diverse measures into one number can obscure important differences, that the methodology can shift in ways that move ratings without real quality change, and that large academic medical centers treating the sickest patients may be disadvantaged despite excellent care. This is the same summary-vs-nuance trade from earlier, now with reputational and competitive stakes.
The practical lesson for anyone working in quality is to treat the star rating as a starting point, not a verdict. It is invaluable for orienting patients and flagging where to look, but real improvement work requires going back into the individual measures and measure groups beneath the star to understand what is actually driving performance.
The overall star rating compresses dozens of measures into one number. It is great for public comparison but hides the detail clinicians need. Methodology changes can also move ratings without underlying quality changing — so always look at the underlying measure groups, not just the star.
A Star Is a Summary, Not the Whole Story

######## clinical-quality-measurement | mips-quality-payment | MIPS and Quality Payment Program Measures
MIPS and Quality Payment Program Measures
When Quality Scores Become Paychecks
So far this course has treated quality measurement mostly as information — scores that inform improvement and public comparison. The Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) is where measurement turns directly into money. Under MIPS, a clinician's measured performance adjusts their Medicare payments up or down.
MIPS was created by the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA), the law that repealed Medicare's old physician-payment formula. MACRA established the Quality Payment Program (QPP), which gives clinicians two tracks: MIPS, and Advanced Alternative Payment Models (APMs) such as certain ACOs that take on financial risk.
MIPS is the default track for most clinicians billing Medicare Part B who are not in an Advanced APM. It consolidated several older, separate programs into one scoring system — making it the largest pay-for-performance program for physicians in the country.
MIPS (Merit-based Incentive Payment System), created by MACRA in 2015, is the track of Medicare's Quality Payment Program that ties a clinician's Medicare Part B payments directly to their measured performance.
The Four Performance Categories
A MIPS score is built from four performance categories, each capturing a different dimension of practice. The first is Quality — clinical quality measures the clinician selects and reports, the direct descendant of the older quality-reporting programs.
The second is Cost, which measures the total cost of care attributed to the clinician and is calculated by CMS from Medicare claims, requiring no separate data submission. The third is Improvement Activities, which credits activities that improve care processes, patient engagement, and access. The fourth is Promoting Interoperability (formerly "Meaningful Use"), which requires using certified EHR technology (CEHRT) to share information and engage patients.
For 2024, the category weights are Quality 30 percent, Cost 30 percent, Promoting Interoperability 25 percent, and Improvement Activities 15 percent. Notably, Quality and Cost are now weighted equally — a deliberate shift reflecting the program's push to hold clinicians accountable not just for doing the right things but for doing them efficiently.
Quality

MIPS Performance Categories (2024 Weights)
From Categories to a Final Score
The four weighted categories combine into a single MIPS final score on a 0-to-100 scale. That number is then compared against a national "performance threshold" to determine whether a clinician's payment goes up, down, or stays flat.
For recent performance years the threshold is 75 points. A final score above 75 earns a positive adjustment, a score below 75 earns a negative adjustment, and a score exactly at 75 is neutral. Clinicians scoring very low (below a separate floor) face the steepest penalties.
Crucially, the categories are not independent silos — a strong showing in Quality and Promoting Interoperability can offset a weaker Cost score, and vice versa. This is why MIPS strategy is about optimizing the weighted total, not maxing out any single category.

How a MIPS Score Becomes a Payment Adjustment
The Payment Adjustment: Stakes and Mechanics
The financial consequences are significant. MIPS applies a Medicare Part B payment adjustment of up to plus or minus 9 percent based on the final score. For a practice with substantial Medicare volume, a 9 percent swing is a major revenue event.
Two design features shape how this plays out. First, MIPS is budget-neutral: the penalties collected from low performers fund the bonuses paid to high performers, and adjustments are distributed on a sliding scale. That means a high score does not guarantee the full 9 percent bonus — the actual upside depends on how everyone else performed.
Second, there is a two-year lag. Performance in one year determines the payment adjustment two years later — for example, 2023 performance affects 2025 Medicare payments. Clinicians must therefore manage MIPS prospectively, because by the time the adjustment hits, the performance period is long closed.

Because MIPS is budget-neutral, bonuses are funded by penalties and distributed on a sliding scale. A top score does not guarantee the full +9% — the real bonus depends on the whole pool's performance, which is why actual positive adjustments have often been far smaller than the maximum.
Budget Neutrality Caps the Upside
Why MIPS Matters — and Its Critics
MIPS matters because it operationalizes everything earlier in this course at national scale: the measure stewards, the measure types, and the quality measures themselves all feed into a program that moves real Medicare dollars for hundreds of thousands of clinicians. It is the clearest example of "what gets measured gets paid for."
It is also heavily criticized. Clinicians cite administrative burden, complexity, and frequent rule changes; researchers question whether MIPS scores correlate well with actual patient outcomes, and whether the program meaningfully improves care relative to its reporting cost. The equally-weighted Cost category in particular is contentious because attribution of cost to an individual clinician is difficult.
CMS has acknowledged these concerns and is steering toward "MIPS Value Pathways" (MVPs) — more focused, specialty-relevant measure sets meant to reduce burden and improve relevance. The direction of travel is toward the Advanced APM track and value-based models, but for most clinicians today, MIPS remains the program that connects quality measurement to their Medicare paycheck.
Under MACRA's Quality Payment Program, clinicians fall into one of two tracks. Most report through MIPS and receive a performance-based Part B adjustment. Others participate in Advanced Alternative Payment Models — such as certain ACOs that bear financial risk — which can exempt them from MIPS and offer separate incentives.
The long-term policy goal is to move more clinicians out of MIPS and into risk-bearing Advanced APMs.
The Two QPP Tracks
MIPS, created by MACRA in 2015, is the Quality Payment Program track that ties a clinician's Medicare Part B payments to measured performance.

######## clinical-quality-measurement | aco-quality-reporting | ACO Quality Reporting: MSSP and Beyond
ACO Quality Reporting: MSSP and Beyond
Quality as a Gate on Savings
Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are groups of providers who take collective responsibility for the cost and quality of a population of patients. If they keep spending below a benchmark, they can share in the savings. But there is a catch built into the design: an ACO cannot simply cut costs and pocket the difference. It must also prove it delivered good care.
That proof comes through quality reporting. In the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) — the largest ACO program — quality performance is the gate that determines whether, and how much, an ACO actually gets to keep of any savings it generates. Score too low on quality, and savings shrink or disappear regardless of how much money was saved.
This makes ACO quality reporting fundamentally different from public reporting or even MIPS. Here, quality measurement is wired directly into a shared-savings contract: it is the safeguard that prevents "savings" from being achieved by stinting on care.
In the Medicare Shared Savings Program, an ACO must meet a quality performance standard to qualify for and keep shared savings. Quality reporting is the gate that ensures cost savings did not come at the expense of care.
The APM Performance Pathway
MSSP ACOs report their quality through a specific channel called the APM Performance Pathway (APP). The APP was designed to align ACO quality reporting with MIPS, so an ACO's quality work satisfies both its Shared Savings Program obligations and the MIPS requirements of its clinicians at once.
For 2024, ACOs had a transitional choice. They could report the legacy CMS Web Interface set of 10 measures, or the newer APP measure set of three clinical quality measures submitted electronically. Those three APP measures are familiar ones from elsewhere in this course: diabetes HbA1c poor control, depression screening and follow-up, and controlling high blood pressure.
On top of those, ACOs must administer the CAHPS patient-experience survey, and CMS calculates additional measures directly from administrative claims data. So even the "three-measure" APP option is really a blend of clinician-reported measures, a patient survey, and claims-based measures — combining several measure types we have already studied.

(Transitional alternative)
What an MSSP ACO Reports (2024 APP)
eCQMs, MIPS CQMs, and Medicare CQMs
A subtle but important wrinkle in ACO reporting is the "collection type" — how the same measure's data is gathered. ACOs can report their APP measures as eCQMs, MIPS CQMs, or Medicare CQMs, and the difference is about which patients are included.
eCQMs and MIPS CQMs are reported on the ACO's entire all-payer, all-patient population — every patient regardless of insurer. Medicare CQMs, by contrast, are MIPS CQMs reported only for the ACO's eligible Medicare fee-for-service population. Medicare CQMs were introduced as a more attainable bridge for ACOs not yet able to pull all-payer data from every practice's EHR.
This distinction matters because all-payer reporting is technically demanding: it requires aggregating standardized clinical data across many practices and EHR systems for patients with every kind of insurance. The collection-type options reflect a real-world tension between the aspiration of comprehensive, all-payer digital measurement and the practical limits of today's data infrastructure.
eCQMs / MIPS CQMs
Cover the ACO's entire all-payer population
Every patient, every insurer
Technically demanding to aggregate
The long-term goal
Medicare CQMs
Cover only eligible Medicare FFS patients

All-Payer vs. Medicare-Only Reporting
The Quality Performance Standard
Reporting the measures is only half the requirement; an ACO must also perform well enough to meet the quality performance standard. This standard is what links the quality score to the dollars.
The standard is defined relative to national benchmarks expressed as percentiles. In recent years, an ACO could meet it by scoring at or above roughly the 30th or 40th percentile (depending on the year) on its measures, with a lower floor (around the 10th percentile) on at least one outcome measure. Beginning in 2025 and beyond, the standard generally requires reaching at least the 40th percentile across the MIPS quality performance category scores.
An ACO that meets the standard is eligible for its full earned share of savings; one that falls short sees its savings reduced or forfeited. The percentile design means the bar is relative — ACOs are effectively measured against each other, so the standard rises as the field improves.

Where ACO Reporting Is Headed
ACO quality reporting is in active transition, all in the direction of fewer, more meaningful, fully digital measures. The legacy 10-measure Web Interface is being retired in favor of the APP. Starting in 2025, CMS introduced the "APP Plus" measure set, which grows the APP to six measures (a mix of eCQMs/Medicare CQMs, an administrative-claims measure, and the CAHPS survey) and expands further in later years.
The throughline is the shift toward electronic, all-payer digital quality measurement — pulling measures directly from EHRs across an ACO's whole patient population rather than from a sampled Medicare subset or manual abstraction. That is exactly the digital-measures future the next lessons of this course explore.
For now, the key takeaway is structural: in an ACO, quality measurement is not a report card on the side — it is a contractual gate on real money. The measures, collection types, and percentile standards all exist to ensure that when an ACO claims savings, it has earned them without shortchanging patients.
For 2024, MSSP ACOs reported three eCQMs through the APP plus CAHPS and claims-based measures. For 2025, CMS finalized the "APP Plus" set of six measures — four eCQMs/Medicare CQMs, one administrative-claims measure, and the CAHPS for MIPS survey — with the measure set scheduled to keep expanding.
The trajectory is clear: retire the old Web Interface, consolidate on the APP, and push ACOs toward electronic, all-payer quality measurement.

######## clinical-quality-measurement | ecqms-explained | eCQMs: Electronic Clinical Quality Measures Explained
eCQMs: Electronic Clinical Quality Measures Explained
Measuring Quality Straight From the Chart
Every measure in this course so far depends on data — and where that data comes from shapes everything about cost, accuracy, and timeliness. Traditionally, quality measures were calculated two ways: from insurance claims, or by humans manually reading patient charts. Both have serious drawbacks. Electronic clinical quality measures, or eCQMs, are the modern alternative.
An eCQM is a quality measure specified in a standardized electronic format that uses data extracted directly from electronic health records (EHRs) and other health IT systems. Instead of a person reading a chart or a measure relying on billing codes, the EHR itself supplies the clinical data — lab results, vital signs, medications, diagnoses — straight from where care was documented.
The promise is significant: capture quality automatically from the same record clinicians already use, minimizing manual effort and human error while producing more clinically rich, consistent results. eCQMs are the bridge between traditional measurement and the fully digital quality future.
An eCQM (electronic clinical quality measure) is a quality measure specified in a standardized electronic format that pulls structured clinical data directly from EHRs — rather than from claims or manual chart abstraction.
Why Not Just Claims or Chart Abstraction?
To appreciate eCQMs, consider the alternatives. Claims-based measures use billing data the payer already has — cheap and complete, but they only capture what was coded for payment. A blood-pressure reading or an A1c result often never appears on a claim, so claims measures miss clinically important detail.
Chart-abstracted measures fill that gap by having trained staff manually read a sample of medical records and key the findings into data-collection tools. This captures clinical richness but is slow, expensive, sampled rather than complete, and prone to human error. Results often arrive weeks after the reporting period ends.
eCQMs aim to combine the best of both: the clinical depth of chart review with the automation and completeness of electronic data. The shift has been decisive — by 2017, eCQMs had begun to outnumber chart-abstracted measures in CMS quality reporting, and the trend has only accelerated since.
Claims & Chart Abstraction
Claims: cheap, complete, but only billed data
Abstraction: clinically rich but manual
Abstraction is sampled, slow, error-prone
Results lag the reporting period
eCQMs
Pull structured data directly from EHRs
Clinically rich AND automated
Cover the full population, not a sample
Faster, more consistent, less manual error
Three Ways to Source Measure Data
The Standards Under the Hood: QDM and CQL
For an eCQM to work, every certified EHR must interpret the measure the exact same way — otherwise two hospitals running "the same" measure would compute different things. That consistency requires shared technical standards. Two are central: the Quality Data Model (QDM) and Clinical Quality Language (CQL).
The Quality Data Model is the conceptual model that defines the clinical concepts a measure uses — what counts as a "diagnosis of hypertension" or an "encounter," in machine-readable terms. Clinical Quality Language (CQL) is the language that expresses the measure's logic — the rules for who is in the denominator, who meets the numerator, and what exclusions apply.
Together, QDM and CQL let a measure developer author a measure once, in a standardized way, so it can be executed reliably across diverse certified EHR systems. Measures are typically authored in the Measure Authoring Tool (MAT), and reporting requires certified EHR technology (CEHRT). This standards stack is what makes "the same eCQM" genuinely the same everywhere it runs.
The Quality Data Model expresses the clinical data elements in machine-readable terms.
Define clinical concepts (QDM)
Clinical Quality Language encodes the denominator, numerator, and exclusion rules.
Express the logic (CQL)
Developers build the standardized measure in the Measure Authoring Tool.
Author in the MAT
Certified EHR technology extracts structured data and computes the measure consistently.

How an eCQM Is Built and Run
Value Sets: Standardizing the Data Itself
Standardizing the logic is not enough if the underlying data is recorded inconsistently. One EHR might code a hemoglobin A1c test one way and another EHR a different way. eCQMs solve this with value sets — curated lists of the standard codes (from terminologies like SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm) that count as a given clinical concept.
A value set is essentially the answer to "which codes mean this?" When an eCQM asks whether a patient had an A1c test, it checks the patient's data against the LOINC codes in the measure's A1c value set. This is why the data-standards lessons elsewhere in this course matter so directly: eCQMs are only as reliable as the standardized coding beneath them.
Get the value sets and coding right, and an eCQM can be computed automatically and compared across organizations. Get them wrong — or document care in unstructured free text the measure cannot read — and the eCQM silently undercounts, making good care look like a gap.
eCQMs depend on value sets — curated lists of standard codes (SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm) that define each clinical concept. An eCQM is only as accurate as the standardized data and coding it reads from the EHR.
The Catch: Data Capture Is Hard
eCQMs sound like a clean win, but implementing them is genuinely difficult. Calculating an eCQM is more complex than chart abstraction: organizations must educate staff, review and adjust clinical workflows so the right data is captured in structured fields, and map and validate that their EHR produces correct results.
The core problem is that eCQMs can only count what is documented in structured, coded form. If a clinician records a key finding in free-text notes, or in a field the measure does not look at, the eCQM cannot see it — and the patient appears non-compliant even though the care happened. Studies have found that some EHR-extracted data elements are captured far less reliably than others, with error rates varying widely across clinical elements.
This is the central tension of eCQMs and a direct lead-in to the next lessons: the measure logic can be perfect, but if the EHR data is incomplete, inconsistent, or buried in free text, the result is wrong. That is why data quality and the move toward FHIR-based digital measures — the subjects of the next two lessons — are so important.
If care is documented in free text or in a field the measure does not read, the eCQM cannot count it — and good care looks like a care gap. eCQM accuracy depends entirely on capturing the right clinical data in structured, coded form in the EHR.
An eCQM Only Sees Structured Data

######## clinical-quality-measurement | fhir-digital-quality-measures | FHIR-Based Digital Quality Measures (dQMs)
FHIR-Based Digital Quality Measures (dQMs)
The Next Step Beyond eCQMs
The previous lesson showed how eCQMs pull quality data directly from EHRs — a big advance over claims and manual chart abstraction. But eCQMs have a limitation: they are tightly bound to a single EHR's data, and they rely on older technical standards. The next evolution, which CMS is actively driving the entire field toward, is the digital quality measure, or dQM, built on the modern FHIR standard.
CMS defines a digital quality measure as a measure that uses standardized digital data from one or more sources, captured and exchanged via interoperable systems, with standards-based specifications and code packages, computable in an integrated environment without additional effort. The key phrases are "one or more sources" and "without additional effort" — dQMs are meant to draw from many data sources and run automatically.
This matters because it is not a niche technical update — CMS has set the strategic goal of transitioning all the quality measures in its reporting programs to dQMs. Everyone working in quality will be living in a dQM world; this lesson explains what that means.
A digital quality measure (dQM) uses standardized digital data from one or more interoperable sources, with standards-based specifications, computable automatically. CMS's goal is to transition all its quality measures to dQMs.
What Makes a dQM Different From an eCQM
eCQMs and dQMs both use digital data and interoperability standards, so the line between them can blur. The clearest distinction is the breadth of data sources. An eCQM is generally tied closely to EHR data — it measures what is in the electronic health record. A dQM can pull standardized digital data from many sources: EHRs, claims, registries, and even patient-generated health data.
This multi-source capability is powerful. Recall the recurring problem of care gaps that are not really gaps — a service happened but the EHR didn't capture it. A dQM that can also see claims and registry data has more places to find evidence of care, producing a more complete and accurate picture than an EHR-only eCQM.
The other key difference is the underlying technology. eCQMs were built on the Quality Data Model (QDM); dQMs are built on FHIR — the same modern, web-based interoperability standard used across health IT — which makes the data far easier to exchange and combine across systems.
eCQM
Closely tied to a single EHR's data
Built on the Quality Data Model (QDM)
Measures what is in the EHR
A major advance over claims/abstraction
dQM (FHIR-based)

Built on FHIR (QI-Core)

eCQM vs. dQM
The FHIR Standards Stack
A FHIR-based measure rests on a specific stack of standards, and the names are worth knowing because they appear constantly in this space. The foundation is FHIR Release 4 (R4), the version of the interoperability standard most measures build on.
On top of FHIR sit two implementation guides. The Quality Improvement Core (QI-Core) defines the data profiles — it replaces the old QDM as the model for representing clinical data, and it is built directly on FHIR resources (including US Core). The Quality Measure Implementation Guide (QM IG) describes how to represent the measure itself using FHIR's Clinical Reasoning module. Notably, Clinical Quality Language (CQL) — the same logic language used in eCQMs — carries forward to express measure logic in dQMs.
So the transition is evolutionary, not a clean break. CMS's first operational step is converting existing QDM-based eCQMs into "FHIR eCQMs" that use QI-Core and the QM IG. From there, measures can expand to the multi-source dQM vision. CQL remains the logic language throughout, which preserves much of the existing measurement know-how.
The base interoperability standard the measure is built on.
FHIR R4
FHIR-based data profiles that replace the QDM for representing clinical data.
QI-Core
Defines how to represent the measure using FHIR's Clinical Reasoning module.
Quality Measure IG (QM IG)

The FHIR dQM Standards Stack
Why CMS Is Pushing dQMs
CMS is not adopting dQMs for technology's own sake. The motivations are the same pain points that have run through this whole course. First, reduced burden: if measures compute automatically from interoperable data "without additional effort," providers spend less time on manual abstraction and submission.
Second, better data and accuracy: drawing from multiple standardized sources captures care that any single source would miss, addressing the care-gap and free-text problems that limit eCQMs. Third, speed: FHIR's real-time, API-based exchange supports the dream of near-real-time quality insight rather than the retrospective, year-end picture that plagues HEDIS-style reporting.
Fourth, interoperability and alignment: because dQMs use the same FHIR standard as patient access APIs, payer data exchange, and the broader health-IT ecosystem, quality measurement stops being a separate data silo and becomes part of one connected data fabric. That alignment is the strategic prize.

The Reality: A Hard, Ongoing Transition
The dQM vision is compelling, but getting there is a multi-year, difficult transition. Targets have shifted, and the practical reality is that providers, vendors, and CMS are all working through a long migration: converting measures, upgrading EHRs to support the FHIR standards, building the data pipelines, and validating that FHIR-based measures produce correct, comparable results.
The same data-quality dependency from the eCQM lesson applies with full force here. A dQM that can pull from many sources is only as good as the standardized data those sources provide. If the underlying FHIR data is incomplete or inconsistently coded, a more sophisticated measure simply computes a wrong answer more efficiently. Multi-source data also raises new challenges around de-duplication and reconciling conflicting records.
For anyone in the field, the practical posture is to understand where the puck is going — FHIR-based, multi-source, automated, near-real-time measurement — while recognizing that today's reporting still leans heavily on eCQMs and even legacy methods. The dQM is the destination; the journey is the work of this decade. That is exactly why the next lesson tackles the foundation everything here depends on: EHR data quality.
dQMs are more powerful because they pull from multiple sources — but that power amplifies the data-quality dependency. If the underlying FHIR data is incomplete or inconsistently coded, a sophisticated dQM just produces a wrong answer faster. Multi-source data also introduces de-duplication and reconciliation challenges.
A Better Measure on Bad Data Is Still Wrong

######## clinical-quality-measurement | ehr-data-quality | EHR Data Quality: Completeness, Accuracy, Timeliness
EHR Data Quality: Completeness, Accuracy, Timeliness
The Foundation Everything Rests On
The last two lessons built toward a clear conclusion: modern quality measurement — eCQMs and FHIR-based digital measures — computes scores automatically from data in the electronic health record. That makes one fact inescapable. The most sophisticated measure in the world is worthless if the underlying EHR data is wrong, missing, or inconsistent.
EHR data quality is therefore not a side topic; it is the foundation the entire digital-measurement enterprise rests on. A measure can have perfect logic, flawless standards, and elegant FHIR plumbing, and still produce a completely misleading result if the data feeding it is poor. "Garbage in, garbage out" is not a cliché here — it is the central operational risk.
This lesson breaks down what "data quality" actually means, the specific ways EHR data goes wrong, and why this matters so much for quality measurement and improvement.
Because modern measures compute automatically from EHR data, data quality is the foundation of all quality measurement: a perfectly specified measure still produces a wrong answer if the underlying data is incomplete, inaccurate, or inconsistent.
The Dimensions of Data Quality
Researchers have worked to define data quality precisely, and while frameworks vary, a consistent core set of dimensions recurs. The three that matter most for quality measurement — and that name this lesson — are completeness, accuracy, and timeliness, joined closely by consistency.
Completeness asks: is the data actually there? A measure needs the relevant facts recorded for every patient in the denominator. Accuracy (sometimes called correctness) asks: is the recorded data right — does it match reality? Timeliness (or currency) asks: is the data available when it is needed, and does it reflect the current state? Consistency (or concordance) asks: does the data agree with itself and across sources?
Other frameworks add dimensions like plausibility (is the value believable — a blood pressure of 900 is not), uniqueness (no duplicate records), and representativeness. Notably, there is still no single standard taxonomy for EHR data quality, which is itself a challenge — but completeness is consistently the most-assessed dimension, because missing data is the most common and most damaging problem.
Completeness
A required A1c result is missing
Is the needed data actually present?
Accuracy
Wrong value entered or coded
Does the recorded data match reality?
Timeliness

Core Data Quality Dimensions
How EHR Data Actually Goes Wrong
These are not theoretical concerns. EHR data quality problems are pervasive and well-documented. Missing data is the headline issue: studies have found missing-data rates exceeding 80 percent for some variables, meaning the fact a measure needs simply is not in the record for most patients.
A second major problem is the free-text trap. The majority of data stored in EHRs is unstructured free text — narrative notes — which automated measures generally cannot read. Important clinical facts (a documented reason a patient declined a screening, a blood pressure mentioned in a note) routinely live in text the eCQM cannot see, so the care vanishes from the measure even though it happened.
A third is copy-paste and note bloat. Copy-paste prevalence has been measured at around 82 percent in residents' progress notes, and more than half of the text in some electronic records is duplicated. Bloated, copied notes propagate stale or wrong information forward, contributing to diagnostic errors, wasted clinician time, and inaccurate billing — and they make it hard to tell what is actually current and true.

Why It Hits Quality Measurement So Hard
Each data-quality failure maps directly onto a wrong measure result. Incomplete data makes delivered care invisible, so a measure understates performance — good care looks like a gap. Inaccurate data can do either: it can falsely credit care that did not happen, or penalize care that did.
The free-text problem is especially insidious because it is systematic, not random. If a particular clinic documents a key step mostly in narrative notes, that clinic will look worse on the eCQM regardless of how good its actual care is — the measure is really measuring documentation behavior, not care. This is how a quality measure can quietly become a measure of "how well you code," which corrodes trust in the whole exercise.
Beyond measurement, these issues carry real safety stakes. EHR-related medication errors have been found to comprise about 34 percent of all medication errors in ICUs, with a substantial share carrying life-threatening potential. So data quality is simultaneously a measurement problem and a patient-safety problem — the same bad data that distorts a score can harm a patient.
When required clinical facts live in free text or go unrecorded, an eCQM measures how care was documented and coded, not how it was delivered. A clinic with excellent care but text-heavy notes can score poorly — eroding trust in the measure and unfairly penalizing good clinicians.
A Quality Measure Can Become a Documentation Measure
Improving Data Quality
Because data quality underpins everything, organizations serious about quality measurement invest in it directly. The first step is assessment: systematically checking data against the dimensions above using methods like comparison to gold standards, validity and plausibility checks, element-presence checks, and data-source agreement. You cannot fix what you have not measured.
The second is capture at the source: redesigning workflows and templates so that the clinical facts measures need are recorded in structured, coded fields as a natural part of care — not buried in free text or skipped. This is the workflow work that the eCQM lesson flagged: getting the right data into the right field the first time. Natural-language processing can help surface facts trapped in free text, but capturing them structurally up front is more reliable.
The third is governance: clear standards for documentation, controls on copy-paste, ongoing validation of EHR outputs, and the external auditing role played by entities like the EQRO and the HEDIS Compliance Audit covered earlier. Data quality is not a one-time cleanup; it is a continuous discipline. As measurement goes fully digital and multi-source with dQMs, this foundation only becomes more important — which is why it sits at the center of this course rather than the margins.
Systematically check data against completeness, accuracy, timeliness, and consistency.
Assess
Redesign workflows/templates so needed facts are recorded in structured fields, not free text.
Capture at the source
Set documentation standards, control copy-paste, and validate EHR outputs continuously.

Use external review (e.g., EQRO, HEDIS Compliance Audit) to verify data reliability.

Improving EHR Data Quality
Because modern measures compute automatically from EHR data, data quality is the foundation of all quality measurement — a perfect measure on bad data still gives a wrong answer.
The core data-quality dimensions are completeness, accuracy, timeliness, and consistency, with completeness the most commonly assessed because missing data is so damaging.
EHR data quality problems are pervasive: missing-data rates above 80% for some variables, ~82% copy-paste in resident notes, and over half of text duplicated in some records.
Most EHR data is unstructured free text that automated measures cannot read, so real care frequently disappears from the measure.
Incomplete or free-text data makes good care look like a gap, turning a quality measure into a measure of documentation and coding behavior.
Poor EHR data is also a safety problem — EHR-related medication errors made up about 34% of ICU medication errors in one analysis.
Improving data quality requires assessment, capturing facts in structured fields at the source, governance (including copy-paste controls), and external auditing.
eCQMs can only count structured, coded data. When care is documented in free text the measure cannot read, delivered care becomes invisible and the clinic appears non-compliant — so the low score reflects a data-capture (completeness) problem, not the true quality of care. This is why the measure can drift into assessing documentation behavior rather than care.

######## clinical-quality-measurement | stratifying-measures-by-race | Stratifying Quality Measures by Race, Ethnicity, and SDOH
Stratifying Quality Measures by Race, Ethnicity, and SDOH
The Average Hides the Inequity
Every measure so far in this course produces a single number for an organization — one breast-cancer-screening rate, one blood-pressure-control rate. That single number is an average across everyone the measure covers. And an average, by design, hides variation. A hospital with an excellent overall score can still be delivering very different care to different groups of patients.
This is the core insight of equity-focused measurement: an aggregate measure can look fine while masking serious disparities underneath. If care is excellent for one population and poor for another, the blended average may land in a perfectly acceptable range — and the inequity stays invisible precisely because no one disaggregated the number.
The remedy is stratification: breaking a measure apart and reporting it separately for different groups — by race, ethnicity, language, and social risk factors. Stratification is how a hidden disparity becomes a visible, addressable problem. It connects directly to "equity," the sixth IOM aim from the first lesson of this course.
Stratification means reporting a quality measure separately for different patient groups (by race, ethnicity, language, social risk) instead of as one average — revealing disparities that an aggregate score hides.
Why the Aggregate Fails — A Concrete Example
The power of stratification is easiest to see in real data. CMS's Office of Minority Health publishes stratified reports of Medicare performance, and they repeatedly show gaps that the overall numbers conceal.
In a 2021 CMS Office of Minority Health report on Medicare Advantage, stratifying by both race and dual-eligibility or low-income-subsidy status (markers of low income) at the same time showed gaps that a single average buries: within every racial group, low-income enrollees did worse on many clinical measures — on 56 percent of measures among White enrollees (including a 12-percentage-point deficit in breast cancer screening) and on 38 percent among Black enrollees.
Crucially, that gap only appeared when race and dual status were crossed together. Stratifying by race alone, or income alone, understated it. This is the intersectionality point: disparities often live at the intersection of factors, so the way you slice the data determines what you can see.

CMS OMH stratifies measures of patient experience and clinical care quality by race, ethnicity, and sex for Medicare Advantage and fee-for-service enrollees, with statistical comparisons to benchmarks.
These reports exist specifically to surface disparities that national averages hide, and to give plans and CMS a target for where to focus equity-improvement work.
CMS Office of Minority Health Stratified Reporting
You Cannot Stratify Without the Data
Stratification has a hard prerequisite: you must have data on the characteristics you want to stratify by. The foundational requirement is race, ethnicity, and language (REL) data, ideally collected directly from patients in a standardized way. Without REL data, the disparity is real but unmeasurable.
In practice, REL data is often incomplete or missing — the same data-quality problem from the previous lesson, now with equity stakes. When self-reported data is unavailable, organizations sometimes estimate race and ethnicity indirectly; for HEDIS, for example, CMS has estimated group membership by combining administrative data, surname analysis, and residential location (geocoding).
Indirect estimation is a stopgap, not a substitute — it introduces error and can misclassify individuals. The durable solution is collecting accurate self-reported REL and social-risk data directly, which is why this is a major focus of equity work and why CMS and Medicaid are increasingly moving to require standardized collection of race, ethnicity, language, disability status, and related factors.
You can only stratify by characteristics you actually record. Missing or low-quality race/ethnicity/language data means disparities exist but stay invisible. Indirect estimation (surname, geocoding) is a stopgap that introduces error — self-reported standardized data is the real fix.
No REL Data, No Disparity Measurement
Beyond Race: Social Risk and SDOH
Equity stratification is not limited to race and ethnicity. Social determinants of health (SDOH) and social risk factors — income, housing instability, food insecurity, disability status, geography, dual-eligibility — are powerful axes for revealing disparities, and often interact with race.
The CMS example above used dual-eligibility as a proxy for low income, and it was the combination with race that exposed the largest gap. Increasingly, quality programs stratify by social risk factors and compare subgroup performance to benchmarks, because where a disparity is driven by social conditions, the improvement strategy differs from one driven by, say, clinical access.
This is also why SDOH data collection (screening for housing, food, transportation needs) and standardized coding of those needs matter for measurement, not just for care. The richer and more standardized the social-risk data, the more precisely an organization can locate and target the inequities in its care.
Gather standardized REL and social-risk/SDOH data, ideally self-reported.
Collect the characteristics
Report the measure separately for each group instead of one average.
Disaggregate the measure
Examine intersections (e.g., race × income) where disparities often hide.
Cross factors
Compare subgroups to benchmarks and direct improvement to the gaps.
Compare and target
How to Stratify a Measure for Equity
From Visibility to Accountability
Stratification is moving from optional analysis to required practice. CMS has built health-equity stratified reporting into its programs, and Medicaid and CHIP have moved toward making standardized, stratifiable quality measures mandatory — including collecting a core set of demographic and social-risk metrics specifically to identify and address disparities.
This shift matters because what is required gets done. As long as stratification was voluntary, many organizations reported only the aggregate and never saw their internal gaps. Mandating disaggregated reporting forces the inequities into view, which is the necessary first step toward closing them.
But stratification only diagnoses; it does not treat. Seeing a 24-point gap tells you a problem exists, not how to fix it — and, as the next lesson explores, it raises a thorny technical question about whether and how to risk-adjust for social factors. Stratification is the indispensable first move of equity-focused quality measurement: you cannot close a gap you refuse to look at.
An aggregate quality score can be entirely acceptable and still conceal a population receiving far worse care. Stratification is how the field stops hiding behind the average.
A single aggregate quality measure is an average that can hide large disparities between patient groups, even when the overall score looks acceptable.
Stratification reports a measure separately by race, ethnicity, language, and social risk factors, making hidden disparities visible and actionable.
A 2021 CMS analysis that crossed race with dual-eligibility found low-income enrollees doing worse within every racial group — gaps the aggregate would have buried.
Disparities often live at intersections (e.g., race × income), so crossing factors reveals gaps that single-factor stratification understates.
Stratification requires data: standardized race, ethnicity, and language (REL) and social-risk data — ideally self-reported, since indirect estimation introduces error.
Social determinants and social risk factors (income, housing, dual-eligibility, disability) are essential stratification axes alongside race and ethnicity.
CMS and Medicaid are moving stratified, disaggregated reporting from optional to mandatory, because requiring it forces inequities into view — the first step to closing them.
