######## population-health-management | care-gap-analysis | Care Gap Analysis and Quality Metrics
Care Gap Analysis and Quality Metrics
Turning Risk Into a To-Do List
Risk stratification tells you who needs attention; predictive analytics sharpens who is about to need it. But "this patient is high-risk" is not yet an action. Care gap analysis is what turns risk into a concrete, closeable list of specific things to do for specific patients — it is where population health becomes operational.
A care gap is, simply, a missed service: a clinical service a patient is due for, based on guidelines and quality measures, that has not happened. A diabetic patient overdue for an eye exam. A 55-year-old who has never had a colonoscopy. A heart-failure patient not on a guideline-recommended medication. Each gap is a precise, actionable item — find it, close it.
This is the workhorse activity of day-to-day population health. While risk models and dashboards set strategy, care gap closure is the relentless operational grind that actually improves measured quality and outcomes: identify every open gap across the panel, and systematically close them.
A care gap is a needed clinical service a patient is due for but has not received. Care gap analysis turns abstract risk into a concrete, closeable to-do list — the workhorse operational activity of population health.
Care Gaps and Quality Measures
Care gaps are defined against quality measures — most prominently HEDIS, the standardized measure set from the National Committee for Quality Assurance (covered in depth in the Clinical Quality Measurement course). A quality measure defines what should happen for a population; a care gap is the missing piece for an individual patient measured against it.
The relationship is precise. Recall that a HEDIS measure has a denominator (everyone eligible for the service) and a numerator (everyone who received it). A care gap is exactly the difference: an eligible patient in the denominator who is NOT yet in the numerator. Closing a gap moves that patient into the numerator and raises the measure rate. Care gap analysis is, in effect, HEDIS improvement done one patient at a time.
Gaps span the full range of measures: cancer screenings, immunizations, chronic-disease management (like the diabetes measures — HbA1c control, blood pressure control, eye exams, and kidney health evaluation — which NCQA split out of the former Comprehensive Diabetes Care bundle in 2022), behavioral health follow-up, and more. As open gaps accumulate across a population, measured quality falls; closing them is how the population's quality scores rise.
A guideline-based measure (e.g., diabetic eye exam in the past year).
Start with a quality measure
All patients who should receive the service.
Identify the eligible denominator
Eligible patients not yet in the numerator = the open care gaps.
Find who is missing (the gap)
Deliver and document the service, moving the patient into the numerator.
Close the gap
How a Care Gap Is Defined
The Closure Workflow
Identifying gaps is necessary but useless without a workflow to close them. Care gap closure is an end-to-end process: identify patients overdue for services, reach out to them, schedule appointments, deliver the service, and document it so the gap actually registers as closed. Each step can fail, so each needs deliberate design.
Two workflow moments are especially high-leverage. The first is pre-visit planning: before a patient's scheduled visit, the team reviews their open gaps and pre-populates them so the provider can address them during the visit they are already having. The second is point-of-care alerts: surfacing a patient's open gaps in the EHR while the provider is with them. Catching the patient who is already in the building is far easier than chasing one who is not.
For gaps that cannot be closed during an existing visit, proactive outreach campaigns reach patients who are not coming in — the whole-population behavior that defines population health. The mechanics matter: outreach that includes a direct self-scheduling link removes a step that outreach asking patients to call the office leaves in place. Reducing friction is as important as sending the reminder.

Why Closing Gaps Pays
Care gap closure is not just good medicine — it is directly tied to revenue and reputation through quality programs. Closing gaps improves HEDIS scores, UDS measures (for community health centers), and CMS Star Ratings, all of which feed value-based contract revenue and quality bonuses (the MIPS, ACO, and Star Ratings mechanics from the Clinical Quality Measurement course).
This creates a powerful alignment: the same activity that improves a patient's health — getting them their overdue screening or controlling their chronic disease — also raises the organization's quality scores and earns it more under value-based payment. Care gap closure is one of the cleaner places in health care where doing right by the patient and doing well financially point in the same direction.
Note the honest tension, though: because gaps are tied to bonuses, there is a risk of "teaching to the test" — chasing the measured gaps while ignoring unmeasured needs. Good programs treat gap closure as a floor (the minimum, guideline-based care everyone deserves) rather than the ceiling of what they do for patients. The metric is a means to better health, not the end in itself.
A diabetic patient is in the denominator for several gaps at once: HbA1c testing, blood-pressure control, a retinal eye exam, and a kidney health evaluation. A care-gap report flags exactly which are open.
During a scheduled visit, point-of-care alerts prompt the team to draw the overdue HbA1c and order the eye exam; an outreach text with a scheduling link gets the patient booked for the screening they keep missing. Each closed gap improves the patient's diabetes control AND the organization's diabetes quality measures.
Comprehensive Diabetes Care Gaps
Doing Gap Analysis Well
Effective care gap analysis rests on the foundations from earlier lessons. It needs solid data infrastructure (a gap is only real if the data is complete — out-of-network care the EHR cannot see can create false gaps for services that actually happened). It uses risk stratification to prioritize (close the highest-risk patients' gaps first). And it depends on accurate documentation and coding so closed gaps actually register.
The operational best practices are concrete: maintain an up-to-date registry of open gaps, run daily huddles and pre-visit planning so the team knows each day's gap opportunities, surface point-of-care alerts to close gaps during existing visits, and run frictionless outreach (direct scheduling links) for the patients who are not coming in. Automation increasingly handles the identification and outreach at scale.
The throughline is that care gap analysis is where population health's strategy meets daily execution. The risk models and predictions point the way, but it is the steady, systematic closing of specific gaps for specific patients — visit by visit, outreach by outreach — that actually moves a population's health and quality scores. The next module turns to the chronic-disease programs where much of this gap closure concentrates.
Care gaps depend entirely on data completeness. If a patient got a screening out-of-network and your EHR cannot see it, you will chase a "gap" that does not exist — wasting effort and annoying the patient. Solid data integration (claims + clinical + HIE) is what makes gap lists trustworthy.
A Gap Is Only Real if the Data Is Complete

######## population-health-management | diabetes-population-management | Managing Diabetes at Scale
Managing Diabetes at Scale
The Defining Chronic Disease of Population Health
If population health has a signature disease, it is diabetes. It is enormously common, enormously expensive, largely manageable, and heavily driven by the social and behavioral factors population health is built to address. Almost every concept in this course — risk stratification, care gaps, the Chronic Care Model, prevention, equity — comes together in diabetes management.
The scale is staggering. About 38 million Americans — roughly 11.6 percent of the population — have diabetes. Its total annual cost in the U.S. is around $413 billion, making it the most expensive chronic condition in the nation: roughly $1 of every $4 spent on U.S. health care goes to caring for people with diabetes.
And yet diabetes is largely controllable. Good management — keeping blood sugar, blood pressure, and cholesterol in range — dramatically reduces the complications (kidney failure, blindness, amputation, heart attack) that drive most of the cost and suffering. But control is hard to achieve at scale: nationally, only about 26 percent of adults with diagnosed diabetes met the combined "ABCS" goals (A1c, blood pressure, cholesterol, and not smoking) in 2017–2018, according to CDC. The gap between what is achievable and what is achieved is exactly the opportunity population health exists to close.
Diabetes affects ~38 million Americans (~11.6%), costs ~$413 billion a year (~$1 of every $4 in U.S. health spending), and is largely controllable — yet only ~26% of adults with diabetes meet combined ABCS control goals. That gap is population health's opportunity.
The Chronic Care Model
Managing diabetes at scale requires a framework, and the foundational one is the Chronic Care Model (CCM), developed by Ed Wagner and colleagues. The CCM was created on the recognition that the traditional, reactive, visit-based model of care fails people with chronic disease, who need continuous, proactive, coordinated support — exactly the population health philosophy.
The CCM has six interacting elements: the health system (organizational support for quality), delivery system design (team-based, planned care), decision support (embedding guidelines into care), clinical information systems (registries and data to track the population), self-management support (helping patients manage their own condition), and community resources (linking to programs beyond the clinic).
For diabetes specifically, CCM-based interventions work: meta-analyses find they produce statistically significant improvements in glycemic control and blood pressure. The model's power is that it is systemic — it does not rely on heroic individual clinicians but redesigns the system so good chronic-disease care happens reliably for the whole population. Notice how the CCM elements map onto this course: clinical information systems are the data infrastructure, delivery system design is team-based care management, and so on.
Organizational leadership and support for chronic-care quality.
Health system
Team-based, planned, proactive care (not reactive visits).
Delivery system design

The Six Elements of the Chronic Care Model
Managing the Diagnosed Population
Operationally, diabetes population management applies the tools from earlier in this course to the diabetic panel. It starts with a registry of every patient with diabetes — the clinical-information-systems element of the CCM — so the team can see and act on the whole population, not just those who show up.
Within that registry, the team works the diabetes care gaps (from the previous lesson): who is overdue for an A1c test, whose blood pressure is uncontrolled, who has not had a retinal eye exam, who needs a kidney health evaluation. Risk stratification prioritizes the work — the patient with an A1c of 11 and rising needs intensive outreach before the well-controlled patient. Predictive analytics flags who is deteriorating.
The delivery is team-based: pharmacists adjusting medications, nurses and care managers coaching and following up, community health workers addressing barriers, with the physician focused where their expertise is essential. Self-management support is central — diabetes is managed by the patient almost all of the time, between visits, so helping them understand and manage their own condition (diet, activity, medication adherence, glucose monitoring) drives outcomes more than any single office visit.
This is the whole course in microcosm: registry + risk stratification + care gaps + team-based delivery + self-management, all aimed at a single high-value, controllable disease.
Prevention: The National Diabetes Prevention Program
Managing diagnosed diabetes is essential, but population health also looks upstream — to the far larger group with prediabetes who can still avoid the disease entirely. The flagship intervention is the CDC's National Diabetes Prevention Program (National DPP), a structured, evidence-based lifestyle-change program for adults at high risk.
The DPP's results are remarkable. The lifestyle program — delivered by trained coaches over a roughly 12-month curriculum, focused on modest weight loss (5 to 7 percent of body weight) and increasing physical activity to at least 150 minutes per week — reduced the risk of developing type 2 diabetes by 58 percent in high-risk adults. And the effect is durable: a 10-year follow-up found participants were still about one-third less likely to develop diabetes than controls.
The DPP is a model for population health prevention generally: it is structured, evidence-based, delivered by non-physician coaches, scalable (including virtual delivery), and it attacks a condition before it becomes expensive and irreversible. For a population health program, identifying prediabetic patients and connecting them to a DPP is one of the highest-return preventive investments available — exactly the "rising risk" intervention the stratification lesson highlighted, applied to diabetes.

Equity and the Bigger Picture
Diabetes is also a stark equity story, which is why it sits squarely in population health. Its prevalence, control rates, and complications are unequally distributed — higher burden and worse outcomes among lower-income communities and several racial and ethnic groups, driven heavily by the social determinants (food access, neighborhood environment, economic stability) from earlier lessons. A diabetes program that ignores these disparities will improve the average while leaving the gap intact.
This means effective diabetes population management must address the social drivers, not just the clinical ones. Food insecurity undermines dietary management; lack of transportation prevents eye exams; cost drives medication non-adherence. Connecting patients to food resources, community programs, and financial assistance (the community-resources element of the CCM) is often as important to control as the prescription itself.
Diabetes thus ties the whole course together: it demands data infrastructure and registries, risk stratification and prediction, care-gap closure, team-based care management, self-management support, prevention, and an equity lens. Master diabetes management and you have essentially practiced every core competency of population health on the disease where it matters most. The next lessons extend these same methods to heart failure, hypertension, and behavioral health.
Diabetes is driven heavily by social and behavioral factors, and its burden is unequally distributed. A program that only optimizes prescriptions and labs — ignoring food insecurity, transportation, cost, and self-management support — will plateau and may widen disparities. Effective diabetes population management is as much social and behavioral as clinical.
Clinical Management Alone Won't Control Diabetes at Scale
Diabetes is population health's signature disease: ~38 million Americans (~11.6%), ~$413 billion/year (~$1 of every $4 in U.S. health spending), and largely controllable.
Only about 26% of adults with diabetes meet combined ABCS control goals — the gap between achievable and achieved control is the core opportunity.

######## population-health-management | heart-failure-hypertension-management | Heart Failure and Hypertension Programs
Heart Failure and Hypertension Programs
The Cardiovascular Core of Population Health
After diabetes, the conditions that most define chronic-disease population health are cardiovascular: hypertension and heart failure. They are connected — uncontrolled high blood pressure is a leading cause of heart failure — and together they represent a huge, costly, and highly manageable target. The same population health methods apply, but the specific programs and signals differ, which is what this lesson covers.
Hypertension is almost unimaginably common. About 120 million U.S. adults — roughly 48 percent — have high blood pressure. Yet control is poor: only about 1 in 4 adults with hypertension have it controlled. Because hypertension is usually symptomless ("the silent killer"), patients often do not feel sick and do not prioritize it — making it a classic population health problem of reaching people who are not seeking care.
Heart failure is less common but far more acute and expensive: about 6.2 million U.S. adults have it, at an estimated national cost of $30.7 billion a year. Its defining population health challenge is the hospital readmission — heart-failure patients have roughly a 25 percent 30-day readmission rate nationally, and each readmission is costly and often preventable. Hypertension is a chronic control problem; heart failure is an acute-decompensation-and-readmission problem. Both are squarely population health territory.
Hypertension (~120M U.S. adults, only ~1 in 4 controlled) is a silent chronic-control problem; heart failure (~6.2M, ~$30.7B/year, ~25% 30-day readmission) is an acute decompensation-and-readmission problem. Both are common, costly, and highly manageable.
Managing Hypertension at Scale
Because hypertension is symptomless and common, managing it is a numbers game: find everyone with it, get them on effective treatment, and keep their blood pressure controlled over time. The registry-and-care-gap machinery from earlier in this course is the engine — a hypertension registry, with gaps for undiagnosed high readings, untreated patients, and uncontrolled patients.
The most effective hypertension programs share two features. The first is self-measured blood pressure (SMBP) monitoring — having patients measure their own pressure at home and report it, which gives far more data than occasional office readings and engages patients in their own control. The second is team-based care, especially pharmacist involvement to titrate medications between physician visits.
The results can be substantial. In a 2024 retrospective study of 6,595 patients with uncontrolled hypertension enrolled in a remote monitoring program (cellular-connected home cuffs plus registered-nurse care navigators), the share still uncontrolled fell from 66 percent to 40 percent after an average of about nine and a half months. This is the population health pattern: technology (home monitoring) plus team-based care (nurse or pharmacist titration) plus data (reported readings) achieving control rates far above the dismal national average. The physician is not the bottleneck; the system is.
In a remote monitoring program studied in 2024 (Smith et al., Healthcare), patients with uncontrolled hypertension used cellular-connected blood-pressure cuffs that transmitted home readings, while registered-nurse care navigators reviewed the data and coordinated medication changes with clinicians between visits.
Among 6,595 patients uncontrolled at baseline, the share still uncontrolled fell from 66.3% to 40.2% after an average of 289 days — by combining home monitoring, team-based follow-up, and continuous data rather than relying on sporadic office visits.
SMBP Plus Pharmacist Management
The Heart Failure Readmission Problem
Heart failure population health centers on a specific, high-stakes event: the hospital readmission. Heart-failure patients decompensate — fluid builds up, symptoms worsen — and end up back in the hospital, often within 30 days of a prior discharge. With a national 30-day readmission rate around 25 percent and each readmission costing many thousands of dollars, preventing readmissions is where the clinical and financial stakes concentrate.
Readmissions are also a quality-and-payment focal point: the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (from the Clinical Quality Measurement course) penalizes hospitals for excess heart-failure readmissions, so reducing them improves both patient outcomes and the bottom line. The key insight is that many heart-failure readmissions are preventable with timely intervention — they result from a gradual decompensation that, if caught early, can be managed at home instead of in the hospital.
Two interventions dominate. Transitional care — structured follow-up in the vulnerable post-discharge window (the ADT-alert-driven outreach from the data-infrastructure lesson, medication reconciliation, an early follow-up visit) — directly attacks the readmission risk. And remote patient monitoring (RPM) catches decompensation before it becomes a crisis.
ADT alerts notify the team the day a heart-failure patient is discharged.
Catch the discharge in real time
Medication reconciliation and an early follow-up visit in the vulnerable window.
Transitional care
Daily home weight/vitals to catch fluid buildup before crisis.
Remote monitoring
Adjust medications at home instead of waiting for a readmission.
Intervene early
Preventing Heart Failure Readmissions
Remote Patient Monitoring
Remote patient monitoring (RPM) is the signature heart-failure intervention and a powerful example of population health technology. Patients are equipped with connected devices — most importantly a scale, because a sudden weight gain signals fluid retention and impending decompensation — plus blood-pressure cuffs. Readings transmit automatically to the care team, which is alerted to abnormal values via a dashboard.
The logic is anticipation, the same theme as predictive analytics: a heart-failure patient who gains several pounds over a few days is decompensating, and a phone call to adjust their diuretic can prevent a hospitalization that is still days away. RPM converts the invisible gradual decline into a visible, actionable signal — catching the problem in the window where a cheap intervention works.
The evidence is promising but uneven. In 2024 UMass Memorial Health–Harrington Hospital reported that its remote monitoring program cut 30-day heart-failure readmissions by 50 percent, though no peer-reviewed study accompanied the announcement, and results vary across programs. RPM is increasingly reimbursed for high-risk heart-failure populations because the logic is favorable: a modest monitoring cost can prevent a very expensive readmission.

Common Threads and the Bigger Picture
Hypertension and heart failure management share the population health DNA seen throughout this course. Both rely on registries and risk stratification to find and prioritize patients; both use home monitoring and continuous data rather than sporadic office visits; both depend on team-based care (pharmacists, nurses, care managers) rather than physician visits alone; and both aim to intervene early, in the cheap window, before a costly event.
And like diabetes, both are equity issues. Hypertension prevalence and control, and heart-failure outcomes and readmissions, are unequally distributed — worse among several racial and ethnic groups and lower-income communities, driven by access, the social determinants, and structural factors. A cardiovascular program that does not address these disparities will improve the average while leaving the gap, so equity-aware design (the focus of a later module) is essential.
The strategic point is that these chronic-disease programs are where population health delivers its clearest return: well-controlled hypertension prevents strokes, heart attacks, and heart failure downstream; prevented heart-failure readmissions save large, immediate costs. They are concrete proof that the proactive, data-driven, team-based, whole-population approach works — and they set up the next lesson, behavioral health integration, which addresses a dimension of health that profoundly affects these very conditions.
Hypertension and heart failure change continuously, but office visits are occasional snapshots. Programs that rely only on periodic visits miss the silent rise in blood pressure or the gradual fluid buildup that precedes a crisis. Continuous data — home BP monitoring, RPM weight tracking — plus team-based response is what actually achieves control and prevents readmissions.

######## population-health-management | behavioral-health-integration-population | Behavioral Health Integration in Population Programs
Behavioral Health Integration in Population Programs
You Cannot Manage the Body Without the Mind
A population health program focused only on physical disease will hit a wall, because mental and physical health are deeply intertwined. Depression makes diabetes harder to control; anxiety drives ER use; serious mental illness shortens lifespan dramatically, largely through untreated physical disease. The chronic-disease programs from the last two lessons cannot fully succeed without addressing behavioral health.
The comorbidity is the rule, not the exception. A patient with diabetes, hypertension, and depression is a common population health profile — and the depression is not a side issue. Untreated depression undermines the self-management (diet, activity, medication adherence) that diabetes and hypertension control depend on. Treating the behavioral health condition often improves the physical ones, and vice versa.
Yet behavioral health has historically been siloed — separated from medical care by different systems, providers, payment, and even buildings. Patients fall through the gap between them. Behavioral health integration is the work of closing that gap, bringing mental health care into the medical setting where most patients are actually seen. It is essential infrastructure for population health.
Mental and physical health are inseparable: untreated depression undermines chronic-disease self-management, and behavioral health has historically been siloed from medical care. Integration brings mental health care into the medical setting where patients are actually seen.
The Collaborative Care Model
The gold-standard approach to behavioral health integration is the Collaborative Care Model (CoCM), developed at the University of Washington in the 1990s. It is, by a wide margin, the most evidence-backed integration model: more than 90 randomized controlled trials, beginning with the landmark IMPACT trial published in 2002, have shown it more effective than usual care for depression, anxiety, and other conditions.
CoCM works through a defined three-role team. The primary care provider (PCP) leads overall care and prescribes. A behavioral health care manager (typically a licensed clinician) does the hands-on work — regular check-ins, brief evidence-based interventions, tracking the patient, and coordinating. And a psychiatric consultant provides expert guidance, reviewing the caseload with the care manager and advising on treatment, without needing to see every patient directly. This structure lets one psychiatrist effectively support a large population — solving the chronic shortage of psychiatric access.
Note how purely this is a population health model: it is team-based (not physician-only), it operates on a caseload/registry, the scarce specialist (psychiatrist) is leveraged across many patients via consultation, and it lives inside primary care where patients already are. CoCM is population health applied to mental health.
Leads care, prescribes, and integrates behavioral and physical health.
Primary care provider
Regular check-ins, brief interventions, tracking, coordination — the hands-on role.
Behavioral health care manager
Reviews the caseload with the care manager and advises, without seeing every patient.
Psychiatric consultant
A tracked caseload so the team manages the whole population, not just walk-ins.
The registry
The Collaborative Care Team
Measurement-Based Care: Treat to Target
A defining principle of CoCM — and a direct bridge to the quality-measurement and care-gap themes of this curriculum — is measurement-based care. Rather than treating depression by impression, CoCM uses a validated, quantitative measure to track each patient and treat toward a specific goal, just as a diabetes program treats toward an A1c target.
The standard tool for depression is the PHQ-9, a nine-item questionnaire scored 0 to 27. The care manager administers it at regular intervals, and the team treats "to target" — for example, a 50 percent reduction in the PHQ-9 score (response) and ultimately a score below 5 (remission). If a patient is not improving on the measure, the team escalates: adjusts medication (with psychiatric-consultant input), changes the intervention, or intensifies follow-up. The number drives the action.
This is profound because it brings the rigor of chronic-disease management to mental health. Just as you would not manage hypertension without measuring blood pressure, CoCM does not manage depression without measuring symptoms — and it does not accept "no improvement" passively. Measurement-based, treat-to-target care is a large part of why CoCM outperforms usual care: it systematically catches and acts on patients who are not getting better.
A primary care patient screens positive for depression and is enrolled in collaborative care. The behavioral health care manager administers the PHQ-9 at baseline (score 18, moderately severe) and re-measures every few weeks.
When the score has not improved after several weeks, the care manager reviews the case with the psychiatric consultant, who recommends a medication change. The team tracks the PHQ-9 down toward the target (at least a 50% drop, aiming for remission below 5) — actively escalating rather than waiting, which is exactly why measurement-based collaborative care beats usual care.
PHQ-9 Treat-to-Target in Action
Making It Sustainable: Payment
A model is only sustainable if it can be paid for, and a major barrier to behavioral health integration was historically the lack of reimbursement for the care-manager and consultation work that happens outside a face-to-face visit. CMS addressed this by creating specific billing codes for the Collaborative Care Model.
The CoCM codes — CPT 99492 (initial month, ~70 minutes), 99493 (subsequent month), and 99494 (additional time), plus G2214 — let a practice bill for the time the behavioral health care manager and psychiatric consultant spend managing a patient in coordination with the billing provider. This created a financial pathway for the team-based, between-visit work that CoCM depends on.
This matters for population health generally: the proactive, team-based, between-visit work that defines the whole field (care management, monitoring, coordination) only scales when there is a way to pay for it. The CoCM codes are one example of payment evolving to support population health activities; chronic care management (CCM) and remote monitoring (RPM) codes are others. Where payment follows, programs become sustainable rather than grant-dependent pilots.
A real-world note: a single complex patient — say, with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and depression — may be served by several of these programs at once (collaborative care for the depression, chronic care management and remote monitoring for the physical conditions), all coordinated in one care plan. Integration is what keeps that from being three disconnected efforts.
Why Integration Is Population Health
Behavioral health integration is not a niche add-on to population health — it is core to it, for three reasons. First, the comorbidity: behavioral health conditions cluster with and worsen the expensive physical conditions population health targets, so ignoring them caps how much a program can achieve. Second, the cost: patients with untreated behavioral health conditions are disproportionately high utilizers, exactly the high-risk group risk stratification surfaces.
Third, the model fit: CoCM is population health in microcosm — registry-based, team-based, measurement-driven, specialist-leveraged, embedded in primary care, and increasingly payable. Everything this course teaches about managing physical chronic disease applies to behavioral health through CoCM, and the two reinforce each other when managed together.
The practical takeaway is that a serious population health program must integrate behavioral health from the start — screening for depression and anxiety as routinely as it checks blood pressure, building a collaborative care team, treating to target with validated measures, and billing the available codes to sustain it. The next module turns from disease-specific programs to the care management roles and models that deliver all of this work across conditions.
Managing physical chronic disease while ignoring co-occurring depression or anxiety caps results, because untreated behavioral health undermines self-management and drives utilization. The evidence-based fix is integration — the Collaborative Care Model with measurement-based, treat-to-target care embedded in primary care — not referring patients off to a disconnected mental health silo.
Don't Treat Behavioral Health as Separate

######## population-health-management | care-manager-roles-models | Care Manager Roles and Care Management Models
Care Manager Roles and Care Management Models
The People Who Do the Work
The first half of this course built the analytic machinery of population health — data, risk stratification, prediction, care gaps, and disease-specific programs. But analytics do not call patients, coordinate their care, or help them manage at home. People do. This lesson is about those people: the care managers, and the models that organize their work.
Care management is the hands-on, relationship-based core of population health — the human layer that turns a risk score into actual help for a real person. A care manager is the team member who takes responsibility for guiding a defined set of high-risk patients: coordinating their care across providers, helping them navigate the system, supporting their self-management, and intervening proactively before problems escalate.
This is where the proactive, whole-population philosophy becomes a job. The risk stratification lesson identified who needs intensive attention; care management is who delivers it. Understanding the roles, the program types, and the structural models is understanding how population health actually reaches patients.
Care management is the hands-on, relationship-based core of population health: a care manager takes responsibility for guiding a defined set of high-risk patients — coordinating care, supporting self-management, and intervening proactively. Analytics identify who needs help; care managers deliver it.
Who Care Managers Are
Care managers come from varied backgrounds, and the mix matters because different patients need different expertise. The most common is the registered nurse (RN) care manager, who handles the clinical work — medication management, disease education, symptom monitoring, coordinating with physicians. RNs are the backbone of complex and chronic care management.
But care management is a team, not a single role. Social workers address the social and behavioral barriers — housing, benefits, mental health, family situations — that often drive a patient's health more than the clinical issues. Community health workers (the subject of a later lesson) bring trusted, culturally-concordant connection to the community and help with on-the-ground barriers. Pharmacists manage complex medication regimens. The right team for a population mixes these roles.
The key principle is matching the role to the need. A patient whose diabetes is uncontrolled because of a complex insulin regimen needs an RN or pharmacist; a patient whose diabetes is uncontrolled because they cannot afford food or get to appointments needs a social worker or community health worker. Effective care management deploys the whole team and routes each patient to the role that addresses their actual barrier.
Clinical core: medication management, disease education, symptom monitoring, physician coordination.
RN care manager
Social and behavioral barriers: housing, benefits, mental health, family.
Social worker
Trusted community connection and on-the-ground barrier support.
Community health worker
Complex medication management and titration.
Pharmacist
The Care Management Team
Types of Care Management
Care management is not one program but several, distinguished by the population and the time horizon. Chronic Care Management (CCM) is ongoing support for patients with two or more chronic conditions expected to last at least a year — the steady, month-to-month work of keeping chronic disease controlled. Medicare reimburses it: CPT 99490 covers 20 minutes of clinical staff time per month for care planning and oversight.
Complex CCM serves patients needing more intensive management, with codes (99487, plus add-on 99489) covering 60+ minutes per month and moderate-to-high-complexity decision-making. Transitional Care Management (TCM) is the time-limited, high-intensity work in the 30 days after a hospital discharge — the post-discharge follow-up that prevents readmissions (connecting to the heart-failure and ADT-alert lessons). And complex (intensive) care management targets the highest-risk, highest-cost patients with hands-on, often in-person support.
These programs each have their own reimbursement, eligibility, and intensity, but they share a logic: match the program to the patient's risk tier and situation. A stable two-chronic-condition patient gets CCM; a patient just discharged from the hospital gets TCM; the complex apex patient gets intensive care management. This is the risk pyramid translated into staffing and programs.

Types of Care Management
Caseload: The Central Design Variable
The single most important operational decision in care management is caseload — how many patients one care manager is responsible for. It is the dial that trades off intensity against reach, and getting it wrong wastes the whole program. Too high, and the care manager cannot meaningfully help anyone; too low, and the program is too expensive to scale.
Caseloads vary enormously by intensity. A typical RN care manager handling high-risk patients carries roughly 50 to 150 patients. But the range is wide: a purely telephonic, light-touch program might run as high as ~500 members per care manager, while intensive in-person case management for the most complex patients might be as low as ~25 to 1. The intensity of the intervention determines the caseload, not the other way around.
The factors that set the right caseload include the clinical and social complexity of the patients, the care manager's experience, the available social supports, the setting, and the target outcomes. The discipline is to match caseload to the population's needs: the highest-risk apex patients need small caseloads and intensive attention; the broader rising-risk tier can be served with larger caseloads and lighter touch. This is, again, the risk pyramid driving resource allocation.

Embedded vs. Centralized Models
Beyond who and how many, there is a structural question: where does the care manager sit? Two models dominate. In the embedded (practice-based) model, the care manager is part of the primary care team — physically and organizationally inside the practice, working alongside the physicians and their patients. In the centralized model, care managers work from a central hub (often a health plan or a system-level team), independent of any one practice's workflow.
Each has trade-offs. Embedded care managers build trust with both physicians and patients, integrate into the clinical workflow, and benefit from warm hand-offs and shared knowledge — evidence suggests embedded models are generally better adopted into practice. Centralized models offer efficiency, consistency, specialized expertise, and easier scaling across many practices, but can feel disconnected from the front-line care team.
Many organizations blend the two — embedded care managers for the highest-touch work where relationship and workflow integration matter most, centralized teams for scalable, telephonic, or specialized functions. There is no single right answer; the choice depends on the population, the organization's structure, and the resources available. The throughline is that care management is the human engine of population health, and how you staff, size, and structure it determines whether all the upstream analytics actually translate into better care. The next lesson turns to what care managers and patients actually do together: care planning and patient engagement.
A care manager given 300 of the most complex patients cannot meaningfully help any of them; one given 25 light-touch patients is wasted capacity. The caseload must match the intervention intensity and patient complexity — small for intensive in-person work, larger for telephonic light-touch — or the program fails on either impact or cost.
Caseload Must Match Intervention Intensity
Care management is the hands-on, relationship-based core of population health — the human layer that turns risk scores into actual help; care managers guide defined sets of high-risk patients.
Care managers come from varied backgrounds — RNs (clinical core), social workers (social barriers), community health workers, pharmacists — and the right team matches the role to the patient's actual barrier.
Care management types include Chronic Care Management (CCM, 2+ conditions, ~20 min/month, CPT 99490), Complex CCM (60+ min), Transitional Care Management (post-discharge), and intensive complex care management.
Medicare reimburses these programs, making team-based, between-visit care management financially sustainable.
Caseload is the central design variable: typically 50-150 high-risk patients per RN, ranging from ~500:1 (telephonic light-touch) to ~25:1 (intensive in-person).
Intervention intensity determines caseload — more intensive work requires smaller caseloads — and should follow the risk pyramid.
Care managers can be embedded (in the practice; better integrated and adopted) or centralized (in a hub; more scalable and consistent); many organizations blend both.
Caseload must match intervention intensity. Intensive, in-person management of the most complex patients requires small caseloads — often as low as ~25 to 1, and typically 50-150 for high-risk RN caseloads. Assigning 300 complex patients to one care manager (a ratio appropriate only for light-touch telephonic work) means none of them get the intensive support they need. The program would fail on impact despite spending the money.

######## population-health-management | care-planning-patient-engagement | Care Planning and Patient Engagement
Care Planning and Patient Engagement
The Patient Does Most of the Work
A profound truth sits beneath all of population health: patients manage their own health almost all of the time. A person with diabetes spends maybe a few hours a year with clinicians and the other ~8,760 hours managing the disease themselves — choosing what to eat, whether to take medications, when to check glucose, how to respond to symptoms. The care team is a small fraction of the equation; the patient is the rest.
This reframes the care manager's job. It is not to manage the patient, but to help the patient manage themselves more effectively. The two tools for doing that are the care plan (the shared roadmap of what the patient and team will do) and patient engagement (the work of getting the patient to actively participate). Without these, even the best analytics and care managers produce instructions the patient ignores.
This is also where many population health programs quietly fail. They identify the right patients, assign a care manager, and create a plan — then the patient does not follow it, because the plan was made for them rather than with them, or because they lack the knowledge, confidence, or means to act. Engagement is the difference between a plan on paper and a change in health.
Patients manage their own health almost all the time; the care team is a small fraction. The care manager's job is to help patients manage themselves — through a shared care plan and genuine patient engagement, not instructions handed down.
The Person-Centered Care Plan
A care plan is the shared roadmap for a patient's care — but the crucial word is "shared." A person-centered care plan is developed WITH the patient, not for them, and reflects not just what is clinically optimal but what the patient is actually willing and able to do given their preferences and real-life constraints.
Its core components are goals and action steps that the patient and care manager set together. Crucially, the goals should be the patient's goals, expressed in terms that matter to them — "be able to play with my grandchildren" or "stop having to take insulin" — not just clinical targets. A plan anchored in what the patient cares about gets followed; one that lists only the clinician's targets often does not.
The mechanism for building such a plan is shared decision-making: the clinician and patient collaborate, with the clinician explaining options, benefits, risks, and tradeoffs in plain language, and the patient contributing their preferences, values, and constraints. The final plan reflects both clinical evidence and what the patient will realistically do. A person-centered plan also unifies medical and behavioral health into one document rather than separate, disconnected plans — connecting to the integration lesson.
Start with what matters to the patient, in their own terms.
Elicit the patient's goals
Discuss options, benefits, risks, and tradeoffs in plain language.
Share decisions
Agree on what the patient is willing and able to do.
Set shared, realistic action steps
Track progress and adjust the plan as life and health change.
Monitor and revise together
Building a Person-Centered Care Plan
Patient Activation and the PAM
Patients differ enormously in their readiness to manage their own health, and meeting them where they are is essential. The key concept is "patient activation" — a patient's knowledge, skills, and confidence to manage their own health and care. It is distinct from engagement: engagement is what a patient does; activation is the underlying capacity that makes engagement possible.
Activation is measurable. The Patient Activation Measure (PAM), developed by Judith Hibbard, is a validated 13-item survey that scores a patient and places them in one of four levels: Level 1 (may not yet believe their role is important), Level 2 (lacks confidence and knowledge to act), Level 3 (beginning to take action), and Level 4 (maintaining healthy behaviors even under stress). Knowing a patient's activation level lets the team tailor its approach.
Why it matters: more-activated patients have better health outcomes and care experiences, and tailoring support to activation level improves results. A Level 1 patient who is overwhelmed needs small, confidence-building steps and basic education, not a complex 10-point self-management regimen that will only set them up to fail. A Level 4 patient can take on more. Treating every patient identically ignores the single biggest predictor of whether the plan will work.
Level_1
May not believe their role is important
Build belief; small steps; basic education

The Four Levels of Patient Activation (PAM)
Engagement Techniques That Work
Engagement is a skill, and several evidence-based techniques make it work. The first is motivational interviewing (MI): a collaborative, non-judgmental communication style that helps patients find their own motivation to change, rather than being lectured. MI is especially effective for behavior change in chronic illness, and brief versions are adapted for short clinical encounters.
The second is the teach-back method: after explaining something, the clinician asks the patient to explain it back in their own words, revealing and correcting misunderstandings on the spot. Teach-back improves health literacy and knowledge retention among patients with chronic disease, and it is far more effective than simply asking "do you understand?" (to which patients almost always say yes).
Underlying both is attention to health literacy — the patient's ability to obtain, understand, and use health information. Much of what clinicians say is not understood, and a plan a patient does not understand is a plan they cannot follow. Plain language, teach-back, and meeting patients at their activation level are how a care plan crosses the gap from the clinician's mind into the patient's actual behavior.
A care manager explains a new insulin regimen, then says: "I want to make sure I explained that clearly — can you walk me through how you'll take your insulin tomorrow morning?" The patient's explanation reveals they think they only take it when they feel symptoms.
The care manager corrects the misunderstanding on the spot. Without teach-back, that error would have gone home with the patient — a "plan" that would have failed silently. Asking "do you understand?" would have gotten a "yes" and missed it entirely.
Teach-Back in a Diabetes Visit
Why This Is the Linchpin
Care planning and patient engagement are the linchpin where all the upstream population health machinery either pays off or stalls. The data found the right patient; risk stratification flagged them; the care manager reached them; a disease program defined the evidence-based care. But none of it changes the patient's health unless the patient actually does something different — and that depends entirely on a plan they own and an engagement that activates them.
This is why the best programs treat engagement as a core competency, not an afterthought. They measure activation (PAM), tailor to it, build plans around patient goals, communicate with teach-back and plain language, and use motivational interviewing to spark intrinsic motivation. They recognize that a beautifully evidence-based plan the patient ignores is worth nothing, while a modest plan the patient embraces changes their trajectory.
The humbling, central lesson is that population health ultimately runs on the patient's own choices, repeated thousands of times between visits. Everything the system does is in service of supporting those choices. Get the engagement right and the analytics, care management, and disease programs all bear fruit; get it wrong and they are expensive machinery producing plans no one follows. The remaining lessons turn to the value-based contracts that pay for all of this, the equity lens that ensures it reaches everyone, and the measurement that proves it works.
Care plans built around clinical targets and handed to patients routinely fail. Plans must be built WITH patients around THEIR goals, tailored to their activation level, and communicated so they actually understand (teach-back, plain language). The most evidence-based plan is worthless if the patient does not own it or cannot follow it.
A Plan Made FOR a Patient Is a Plan They Ignore
Patients manage their own health almost all the time, so the care manager's job is to help them self-manage — via a shared care plan and genuine engagement — not to manage them.

######## population-health-management | aco-population-health-strategy | ACO Population Health Strategy
ACO Population Health Strategy
Why ACOs and Population Health Are Inseparable
Everything in this course has assumed a financial reason to manage a population proactively. The Accountable Care Organization (ACO) is the structure that creates that reason. An ACO is a group of providers that agrees to be collectively accountable for the cost and quality of a defined population of patients — and to share in the savings if they keep spending below a benchmark while meeting quality standards.
This is the economic engine. Under fee-for-service, there is no payoff for preventing an avoidable hospitalization — the hospital is paid for the admission. Under an ACO, preventing that admission keeps spending below benchmark and earns shared savings. The ACO flips the incentive so that the proactive, whole-population work this course describes finally pays. ACO strategy IS population health strategy, applied to a financial contract.
And it works at scale. In 2024, the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) — the largest ACO program — had 476 ACOs covering about 10.3 million assigned beneficiaries and generated record net savings of roughly $2.5 billion, the eighth consecutive year of savings. ACOs are no longer an experiment; they are a proven, growing model, and population health is how they succeed.
An ACO is a group of providers accountable for the cost and quality of a defined population, sharing in savings if they beat a spending benchmark while meeting quality. It is the financial engine that makes proactive population health pay — ACO strategy IS population health strategy.
How ACO Economics Work
Three mechanics define an ACO, and all three connect to earlier lessons. First, attribution: patients are assigned to the ACO, usually based on where they get their primary care — this is the "defined population" from the very first lesson. Second, the benchmark: CMS sets an expected spending target for the ACO's attributed population. Third, shared savings: if actual spending comes in below the benchmark AND the ACO meets quality standards, the ACO keeps a share of the difference.
The quality gate matters: an ACO cannot earn savings simply by spending less — it must also hit quality measures (the ACO quality reporting from the Clinical Quality Measurement course), so "savings" cannot come from stinting on care. This is what aligns the financial and clinical goals.
A critical evolution is two-sided risk. Early ACOs took only upside (shared savings with no penalty for overspending). Increasingly, ACOs take two-sided risk — they share in savings but also owe money if they overspend. In 2024, ACOs in the risk-bearing Level E and ENHANCED tracks delivered more than two-thirds of all program savings, and real downside risk drives serious population health investment: the more an ACO has at stake, the harder it works the population health levers.
Patients are assigned to the ACO, usually via their primary care.
Attribution
CMS sets an expected spending target for the attributed population.
Benchmark
Spend below benchmark while meeting quality measures.
Beat the benchmark on cost AND quality
Keep a share of the difference (and, under two-sided risk, owe money if over).
Share the savings
How an ACO Earns Shared Savings
The Strategic Levers
How does an ACO actually beat its benchmark? Not by denying care, but by reducing avoidable, low-value utilization — the high-cost events that add little clinical benefit. The primary targets are preventable inpatient admissions, avoidable emergency department visits, and destabilizing care transitions. Every lever in this course points at these.
The strategy is built on the population health toolkit: risk-stratify the attributed population to find the high-risk and rising-risk patients; deploy care management to those tiers; run chronic-disease programs (diabetes, heart failure, hypertension) to prevent the complications that drive admissions; integrate behavioral health; close care gaps for quality; and use transitional care and remote monitoring to prevent readmissions. The ACO is where all the previous lessons combine into one financial strategy.
Two ACO-specific levers deserve emphasis. Post-acute care management: a huge share of avoidable spending is in skilled nursing facilities (SNFs) and other post-acute care, so top ACOs build preferred, high-quality SNF networks and manage length of stay and readmissions there. And primary care investment: ACOs composed predominantly of primary care clinicians saved Medicare $403 per beneficiary in 2024 versus $224 for ACOs with fewer primary care clinicians (CMS), because strong primary care prevents the downstream expensive events. ACOs that invest in primary care and post-acute management win.

The Leakage Problem
A distinctive ACO challenge is "network leakage" — attributed patients getting care outside the ACO's network. Leakage hurts an ACO two ways: it loses visibility into the patient's care (the out-of-network data blind spot from the data-infrastructure lesson), and it loses the ability to manage cost and quality for care it does not control. Out-of-network utilization can seriously derail an ACO's savings.
The data bears this out: costs are higher for ACOs whose patients see primary care physicians outside the ACO's network. When a patient's care fragments across providers the ACO cannot coordinate, avoidable duplication, gaps, and high-cost events multiply — exactly the fragmentation population health exists to fix, now with direct financial consequences.
Managing leakage is therefore a core ACO strategy: building strong primary-care relationships so patients stay in-network, establishing preferred specialist and post-acute networks, and using data (including ADT alerts and predictive analytics) to detect and respond to leakage. This is the financial expression of the whole course's theme — fragmented care is bad care and expensive care, and keeping the patient within a coordinated, accountable network is how an ACO delivers better outcomes at lower cost.
When attributed patients get care outside the ACO's network, the ACO loses both visibility (the out-of-network data blind spot) and control over cost and quality — and its costs rise. Strong primary care relationships, preferred networks, and leakage-detection analytics are essential, because uncoordinated out-of-network care directly erodes shared savings.
Leakage Quietly Destroys ACO Savings
Where the Course Comes Together
The ACO is where this entire course resolves into a coherent business strategy. Each earlier lesson is a lever an ACO pulls: data infrastructure gives the ACO visibility into its attributed population; risk stratification and prediction target its limited resources; care gap closure earns the quality gate; chronic-disease and behavioral programs prevent the complications that drive cost; care management and patient engagement deliver the interventions; and leakage management keeps it all coordinated.
This also clarifies why population health and value-based payment are inseparable, as the first lesson claimed. Population health is the operational method; the ACO (and value-based contracts generally) is the payment model that rewards it. Neither works alone: value-based payment without population health capability just shifts risk onto unprepared providers; population health without value-based payment has no business case. Together, they form the model.
The strategic takeaway for any provider entering value-based care is that succeeding as an ACO is not about a single trick — it is about systematically building the full population health stack and pointing it at avoidable utilization, while keeping patients coordinated within the network and meeting quality. The ACOs that win are the ones that do population health well. The next lesson goes deeper into the financial discipline of managing the total cost of care that underlies all of this.
A successful two-sided-risk MSSP ACO invests heavily in primary care (driving PCP utilization well above average), risk-stratifies its attributed population, and deploys care managers to the high-risk and rising-risk tiers. It runs diabetes, heart-failure, and behavioral-health programs, uses ADT alerts for transitional care, and builds a preferred high-quality SNF network to cut avoidable post-acute spending.
The result: fewer preventable admissions and readmissions, strong quality scores, and shared savings earned by keeping its defined population healthier and better coordinated — population health as financial strategy.
A High-Performing ACO's Playbook

######## population-health-management | total-cost-of-care-management | Managing Total Cost of Care
Managing Total Cost of Care
The Number an ACO Lives or Dies By
The previous lesson showed that an ACO earns savings by keeping spending below a benchmark. This lesson is about the spending itself: total cost of care (TCOC), the single number that determines whether a value-based organization succeeds or fails financially. If population health is the method and the ACO is the contract, TCOC is the scoreboard.
Total cost of care is a holistic view of all healthcare spending for an entire population over a period — inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, and ancillary services, everything. It is typically expressed as a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month (PMPM) figure, so populations of different sizes and health profiles can be compared fairly. The HealthPartners TCOC framework is a widely used standard for measuring it.
The discipline of managing TCOC is different from managing a single disease or a single patient. It requires zooming out to the whole population's spending, finding where the money actually goes, and pulling the levers that reduce avoidable cost without harming care. This lesson covers where the cost concentrates and how to manage it down.
Total cost of care (TCOC) is all healthcare spending for a population over a period — inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, ancillary — usually expressed as a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month (PMPM) figure. It is the scoreboard for value-based success.
PMPM and Risk Adjustment
The standard unit of TCOC is per member per month (PMPM): total healthcare spending divided by the number of member-months in the population. PMPM normalizes cost to a comparable per-person, per-month figure, which is how value-based contracts, budgets, and benchmarks are expressed. A population's PMPM is the headline number leaders watch.
But raw PMPM is misleading without risk adjustment, because populations differ in how sick they are. A practice serving older, sicker patients will have a higher PMPM than one serving young, healthy patients — not because it is wasteful, but because its patients are genuinely more costly. Risk adjustment (the HCC/RAF methods from the risk-stratification lesson) corrects for this, so a risk-adjusted PMPM reflects efficiency rather than just patient mix.
This connects directly to the equity and risk-adjustment debates elsewhere in the curriculum: how you risk-adjust shapes whether comparisons are fair, and poorly done risk adjustment can either penalize those serving the sickest or mask real inefficiency. For TCOC management, the practical point is that you manage the risk-adjusted number — comparing your population's cost to what it "should" be given its risk, then attacking the gap.
Inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, and ancillary for the whole population.
Sum all spending
Total cost divided by member-months = per-member-per-month figure.
Divide to PMPM
Correct for the population's health profile so comparisons reflect efficiency, not patient mix.
Risk-adjust
Measure the risk-adjusted PMPM against the target and attack the gap.
Compare to benchmark
How TCOC Is Measured
Where the Money Actually Goes
Managing TCOC starts with knowing where cost concentrates — and it concentrates dramatically, echoing the risk-stratification lesson. High-cost claimants (HiCCs) are a tiny fraction of the population but a huge share of spend: nationally, the top 5 percent of spenders account for roughly half of all health care spending, and the top 1 percent for about a fifth (AHRQ Medical Expenditure Panel Survey).
A second concentrated and fast-growing driver is specialty pharmacy. Specialty drugs are only about 2 percent of prescriptions but often drive 50 percent or more of total pharmacy spend. A small number of patients on high-cost specialty and infused medications can dominate a population's pharmacy budget, and this spend is growing rapidly — making pharmacy management a central TCOC concern, not an afterthought.
A third driver is avoidable acute utilization, especially emergency department visits. UnitedHealth Group estimated in 2019 that 18 million of the 27 million ED visits made each year by privately insured people are avoidable, costing about $32 billion — roughly $1,800 per visit — because treating the same problem in the ED costs far more than in urgent care, primary care, or telehealth (other researchers estimate a smaller avoidable share). Knowing this map — high-cost claimants, specialty pharmacy, avoidable acute care — tells you exactly where to aim TCOC management.

The Levers to Pull
With the cost map in hand, TCOC management deploys specific levers at each concentration. For high-cost claimants, the lever is intensive care management — the population health toolkit aimed at the highest tier of the pyramid, preventing the complications and acute events that drive their cost (often combined with case-by-case review of these expensive patients).
For specialty pharmacy, the levers are pharmacy-specific: prior authorization and step therapy to ensure appropriate use, biosimilar adoption (lower-cost versions of biologic drugs), rebate negotiation, and especially site-of-care steerage. Site-of-care steerage means directing where a patient receives an expensive infusion — a hospital outpatient setting can cost dramatically more than a physician's office or the patient's home for the identical drug. The savings depend on the drug and on the price gap between settings.
For avoidable acute utilization, the levers are the prevention and access strategies from across this course: strong primary care and same-day access so patients do not default to the ED, care management and chronic-disease programs to prevent the crises that lead to admissions, transitional care to prevent readmissions, and patient education on appropriate care settings. The throughline is that almost every TCOC lever is a population health activity from an earlier lesson, now aimed explicitly at the dollars.
A patient needs a regular high-cost infused medication. Administered in a hospital outpatient department, it might cost several times more than the identical drug given in a physician's office or at home.
A TCOC program identifies these patients and works with the PBM/medical vendor to steer the infusions to the lower-cost site — saving the price difference between settings, with no change in the actual treatment the patient receives. Same drug, same dose, lower total cost of care.
Site-of-Care Steerage for an Infusion
Managing Cost Without Harming Care
The defining discipline of TCOC management is reducing cost without reducing necessary care — and the distinction is everything. The legitimate target is avoidable, low-value spending: the preventable admission, the duplicate test, the ED visit that should have been a primary care visit, the specialty drug given in a needlessly expensive setting. Cutting these improves value. Cutting necessary care to hit a number is both unethical and, in a value-based contract with a quality gate, financially self-defeating.
This is why TCOC is always managed alongside quality. An ACO that lowers its PMPM by skimping on care will fail its quality measures and forfeit savings (and harm patients). The right framing is efficiency: deliver the same or better outcomes at lower cost by eliminating waste, not by withholding value. Risk adjustment and quality gates are the guardrails that keep TCOC management honest.
TCOC ties the financial story of this course together. Population health's clinical activities — risk stratification, care management, chronic-disease programs, prevention — all ultimately express themselves in this one risk-adjusted PMPM number. Master where cost concentrates and which levers move it without harming care, and you have the financial discipline that makes value-based population health sustainable. The final module turns to ensuring all of this reaches everyone equitably, and to measuring whether it actually works.
The only legitimate way to reduce total cost of care is to eliminate avoidable, low-value spending — preventable admissions, duplicate tests, misplaced sites of care — never necessary care. In a value-based contract, skimping on care fails the quality gate and forfeits savings anyway. Risk adjustment and quality measures are the guardrails that keep TCOC management honest.
Lower Cost by Cutting Waste, Not Care
Total cost of care (TCOC) is all spending for a population over a period (inpatient, outpatient, professional, pharmacy, ancillary), usually a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month (PMPM) figure.
PMPM normalizes cost per person per month; risk adjustment corrects for the population's health profile so the number reflects efficiency, not just patient mix.
Cost concentrates: the top 5% of spenders account for about half of all health spending, and the top 1% for about a fifth (AHRQ MEPS).
Specialty pharmacy is ~2% of prescriptions but often 50%+ of pharmacy spend, and avoidable ED visits (an estimated 18M/year among the privately insured, ~$32B) are major drivers.
Levers: intensive care management for high-cost claimants; prior auth, step therapy, biosimilars, rebates, and site-of-care steerage for specialty pharmacy; prevention and access for avoidable acute care.
Site-of-care steerage (e.g., moving infusions to lower-cost settings) captures the price gap between settings with no change to treatment.
TCOC must be lowered by cutting avoidable waste, never necessary care; risk adjustment and quality gates keep it honest, and almost every lever is a population health activity aimed at the dollars.
TCOC must be reduced by cutting avoidable, low-value spending — not necessary care. Cutting necessary care harms patients and, in a value-based contract with a quality gate, fails quality measures and forfeits savings anyway. Legitimate levers target waste: intensive care management for high-cost claimants, site-of-care steerage for specialty drugs, and prevention/access strategies for avoidable ED and inpatient use. Risk adjustment and quality gates are the guardrails that keep cost management honest.

######## population-health-management | stratifying-by-equity | Stratifying Quality Data by Race, Ethnicity, and Language
Stratifying Quality Data by Race, Ethnicity, and Language
Equity Is Built Into Population Health
Recall the founding definition from the first lesson: population health is the health outcomes of a group AND the distribution of those outcomes within it. That word "distribution" makes equity intrinsic — a population health program that improves the average while leaving disparities intact has, by definition, failed at half its job. This module is about making that equity commitment operational.
The core tool is the same one from the Clinical Quality Measurement course: stratification — breaking apart an aggregate metric and reporting it separately for different groups. An overall diabetes-control rate of 70 percent can hide that one group is at 85 percent and another at 50 percent. Only by disaggregating do you see the gap; the average actively conceals it.
For population health specifically, stratification is not just a reporting exercise — it is a targeting tool. Once you can see which subgroups of your defined population are faring worse, you can direct your finite care-management, outreach, and program resources to close those gaps, the same way risk stratification directs resources by risk. Equity stratification is risk stratification with an equity lens.
Equity is intrinsic to population health's definition (outcomes AND their distribution). Stratification — reporting a metric separately by subgroup instead of as one average — is how you see disparities the average hides, and then target resources to close them.
The Prerequisite: REL Data
You cannot stratify by characteristics you do not record. The foundational requirement is REL data — race, ethnicity, and language — collected in a standardized, codable way. Without it, disparities in your population are real but invisible, and equity work cannot even begin. REL data is the bedrock of equity stratification.
Good REL data follows standards. The gold standard is self-reported data (patients identify their own race, ethnicity, and language), collected using categories aligned to federal Office of Management and Budget (OMB) standards and allowing people to select multiple races. Critically, standards encourage granular data that can be aggregated up — because broad categories hide disparities within them (the experiences of different Asian or Hispanic subgroups, for example, can differ enormously).
These standards are evolving. In 2024, OMB updated its race/ethnicity standards — moving to a combined race-and-ethnicity question, adding a new "Middle Eastern and North African" (MENA) category, and requiring collection of detailed responses. The trend is toward more granular, more self-determined, more complete REL data, precisely because better data reveals disparities that coarser data conceals. For a population health program, building robust self-reported REL collection is foundational equity infrastructure.
Have patients identify their own race, ethnicity, and language (the gold standard).
Self-report
Standardized categories, allowing multiple-race selection.
Use OMB-aligned categories
Capture subgroups that aggregate up, since broad categories hide within-group disparities.
Collect granular detail
Reflect updates like the 2024 combined question and MENA category.
Keep current with standards
Collecting REL Data Well
When the Data Is Missing: Indirect Estimation
The hard reality is that most health plans and delivery systems lack complete REL data — large shares of patients have missing or unrecorded race and ethnicity. This is the equity version of the data-quality problem that runs through this curriculum: the information that would reveal disparities is simply not there, hampering efforts to monitor utilization, track quality by group, and target interventions.
When self-reported data is incomplete, organizations use indirect estimation. The standard method is BISG — Bayesian Improved Surname Geocoding, developed by RAND — which combines the probability of race/ethnicity from a person's surname (using Census surname data) with the racial/ethnic composition of their neighborhood (Census geocoding) to estimate likely race/ethnicity. It is reasonably accurate at the group level, with C-statistics around 0.93 to 0.94 for major groups.
But BISG carries a crucial limitation that must be respected: it is designed to estimate disparities at the GROUP or population level, not to classify any specific individual's race. Its individual-level accuracy (sensitivity and predictive value) is far lower than its group-level performance. So BISG is appropriate for measuring population disparities and targeting community-level interventions — but using it to label an individual patient's race would be both inaccurate and ethically fraught. Indirect estimation is a stopgap for population analysis, never a substitute for asking the patient.
Indirect estimation methods like BISG estimate race/ethnicity well at the group level (for measuring population disparities) but are far less accurate for any single person. Using BISG to classify an individual patient's race is inaccurate and ethically problematic. It is a population-analysis stopgap when self-reported data is missing — not a replacement for asking patients directly.
BISG Is for Populations, Not Individuals
Beyond Race: Language, SDOH, and Intersections
Equity stratification is not limited to race and ethnicity. Language is a powerful and actionable axis — patients with limited English proficiency face real barriers, and stratifying by preferred language reveals gaps that language-access services (interpreters, translated materials) can directly close. This is why the "L" in REL matters as much as the R and E.
Social determinants and social risk factors (the SDOH and Z-code data from the determinants lesson) are equally important stratification axes — income, housing instability, food insecurity, disability, geography. And as the Clinical Quality Measurement course emphasized, disparities often live at the INTERSECTION of factors: stratifying by race alone, or income alone, can understate a gap that only appears when you cross them (e.g., race by dual-eligibility). The richer and more standardized the data, the more precisely a population health program can locate its inequities.
The practical upshot is that equity stratification draws on the whole data infrastructure built earlier in this course — REL data, language, SDOH/Z codes — and slices the population's metrics along all of them, looking especially at intersections, to find where care is falling short for whom.
A population health program reports an overall hypertension-control rate of 68%, which meets its target. Stratified by race and preferred language, it discovers control is 78% among English-speaking White patients but only 52% among Spanish-speaking Hispanic patients.
The aggregate hid a 26-point gap. Now visible, it points to a concrete fix: Spanish-language self-measured-BP education and interpreter-supported care management for that subgroup — equity stratification turning an invisible disparity into a targeted intervention.
Finding a Hidden Disparity by Stratifying
From Seeing to Closing the Gap
Stratification only diagnoses; it does not treat. Seeing a disparity is the necessary first step, but the value comes from acting on it — directing population health resources to the lagging subgroups and tracking whether the gap narrows. The equity-focused quality improvement principles from the Clinical Quality Measurement course apply directly: put the disparity itself on the dashboard as a tracked metric, and judge success by whether it shrinks, not just whether the average rises.
This guards against a real failure mode: a program can improve its overall metrics while the gap widens, if its interventions reach the already-advantaged faster than the disadvantaged. Population health, with its proactive outreach and care management, is well-positioned to prevent this — by deliberately targeting the subgroups stratification flags as behind, rather than letting improvement flow to whoever is easiest to reach.
The throughline is that equity is not a separate program bolted onto population health — it is woven through every step. Risk stratification should consider equity; care management should be deployed to close disparities; chronic-disease and behavioral programs should be designed to reach the groups faring worst. Stratification is the lens that makes all of this visible and actionable. The next lesson covers community health workers — one of the most effective tools for actually reaching and closing gaps in underserved populations.
A practical equity-stratification routine for any population health program: collect standardized self-reported REL (supplemented by careful population-level indirect estimation where needed), stratify every key metric by race, ethnicity, language, and social risk — including intersections — put the gaps on the dashboard, target resources to the lagging groups, and re-measure to confirm the disparities are actually closing.
