The Precision Oncology Landscape
Immunotherapy Biomarkers: PD-L1, MSI-H, and TMB
Not all precision oncology involves targeted kinase inhibitors. Immunotherapy — specifically immune checkpoint inhibitors — represents a second major category. These drugs work by releasing the brakes on the immune system, allowing it to recognize and destroy cancer cells. The challenge is predicting who will respond.
Three key biomarkers predict immunotherapy response: PD-L1 expression (a protein on tumor cells that suppresses immune attack), MSI-H/dMMR status (microsatellite instability-high, indicating a defect in DNA mismatch repair that creates many mutant proteins for the immune system to target), and TMB (tumor mutational burden, the total number of mutations in the tumor genome). Higher values on each measure generally predict better response to checkpoint inhibitors.
Pembrolizumab (Keytruda) received the first tumor-agnostic FDA approval in 2017 — it is approved for any solid tumor that is MSI-H or dMMR, regardless of where in the body the cancer originated. This was a regulatory landmark: for the first time, a cancer drug was approved based on a molecular biomarker alone, not a tissue type.
Basket Trials and the MATCH Trial: Rethinking Clinical Research
Precision oncology has also forced a rethinking of how clinical trials are designed. Traditional trials enroll patients by cancer type — all participants have the same cancer. But if we are treating based on mutation rather than tissue type, we need new trial architectures.
A basket trial enrolls patients based on a shared molecular alteration (e.g., a specific mutation), regardless of cancer type. Multiple tumor types are tested in 'baskets' within the same trial. A platform trial or umbrella trial tests multiple targeted agents within a single cancer type, matching each patient to the arm that targets their specific mutation.
The NCI-MATCH (Molecular Analysis for Therapy Choice) trial, launched in 2015, became the flagship example of this approach. It screens patients with any solid tumor or lymphoma for specific genetic alterations and then assigns them to treatment arms targeting those alterations. By 2024, MATCH had screened over 6,000 patients across dozens of molecular arms, generating data no traditional trial structure could have produced.
The National Cancer Institute's Molecular Analysis for Therapy Choice (MATCH) trial launched in 2015 as the largest precision oncology trial in U.S. history. Patients with any refractory solid tumor or lymphoma undergo tumor sequencing; if an actionable mutation is found, they are matched to a corresponding treatment arm. The trial simultaneously tests dozens of targeted agents across multiple cancer types, dramatically accelerating evidence generation for rare mutation-treatment combinations.
Real-World Example
By 2024, MATCH had enrolled over 6,000 patients and produced published results for more than 30 molecular treatment arms, providing FDA-relevant efficacy data for mutation-drug pairings that would have taken decades to study in traditional single-cancer trials.
National Cancer Institute, NCI-MATCH Trial; NEJM Evidence, 2022
NCI-MATCH Trial
Pharmacogenomics in Primary Care: The Drugs Your Patients Are Already Taking
Precision medicine is not confined to oncology. Pharmacogenomics — the study of how genetic variation affects drug metabolism and response — is increasingly relevant to primary care prescribing. Millions of patients are on medications whose effectiveness or safety is meaningfully affected by common genetic variants.
The cytochrome P450 (CYP) enzyme family metabolizes the majority of clinically used drugs. Genetic variants in CYP genes create four metabolizer categories: poor metabolizers (drug builds up to toxic levels), intermediate metabolizers (reduced clearance), normal metabolizers, and ultra-rapid metabolizers (drug is cleared so fast it never reaches therapeutic levels). A single blood or saliva test can identify a patient's metabolizer status across multiple CYP genes simultaneously.
CYP2C19 is clinically critical for clopidogrel (Plavix), the antiplatelet drug used after heart attacks and stent placement. Clopidogrel is a prodrug — it must be converted by CYP2C19 into its active form. Patients who are CYP2C19 poor metabolizers cannot convert the drug effectively, which means they are not getting the antiplatelet protection they need. This is associated with higher rates of stent thrombosis and adverse cardiac events.
CYP2D6 metabolizes many commonly prescribed antidepressants and antipsychotics, including fluoxetine, paroxetine, codeine, and tramadol. Ultra-rapid CYP2D6 metabolizers who receive codeine may convert it to morphine so rapidly that they experience dangerous opioid toxicity — a phenomenon that has caused fatalities, including in children who received codeine after tonsillectomy.
Pharmacogenomic testing is only relevant for cancer patients or those on specialty medications.
Some of the most clinically consequential pharmacogenomic interactions involve common primary care drugs: clopidogrel (cardiovascular), codeine (pain), SSRIs (mental health), and warfarin (anticoagulation). CYP2C19 poor metabolizer status affects roughly 2-3% of the U.S. population and has direct implications for antiplatelet therapy after cardiac events.
HLA-B*5701 and abacavir represents one of the clearest success stories in pharmacogenomics. Abacavir is a key antiretroviral medication used in HIV treatment. Approximately 5-8% of patients with the HLA-B*5701 allele develop a severe, potentially fatal hypersensitivity reaction to the drug. Prospective screening for this allele before prescribing abacavir has essentially eliminated abacavir hypersensitivity reactions in clinical practice — a model example of precision medicine preventing harm.

Pharmacogenomics by the Numbers
The Rare Disease Diagnostic Odyssey — and How Genomics Is Ending It
Rare diseases affect approximately 1 in 10 Americans — about 30 million people — yet most are caused by single-gene mutations and individually affect fewer than 200,000 people. This combination of commonality in aggregate and rarity in specificity has historically made them profoundly difficult to diagnose.
The 'diagnostic odyssey' describes the years-long journey rare disease patients typically travel before receiving a correct diagnosis. On average, patients with rare genetic diseases see 7-8 physicians over 4-5 years before getting an accurate diagnosis. During that time, they often receive incorrect diagnoses, inappropriate treatments, and significant psychological burden.
Whole-exome sequencing (WES) sequences the approximately 1-2% of the genome that encodes proteins — the exome. Because most disease-causing mutations affect protein-coding genes, WES captures the clinically relevant variation at a fraction of the cost of whole-genome sequencing. For rare disease diagnosis, WES has transformed the landscape.
Studies of WES in pediatric rare disease patients have reported diagnostic yields of 25-40%, meaning that roughly one-third of children who had previously been undiagnosed receive a molecular diagnosis from WES. More importantly, in many cases WES compresses the diagnostic timeline from years to weeks. For families who have spent years in uncertainty, this can be transformative even when treatment options are limited.
The NIH Undiagnosed Diseases Network was established in 2014 to bring the power of whole-genome and whole-exome sequencing to patients who had exhausted conventional diagnostic workup. Patients are evaluated at one of the UDN's clinical sites, which includes comprehensive sequencing and expert multidisciplinary review. The program has identified novel disease-causing genes and provided diagnoses to patients who had been undiagnosed for decades.
Real-World Example
By 2024, the UDN had evaluated over 2,000 participants and identified diagnoses in approximately 35% of cases, including novel gene discoveries that expanded the scientific understanding of human disease.
NIH Undiagnosed Diseases Network; NEJM, 2021
Undiagnosed Diseases Network (UDN)
Genetic Counseling: The Clinical Skill That Makes Genomics Actionable
A genomic test result is not self-interpreting. The clinical value of a genetic test depends entirely on whether the patient understands what the result means — and does not mean — and can act on that understanding. This is the role of genetic counseling.
Genetic counselors are healthcare professionals with specialized graduate training in medical genetics and counseling. They help patients understand what genetic tests measure, interpret results in the context of personal and family history, communicate implications for family members, and support decision-making about testing, surveillance, and intervention. Pre-test counseling occurs before testing; post-test counseling interprets results after they arrive.
One of the most challenging communications in clinical genetics involves variants of uncertain significance (VUS). A VUS is a genetic change found in a patient's DNA that has not yet been classified as either pathogenic (disease-causing) or benign. With the expanding use of genomic testing, VUS findings are extremely common — and they create real clinical and psychological challenges.
A variant of uncertain significance is NOT a diagnosis. Patients and providers sometimes interpret VUS findings as evidence of disease, leading to unnecessary anxiety, surveillance, and even preventive surgery. Communicating clearly that 'uncertain' does not mean 'dangerous' requires counseling skill — not just medical knowledge.
The genetic counselor reviews the patient's personal and family history, explains what the test measures and its limitations, discusses possible result categories (positive, negative, VUS), and explores what the patient will do with different results.
Pre-test counseling session
The patient provides informed consent for testing, understanding the implications including potential insurance or employment considerations. The test is ordered — often requiring prior authorization from the insurer.
Informed consent and test ordering
Results typically arrive in 2-4 weeks. The laboratory report classifies variants as pathogenic, likely pathogenic, VUS, likely benign, or benign. The genetic counselor reviews the report and prepares to communicate findings.
Result interpretation
The counselor explains the result in plain language, addresses the clinical implications, discusses implications for biological relatives, and develops a surveillance or management plan in coordination with the patient's clinical team.
Post-test counseling session
The counselor helps the patient communicate results to at-risk family members, who may then pursue cascade testing. This is often the most emotionally complex part of the process.
Family communication support
The Genetic Counseling Process: From Referral to Follow-Up
BRCA Testing and Preventive Decisions: When Genomics Meets Surgery
BRCA1 and BRCA2 are tumor suppressor genes. Pathogenic variants in these genes substantially increase lifetime risk of breast and ovarian cancer. Women with BRCA1 pathogenic variants face roughly 55-72% lifetime risk of breast cancer and 44-46% lifetime risk of ovarian cancer — compared with approximately 12% and 1.3% in the general population.
These risk estimates are high enough that many BRCA-positive individuals choose risk-reducing surgeries — prophylactic bilateral mastectomy and/or salpingo-oophorectomy (removal of the fallopian tubes and ovaries). These decisions are deeply personal and require extensive counseling about risk reduction, surgical menopause, fertility implications, and reconstruction options.
Angelina Jolie's public disclosure of her BRCA1 status and prophylactic mastectomy in 2013 created what researchers called the 'Angelina Jolie effect' — a measurable increase in BRCA testing rates following her op-ed in the New York Times. This is a reminder that celebrity disclosure can function as a form of public health communication, with both beneficial (increased testing) and complex (inappropriate testing outside guidelines) effects.
Liquid Biopsy: Reading the Blood to Monitor Cancer
A liquid biopsy is a blood test that detects circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) — fragments of cancer cell DNA that are shed into the bloodstream as tumors grow, respond to treatment, or acquire new mutations. Unlike a traditional tissue biopsy, a liquid biopsy is non-invasive, can be repeated frequently, and can capture heterogeneity across multiple tumor sites simultaneously.
Liquid biopsy has multiple clinical applications: early cancer detection (screening asymptomatic individuals), treatment monitoring (is the tumor responding?), minimal residual disease detection (are there still cancer cells after treatment?), and resistance mutation identification (what mutation caused the tumor to stop responding to treatment?).
Think of ctDNA in the bloodstream like exhaust from a car engine. If the engine is running hard, there is a lot of exhaust. If the engine is well-tuned, there is very little. And if the engine stops entirely, the exhaust disappears. You can assess what the engine is doing without opening the hood — just by sampling what comes out.
When cancer cells are active, they shed more ctDNA into the bloodstream. When treatment is working, ctDNA levels fall. When resistance develops and the tumor starts growing again, ctDNA rises — often weeks before the tumor is large enough to appear on imaging.
Liquid biopsy for treatment monitoring
Newborn Screening: Precision Medicine at Population Scale
Newborn screening (NBS) programs represent one of the oldest and most successful applications of precision medicine — though they predate the term. A few drops of blood from a heel stick, collected within 24-48 hours of birth, are tested for dozens of metabolic, endocrine, and genetic disorders. Early identification allows treatment to begin before symptoms appear, preventing intellectual disability, organ damage, or death.
The Recommended Uniform Screening Panel (RUSP) in the United States currently includes 35 core conditions and 26 secondary conditions. States implement the RUSP at their own pace; Vermont screens for all RUSP core conditions plus several additional disorders. Phenylketonuria (PKU), congenital hypothyroidism, and sickle cell disease are among the most well-known conditions detected through NBS.
Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) is now on the RUSP and represents a new frontier in NBS. SMA is caused by mutations in the SMN1 gene and, without treatment, leads to progressive muscle weakness and early death. Gene therapy with onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma) — when given in the first weeks of life before symptom onset — can prevent disease progression entirely. This is precision medicine at its most dramatic: a single treatment delivering near-normal outcomes for what was once a fatal disease.
More than 4 million babies are screened through state newborn screening programs each year, making NBS the most universal public health genomics program in the country. (ACMG, 2024)

Clinical Decision Support Tools for Genomic Prescribing
Even when pharmacogenomic data is available, it has little clinical value if physicians cannot access it at the point of care. Clinical decision support (CDS) tools embedded in electronic health record (EHR) systems are the mechanism through which genomic information becomes actionable in real-time prescribing.
The CPIC (Clinical Pharmacogenomics Implementation Consortium) publishes evidence-based guidelines for gene-drug pairs, which EHR vendors and health systems use to build CDS alerts. When a provider orders clopidogrel for a patient whose CYP2C19 status is already on file as a poor metabolizer, the EHR can fire an alert recommending an alternative antiplatelet agent — preventing a potentially catastrophic prescribing error.
The challenge is that most patients do not have pharmacogenomic data in their EHR. This is changing as health systems implement pre-emptive genotyping programs — testing patients for a panel of pharmacogenomic variants before they need any specific drug, then storing results in the EHR to inform future prescribing. Vanderbilt University Medical Center's PREDICT program, launched in 2010, was among the first large-scale implementations of this model.
Integrating Genomics into Primary Care: Vermont's Context
Vermont's primary care landscape presents both opportunities and challenges for genomic medicine integration. The state has a relatively small, relationship-based primary care system where patients often have long-term relationships with their providers — an ideal environment for the longitudinal conversations that genomic medicine requires.
The University of Vermont Medical Center (UVMMC) has a genetics and genomics program that provides consultation services and collaborates with Vermont's regional critical access hospitals. Vermont's participation in the NIH All of Us Research Program gives Vermont residents the opportunity to contribute their genomic and health data to a nationally representative biobank — and to receive their own genetic results as part of participation.
However, Vermont's rural geography creates access barriers. Genetic counselors are concentrated at UVMMC in Burlington, and many Vermont residents face significant travel burdens to access in-person genetic services. Telegenetics — genetic counseling delivered via telehealth — has become increasingly important in Vermont, particularly following the expansion of telehealth infrastructure during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Genetic counseling is only needed for patients with a known family history of genetic disease.
Genetic counseling is appropriate before any genetic test that could have significant clinical or psychological implications — including BRCA testing in patients without a family history who qualify under USPSTF guidelines, pharmacogenomic testing before starting psychiatric medications, and prenatal testing for all pregnant individuals regardless of family history. Counseling ensures informed decision-making, not just result interpretation.
Clopidogrel is a prodrug that requires conversion by CYP2C19 into its active antiplatelet form. A CYP2C19 poor metabolizer cannot perform this conversion effectively, meaning the patient was not receiving adequate antiplatelet protection despite being prescribed the drug at standard dose. The stent thrombosis is most likely attributable to inadequate platelet inhibition due to her metabolizer status. The next step should be switching to an antiplatelet agent that does not require CYP2C19 activation — such as prasugrel or ticagrelor — both of which are recommended alternatives in CPIC guidelines for CYP2C19 poor metabolizers after ACS.
Think about what CYP2C19 does to clopidogrel and what 'poor metabolizer' means for a prodrug.
A 58-year-old patient receives a coronary stent after an acute MI and is started on clopidogrel. Two weeks later, she suffers a stent thrombosis. A pharmacogenomic test reveals she is a CYP2C19 poor metabolizer. What is the most likely explanation for the stent thrombosis, and what should happen next?
A variant of uncertain significance (VUS) is not a diagnosis of increased cancer risk. It means that the laboratory has identified a change in the BRCA2 gene, but there is currently insufficient evidence to determine whether that change is harmful, benign, or irrelevant. A VUS finding should NOT prompt preventive surgery. The appropriate clinical response is: (1) refer to a board-certified genetic counselor who can explain VUS in plain language and review the patient's full family history; (2) confirm that DTC test results for VUS findings should be validated in a CLIA-certified clinical laboratory before any clinical action; (3) reassure the patient that VUS reclassification over time (often toward benign) is common as more data accumulates; and (4) screen for and address the patient's anxiety, which is a real and valid consequence of this type of ambiguous result.
What does 'uncertain significance' mean, and how does VUS status differ from a pathogenic variant finding?
A patient returns from a direct-to-consumer (DTC) genetic test with a report showing a 'variant of uncertain significance' in BRCA2. She is very distressed and asks if she should have a preventive mastectomy. How should a clinician respond?
Tumor profiling identifies the specific mutations driving a cancer, enabling targeted therapies that block those mutations with greater precision and often fewer side effects than traditional chemotherapy.
Immunotherapy biomarkers — PD-L1, MSI-H, and TMB — help predict which patients will respond to immune checkpoint inhibitors, which are now approved in a tumor-agnostic manner for MSI-H cancers.
Basket trials and platform trials are clinical research innovations designed for precision oncology, testing drugs across multiple cancer types based on shared molecular alterations rather than tissue of origin.
Pharmacogenomics affects primary care prescribing: CYP2C19 status is critical for clopidogrel effectiveness, CYP2D6 affects metabolism of many antidepressants and opioids, and HLA-B*5701 screening prevents abacavir hypersensitivity.
Whole-exome sequencing is transforming rare disease diagnosis, compressing the diagnostic odyssey from years to weeks for many patients and achieving diagnostic yields of 25-40%.
Genetic counselors are essential clinical partners for interpreting genomic results, communicating uncertainty (especially VUS findings), and supporting decision-making for patients facing high-stakes choices like preventive surgery.
Newborn screening programs are one of the most successful applications of precision medicine, screening millions of infants annually and enabling early treatment that prevents disability and death.
Liquid biopsy uses circulating tumor DNA from blood samples to monitor cancer treatment response, detect minimal residual disease, and identify resistance mutations non-invasively.
Module 5 Key Takeaways
Precision medicine is no longer a research concept — it is reshaping the clinical encounter in oncology, primary care, and rare disease diagnosis. This module traces how tumor profiling, pharmacogenomics, and whole-exome sequencing are moving from academic medical centers into everyday practice. You will see how clinical decision support, newborn screening programs, and genetic counseling translate genomic science into patient care decisions. By the end, you will understand what precision medicine looks like from the clinician's perspective and how Vermont providers are beginning to integrate these tools.
######## genomics-precision-medicine | precision-medicine-m6-equity | The Diversity Deficit: Why Precision Medicine Must Work for Everyone
The Diversity Deficit: Why Precision Medicine Must Work for Everyone
Imagine a medical technology that works brilliantly for some patients but delivers systematically inferior results for others — not because of differences in the patients' underlying biology, but because the technology was built using data that did not include people like them. This is not a hypothetical. It is the current state of precision medicine.
The power of precision medicine comes from comparison: we understand whether a genetic variant is disease-causing by comparing its frequency in affected versus unaffected individuals, and by observing what happens to people who carry it. But if almost all the people in those comparisons share a similar ancestry, the insights generated are primarily valid for people of that ancestry.
The GWAS Diversity Problem: A Scientific Crisis, Not Just an Ethical One
A genome-wide association study (GWAS) is a research approach that scans the entire genome of thousands of people to find genetic variants that are statistically associated with a trait or disease. GWAS has identified tens of thousands of genetic associations across hundreds of conditions. But most GWAS participants have been of European ancestry, so the variants discovered — and the risk tools built on them — reflect European genomes far better than those of any other population.
Why does this matter scientifically? Genetic associations found in European populations do not always replicate in other ancestry groups. The specific variants tagged in a GWAS study may differ by ancestry because linkage disequilibrium patterns — the way genetic variants are inherited together — vary between populations. A variant that reliably tags a disease-causing mutation in a European population may not tag the same mutation in an African or Asian population.
African-ancestry populations also have greater genetic diversity than European populations — a consequence of modern human populations originating in Africa and experiencing thousands of additional generations of evolution there before migrating to other continents. This means that studies restricted to European ancestry samples are sampling a genetically less diverse slice of humanity, potentially missing variants and associations that only exist in higher frequency in African or other non-European populations.
As of 2018, 78% of genome-wide association study participants were of European ancestry, 10% Asian, and 2% African. (Sirugo, Williams & Tishkoff, Cell, 2019)

The Genomic Diversity Gap
Imagine you want to build a highly accurate autocorrect algorithm for English. You train it almost exclusively on text written in British English — newspapers, novels, government documents. The algorithm works well for British English speakers. But when Australian, Nigerian, or Jamaican English speakers use it, it keeps flagging their perfectly correct words as mistakes, because those word patterns were absent from the training data. The algorithm is not wrong, exactly — it is just incomplete in a way that systematically disadvantages non-British users.
Genomic databases trained predominantly on European ancestry populations make better predictions for European ancestry individuals. For African, Indigenous, South Asian, and other non-European ancestry individuals, the predictions are less accurate — and clinical decisions based on those predictions are therefore less reliable.
Why GWAS diversity matters for scientific validity
Polygenic Risk Scores: When the Training Data Is Not Diverse
A polygenic risk score (PRS) is a number calculated by summing up the small effects of hundreds or thousands of genetic variants to estimate a person's inherited risk for a complex trait or disease. PRS for conditions like coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes, and breast cancer are moving toward clinical use. But PRS accuracy is strongly ancestry-dependent: a PRS trained on European data performs poorly when applied to individuals of African or Asian ancestry.
A 2019 study in Nature Genetics (Martin et al.) found that polygenic scores built from predominantly European data predicted risk about 4.5 times more accurately for people of European ancestry than for people of African ancestry, who are genetically farthest from the training population. Using a PRS with known poor accuracy for a patient of African ancestry without disclosing this limitation is a form of health inequity embedded in the technology itself.
If a cardiologist uses a coronary artery disease PRS to decide whether to intensify preventive treatment, and that PRS was trained entirely on European ancestry data, she is making decisions based on a risk estimate that is less accurate for her Black or South Asian patients than for her white patients. This is a clinical accuracy problem — and one that many providers do not know to ask about.
Algorithmic Bias in Genomic Interpretation Tools
The GWAS diversity gap has a direct clinical consequence: variant classification databases — the tools laboratories use to determine whether a genetic variant is pathogenic or benign — are also skewed toward European ancestry populations. When a clinical genetics lab identifies a variant in a patient of African ancestry, they look it up in databases like ClinVar. If that variant has only been observed in European populations before, it may be classified as a VUS (variant of uncertain significance) even if its clinical significance is actually well-established in other contexts.
This produces a systematic disparity in BRCA testing outcomes. Multiple studies have found that Black women receive VUS results from BRCA testing at substantially higher rates than white women — not because Black women's BRCA variants are intrinsically more ambiguous, but because there is less reference data from individuals of African ancestry in the databases used to classify variants. The result is diagnostic uncertainty that falls disproportionately on the patients who already face the most barriers to cancer care.
If a genetic test result comes back 'uncertain,' that reflects something ambiguous about the patient's biology.
VUS findings often reflect gaps in the reference database, not ambiguity in the patient's biology. The same variant may be reclassified as benign or pathogenic as more data is added — especially data from underrepresented ancestries. Higher VUS rates in non-European patients are a measure of database inadequacy, not biological complexity.
The Economic Access Barrier: Who Can Actually Get Precision Medicine
Even if the genomic databases were fully equitable, precision medicine therapies face another equity barrier: cost. Many targeted cancer therapies, gene therapies, and genomic testing services are extraordinarily expensive — and coverage by Medicaid, the insurance program for low-income Americans, is inconsistent.
Consider Zolgensma, the gene therapy for spinal muscular atrophy discussed in Module 5. At approximately $2.1 million for a single infusion, it is one of the most expensive drugs ever approved. While manufacturers have patient assistance programs, access for Medicaid-enrolled patients has been inconsistent across states, and disparities in newborn screening follow-up — needed to identify eligible infants — have been documented along racial and socioeconomic lines.
Genetic counseling services face a similar access problem. There is a national shortage of genetic counselors — approximately 6,000 board-certified genetic counselors serve the entire United States, compared with over 300,000 primary care physicians. They are concentrated in urban academic medical centers. Rural patients, low-income patients without transportation, and patients who need counseling in languages other than English face significant barriers to accessing services that are increasingly central to precision medicine care.

Precision Medicine Access: High-Income Urban vs. Low-Income Rural Patient
Direct-to-Consumer Genomics: Promise vs. Reality for Low-Income Patients
Companies like 23andMe and AncestryDNA have made genetic testing accessible to millions of Americans at a price point of $100-300. In theory, this democratizes genomics. In practice, the equity picture is more complicated.
DTC tests are research-grade, not clinical-grade. They use genotyping arrays that detect a fixed set of known variants, not the comprehensive sequencing used in clinical laboratories. Health reports from DTC companies have documented accuracy limitations, particularly for non-European ancestry individuals, and the regulatory oversight of health claims is lighter than for clinical tests. A person who receives a DTC 'low risk for BRCA' result may have a false sense of reassurance if they carry a pathogenic variant the DTC array does not detect.
Furthermore, DTC genomic results require health literacy and access to clinical follow-up to be actionable. A low-income patient without a primary care provider who receives a 23andMe report showing elevated Alzheimer's or cancer risk faces the result without clinical support. For patients who have the least access to care, DTC genomics may create anxiety and confusion more often than clinical benefit.
NIH All of Us: Building the Diverse Biobank Precision Medicine Requires
The NIH All of Us Research Program, launched in 2018, is a national effort to build a biobank of 1 million or more diverse U.S. participants. The program explicitly prioritizes recruitment of communities that have historically been underrepresented in biomedical research: racial and ethnic minorities, rural residents, sexual and gender minorities, people with disabilities, and those without a college education. Participants donate health data, biological samples, and electronic health record access; in return, they receive their own genetic results.
As of 2025, All of Us had enrolled over 800,000 participants, with approximately 50% from racial or ethnic minority groups — a dramatic improvement over prior NIH biobank initiatives. The program has made its data available to approved researchers through a secure cloud-based platform, with the goal of generating genomic insights that are valid and actionable across the full diversity of the American population.
Vermont has been an active participant in the All of Us program, with enrollment sites at the University of Vermont Medical Center and community health centers across the state. The program's emphasis on rural participants — one of the most underrepresented groups in prior genomic research — has made Vermont an important recruiting ground. Vermont participants include residents from the Northeast Kingdom and other rural regions who would rarely have access to academic genomic research programs.
Real-World Example
Vermont's All of Us enrollment has contributed to the program's goal of including rural Americans as a distinct population of interest, generating data relevant to understanding how geography, environmental exposures, and rural social determinants interact with genomic risk factors.

NIH All of Us and Genomic Equity Progress
Historical Trauma and the Research Trust Deficit
Recruitment of underrepresented communities into genomic research cannot be separated from the history of exploitation in biomedical research. That history is not ancient — it extends into living memory and continues to shape how communities respond to research recruitment today.
The U.S. Public Health Service Syphilis Study at Tuskegee (1932-1972) enrolled 399 Black men with syphilis and 201 uninfected controls, promising free medical care and burial insurance while deliberately withholding treatment — including penicillin after it became the standard of care in 1947 — to study the natural progression of untreated syphilis. The study ended only when a whistleblower leaked details to the press. Its legacy is a documented, rational distrust of biomedical research and institutions among many Black Americans.
The story of Henrietta Lacks and the HeLa cell line adds another dimension. Lacks was a Black woman whose cervical cancer cells were taken without her knowledge or consent at Johns Hopkins Hospital in 1951. Her cells — known as HeLa cells — became the first human cell line that could be kept alive and grown in the laboratory indefinitely. They have been used in thousands of scientific studies and generated billions of dollars in commercial value. The Lacks family received no compensation and was not informed for decades.
These histories matter for precision medicine recruitment because trust is the prerequisite for participation. When researchers approach Black, Indigenous, or other historically exploited communities with genomic research offers, they are entering those conversations carrying this institutional history — whether or not individual researchers know it or intend it. Effective, ethical recruitment requires community engagement, transparent data governance, and demonstrated benefit to the communities being recruited.
Imagine a bank that, for decades, systematically overcharged customers from a particular neighborhood, denied them loans based on their address, and never faced consequences. Now the bank has new leadership, new policies, and genuinely wants to serve that neighborhood. But residents remember — or their parents remember — and they are not wrong to be cautious. The bank's new good intentions do not erase the institutional memory of harm.
Research institutions that previously exploited communities of color now seek to recruit those communities into genomic research for what they believe are legitimate scientific and equity goals. The skepticism these communities exhibit is not irrational — it is a rational protective response to documented institutional harm. Building trust requires time, transparency, community control over data, and demonstrated reciprocal benefit.
Why historical research exploitation creates present-day trust deficits
Indigenous Data Sovereignty and the CARE Principles
Indigenous communities face a distinct set of concerns around genomic research. Beyond the shared history of exploitation that many minority communities experience, Indigenous peoples have specific legal and political status as sovereign nations, with implications for how data about their members is collected, stored, shared, and used.
Indigenous data sovereignty is the right of Indigenous peoples to govern the collection, ownership, and application of data about their communities. The CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance — Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, and Ethics — provide a framework for how genomic research involving Indigenous communities should be structured. These principles assert that data about Indigenous peoples belongs to and should serve Indigenous peoples, not external researchers or corporations.
Specific cases have illustrated the stakes. The Havasupai Tribe of Arizona participated in a diabetes genetics study at Arizona State University in the 1990s, donating blood samples for that specific purpose. Researchers then used the samples for other studies — including research on schizophrenia, population migration, and inbreeding — without tribal consent. The Havasupai sued, eventually settling in 2010, and the case has since been a touchstone for discussions of Indigenous research ethics.
In Vermont, the Abenaki Nation — Vermont's only state-recognized Indigenous nation — has its own community priorities and sensitivities around research and data governance. Any genomic research initiative seeking to include Abenaki community members must engage tribal leadership as partners, not merely as a recruitment population, and must respect the community's authority to decide whether and on what terms genomic research is appropriate.
LGBTQ+ Populations and Genomic Research Gaps
LGBTQ+ populations — lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, queer, and other sexual and gender minority (SGM) individuals — represent another group systematically underrepresented in genomic and biomedical research. This is partly a data collection problem: most electronic health records and research databases have not systematically collected sexual orientation or gender identity (SOGI) data, making it impossible to study health disparities that may have genetic or gene-environment interaction components.
LGBTQ+ individuals also have documented higher rates of several conditions with potential genomic components — including depression, anxiety, substance use disorders, and certain cancers — but the research to disentangle genetic from social and minority stress contributions to these disparities is in its infancy. The NIH Sexual & Gender Minority Research Office and the All of Us program's explicit SGM inclusion goals are beginning to address this gap.
Rural Populations and Precision Medicine Access Barriers
Rural populations face a distinct set of precision medicine access barriers that are structural rather than cultural. These include geographic distance from specialized genetic services, limited broadband access needed for telegenetics, provider shortages that mean primary care physicians have little time to engage with genomic complexity, and insurance gaps that make high-cost genomic testing and targeted therapies financially inaccessible.
Rural patients with cancer have historically had less access to tumor genomic profiling — the first step in precision oncology — because testing and molecular expertise concentrate in academic centers. Programs that bring testing to community practices can close that gap: a 2024 study in JNCI Cancer Spectrum of 1,258 patients in the Maine Cancer Genomics Initiative, which deployed tumor testing through community and rural oncology practices, found that rurality was not associated with receipt of genome-matched treatment. Access, not geography itself, is the barrier.
Urban areas have approximately 3.5 times more genetic counselors per capita than rural areas, creating a profound service desert in rural states like Vermont. (NSGC Workforce Survey, 2023)

Rural and Structural Access Gaps in Precision Medicine
Vermont-Specific Equity Challenges: Refugee Populations and Rural Geography
Vermont is among the whitest states in the nation by percentage, but it hosts a significant and growing refugee population — particularly in Burlington and surrounding communities — that represents extraordinary genetic and ancestral diversity. Vermont has resettled refugees from Bhutan, Somalia, Democratic Republic of Congo, Bosnia, Sudan, and dozens of other countries.
For refugee populations, precision medicine access barriers multiply. Language barriers complicate genetic counseling, which is inherently nuanced and requires precise communication about probability, uncertainty, and family implications. Reference databases have almost no data from many refugee-origin populations, increasing VUS rates dramatically. Cultural frameworks around fate, family disclosure, and heredity may differ significantly from those embedded in standard genetic counseling practice.
Genetic counselors working with Vermont's refugee communities need cultural competence, access to professional medical interpreters (not family members, who may selectively filter difficult information), and awareness that the Western individualistic framework for genetic decision-making — emphasizing personal autonomy and individual disclosure choices — may not fit the community-oriented decision-making frameworks of many refugee cultures.
UVMMC's Global Health Program and its associated refugee health clinic provide primary care to Burlington's refugee communities. The program has developed culturally adapted health communication approaches and works with community health workers who share cultural and linguistic backgrounds with patient populations. As genomic medicine becomes more integrated into primary care, these established community relationships represent a critical infrastructure for equitable genomic service delivery.
Real-World Example
The Global Health Program model — community health workers as cultural bridges, professional interpreter use, and community engagement in service design — represents a replicable approach for extending precision medicine services to linguistically and culturally diverse populations in rural states.
UVMMC Global Health Program; Vermont Refugee Health Program Annual Reports
University of Vermont Medical Center Global Health Program
What Equitable Precision Medicine Actually Requires
Equitable precision medicine is not simply a matter of increasing diversity in research databases, though that is essential. It requires changes at multiple levels — research design, clinical service delivery, technology development, insurance policy, and community trust-building — working simultaneously.
Genomic databases, GWAS studies, and variant interpretation tools must include sufficient representation from all major ancestry groups to ensure that polygenic risk scores and variant classifications are valid across populations — not just European ancestry individuals.
Diverse, representative research databases
Underrepresented communities must be partners in research design, not merely recruitment targets. This means tribal consultation for Indigenous communities, community advisory boards for other groups, and genuine power-sharing over data governance and benefit distribution.
Community-engaged research design
Genomic testing and precision medicine therapies must be covered by Medicaid and other public payers at rates that ensure access regardless of income. Inconsistent Medicaid coverage for tumor profiling, targeted therapies, and genetic counseling is a structural equity failure.
Insurance coverage and payment reform
The genetic counseling workforce must expand dramatically, and telegenetics must be fully reimbursed to extend services to rural areas. Community health workers trained in genomic health communication can extend the reach of genetic counselors in underserved communities.
Workforce expansion and telegenetics
Genetic counseling and genomic health communication must be available in the languages spoken by patients, with cultural adaptation for communities whose frameworks for understanding heredity, family, and risk differ from the Western individualistic model embedded in standard practice.
Culturally and linguistically adapted services
What Equitable Precision Medicine Requires: A Framework
The equity failures in precision medicine are not primarily failures of individual prejudice — they are failures of system design. Genomic databases were built with the researchers available, which happened to be primarily from European ancestry academic institutions. Fixing this requires intentional redesign of research infrastructure, not just increased awareness.
The solution to genomic inequity is simply to recruit more diverse participants into existing research frameworks.
Recruiting diverse participants into research systems that were not designed with their interests, governance preferences, or data sovereignty in mind replicates historical exploitation in a new form. Equitable genomic research requires restructuring how data governance works — giving communities authority over their data, ensuring benefit flows back to participating communities, and building infrastructure that serves underrepresented populations rather than merely extracting data from them.
VUS findings are more common in patients of African ancestry because the databases used to classify variants — such as ClinVar — have been built predominantly from research on European ancestry populations. A variant that has been observed many times in European ancestry individuals may be well-classified as benign or pathogenic; a variant that appears primarily in African ancestry individuals may lack sufficient reference data for classification, resulting in VUS status. This is a limitation of the database, not a feature of the patient's biology. The provider should: (1) explain clearly that VUS does not mean dangerous and is not a basis for preventive surgery; (2) refer to a board-certified genetic counselor for comprehensive counseling; (3) encourage the patient's relatives to be tested, as additional family data can help reclassify variants; (4) inform the patient that VUS classifications are frequently updated as databases improve, and her lab should re-analyze her variants over time; and (5) acknowledge that the higher VUS rate in patients of African ancestry is a systemic inequity in the genomic research infrastructure, not a personal or biological characteristic.
Think about what drives VUS classification and how variant databases are constructed.
A Black woman in Vermont receives BRCA1/2 testing through her OB/GYN after a family history of breast cancer. Her result shows three variants of uncertain significance (VUS). She is devastated and asks whether she should have a prophylactic mastectomy. What should her provider understand about why VUS findings are more common in patients of African ancestry, and how should this be communicated?
The CARE Principles require: Collective Benefit — the research must generate direct benefit to the Abenaki community, not just academic publications or commercial applications that flow back to the research institution; Authority to Control — the Abenaki Nation must have genuine authority over how their members' data is collected, stored, analyzed, and shared, including veto power over secondary uses; Responsibility — researchers have an ongoing obligation to the community that extends beyond the data collection period; and Ethics — research must be consistent with the community's own values and governance processes. In practice, a genuine data sovereignty approach would: involve tribal leadership as co-investigators with intellectual property rights, not just as a community advisory board; require that data be stored in systems the tribe controls; require explicit consent for every new use case rather than blanket consent; specify that data cannot be shared with commercial genomics companies; guarantee that research results and benefits flow back to the community; and include community health workers as co-researchers who will remain in the community after the study ends. The Havasupai case specifically teaches that researchers must obtain specific consent for each study use — blanket consent for 'diabetes research' does not authorize use of samples for ancestry, migration, or psychiatric studies.
Think about what CARE stands for and what the Havasupai case taught the field about scope of consent.
A Vermont health system wants to partner with the Western Abenaki community to study genetic factors in type 2 diabetes, which affects the community at elevated rates. Community members have expressed interest in the health question but concern about how their genetic data will be used. What does the CARE framework require of researchers in this situation, and what would a genuine data sovereignty approach look like?
More than 78% of GWAS participants have been of European ancestry, making precision medicine less scientifically valid for the 84% of the global population that is not of European ancestry — this is a scientific accuracy problem, not just an ethical concern.
Polygenic risk scores trained on European data perform substantially worse in non-European populations, meaning clinical decisions based on these scores are systematically less accurate for patients of African, Asian, Indigenous, and other non-European ancestry.
Higher rates of variants of uncertain significance in non-European BRCA testing reflect database inadequacy, not biological ambiguity — variant classification databases are built from skewed reference populations.
The Tuskegee syphilis study and the Henrietta Lacks/HeLa cell case are not historical curiosities — they established patterns of research exploitation whose legacy shapes community participation in genomic research today.
Indigenous data sovereignty and the CARE principles (Collective Benefit, Authority to Control, Responsibility, Ethics) require that research involving Indigenous communities be governed by those communities, not by external institutions.
Economic barriers — inconsistent Medicaid coverage for tumor profiling, targeted therapies, and genetic counseling — mean that precision medicine's benefits are currently distributed along income lines.
Vermont's refugee communities face compounded barriers to genomic equity: language barriers in genetic counseling, near-complete absence of their ancestries in reference databases, and cultural frameworks that differ from the individualistic model embedded in standard genetic counseling.
Equitable precision medicine requires redesigning research infrastructure, not merely recruiting more diverse participants — communities must have authority over their data and receive direct benefit from research participation.
Module 6 Key Takeaways
Precision medicine's promise is undermined by a fundamental problem: the genomic databases and research studies that power it are built overwhelmingly from people of European ancestry. This is not just an ethical concern — it is a scientific validity problem that produces less accurate polygenic risk scores, higher rates of ambiguous genetic findings, and systematically worse care for non-European patients. This module examines the structural causes of genomic inequity, the historical trauma that makes diverse participation in research difficult, and what equitable precision medicine actually requires — including Vermont-specific challenges around refugee populations, Abenaki communities, and rural access.
######## medicare-fundamentals | medicare-history-structure | Medicare: History, Structure, and Enrollment
Medicare: History, Structure, and Enrollment
Why Medicare Was Created
Before 1965, growing old in America often meant losing health coverage exactly when you needed it most. Private insurers either refused to cover older adults or charged premiums most retirees could not afford, and roughly half of Americans over 65 had no health insurance at all. Aging was, in effect, a pre-existing condition that the private market would not insure.
President Lyndon B. Johnson signed Medicare into law on July 30, 1965, as part of the Social Security Amendments of 1965. The same statute created Medicaid. Medicare became Title XVIII of the Social Security Act and Medicaid became Title XIX — the legal "titles" you still hear referenced today.
Johnson held the signing ceremony at the Truman Library in Independence, Missouri, to honor former President Harry Truman, who had proposed national health insurance back in 1945 only to be blocked by Congress. Truman was enrolled as Medicare’s very first beneficiary and received the first Medicare card.
Medicare is a social insurance program: workers pay into it through payroll taxes during their careers and draw benefits in retirement, regardless of income. This is fundamentally different from Medicaid, which is means-tested and targets low-income people.
When Johnson signed Medicare into law at the Truman Library on July 30, 1965, he enrolled 81-year-old former President Harry Truman as the program’s first beneficiary. Truman and his wife Bess received the first two Medicare cards. Johnson chose the venue deliberately to credit Truman, who had first proposed national health insurance two decades earlier.
Harry Truman, Medicare Card #1
The Four Parts of Medicare
Medicare grew from a two-part program into a four-part program over four decades. Parts A and B existed from the start in 1965 and together are called "Original" or "Traditional" Medicare. Part C (Medicare Advantage) was created by the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 — originally called Medicare+Choice — letting beneficiaries get their benefits through private plans. Part D, the outpatient prescription drug benefit, was created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 and took effect on January 1, 2006.
Part A is Hospital Insurance. It covers inpatient hospital stays, skilled nursing facility care following a qualifying hospital stay, hospice, and some home health. Most beneficiaries pay no Part A premium because they (or a spouse) paid Medicare payroll taxes for at least 40 quarters — ten years — of work.
Part B is Medical Insurance. It covers physician visits, outpatient care, preventive services, durable medical equipment, and drugs administered in a clinical setting. Part B requires a monthly premium. Part C, Medicare Advantage, is a private-plan alternative that must cover everything A and B cover and usually bundles in Part D drug coverage. Part D is the standalone voluntary prescription drug benefit delivered by private plans.
Original Medicare (Parts A + B)
Run directly by the federal government
See any provider that accepts Medicare nationwide

Medicare Advantage (Part C)
Run by private insurers paid a capitated rate by CMS

Original Medicare vs. Medicare Advantage (Part C)
Who Is Eligible
Medicare eligibility is not purely about turning 65. The program has four distinct pathways to coverage, and understanding them is essential because they carry different rules about premiums and waiting periods.
The main pathway is age. U.S. citizens and lawful permanent residents who have worked 40 quarters (ten years) in Medicare-covered employment are entitled to premium-free Part A at 65 and can enroll in Part B for a monthly premium. People who reach 65 without enough work quarters can still buy into Part A by paying a premium.
The disability pathway covers people under 65 who have received Social Security Disability Insurance (SSDI) for 24 months; they are then automatically enrolled in Parts A and B. Two conditions bypass the standard 24-month wait: people with End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) generally qualify about three months after starting regular dialysis or after a kidney transplant, and people with ALS (amyotrophic lateral sclerosis) qualify immediately upon receiving SSDI.
Citizens/permanent residents with 40 quarters of Medicare-taxed work get premium-free Part A; those with fewer quarters can buy in.
Age 65+
People under 65 are auto-enrolled in Parts A and B after 24 months of Social Security Disability Insurance benefits.
SSDI for 24 months
Qualify at any age, generally ~3 months after regular dialysis begins or after a kidney transplant — no 24-month wait.

People with ALS receive Medicare immediately upon collecting SSDI — no 24-month wait.

The Four Pathways to Medicare Eligibility
Medicare is federal, age/disability-based, and not means-tested. Medicaid is a joint federal-state program that is means-tested for low-income people. About 12 million Americans are "dual eligibles" enrolled in both at once — Medicare pays first, Medicaid fills gaps.
Don’t confuse Medicare with Medicaid
How Big Medicare Is
Medicare is one of the largest payers in the world. In 2024, Medicare covered about 68 million people: roughly 61 million (about 90 percent) age 65 or older and 7 million younger people who qualify through disability, ESRD, or ALS.
The program is also a massive share of public finances. Medicare made up roughly 13.5 percent of the federal budget in 2024, Medicare benefit payments are estimated at about $1.1 trillion in 2025, and Medicare accounted for about 21 percent of all national health expenditures in 2023. In short, more than one in five U.S. health care dollars flows through Medicare.
The pressure is demographic. The United States entered "Peak 65" in 2024: about 4.1 million people are turning 65 each year from 2024 through 2027 — roughly 11,000 every day. This wave of aging baby boomers is why Medicare financing, payment reform, and the shift toward value-based care dominate health policy debates.

Why Medicare’s Structure Matters
Medicare’s four-part design shapes nearly everything about how American health care is paid for. Because Part A is funded by a dedicated payroll-tax trust fund while Part B and Part D draw heavily on general revenue and premiums, the parts face very different fiscal pressures — a distinction explored in the next lesson on financing.
Medicare also sets the pace for the entire system. Private insurers frequently benchmark their payment rates to Medicare, and Medicare’s policy experiments — prospective payment, accountable care organizations, bundled payments — ripple outward to Medicaid and commercial payers. When Medicare changes how it pays, the whole market tends to follow.
Finally, the rapid growth of Medicare Advantage has shifted the program toward private administration. More than half of eligible beneficiaries are now in Part C plans, which changes how care is managed, how providers are reimbursed, and where federal dollars actually go.
Medicare did not just insure older Americans — it became the single most powerful force shaping how the entire U.S. health care system is financed and delivered.
Medicare was signed into law on July 30, 1965, by President Johnson as Title XVIII of the Social Security Act, alongside Medicaid (Title XIX); Harry Truman was its first beneficiary.
Medicare is social insurance — funded by payroll taxes and available regardless of income — not a means-tested program like Medicaid.
Part A covers hospital care, Part B covers outpatient/physician care, Part C (Medicare Advantage) is the private-plan alternative, and Part D covers prescription drugs.
Parts A and B date to 1965; Part C came from the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 and Part D from the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 (effective 2006).
Eligibility has four pathways: age 65+ with 40 work quarters, 24 months of SSDI, ESRD, and ALS (the last two skip the 24-month wait).
In 2024, about 68 million people were enrolled, ~90% of them age 65 or older.
Medicare benefit payments are estimated at about $1.1 trillion in 2025 — Medicare is about 21% of national health spending and ~13.5% of the federal budget — and the "Peak 65" wave is intensifying fiscal pressure.

Part A covers hospital/inpatient care, Part B covers outpatient and physician services, and Part D covers prescription drugs — so the other three options mismatch the part with its coverage.

######## medicare-fundamentals | medicare-financing | How Medicare Is Financed
How Medicare Is Financed
Two Trust Funds, Two Very Different Designs
Medicare does not run on a single pot of money. It runs on two separate trust funds with fundamentally different financing rules, and understanding the split is the key to understanding every Medicare solvency headline you will ever read. The Hospital Insurance (HI) Trust Fund pays for Part A. The Supplementary Medical Insurance (SMI) Trust Fund pays for Part B and Part D.
The HI Trust Fund works like Social Security: dedicated payroll taxes flow in while workers are employed, and benefits flow out in retirement. When payroll-tax revenue exceeds Part A spending, the surplus accumulates in the trust fund; when spending exceeds revenue, the fund is drawn down. Because its income is capped by what the tax brings in, the HI fund can actually run dry.
The SMI Trust Fund is the opposite. No payroll taxes are dedicated to it. Instead it is filled each year by general federal revenue plus beneficiary premiums, and the federal contribution is set prospectively to cover projected costs. Because Congress simply appropriates whatever is needed, the SMI fund is, by design, always solvent — it cannot "go broke."
HI (Part A) is funded by dedicated payroll taxes and can be exhausted. SMI (Parts B and D) is funded by general revenue and premiums set to cover costs, so it is automatically solvent. Almost every "Medicare is going bankrupt" story is really about the HI Trust Fund only.
HI Trust Fund (Part A)
Funded by the 2.9% Medicare payroll tax
Works like a savings account — surplus or drawdown
Can be depleted if spending outruns tax revenue
Solvency is a recurring fiscal concern
SMI Trust Fund (Parts B & D)
Funded ~75% general revenue, ~25% premiums
Federal contribution set prospectively each year
Cannot be depleted — automatically solvent
But it adds to the federal deficit instead
The Two Medicare Trust Funds
Part A: The Medicare Payroll Tax
Part A is financed primarily by the Medicare payroll tax. Employees pay 1.45 percent of their earnings and employers pay a matching 1.45 percent, for a combined 2.9 percent. Self-employed workers pay the full 2.9 percent themselves. Unlike the Social Security tax, the Medicare payroll tax has no wage cap — it applies to every dollar of earnings.
Since 2013, an Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9 percent applies to high earners — on wages above $200,000 for individual filers and above $250,000 for joint filers. This extra tax is paid only by the employee, not matched by the employer, and was added by the Affordable Care Act to shore up HI financing.
This pay-as-you-go design means today’s workers are largely funding today’s retirees. That works well when there are many workers per beneficiary and strains badly when there are few — which is exactly the demographic squeeze Medicare now faces.
1.45% employee + 1.45% employer (CMS / Treasury)
Combined Payroll Tax
2.9%
On wages over $200K single / $250K joint (ACA)

Part B & D Funding Split

On Medicare Payroll Tax
No cap
Parts B and D: General Revenue and Premiums
Part B and Part D are paid out of the SMI Trust Fund. For Part B, the law sets standard beneficiary premiums to cover about 25 percent of projected per-enrollee costs, with the remaining roughly 75 percent coming from general federal revenue — that is, from the broad federal budget funded by income taxes and borrowing.
Higher-income beneficiaries pay more through the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount (IRMAA), a surcharge added to both Part B and Part D premiums above certain income thresholds. Part D is financed similarly: enrollee premiums plus a large federal subsidy, with additional support for low-income beneficiaries.
The trade-off is important. Because SMI leans so heavily on general revenue, it never faces insolvency — but every dollar of growth in Part B and Part D spending directly enlarges the federal deficit. So SMI’s fiscal pressure shows up not as a trust-fund crisis but as a rising claim on the overall federal budget.
Medicare Advantage (Part C) does not have its own trust fund. CMS pays MA plans a risk-adjusted per-member-per-month capitation rate drawn from both the HI and SMI trust funds, in proportion to the Part A and Part B services those plans cover. So as MA enrollment grows past half of all beneficiaries, a growing share of both trust funds flows through private plans rather than directly to providers.
Medicare Advantage and Both Trust Funds
The HI Trust Fund Solvency Problem
Each year the Medicare Trustees publish projections of when the HI Trust Fund will run short. The 2025 Trustees Report projects HI depletion in 2033 — three years earlier than the prior report’s 2036 estimate, a change driven mainly by higher projected health care costs.
Crucially, depletion does not mean Medicare ends or that Part A stops. It means incoming payroll-tax revenue would cover only about 89 percent of Part A costs in 2033 — leaving an 11 percent shortfall that Congress would have to close through higher taxes, lower payments, or other policy changes.
The underlying driver is demographic. The number of workers paying HI payroll taxes for each Medicare beneficiary has been falling and will keep falling as baby boomers retire. Fewer workers supporting more retirees is the core arithmetic behind every solvency warning.
If the HI Trust Fund is depleted in 2033, Part A would still pay roughly 89 cents on the dollar from ongoing payroll taxes — it would not shut down. The depletion date is a policy deadline, not the end of the program.
"Trust fund depletion" is not bankruptcy

Why Financing Drives Payment Reform
Medicare’s financing structure is the engine behind decades of payment reform. Because the HI Trust Fund cannot simply print money and SMI growth widens the deficit, CMS has a powerful incentive to slow the rate of spending growth rather than just cut benefits.
That is why CMS has invested so heavily in delivery-system reform — accountable care organizations, bundled payments, value-based purchasing, and the work of the CMS Innovation Center. Each is an attempt to get the same or better care for less money, extending trust-fund solvency without slashing eligibility or coverage.
For anyone working in health care, the lesson is direct: Medicare’s payment changes are not arbitrary. They are downstream of a financing system under demographic strain, and they will keep coming as long as the worker-to-beneficiary ratio keeps falling.
Medicare’s solvency math — fewer workers funding more retirees — is the quiet force pushing American health care from paying for volume toward paying for value.
Medicare runs on two separate trust funds: HI (Part A), funded by payroll taxes, and SMI (Parts B and D), funded by general revenue and premiums.
The Part A payroll tax is 2.9% combined (1.45% employee + 1.45% employer), with an extra 0.9% on high earners and no wage cap.
Part B premiums are set to cover about 25% of costs, with roughly 75% paid from general federal revenue; Part D is financed similarly.
The SMI fund cannot be depleted because Congress funds it annually — but that means its growth enlarges the federal deficit instead.
The 2025 Trustees Report projects the HI Trust Fund will be depleted in 2033, after which payroll taxes would cover about 89% of Part A costs.
Depletion is not bankruptcy: Part A keeps paying most benefits and the date is really a deadline for Congress to act.
The falling number of workers per beneficiary is the central reason Medicare keeps pushing payment reform.
Unlike the HI fund (which depends on a fixed payroll tax and can run dry), the SMI fund is filled annually with general federal revenue plus premiums, with the federal contribution set prospectively to match projected costs. That makes it automatically solvent — but it adds to the federal deficit rather than risking depletion.

######## medicare-fundamentals | medicare-coverage-benefits | Medicare Coverage: What's Covered, What's Not
Medicare Coverage: What's Covered, What's Not
A Safety Net, Not Comprehensive Insurance
A common misconception is that Medicare pays for everything once you turn 65. It does not. Traditional Medicare was designed in 1965 as a safety net against catastrophic costs, not as a comprehensive benefit, and it still carries substantial cost-sharing and significant coverage exclusions. Understanding these gaps is the single best way to understand why the Medigap and Medicare Advantage markets exist.
Cost-sharing in traditional Medicare comes in three forms: deductibles you pay before coverage kicks in, coinsurance (a share of each cost), and premiums for ongoing coverage. The dollar figures change every year; the structure does not.
The most consequential design feature is what traditional Medicare lacks: an out-of-pocket maximum. Unlike employer plans and Medicare Advantage, Original Medicare Parts A and B set no annual cap on what a beneficiary can owe — a single catastrophic illness can generate unlimited 20 percent coinsurance.
Original Medicare (Parts A + B) has no annual out-of-pocket maximum. This is the central financial risk of traditional Medicare and the main reason most beneficiaries add Medigap or choose Medicare Advantage.
Part A Cost-Sharing (Hospital)
Part A cost-sharing is organized around the "benefit period," a concept that surprises many beneficiaries. A benefit period begins when you are admitted as an inpatient and ends only after you have been out of a hospital or skilled nursing facility for 60 consecutive days. The deductible is charged per benefit period, not per year — so two separate hospitalizations months apart can each trigger the full deductible.
In 2025, the inpatient hospital deductible is $1,676 per benefit period. Days 1–60 carry no additional coinsurance after the deductible. Days 61–90 cost $419 per day. Beyond 90 days, you tap into 60 "lifetime reserve days" at $838 per day — and once used, those reserve days are gone forever.
Skilled nursing facility (SNF) coverage follows a separate schedule and has a critical precondition: Medicare only pays for SNF care after a qualifying inpatient hospital stay of at least three days. SNF days 1–20 carry no coinsurance; days 21–100 cost $209.50 per day in 2025; and after day 100, the beneficiary pays the full cost.

2025 Part A Cost-Sharing
Medicare only covers SNF care after a 3-day inpatient hospital stay. Time spent under "observation status" — even overnight — does not count as inpatient, so patients who think they were admitted can be denied SNF coverage. This is a frequent and costly trap.
The 3-day rule and "observation status"
Part B Cost-Sharing (Medical)
Part B covers physician visits, outpatient care, preventive services, and durable medical equipment. In 2025, the standard Part B premium is $185.00 per month and the annual deductible is $257. After the deductible, beneficiaries typically pay 20 percent coinsurance of the Medicare-approved amount for most services.
That 20 percent has no ceiling. For a routine office visit it is trivial; for an expensive course of chemotherapy, dialysis, or specialty infusions billed under Part B, the 20 percent share can run into the tens of thousands of dollars in a single year — with no out-of-pocket maximum to stop it.
Higher-income beneficiaries pay more than the standard premium through IRMAA, the Income-Related Monthly Adjustment Amount, which adds surcharges to both Part B and Part D premiums above set income thresholds.

What Medicare Does NOT Cover
Beyond cost-sharing, traditional Medicare simply excludes whole categories of care that older adults frequently need. Routine dental, vision, and hearing care — including most dentures, eyeglasses, and hearing aids — are not covered by Original Medicare.
The largest gap is long-term care. Medicare does not pay for custodial long-term care — help with bathing, dressing, eating, and other daily activities in a nursing home or at home over the long run. Medicare covers only short-term, skilled care for recovery. Long-term custodial care is paid out of pocket, by long-term care insurance, or by Medicaid once a person spends down their assets.
These exclusions are not minor. They are precisely the benefits that Medicare Advantage plans advertise — many MA plans add dental, vision, and hearing benefits — and they are a major reason beneficiaries weigh MA against Original Medicare plus a supplement.

Covered vs. Not Covered by Original Medicare
How Medigap Fills the Gaps
Because Original Medicare has no out-of-pocket maximum and substantial cost-sharing, about 43 percent of traditional-Medicare beneficiaries (12.2 million people in 2023) buy a Medicare Supplement policy, known as Medigap; others rely on employer retiree coverage or Medicaid. Sold by private insurers, Medigap plans are standardized into lettered plans (such as Plan G and Plan N) so that the same letter offers the same benefits no matter which company sells it.
Medigap covers cost-sharing in Original Medicare — Part A and Part B coinsurance and copayments, and depending on the plan, deductibles. By capping the beneficiary’s exposure, Medigap effectively creates the out-of-pocket protection that Original Medicare itself lacks.
But Medigap does not fill the benefit gaps. Medigap plans generally do not cover dental, vision, hearing, or long-term care. For those, beneficiaries must buy separate standalone policies — or choose a Medicare Advantage plan that bundles such benefits in. This trade-off, cost protection versus added benefits, is the core choice every new beneficiary faces.
Consider a Part B patient on an expensive specialty infusion drug billed at $300,000 a year. Under Original Medicare alone, the 20% coinsurance — about $60,000 — would fall on the patient with no cap to stop it. A Medigap Plan G would cover that Part B coinsurance after the small Part B deductible, turning a potentially ruinous bill into a predictable, modest cost. This is exactly the financial risk Medigap was built to address.
The Catastrophic-Cost Scenario
