######## medicare-fundamentals | inpatient-pps-drg | Inpatient Payment: DRGs and the Prospective Payment System
Inpatient Payment: DRGs and the Prospective Payment System
The Problem Medicare Had to Solve
For Medicare’s first 18 years, hospitals were paid retrospectively for whatever it cost them to treat a patient. Under this cost-based reimbursement hospitals bore almost no financial risk: the more services they delivered and the longer patients stayed, the more Medicare paid. There was no built-in reason to be efficient.
Predictably, costs spiraled. Cost-based payment rewarded volume and length of stay, not value, and Medicare hospital spending grew faster than the program could sustain. By the early 1980s, policymakers concluded the incentives themselves had to change.
The solution was a prospective payment system — pay a fixed, predetermined amount per case based on the patient’s diagnosis, set in advance. If a hospital treats the patient for less, it keeps the difference; if it spends more, it absorbs the loss. This single change shifted financial risk from Medicare onto hospitals and rewired the incentives of American hospital care.
Prospective payment means the price is set before the care is delivered, based on the patient’s diagnosis — not on the hospital’s actual costs. Efficiency becomes the hospital’s reward; inefficiency becomes its loss.
Cost-Based (pre-1983)
Hospital paid for actual costs incurred
More services and longer stays = more revenue
Hospital bears almost no financial risk
Incentive: do more, stay longer
Prospective (IPPS, 1983+)
Fixed payment set in advance per diagnosis
Treat efficiently and keep the difference
Hospital bears the financial risk
Incentive: treat efficiently, discharge appropriately
Cost-Based vs. Prospective Payment
What Is a DRG?
The unit of payment under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS) is the Diagnosis-Related Group, or DRG. DRGs were developed at Yale University in the early 1970s by Robert Fetter and John Thompson as a way to classify hospital cases into clinically similar groups that consume similar resources.
The core idea is patient classification by "case mix." Instead of paying for each test, drug, and bed-day, Medicare assigns each inpatient stay to a single DRG based on the principal diagnosis, procedures performed, complications, comorbidities, age, and discharge status. Each DRG carries a relative weight reflecting how resource-intensive that type of case is on average.
Medicare uses a refined version called MS-DRGs (Medicare Severity DRGs), which account for the severity of illness through complication and comorbidity tiers. For fiscal year 2025, CMS uses a total of 773 MS-DRGs. A high-weight DRG such as a major organ transplant pays far more than a low-weight DRG such as a simple medical admission.
In the early 1970s, Robert B. Fetter, Ph.D., and John D. Thompson, MPH, at Yale University built the first operational set of Diagnosis-Related Groups to relate the types of patients a hospital treats to the costs it incurs. A decade later, Congress adopted their classification system as the backbone of Medicare’s national prospective payment system — turning an academic case-mix tool into the engine of U.S. hospital reimbursement.
Yale University and the Birth of DRGs
How a DRG Payment Is Calculated
The base IPPS payment for a case is, at its heart, a multiplication: a standardized base payment rate multiplied by the DRG’s relative weight. The base rate is split into a labor-related share and a non-labor share, and the labor share is adjusted by the local area wage index so that hospitals in high-cost labor markets receive more.
On top of that base payment, Medicare adds several adjustments. Teaching hospitals receive an Indirect Medical Education (IME) add-on tied to their resident-to-bed ratio. Hospitals serving many low-income patients receive a Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) add-on. And unusually expensive cases can qualify for outlier payments once costs exceed a high threshold.
The combined formula means two hospitals treating the identical DRG can be paid different amounts based on where they are, whether they teach, whom they serve, and whether the case became catastrophically expensive — but the starting point is always the same: base rate times relative weight.
Take the standardized amount, split into labor and non-labor shares.
Start with the base rate
Apply the area wage index to the labor share for geographic cost differences.
Adjust for local wages
Multiply the wage-adjusted base rate by the MS-DRG relative weight.
Multiply by the DRG weight
Add IME (teaching), DSH (low-income), and any new-technology add-ons.
Add policy adjustments
For extraordinarily costly cases that exceed the outlier threshold.
Apply outlier payment if needed
Building an IPPS Payment

How IPPS Changed Hospital Behavior
Because a hospital now earns a fixed amount per DRG regardless of how long the patient stays, IPPS created powerful pressure to reduce length of stay and eliminate unnecessary days and tests. After 1983, hospitals intensified their scrutiny of length of stay, and average inpatient stays fell substantially across the system.
IPPS also made accurate clinical documentation and coding financially critical. Since the DRG assignment — and thus the payment — depends on documented diagnoses, complications, and comorbidities, hospitals invested heavily in coding, case management, and clinical documentation improvement programs.
The same incentives carry risks regulators watch closely: "upcoding" (assigning a higher-paying DRG than warranted) and premature discharge ("quicker and sicker"). These concerns are exactly why Medicare layered on quality and readmissions programs in later decades — covered later in this course.
A fixed payment per DRG rewards efficiency but can incentivize premature discharge and upcoding. Medicare’s later quality programs — like the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program — exist partly to counterbalance these inpatient-payment incentives.
The downside of paying per case
Why IPPS Still Matters
IPPS was the first large-scale demonstration that changing how you pay providers changes how they deliver care. It proved that Medicare’s purchasing power could reshape behavior across thousands of hospitals at once — a lesson that underpins every later payment reform.
The prospective-payment logic spread far beyond hospitals. Medicare went on to build prospective payment systems for skilled nursing facilities, home health, inpatient rehabilitation, and more — each applying the same principle of paying a predetermined amount per episode or unit of care rather than per service.
And the DRG concept itself became foundational to bundled payments and value-based care. Once you can define and price a discrete episode of care, you can begin holding providers accountable for the cost and quality of that whole episode — which is precisely where Medicare payment policy has been heading ever since.
The 1983 shift to DRG-based prospective payment proved a principle that still drives reform today: change how you pay, and you change how care is delivered.
Before 1983, Medicare paid hospitals retrospectively for their costs, rewarding volume and long stays with almost no financial risk to the hospital.
In 1983 Congress authorized the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS), paying a fixed amount per case set in advance by diagnosis.
The unit of payment is the Diagnosis-Related Group (DRG), developed at Yale by Fetter and Thompson; Medicare uses MS-DRGs that reflect severity.
For FY2025 there are 773 MS-DRGs, each with a relative weight reflecting average resource use.
Base IPPS payment = standardized base rate × DRG relative weight, adjusted by the area wage index, plus IME, DSH, and outlier add-ons.
IPPS shifted financial risk to hospitals, drove down length of stay, and made coding and documentation financially critical.
The prospective-payment model spread to other settings and laid the conceptual groundwork for bundled payments and value-based care.
IPPS pays prospectively: a standardized base rate (split into labor/non-labor shares and wage-index adjusted) is multiplied by the MS-DRG relative weight, with add-ons for teaching (IME), low-income share (DSH), and outliers. It deliberately does not pay based on the hospital’s actual costs, charges, or length of stay — that was the pre-1983 cost-based system it replaced.

######## medicare-fundamentals | physician-payment-fee-schedule | Physician Payment: The Medicare Fee Schedule and RBRVS
Physician Payment: The Medicare Fee Schedule and RBRVS
From "Usual and Customary" to a Resource-Based Scale
Just as hospitals were paid by cost before 1983, physicians were originally paid by their own charges — Medicare reimbursed "usual, customary, and reasonable" fees. The result was the same problem in a different form: payments tracked what doctors billed, not what services actually required, and rates varied wildly with no consistent logic.
The solution was the Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS), developed in the 1980s by Harvard researchers led by economist William Hsiao. The idea was to pay physicians based on the relative resources each service consumes, not on what any individual doctor chooses to charge.
Congress authorized the RBRVS-based Medicare Physician Fee Schedule in the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989, and it took effect on January 1, 1992. It remains the basis for how Medicare pays physicians — and, because private insurers benchmark to it, how much of American medicine is priced.
RBRVS pays for the resources a service requires — physician work, practice overhead, and malpractice cost — rather than whatever a physician chooses to charge. It is the physician-side analog to the hospital DRG system.
The Three Components of an RVU
Every service in the fee schedule — identified by a CPT/HCPCS code — is assigned Relative Value Units (RVUs) across three categories. Physician Work RVUs capture the physician’s time, skill, mental effort, and the intensity and stress of the service. These were implemented at the start in 1992.
Practice Expense RVUs capture the overhead of delivering the service: non-physician staff labor, medical equipment, supplies, and the cost of office space. These were phased in starting in 1999. Malpractice (Professional Liability) RVUs capture the cost of malpractice insurance attributable to the service and were added in 2000.
A service that demands great physician skill but little equipment — like complex medical decision-making — is weighted heavily toward work RVUs. A service performed with expensive equipment in an office — like imaging — carries large practice-expense RVUs. The three components together describe the full resource cost of each service.
What they measure
Work RVU: physician time, skill, effort, intensity
Practice Expense RVU: staff, equipment, supplies, space
Malpractice RVU: liability insurance cost
When added
Work RVUs implemented in 1992
Practice Expense RVUs phased in from 1999
Malpractice RVUs added in 2000
The Three RVU Components
How a Fee Is Calculated
The fee for a service is a formula. First, each of the three RVU components is adjusted for local cost differences using its Geographic Practice Cost Index (GPCI) — there is a separate GPCI for work, practice expense, and malpractice, so a service in Manhattan is priced differently than the same service in rural Iowa.
The geographically adjusted RVUs are summed and then multiplied by a single national Conversion Factor (CF), a dollar amount that translates RVUs into actual payment. For calendar year 2025, the conversion factor is $32.35 — a decrease of $0.94, or 2.83 percent, from the 2024 figure of $33.29.
So the full formula is: payment = [(Work RVU × Work GPCI) + (PE RVU × PE GPCI) + (MP RVU × MP GPCI)] × Conversion Factor. Change any RVU, GPCI, or the conversion factor, and physician payment changes accordingly.
Each CPT/HCPCS code has Work, Practice Expense, and Malpractice RVUs.
Identify the service
Multiply each RVU by its local GPCI (separate index for each component).
Apply geographic adjustment
Add the three geographically adjusted RVUs together.
Sum the adjusted RVUs
Multiply the total by the national CF ($32.35 in 2025) to get the dollar payment.

Who Sets the RVUs — and the Budget-Neutrality Trap
RVU values are not set in a vacuum. The AMA/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale Update Committee — known as the RUC — is a multispecialty committee that recommends RVU values to CMS for new and revised services. The RUC only advises; CMS makes all final decisions about Medicare payment.
A critical constraint shapes the whole system: budget neutrality. By law, changes to the fee schedule that would increase total spending beyond a threshold must be offset elsewhere, typically by adjusting the conversion factor downward. This means raising the value of one service effectively lowers payment for others — the system is largely a fixed pie being re-sliced.
Budget neutrality is a major reason physician payment has lagged inflation for years. When new high-value services are added or work RVUs rise, the conversion factor is cut to keep the total budget neutral, which is part of why the 2025 conversion factor fell rather than rose.
The AMA RUC is influential but advisory. CMS is not bound by its recommendations and makes the final call on every RVU and on the conversion factor. Budget neutrality means a payment increase for one specialty is often funded by cuts to others.
The RUC recommends; CMS decides
From the SGR to MACRA
For nearly two decades, fee-schedule updates were governed by the Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR), a formula meant to tie physician payment growth to the broader economy. When spending outpaced the target, the SGR called for steep automatic cuts — cuts so politically untenable that Congress passed temporary "doc fix" patches year after year to override them.
The Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 (MACRA) finally repealed the SGR, ending the annual doc-fix drama. In its place, MACRA set modest statutory update paths and tied a growing share of physician payment to quality and value through the Quality Payment Program — moving physician reimbursement, like hospital payment, toward value-based incentives.
Yet the fee schedule still rests on RBRVS at its core. Even value-based programs are layered on top of fee-for-service RVU payments, which is why understanding work RVUs, GPCIs, and the conversion factor remains essential to understanding how physicians actually get paid today.
Three decades after RBRVS replaced "usual and customary" charges, the relative value unit remains the atom of physician payment — even as value-based programs are built on top of it.
Before 1992, Medicare paid physicians based on their own "usual, customary, and reasonable" charges, producing wide and illogical variation.

######## medicare-fundamentals | post-acute-care-payment | Post-Acute Care Payment: SNF, Home Health, and PDPM
Post-Acute Care Payment: SNF, Home Health, and PDPM
The World Beyond the Hospital
When a Medicare patient leaves the hospital, their care often continues elsewhere — in a skilled nursing facility for rehabilitation, at home with a visiting nurse and therapist, or in an inpatient rehabilitation facility for intensive therapy. This is post-acute care (PAC), and it is one of the most consequential and most scrutinized areas of Medicare spending.
Each post-acute setting has its own prospective payment system, all descended from the same 1983 IPPS logic: pay a predetermined amount per episode or period rather than per service. But because so much of post-acute care is therapy-driven, these systems faced a recurring problem — the old rules paid more when providers delivered more therapy, regardless of whether the patient needed it.
That perverse incentive is the thread running through every recent post-acute reform. In setting after setting, CMS has rebuilt payment to reward clinical characteristics and patient needs instead of raw therapy volume. This lesson walks through the three main settings and the reforms that reshaped them.
Post-acute care is the care that follows a hospital stay: skilled nursing facilities (SNF), home health, and inpatient rehabilitation facilities (IRF). The defining payment story is the shift from rewarding therapy volume to rewarding patient need.
Skilled Nursing Facilities: From RUG-IV to PDPM
Skilled nursing facilities are paid a per-diem (daily) rate under the SNF Prospective Payment System. For two decades that rate was set by the Resource Utilization Groups system — most recently version IV (RUG-IV, from 2010) — which based payment primarily on the volume of therapy minutes a patient received — more therapy meant more money, largely independent of the patient’s actual clinical needs.
This created an obvious incentive to over-deliver therapy. On October 1, 2019, CMS replaced RUG-IV with the Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM). PDPM ties payment to clinically relevant patient characteristics — using ICD-10 diagnoses to sort residents into one of ten clinical categories — rather than to the sheer quantity of therapy provided.
PDPM sets the per-diem from six payment components, five of which are case-mix adjusted based on patient characteristics (such as physical therapy, occupational therapy, speech-language pathology, nursing, and non-therapy ancillaries), plus a non-case-mix component. By breaking payment into need-based components, PDPM aimed to pay more accurately and reduce the administrative burden of constant therapy-minute tracking.
RUG-IV (pre-Oct 2019)
Payment driven mainly by therapy minutes
More therapy delivered = higher payment
Incentive to over-provide therapy
Heavy therapy-minute documentation burden
PDPM (Oct 1, 2019+)
Payment driven by clinical characteristics
ICD-10 diagnosis sorts patients into clinical categories
Six components, five case-mix adjusted

SNF Payment: RUG-IV vs. PDPM
Home Health: From 60-Day Episodes to PDGM
Home health agencies were historically paid for 60-day episodes of care, with payment heavily influenced by therapy thresholds — the more therapy visits delivered, the higher the payment tier. As with SNFs, this rewarded volume over need.
The Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 mandated reform, and on January 1, 2020, CMS implemented the Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM). PDGM made two major changes: it cut the unit of payment from a 60-day episode to a 30-day period, and it eliminated therapy thresholds entirely, shifting payment toward clinical characteristics drawn from the OASIS assessment and claims data.
PDGM classifies each 30-day period into one of 432 case-mix groups (home health resource groups). It also refined the Low-Utilization Payment Adjustment (LUPA): instead of a single visit threshold, each of the 432 groups has its own threshold below which the period is paid per-visit rather than as a full case. The goal, once again, was to remove the incentive to over-provide therapy.
Payment unit shrank from a 60-day episode to a 30-day period of care.
Define a 30-day period
Use the OASIS assessment and claims to capture patient characteristics, not therapy counts.
Collect clinical data

Inpatient Rehabilitation Facilities and the 60% Rule
Inpatient rehabilitation facilities (IRFs) provide intensive, hospital-level rehabilitation — for example, after a stroke, spinal-cord injury, or major joint replacement. IRFs are paid under their own prospective payment system that classifies patients into Case-Mix Groups (CMGs) using the IRF Patient Assessment Instrument (IRF-PAI), with each CMG carrying a relative weight reflecting expected resource use.
A distinctive feature governs which facilities even qualify as IRFs: the "60 percent rule." To be paid under the IRF PPS rather than as a regular acute-care hospital, at least 60 percent of an IRF’s patients must require intensive rehabilitation for one or more of 13 specified conditions listed in federal regulation.
The 60 percent rule exists to keep the IRF benefit targeted at patients who genuinely need intensive inpatient rehabilitation, distinguishing true rehab hospitals from facilities that might otherwise reclassify to capture higher payment. Facilities that fail the threshold are paid under the standard inpatient hospital system instead.
SNF, home health, and IRF each have different payment systems, intensity levels, and eligibility rules. Where a patient goes after the hospital can dramatically change Medicare’s cost and the patient’s out-of-pocket exposure — which is why discharge planning is a major focus of value-based programs.
Post-acute settings are not interchangeable
Why Post-Acute Payment Is a Battleground
Post-acute care is one of the largest sources of variation in Medicare spending. Two patients with the same hospital diagnosis can generate vastly different total costs depending on whether they go home, to a SNF, or to an IRF — and historically much of that variation reflected payment incentives more than clinical need.
That is exactly why PDPM and PDGM both deliberately decoupled payment from therapy volume. By paying for patient characteristics instead, CMS aimed to neutralize the incentive to deliver unnecessary therapy and to make spending track actual need.
Post-acute care is also central to bundled payments and accountable care. When a provider is held accountable for the total cost of an episode — say, a joint replacement and the 90 days after — post-acute spending becomes the biggest lever they can pull. Understanding how SNF, home health, and IRF payment works is therefore essential to understanding value-based care, the focus of later lessons.
In post-acute care, the question driving every recent reform is the same: are we paying for how much therapy was delivered, or for what the patient actually needed?
Post-acute care — SNF, home health, and IRF — is the care that follows a hospital stay and a major, highly scrutinized area of Medicare spending.
Each post-acute setting has its own prospective payment system descended from the 1983 IPPS logic of paying per episode rather than per service.
On October 1, 2019, the SNF Patient-Driven Payment Model (PDPM) replaced RUG-IV, basing per-diem payment on clinical characteristics instead of therapy minutes.
PDPM uses six payment components (five case-mix adjusted) and ICD-10 diagnoses to sort residents into ten clinical categories.
On January 1, 2020, the home health Patient-Driven Groupings Model (PDGM) cut the payment period from 60 to 30 days and eliminated therapy thresholds, using 432 case-mix groups.
IRFs are paid via Case-Mix Groups from the IRF-PAI and must satisfy the "60 percent rule" — at least 60% of patients needing intensive rehab for one of 13 conditions.
The unifying theme of PDPM and PDGM is paying for patient need rather than therapy volume, which is also central to bundled payments and value-based care.
Both PDPM and PDGM were designed to remove the old incentive to over-provide therapy. They shifted payment toward clinically relevant patient characteristics (diagnoses, functional status, OASIS data) and away from raw therapy minutes/thresholds — they did not increase therapy-based pay, return to cost-based reimbursement, or merge the two systems.

######## medicare-fundamentals | medicare-advantage-overview | Medicare Advantage: Structure and Growth
Medicare Advantage: Structure and Growth
The Private Option Inside Medicare
Medicare Advantage (Part C) lets beneficiaries receive their Medicare benefits through a private health plan instead of directly from the government. An MA plan must cover everything Original Medicare Parts A and B cover, and the great majority also bundle in Part D drug coverage. In exchange for taking on this role, the plan receives a fixed monthly payment from CMS for each enrollee.
The trade-off for beneficiaries is real. In return for using a plan’s provider network and following its rules — including prior authorization for many services — enrollees often get extra benefits Original Medicare lacks, like dental, vision, hearing, and an annual out-of-pocket maximum that traditional Medicare does not have.
Medicare Advantage grew from the Balanced Budget Act of 1997 (originally "Medicare+Choice") and was renamed and expanded by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003. Over the following two decades it went from a niche option to the way most beneficiaries now get their Medicare.
Medicare Advantage plans are paid a risk-adjusted, capitated (per-member-per-month) amount by CMS to cover all Part A and B benefits — a fundamentally different payment model from the fee-for-service of Original Medicare.
From Niche to Majority
The headline fact about Medicare Advantage is its explosive growth. In 2024, more than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries — about 32.8 million people, or 54 percent — were enrolled in MA plans, up from 25 percent in 2010.
This shift has profound consequences. As MA crosses the majority threshold, a growing share of all Medicare dollars flows through private insurers rather than directly to providers, and the largest insurers (such as UnitedHealthcare and Humana) have become dominant players in Medicare. Provider networks, prior authorization, and plan marketing now shape the experience of most beneficiaries.
Growth has been fueled by generous extra benefits, heavy marketing, and a payment structure that — as later sections explain — has tended to pay plans well. For the health system, MA is no longer an alternative to Medicare; for most beneficiaries, it is Medicare.

How Medicare Pays MA Plans: Benchmarks, Bids, and Rebates
Medicare pays MA plans through a benchmark-and-bid system. The benchmark is the maximum CMS will pay for an enrollee in a given county, set as a percentage of estimated traditional-Medicare spending in that county — ranging from 95 percent in high-cost counties to 115 percent in low-cost counties. Each plan then submits a bid: its estimated cost to provide Part A and B benefits.
If a plan bids below its benchmark — which nearly all plans do — it receives a rebate equal to a share of the difference between the benchmark and its bid. That share depends on the plan’s star rating: 70 percent for plans with at least 4.5 stars, 65 percent for 3.5–4 stars, and 50 percent for lower-rated plans. Plans must return rebates to enrollees as lower premiums, reduced cost-sharing, or supplemental benefits.
This is why MA plans can offer "$0 premium" coverage with dental and vision: the rebate funds those extras. It also ties plan revenue directly to quality ratings, since higher stars mean both a larger rebate share and quality-bonus increases to the benchmark itself.
A county-specific cap, 95%–115% of local traditional-Medicare spending.

How an MA Plan Gets Paid
Risk Adjustment and Star Ratings
Capitated payment creates an obvious risk: a plan could profit by enrolling only healthy people. Medicare counters this with risk adjustment. The CMS-HCC (Hierarchical Condition Categories) model raises a plan’s per-enrollee payment for sicker members based on their documented diagnoses, so plans are paid more to care for higher-need patients.
Quality is governed by the Star Ratings system, which rates plans from 1 to 5 stars on dozens of measures spanning clinical quality, patient experience, and customer service. Stars do double duty: they determine quality-bonus payments and they set the rebate share a plan keeps. In 2025, about 75 percent of MA enrollees were in plans receiving bonus payments, at an estimated federal cost of at least $12.7 billion.
Together, risk adjustment and star ratings are the levers that make capitation workable — paying more for sicker patients and rewarding measured quality — but, as the next section shows, they are also where the program’s biggest controversies live.
In 2025, federal spending on Medicare Advantage quality-bonus payments totaled at least $12.7 billion, with roughly 75% of MA enrollees in plans that earned bonuses. Bonuses raise a plan’s benchmark (most by 5 percentage points, and "double bonus" counties by 10), which is why plans invest heavily in their star ratings — even small movements across a star threshold can mean large revenue swings.
The $12.7 Billion Quality Bonus
The Overpayment Controversy
For all its popularity, Medicare Advantage faces a serious and well-documented critique: it costs taxpayers more than traditional Medicare would for similar enrollees. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC) estimated that Medicare spends about 22 percent more for MA enrollees than it would if they were in fee-for-service — roughly $83 billion in 2024 alone.
MedPAC attributes this to two forces. "Coding intensity" — plans documenting more diagnoses to raise risk scores — made MA risk scores about 20 percent higher than for comparable traditional-Medicare beneficiaries — about 13 percent even after CMS’s mandatory 5.9 percent coding adjustment, worth roughly $50 billion in 2024. "Favorable selection" — MA tending to enroll healthier-than-average beneficiaries relative to their risk scores — accounts for most of the remainder.
These findings drive ongoing policy fights over how to reform risk adjustment, audit coding, and recalibrate benchmarks. They are essential context: Medicare Advantage delivers real benefits to enrollees, but its payment design has produced systematic overpayments that strain the very trust funds discussed earlier in this course.
Medicare Advantage often gives enrollees richer benefits and an out-of-pocket cap — but MedPAC estimates it cost taxpayers about $83 billion more than traditional Medicare in 2024, mostly from coding intensity and favorable selection. Both can be true at once.
Popular with enrollees, costly to taxpayers
Medicare Advantage (Part C) delivers Medicare benefits through private plans paid a risk-adjusted, capitated amount by CMS.
MA plans must cover everything Parts A and B cover, usually include Part D, and are required to have an annual out-of-pocket maximum that Original Medicare lacks.
In 2024 about 54% of beneficiaries (~32.8 million) were enrolled in MA, making it how most people now get their Medicare.

Rebates must fund lower premiums, reduced cost-sharing, or supplemental benefits — which is how "$0 premium" plans with dental/vision are financed.
The CMS-HCC model risk-adjusts payment for sicker enrollees, and Star Ratings drive both quality bonuses (~$12.7B in 2025) and the rebate share.
MedPAC estimates Medicare spends ~22% more on MA enrollees than traditional Medicare would (~$83B in 2024), driven mainly by coding intensity (~$50B) and favorable selection.
Nearly all MA plans bid below their county benchmark. The rebate — a star-rating-dependent share of the difference between benchmark and bid — must by law be returned to enrollees as lower premiums, reduced cost-sharing, or supplemental benefits, which is how plans fund $0-premium offerings with dental and vision. MA plans must still cover all Part A and B benefits.

######## medicare-fundamentals | medicare-advantage-market-dynamics | MA Market Dynamics: Special Needs Plans and D-SNPs
MA Market Dynamics: Special Needs Plans and D-SNPs
Special Needs Plans: Targeting the Highest-Need Beneficiaries
Not every Medicare Advantage plan is open to everyone. Special Needs Plans (SNPs) are a category of MA plan restricted to beneficiaries with specific characteristics, designed to tailor benefits, provider networks, and care management to populations with concentrated needs. They are one of the fastest-growing parts of the entire Medicare program.
There are three types. Chronic Condition SNPs (C-SNPs) serve people with specific severe or disabling chronic conditions, such as diabetes or heart failure. Institutional SNPs (I-SNPs) serve people who live in institutions like skilled nursing facilities (or who need that level of care). Dual Eligible SNPs (D-SNPs) serve people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid.
SNPs have grown dramatically. They now account for about 21 percent of all Medicare Advantage enrollees, up from just 13 percent in 2018, and between 2024 and 2025 they made up nearly half of the total growth in MA enrollment. SNPs are no longer a niche — they are a major engine of MA expansion.
There are three SNP types: C-SNP (chronic conditions), I-SNP (institutional), and D-SNP (dual eligible). All are Medicare Advantage plans, but enrollment is limited to beneficiaries who meet the plan’s specific eligibility criteria.
Who they serve
C-SNP: people with specific chronic/disabling conditions
I-SNP: people in (or needing) institutional-level care
D-SNP: people eligible for both Medicare and Medicaid
Why they exist
Tailor benefits and care management to high-need groups
Concentrate clinical expertise for complex patients
Coordinate the notoriously fragmented dual-eligible experience
The Three Types of Special Needs Plans
Dual Eligibles and the Rise of D-SNPs
Dual eligibles — people enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid — are among the most complex and expensive beneficiaries in the entire health system. They tend to be poorer, sicker, and more likely to need long-term services and supports, and historically they have had to navigate two completely separate programs with separate rules, cards, and benefits.
D-SNPs are designed to bring those two programs together. They are by far the largest SNP category: over 80 percent of all SNP enrollees are in D-SNPs, and D-SNP enrollment grew from about 2.2 million in 2018 to roughly 5.8 million in 2024. As more duals enroll, D-SNPs increasingly define how this high-need population experiences coverage.
The core challenge is integration. A D-SNP can be loosely or tightly coordinated with the enrollee’s Medicaid coverage, and CMS classifies the more integrated forms as Highly Integrated Dual Eligible (HIDE) SNPs and Fully Integrated Dual Eligible (FIDE) SNPs. FIDE SNPs go furthest — covering nearly all Medicaid services, including long-term services and supports, under one coordinated umbrella.

The 2025 Push Toward Integration
CMS has made integrating Medicare and Medicaid for dual eligibles a top priority, and a set of rules taking effect in 2025 sharply accelerates that push. The central change is a new integrated-care Special Enrollment Period (SEP): starting January 1, 2025, full-benefit dual eligibles can switch into an integrated D-SNP (FIDE, HIDE, or an applicable integrated plan) once per month to align their Medicare and Medicaid coverage.
At the same time, FIDE SNPs are now required to operate with "exclusively aligned enrollment," meaning their members must also be in the affiliated Medicaid managed care plan — so the two halves of coverage finally move together. Additional requirements phase in over the following years to further consolidate and align dual coverage.
The goal is to end the fragmentation that has long plagued dual eligibles: a single, coordinated plan responsible for both Medicare and Medicaid benefits, with unified care management and appeals. For the dual-eligible population, these rules represent one of the most significant structural changes in years.

Toward unified coverage
The 2025 Integration Changes (Dual Eligibles)
A Fully Integrated Dual Eligible (FIDE) SNP is the most tightly integrated D-SNP. It must provide nearly all Medicaid services — including long-term services and supports (LTSS), Medicaid behavioral health, home health, and durable medical equipment — under one plan with exclusively aligned enrollment. For a dual eligible needing nursing-home-level care, that means a single entity coordinating both their Medicare medical care and their Medicaid long-term care, rather than two disconnected programs.
FIDE SNPs and Long-Term Services
A Concentrated Market
As Medicare Advantage has grown, it has also consolidated. A handful of large insurers now dominate. In 2024, UnitedHealthcare and Humana together accounted for nearly half — about 47 percent — of all Medicare Advantage enrollment nationwide.
At the local level the concentration is even starker. As of 2024, about 90 percent of eligible Medicare beneficiaries lived in a county where at least half of MA enrollees were in plans sponsored by just one or two insurers, and 79 percent of counties were classified as highly concentrated MA markets. Rural counties were the most concentrated of all: 39 percent of the most rural counties were very highly concentrated, versus 6 percent of urban counties.
This concentration matters for policy. Limited competition can mean less pressure on plans to improve benefits or restrain costs, and it gives a few firms enormous influence over how most Medicare beneficiaries receive care. Market structure, not just payment formulas, shapes what Medicare Advantage actually delivers.
Beneficiaries often see dozens of MA plan options, but most of those plans are offered by the same few insurers. With UnitedHealthcare and Humana alone holding ~47% of national enrollment and most counties dominated by one or two firms, the MA "marketplace" is far less competitive than the plan count suggests.
Choice on paper, concentration in practice
Why MA Market Dynamics Matter
The growth of SNPs and the consolidation of the MA market are reshaping who controls high-need care. D-SNPs in particular are becoming the dominant vehicle for the dual-eligible population — the very people whose care is most expensive and most fragmented — putting private plans at the center of one of health policy’s hardest problems.
These dynamics also intersect with the overpayment concerns from the previous lesson. SNPs enroll sicker patients with higher risk scores, and concentrated markets reduce competitive pressure, both of which influence how much Medicare ultimately pays and what beneficiaries receive in return.
For anyone working in Medicare, the lesson is that Medicare Advantage is not a single uniform product. It is a fast-evolving market of specialized plans and dominant insurers, and the 2025 integration rules show that policymakers are actively trying to steer that market toward better-coordinated care for the people who need it most.
Medicare Advantage is no longer one product but a consolidating market of specialized plans — and D-SNPs are quietly becoming the front door to care for America’s sickest, poorest beneficiaries.

######## medicare-fundamentals | hospital-vbp-hrrp-hacrp | Hospital Value-Based Programs: VBP, HRRP, and HACRP
Hospital Value-Based Programs: VBP, HRRP, and HACRP
Adding Quality to the Payment Equation
The Inpatient Prospective Payment System pays hospitals a fixed amount per case — which rewards efficiency but says nothing about whether the care was good. A hospital could discharge a patient quickly and cheaply, only to have them bounce back a week later with a complication, and IPPS alone would simply pay for both stays.
The Affordable Care Act of 2010 set out to fix that gap by tying a slice of Medicare hospital payment to quality and outcomes, not just volume. It created three mandatory pay-for-performance programs that now sit on top of IPPS: the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing Program (VBP), the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), and the Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program (HACRP), which started two years later.
Together these three programs adjust a meaningful portion of a hospital’s Medicare revenue based on how well it performs on safety, outcomes, patient experience, and cost. They are the hospital-level expression of Medicare’s broader shift from paying for volume to paying for value.
VBP, HRRP, and HACRP are three distinct ACA-era programs that adjust hospital IPPS payments based on quality. A hospital can be affected by all three at once, with the adjustments stacking on top of its base DRG payments.
Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP)
The Hospital VBP Program rewards or penalizes hospitals based on their performance across four evenly weighted domains: Clinical Outcomes, Safety, Person and Community Engagement (patient experience), and Efficiency and Cost Reduction. A hospital’s scores combine into a Total Performance Score.
VBP has a defining feature: it is budget-neutral. CMS withholds 2 percent of each participating hospital’s base operating DRG payments and redistributes the entire pool back to hospitals as value-based incentive payments. High performers can earn back more than they contributed; low performers get back less. No money leaves the system — it is redistributed from worse to better performers.
The Clinical Outcomes domain illustrates what VBP measures: mortality after acute myocardial infarction (AMI), heart failure, pneumonia, COPD, and coronary artery bypass graft (CABG), plus complications from elective hip and knee replacement. VBP is the broadest of the three programs because it can move payment in either direction.
Of base operating DRG payments (CMS)
VBP Withhold
Outcomes, Safety, Experience, Efficiency (evenly weighted)
VBP Domains

VBP Design
Budget-neutral
Affordable Care Act value-based programs

2010
Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP)
The HRRP, also created by the ACA and launched in October 2012, targets a specific waste-and-quality problem: patients who are discharged and then readmitted within 30 days, often because of poor discharge planning or inadequate follow-up. It penalizes hospitals with worse-than-expected, risk-adjusted readmission rates.
Unlike VBP, HRRP is a one-way penalty: there is no upside. Hospitals with excess readmissions lose up to 3 percent of their inpatient Medicare payments. The program focuses on six conditions and procedures: heart attack (AMI), heart failure, pneumonia, COPD, CABG, and elective hip/knee replacement.
HRRP is credited with helping drive down national readmission rates, but it is also one of the most debated programs in Medicare. Critics argue it disproportionately penalizes safety-net hospitals that serve sicker, poorer patients, prompting CMS to later stratify hospitals into peer groups by their share of dual-eligible patients to make comparisons fairer.
A hospital that discharges a heart-failure patient without arranging medications, follow-up appointments, and home monitoring may see that patient return within days. HRRP makes such readmissions financially painful — up to a 3% cut on all inpatient Medicare payments — which is why hospitals invested heavily in discharge planning, transitional care, and post-discharge follow-up after 2012.
Why the 30-Day Window Matters
Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program (HACRP)
The HACRP, which began in October 2014, targets harms that happen inside the hospital — conditions patients acquire during their stay that should largely be preventable. It is the bluntest of the three programs: every year, the hospitals scoring in the worst-performing quartile (the bottom 25 percent) lose 1 percent of all their Medicare fee-for-service payments.
HACRP scoring rests on six measures: the CMS Patient Safety and Adverse Events Composite (PSI 90), plus five healthcare-associated infection measures — central line-associated bloodstream infections (CLABSI), catheter-associated urinary tract infections (CAUTI), surgical site infections (SSI) for colon surgery and hysterectomy, MRSA bacteremia, and Clostridioides difficile infection (CDI).
Because HACRP penalizes a fixed bottom quartile every year regardless of absolute improvement, even hospitals that get safer can still be penalized if others improve faster — a design feature that has drawn criticism, particularly for its disproportionate impact on safety-net and teaching hospitals.
Because HACRP penalizes the worst-performing 25% of hospitals each year by definition, a hospital can reduce its infection rates and still be penalized if it remains in the bottom quartile. It is a relative-ranking penalty, not an absolute-threshold one.

The Three Hospital Quality Programs at a Glance
How the Programs Fit Together
These three programs operate simultaneously and independently. A single hospital can earn a VBP bonus, take an HRRP readmissions penalty, and avoid (or incur) a HACRP penalty all in the same year — the adjustments stack on top of its base IPPS payments, sometimes pulling in different directions.
Collectively they pushed hospitals to invest in things IPPS alone never rewarded: infection prevention, discharge planning, care transitions, patient experience, and mortality reduction. They demonstrated that even modest payment adjustments — a few percent of Medicare revenue — can reshape hospital priorities.
They also exposed the hard problems of pay-for-performance: how to risk-adjust fairly, how to avoid punishing hospitals that serve disadvantaged patients, and how to measure quality without creating perverse incentives. Those lessons feed directly into the next stage of reform — accountable care organizations and bundled payments — covered in the lessons ahead.
VBP, HRRP, and HACRP proved that Medicare could put a hospital’s money where its quality was — and revealed just how hard it is to measure quality fairly.
The ACA created three mandatory hospital pay-for-performance programs layered on top of IPPS to tie payment to quality, not just volume.

######## medicare-fundamentals | mssp-aco-overview | Medicare Shared Savings Program and ACOs
Medicare Shared Savings Program and ACOs
Accountability for the Whole Patient
Every payment system covered so far pays for a piece of care — a hospital stay, a physician visit, a post-acute episode. The Accountable Care Organization (ACO) model takes a different angle entirely: it holds a group of providers accountable for the total cost and quality of care for a defined population of patients, no matter where that care happens.
An ACO is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other providers who voluntarily join together to coordinate care for a population of Medicare beneficiaries. If they keep total spending below a target while meeting quality standards, they share in the savings. The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) is Medicare’s largest and permanent ACO program, created by the Affordable Care Act of 2010.
Crucially, MSSP is built on top of traditional fee-for-service, not instead of it. Providers in an ACO keep billing and getting paid the normal Part A and B way. The shared-savings (or shared-loss) settlement happens afterward, based on how total spending for their attributed patients compared to a benchmark.
An ACO is held accountable for the total cost and quality of care for a population of patients. Under MSSP, providers keep receiving normal fee-for-service payments, then settle up against a spending benchmark at year-end — sharing savings if they beat it, and (in two-sided models) losses if they exceed it.
How the Shared Savings Program Works
MSSP works through three core mechanics: attribution, benchmarking, and settlement. First, Medicare beneficiaries are attributed (assigned) to an ACO based on where they get most of their primary care. An ACO must have at least 5,000 attributed fee-for-service beneficiaries to participate.
Second, CMS sets a spending benchmark — an expected total cost of care for those attributed patients, based on history and regional spending. Third, at the end of the performance year, CMS compares actual spending to the benchmark. If the ACO spent less and met quality standards, it shares in the savings; if it spent more, it may owe a share of the losses, depending on its track.
Quality is a gate, not an afterthought. An ACO that generates savings but fails to meet CMS quality standards does not get to keep the money. This pairing — savings only if quality holds — is what distinguishes shared savings from simple cost-cutting.
Patients are assigned to the ACO based on their primary care; minimum 5,000 required.
Attribute beneficiaries
CMS establishes an expected total cost of care using historical and regional data.
Set the benchmark
Providers keep billing FFS while managing the population’s overall cost and quality.
Deliver coordinated care
The ACO must meet CMS quality standards to qualify for savings.
Measure quality
Spend below it and pass quality = share savings; spend above it = potential shared losses.
Settle against the benchmark
The MSSP Cycle
One-Sided vs. Two-Sided Risk
The single most important variable in an ACO arrangement is how much financial risk it bears. In one-sided (upside-only) models, the ACO shares in savings if it beats the benchmark but owes nothing if it overspends — a gentle on-ramp that protects new ACOs from losses while they build capabilities.
In two-sided (downside) risk models, the ACO shares in savings but also must repay a share of losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. In exchange for that risk, two-sided ACOs keep a larger share of any savings they generate. MSSP organizes these options into the BASIC track (which glides from upside-only Level A up to risk-bearing Level E) and the ENHANCED track (the highest level of risk and reward).
CMS has steadily pushed ACOs toward downside risk because that is where the savings are. In 2024, roughly two-thirds of ACOs were in the higher-risk Level E or ENHANCED arrangements, and those risk-bearing ACOs generated the large majority of the program’s total savings. Skin in the game changes behavior.
One-Sided (Upside Only)
Share in savings if you beat the benchmark
Owe nothing if you overspend
Lower savings share kept
On-ramp for newer ACOs (e.g., BASIC Levels A-D)
Two-Sided (Downside) Risk
Share in savings AND repay a share of losses
Real financial accountability for overspending
Higher savings share kept
Where most program savings come from (Level E / ENHANCED)
One-Sided vs. Two-Sided Risk
Does It Work? The Evidence
After a slow start, MSSP has become the largest accountable-care program in the country and is now producing record results. For performance year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated nearly $2.5 billion in net savings to Medicare — the highest in the program’s history — while nearly every ACO met CMS quality standards.
Participation keeps growing. For 2025, 476 ACOs participated, and the program serves millions of traditional-Medicare beneficiaries through hundreds of thousands of providers. The data consistently show that two-sided, risk-bearing ACOs deliver most of the savings, which is why the program’s design keeps nudging organizations toward downside risk.
Alongside the permanent MSSP, the CMS Innovation Center runs ACO models that test more aggressive designs — most notably ACO REACH, which uses full or partial capitation and a strong health-equity focus, serving millions of beneficiaries through participating ACOs. MSSP is the durable backbone; the Innovation Center models are the laboratory.

Why ACOs Matter
ACOs represent a fundamentally different theory of payment reform than the per-case programs that came before. Instead of fine-tuning the price of each service, they make providers accountable for the whole — the total spending and quality of a population — and let the providers figure out how to deliver better care for less.
This shifts incentives toward exactly the activities fee-for-service neglects: care coordination, prevention, managing chronic disease, reducing avoidable hospitalizations, and steering patients to high-value post-acute care. An ACO profits by keeping people healthy and out of the hospital, not by doing more to them.
For Medicare, ACOs are central to the long-term strategy of moving traditional fee-for-service toward value. CMS has set goals to have all traditional-Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship — making the ACO model not a side experiment but the intended future of the program.
The ACO flips the core question of payment: not "how do we price each service?" but "who is accountable for the whole patient?"
An Accountable Care Organization (ACO) is a voluntary group of providers held accountable for the total cost and quality of care for a population of patients.
The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), created by the ACA in 2010, is Medicare’s largest, permanent ACO program.
MSSP runs on attribution (minimum 5,000 beneficiaries), a spending benchmark, and a year-end settlement — built on top of normal fee-for-service payments.
Quality is a gate: an ACO must meet CMS quality standards to keep any shared savings.

In exchange for taking that risk, two-sided ACOs keep a larger share of any savings. One-sided ACOs, by contrast, have upside only and owe nothing for overspending.

######## medicare-fundamentals | bundled-payments-and-innovation | Bundled Payments and CMS Innovation Center Models
Bundled Payments and CMS Innovation Center Models
Paying for an Episode, Not a Service
A bundled payment sits conceptually between fee-for-service and the population accountability of an ACO. Instead of paying separately for the surgeon, the hospital stay, the rehab facility, and every follow-up visit, a bundle holds providers accountable for the total cost of a defined clinical episode — for example, a hip replacement and everything that happens in the 90 days after it.
The mechanics are usually retrospective. Providers keep billing fee-for-service throughout the episode, then at the end Medicare reconciles total spending against a predetermined target price. If actual spending came in under the target and quality held, the providers keep the difference; if it ran over, they may owe Medicare back.
Bundling targets a specific weakness of fee-for-service: fragmentation. When no one is accountable for the whole episode, costs leak — especially into post-acute care, where discharge decisions vary enormously. A bundle gives providers a direct financial reason to coordinate the entire arc of care.
A bundled payment sets a single target price for a whole episode of care (often 90 days). Spending is reconciled against that target: beat it with good quality and keep the savings; exceed it and potentially repay. The episode — not the individual service — becomes the unit of accountability.
The CMS Innovation Center (CMMI)
Most of Medicare’s bundled-payment and value-based experiments come from one place: the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), known as the CMS Innovation Center. It was created by Section 3021 of the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a specific mission — to test new payment and delivery models that could reduce spending while preserving or improving quality.
CMMI has a powerful and unusual authority: if a model is certified by the actuary to lower spending without harming quality (or improve quality without raising spending), the Secretary of HHS can expand it nationally without an act of Congress. That ability to scale successful models is what makes CMMI Medicare’s primary engine of payment innovation.
CMMI is also why models can be made mandatory in selected regions. Voluntary models suffer from selection bias — only providers who expect to benefit join — so CMMI sometimes requires all hospitals in chosen markets to participate, producing cleaner evidence about whether a model actually works.
Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced), launched in 2018, let participants take accountability for 90-day episodes across a menu of medical and surgical conditions, with target prices based partly on their own historical spending. It was the first episode model to include an outpatient surgical condition (spine surgery). Like other episode models, it billed fee-for-service throughout and reconciled spending against the target price at the end of each episode.
BPCI Advanced
CJR: Testing Mandatory Bundles
The clearest test of bundled payment was the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model, which ran from April 2016 through December 2024. CJR was mandatory for hospitals in selected metropolitan areas and covered hip and knee replacements — high-volume, high-cost procedures with notoriously variable post-acute spending.
The results validated the core theory. A rigorous evaluation found CJR reduced institutional spending per joint-replacement episode by roughly $812 (about a 3 percent relative decrease), driven largely by a meaningful drop in patients being discharged to costly post-acute facilities instead of home. Critically, CMS found no adverse effects on quality — complication rates, mortality, readmissions, and ED use did not worsen.
CJR demonstrated that a well-designed bundle could squeeze out wasteful post-acute spending without harming patients. Its success directly shaped the next generation of mandatory models, proving that the lever to pull in episode payment is usually post-acute care.

From CJR to TEAM
The lessons from CJR fed directly into its successor: the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), a mandatory episode-based payment model launching in January 2026. TEAM expands the bundled-payment approach beyond joint replacement to five surgical episode categories and adds enhanced protections for safety-net hospitals.
TEAM reflects how Medicare’s thinking has matured. It is mandatory (for cleaner evidence and broader impact), it spans multiple procedures (not just one), and it explicitly builds in equity safeguards to avoid penalizing hospitals that serve disadvantaged patients — addressing a recurring critique of earlier value programs.
TEAM also illustrates the cumulative nature of payment reform: each model learns from the last. CJR proved bundles work for joint replacement; TEAM extends that proof across more surgeries while patching the equity gaps the earlier models exposed.
Voluntary models attract providers who expect to win, biasing results. Mandatory models like CJR and TEAM require everyone in selected markets to participate, which gives CMS cleaner evidence about whether a payment model truly works — but also generates strong provider pushback.
Mandatory models produce better evidence
CMMI’s Mixed Track Record
For all its importance, CMMI’s overall record is sobering and politically contested. In roughly 14 years it has launched more than 50 models, but a 2023 Congressional Budget Office analysis found that only six of the 49 models it examined produced statistically significant savings, and that over 2011–2020 CMMI increased federal direct spending by about $5.4 billion — roughly 0.1 percent of net Medicare spending — once its operating costs were counted.
Very few models have cleared the high bar required for national expansion. To date, only the Diabetes Prevention Program and the Pioneer ACO model met the statutory criteria, and even the Pioneer ACO model was never fully folded into permanent Medicare. Many promising-looking models simply did not save money once rigorously evaluated.
This record is essential context, not a footnote. It shows that paying for value is genuinely hard — good ideas frequently fail to deliver net savings — and it fuels ongoing debate about how CMMI should be reformed. But the standouts, like CJR’s bundled-payment success, are exactly why Medicare keeps testing, refining, and occasionally scaling new models.
CMMI’s history is a humbling lesson: most payment experiments do not save money — but the few that do, like mandatory bundles, point the way for the rest of the system.

######## medicare-fundamentals | part-d-structure-formulary | Part D: Structure, Formularies, and the IRA Drug Reforms
Part D: Structure, Formularies, and the IRA Drug Reforms
The Newest Pillar of Medicare
For its first four decades, Medicare had a glaring gap: it generally did not cover outpatient prescription drugs. A senior could have a heart attack covered under Part A, but the medications to prevent the next one were largely on their own dime. Part D, created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 and effective January 1, 2006, finally closed that gap.
Part D is unusual in its structure. Rather than the government providing the benefit directly, it is delivered entirely by private plans — either standalone Prescription Drug Plans (PDPs) that attach to Original Medicare, or drug coverage built into Medicare Advantage plans (MA-PDs). Beneficiaries pay premiums, and the federal government heavily subsidizes the cost.
Enrollment is voluntary, but there is a catch: beneficiaries who go without creditable drug coverage and sign up late face a permanent late-enrollment penalty added to their premium. This nudge is designed to keep healthy beneficiaries in the risk pool rather than waiting until they get sick.
Part D is the Medicare outpatient prescription drug benefit, created by the Medicare Modernization Act of 2003 (effective 2006). It is delivered entirely through private plans — standalone PDPs or Medicare Advantage drug plans — and subsidized by the federal government.
Formularies and Tiers
Every Part D plan has a formulary — its list of covered drugs. Plans are not required to cover every drug, but they must cover a wide range across therapeutic categories and include certain protected classes. Two plans can cover very different drugs at very different prices, which is why drug coverage, not just premium, should drive plan choice.
Within a formulary, drugs are sorted into tiers. Lower tiers (preferred generics, generics) carry low copays; higher tiers (preferred brand, non-preferred, and specialty) carry higher copays or coinsurance. Plans use tiering to steer patients toward lower-cost drugs and to negotiate with manufacturers.
Plans also use utilization management tools: prior authorization (requiring approval before a drug is covered), step therapy (try a cheaper drug first), and quantity limits. These tools control costs but can create access barriers, making formulary design one of the most consequential — and contested — features of any Part D plan.

Choosing a Part D Plan: What Matters
The Benefit Structure — and the End of the Donut Hole
The standard Part D benefit has long moved through phases. A beneficiary first pays a deductible (up to $590 in 2025), then enters an initial coverage phase sharing costs with the plan. Historically, beneficiaries then hit the infamous "donut hole" — a coverage gap where they paid a much larger share — before reaching catastrophic coverage.
That donut hole is now gone. As of 2025, the Inflation Reduction Act restructured Part D into a simpler three-phase benefit — deductible, initial coverage, and catastrophic — with no coverage gap in between. The change makes drug costs far more predictable for beneficiaries.
The headline reform is a hard out-of-pocket cap. Beginning in 2025, beneficiary out-of-pocket spending on covered Part D drugs is capped at $2,000 per year (indexed thereafter; the cap is $2,100 in 2026). Once a beneficiary hits the cap, the plan covers the rest of their covered drug costs for the year — a profound change for people on expensive medications.

The Inflation Reduction Act Transformation
The 2022 Inflation Reduction Act (IRA) is the most significant change to Medicare drug coverage since Part D itself. Beyond the out-of-pocket cap and donut-hole elimination, it capped insulin cost-sharing at $35 per month (effective 2023 for Part D insulin), making a life-sustaining drug affordable for millions.
The IRA also requires drug manufacturers to pay rebates to Medicare if they raise prices faster than inflation — an inflation-rebate provision designed to restrain price growth. And it created the Medicare Prescription Payment Plan, effective January 1, 2025, which lets any Part D enrollee spread their out-of-pocket costs into capped, interest-free monthly installments instead of paying a large bill all at once at the pharmacy.
Most historically, the IRA gave Medicare the power to negotiate prices for certain high-spend drugs — something the original 2003 law had explicitly forbidden. CMS selected the first 10 drugs, and the negotiated prices (ranging from a 38 percent to a 79 percent discount off 2023 list prices) take effect in 2026, with more drugs added in later years.
For the first negotiation cycle, CMS reached agreed prices on 10 high-spend Part D drugs — including Januvia, Eliquis, Xarelto, and Imbruvica — with discounts ranging from 38% to 79% off 2023 list prices. Effective in 2026, these prices are estimated to save Medicare beneficiaries about $1.5 billion in out-of-pocket costs and the Medicare program roughly $6 billion per year. It is the first time in Part D’s history that Medicare has directly negotiated drug prices.
The First Round of Drug Price Negotiation
Why Part D Matters Now
Part D sits at the intersection of Medicare’s biggest tensions: access, cost, and the role of private plans. It made drugs vastly more accessible to seniors, but it also embodied the original political bargain of relying on private plans and barring price negotiation — a bargain the IRA has now substantially rewritten.
The IRA reforms ripple far beyond beneficiaries’ wallets. The out-of-pocket cap shifts more cost onto plans and manufacturers, reshaping plan bids and premiums. Price negotiation challenges the pharmaceutical industry’s pricing model and has prompted litigation. And inflation rebates change manufacturers’ incentives to raise prices.
For anyone working in Medicare, Part D is now one of the most dynamic areas of the program. Understanding formularies, the new three-phase benefit, the $2,000 cap, and drug price negotiation is essential to understanding where Medicare — and American drug policy — is heading.
With the Inflation Reduction Act, Medicare crossed a line it had refused to cross for two decades: it began negotiating what it pays for drugs.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | why-states-move-to-managed-care | Why States Move to Managed Care: History and Rationale
Why States Move to Managed Care: History and Rationale
The Quiet Revolution in How America Covers the Poor
Medicaid is the largest health insurance program in the United States, covering tens of millions of low-income children, adults, seniors, and people with disabilities. But the way most of those people actually receive their care has been transformed over the past three decades, largely out of public view. Today, the dominant model is not the government paying doctors and hospitals directly for each service — it is the state paying private managed care organizations (MCOs) a fixed amount per enrollee to take responsibility for their care. As of July 2024, over 66 million Medicaid enrollees — about 78% of all enrollees — received their care through risk-based MCOs.
This shift from traditional fee-for-service Medicaid to managed care is one of the most consequential and least understood changes in American health policy. It reshaped the relationships among states, the federal government, private insurers, and providers, and it created an entire industry of Medicaid managed care plans operating in most states. Understanding why states made this move — and what they gained and gave up — is the foundation for everything else in Medicaid managed care operations.
The story is not a simple one of cost savings. As we will see, the evidence on whether managed care actually saves money or improves quality is surprisingly mixed. The clearest thing states gained was something subtler but, to a state budget officer, enormously valuable: predictability. This lesson traces the history of the move to managed care and the real rationale behind it.
Key Concept: Medicaid managed care means a state pays a private managed care organization (MCO) a fixed, capitated amount per enrollee to provide their care, shifting financial risk to the MCO — in contrast to traditional fee-for-service Medicaid, where the state pays providers directly for each service.

From Experiment to Dominant Model: A Brief History
Medicaid began in 1965 as a fee-for-service program: providers delivered care and billed the state, which paid them for each service. By the late 1980s and early 1990s, Medicaid costs were rising sharply, and states began experimenting with more cost-effective ways to deliver care. The answer they reached for was managed care — borrowing the model spreading through private insurance, in which a plan accepts a fixed payment and takes responsibility for managing a population’s care and cost.
The growth was rapid. In 1991, about 2.7 million beneficiaries were enrolled in some form of Medicaid managed care — roughly 10% of the program; by 1996, nearly 40% of Medicaid beneficiaries were enrolled in managed care plans. A key legal turning point came with the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which eliminated the requirement that states obtain a federal waiver before launching mandatory Medicaid managed care programs. That change removed a major bureaucratic hurdle and accelerated adoption, helping push managed care toward the near-universal model it is today.
Before 1997, and still today for certain populations and program designs, states needed federal permission to depart from traditional Medicaid rules — typically through Section 1915 or Section 1115 waivers, which grant exemptions from standard Medicaid guidelines. These waivers remain central to Medicaid managed care and are covered in depth later in this course. The history matters because it shows managed care was not imposed from Washington; it grew from states’ own efforts to control costs, enabled by federal flexibility.
States pay providers directly for each service delivered to beneficiaries.

The Path to Managed Care Dominance
The Real Rationale: Predictability and Coordination
Why did states embrace managed care so thoroughly? Two rationales are cited most often: increasing the predictability of spending and improving the coordination of care. The predictability argument is the more powerful one in practice. Under fee-for-service, a state’s Medicaid spending is the unpredictable sum of millions of individual claims — if utilization spikes, so does the bill, often after the budget is set. Under managed care, the state pays MCOs a capitated rate per person per month, so it knows its per-enrollee cost in advance. This lets state policymakers predict and manage Medicaid budgets far more reliably.
For a state budget officer, this predictability is enormously valuable. Medicaid is one of the largest items in every state budget, and states (unlike the federal government) must generally balance their budgets each year. Converting an open-ended, volatile fee-for-service liability into a fixed per-member payment transfers the risk of cost overruns to the MCO and gives the state a number it can plan around. The capitation payment effectively caps the state’s per-enrollee exposure.
The second rationale, care coordination, holds that an MCO responsible for a member’s total care — and bearing the financial risk for it — has both the incentive and the tools to coordinate that care, manage chronic conditions, emphasize prevention, and steer members away from costly avoidable utilization. In theory, the same capitation that delivers budget predictability also aligns the plan’s incentives with keeping members healthy. Whether that theory holds up in practice is a separate and contested question.
Did It Deliver? The Honest Evidence
Given how completely managed care has taken over Medicaid, one might assume the evidence for its benefits is overwhelming. It is not. Research has repeatedly challenged whether managed care has delivered on its promises. While states have reliably achieved more predictability in their Medicaid budgets, only a very small number of studies show that managed care has actually helped states lower costs or improve quality. The most confident claim that can be made is about predictability — not savings, and not better outcomes.
Even the predictability gain is more limited than it appears. Research has found that managed care use has been concentrated among the enrollees with the most stable spending — historically healthier children and families — which means the budget predictability gains were smaller than hoped, because the unpredictable, high-cost populations (the aged and people with disabilities) were often kept in fee-for-service. As states increasingly move these complex populations into MCOs, the stakes — and the difficulty — rise.
Capitated managed care can create an incentive to avoid expensive members. Plans have been criticized for prioritizing cost containment over necessary care and for directly or indirectly selecting healthier enrollees or avoiding patients with complex needs. Guarding against this is a central purpose of the oversight, risk adjustment, and contract rules covered later in this course.
The Cherry-Picking Concern
Where Managed Care Stands Today
Despite the mixed evidence, Medicaid managed care is now the dominant delivery model and continues to expand. As of 2024, thirty MCO states covered at least 75% of their Medicaid beneficiaries through MCOs. The populations enrolled tell an important story: children and ACA expansion adults are the most likely to be in comprehensive MCOs (around 90% and 86% respectively), while people eligible through a disability pathway and adults 65 and older have historically been less likely to be enrolled — though states are steadily moving these higher-need groups into managed care too.
A state moving Medicaid to managed care is like a company switching from paying every employee’s medical bills directly to buying a fixed-price health plan for all of them. The company no longer faces a surprise bill when costs spike — it pays a known premium and the insurer absorbs the risk. That predictability is the main attraction. But the company also gives up direct control, and must now watch carefully that the insurer doesn’t skimp on care or shun its sickest workers to protect its own margin.
Why states adopt Medicaid managed care
This trajectory sets up the rest of the course. Because states have handed responsibility for most of their Medicaid populations to private MCOs, the critical questions become operational: How do states choose which MCOs to contract with? How are the capitation rates calculated so they are adequate but not excessive? How do states hold plans accountable for network adequacy, quality, and fair treatment of complex members? Each of these exists precisely because the move to managed care transferred enormous responsibility — and public dollars — to private organizations that must be carefully governed.
The fundamental tension introduced here runs through everything that follows. Managed care offers states budget predictability and the promise of coordinated care, but it does so by giving private plans a financial incentive that can cut against members’ interests. The entire apparatus of Medicaid managed care operations — procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality measurement, and value-based purchasing — exists to capture the benefits of the model while guarding against its risks. Understanding why states made this move is understanding why all that machinery is necessary.
Medicaid managed care means a state pays private managed care organizations (MCOs) a fixed capitated amount per enrollee to provide care, shifting financial risk to the MCO instead of paying providers per service as in fee-for-service.
It is now the dominant model: over 66 million enrollees (~78%) received care through risk-based MCOs as of July 2024, and 30 states cover at least 75% of beneficiaries in MCOs.
Managed care grew rapidly in the 1990s (from ~10% of beneficiaries in 1991 to nearly 40% by 1996), accelerated by the Balanced Budget Act of 1997, which eliminated the waiver requirement for mandatory managed care.
The two most-cited rationales are increasing budget predictability and improving care coordination, with predictability the most powerful in practice because it converts volatile fee-for-service costs into a fixed per-member payment.
Budget predictability matters because Medicaid is a huge share of state budgets that must generally balance annually, so capitation caps the state’s per-enrollee exposure and transfers overrun risk to the MCO.
The evidence is mixed: states reliably gained predictability, but few studies show managed care lowered costs or improved quality, and predictability gains were limited because managed care first covered the most stable-spending populations.
Capitation creates a cherry-picking risk — incentives to avoid expensive, complex members — which oversight, risk adjustment, and contract rules are designed to counter.
The transfer of most Medicaid populations and dollars to private MCOs is exactly why the rest of Medicaid managed care operations (procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality, value-based purchasing) is necessary.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | medicaid-delivery-system-models | MCO vs PCCM vs ACO: Medicaid Delivery System Models
MCO vs. PCCM vs. ACO: Medicaid Delivery System Models
Not All "Managed Care" Is the Same
The previous lesson established that most Medicaid beneficiaries now receive care through "managed care." But that umbrella term hides important distinctions. A state can manage and coordinate Medicaid care through several different delivery system models, and they differ enormously in how much financial risk is transferred to private organizations, how providers are paid, and how much control the state retains. Choosing among these models is one of the most fundamental decisions a state Medicaid program makes — and understanding the differences is essential to understanding everything else in this course.
The three models most worth knowing are the comprehensive risk-based managed care organization (MCO), primary care case management (PCCM), and the accountable care organization (ACO). They sit at different points on a spectrum of risk transfer, much like the value-based-care risk continuum: from full capitated risk borne by a private plan (MCO), to coordinated fee-for-service with no provider risk (PCCM), to newer accountable-care arrangements layered on top. States often use more than one at once for different populations.
The key question that distinguishes these models is simple: who bears the financial risk, and how are providers paid? Once you can answer that for any arrangement, you understand its core incentives — and the operational machinery that must surround it.
Key Concept: Medicaid delivery models differ by who bears financial risk. A comprehensive MCO takes full capitated risk; PCCM keeps providers on fee-for-service with a small care-coordination fee and no provider risk; ACOs layer accountability for cost and quality on top of existing arrangements.
As of July 2025, 42 states (including DC) contract with comprehensive, risk-based managed care plans for at least some beneficiaries (KFF)
