The Comprehensive MCO: Full Risk Transfer
The dominant model is the comprehensive risk-based MCO. Under this arrangement, the state pays the plan a capitation rate — a fixed dollar amount per member per month — to cover a defined set of services. The defining feature is risk: the plan is at financial risk if its spending on benefits and administration exceeds the payments it receives. If the MCO manages care efficiently and spends less than its capitation, it keeps the difference; if it overspends, it absorbs the loss.
This full risk transfer is exactly what gives the state the budget predictability discussed in the prior lesson, and it gives the MCO a powerful incentive to manage utilization, coordinate care, and emphasize prevention. But it is also what creates the need for nearly all the oversight this course covers — because a plan at risk for costs has an incentive to under-provide care or avoid expensive members. The MCO model maximizes both the potential benefits of managed care and the potential harms, which is why it is the most heavily regulated.
PCCM: Coordinated Fee-for-Service
At a very different point on the spectrum sits primary care case management (PCCM). Under PCCM, beneficiaries are enrolled with a primary care provider who is paid a small monthly fee — typically a few dollars per member per month — to provide case management and care coordination, on top of being paid the usual fee-for-service rates for the actual care delivered. The critical distinction is that individual providers are not at financial risk; they continue to be paid fee-for-service and simply receive an extra fee for coordinating care.
This makes PCCM a kind of hybrid. Federal Medicaid law considers PCCM a form of managed care, but in practice it is more akin to traditional fee-for-service Medicaid with care coordination layered on. The state retains the cost risk (it still pays per service), so it gives up the budget predictability of capitation — but it also avoids the under-provision incentives of full risk transfer, since providers have no financial reason to withhold care. PCCM is often favored in rural areas where there are too few providers to support competing MCO networks.
Many states have strengthened this model into Enhanced PCCM (PCCM-E), which adds features such as more intensive case management, dedicated care-coordination staff, additional resources for beneficiaries, and improved financial incentives for primary care physicians tied to performance goals. PCCM-E aims to capture more of the care-coordination benefits of managed care while keeping providers out of full financial risk — a middle path between fee-for-service and the comprehensive MCO.
Comprehensive MCO

Medicaid ACOs: Accountability Layered On Top
A newer model is the Medicaid accountable care organization (ACO). Rather than replacing the existing delivery system, states are increasingly layering ACOs — newer forms of care management and accountability for total cost and quality — on top of their traditional arrangements, including comprehensive MCOs. A Medicaid ACO holds a group of providers accountable for the cost and quality of care for an attributed population, typically through shared-savings or risk arrangements, mirroring the ACO concept from the value-based-care world but adapted to Medicaid.
Because ACOs are layered on rather than standardized in federal regulation the way MCOs are (under 42 CFR Part 438, covered in the next lesson), they vary widely by state. Massachusetts and Minnesota are prominent examples of states that have implemented Medicaid ACO models for their managed care populations, each making its own choices about stakeholder engagement, how beneficiaries are attributed to an ACO, and the payment methodology. The ACO model reflects Medicaid’s movement toward value-based payment — paying for outcomes and total cost of care rather than simply transferring risk to a plan.
There is also a fourth, narrower category worth knowing: limited-benefit plans, which manage only a specific slice of care — such as behavioral health, dental, or non-emergency transportation — rather than a member’s comprehensive needs. These "carve-outs" let a state apply managed care to a particular benefit while handling the rest differently, and they are discussed further in the benefits lesson. Together, comprehensive MCOs, PCCM/PCCM-E, ACOs, and limited-benefit plans give states a toolkit of delivery models to combine.
How States Mix and Match
In practice, states rarely use a single model for everyone. Analysts have grouped states by their dominant approach: some have historically been PCCM-predominant (enrolling most beneficiaries in PCCM, few in MCOs), some MCO-predominant (the now-common pattern), some used both extensively, and others fell into mixed categories. A typical state might enroll its children and expansion adults in comprehensive MCOs, manage a rural region through PCCM, carve out behavioral health to a limited-benefit plan, and layer an ACO arrangement on top to push toward value — all at once.
The delivery models are like different ways a city might run its bus system. A comprehensive MCO is like hiring a private company for a fixed annual fee to run all the routes — predictable cost, but you must watch that they don’t cut service to save money. PCCM is like keeping the buses public but paying each route a bonus to coordinate schedules — no incentive to skimp, but the city still pays per mile. An ACO is like setting a performance target for on-time arrivals and sharing the savings — accountability layered onto whatever system already runs the buses.
Comparing Medicaid delivery system models
The choice among models reflects a state’s priorities and constraints. A state prioritizing budget predictability and willing to invest in oversight leans toward comprehensive MCOs. A state with thin rural provider networks or wary of full risk transfer may favor PCCM or PCCM-E. A state pushing toward value-based, outcomes-focused care builds ACO arrangements. And nearly every state uses carve-outs for specialized benefits. There is no single right answer — only trade-offs among predictability, control, provider incentives, and administrative complexity.
This sets up the rest of the course. Because the comprehensive MCO is the dominant and most heavily regulated model, most of what follows — the federal framework, procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, and quality measurement — focuses on it. But understanding that PCCM, ACOs, and carve-outs exist alongside it is essential to seeing the full Medicaid managed care landscape. The model a state chooses determines who bears risk, how providers are paid, and what oversight is required — the questions that organize everything still to come.
Medicaid delivery models differ chiefly by who bears financial risk and how providers are paid — the question that defines each model’s incentives.
A comprehensive risk-based MCO is paid a capitation rate (PMPM) and bears full financial risk, giving the state budget predictability but creating under-provision incentives that require heavy oversight; 42 states plus DC use comprehensive MCOs as of July 2025.
Primary care case management (PCCM) keeps providers on fee-for-service plus a small monthly care-coordination fee, placing no additional financial risk on providers — managed care in name, closer to coordinated fee-for-service in practice.
Enhanced PCCM (PCCM-E) strengthens the model with intensive case management, dedicated coordination staff, and performance-based incentives while still avoiding full provider risk — a middle path often used in rural areas.
Medicaid ACOs layer accountability for total cost and quality (via shared savings or risk) on top of existing arrangements rather than replacing them; they vary widely by state, with Massachusetts and Minnesota as prominent examples.
Limited-benefit plans (carve-outs) apply managed care to a single slice of care such as behavioral health, dental, or transportation, rather than comprehensive needs.
States mix and match models — e.g., MCOs for children and expansion adults, PCCM in rural areas, behavioral-health carve-outs, and an ACO layer — choosing based on predictability, control, provider incentives, and complexity.
Because the comprehensive MCO is the dominant and most regulated model, most Medicaid managed care operations (federal framework, procurement, rate-setting, network standards, oversight, quality) focus on it.

Federal Framework: 42 CFR Part 438 and CHIP Rules
The Rulebook Behind Every Medicaid Managed Care Contract
Medicaid is a federal-state partnership: states run their programs, but they do so within rules set by the federal government, and they receive federal matching dollars only if they follow those rules. For managed care, the master rulebook has a name worth memorizing: 42 CFR Part 438. This section of the Code of Federal Regulations governs Medicaid managed care organizations and defines what states must require of the plans they contract with — from network adequacy to financial standards to quality and beneficiary protections.
Understanding Part 438 is essential because it is the framework within which everything else in this course operates. When a state writes an MCO contract, sets capitation rates, defines network standards, or oversees plan performance, it is implementing requirements that ultimately trace back to Part 438. The companion rules for the Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP) live at 42 CFR Part 457, applying parallel managed care protections to CHIP enrollees. Together, these regulations are the federal floor for Medicaid and CHIP managed care.
This framework is not static. In 2024, CMS substantially updated it through a major final rule, raising the bar on access, finance, and quality. This lesson covers both the enduring structure of Part 438 and the significant 2024 changes that now shape how states must manage their managed care programs.
Key Concept: 42 CFR Part 438 is the federal regulation governing Medicaid managed care, setting the rules states must follow for network adequacy, finance (including MLR), quality, and beneficiary protections. CHIP managed care is governed by the parallel 42 CFR Part 457.
If a state sets a minimum MLR for its managed care plans under Part 438, it must be equal to or higher than 85 percent (42 CFR 438.8)
Minimum Medical Loss Ratio
≥85%
The 2024 rule requires appointment within 15 business days for primary care and OB/GYN, and 10 business days for outpatient behavioral health (CMS 2024 final rule)
New Wait-Time Standards
15 / 10 days
What Part 438 Requires
Part 438 is organized around the state’s responsibilities as the entity contracting with private plans. Its core requirements span the operational territory this course will explore. On network adequacy, a state that contracts with a managed care plan must develop and enforce network adequacy standards, including quantitative standards for specified provider types. On finance, it governs how capitation rates must be actuarially sound and sets the rules for the medical loss ratio. On quality, it requires quality assessment and improvement programs and external review. And throughout, it establishes beneficiary protections — enrollment, grievances and appeals, and access to care.
A central financial requirement is the medical loss ratio (MLR). Part 438 provides that if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR for its plans, that minimum must be equal to or higher than 85 percent, and the MLR must be calculated and reported each year by the plan. The MLR — covered in depth in its own lesson — ensures that at least 85 cents of every capitation dollar goes toward medical care and quality rather than profit and administration. States have been required to submit summary MLR reports to CMS since rating periods beginning July 1, 2017.
Part 438 also imposes detailed network adequacy requirements at section 438.68. States must develop quantitative network adequacy standards for certain provider types covered under the contract, and states whose contracts cover long-term services and supports (LTSS) must develop quantitative standards for LTSS provider types as well. These requirements exist to ensure that the promise of a "network" is real — that enrollees can actually reach the providers their plan claims to offer.
The 2024 Final Rule: Access, Finance, and Quality
In 2024, CMS issued one of the most significant updates to the managed care framework in years. The "Medicaid and CHIP Managed Care Access, Finance, and Quality" final rule (CMS-2439-F) was published May 10, 2024, and became effective July 9, 2024. It advances CMS’s efforts to improve access to care, quality and health outcomes, and health equity for Medicaid and CHIP managed care enrollees — and it applies to both Part 438 (Medicaid) and Part 457 (CHIP). The rule is best understood through its three named pillars: access, finance, and quality.
The most concrete and consequential changes are on access. For the first time, the rule sets specific, enforceable appointment wait time standards: enrollees must be able to get a routine appointment within 15 business days for primary care (adult and pediatric) and for OB/GYN services, and within 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use services. These are national floors that translate the abstract idea of "network adequacy" into a measurable patient experience — how long someone actually has to wait to see a provider.
On finance, the rule addresses state directed payments and reduces some state burdens while specifying MLR requirements and adding standards for "in lieu of services and settings" (ILOS) — alternative services like housing or nutrition supports that plans can offer in place of traditional covered benefits. On quality, it establishes a quality rating system for Medicaid and CHIP managed care plans, a kind of consumer-facing report card. Together these pillars push the framework from process requirements toward measurable outcomes and transparency.
New appointment wait-time standards (15 days primary/OB-GYN, 10 days behavioral health) enforced through secret shopper surveys.
Access
Clarified state directed payment and MLR requirements; new standards for in lieu of services and settings (ILOS).

The 2024 Final Rule’s Three Pillars
Enforcement: The Secret Shopper
A standard means nothing without enforcement, and the 2024 rule pairs its access requirements with a specific monitoring tool: the secret shopper survey. States must use annual secret shopper surveys to determine plan compliance with the appointment wait time standards and to assess the accuracy of electronic provider directories. A secret shopper survey involves a third party posing as an enrollee and attempting to schedule an appointment with a provider listed in the plan’s directory — testing whether the network is real and accessible in practice, not just on paper.
The methodology is specified to make the results meaningful. The surveys must use a random sample, cover all areas of the state served by the plan, and reach a statistically valid sample of providers for the wait-time tests. Crucially, the results must be submitted to CMS and posted on the state agency’s public website — building in transparency and accountability. This directly targets the long-standing problem of "ghost networks," where provider directories list doctors who are not actually accepting new Medicaid patients or who cannot be reached.
For decades, network adequacy was judged on paper — a plan could list thousands of providers while enrollees struggled to get appointments. The secret shopper survey tests the directory against reality, exposing "ghost networks" and inaccurate listings, and forcing plans to maintain networks that actually deliver timely care.
Why the Secret Shopper Matters
Why the Framework Matters
It is easy to dismiss regulatory citations like "42 CFR Part 438" as bureaucratic detail, but the framework is where the public interest in Medicaid managed care is actually protected. Recall the central tension from earlier lessons: capitation gives plans a financial incentive to under-provide care and avoid expensive members. Part 438 and its CHIP counterpart are the legal counterweight — the binding rules that require plans to maintain adequate networks, spend most of their capitation on care, meet quality standards, and treat beneficiaries fairly. Without this framework, managed care would be risk transfer with no guardrails.
If a Medicaid MCO contract is the lease on an apartment, 42 CFR Part 438 is the housing code behind it. The lease sets the specific terms between landlord and tenant, but the housing code sets the floor no lease can fall below — working heat, safe wiring, a real door that locks. The 2024 rule is like the code being updated to add a new requirement that the heat actually reach a measured temperature, with inspectors (secret shoppers) sent to verify it. The code is what makes the lease’s promises enforceable.
How the federal framework backs managed care contracts
The framework also illustrates the federal-state dynamic that runs through all of Medicaid. The federal government sets the floor through Part 438; states build on top of it through their own contracts, which can be more demanding but not less. This is why two states’ Medicaid managed care programs can look quite different while both complying with the same federal rules — and why a major federal rule change, like the 2024 update, ripples through every state’s program at once, forcing contract amendments, new monitoring, and new reporting nationwide.
For the rest of this course, Part 438 is the connective tissue. The procurement and contracting lessons implement its requirements; the rate-setting and MLR lessons implement its financial standards; the network adequacy and quality lessons implement its access and quality provisions; and the oversight lesson implements its monitoring and enforcement expectations. When you encounter a specific operational requirement later, it is worth asking where it traces back to in the federal framework — because almost always, the answer is here.
42 CFR Part 438 is the federal regulation governing Medicaid managed care, setting the rules states must follow for network adequacy, finance (including MLR), quality, and beneficiary protections; CHIP managed care is governed by the parallel 42 CFR Part 457.
Part 438 requires actuarially sound capitation rates and provides that any state-mandated minimum medical loss ratio must be at least 85 percent, reported annually by each plan.
Network adequacy requirements (section 438.68) require states to set quantitative standards for specified provider types, including LTSS provider types when LTSS is covered.
The 2024 "Access, Finance, and Quality" final rule (CMS-2439-F, effective July 9, 2024) significantly updated the framework across three pillars — access, finance, and quality — for both Medicaid and CHIP.
The rule established first-of-their-kind appointment wait-time standards: 15 business days for primary care and OB/GYN, and 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use services.
It also addressed state directed payments, added standards for in lieu of services and settings (ILOS), and established a new quality rating system (a public report card) for managed care plans.
Enforcement relies on annual secret shopper surveys — a third party posing as an enrollee to test appointment availability and directory accuracy — with results reported to CMS and posted publicly to expose "ghost networks."
The framework is the legal counterweight to capitation’s under-provision incentives, sets a federal floor states can exceed but not fall below, and is the connective tissue linking procurement, rate-setting, network, quality, and oversight throughout this course.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | rfp-process-mco-selection | The RFP Process: How States Select MCOs
The RFP Process: How States Select MCOs
Choosing Who Will Manage Billions in Public Care
When a state decides to run its Medicaid program through managed care, it must choose which private organizations will receive billions of dollars to care for its most vulnerable residents. This choice is made through a procurement — a formal, competitive process built around a Request for Proposals (RFP). The stakes could hardly be higher: a single state’s Medicaid managed care contracts can be worth tens of billions of dollars over their life and determine the care of millions of people. Getting the procurement right is one of the most consequential things a state Medicaid agency does.
The procurement is also where the abstract requirements of the federal framework become concrete commitments. The RFP translates Part 438’s rules and the state’s own priorities into specific demands that bidding plans must meet, and the evaluation determines which plans best satisfy them. Increasingly, procurement is also how states drive innovation — using the competition to push plans toward value-based payment, health equity, and better member experience. The RFP is not just a purchasing document; it is a policy instrument.
This lesson walks through how the process works, from RFP development to contract award, and confronts a reality that has come to dominate Medicaid procurement in recent years: the explosion of bid protests and litigation that can delay or undo even a carefully run selection.
Key Concept: States select Medicaid MCOs through a competitive procurement built around a Request for Proposals (RFP). Plans submit bids that are scored against predetermined criteria; the highest-scoring bidders are awarded contracts, subject to negotiation, readiness review, and an increasingly common gauntlet of protests.
A full Medicaid managed care procurement — preplanning, bidding, and implementation — typically lasts 18 to 24 months (MACPAC)
Length of a Procurement

Bid protests, now common, frequently delay implementation by six months or more, and in some states by years (HealthScape Advisors)

6+ months
The Procurement Process, Step by Step
A Medicaid managed care procurement follows a structured sequence. It begins with the state developing the RFP, which includes a scope of work or model contract specifying what plans must do, and a set of predetermined questions and criteria. The state publicly advertises the procurement and accepts bids. It then evaluates the proposals — typically using a formal scoring system — announces its intent to award contracts to the winning bidders, negotiates final contracts, conducts "readiness reviews" to verify the new plans can actually operate, and finally implements. The whole process typically takes 18 to 24 months.
A key structural choice is how many plans to admit. Some states use an "any willing and qualified bidder" approach, contracting with every plan that meets the requirements. But most states limit the number of MCOs through a competitive procurement, awarding contracts only to the highest-scoring bidders. Limiting the field gives the state more leverage and concentrates enrollment (helping plans achieve scale), but it also raises the stakes of each award — and the incentive for losing bidders to challenge it.
Write the scope of work / model contract and the scored questions reflecting Part 438 rules and state priorities.
Develop the RFP
Publicly solicit proposals from interested managed care plans.

Rate bids against predetermined criteria using a formal scoring rubric.

Announce intent to award, negotiate final contracts, and verify each plan can actually operate before go-live.

The MCO Procurement Sequence
The readiness review deserves emphasis. Winning a contract on paper is not the same as being able to deliver care on day one. Before implementation, the state verifies that each selected plan has an adequate provider network, functioning claims systems, member services, and the operational infrastructure to serve enrollees. A plan that cannot pass readiness review can delay an entire program’s launch, which is why the period between award and go-live is intensely operational.
How Bids Are Scored
The heart of the procurement is the evaluation, and most Medicaid agencies use formal scoring rubrics to ensure a fair and standardized process. The state typically releases the scoring rubric along with the RFP, so bidders know in advance how their answers will be judged. Each question carries a point value, and evaluators rate responses against a defined scale. In Hawaii’s 2021 procurement, for example, answers were rated on a zero-to-five scale — zero being "Very Poor" and five "Excellent" — with each RFP question worth a set number of points.
What states ask for in those questions has been evolving. States are increasingly asking bidders to demonstrate actual results rather than make promises — to respond to case scenarios showing how the plan would handle needs unique to the Medicaid population, and to provide evidence of past performance. A rubric can be deliberately designed to reward innovation, steering the competition toward the state’s policy goals. This is how a procurement becomes a policy lever: by attaching points to value-based payment commitments, health-equity strategies, or member-experience improvements, the state pulls the whole market in that direction.
The discipline of releasing a clear rubric in advance serves a second purpose beyond fairness: defensibility. As the next section shows, procurements are now routinely challenged, and a transparent, well-documented scoring process is a state’s best protection against having its award overturned. States are responding by strengthening evaluation frameworks, clarifying scoring criteria, and emphasizing transparency precisely so their decisions can withstand scrutiny.
The Protest Problem
In recent years, bid protests and litigation have become a structural feature of Medicaid procurement rather than an occasional exception. Because a single award can be worth billions and losing bidders may be shut out of a state’s market for years, the incentive to challenge an unfavorable decision is enormous. Protests are now an increasingly anticipated component of competitive procurements, frequently delaying implementation by six months or more — and sometimes far longer.
The 2024–2025 period offered vivid examples across the country. In Florida, a losing bidder sued to block new contracts while protests continued. In Rhode Island, bidders protested a roughly $15 billion award — pointing out, among other things, that the review team was composed entirely of agency employees in violation of state procurement rules — prompting the state to reevaluate proposals, cancel the solicitation, extend incumbent contracts, and prepare a revised RFP. In Texas, the STAR and CHIP procurement was tied up in litigation for nearly two years, with courts pausing the process over deficiencies in the state’s evaluation methodology, including the premature disclosure of competitors’ proposals to one bidder. In Georgia, incumbent protests pushed an anticipated July 2025 go-live to late 2026 or early 2027.
While some protests are simply losing bidders fighting to stay in the market, others expose legitimate procedural gaps — flawed scoring, insufficient documentation, conflicts of interest, or unclear criteria. Either way, the delay is real: members keep their current plans, new innovations wait, and the state’s timeline can slip by months or years.
Protests Expose Real Flaws — and Cause Real Delays
Why Procurement Defensibility Now Drives the Process
The rise of protests has fundamentally changed how states approach procurement. Escalating protest activity and judicial scrutiny have raised the bar for procurement defensibility — meaning a state must be able to prove, in detail, that its process was fair, well-documented, free of conflicts, and faithful to its own published rules. This has slowed procurements down, but the slowdown does not mean states are abandoning managed care. It reflects a recalibration toward more durable, defensible procurement structures built to withstand litigation, policy volatility, and operational complexity.
A Medicaid procurement is like a high-stakes talent competition where the prize is a multibillion-dollar contract. The judges must publish their scorecard in advance, score every contestant the same way, document their reasoning, and avoid any appearance of favoritism — because every losing contestant has a lawyer ready to challenge the result. A sloppy or biased judging process doesn’t just produce a bad winner; it can get the whole competition thrown out and restarted, leaving everyone in limbo for a year.
Why procurement fairness and documentation matter
For the state, the practical lesson is that the quality of the process matters as much as the quality of the choice. A perfectly reasonable selection can be undone by a flawed procedure — an evaluator with an undisclosed conflict, a scoring inconsistency, a leaked document. The defensibility imperative pushes states toward independent evaluators, meticulous documentation, clear criteria, and transparency, all of which also tend to produce better, fairer selections. Good process and good outcomes increasingly go together.
This lesson connects directly to what follows. The RFP and resulting contract are where the state codifies everything it will require of its plans — the network adequacy standards, quality requirements, and reporting obligations covered in the next lesson; the capitation rates and MLR rules covered in the rate-setting module; and the value-based purchasing goals covered later. The procurement is the moment the state exercises its leverage, because once the contract is signed, the state must work within its terms. Choosing the right plans through a defensible process is the foundation on which all subsequent oversight rests.
States select Medicaid MCOs through a competitive procurement built around a Request for Proposals (RFP) that translates federal rules and state priorities into specific, scored requirements.
The process follows a sequence — RFP development, advertising and bid receipt, scored evaluation, intent to award, contract negotiation, readiness review, and implementation — typically lasting 18 to 24 months.
Most states limit the number of MCOs by awarding contracts only to the highest-scoring bidders (rather than accepting any willing qualified bidder), which raises the leverage and the stakes of each award.
Readiness review verifies that a selected plan can actually operate — adequate network, claims systems, member services — before go-live, and a plan that fails it can delay an entire program launch.
Bids are scored with formal rubrics released alongside the RFP (e.g., Hawaii’s 0–5 scale), and states increasingly require evidence of results and case-scenario responses, using point allocations to reward innovation and steer the market.
Bid protests and litigation have become a structural feature of procurement, frequently delaying implementation by six months or more, with 2024–2025 examples in Florida, Rhode Island, Texas, and Georgia.
Protests can expose real procedural flaws — biased or all-internal review teams, flawed scoring, leaked competitor proposals, conflicts of interest — and can force reevaluation, cancellation, or multi-year delays.
Escalating scrutiny has made procurement defensibility paramount, pushing states toward independent evaluators, meticulous documentation, clear criteria, and transparency — which also produce fairer, better selections.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | contract-requirements | Contract Requirements: Network Adequacy, QA, Reporting
Contract Requirements: Network Adequacy, Quality Assurance, and Reporting
The Contract Is Where Promises Become Obligations
Once a state selects its MCOs through the procurement covered in the last lesson, it translates the winning proposals into a binding contract. That contract — often hundreds of pages long — is the single most important operational document in Medicaid managed care. It converts the federal requirements of 42 CFR Part 438 and the state’s own priorities into specific, enforceable obligations the plan must meet. If the procurement is where the state chooses its partners, the contract is where it defines exactly what those partners must do.
Three categories of contract requirements form the operational backbone of every Medicaid MCO contract: network adequacy (ensuring enrollees can actually access providers), quality assurance (ensuring the care is good), and reporting (ensuring the state can see what the plan is doing). These three threads run through the entire relationship, and each is anchored in federal regulation. Together they are how a state holds a risk-bearing private plan accountable for serving a vulnerable public population.
Understanding these requirements matters because they are the mechanism that addresses the central tension of managed care. A capitated plan has an incentive to spend less — which could mean a thin network, skimpy care, or hidden problems. Network, quality, and reporting requirements are the contractual counterweights: they force the plan to maintain real access, demonstrate real quality, and show the state real data.
Key Concept: An MCO contract converts federal rules and state priorities into binding obligations across three core areas — network adequacy (access), quality assurance (good care), and reporting (transparency) — backed by enforcement tools like sanctions and liquidated damages.
Network Adequacy Requirements
The first pillar is network adequacy: the contract must require the plan to maintain a provider network sufficient to deliver the covered services. Under 42 CFR 438.68, states must develop and publish a quantitative network adequacy standard (other than appointment wait times — often time-and-distance or provider-to-enrollee ratios) for a defined set of provider types — primary care (adult and pediatric), OB/GYN, behavioral health, adult and pediatric specialists, hospitals, pharmacy, and pediatric dental — plus additional types as CMS determines. The 2024 final rule layered appointment wait-time standards on top of these, as the federal-framework lesson described, so adequacy is now judged by both the state’s quantitative standards and timeliness.
Crucially, network adequacy is not just about counting providers. In setting standards, states must consider factors such as providers’ ability to communicate with limited-English-proficient enrollees, accommodation of disabilities, the availability of triage or screening lines, and the use of telemedicine and other innovative technologies. This reflects a recognition that a "provider in the network" is only meaningful if a real enrollee — who may have a disability, speak limited English, or live far from care — can actually reach and use them. The contract embeds these considerations as binding requirements.
To verify adequacy, states require plans to support a Network Adequacy and Access Assurances Report (NAAAR), documenting an analysis that supports the assurance that each plan’s network is adequate. Combined with the secret-shopper surveys from the federal-framework lesson, this gives the state both the plan’s self-reported network data and an independent test of whether that network functions in practice — closing the gap between paper networks and real access.
Quality Assurance Requirements
The second pillar is quality assurance. The contract must require the plan to participate in the state’s quality apparatus, which federal rules build around several components. Each state contracting with managed care plans must draft and implement a written quality strategy for assessing and improving the quality of care (42 CFR 438.340). Within that, each plan must operate a Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) program, undergo external quality review (EQR) by an independent organization, and meet accreditation and reporting requirements.
These requirements work together as a system. The state’s quality strategy sets the overall direction and goals. Each plan’s QAPI program is its internal engine for measuring and improving care. External quality review provides an independent, expert assessment of each plan’s performance — the subject of its own lesson later in this course. And quality measure reporting (including HEDIS, also covered later) generates the data that feeds all of it. The contract binds the plan into this entire structure, making quality not optional but a condition of payment.
Because a capitated plan profits by spending less, there is a risk it could cut corners on care. The quality strategy, QAPI, external quality review, and measure reporting exist precisely to detect under-provision and force improvement — turning "good care" from a hope into a measured, enforceable obligation.
Quality Requirements Counter the Skimping Incentive
Reporting Requirements and Enrollee Protections
The third pillar is reporting — the data flow that lets the state see what its plans are doing. The centerpiece is the requirement under 42 CFR 438.66 that each state submit to CMS, no later than 180 days after each contract year, a Managed Care Program Annual Report (MCPAR) on each program. That report must assess, at minimum, each plan’s financial performance (including medical loss ratio), the quality and timeliness of encounter data, enrollment and benefit changes, a summary of grievances, appeals, and state fair hearings, network adequacy and access, and performance on quality measures. The MCPAR is essentially the state’s annual accountability ledger for managed care.
Two reporting streams deserve special note. Encounter data — the information about every item or service an enrollee receives under the contract — is the managed care equivalent of fee-for-service claims data, and it is essential for rate-setting, quality measurement, and oversight; the timeliness and accuracy of encounter data is itself a monitored requirement. And appeals and grievances data give a direct window into enrollee experience: enrollees can appeal service denials and file grievances about any dissatisfaction, and states must summarize each plan’s appeals, grievances, and state fair hearings for CMS in the annual MCPAR, so the state can spot a plan that is denying too much care.
These reporting requirements connect to enforcement. Federal rules require states to maintain a monitoring system spanning administration, appeals and grievances, claims, enrollee materials, finance and MLR, information systems and encounter data, marketing, medical and utilization management, program integrity, network management, quality improvement, and LTSS delivery. When monitoring reveals problems, contracts give states enforcement tools: monetary penalties, corrective action plans, suspension of new enrollment, and liquidated damages — predetermined monetary penalties written into the contract for specific failures. These are the teeth behind the requirements.
Time-and-distance and wait-time standards, LEP/disability/telehealth considerations, and network assurance reporting (NAAAR).
Network adequacy
State quality strategy, plan QAPI program, external quality review, accreditation, and quality-measure reporting.
Quality assurance
Annual MCPAR (within 180 days), encounter data, appeals/grievances reporting, backed by sanctions and liquidated damages.
Reporting and oversight
The Three Pillars of an MCO Contract
Why the Contract Is the Heart of Oversight
Everything a state can require of a plan after the contract is signed must be in the contract. This makes contract design enormously consequential — it is the state’s last and best chance to exercise leverage. A weak contract with vague standards and few reporting requirements leaves the state with little ability to hold a plan accountable; a strong contract with clear, measurable, enforceable requirements gives the state real oversight. Because the relationship runs for years, the quality of the contract determines the quality of the accountability for the entire contract term.
An MCO contract is like the franchise agreement behind a restaurant chain. The franchisee (the plan) runs the day-to-day operation, but the agreement dictates the standards it must meet — the menu it must offer (covered services), the locations it must staff (network adequacy), the inspections it must pass (quality review), and the sales reports it must file (reporting). If a location skimps, the franchise agreement’s penalty clauses (sanctions and liquidated damages) are what let headquarters force a fix. A vague agreement means a chain that can’t control its own restaurants.
How the MCO contract enables oversight
The three pillars also illustrate how managed care’s components interlock. Network adequacy without reporting would be unverifiable; quality requirements without enforcement would be toothless; reporting without standards to measure against would be meaningless. The contract weaves them together: it sets the standards (network and quality), requires the data to verify them (reporting), and attaches the consequences for failure (sanctions). Each pillar depends on the others, and the contract is what binds them into a coherent system of accountability.
This lesson sets up the rest of the course in a direct way. The monitoring and oversight lesson that follows explains how the state actually uses the reporting and enforcement provisions established here. The rate-setting module explains how the financial terms — including the encounter data and MLR provisions referenced above — are calculated. The network adequacy and quality lessons go deeper into those specific contract requirements. The contract is the hub; the operational details radiate out from it. Master what the contract requires, and you understand the structure within which all of Medicaid managed care operates.
The MCO contract converts federal rules (42 CFR Part 438) and state priorities into binding, enforceable obligations, organized around three core pillars: network adequacy, quality assurance, and reporting.
Network adequacy requirements (438.68) include quantitative standards (such as time-and-distance or provider ratios) for specified provider types plus 2024 appointment wait-time standards, and must consider LEP communication, disability accommodation, and telehealth.
States require network assurance documentation (the NAAAR) and, combined with secret-shopper surveys, verify that paper networks deliver real access.
Quality assurance requires a state quality strategy (438.340), a plan QAPI program, external quality review by an independent organization, and accreditation/measure reporting — a system that exists to counter the skimping incentive of capitation.
Reporting centers on the Managed Care Program Annual Report (MCPAR) under 438.66, due within 180 days of the contract year, covering financial performance/MLR, encounter data, enrollment/benefit changes, grievances and appeals, network adequacy, and quality measures.
Encounter data (the record of every service an enrollee receives) is the managed care equivalent of claims data and is essential for rate-setting, quality, and oversight; appeals and grievances data (summarized for CMS in the annual MCPAR) reveal enrollee experience and over-denial.
Federal rules require a broad state monitoring system, and contracts provide enforcement teeth — monetary penalties, corrective action plans, enrollment suspension, and liquidated damages (predetermined penalties for specific failures).
Because anything the state can require after signing must be in the contract, contract design is the state’s key point of leverage — a strong, measurable contract enables real oversight for the entire multi-year term.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | monitoring-oversight-eqro | Monitoring and Oversight: EQRO and State Responsibilities
Monitoring and Oversight: EQRO and State Responsibilities
Trust, but Verify — Independently
A state can write a strong contract with detailed network, quality, and reporting requirements, but a contract is only as good as the oversight behind it. How does a state actually know whether its MCOs are delivering quality care, maintaining adequate networks, and treating enrollees fairly — rather than simply claiming to? The answer combines two layers: the state’s own ongoing monitoring, and an independent, expert review conducted by a third party called an External Quality Review Organization (EQRO). This lesson is about how Medicaid managed care is actually watched.
The need for independent review flows directly from the central tension of managed care. A capitated plan has both the incentive to under-provide care and control over much of the data used to judge it. Relying solely on the plan’s self-reporting would be like grading students on tests they score themselves. The EQRO exists to break that conflict — to provide the state and CMS an objective, expert assessment of each plan’s quality, timeliness, and access, based on validated data rather than the plan’s word.
Understanding monitoring and oversight completes the procurement-and-contracting story. The procurement chose the plans; the contract defined their obligations; and oversight — anchored by the EQRO — is how the state verifies those obligations are met and acts when they are not.
Key Concept: States oversee MCOs through ongoing monitoring plus an annual External Quality Review (EQR) conducted by an independent External Quality Review Organization (EQRO), which assesses each plan’s quality, timeliness, and access and reports findings the state uses to hold plans accountable.
What External Quality Review Is
External Quality Review (EQR) is the analysis and evaluation, by an independent EQRO, of aggregated information on the quality, timeliness, and access to health care services that a managed care plan furnishes to Medicaid or CHIP enrollees. Those three dimensions — quality, timeliness, and access — are the lens through which every EQR assesses a plan. The federal parameters that states must follow when conducting EQR are set out at 42 CFR §§ 438.350, 438.354, 438.358, 438.360, and 438.364, making EQR a federally required, structured process rather than an ad hoc review.
The EQRO must be genuinely independent and qualified. Federal rules require the EQRO to have staff with demonstrated experience and knowledge of Medicaid beneficiaries, managed care delivery systems, and quality assessment methods; sufficient physical, technological, and financial resources; and the clinical and nonclinical skills to carry out the work. This independence and expertise are what give the EQRO’s findings credibility — it is not the plan grading itself, and it is not a generalist auditor, but a specialized organization equipped to evaluate managed care quality.
The Mandatory EQR Activities
EQR is built from a defined set of EQR-related activities — the work, set out at 42 CFR § 438.358, that produces the data the EQRO analyzes. Several activities are mandatory, performed on each plan. One is a compliance review, which states must conduct on each plan once within a three-year period, assessing the plan’s compliance with structural and operational standards. Another is the validation of performance measures — independently confirming that the quality measures a plan reports (such as HEDIS measures, covered later) are accurate rather than self-flattering. A third is the validation of performance improvement projects (PIPs) that are part of the plan’s QAPI program. A fourth, added by the 2016 rule, is validation of each plan’s network adequacy against the state’s §438.68 standards.
The crucial word in those activities is "validation." The EQRO does not simply accept the numbers a plan reports; it validates them — checking the methodology and data so that a plan cannot inflate its measured performance. This is the heart of breaking the self-reporting conflict. Beyond the mandatory activities, federal rules also define optional activities states may add — such as validating encounter data, administering or validating consumer and provider surveys, and conducting focused quality studies — and the 2024 final rule added EQRO help with the new managed care quality ratings. The mandatory core ensures every state’s EQR covers the essentials, while options let states tailor deeper scrutiny.
Assess each plan’s compliance with structural and operational standards once every three years.
Compliance review
Independently verify that the quality measures a plan reports are accurate.
Validation of performance measures
Confirm that the plan’s quality-improvement projects are sound and producing real improvement.
Validation of performance improvement projects (PIPs)
Validate each plan’s network against the state’s §438.68 standards (mandatory); states may add optional reviews such as encounter data validation, consumer surveys, or focused quality studies.
Validation of network adequacy (plus optional activities)
Core Mandatory EQR Activities
The EQR Technical Report — and What States Do With It
The product of all this work is the annual EQR technical report, which the EQRO must provide to the state and CMS for each plan. The report describes how the data was aggregated and analyzed for each EQR activity and draws conclusions about the quality, timeliness, and access to care the plan furnishes. Critically, it assesses each plan’s strengths and weaknesses on those dimensions and offers recommendations for improving services and for how the state can target the goals and objectives in its quality strategy. The technical report is the authoritative, independent scorecard on each plan.
But a report only matters if the state acts on it, and here states vary considerably. They range from simply noting plan performance to taking real consequences — using EQR findings to inform contract changes, require corrective action plans (CAPs), impose financial penalties, and reduce or freeze the auto-assignment of new enrollees to a poor-performing plan. That last tool is particularly powerful: auto-assignment (how the state distributes enrollees who do not choose a plan) is a major source of membership, so freezing it directly hits a plan’s growth and revenue. The strongest oversight ties EQR findings to tangible consequences.
The EQR technical report is only as effective as the state’s willingness to act on it. States that merely "note" poor performance exert little pressure; states that link EQR findings to corrective action plans, financial penalties, and frozen auto-assignment turn independent review into real accountability. Oversight is a choice, not just a process.
A Report Without Consequences Changes Nothing
The State’s Broader Monitoring Role
The EQRO is the centerpiece, but the state retains a broad, ongoing monitoring role that surrounds it. As the contract lesson described, federal rules require states to maintain a monitoring system spanning administration, appeals and grievances, claims, finance and MLR, encounter data, medical and utilization management, program integrity, network management, quality improvement, and LTSS. CMS reinforces this with required reports — the Managed Care Program Annual Report (MCPAR) under 42 CFR § 438.66(e), the medical loss ratio summary reports under § 438.74, and the network adequacy assurance under § 438.207(d) — that compel states to compile and submit evidence of their oversight to the federal government.
State oversight of MCOs works like the oversight of a restaurant. The state’s ongoing monitoring is the manager checking the books, the complaints, and the daily operations. The EQRO is the independent health inspector who arrives annually, validates that the kitchen really meets standards rather than taking the owner’s word, and files a detailed report on what is clean and what is not. And the enforcement tools — corrective action plans, fines, freezing new business — are what give the inspection teeth. Without the independent inspector, the owner grades their own kitchen; without enforcement, even a damning inspection changes nothing.
The layers of Medicaid managed care oversight
This layered structure — independent expert review (EQRO) plus continuous state monitoring plus federal reporting — exists because the stakes are so high and the conflict of interest so real. Billions in public dollars flow to private plans serving vulnerable populations, and those plans profit by spending less. Oversight is the mechanism that lets a state capture managed care’s benefits (predictability, coordination) while guarding against its risks (under-provision, cherry-picking, poor quality). It is the practical answer to the question that opened the course: how do you trust private plans with public care?
This lesson closes the procurement-and-contracting arc and opens onto the rest of the course. Oversight depends on the data and standards established elsewhere: the quality measures validated by the EQRO are detailed in the HEDIS and quality lessons; the financial oversight connects to the rate-setting and MLR module; the network reviews connect to the network-adequacy lesson. Monitoring is not a separate silo but the verification layer that makes every other requirement real. A state that selects good plans, writes a strong contract, and oversees rigorously has built the full machinery of accountable Medicaid managed care.
States oversee MCOs through two layers: their own ongoing monitoring and an annual External Quality Review (EQR) conducted by an independent External Quality Review Organization (EQRO).
EQR is the independent analysis of aggregated information on the quality, timeliness, and access to care a plan furnishes, governed by federal parameters at 42 CFR §§ 438.350–438.364.
The EQRO must be independent and qualified, with demonstrated expertise in Medicaid beneficiaries, managed care delivery, and quality assessment — so findings come from a specialized third party, not the plan grading itself.
Mandatory EQR activities (438.358) include a compliance review once every three years, validation of reported performance measures, validation of performance improvement projects (PIPs), and validation of network adequacy; states may add optional activities such as encounter data validation or consumer surveys.
The key word is "validation" — the EQRO verifies the accuracy of what plans report rather than accepting it, breaking the self-reporting conflict of interest.
The annual EQR technical report assesses each plan’s strengths, weaknesses, and recommendations on quality, timeliness, and access, and is provided to the state and CMS as the authoritative independent scorecard.
States vary in acting on findings — from merely noting performance to imposing corrective action plans, financial penalties, and reducing or freezing auto-assignment of enrollees (a powerful lever on a plan’s revenue).
Surrounding the EQRO, states maintain a broad monitoring system and submit federally required reports (the Managed Care Program Annual Report under 438.66(e), MLR summary reports under 438.74, and network adequacy assurances under 438.207(d)), creating a layered structure that lets states capture managed care’s benefits while guarding against its risks.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | capitation-rate-setting | How Medicaid Capitation Rates Are Set
How Medicaid Capitation Rates Are Set
The Single Number That Makes Managed Care Work
Everything about Medicaid managed care hinges on one number: the capitation rate — the fixed amount per member per month (PMPM) that a state pays an MCO to cover a defined population’s care. Set that number too high, and the state wastes taxpayer money and overpays plans for little benefit. Set it too low, and plans cannot deliver adequate care, may cut corners or avoid sick members, and could exit the market entirely. The entire promise of managed care — budget predictability with adequate care — depends on getting this number right. This lesson explains how that number is actually built.
Capitation rate-setting is a technical, actuarial discipline, but its logic is comprehensible and its stakes are enormous. Because the rate determines both the state’s spending and the plans’ resources, federal law surrounds it with a strict requirement: actuarial soundness. Rates cannot be a political guess or a budget target imposed from above; they must be developed by qualified actuaries according to professional standards and certified to CMS. Understanding actuarial soundness and the rate-development process is understanding the financial heart of Medicaid managed care.
The governing rule is 42 CFR 438.4, the federal regulation on actuarial soundness, supported by detailed annual CMS rate development guides. Together they define what a sound rate is, how it must be built, and how it must be documented — turning a single PMPM figure into a rigorously justified calculation.
Key Concept: A Medicaid capitation rate is the fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment to an MCO. Federal law (42 CFR 438.4) requires rates to be "actuarially sound" — projected to cover all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs for the population and services, developed by qualified actuaries and certified to CMS.
When a state certifies a range of rates per cell, the upper bound cannot exceed the lower bound multiplied by 1.05 — a 5% maximum range (CMS final rule)
Maximum Rate Range
≤ 5%
A state may move up to 1.5% in either direction from the certified rate without notifying CMS — roughly the typical risk margin in rate-setting (CMS)
Movement Without Notice
±1.5%
What "Actuarially Sound" Means
Actuarial soundness is the legal and professional standard that governs every Medicaid capitation rate. Under the regulation, actuarially sound capitation rates are those projected to provide for all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs required under the contract and for the operation of the plan, for the covered time period and population, developed in accordance with generally accepted actuarial principles and practices. In plain terms: the rate must realistically cover what it actually costs to care for the population, plus the legitimate costs of running the plan — no more, no less.
Two features of this standard matter. First, rates must be developed and certified by qualified actuaries, professionals bound by actuarial standards of practice — not set by political fiat. This is a safeguard against states lowballing rates to fit a budget, which would undermine care, and against plans inflating rates beyond justified costs. Second, the standard is forward-looking and population-specific: it asks what the defined population will reasonably cost in the coming period, which requires projecting from historical experience into the future.
Actuarial soundness is not just a technicality — it is the guardrail that keeps rates honest. It prevents states from setting rates so low that plans must skimp on care or flee the market, and prevents rates so high that taxpayers overpay. The requirement that a qualified actuary certify the rate is what gives that guardrail teeth.
Soundness Protects Both Sides
Building the Rate: Base Data, Trend, and Adjustments
How does an actuary actually build a sound rate? The process, outlined in federal rules (42 CFR 438.5(b)), follows a logical sequence. It begins with base data: identifying and developing base utilization and price data from the actual experience of the Medicaid population (or a similar population) — essentially, what did it cost to provide care to these people recently, drawn largely from the encounter data discussed in earlier lessons. This historical experience is the foundation everything else builds on.
Next comes trend: the actuary develops and applies trend factors to project the base data forward, accounting for how costs will change due to medical inflation, shifts in utilization, new treatments, and price growth. A rate for next year cannot simply repeat last year’s costs; it must anticipate where costs are heading. After trending, the actuary applies adjustments — for changes in covered benefits, eligibility, program design, and special considerations for individuals with chronic illness, disability, ongoing needs, or catastrophic claims. Finally, the rate must account for the plan’s non-medical costs: an administrative load (the cost of running the plan) and a risk margin (compensation for bearing financial risk).
Use actual historical utilization and price data from the Medicaid (or similar) population, drawn largely from encounter data.
Start with base data
Project costs forward for medical inflation, utilization changes, and new treatments.
Apply trend factors
Account for benefit, eligibility, and program changes, plus chronic illness, disability, and catastrophic claims.
Make adjustments
Include the legitimate cost of operating the plan and compensation for bearing financial risk.
Add administrative load and risk margin
How a Capitation Rate Is Built
The result is not a single statewide number but a set of rates organized into rate cells — rate groupings specific to eligibility category, age, gender, locality or region, and optionally diagnosis or health status. Rate cells matter because different populations cost vastly different amounts: a healthy child costs far less than an elderly person with disabilities. By setting a distinct rate for each cell, the system pays plans appropriately for whatever mix of members they actually enroll — and reduces (though does not eliminate) the incentive to cherry-pick, a problem addressed more directly by risk adjustment in the next lesson.
Rate Ranges, MLR Targets, and Certification
Rate development does not always produce a single point; states may develop and certify a range of capitation rates per rate cell, as long as the certification identifies and justifies the assumptions, data, and methodologies for both the upper and lower bounds. But the range is bounded: the upper bound of a rate range cannot exceed the lower bound multiplied by 1.05 — a maximum 5% range. Separately, the rules permit a state to move up to 1.5% in either direction from the certified rate without notifying CMS, a figure CMS chose because it is generally not more than the risk margin in a typical rate-setting process. These guardrails prevent rate ranges from becoming a backdoor for arbitrary rate-setting.
The rate must also align with the medical loss ratio standard from earlier lessons. The certified rates must target an MLR of at least 85%, meaning the rate is built so that at least 85 cents of every dollar is expected to go to medical care and quality rather than administration and profit; states may target a higher MLR if they choose. This links rate-setting to the MLR requirement covered in its own lesson — the rate is constructed with the MLR floor in mind, and the MLR is then measured against actual experience.
Finally, none of this is valid until certified. CMS uses "rate certification" to mean both the actuary’s letter attesting that the rates are actuarially sound and meet federal requirements, and all the supporting documentation — the actuarial report, data, memos, and workbooks behind it. CMS reviews this certification before approving the rates, and only approved rates can be paid with federal matching funds. The certification is the formal proof that the single PMPM number rests on a rigorous, documented, professionally sound foundation.
Why Rate-Setting Is the Make-or-Break Function
Capitation rate-setting is where the abstract promise of managed care meets hard arithmetic. Every other element of the program — network adequacy, quality, care management — depends on plans having enough money to deliver, and not so much that the program is wasteful. Get the rate right, and plans can build real networks and manage care well while the state controls spending. Get it wrong in either direction, and the whole edifice wobbles: underfunded plans skimp or exit, overfunded plans pocket the difference, and either way the public interest suffers.
Setting a capitation rate is like a city setting the fixed annual fee it pays a contractor to maintain all its parks. Set it from real data on what upkeep actually costs (base data), adjusted for rising wages and materials (trend) and for how many parks and how big (rate cells and adjustments), plus a fair amount for the contractor’s overhead and risk. Pay too little and the parks go to seed; pay too much and taxpayers are fleeced. And a qualified, independent estimator (the actuary) must certify the number is honest before the city signs the check.
How Medicaid capitation rates are built
This is also why rate-setting connects to so much else in the course. The base data comes from encounter data, whose accuracy the contract and oversight lessons emphasized. The rate cells set the stage for risk adjustment, the next lesson’s subject, which refines payment for the actual health of enrolled members. The 85% MLR target ties to the MLR lesson that follows. And the actuarial soundness requirement is itself a Part 438 mandate from the federal-framework lesson. Rate-setting is the financial hub where data, regulation, and the other operational pieces converge into the payment that drives the entire system.
For the student, the key insight is that the capitation rate is neither a guess nor a negotiation in the ordinary sense — it is a regulated, actuarial calculation built from real experience, projected forward, adjusted for population and program, and certified by professionals. The discipline of actuarial soundness exists precisely because the number is so consequential. When you understand how a Medicaid capitation rate is set, you understand how a state turns its budget into adequate care for millions of people — and why so much regulatory care surrounds that single PMPM figure.
A Medicaid capitation rate is the fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment to an MCO, and federal law (42 CFR 438.4) requires it to be "actuarially sound" — projected to cover all reasonable, appropriate, and attainable costs for the population and services.
Actuarial soundness requires rates to be developed and certified by qualified actuaries per generally accepted actuarial principles, protecting against rates set too low (forcing skimping or market exit) or too high (wasting taxpayer money).
Rates are built in a sequence: start with base utilization and price data from actual experience (largely encounter data), apply trend factors to project forward, make adjustments for benefit/eligibility/program changes and high-need members, and add administrative load and risk margin.
Rates are organized into rate cells specific to eligibility category, age, gender, region, and optionally health status, so plans are paid appropriately for the mix of members they enroll.
States may certify a range of rates per cell, but the upper bound cannot exceed 1.05× the lower bound (a 5% maximum range), and a state may move ±1.5% from the certified rate without notifying CMS (roughly the typical risk margin).
Certified rates must target a medical loss ratio of at least 85%, linking rate-setting to the MLR requirement, with states free to target a higher MLR.
A rate is valid only when certified — the actuary’s attestation plus all supporting documentation — which CMS reviews before approving rates for federal matching funds.
Rate-setting is the financial hub of managed care: it draws on encounter data, sets the stage for risk adjustment, ties to the MLR standard, and determines whether plans can deliver adequate care while the state controls spending.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | risk-adjustment-medicaid | Risk Adjustment in Medicaid Managed Care
Risk Adjustment in Medicaid Managed Care
The Problem That Risk Adjustment Solves
The previous lesson showed how states set capitation rates and organize them into rate cells by age, gender, eligibility, and region. But those broad cells leave a dangerous gap. Within the same cell — say, adult expansion enrollees in one region — one plan might enroll relatively healthy members while another enrolls people with diabetes, serious mental illness, and disabilities. If both plans receive the same capitation, the plan with sicker members is badly underpaid and the plan with healthier members is overpaid. Worse, every plan now has a powerful incentive to attract the healthy and avoid the sick. This is the cherry-picking problem, and risk adjustment is the tool built to solve it.
Risk adjustment modifies the capitation payment to each plan based on the measured health status of the members it actually enrolls. A plan that enrolls sicker, more expensive members receives more; a plan that enrolls healthier, cheaper members receives less. The goal, in the words of the field, is to align expected revenues with expected costs so that both high- and low-cost enrollees are attractive to plans. When risk adjustment works, a plan no longer profits by avoiding sick people — it is paid fairly to care for them.
This makes risk adjustment one of the most important safeguards in all of Medicaid managed care. It directly attacks the central risk of capitation — that plans will select healthy members and shun expensive ones — by changing the economics so that caring for the sick is financially viable. Understanding how it works is essential to understanding how managed care can serve vulnerable, high-need populations at all.
Key Concept: Risk adjustment modifies capitation payments based on the measured health status of each plan’s enrolled members — paying more for sicker members and less for healthier ones — to align expected revenue with expected cost and remove the incentive to cherry-pick healthy enrollees.
Of the 38 Medicaid programs that risk-adjust MCO payments, 33 use the Chronic Illness and Disability Payment System (CDPS) or a related model (Medical Care, 2024 — UC San Diego and the Institute for Medicaid Innovation)
States Using CDPS
33 of 38
CDPS uses ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes grouped into condition categories to measure each member’s illness burden (UC San Diego / Find-A-Code)
How CDPS Measures Risk
Diagnosis-based
How Risk Adjustment Works
At its core, risk adjustment assigns each member a risk score reflecting their predicted health care costs relative to the average. A member with no significant conditions might have a risk score near 1.0 (average); a member with multiple chronic illnesses might score 3.0 or higher, signaling expected costs three times the average. The plan’s overall risk score is the average across its members, and its capitation is adjusted up or down accordingly. A plan with a population risk score of 1.2 enrolls members who are 20% costlier than average and is paid more to reflect that.
These risk scores are built from data the program already collects. Risk-adjustment models typically use diagnosis or pharmaceutical codes from claims or encounter data to measure illness burden among enrolled members. This is another reason the encounter data emphasized in the contract and oversight lessons matters so much: it is the raw material from which risk scores — and therefore payments — are calculated. Inaccurate or incomplete encounter data produces inaccurate risk scores and unfair payments.
Risk adjustment can be applied prospectively (using a member’s diagnoses from a prior period to set payment for the coming period) or concurrently/retrospectively (adjusting for conditions in the same period being paid). Prospective adjustment is more common and predictable, but retrospective adjustment can better reduce a plan’s worry about unexpectedly sick enrollees. Either way, the model translates clinical reality into a payment signal that follows the patient to whichever plan enrolls them.
CDPS: The Workhorse Model
The dominant risk-adjustment model in Medicaid is the Chronic Illness and Disability Payment System (CDPS), developed at the University of California, San Diego. CDPS is a diagnosis-based model: it uses ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes, grouped into categories for different diseases and conditions (such as psychiatric or cancer categories), to measure each member’s illness burden. Its adoption is striking — of the 38 Medicaid programs that risk-adjust MCO payments, 33 use CDPS or a related model, making it the de facto standard for Medicaid.
CDPS was designed specifically for the Medicaid population, which is exactly why it dominates. Unlike models built for commercial or Medicare populations, CDPS accounts for the chronic illnesses, disabilities, and complex conditions disproportionately present among Medicaid enrollees, helping ensure more accurate funding for complex care needs. This Medicaid-specific calibration matters: a risk model that underweighted the conditions common in Medicaid would systematically underpay the plans serving the neediest members.
The model has enhanced variants that add pharmacy data. Medicaid Rx (MRx) is a pharmacy-based system that uses National Drug Code (NDC) data to infer conditions from the drugs a member takes, and CDPS+Rx combines diagnosis-based CDPS with pharmacy-based MRx for a fuller picture. Pharmacy data can capture conditions that diagnosis codes miss and can be timelier. The model is also periodically updated — the Institute for Medicaid Innovation partnered with UC San Diego to refresh the weights using national Medicaid managed care data, producing CDPS+Rx version 7 — so the payment signal stays calibrated to current clinical and cost patterns.
Gather the diagnosis (ICD-10-CM) and pharmacy (NDC) codes for each member.
Collect encounter/claims data
CDPS/CDPS+Rx groups codes into disease categories reflecting cost burden.
Map codes to condition categories
Combine the member’s conditions into a risk score relative to the average (1.0).
Calculate a risk score
Pay each plan according to the average risk score of its enrolled members.
Adjust the capitation payment
From Diagnosis to Adjusted Payment
Reallocation, Budget Neutrality, and Limits
Risk adjustment is typically applied in a budget-neutral way: it does not change the total amount the state spends, but reallocates it among plans. The mechanism effectively shifts capitation payments away from plans with healthier-than-average members toward plans with sicker-than-average members, bringing each plan’s payment closer to the expected cost of the members it actually enrolls. The total pie stays the same; risk adjustment just slices it according to who is caring for whom. This is what makes it a fairness mechanism rather than a spending increase.
The better the model predicts cost, the better it works. The stronger a risk-adjustment tool’s predictive capacity, the less incentive plans have to cherry-pick healthy enrollees, because plans can trust that the system will adequately compensate them if they end up with relatively expensive members. A precise model makes sick members no less attractive than healthy ones, which is the entire point. A crude model leaves residual incentives to select, undermining the goal.
No risk model predicts cost perfectly. Research from Medicare Advantage shows that even after risk adjustment, plans can enroll members with high risk scores but lower-than-predicted actual costs — "overpriced" enrollees. Risk adjustment dramatically reduces the incentive to cherry-pick, but it does not eliminate selection entirely, which is why oversight of enrollment and quality remains necessary.
Risk Adjustment Is Powerful but Imperfect
Why Risk Adjustment Holds the System Together
Risk adjustment is the quiet linchpin that makes Medicaid managed care viable for vulnerable populations. Without it, the financial logic of capitation would steadily push plans to compete for the healthy and shun the sick, leaving the most expensive and most needy members — people with disabilities, serious mental illness, and complex chronic conditions — as financial liabilities no plan wants. Risk adjustment flips that logic: by paying more for sicker members, it makes those members financially viable to enroll and care for, which is a precondition for serving them at all.
Risk adjustment is like adjusting a potluck contribution by what each guest will actually eat. If everyone paid the same flat amount, hosts would compete to invite light eaters and shun anyone with a big appetite. Instead, the organizer estimates each guest’s appetite (risk score) and pays the host accordingly, so a host who welcomes the hungriest guests is funded to feed them — and no host has a reason to turn anyone away. The total budget is the same; it is just shared out to match who is actually being fed.
How risk adjustment reallocates capitation
This lesson sits at the center of the rate-setting module for a reason. The previous lesson built the base capitation rate; this one refines it to match the actual health of enrolled members; and the next lesson, on medical loss ratios, ensures that whatever a plan is paid, enough of it goes to care. Together they form the financial spine of managed care: a sound rate, adjusted for risk, with a floor on how much must be spent on members. Risk adjustment is the part that makes the system fair across plans serving different populations.
For the student, the essential takeaway is that risk adjustment is what allows a capitated system to serve the sick. It is imperfect — no model captures cost perfectly, and residual selection incentives remain — but it transforms the economics enough that plans can compete on managing care well rather than on avoiding expensive people. When you see a Medicaid program risk-adjust its payments with CDPS, you are watching the mechanism that keeps the promise of managed care honest for the members who need care the most.
Risk adjustment modifies capitation payments based on the measured health status of each plan’s enrolled members — more for sicker members, less for healthier ones — to align expected revenue with expected cost.
Its central purpose is to remove the cherry-picking incentive: by paying fairly for sick members, it makes both high- and low-cost enrollees attractive to plans.
Each member gets a risk score relative to the average (1.0); a plan’s payment is adjusted by the average risk score of its members, calculated from diagnosis and pharmacy codes in claims/encounter data.
Risk adjustment can be prospective (prior-period diagnoses set future payment) or concurrent/retrospective; prospective is more common, while retrospective can better reduce plans’ fear of unexpectedly sick enrollees.
The dominant model is the diagnosis-based Chronic Illness and Disability Payment System (CDPS) from UC San Diego — used by 33 of the 38 Medicaid programs that risk-adjust — designed specifically for the Medicaid population’s chronic and disabling conditions.
Enhanced variants add pharmacy data: MRx uses NDC drug codes, and CDPS+Rx combines diagnosis- and pharmacy-based measurement; the model is periodically updated (e.g., CDPS+Rx version 7) to stay calibrated.
Risk adjustment is typically budget-neutral, reallocating the same total spending away from healthier plans toward sicker plans rather than increasing overall cost.
It is powerful but imperfect — even after risk adjustment, plans can enroll high-scoring but lower-cost "overpriced" members — so it greatly reduces but does not eliminate selection, and oversight remains necessary.
