######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | mlr-requirements | MLR Requirements and Profit Limits
MLR Requirements and Profit Limits
The Rule That Limits How Much a Plan Can Keep
The previous two lessons explained how a state sets a capitation rate and adjusts it for the health of each plan’s members. But once the money is paid, a new question arises: how much of it must actually be spent on care, versus kept by the plan as administration and profit? Without an answer, a capitated plan could pocket a large share of public dollars while delivering minimal care — the worst version of the under-provision incentive that runs through this entire course. The medical loss ratio (MLR) is the rule that answers this question and sets a floor on how much of each capitation dollar must go to members.
The medical loss ratio is the share of premium (capitation) revenue that a plan spends on medical care and quality improvement, rather than on administration, marketing, and profit. An 85% MLR means at least 85 cents of every dollar goes to care and quality, leaving at most 15 cents for everything else. The MLR is, in effect, a profit-and-overhead limit expressed from the other direction: by requiring most of the money to be spent on care, it caps how much can be retained.
For Medicaid, the MLR is both a financial-integrity safeguard and a complement to rate-setting. Recall from the rate-setting lesson that certified rates must target an MLR of at least 85%; the MLR requirement then measures whether actual spending lived up to that target. Together, they ensure rates are built to fund care and that the money paid actually reaches care. This lesson explains how the MLR is calculated, enforced, and where it differs from its better-known commercial cousin.
Key Concept: The medical loss ratio (MLR) is the share of capitation revenue a plan spends on medical care and quality improvement rather than administration and profit. Under 42 CFR 438.8, any state-mandated minimum MLR must be at least 85%, functioning as a floor on care spending and a cap on overhead and profit.
If a state mandates a minimum MLR, it must be equal to or higher than 85 percent — at least 85 cents of every dollar spent on care and quality (42 CFR 438.8)
Minimum MLR Floor
≥ 85%
In the ACA Marketplaces, plans rebated $1.1 billion to enrollees in 2023 for missing MLR targets — a contrast with Medicaid, where remittances go to the state and are optional (KFF)
ACA Rebates (2023)
$1.1B
How the MLR Is Calculated
The MLR is a fraction: care-and-quality spending divided by adjusted revenue. Federal rules (42 CFR 438.8) define each part precisely. The numerator is the sum of the plan’s incurred claims (the direct cost of covered services, including payments to network providers and amounts for claims still being processed or incurred but not yet reported), plus expenditures for activities that improve health care quality, plus fraud prevention activities. In other words, the numerator captures money spent on actual care and on legitimate quality and integrity work — the things the MLR is meant to reward.
The denominator is adjusted premium revenue: the plan’s premium (capitation) revenue minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing and regulatory fees. Subtracting those taxes and fees is important — it ensures the plan is not penalized for money it never really had to spend on care, because that money went to the government, not to overhead or profit. Dividing the care-and-quality numerator by the adjusted-revenue denominator yields the MLR percentage.
One technical refinement matters: the credibility adjustment. Small plans with few enrollees have MLRs that swing widely due to random statistical variation — a single catastrophic case can distort a small plan’s ratio. The credibility adjustment accounts for this random variation related to the number of enrollees, giving smaller plans some allowance so they are not unfairly penalized (or rewarded) for what is essentially statistical noise rather than how they actually managed care. Larger plans, whose numbers are statistically stable, receive little or no adjustment.
Add incurred claims, quality-improvement expenditures, and fraud-prevention activities — money spent on care and quality.
Build the numerator
Take premium (capitation) revenue and subtract federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees.
Build the denominator
Numerator ÷ denominator, adjusted for random variation in small plans, yields the MLR percentage.
Divide and apply credibility adjustment
Measure the result against the state’s minimum (at least 85%) to determine compliance.
Compare to the minimum
The MLR Calculation
Remittance: What Happens When a Plan Falls Short
Setting a minimum MLR is meaningless without a consequence for missing it, and that consequence is the remittance — a payment a plan must make when its MLR falls below the minimum. If a plan’s MLR comes in below 85% (meaning it spent less than 85% on care and kept more than 15%), the state can require the plan to remit the shortfall. This is what gives the MLR teeth: a plan cannot simply under-spend on care and pocket the difference, because the difference must be paid back.
Some states have built creative alternatives to a straight cash remittance. In North Carolina, plans that miss the MLR may contribute to health-related resources in lieu of all or part of the remittance, submitting proposals that align with the state’s quality strategy for approval. Tennessee similarly lets a plan below 85% either remit funds or propose a community reinvestment plan for state approval. These approaches turn the penalty into reinvestment — redirecting underspent dollars back into community health rather than simply clawing them to the treasury.
Because the numerator includes quality-improvement and provider-incentive spending, plans can be tempted to inflate those categories to artificially raise their MLR and avoid remittances. The 2024 final rule specifically targets this, noting that disconnecting provider incentive payments from actual measurable quality standards creates a risk of artificially inflated qualifying costs and manipulated MLR percentages.
Watch for MLR Manipulation
How Medicaid MLR Differs From Commercial
The MLR concept is most famous from the Affordable Care Act, which applies it to commercial insurance — but the Medicaid version differs in two crucial ways. First, enforcement and where the money goes. In the ACA Marketplaces, plans that miss the MLR target must return the excess to enrollees as rebates — totaling $1.1 billion in 2023. In Medicaid, by contrast, any remittance goes to the state (and ultimately back to federal and state taxpayers who funded the capitation), not to individual enrollees, because Medicaid enrollees did not pay premiums in the first place.
Second, and more striking, is that the Medicaid MLR is largely optional for states. Under federal law, states that contract with MCOs have the flexibility to decide whether to impose a minimum MLR requirement at all, and if so, whether to collect remittances from plans that fall short. Federal rules require that all plans calculate and report their MLR, and that any state-set minimum be at least 85% — but they do not force a state to set a minimum or to collect a remittance. CMS considers a minimum MLR with a remittance to be a reasonable program-integrity approach, but it is the state’s choice.
This flexibility is consequential and controversial. It means a state could require plans to report MLRs that reveal low care spending and high retention, yet collect nothing back — a gap critics have noted, observing that Congress and CMS have stopped short of a uniform, mandatory Medicaid MLR with required rebates. The reporting requirement still creates transparency and pressure, but the actual financial bite depends on whether each state chooses to wield it.
Why the MLR Completes the Financial Spine
The MLR is the final piece of the rate-setting module’s financial spine, and it interlocks with the other two. Rate-setting determines how much a plan is paid; risk adjustment ensures that payment matches the health of the members enrolled; and the MLR ensures that, whatever the plan is paid, most of it is actually spent on care. Remove any one and the system fails: a sound, risk-adjusted rate could still be largely pocketed without an MLR floor, and an MLR floor on an unsound rate would just enforce inadequate spending. The three work only together.
The MLR is like a rule that a charity must spend at least 85 cents of every donated dollar on its mission, keeping no more than 15 cents for overhead and salaries. Donors (here, taxpayers) get assurance their money reaches the cause rather than the office. And if the charity spends too little on the mission, it must give the surplus back. The Medicaid twist is that whether the "give it back" rule is enforced — and how strictly — is left to each state to decide.
How the medical loss ratio works
The MLR also reframes how to think about a managed care plan’s profit. A plan does not profit by being paid more — the capitation is fixed and risk-adjusted — nor simply by spending less on care, because the MLR floor limits that. In principle, a plan profits by managing care efficiently: reducing avoidable utilization and administrative waste while still meeting the MLR and quality requirements. The MLR is designed to channel the plan’s drive for profit away from skimping on care and toward genuine efficiency, which is the behavior managed care is supposed to reward.
For the student, the MLR is the clearest expression of how Medicaid managed care tries to reconcile private profit with public purpose. By requiring most of every public dollar to reach care, it limits the harm a profit motive can do; by leaving plans room for efficiency gains, it preserves the incentive that makes managed care work. Its optional, state-by-state enforcement also illustrates the federal-state tension that runs through Medicaid — a federal floor on the percentage, but state discretion on whether to enforce it. Master the MLR, and you understand the rule that keeps capitation honest about where the money goes.
The medical loss ratio (MLR) is the share of capitation revenue a plan spends on medical care and quality improvement rather than administration and profit; an 85% MLR means at least 85 cents of every dollar goes to care.
Under 42 CFR 438.8, any state-mandated minimum MLR must be at least 85%, functioning simultaneously as a floor on care spending and a cap on overhead and profit.
The MLR numerator is incurred claims plus quality-improvement and fraud-prevention spending; the denominator is adjusted premium revenue (premium minus federal, state, and local taxes and licensing/regulatory fees).
A credibility adjustment accounts for random statistical variation in small plans, so a few catastrophic cases do not unfairly distort a small plan’s MLR.
When a plan’s MLR falls below the minimum, the state can require a remittance (paying back the shortfall); some states (e.g., North Carolina, Tennessee) allow community reinvestment plans in lieu of cash remittance.
Medicaid MLR differs from commercial/ACA MLR in two ways: remittances go to the state (not rebated to enrollees as in the ACA’s $1.1 billion in 2023 rebates), and setting a minimum MLR and collecting remittances is largely optional for states.
Because the numerator includes quality and provider-incentive spending, plans can attempt to inflate it to avoid remittances — a manipulation the 2024 final rule specifically targets by tightening the link between incentive payments and measurable quality.
The MLR completes the financial spine with rate-setting and risk adjustment, channeling a plan’s profit motive away from skimping on care and toward genuine efficiency.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | covered-benefits-carveins-carveouts | Covered Benefits: Carve-Ins vs Carve-Outs
Covered Benefits: Carve-Ins vs. Carve-Outs
Deciding What the Plan Is Responsible For
When a state contracts with an MCO, one of the most consequential design decisions is also one of the least visible: exactly which services the plan is responsible for. It would seem obvious that a comprehensive plan should cover everything, but Medicaid programs routinely pull certain services out of the MCO contract and manage them separately. These decisions — to "carve in" or "carve out" a benefit — shape how care is delivered, how it is coordinated, and whether a member’s care is unified or fragmented across multiple systems.
The terminology is simple. A carve-in is a service that remains within or is integrated into the MCO’s responsibility — the plan provides it and is paid (through capitation) to cover it. A carve-out is a service removed from the MCO benefit package — the plan neither provides it nor receives payment for it, and the state manages that service through a separate arrangement, such as a limited-benefit plan or fee-for-service. Every Medicaid managed care program is, in effect, a set of decisions about which benefits to carve in and which to carve out.
These decisions carry real stakes for members and for the system. Carve-outs can bring specialized expertise to complex services but risk fragmenting a person’s care across disconnected plans; carve-ins promise integration and "whole-person care" but depend on the MCO actually coordinating well. This lesson examines which services are commonly carved out, the strong recent trend toward carving them back in, and the surprisingly mixed evidence on whether integration delivers.
Key Concept: A carve-in keeps a service within the MCO’s capitated responsibility; a carve-out removes it, so the plan neither provides nor is paid for it and the state manages it separately. The mix of carve-ins and carve-outs defines the scope of each MCO contract and how integrated a member’s care is.
In 2023, over two-thirds of comprehensive MCO enrollees were also in at least one limited-benefit plan and/or received fee-for-service care outside their MCO (KFF)
MCO Enrollees Also Using Carved-Out Care
2/3+
California, Missouri, North Dakota, Tennessee, West Virginia, and Wisconsin as of July 2022 (KFF), plus New York from April 2023
Carving Pharmacy Out of MCOs
7 states
What Gets Carved Out — and Why
A handful of services are carved out far more often than others, and they share a common trait: they are specialized, distinct from general medical care, and historically managed through their own systems. The services most frequently carved out of Medicaid managed care are behavioral health (mental health and substance use), dental, pharmacy, and non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT). Behavioral health is the most commonly carved-out service of all, reflecting a long history of separate mental health systems and specialized provider networks.
The rationale for carving out is real. A specialized service may benefit from a vendor with deep, focused expertise — a behavioral health organization that understands serious mental illness, a dental plan with a dedicated dentist network, a transportation broker that manages rides. Carving out lets the state contract with an entity built specifically for that service, rather than expecting a general medical MCO to manage something far outside its core competence. When done well, a carve-out delivers specialized management that a comprehensive plan might handle poorly.
But carve-outs come at a cost: fragmentation. When a member’s behavioral health is managed by one entity, their physical health by another, their pharmacy by a third, and their transportation by a fourth, no single organization sees the whole person. A patient with serious mental illness and diabetes may have their psychiatric care and their diabetes care managed by entities that never communicate. This fragmentation is precisely the problem that the integration movement, discussed next, aims to solve.
Carve-In (Integrated)
Service stays within the MCO’s capitation
One plan responsible for the whole person
Easier coordination across physical and other care
Depends on the MCO actually integrating care
Aligned with "whole-person care" goals
Carve-Out (Separate)
Service removed from the MCO benefit package
Managed by a specialized vendor or fee-for-service
Brings focused expertise to complex services
Risks fragmenting a member’s care across systems
Requires deliberate cross-system coordination
Carve-In vs. Carve-Out
The Trend: Carving Back In
Over the past decade, the dominant trend has been to carve services back in — to integrate them into comprehensive MCOs in pursuit of "whole-person care." The shift in behavioral health is striking: over the last decade many states moved from carving behavioral health out to carving it in, and a significant majority of states with Medicaid managed care now carve in behavioral health services for at least some enrollees, while others use mixed "carve-up" approaches that carve in some populations or services and carve out others — driven by a clear policy preference for integration.
Pharmacy is the notable exception: most MCO states still carve pharmacy in, but a handful — including California (2022) and New York (2023) — have carved prescription drugs out of MCO contracts to centralize purchasing. The logic behind carving in is intuitive and powerful — when one plan is responsible for all of a member’s care, it has both the information and the financial incentive to coordinate across physical health, behavioral health, and pharmacy, treating the person as a whole rather than a collection of disconnected benefits.
This integration goal connects directly to the financial model. A fully capitated MCO responsible for the whole person internalizes the trade-offs: it benefits financially when better behavioral health care reduces avoidable medical admissions, or when managing medications prevents hospitalizations. Under carve-outs, those savings flow to a different entity — a version of the "wrong pocket problem." Carving in aligns the incentives so that one plan profits from coordinating the member’s total care, which is the theoretical heart of the whole-person-care argument.
Does Integration Actually Work?
Given the strength of the carve-in trend, one might expect clear evidence that integration improves care. The reality is more humbling. Research on whether carve-in models deliver better outcomes is genuinely mixed. Some studies have found that access to and utilization of services was not better at integrated MCOs compared to carve-out models, finding no consistent association between integration and claims-based measures of utilization and quality. In other words, simply putting a benefit inside the MCO contract did not, by itself, produce better care.
Yet other evidence is more encouraging. In New York and Oregon, behavioral health integration led to higher use of both behavioral and physical health outpatient services among individuals with serious mental illness and those with milder behavioral health needs — suggesting integration can improve access when implemented well. The divergence points to a crucial lesson: the outcome depends not on the contracting structure alone, but on how the integration is actually executed.
Putting two benefits in the same MCO contract (financial integration) does not guarantee that the administration and delivery of care are actually coordinated (clinical integration). States seeking real integration must pair the contracting change with investments in workforce, data analytics, and performance oversight — otherwise a carve-in is integration in name only.
Financial Integration Is Not Clinical Integration
Designing the Benefit Package
For a state Medicaid program, the carve-in/carve-out decision is a balancing act with no universally right answer. Carving in offers the promise of coordinated, whole-person care and aligned incentives, but only if the MCO genuinely integrates the service rather than administering it in a silo. Carving out offers specialized expertise and focused management, but at the risk of fragmenting the member’s experience. The right choice depends on the service, the state’s MCO capabilities, the strength of specialized vendors, and how much the state is willing to invest in making integration real.
Carve-ins and carve-outs are like deciding whether one general contractor handles your entire home renovation or you hire separate specialists for plumbing, electrical, and roofing. The single contractor (carve-in) can coordinate everything and is accountable for the whole project — but only if they actually manage the subtrades well. Hiring separate specialists (carve-out) gets you deep expertise in each area, but now someone has to make sure the plumber and electrician don’t work at cross-purposes. Neither is automatically better; it depends on the contractor’s coordinating skill.
Carve-in vs. carve-out benefit design
Two requirements cut across the decision regardless of structure. First, care coordination: whether a service is carved in or out, states and plans are responsible for coordinating care across delivery systems so the member does not fall through the cracks. Second, behavioral health parity: federal rules require that behavioral health benefits be covered on par with medical benefits, a requirement that applies however behavioral health is structured. These obligations mean that even a carve-out cannot be an excuse to ignore a service or treat mental health as second-class.
This lesson opens the benefits-and-network module by defining the scope of what an MCO actually manages. The next lessons build on it: network adequacy standards apply to the services a plan covers, and provider credentialing concerns the providers a plan must contract with for those covered benefits. The carve-in/carve-out decision is logically first because it determines the boundaries of the plan’s responsibility — everything else in benefit and network management operates within the scope these decisions set.
A carve-in keeps a service within the MCO’s capitated responsibility, while a carve-out removes it so the plan neither provides nor is paid for it and the state manages it separately.
The services most commonly carved out are behavioral health (the most frequent), dental, pharmacy, and non-emergency medical transportation — specialized services historically run through their own systems.
Carve-outs bring specialized vendor expertise but risk fragmenting a member’s care across disconnected entities that may never communicate.

Carving in aligns incentives by making one capitated plan responsible for the whole person, so it benefits financially from coordinating across physical, behavioral, and pharmacy care (avoiding a "wrong pocket" problem).

Regardless of structure, states and plans must coordinate care across delivery systems and comply with behavioral health parity, and the carve-in/carve-out decision sets the scope within which network adequacy and credentialing then operate.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | network-adequacy-standards | Network Adequacy Standards and Time-Distance Requirements
Network Adequacy Standards and Time-Distance Requirements
A Network Is Only Real If You Can Reach It
A managed care plan’s most basic promise is access: that its enrollees can actually get the care they need from the providers in its network. But "having a network" on paper means nothing if the listed doctors are too far away, booked for months, no longer practicing, or not accepting Medicaid patients. Network adequacy is the set of standards and oversight that turns the promise of a network into a reality enrollees can use. It is where the abstract idea of "access to care" becomes measurable — in miles, minutes, ratios, and days.
The stakes are not theoretical. Medicaid serves people who often face transportation barriers, limited time off work, disabilities, and language barriers. For them, a provider 90 minutes away or with a three-month wait is effectively no provider at all. Network adequacy standards exist precisely because a capitated plan has a financial incentive to keep its network lean — and because a thin network is one of the quietest ways a plan can under-deliver care while still technically covering the benefit.
This lesson goes deeper into the network adequacy requirements introduced in the federal-framework lesson, focusing on how adequacy is actually defined and measured — and confronting the persistent gap between networks as reported and networks as experienced, the problem of "ghost networks."
Key Concept: Network adequacy standards require a plan to maintain enough accessible providers to serve its enrollees, measured through time-and-distance limits, provider-to-enrollee ratios, and appointment wait-time standards (42 CFR 438.68). The challenge is ensuring the network is real in practice, not just on paper.
More than one-third of doctors listed in Medicaid networks did not provide care to Medicaid patients in 2023 — inflating networks on paper (Lown Institute)
Medicaid "Ghost" Providers

How Network Adequacy Is Measured
States use several complementary types of standards to measure network adequacy, and most use more than one. Time-and-distance standards limit how far or how long an enrollee should have to travel to reach a provider of a given type — for example, a primary care physician within 30 minutes or 15 miles. Provider-to-enrollee ratios require a minimum number of providers relative to the enrolled population, ensuring there are enough providers to go around. And appointment wait-time standards, added by the 2024 final rule, limit how long an enrollee must wait to be seen.
Under 42 CFR 438.68, states must develop quantitative network adequacy standards (other than wait times) for specified provider types if covered under the contract — primary care (adult and pediatric), OB/GYN, behavioral health, specialists, hospitals, pharmacy, and pediatric dental, among others. In setting time-and-distance standards, states must consider the geographic location of providers and enrollees, the distance and travel time involved, and the means of transportation Medicaid enrollees ordinarily use — a recognition that a car-owning suburbanite and a bus-dependent rural enrollee face very different "distances" to the same provider.
The 2024 final rule added the appointment wait-time standards covered in the federal-framework lesson: routine appointments within 15 business days for primary care and OB/GYN, and within 10 business days for outpatient mental health and substance use care. These standards phase in over time — the rule’s key provisions apply to contracts beginning roughly three to four years after the rule’s July 9, 2024 effective date — giving states and plans time to build the monitoring infrastructure. Wait-time standards matter because they capture a dimension that geography misses: a provider can be close by and still inaccessible if they cannot see the patient for months.
Limit how far/long an enrollee travels to reach each provider type, considering transportation actually used.
Time-and-distance standards
Require enough providers relative to the enrolled population.
Provider-to-enrollee ratios
Cap how long an enrollee waits (15 days primary/OB-GYN, 10 days behavioral health under the 2024 rule).
Appointment wait-time standards
Account for telemedicine and innovative access, especially where in-person providers are scarce.
Telehealth and flexibility
The Tools for Measuring Network Adequacy
The Ghost Network Problem
For decades, network adequacy was judged largely on the provider lists plans submitted — and that created a gaping vulnerability. Plans can report large networks that bear little relation to the care enrollees can actually obtain, a phenomenon known as "ghost networks" or "phantom networks." The numbers are alarming: research found that more than one-third of doctors listed in Medicaid networks did not provide care to Medicaid patients in 2023, and in one study of Oregon Medicaid behavioral health, 58.2% of network directory listings were phantom providers who did not see Medicaid patients.
Ghost networks arise in several ways. A listed provider may have moved, retired, or died; may not actually accept the plan’s Medicaid product; or may not be taking new patients. Sometimes the directory information is simply wrong. The effect is the same regardless of cause: the network looks adequate on paper while enrollees, especially those seeking behavioral health care, call provider after provider and cannot get an appointment. The problem is most severe precisely where access is most critical — behavioral health, where directories are notoriously inaccurate and HHS oversight has repeatedly found limited networks padded with inactive providers.
A plan can fully satisfy a count-based or distance-based standard while delivering little actual access, because the listed providers are inactive, mislisted, or closed to new Medicaid patients. This is why modern oversight tests directories against reality rather than trusting the plan’s submitted lists.
A Paper Network Is Not a Real Network
Testing the Network Against Reality
Closing the gap between reported and real networks requires verification, and the 2024 rule’s central tool is the secret shopper survey. States must use annual secret shopper surveys to test plan compliance with appointment wait-time standards and to assess the accuracy of provider directories. A third party — independent of both the state and the plans — poses as an enrollee and tries to schedule an appointment with a directory-listed provider. This directly tests what a real member experiences, exposing the ghost providers that paper reviews miss.
Network adequacy verification is also built into the oversight system covered earlier: validation of plan network adequacy is a mandatory External Quality Review activity, with states and EQROs required to use a network adequacy validation protocol. This layers independent EQRO validation on top of secret-shopper testing and the plans’ own Network Adequacy and Access Assurances Reports — multiple checks designed to catch the discrepancy between what plans claim and what enrollees can actually access.
Yet verification means little without enforcement, and here the record has been weak. In Medicare Advantage, where CMS enforces network rules directly, a KFF Health News inquiry found that CMS sent letters to only five insurers whose plans failed network adequacy requirements from 2016 to 2022, and had imposed no sanctions for network failures as of 2024. In Medicaid managed care, enforcement rests with each state, and its strength varies with each state’s contract terms and willingness to use them. The 2024 rule’s stronger measurement tools are a meaningful step, but the persistent gap between detecting inadequacy and penalizing it remains the field’s central unsolved problem.
Why Network Adequacy Is the Truest Test of Access
Network adequacy is where managed care’s promise is most directly tested, because it concerns the single thing enrollees care about most: can I actually see a doctor when I need one? Every other element — the capitation rate, the quality measures, the contract terms — is ultimately in service of this. A program can be financially sound and well-governed and still fail its members if they cannot get appointments. This is why network adequacy has become a focal point of regulation, and why the 2024 rule invested so heavily in measuring it more honestly.
A provider directory without verification is like a restaurant guide that lists hundreds of places without checking which are still open. The guide looks impressive and the "network" seems vast — until you drive across town to three listings that turned out to be closed, moved, or not taking reservations. The secret shopper survey is the guide’s editor actually calling each restaurant to confirm it exists and can seat you. A directory is only as good as the verification behind it; the same is true of a provider network.
Reported networks vs. verified access
The flexibility states have in defining standards is both a strength and a weakness. It lets a state tailor standards to its geography — a rural state needs different time-and-distance limits than a dense urban one, and telehealth can legitimately extend access where in-person providers are scarce. But that same flexibility means standards vary widely in rigor, and a state can set standards loose enough that almost any network passes. Combined with weak enforcement, this is how inadequate networks persist despite a framework designed to prevent them. Stronger measurement helps only if states are willing to set meaningful standards and act on violations.
This lesson connects the benefits-and-network module to the access goals at the heart of the federal framework. The carve-in/carve-out decision set the scope of what a plan covers; network adequacy ensures the plan has real providers for those covered services; and the next lesson, on provider credentialing, concerns how plans actually bring providers into the network. Network adequacy is the bridge between a covered benefit and a delivered service — and the place where the difference between a network that exists on paper and one that works in practice is decided.
Network adequacy standards require a plan to maintain enough accessible providers to serve its enrollees, turning the abstract promise of "access" into measurable limits — and they counter a capitated plan’s incentive to keep networks lean.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | provider-credentialing-mco | Provider Credentialing and Contracting with MCOs
Provider Credentialing and Contracting with MCOs
The Gatekeeping That Builds the Network
The previous lesson showed that a plan must maintain an adequate network of real, accessible providers. But how do providers actually get into that network — and how does the system verify they are qualified and trustworthy enough to care for Medicaid members? The answer is a two-track process of credentialing and enrollment screening, followed by contracting. This is the gatekeeping that determines who is allowed to deliver care, and it is both a patient-safety safeguard and one of the most notorious sources of administrative burden in all of health care.
Two related but distinct processes govern provider participation. Credentialing is the verification that a provider has the qualifications they claim — valid license, education, training, board certification, and a clean history. Provider enrollment screening is the state Medicaid program’s separate process of vetting providers for the risk of fraud, waste, and abuse before they can bill Medicaid at all. A provider serving Medicaid managed care members typically must clear both, and then sign a contract with the plan to join its network.
These processes matter because they sit at the intersection of three goals that sometimes conflict: protecting patients from unqualified or fraudulent providers, building a network large enough to meet adequacy standards, and not burying providers in so much paperwork that they refuse to participate in Medicaid at all. Understanding credentialing and enrollment is understanding how the network is actually assembled — and why doing it well is harder than it sounds.
Key Concept: Credentialing verifies a provider’s qualifications (license, education, history) through primary source verification, while Medicaid enrollment screening (42 CFR Part 455) vets providers for fraud/abuse risk. Providers typically must clear both and sign a network contract before serving managed care members.
Health plans must recredential all network providers at least once every three years to confirm continued compliance (NCQA)
Recredentialing Cycle
Every 3 years
Medicaid screens providers at "limited," "moderate," or "high" risk levels with escalating requirements (42 CFR 455.450)
Medicaid Screening Tiers

Credentialing: Verifying Qualifications
Credentialing is the process by which a plan confirms that a provider is who and what they claim to be. Its core discipline is primary source verification (PSV) — confirming credentials directly with the issuing source rather than taking the provider’s word. Several elements must be verified at the primary source: the provider’s license, their highest level of education and training, their Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) certificate, and board certification if applicable. Verifying through the primary source (or a recognized agent of it) is a foundational standard, because a forged or expired credential is exactly what PSV exists to catch.
The dominant framework for credentialing is set by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), whose standards most health plans — including Medicaid MCOs — follow. NCQA requires a designated credentialing committee that reviews applications and makes participation decisions, and it sets the timelines and elements of the process. Recent NCQA updates have tightened these: the PSV window was reduced (to as little as 90–120 days depending on the program), so verifications like license checks, malpractice review, and board confirmation must be completed within tighter timeframes before the committee decides.
Much of this verification flows through a centralized system. CAQH (and its ProView database) serves as a central point of verification used by virtually every commercial payer, Medicaid MCO, and Medicare Advantage plan, certified to NCQA and other standards. A provider uploads their credentialing information once into CAQH, and multiple plans can draw on it — reducing the burden of submitting the same documents to every plan separately. CAQH is one of the main mechanisms by which the system tries to tame credentialing’s administrative load.
Often via CAQH ProView — license, education, DEA certificate, board certification, work history.
Provider submits credentials
The plan confirms each credential directly with the issuing source within tightened time windows.

A designated committee reviews the verified file and approves or denies participation.

The Credentialing Process
Ongoing Monitoring and Recredentialing
Credentialing is not a one-time event. A provider who was qualified at enrollment can later lose their license, be sanctioned, or be excluded from federal programs — so plans must monitor continuously between full reviews. NCQA requires that health plans recredential all providers at least once every three years to demonstrate continued compliance, re-verifying the key credentials and reviewing any complaints, sanctions, or quality issues that arose since the last cycle.
Between recredentialing cycles, monitoring has become much more frequent. Updated standards require monthly tracking of license expirations and, critically, regular checks against exclusion and sanction databases — Medicare and Medicaid exclusion lists, SAM.gov, OIG queries, and state board sanctions — often every 30 days. These exclusion checks are essential program-integrity safeguards: a provider excluded from federal health programs (for fraud, patient harm, or other serious misconduct) must not be paid with Medicaid dollars, and frequent screening ensures an excluded provider is caught quickly rather than continuing to bill until the next three-year review.
Medicaid Provider Enrollment Screening
Running parallel to plan credentialing is the state’s own provider enrollment screening, a program-integrity process governed by federal regulation at 42 CFR Part 455. Under 42 CFR 455.410, state Medicaid agencies must screen participating providers, and the rigor of that screening scales with risk. Under 42 CFR 455.450, providers are assigned a categorical risk level — "limited," "moderate," or "high" — based on their potential for fraud, waste, or abuse, with screening requirements escalating accordingly.
The tiers build on one another. Limited-risk providers (such as physicians and most established provider types) undergo license verifications — including in other states where they may be licensed — and database checks before and after enrollment. Moderate-risk providers must meet the limited requirements plus undergo on-site visits. High-risk providers (newer or higher-fraud-risk types, such as certain suppliers) must meet the limited and moderate requirements and face the most intensive scrutiny, which can include fingerprint-based criminal background checks. This risk-based approach concentrates the most burdensome screening where the fraud risk is greatest.
Importantly, the system tries to avoid redundant screening. A state Medicaid agency may rely on the results of provider screening performed by other entities — such as Medicare or another state’s Medicaid program — rather than duplicating verification that has already been done. This reflects a broader theme: enrollment screening and credentialing are both essential, but they impose real burden, and policymakers continually look for ways (shared screening, centralized databases, reliance on others’ results) to protect program integrity without making participation so onerous that providers walk away.
Credentialing (verifying qualifications, typically NCQA-driven and plan-run) and Medicaid enrollment screening (vetting fraud/abuse risk, state-run under 42 CFR 455) are distinct processes with different purposes. A provider generally must satisfy both — being qualified is not the same as being cleared to bill Medicaid, and vice versa.
Credentialing and Enrollment Are Not the Same Thing
Contracting, Burden, and the Network
Once a provider is credentialed and enrolled, the final step is contracting — the agreement between the provider and the MCO that brings them into the network, setting payment terms and obligations. Many plans use delegated credentialing, in which a plan delegates the credentialing function to a qualified group or entity (which then credentials its own providers under the plan’s oversight), streamlining participation for large practices and systems. The credentialed, enrolled, contracted provider is now a network provider who can serve the plan’s members and count toward its network adequacy.
Getting a provider into an MCO network is like onboarding a pilot at an airline. Credentialing is verifying the pilot’s license, training, and flight record directly with the issuing authorities (primary source verification). Enrollment screening is the security background check for fraud and prior misconduct. Recredentialing and monthly monitoring are the recurring medical exams and license checks that keep the pilot cleared to fly. Only after all of it does the pilot sign on (contracting) and join the roster. Skip any step and you risk an unqualified or barred person in the cockpit — or, here, the exam room.
How a provider joins a managed care network
The persistent tension across all of this is administrative burden. Credentialing and enrollment are genuine safeguards — they keep unqualified and fraudulent providers away from Medicaid patients and dollars — but they are also slow, repetitive, and costly, and excessive burden can discourage providers from participating in Medicaid at all, worsening the network adequacy problems from the last lesson. This is why the field invests so heavily in centralized credentialing (CAQH), shared screening across programs, and delegated credentialing: each is an attempt to preserve the safeguards while reducing the friction that thins Medicaid networks.
This lesson completes the benefits-and-network module by explaining how the network is actually built. The carve-in/carve-out decision set what the plan covers; network adequacy set how many accessible providers it needs; and credentialing, enrollment, and contracting are how those providers are vetted and brought in. Together they answer the practical question behind every covered benefit: who, exactly, is qualified and authorized to deliver it — and how do we make sure of that without making participation so painful that no one shows up?
Two distinct processes govern provider participation: credentialing (verifying qualifications) and Medicaid enrollment screening (vetting fraud/abuse risk under 42 CFR Part 455); providers typically must clear both, then sign a network contract.
Credentialing relies on primary source verification (PSV) — confirming license, education, DEA certificate, and board certification directly with the issuing source — under standards set largely by NCQA.
NCQA requires a designated credentialing committee and has tightened PSV windows (to as little as 90–120 days); CAQH ProView serves as a centralized verification database used across payers to reduce duplicate paperwork.
Credentialing is ongoing: plans must recredential at least every three years and monitor continuously, with monthly license tracking and roughly every-30-day checks against Medicare/Medicaid exclusion lists, SAM.gov, OIG, and state board sanctions.
Medicaid enrollment screening (42 CFR 455.410/455.450) assigns providers a "limited," "moderate," or "high" risk level, with escalating requirements — license/database checks, then on-site visits, then the most intensive scrutiny (e.g., fingerprint background checks).
States may rely on screening already performed by Medicare or other states to avoid redundant verification, reflecting an ongoing effort to balance program integrity against administrative burden.
After credentialing and enrollment, contracting brings the provider into the network; delegated credentialing (delegating the function to a qualified group under plan oversight) streamlines participation for large practices and systems.
The central tension is that these safeguards protect patients and program integrity but impose real burden that can thin Medicaid networks — driving investment in centralized credentialing, shared screening, and delegation to preserve protections while reducing friction.

[3] Andros: "Breaking It Down — Understanding NCQA and CMS Requirements" — https://andros.co/insights/breaking-it-down-understanding-ncqa-and-cms-requirements/ — CMS requirement that Medicaid MCOs and MA plans demonstrate compliance with federal credentialing standards; CAQH as a central verification point.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | hedis-medicaid-reporting | HEDIS in Medicaid: Reporting Requirements and Benchmarks
HEDIS in Medicaid: Reporting Requirements and Benchmarks
How We Actually Measure Whether a Plan Delivers Good Care
Throughout this course, the requirement that managed care plans deliver "quality" care has appeared again and again — in the contract, in the federal framework, in external quality review. But quality is meaningless unless it can be measured in a standardized, comparable way. How do you actually tell whether one plan delivers better diabetes care than another, or whether a plan is screening children appropriately? The dominant answer in American health care is HEDIS — the Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — and for Medicaid specifically, a set of mandatory Core Set measures built largely on it.
HEDIS is the closest thing health care has to a universal report card for health plans. Managed by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA), it defines standardized measures so precisely that a plan in Vermont and a plan in Texas calculate "the percentage of diabetics whose blood sugar is controlled" exactly the same way — making their results genuinely comparable. More than 235 million people are enrolled in plans that report HEDIS, and more than 90% of health plans use it. For Medicaid, HEDIS measures and the federal Core Sets are how states judge plan quality, hold plans accountable, and drive improvement.
This lesson explains what HEDIS is, how the data is collected and audited, how benchmarks turn raw rates into judgments, and how the mandatory Medicaid Core Sets layer specific reporting requirements on top of HEDIS. It is the measurement engine behind the quality requirements established earlier in the course.
Key Concept: HEDIS (Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set), managed by NCQA, is a set of precisely standardized quality measures that let health plans be compared on the same basis. Medicaid plans report HEDIS measures and the mandatory federal Core Sets, which became required for all states starting in 2024.
HEDIS includes more than 90 measures across 6 domains of care, reported by plans covering more than 235 million people (NCQA)
HEDIS Scope
90+ measures

Medicaid Core Sets
Mandatory 2024
What HEDIS Measures and How
HEDIS includes more than 90 measures organized across six domains of care: Effectiveness of Care, Access/Availability of Care, Experience of Care, Utilization and Risk-Adjusted Utilization, Health Plan Descriptive Information, and measures collected through electronic data. The measures span the full range of what good care looks like — childhood immunizations, cancer screenings, diabetes and blood pressure control, postpartum care, behavioral health follow-up, and many more. Each is defined with technical precision: exactly which patients are in the denominator, what counts as the numerator, and how to calculate the rate.
The precision is the entire point. Because HEDIS specifies measures so exactly, results are comparable across plans, states, and time — the foundation of any meaningful quality judgment. The data comes from several sources: most HEDIS data is collected through insurance claims, medical charts, and surveys. Clinical measures use either an administrative methodology (drawing purely on electronic records like claims and pharmacy data) or a hybrid methodology (combining administrative data with a sample of medical-record review to capture care that claims miss). The choice of method affects both the accuracy and the cost of measurement.
HEDIS also pairs with CAHPS — the Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems surveys — which capture the patient experience dimension (the patient-reported experience measures, or PREMs, distinct from the clinical outcomes HEDIS emphasizes). Together, HEDIS (largely clinical process and outcome measures) and CAHPS (experience) give a fuller picture of a plan’s performance than either alone, and both feed the plan ratings and benchmarks discussed below.
Audit and the Measurement Year
Numbers a plan reports about itself are only trustworthy if they are verified — the same self-reporting conflict that motivated external quality review. HEDIS addresses this through a formal audit. HEDIS results must be audited by an NCQA-approved auditing firm before they can be publicly reported, conducted by Certified HEDIS Compliance Auditors who follow NCQA standards. The audit includes an assessment of the plan’s information-systems capabilities and an evaluation of compliance with HEDIS specifications — confirming that the plan calculated the measures correctly rather than in a self-flattering way.
HEDIS uses specific timing language worth understanding. The Measurement Year (MY) is the calendar year in which the care was delivered; the audit and reporting happen the following year. So MY 2024 measures care provided during 2024, audited and reported in 2025. Plans submit their final, locked rates through NCQA’s Interactive Data Submission System (IDSS), and the audited results are captured in Final Audit Reports (FARs). This MY/reporting-year structure is why HEDIS results always lag the care they describe by roughly a year.
An unaudited HEDIS rate is just a plan’s claim about itself. The NCQA-approved compliance audit — validating the data systems and the calculation — is what turns a self-reported number into a trustworthy, comparable result. This audit also feeds the mandatory performance-measure validation that external quality review organizations conduct.
Audit Is What Makes the Numbers Mean Anything
Benchmarks: Turning Rates Into Judgments
A HEDIS rate by itself — say, 58% of diabetics with controlled blood sugar — means little without context. Is 58% good or bad? Benchmarks supply the answer by showing how a plan compares to others. NCQA’s Quality Compass provides national, state, and regional HEDIS and CAHPS benchmarks, along with plan-level results, so a plan can see where it stands against peers and competitors. Benchmarks transform an isolated number into a judgment: a rate at the 90th percentile is excellent; one at the 25th percentile signals a problem.
Percentiles are the key tool. Organizations analyze performance against the 25th, 50th (median), 75th, and 90th percentiles to understand where they fall in the distribution and how much room they have to improve. A state can set a contractual quality threshold at, say, the 50th percentile, requiring plans to perform at least as well as the national median. This is how benchmarks become accountability: by attaching consequences (in contracts, ratings, or payment) to where a plan’s HEDIS rates land relative to peers.
These measures also feed broader rating and payment programs. NCQA’s HEDIS measures are used for health plan ratings and payment programs including CMS Star Ratings, state Medicaid quality reporting, and many alternative payment and value-based care programs. A single HEDIS rate can thus ripple outward — informing a plan’s public rating, its standing in a state’s quality strategy, and even its payment under value-based arrangements. This is why plans invest enormous effort in HEDIS performance: the measures are consequential far beyond the report itself.
The Medicaid Core Sets
For Medicaid specifically, HEDIS connects to a parallel federal requirement: the Medicaid and CHIP Core Sets of Health Care Quality Measures. These are standardized measure sets — the Adult Core Set, the Child Core Set, and a Behavioral Health Core Set — that CMS and states use to measure the quality of care delivered to the roughly 78 million Medicaid and CHIP beneficiaries. Many Core Set measures are HEDIS measures, calculated following HEDIS specifications, which is why HEDIS reporting and Core Set reporting are tightly intertwined for Medicaid plans.
A major change took effect recently: starting in 2024, reporting of the Child Core Set and the behavioral health measures on the Adult Core Set became mandatory for all states, the District of Columbia, Puerto Rico, and the territories, with the first round required to be submitted and certified by December 31, 2024. Before this, much Core Set reporting was voluntary and uneven; the mandate creates, for the first time, a consistent national picture of Medicaid quality. States submit state-level data annually, and CMS publicly publishes measures reported by at least 25 states that meet data-quality standards — building transparency and cross-state comparison.
HEDIS is like a standardized exam for health plans. Just as the SAT defines each question precisely so a score in one state means the same as in another, HEDIS defines each measure so "diabetes control rate" is calculated identically everywhere — making plans comparable. The NCQA audit is the proctor ensuring no one cheats on their own score. Benchmarks (percentiles) are the score report showing how you rank against everyone else. And the Medicaid Core Sets are like a required subset of that exam that every state must now take and report.
How HEDIS standardizes quality measurement
This lesson is the measurement backbone of the care-management-and-quality module and connects to much that came before. The performance-measure validation that EQROs perform (from the oversight lesson) largely validates these HEDIS and Core Set measures. The quality requirements written into MCO contracts are largely defined in terms of HEDIS rates and benchmarks. And the value-based purchasing covered in the next module ties plan and provider payment to performance on exactly these measures. HEDIS is not a standalone report — it is the common currency of quality that flows through contracting, oversight, and payment alike. Master HEDIS and the Core Sets, and you understand how "quality" stops being a slogan and becomes a measured, audited, benchmarked, and consequential number.
HEDIS (Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set), managed by NCQA, is a set of precisely standardized quality measures that make health plans comparable on the same basis; plans covering more than 235 million people report it.
HEDIS includes more than 90 measures across six domains (effectiveness, access/availability, experience, utilization/risk-adjusted utilization, descriptive information, and electronic data), each defined with exact numerator/denominator specifications.
Data is collected via administrative methodology (claims and electronic records) or hybrid methodology (administrative data plus medical-record review), and HEDIS pairs with CAHPS surveys to capture patient experience.
HEDIS results must be audited by NCQA-approved Certified HEDIS Compliance Auditors before public reporting, verifying data systems and correct calculation — the safeguard that makes self-reported rates trustworthy.
HEDIS uses the "Measurement Year" (MY) for the year care was delivered, audited and reported the following year via NCQA’s IDSS, so results lag the care by about a year.
Benchmarks (via NCQA’s Quality Compass) and percentiles (25th, 50th, 75th, 90th) turn isolated rates into judgments and accountability, and HEDIS measures feed CMS Star Ratings, state Medicaid reporting, and value-based programs.
The Medicaid/CHIP Core Sets (Adult, Child, Behavioral Health) measure quality for ~78 million beneficiaries and draw heavily on HEDIS specifications; the Child Core Set and Adult behavioral health measures became mandatory for all states in 2024 (first submission due December 31, 2024).
HEDIS is the common currency of quality across the course — EQROs validate these measures, contracts define quality in their terms, and value-based purchasing ties payment to performance on them.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | ltss-mltss-care-coordination | LTSS and MLTSS: Care Coordination for Complex Members
LTSS and MLTSS: Care Coordination for Complex Members
The Members Who Need the Most — and Cost the Most
Most of Medicaid managed care concerns medical care — doctor visits, hospital stays, prescriptions. But a distinct and enormously important category of need falls outside acute medical care entirely: help with the basic activities of daily living for people who cannot manage them alone. An elderly person who can no longer bathe or dress safely, an adult with a disability who needs daily support, a person with a serious chronic condition who requires ongoing assistance — these people need long-term services and supports (LTSS). They are among Medicaid’s most complex and most expensive members, and how managed care serves them is the subject of this lesson.
LTSS refers to the hands-on services that help people live safely when they need assistance with daily life because of age, disability, or chronic conditions. It spans two settings: institutional care (nursing facilities) and home- and community-based services (HCBS) that let a person receive the same support while remaining in their own home or community. When a state delivers these services through capitated managed care, the result is Managed Long-Term Services and Supports (MLTSS) — and it represents one of the most consequential and challenging frontiers of Medicaid managed care.
This matters because LTSS is where managed care’s stakes are highest. The members are vulnerable, the services are intensely personal, the costs are large, and the central policy goal — helping people live in the community rather than in institutions — depends heavily on how well the plan coordinates care. Done well, MLTSS can integrate fragmented services and keep people at home; done poorly, it can fail the people least able to advocate for themselves.
Key Concept: Long-term services and supports (LTSS) help people with daily living due to age, disability, or chronic conditions, spanning institutional care and home- and community-based services (HCBS). Managed LTSS (MLTSS) delivers these through capitated managed care, with the plan coordinating all approved supports for each participant.
As of December 2023, 24 states contracted with managed care organizations to deliver long-term services and supports, a number expected to grow (industry analyses)

2 settings
What LTSS Covers
LTSS encompasses the supports a person needs to manage activities of daily living (ADLs) — bathing, dressing, eating, toileting, mobility — and related needs, when age, disability, or chronic illness makes them unable to do so independently. In an institutional setting, both fee-for-service and MLTSS programs provide room and board, nursing care, personal care, and therapy services for low-income individuals who need this level of assistance. The nursing facility has historically been the default setting for people who cannot live safely on their own.
But institutions are not the only option, and increasingly not the preferred one. States may choose to provide home- and community-based services (HCBS) — the same kinds of personal care, assistance, and supports, delivered in a person’s own home or community rather than in a facility. HCBS lets a beneficiary receive help with daily living while continuing to live at home, preserving independence and community connection. The choice between institutional and community-based LTSS is at the heart of LTSS policy, and as we will see, shifting the balance toward HCBS is a central goal of MLTSS.
LTSS is distinct from acute medical care in ways that shape how it must be managed. It is ongoing rather than episodic, deeply personal, often delivered in the home by aides rather than in clinics by physicians, and intertwined with a person’s housing, family, and community. Managing it well requires skills and infrastructure quite different from managing medical care — which is exactly why bringing LTSS into managed care is both promising and difficult.
MLTSS and Care Coordination
Under MLTSS, a state contracts with capitated managed care plans to deliver and, crucially, coordinate long-term services and supports. Under a MLTSS system, the managed care plan coordinates the delivery of all approved supports and services for each program participant — acting as the single entity responsible for assembling a coherent package of care around a person with complex, often multiple needs. This coordination role is the heart of MLTSS’s promise.
The appeal of capitated MLTSS is that it can integrate what fee-for-service fragments. A capitated managed care plan can offer more flexible benefit packages and opportunities for integrating acute and long-term services and supports — bringing a member’s medical care and their daily-living supports under one coordinated roof. For a person with both serious medical conditions and functional needs, this integration can mean the difference between disjointed services and a single care plan that addresses the whole person. The capitation also gives the plan flexibility to fund non-traditional supports that keep someone safely at home.
For acute care, a plan’s main task is paying for and managing discrete medical services. For MLTSS, coordination IS the service — assembling personal care, medical care, housing supports, and family involvement into a workable daily-living plan for a vulnerable person. A plan that pays claims but fails to coordinate has failed at the core purpose of MLTSS.
Coordination Is the Whole Job
Rebalancing: Moving Care Into the Community
The dominant policy goal driving MLTSS is rebalancing — shifting the LTSS system away from costly, less-integrated institutional settings toward more cost-effective, more integrated community settings. Nursing facility care is expensive and, for most people, far less desirable than living at home. States see MLTSS as a useful tool to rebalance their LTSS systems toward HCBS, simultaneously honoring members’ strong preference to remain in the community and reducing the cost of institutional care.
States use specific mechanisms to drive rebalancing through MLTSS. These include paying plans a blended per-member-per-month capitation rate (blending the cost of institutional and community members so the plan is not penalized for moving someone home), implementing financial incentives to transition enrollees from institutional facilities to community settings, and requiring plans to report on rebalancing-related quality metrics to measure progress. The capitation structure is what makes this work: because the plan bears the full cost, it benefits financially when it can safely support someone in lower-cost community care rather than an expensive nursing facility — aligning the financial incentive with the member’s preference.
Beyond rebalancing, states increasingly use MLTSS as a platform to integrate Medicare and Medicaid for dual-eligible individuals — the people enrolled in both programs, who are often the highest-need and highest-cost population in all of health care. Because dual eligibles get acute care through Medicare and LTSS through Medicaid, their care is notoriously fragmented across two programs that rarely coordinate. MLTSS programs can serve as the vehicle to integrate Medicare and Medicaid services in one health plan responsible for delivering all covered services — a powerful (if complex) opportunity to unify the care of those who need coordination most.
Pay one PMPM blending institutional and community costs, so moving a member home doesn’t cut the plan’s payment.

How MLTSS Drives Rebalancing
The Promise and the Difficulty
MLTSS sits at the frontier of Medicaid managed care precisely because it is the hardest thing managed care attempts. The members are the most vulnerable, the services the most personal, the coordination the most demanding, and the consequences of failure the most severe. The promise is real: an integrated, capitated plan can coordinate fragmented services, fund flexible community supports, align incentives with keeping people at home, and unify Medicare and Medicaid for dual eligibles. Increasing numbers of states are pursuing MLTSS for exactly these reasons — expanding HCBS, promoting community inclusion, ensuring quality, and increasing efficiency.
Managing acute care is like a plan paying for occasional repairs on a house — discrete jobs, billed and managed one at a time. MLTSS is more like being responsible for helping an aging person stay in their home: it means coordinating the aide who helps them dress, the doctor who manages their conditions, the ramp that lets them reach the door, and the family who checks in — all woven into one daily plan. The capitated plan profits not by doing more procedures, but by keeping the person safe and at home, which is cheaper than a nursing facility and what the person wanted anyway.
How MLTSS coordinates care for complex members
But the difficulty is equally real, and it amplifies every concern raised earlier in the course. The under-provision incentive is especially dangerous when the member cannot easily advocate for themselves and the "service" is hands-on personal care. Network adequacy is harder when the providers are home-care aides facing chronic workforce shortages. Quality measurement is harder for personal supports than for clinical procedures. And the capitation incentive to move people into the community, while generally aligned with member preference, must be carefully overseen to ensure no one is pushed out of needed institutional care prematurely. MLTSS magnifies both the benefits and the risks of managed care.
This lesson closes the care-management-and-quality module by showing managed care applied to its most demanding population. It draws together threads from across the course: the capitation and rate-setting that make blended rates possible, the network adequacy that must extend to home-care providers, the quality measurement that must capture rebalancing, and the oversight that must protect members who cannot protect themselves. MLTSS is where the abstract machinery of Medicaid managed care meets the most human stakes — and where doing it well, or badly, most directly shapes whether vulnerable people live with dignity in their own homes or not.
Long-term services and supports (LTSS) are the hands-on services that help people manage daily living due to age, disability, or chronic conditions, spanning institutional care (nursing facilities) and home- and community-based services (HCBS).
Managed LTSS (MLTSS) delivers these services through capitated managed care, with the plan responsible for coordinating all approved supports for each participant; 24 states used MLTSS as of December 2023.
LTSS differs from acute care — it is ongoing, deeply personal, often home-based, and intertwined with housing and family — so coordination, not claims payment, is the core job of an MLTSS plan.
Capitated MLTSS can integrate acute and long-term services under one coordinated plan and fund flexible community supports, addressing the whole person rather than fragmented services.
The dominant goal is rebalancing — shifting LTSS from costly institutional settings toward community-based HCBS — driven by blended capitation rates, transition incentives, and rebalancing quality metrics that align the plan’s financial interest with members’ preference to stay home.
States increasingly use MLTSS as a platform to integrate Medicare (acute) and Medicaid (LTSS) for dual-eligible members, the highest-need population whose care is otherwise fragmented across two programs.
MLTSS magnifies managed care’s risks: the under-provision incentive is most dangerous for members who cannot self-advocate, home-care network adequacy is strained by workforce shortages, and quality is harder to measure for personal supports.
MLTSS is the frontier of Medicaid managed care, drawing together capitation, network adequacy, quality measurement, and oversight, where doing the job well or badly most directly determines whether vulnerable people can live with dignity at home.
