######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | value-based-purchasing-medicaid | Value-Based Purchasing in Medicaid Managed Care
Value-Based Purchasing in Medicaid Managed Care
Pushing Value Down to the Provider
A subtle but important point runs through this entire course: capitating an MCO transfers risk to the plan, but it does not automatically change how that plan pays the doctors and hospitals delivering care. An MCO can receive a capitated, value-oriented payment from the state and then turn around and pay its providers on straight fee-for-service — recreating the very volume incentives managed care was supposed to escape, just one layer down. Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the effort to close that gap: to push value-based payment all the way down from the state, through the MCO, to the providers who actually deliver care.
This matters because the state’s ultimate goal is better care at sustainable cost, and that depends on the incentives facing the people at the bedside, not just the plan’s balance sheet. So states increasingly use their contracts with MCOs to require or encourage the plans to adopt value-based arrangements with their providers — shared savings, bundled payments, capitation, pay-for-performance, and the like. VBP in Medicaid is, in essence, the state using its leverage over MCOs to spread value-based payment throughout the delivery system.
This lesson examines how states drive provider-level value-based payment through their MCOs, the frameworks they use to define it, the targets they set, and the powerful financial mechanism — state directed payments — that increasingly carries these efforts. It connects the risk continuum from the hospital-finance course directly to the Medicaid managed care machinery built throughout this one.
Key Concept: Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the state’s use of its MCO contracts to require or encourage plans to pay their providers through value-based arrangements (shared savings, bundles, capitation, pay-for-performance) — pushing value-based payment from the state, through the plan, to the provider level.
About 26 states define the types of value-based payment model their MCOs must use with providers, and 19 set minimum VBP "saturation" targets (Guidehouse / MACPAC)
Define Required VBP Models
26 states
State directed payment arrangements approved as of August 2024 are projected to total $110.2 billion a year — up nearly 60% from $69.3 billion in early 2023 (MACPAC)
State Directed Payments
$110.2B/yr
How States Drive VBP Through MCOs
States generally use two approaches to drive value-based payment through their Medicaid MCOs. The first is setting value-based payment targets — requiring that a certain percentage of an MCO’s provider payments flow through value-based arrangements, without dictating exactly which models. The second is prescriptively directing MCOs to adopt specific payment models — telling plans precisely what kind of value-based arrangement to use. Many states blend the two: setting an overall target while specifying acceptable model types.
The trend is unmistakably toward more requirements. More states are requiring the use of VBP or alternative payment models in the contracts between their MCOs and providers, with roughly 26 states defining the types of VBP model that MCOs must use. This reflects a recognition that simply capitating the MCO is not enough — the state must affirmatively require the plan to transmit value-based incentives to providers, or the plan may default to paying providers in ways that perpetuate volume-driven care.
To make targets concrete, states set saturation targets — the share of MCO payments that must be value-based — and often ramp them up over time. About 19 states have set required minimum saturation targets, and a classic example is Arizona, where the required proportion of MCO revenues in value-based arrangements started at 5% in 2013, rose to 10% in 2014, and climbed to 20% in 2015 and 2016. This gradual ramp gives plans and providers time to build the capabilities value-based payment requires while steadily increasing the pressure to adopt it.
Require a minimum percentage of MCO provider payments to flow through value-based arrangements, ramped up over time.
Set VBP targets
Direct MCOs to adopt particular payment models (e.g., shared savings, bundled payments, or specified arrangements).
Prescribe specific models
Specify which model types qualify, often using a common framework like HCP-LAN categories.
Define acceptable arrangements
Track each MCO’s VBP saturation and tie it to contract compliance.
Measure and enforce
Two State Approaches to VBP
The HCP-LAN Framework: A Common Language
A challenge in requiring VBP is defining what actually counts as "value-based." Without a common standard, every state and plan might define it differently, making targets meaningless and comparison impossible. To solve this, many states adopt the Health Care Payment Learning & Action Network (HCP-LAN) framework, a widely used classification that sorts payment arrangements into categories by how much they tie payment to value and risk — from pure fee-for-service (Category 1), to fee-for-service linked to quality (Category 2), to alternative payment models built on fee-for-service architecture (Category 3), to population-based payment (Category 4).
The framework gives states a precise vocabulary for their requirements. About 17 states specifically reference the HCP-LAN framework in defining acceptable VBP arrangements, and of those, 10 specify the categories MCOs should use — usually HCP-LAN Category 2C or higher, meaning at least fee-for-service tied to quality and ideally more advanced models. Even states that do not explicitly cite HCP-LAN typically use definitions that align with or overlap its categories. The framework has become the de facto common language for Medicaid VBP, letting a state say exactly how far up the value ladder it expects its plans to push.
This connects directly to the risk continuum from earlier study. HCP-LAN’s categories essentially map the same spectrum — from no risk (fee-for-service) through pay-for-performance and shared savings up to full population-based capitation. When a state requires its MCOs to move providers to "Category 3 or higher," it is requiring them to move providers up the risk continuum into shared savings and beyond. The framework is how that abstract continuum becomes a concrete, measurable contract requirement.
State Directed Payments: The Growing Mechanism
The most consequential and fastest-growing tool for VBP in Medicaid managed care is the state directed payment (SDP). Created when CMS updated the managed care regulations in 2016, SDPs allow a state to direct how its MCOs pay providers — overriding the normal rule that plans set their own provider rates. Through SDPs, a state can require MCOs to use minimum or maximum fee schedules, make uniform rate increases for selected providers, require participation in multi-payer models, or require providers to participate in value-based purchasing arrangements. SDPs are how a state reaches through the MCO to shape provider payment directly.
SDPs have exploded in scale. Between February 2023 and August 2024, CMS approved 302 state directed payment arrangements across 40 states and Puerto Rico, and the arrangements approved as of August 2024 are projected to spend $110.2 billion a year — nearly a 60% increase over the $69.3 billion projected just eighteen months earlier. This staggering growth reflects how central SDPs have become to state Medicaid strategy, both for raising provider payment (often toward Medicare levels) and for advancing value-based and quality goals. The VBP-oriented SDPs tie payments to metrics like patient satisfaction, reduced readmissions, and improved chronic-disease management.
This rapid growth drew regulatory attention. In 2024, CMS released a managed care rule with additional updates intended to improve the oversight and transparency of directed payments — a response to concerns that SDPs were growing so fast, and channeling so much money, that they needed tighter guardrails. States now report a range of evaluation measures for their SDPs, such as hospitalization and readmission rates, utilization and timeliness of preventive and specialty care, and outcomes for common chronic conditions, so the billions flowing through SDPs can be tied to demonstrable results rather than simply raising payments.
State directed payments let states reach through MCOs to shape provider payment and advance value-based goals, but their explosive growth to $110+ billion a year prompted CMS to tighten oversight and transparency in 2024. The same mechanism that can drive value-based purchasing can also simply inflate payments, which is why CMS is demanding clearer evaluation of what SDPs actually achieve.
SDPs Are Powerful — and Under Scrutiny
Why VBP Ties the Course Together
Value-based purchasing is where Medicaid managed care reconnects with the broader value-based-care movement that this body of study began with. Everything earlier in this course built the machinery of managed care — selecting plans, setting rates, ensuring networks and quality, overseeing performance. VBP is the layer that aims that machinery at the ultimate goal: not just transferring risk to plans, but actually changing how care is paid for and delivered all the way to the provider, so that value, not volume, drives the system from top to bottom.
A state requiring VBP through its MCOs is like a parent company that pays its regional managers (the MCOs) a fixed budget and then insists those managers also pay their store employees (providers) based on customer satisfaction and results, not just hours worked. Without that insistence, a regional manager might pocket the efficiency and still pay employees the old way — so the incentive to improve never reaches the front line. VBP requirements, HCP-LAN categories, and state directed payments are the parent company’s way of making sure the new incentives flow all the way down to where the work actually happens.
Pushing value-based payment to the provider level
The honest caveat is that requiring VBP does not guarantee it works. As the hospital-finance course showed, value-based payment’s benefits depend on execution — providers must have the data, scale, and capabilities to manage risk, and shared savings must actually offset lost volume. A state can mandate that 50% of MCO payments be "value-based" and still see little change if the underlying arrangements are weak (mere pay-for-performance bonuses rather than real risk) or if providers lack the infrastructure to respond. The targets and frameworks are necessary scaffolding, but the building still depends on genuine capability beneath them.
This lesson opens the final module by showing Medicaid managed care reaching toward value. The next lesson, on Section 1115 waivers, examines the federal authority that lets states innovate beyond standard rules — including many of the boldest VBP and delivery-reform experiments. And the closing lesson looks at where the whole field is heading, toward social determinants and whole-person care. Value-based purchasing is the bridge: it takes the managed care structure built across this course and points it at the same destination the entire value-based-care movement is pursuing — paying for health and outcomes rather than volume of services.
Value-based purchasing (VBP) in Medicaid managed care is the state’s use of MCO contracts to require or encourage plans to pay their providers through value-based arrangements, pushing value-based payment from the state through the plan to the provider level.
It matters because capitating an MCO does not change how the MCO pays providers; without VBP requirements, plans may keep paying providers fee-for-service and recreate volume incentives one layer down.
States drive VBP two ways: setting value-based payment targets (a minimum share of payments that must be value-based) and prescriptively directing MCOs to adopt specific models, often combined.
About 26 states define required VBP model types and 19 set minimum saturation targets, frequently ramped over time — Arizona moved from 5% of MCO revenues in value-based arrangements in 2013 to 20% by 2015–2016.
Many states use the HCP-LAN framework to define "value-based," with ~17 referencing it and 10 specifying categories (usually Category 2C or higher); the framework maps the same risk continuum from fee-for-service to population-based payment.
State directed payments (SDPs), created by CMS in 2016, let states direct how MCOs pay providers — including requiring VBP participation — and have grown explosively to a projected $110.2 billion a year as of August 2024 (302 arrangements in 40 states), up ~60% in 18 months.
The rapid SDP growth prompted CMS to tighten oversight and transparency in 2024 and to require evaluation measures (readmissions, preventive care, chronic-disease outcomes), since SDPs can either advance value or simply inflate payments.
Requiring VBP does not guarantee results — benefits depend on execution, provider capability, and whether the arrangements involve real risk — so targets and frameworks are necessary scaffolding but not sufficient on their own.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | section-1115-waivers | Section 1115 Waivers and Managed Care Innovation
Section 1115 Waivers and Managed Care Innovation
The Authority That Lets States Reinvent Medicaid
Medicaid is governed by detailed federal rules — who must be covered, what services must be offered, how programs must operate. These rules create consistency, but they also constrain experimentation. So how do states test bold new approaches, like covering housing as a health benefit or running an all-payer global budget, when the standard rules would not allow it? The answer is the Section 1115 demonstration waiver — the single most powerful tool states have to reinvent their Medicaid programs, and the engine behind most major Medicaid managed care innovation.
Section 1115 of the Social Security Act gives the Secretary of Health and Human Services authority to approve experimental, pilot, or demonstration projects likely to promote the objectives of the Medicaid program. What makes Section 1115 uniquely powerful is its breadth: it combines extensive waiver authority with a broadly defined purpose. The Secretary can waive almost any Medicaid state plan requirement and can permit federal matching funds for costs not otherwise matchable — letting states cover services and populations Medicaid normally would not. In effect, Section 1115 is a license to experiment with the program’s core rules.
For Medicaid managed care, 1115 waivers are foundational. Many states’ entire managed care programs operate under 1115 authority, and the boldest delivery and payment innovations — from value-based reforms to addressing social needs — are tested through these demonstrations. Understanding Section 1115 is understanding how Medicaid changes and how the most ambitious managed care experiments become possible.
Key Concept: A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary waive most Medicaid rules and authorize federal funding for normally non-matchable costs, so states can test experimental approaches. Demonstrations must be "budget neutral" to the federal government and are generally approved for five years, then renewable.
Section 1115 lets the Secretary waive almost any Medicaid state plan requirement under §1902 to carry out a demonstration (MACPAC / KFF)
Breadth of Authority
~Any §1902 rule
Section 1115 waivers are generally approved for an initial five-year period and renewable for three-to-five-year periods (KFF)
Typical Approval Period
5 years
How Section 1115 Works
A Section 1115 demonstration is, formally, a research and demonstration project: states must have an approved, publicly available evaluation strategy, because the authority is meant to test and evaluate new policy approaches, not simply to expand programs. The breadth is remarkable — under Section 1115, the Secretary can waive almost any state plan requirement under §1902 (with narrow exceptions like citizenship rules), to the extent necessary to carry out the demonstration. This lets states restructure eligibility, benefits, delivery systems, and payment in ways the standard rules would forbid.
Equally important is the "expenditure authority" that comes with 1115: the Secretary can permit federal financial participation for costs not otherwise matchable (CNOM) — federal dollars for services and populations not included in the regular Medicaid state plan. CNOM authority is how a state can use Medicaid funds for things like housing supports or services for populations Medicaid does not normally cover. Without it, the boldest innovations would have no funding mechanism; with it, states can finance genuinely new approaches with federal matching dollars.
The approval process is rigorous and often slow. A state submits a detailed application — describing the demonstration, enrollment estimates, requested authorities, research hypotheses, and documentation of public comment — and CMS reviews it case by case to determine whether the objectives align with Medicaid’s. There is a federal 30-day public comment period, and CMS must consider all comments. Negotiation typically takes anywhere from six months to two years, longer for comprehensive waivers that may encompass most of a state’s Medicaid spending, because each program element must be separately negotiated.
Defines the experimental approach, the populations affected, and research hypotheses to evaluate.
State designs the demonstration
Holds public notice/comment, then submits a detailed application requesting specific waiver and expenditure authorities.
Public comment and application
CMS reviews for alignment with Medicaid objectives, runs a 30-day federal comment period, and negotiates terms (often 6 months–2 years).
CMS case-by-case review
Approved for ~5 years with budget-neutrality limits and a required, public evaluation; renewable for 3–5 year periods.
Approval, operation, evaluation
The 1115 Waiver Process
Budget Neutrality: The Central Constraint
The most important limit on Section 1115 is budget neutrality: a demonstration must not cost the federal government more than it would have spent without the waiver. Federal Medicaid expenditures under the demonstration cannot exceed what federal spending would have been without it, over the course of the project. This single rule shapes nearly every 1115 design, because it means a state cannot simply ask the federal government to pay for new things — it must show that, on net, the demonstration stays within the federal spending it would have incurred anyway.
Budget neutrality is typically calculated on a per-enrollee basis: per-enrollee spending under the demonstration cannot exceed the projected per-enrollee spending in the "without-waiver baseline." This creates a powerful dynamic. If a state spends below that baseline, the difference counts as savings — and the state can use accumulated savings to finance the costs-not-otherwise-matchable spending on populations or services Medicaid does not normally cover. In other words, a state that manages care efficiently enough to come in under its baseline can reinvest the savings into innovative services. Budget neutrality is both a constraint and, paradoxically, the funding source for innovation.
Budget neutrality means an 1115 demonstration cannot simply add federal cost — new services and populations must generally be financed from savings the demonstration itself generates against the without-waiver baseline. This is why 1115 innovations are framed as investments expected to reduce other spending, not as straightforward expansions.
Innovation Must Pay for Itself
What States Are Testing
Section 1115 has become the primary vehicle for the most ambitious Medicaid innovations, and recent years have seen a wave of demonstrations addressing health-related social needs (HRSN) — the social factors like housing and food that drive health outcomes. In 2022 CMS announced a demonstration opportunity to expand states’ tools to address enrollees’ health-related social needs, and by February 2024 had approved eight states under the HRSN framework — Arizona, Arkansas, California, Massachusetts, New Jersey, New York, Oregon, and Washington. These waivers authorize evidence-based housing and nutrition services for high-need populations, including coverage of rent or temporary housing and utilities for up to six months and meal support for up to six months.
The specific demonstrations are striking in scope. New York’s January 2024 waiver amendment included up to $3.673 billion to build HRSN infrastructure, including new "Social Care Networks," and to reimburse for HRSN services through Medicaid. Massachusetts’s MassHealth waiver supports housing (security deposits, rent, relocation, home modifications, housing case management), food security, and transportation. Arkansas’s supports housing deposits, moving costs, and tenancy-sustaining services. A separate 1115 opportunity addressed reentry for justice-involved individuals — partially waiving the Medicaid "inmate exclusion" so states can provide pre-release services — with the Biden administration approving 19 state reentry waivers.
These innovations are politically contingent, which is itself a defining feature of 1115. Because demonstrations are approved at the Secretary’s discretion, their direction shifts with administrations. In March 2025, the Trump administration rescinded the Biden administration’s HRSN guidance; CMS indicated this does not nullify existing HRSN approvals, but that it will consider HRSN and social-determinant requests on a case-by-case basis going forward. This illustrates a core truth about 1115: it is a powerful tool for innovation precisely because it is discretionary, which also means the innovations it enables can be expanded or curtailed as federal priorities change.
Why 1115 Is the Engine of Medicaid Innovation
Section 1115 occupies a unique place in Medicaid: it is the mechanism through which the program evolves. Almost every major delivery and payment innovation — including the all-payer and global-budget models discussed in the value-based-care course, comprehensive managed care expansions, and the social-needs demonstrations above — runs through 1115 authority. When a state wants to do something genuinely new with Medicaid, the path almost always leads to a Section 1115 waiver. It is, in a real sense, where the future of Medicaid is tested before it becomes standard.
Section 1115 is like a sanctioned "sandbox" or pilot program within a heavily regulated system. The standard Medicaid rules are the building code everyone must follow; an 1115 waiver is special permission to construct an experimental building that breaks some of those rules — but only if you can prove it won’t cost the city more than a normal building (budget neutrality), you document what you’re testing (evaluation), and you get the regulator’s sign-off (case-by-case approval). The sandbox is where new designs get proven before, sometimes, becoming the new code.
How Section 1115 enables Medicaid innovation
The tension at the heart of 1115 is between flexibility and accountability. Its flexibility is what makes innovation possible — without it, Medicaid would be frozen in its statutory form. But that same discretionary flexibility means demonstrations can advance one administration’s priorities and be unwound by the next, that budget-neutrality calculations can be contested, and that "demonstrations" sometimes operate for decades without ever conclusively demonstrating anything. The required evaluations are meant to provide accountability, but the political nature of approval means 1115 is as much a policy instrument as a research tool.
This lesson sets up the course’s conclusion. The next and final lesson looks at where Medicaid managed care is heading — toward social determinants of health and whole-person care — and Section 1115 is precisely the authority making that direction possible. The HRSN demonstrations covered here are the leading edge of that future. Understanding 1115 means understanding not just a regulatory mechanism, but the very channel through which Medicaid managed care reaches beyond medical care toward the social factors that shape health, and through which the program will continue to transform in the years ahead.
A Section 1115 demonstration waiver lets the HHS Secretary waive almost any Medicaid state plan requirement (§1902) and authorize federal funding for normally non-matchable costs, so states can test experimental approaches — the most powerful tool for Medicaid innovation.

######## medicaid-managed-care-operations | future-medicaid-managed-care | The Future of Medicaid Managed Care: SDOH and Whole-Person Care
The Future of Medicaid Managed Care: SDOH and Whole-Person Care
Two Forces Shaping What Comes Next
Having built up the full machinery of Medicaid managed care across this course — delivery models, federal rules, procurement, rate-setting, networks, quality, and value-based payment — we close by looking forward. Where is this system heading? The answer is shaped by two powerful forces pulling in different directions. One is aspirational: a sustained movement toward "whole-person care" that addresses the social factors driving health, not just medical services. The other is fiscal and political: looming federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten to reshape the program’s scale and strain its finances. The future of Medicaid managed care lies in the tension between these two forces.
The whole-person-care movement reflects a genuine intellectual shift. There is growing recognition that medical care alone cannot produce health when a person lacks stable housing, adequate food, reliable transportation, or employment — the social determinants of health (SDOH). Medicaid managed care, with its capitated, population-focused structure and (via Section 1115) its flexibility to fund non-traditional services, has become a leading vehicle for acting on this recognition. The direction of travel is toward MCOs that address the whole person and their social context, not just their diagnoses.
But that aspiration now collides with a harsh fiscal environment. Major federal Medicaid cuts and policy changes are projected to shrink enrollment and squeeze financing precisely as states aspire to do more. Understanding the future of Medicaid managed care means holding both realities at once — the expansive vision of whole-person care and the contractionary pressure of cuts that could undermine it.
Key Concept: The future of Medicaid managed care is shaped by two forces — an aspirational shift toward whole-person care addressing social determinants of health (SDOH), and a fiscal/political shift toward major federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten the program’s scale and finances.
Federal Medicaid spending is projected to fall by about $911 billion (~14%) over a decade under recent law (H.R.1/OBBBA), increasing the uninsured by ~7.5 million (KFF)

Whole-Person Care: The Aspirational Direction
The defining aspiration of modern Medicaid managed care is whole-person care — integrating physical health, behavioral health, services for intellectual and developmental disabilities, pharmacy, and social supports into a single coordinated approach centered on the member rather than fragmented by service type. This is the through-line connecting many earlier lessons: the carve-in trend toward integration, MLTSS coordination for complex members, and value-based payment all point toward treating the whole person rather than a collection of disconnected benefits.
Increasingly, that integration extends beyond clinical care to social needs. Medicaid managed care organizations are using Medicaid funds to address social determinants of health, supporting members’ broader needs including housing, nutrition, and employment, in recognition of the adverse health impacts of unmet social needs. The mechanisms are ones this course has already covered: Section 1115 demonstrations (the HRSN waivers), "in lieu of services and settings" (ILOS) authority from the 2024 final rule, and value-based arrangements that reward keeping people healthy. Together they let plans pay for a food prescription or a housing navigator when those interventions improve health more than another clinical visit would.
Effective whole-person care depends on partnership and infrastructure. Plans are increasingly partnering with community-based organizations to connect members with critical resources, recognizing that an MCO cannot itself provide housing or food but can fund and coordinate with the organizations that do. Key elements of doing this well include member- and community-centeredness, structured programming, and realignment of the delivery system. Some states are even beginning to integrate SDOH factors into risk adjustment, so plans serving members with greater social needs are paid appropriately — extending the risk-adjustment logic from clinical conditions to social circumstances.
Unify physical, behavioral, IDD, and pharmacy care around the member rather than by service silo.
Clinical integration
Use 1115 HRSN waivers, ILOS authority, and VBP to fund housing, nutrition, and employment supports.
Social needs services
Partner with community-based organizations that actually deliver social supports.
Community partnerships
Reward whole-person outcomes through value-based arrangements and, increasingly, SDOH-informed risk adjustment.
Aligned payment
Building Blocks of Whole-Person Care
The Fiscal and Political Headwinds
Against this expansive vision stand serious headwinds. Recent federal law (H.R.1, also discussed as OBBBA in the hospital-finance course) is projected to reduce federal Medicaid spending by roughly $911 billion — about 14% — over a decade, and to increase the number of uninsured people by around 7.5 million, with impacts varying widely by state (spending cuts ranging from about 4% to nearly a fifth of federal Medicaid spending in some states). These are not marginal adjustments; they represent a structural contraction of the program’s federal financing.
The enrollment effects are projected to be large and are already beginning. Since H.R.1 was enacted, the five largest Medicaid insurers have already lost a net 1.4 million members (3.8%), and the Urban Institute projects that expansion-adult enrollment in 2028 could be 4.9 to 10.1 million (27–55%) lower than otherwise expected, depending on how much states mitigate coverage losses. The drivers include work reporting requirements and more frequent (six-month) eligibility redeterminations beginning January 1, 2027, which research consistently shows cause eligible people to lose coverage through administrative churn, not just genuine ineligibility.
These pressures cascade through the system in ways this course has mapped. As enrollment falls and financing tightens, the Medicaid segment’s already-thin profitability comes under further pressure. Providers, already reimbursed below fee-for-service levels in many cases, face reduced or stagnant rates alongside more uninsured patients, pressuring them to cut staff and services or close — a particular threat to rural and safety-net providers. The network adequacy, payer-mix, and sustainability problems from earlier lessons all intensify under fiscal contraction.
Whole-person care asks Medicaid managed care to do more — addressing housing, food, and social needs. Federal cuts and enrollment losses push it to do less, with shrinking budgets and fewer members. How states and plans navigate between this expansive vision and contractionary pressure will define Medicaid managed care for the rest of the decade.
The Core Tension of the Coming Years
What States and Plans Are Prioritizing
Facing these crosscurrents, states and advocates are converging on a set of priorities for the years ahead. The most pressing concerns for Medicaid managed care include enrollment oversight (ensuring that eligible people are not wrongly disenrolled amid redeterminations and work requirements), network adequacy (keeping real access as financing tightens), benefit design (deciding what to cover when budgets shrink), and MCO accountability (holding plans to their obligations even under fiscal stress). These priorities are, notably, the very subjects of this course — the machinery built to govern managed care becomes more important, not less, when the program is under strain.
The 2024 final rule’s quality rating system, the strengthened network adequacy and secret-shopper requirements, the tightened MLR and directed-payment oversight — all of these accountability tools take on heightened significance in a contracting environment. When budgets are ample, oversight catches occasional problems; when budgets are cut and plans face negative margins, the temptation to under-provide care, thin networks, and avoid expensive members grows, and robust oversight becomes the main protection for vulnerable enrollees. The future will test whether the accountability framework this course described can hold under real fiscal pressure.
Medicaid managed care’s future is like a household that has finally decided to invest in long-term health — better food, a safer home, preventive care (whole-person care) — just as its income is cut. The wisest response is not to abandon the vision but to protect the investments that actually keep people well and out of expensive crises, while watching spending carefully. The danger is that under financial stress, the household cuts exactly the preventive investments that would have saved money later. States face the same choice: whether cuts fall on the whole-person investments that improve health or are absorbed without gutting them.
Navigating between vision and fiscal constraint
Conclusion: Where the Course Has Led
This final lesson completes a journey that began with a simple question: why do states pay private plans to manage Medicaid, and how is that arrangement governed? The answer unfolded across the course. States moved to managed care chiefly for budget predictability; they choose among delivery models that transfer different amounts of risk; they operate within the federal framework of 42 CFR Part 438; they select plans through procurement, pay them through actuarially sound risk-adjusted capitation bounded by medical loss ratios, require adequate networks and credentialed providers, measure quality through HEDIS, oversee performance through external review, and increasingly push value-based payment and whole-person care. Every piece exists to capture managed care’s benefits while guarding against its central risk: that a plan paid a fixed amount will under-serve the vulnerable people who depend on it.
The future will stress-test that entire structure. Whole-person care represents Medicaid managed care reaching toward its highest ambition — using its capitated, population-based design to address the social roots of health, not just treat illness. The fiscal and political headwinds represent the constraint within which that ambition must be pursued. The same tools that govern managed care in good times — risk adjustment, network standards, quality measurement, MLR floors, oversight — are what will protect enrollees if the cuts arrive as projected. The machinery is not bureaucratic overhead; it is the safeguard that determines whether managed care serves its members or fails them when money is tight.
For the student who has worked through this course, the enduring lesson is that Medicaid managed care is neither inherently good nor bad — it is a powerful financial and delivery structure whose outcomes depend entirely on how well it is designed, paid, and overseen. It can deliver coordinated, whole-person care to tens of millions, or it can become risk transfer with thin networks and under-provided care. The difference lies in the operational details this course has covered. As Medicaid managed care moves into a future of expansive vision and fiscal pressure, those details — the rates, the rules, the networks, the measures, the oversight — will determine whether the system honors its purpose: caring for the people who have nowhere else to turn.
The future of Medicaid managed care is shaped by two opposing forces: an aspirational shift toward whole-person care addressing social determinants of health (SDOH), and major federal cuts and enrollment losses that threaten the program’s scale and finances.
Whole-person care integrates physical health, behavioral health, IDD services, pharmacy, and social supports around the member, extending beyond clinical care to address housing, nutrition, and employment.
Plans address social needs through Section 1115 HRSN waivers, "in lieu of services" (ILOS) authority, value-based arrangements, community-based partnerships, and emerging SDOH-informed risk adjustment.
Recent federal law (H.R.1/OBBBA) is projected to cut federal Medicaid spending ~$911 billion (~14%) over a decade and raise the uninsured by ~7.5 million, with impacts varying widely by state.
Medicaid expansion enrollment could be 4.9–10.1 million lower in 2028 than otherwise projected (Urban Institute), driven by work reporting requirements and six-month redeterminations starting January 1, 2027, with declines already underway.
Fiscal pressure cascades through the system: already-thin Medicaid-segment profitability comes under further pressure, and providers face below-FFS rates plus more uninsured patients, threatening staff cuts and rural/safety-net closures.
States and advocates prioritize enrollment oversight, network adequacy, benefit design, and MCO accountability — the very machinery of this course — which becomes more important under fiscal strain because the incentive to under-provide grows.
The enduring lesson is that Medicaid managed care is neither inherently good nor bad; its outcomes depend on how well it is designed, paid, and overseen — the operational details that determine whether it delivers whole-person care or becomes risk transfer that fails vulnerable members.

######## value-based-care | fee-for-service-origins | Why Fee-for-Service Fails: Incentives & Consequences
Why Fee-for-Service Fails: Incentives & Consequences
The Birth of Fee-for-Service: A 1965 Bargain With Medicine
When President Lyndon B. Johnson signed the Social Security Amendments of 1965 on July 30, Medicare and Medicaid were created to extend health coverage to elderly and low-income Americans. To win the cooperation of organized medicine — particularly the American Medical Association, which had fiercely opposed government health insurance — the law was structured around a simple payment principle: physicians would be paid a fee for each service they delivered, just as they billed private patients. Fee-for-service (FFS) was not a deliberate policy choice so much as a political accommodation to secure physician participation.
When Medicare services formally began on July 1, 1966, more than 19 million Americans age 65 and older enrolled in the program. Physician payments were based on "customary, prevailing, and reasonable" (CPR) charges — essentially whatever a doctor had historically charged. This created an immediate structural problem: every new claim submitted at a higher charge raised the future benchmark, producing a ratchet effect that drove spending upward with no automatic governor.
For the first two decades, policymakers treated the escalating costs as a managed problem rather than a systemic one. Various fee schedule updates, assignment rules, and charge limits were layered on top of CPR without fundamentally questioning the underlying incentive architecture. By the 1980s, it was clear that the "more services = more revenue" logic was deeply embedded in American healthcare finance — and that it was not going away without deliberate reform.
Key Concept: Fee-for-service is a payment model in which a provider receives a separate, discrete payment for each individual service rendered — a visit, a test, a procedure, a prescription. Volume, not value, drives revenue under this model.

How Fee-for-Service Distorts Clinical Incentives
The defining feature of fee-for-service is that it pays providers for activity, not outcomes. A surgeon who performs an operation is paid regardless of whether the patient recovers well or poorly. A primary care physician who spends 45 minutes counseling a patient on lifestyle changes to prevent diabetes earns less than a specialist who performs a 15-minute procedure. A hospital that discharges a patient quickly — reducing the episode cost — earns less than one that extends the stay. In each case, the financial incentives and the clinical incentives point in opposite directions.
This misalignment is not a flaw in individual physician character; it is the predictable output of a well-functioning incentive system pointed in the wrong direction. When volume is the revenue driver, rational economic actors — hospitals, physician groups, imaging centers — respond by increasing volume. This dynamic is widely documented. A 2017 survey of 2,106 physicians published in PLOS ONE found that physicians themselves reported approximately 20% of overall medical care as unnecessary, including 22% of prescriptions, 25% of tests, and 11% of procedures.
The consequences extend beyond wasteful spending. Overutilization exposes patients to real harms: unnecessary surgeries carry surgical risk, excessive imaging involves radiation exposure, and over-prescription of antibiotics contributes to antimicrobial resistance. Fee-for-service also systematically under-incentivizes prevention, care coordination, and the management of chronic disease — precisely the areas where the U.S. population most urgently needs investment, given rising rates of diabetes, hypertension, and heart disease.

What Fee-for-Service Rewards vs. What Patients Need
Overutilization: The $750 Billion Problem
The scale of waste in fee-for-service medicine is staggering and well-documented. A landmark 2012 analysis by the Institute of Medicine (now the National Academy of Medicine) estimated that the United States wasted roughly $750 billion out of $2.6 trillion in annual healthcare spending — approximately 30% of all health expenditures. That analysis identified six categories of waste: unnecessary services, inefficient care delivery, excess administrative costs, inflated prices, prevention failures, and fraud. Unnecessary services — a direct product of FFS incentives — was the single largest category.
More recent estimates have adjusted the figures but not the conclusion. Overtreatment and low-value care are estimated to cost approximately $200 billion annually in the United States. These are not edge cases or outlier events; they are the normal output of a system designed to pay for doing more. The geographic variation in Medicare spending — a well-studied phenomenon — illustrates this clearly: regions with more FFS-driven care often show higher spending but not better health outcomes than lower-spending peers.
Defensive medicine — the practice of ordering additional tests or procedures primarily to guard against malpractice liability rather than for clinical necessity — compounds the problem. Physicians practicing under FFS are simultaneously incentivized by payment and by fear of liability to order more. The result is a system with two powerful engines pushing utilization upward and few structural forces pulling it back.
Imagine paying a taxi driver by the mile, then asking them to recommend the best route across town. They might genuinely believe the longer route is better — more scenic, fewer lights — but the meter is also running in their favor. In fee-for-service medicine, providers have the same structural conflict: the payment system rewards more care, even when the right clinical answer is less.

The Outcomes Paradox: Spending More, Getting Less
The United States spends more on healthcare than any other country on Earth — by a significant margin. In 2023, the U.S. spent approximately $14,885 per capita on health, compared to an OECD average of $5,967. That is more than two-and-a-half times the average spending of other wealthy nations. And yet, by nearly every population health measure, the U.S. performs poorly relative to its peer countries.
U.S. life expectancy was 78.4 years in 2023 — 2.7 years below the OECD average and nearly 4 years shorter than the average among comparable high-income nations (82.5 years). The U.S. performs worse than the OECD average on 77% of health status indicators, including obesity rates (43% in the U.S. versus 26% OECD average) and opioid mortality (223 per million in the U.S. versus 30 per million OECD average). The fee-for-service structure contributes to this paradox by over-investing in acute, high-intensity intervention while systematically under-investing in the primary and preventive care that drives population health.
This mismatch between spending and outcomes is not inevitable. Countries that organize care around primary care-centered, capitated or globally budgeted payment models consistently achieve better population health at lower cost. The evidence from international comparison does not indict American physicians or hospitals — it indicts the payment architecture that shapes how those physicians and hospitals behave.
Vermont launched the nation's first statewide All-Payer Accountable Care Organization (ACO) model in 2018, moving the state's major payers — Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurers — toward value-based payment simultaneously. Rather than paying providers separately for each service, the model provides a single, globally-negotiated budget for a defined population. Vermont has historically had one of the highest rates of primary care utilization in the nation, contributing to better health outcomes relative to its spending level.
The model demonstrates that shifting the payment architecture — not just layering quality bonuses onto FFS — is what produces durable change in care delivery patterns.
Vermont All-Payer ACO Model
Early Attempts to Fix the System: Managed Care and the SGR
Policymakers began serious attempts to constrain FFS-driven spending in the 1980s and 1990s. The most influential structural response was managed care — health maintenance organizations (HMOs) and preferred provider organizations (PPOs) that used capitation, utilization review, and gatekeeping to moderate volume. Managed care did succeed in slowing spending growth through the mid-1990s, but a political and consumer backlash against restricted access and coverage denials led Congress to pass patient protection legislation and effectively defanged many of managed care's cost-control mechanisms by the early 2000s.
For Medicare, Congress attempted a different fix with the Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR) formula, enacted as part of the Balanced Budget Act of 1997. The SGR tied aggregate physician payment updates to GDP growth, theoretically preventing physician spending from outpacing the broader economy. In practice, it failed. When physician spending exceeded the SGR target, the formula required automatic fee cuts — often exceeding 20% — that Congress consistently overrode with emergency "doc fix" legislation rather than allow payments to fall. By 2015, the proposed SGR-driven cut was 21.2% — an amount both politically and practically impossible to implement.
The SGR experience illustrated a fundamental truth: you cannot fix a volume-driven payment system by threatening to reduce the per-unit price when volume rises, because those whose livelihoods depend on that volume will always find a way to reverse the cuts. The only durable solution is to restructure the underlying payment model — to make it financially neutral or advantageous to deliver less but better care. That insight became the foundation for the value-based care movement.
Social Security Amendments of 1965 established FFS as the default payment architecture for government health insurance programs.

The Path from FFS to Value: Key Legislative Milestones
Why FFS Persists Despite Its Flaws
Given the weight of evidence against fee-for-service, a reasonable question is why it remains the dominant payment model in American healthcare. The answer involves entrenched financial interests, administrative complexity, and the genuine difficulty of measuring "value" in health. Provider organizations that have built their revenue models, staffing levels, and capital investments around FFS volume face existential risk in a rapid transition to different payment structures. Hospitals whose margins depend on high-acuity inpatient admissions cannot easily restructure overnight.
There is also the measurement problem. Value-based payment requires robust quality metrics, attribution methodologies (to determine which provider is responsible for a patient's outcomes), risk adjustment (to avoid penalizing providers who care for sicker patients), and data infrastructure capable of tracking patients across settings over time. These systems are expensive to build, slow to validate, and contested in their design. FFS, by contrast, is administratively simple: the claim defines the service, the fee schedule defines the payment, and the transaction is complete.
Despite these barriers, the trajectory is clear. CMS has set explicit targets for moving Medicare toward value-based payment, and the commercial insurance market has followed. Understanding why FFS fails — at the level of incentive structure, not just cost — is the essential first step toward understanding why every major reform initiative of the past 15 years has been an attempt to move away from it.
Fee-for-service is sometimes confused with "privatized" healthcare, but it is actually the dominant payment model within both public (Medicare, Medicaid) and private insurance programs in the United States. The problem is not who pays, but what behavior the payment incentivizes. Both public and private FFS payers face the same volume-driven cost dynamic.

######## value-based-care | relative-value-units | RVUs: How Physician Payment Works — and Why It Favors Procedures
RVUs: How Physician Payment Works — and Why It Favors Procedures
From Customary Charges to a Standardized Scale: The RBRVS Origin Story
Before 1992, Medicare paid physicians based on "customary, prevailing, and reasonable" (CPR) charges — essentially whatever a doctor had historically billed, benchmarked against regional and specialty norms. This system was both inflationary and opaque. Surgeons and proceduralists, who had established high historical charges, received payments that bore little relationship to the actual time, skill, or effort their work required. Primary care physicians, whose cognitive work left a smaller billing footprint, were systematically underpaid by comparison.
In the late 1980s, Harvard economist William Hsiao led a landmark study commissioned by the Health Care Financing Administration (now CMS) to develop a more rational basis for physician payment. The resulting system — the Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS) — assigned each physician service a relative value unit (RVU) intended to reflect the actual resources required: physician time and effort, practice overhead, and malpractice insurance. The Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989 authorized the creation of the Medicare Fee Schedule based on RBRVS, which took effect on January 1, 1992.
The introduction of RBRVS was a genuine improvement over CPR. It replaced an arbitrary, charge-history-based system with one grounded in explicit resource measurement. However, as decades of subsequent evidence would show, the RBRVS contained structural biases — particularly in how it valued procedural work relative to cognitive work — that would persist and intensify over time.
Key Concept: The Resource-Based Relative Value Scale (RBRVS) is the payment system used by Medicare and most other payers to set physician fees. Each service is assigned relative value units (RVUs) that reflect the estimated resource cost — physician work, practice expense, and malpractice — and then multiplied by a dollar conversion factor to produce the actual payment.
Medicare Physician Fee Schedule based on RBRVS replaced CPR charges beginning January 1, 1992 — Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act of 1989

Anatomy of an RVU: Three Components, One Payment
Every Medicare-covered physician service is assigned a total RVU that is the sum of three distinct components. The first is the physician work RVU (wRVU) — intended to capture the time, technical skill, physical effort, mental effort and judgment, and stress associated with the service. The second is the practice expense RVU (PE RVU) — reflecting the overhead costs of running a medical practice: staff, equipment, supplies, and facilities. The third is the malpractice RVU (PLI RVU) — representing the professional liability insurance costs attributable to the service.
To produce a payment amount, each RVU component is first adjusted by a geographic practice cost index (GPCI) — a locality-based multiplier that reflects cost differences across regions. The adjusted RVUs are then summed and multiplied by the national conversion factor. For example, in 2025 the conversion factor is $32.35. A service assigned 2.0 work RVUs in a locality with a GPCI of 1.0, combined with practice expense and malpractice components, might yield a total payment in the range of $80–$120 depending on the specific service. The formula is: Payment = (wRVU × work GPCI + PE RVU × PE GPCI + PLI RVU × PLI GPCI) × Conversion Factor.
The conversion factor is set annually by CMS through the Physician Fee Schedule rulemaking process. Critically, the conversion factor has largely stagnated or declined in real (inflation-adjusted) terms over the past two decades, even as practice costs have risen. For CY 2025, CMS finalized a conversion factor of $32.3465 — a decrease of $0.94 (approximately 2.83%) from the CY 2024 rate of $33.29. This persistent downward pressure on the conversion factor, combined with rising overhead costs, has squeezed physician practice margins — particularly in primary care specialties that cannot offset revenue declines with high procedure volume.
The physician selects the Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code that describes the service rendered — a 99214 office visit, a 27447 total knee replacement, and so on.
Assign CPT Code
CMS publishes the wRVU, PE RVU, and PLI RVU for each CPT code in the annual Medicare Physician Fee Schedule.
Look Up RVU Components
Each RVU component is multiplied by the locality-specific Geographic Practice Cost Index (GPCI) to reflect regional cost differences.
Apply Geographic Adjustments
The three geographically adjusted RVU components are added together to produce total adjusted RVUs for the service.
Sum Adjusted RVUs
Total adjusted RVUs are multiplied by the national conversion factor (e.g., $32.35 in 2025) to produce the Medicare payment amount.
Multiply by Conversion Factor
How a Physician Payment Is Calculated Under RBRVS
The RUC: The Committee That Sets the Scale
RVU values are not set unilaterally by CMS. They are developed and recommended primarily through the AMA/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale Update Committee — universally known as the RUC. The RUC is a private advisory body convened by the American Medical Association whose 32 members are drawn largely from physician specialty societies. CMS accepts the large majority of RUC recommendations: a 2012 Health Affairs study found it agreed with about 87% of the RUC's work-value recommendations from 1994 to 2010.
The composition of the RUC has been a persistent source of criticism. Primary care physicians — family physicians, general internists, general pediatricians — represent only about 19% of RUC seats, despite accounting for nearly a quarter of the physician workforce and handling approximately 35% of all patient visits. Procedural and surgical specialties, by contrast, hold the majority of seats and have historically proposed RVU values that favor their own services. Since CMS adopted most of those recommendations, the result has been a payment schedule that systematically overvalues procedures relative to the cognitive work of primary care.
The RUC process has also been criticized for its opacity. RUC deliberations are not public, and the specialty society survey instruments used to estimate physician time and effort have been questioned for their reliability. When the Government Accountability Office (GAO) examined the RUC process in 2015, it found that CMS lacked the independent data it needed to validate RUC recommendations and recommended that CMS develop additional mechanisms to review values. Despite these critiques, the RUC remains the central institution through which RBRVS values are set.
In 2021, CMS substantially revised the work RVU values for office-based evaluation and management (E/M) codes — the CPT codes used for primary care and specialist office visits. The revision increased wRVUs for complex visits by roughly 28–33% (99214 from 1.50 to 1.92; 99215 from 2.11 to 2.80), representing the most significant effort in RBRVS history to correct the documented undervaluation of cognitive, relationship-based care.
However, because the Medicare fee schedule is budget-neutral by law, the increases for E/M codes required offsetting reductions in other services. Procedural specialties — including surgery, radiology, and others — saw payment reductions as a consequence. The revaluation also had limited impact on total physician compensation because commercial insurers, which cover the majority of patient visits for most physicians, did not uniformly follow Medicare's revised relativities.
The 2021 Evaluation and Management Code Revaluation
Why RVUs Favor Procedures Over Primary Care
The structural bias toward procedures in the RBRVS system is not a subtle phenomenon — it is the defining driver of the specialty income gap in American medicine. A 30-minute surgical procedure routinely generates more wRVUs than an hour of complex cognitive work with a patient managing multiple chronic conditions. This is partly a historical artifact of how the original RVU values were set — based on physician surveys of time and effort conducted in the late 1980s, when procedural work was more clearly demarcated and more easily quantified than the diffuse cognitive labor of primary care.
The consequence is a compensation structure that sends powerful signals to medical students choosing specialties. When primary care physicians can earn $250,000–$280,000 annually while surgical subspecialists routinely earn $400,000–$700,000 or more, the RBRVS payment differential is a major factor driving specialty selection. The United States has a well-documented shortage of primary care physicians — a shortage that worsens as each cohort of medical graduates makes rational economic choices in response to the signals embedded in the payment system.
The problem is compounded by the fact that primary care is where prevention, early detection, and chronic disease management happen — the services that could most efficiently reduce downstream high-cost utilization. A payment system that chronically under-reimburses primary care is, in effect, a system that chronically underinvests in the part of the healthcare pipeline most capable of reducing total spending and improving population health.

Procedural vs. Cognitive Services: Payment Comparison
wRVUs as a Productivity Metric: How Employers Use RVUs
Beyond Medicare payment, wRVUs have become the dominant productivity benchmark in physician employment contracts. Hospitals, health systems, and large group practices routinely compensate employed physicians based on wRVU production — a physician who generates more wRVUs earns a higher base or bonus. This adoption of the Medicare payment unit as an internal incentive metric has propagated the procedural bias of the RBRVS system into the employment structures of academic medical centers, community hospitals, and private practices across the country.
The wRVU-based compensation model was widely adopted because it seemed to solve the problem of measuring physician productivity in a consistent, specialty-comparable way. A wRVU is a wRVU whether earned by a cardiologist, a hospitalist, or a family physician. However, using wRVUs as the compensation metric imports all the valuation biases of the RBRVS directly into compensation design. A physician whose work consists of managing complex elderly patients with multiple chronic conditions — the kind of patient for whom cognitive coordination is the primary clinical need — will produce fewer wRVUs per hour than a physician who performs high-volume, lower-complexity procedures.
The shift toward value-based care is creating pressure on wRVU-based compensation models because many of the activities that generate value under population health contracts — care gap closure, panel management, preventive outreach, care coordination — do not correspond to any billable CPT code and generate no wRVUs. Forward-thinking health systems are beginning to supplement or replace wRVU compensation with models that include panel quality metrics, total cost of care performance, and population health outcomes. This transition, however, requires significant investment in data infrastructure and a willingness to bear transition risk.
The wRVU is now used in two ways: (1) as the unit for Medicare physician fee calculation, and (2) as the dominant internal productivity metric in physician employment contracts. Both uses carry the same procedural bias — and both will need to evolve as healthcare moves toward value-based payment.
The Conversion Factor Problem: Stagnant Pay in an Inflationary World
The conversion factor translates RVU relativities into actual dollar payments. Its trajectory over the past two decades has been a consistent source of concern for physician organizations. The conversion factor has not kept pace with the Medicare Economic Index (MEI) — CMS's own measure of the inflation in physician practice costs — for most of the post-2002 period. The result is that even as the nominal conversion factor has fluctuated, its real purchasing power has declined. Physicians who relied on Medicare payment for a substantial share of their revenue faced compounding economic pressure.
The CY 2025 conversion factor of $32.3465 represents a 2.83% decrease from the 2024 rate of $33.29. This reduction followed the expiration of a temporary 2.93% increase Congress enacted for 2024. Without periodic congressional action to boost the conversion factor above its statutory baseline, it will continue to decline as the budget-neutrality requirement and the absence of an inflation adjustment built into the fee schedule law compound over time.
This dynamic has important implications for the transition to value-based care. If FFS payment is declining in real terms but value-based payment models remain in development and carry financial risk, the intermediate period — when providers are partially in FFS and partially in value-based contracts — is economically dangerous for practices. CMS and Congress have repeatedly acknowledged this "valley of death" between FFS and value-based payment without fully resolving it. Physician organizations have argued that stabilizing the conversion factor is a precondition for the kind of patient investment in value-based infrastructure that the transition requires.
RVUs and CPT codes are related but distinct. A CPT code identifies what service was rendered; an RVU is the assigned value of that service. The same CPT code can have different payment amounts in different payers' fee schedules — commercial insurers negotiate their own conversion factors and may apply different relative values. Medicare's RBRVS is the anchor, but it is not the only fee schedule in use.
Important Distinction
The RBRVS physician payment system was developed by Harvard economist William Hsiao and implemented in 1992 to replace arbitrary CPR charges with a resource-based fee schedule.
Each Medicare payment is calculated by multiplying geographically adjusted RVUs (work + practice expense + malpractice) by the national conversion factor — set at $32.35 for 2025.
RVU values are primarily set by the AMA's Relative Value Scale Update Committee (RUC), where procedural specialists hold the majority of seats and primary care is underrepresented at roughly 19%.
The RBRVS systematically overvalues procedural services relative to cognitive and primary care work, driving the specialty income gap and medical student specialty selection away from primary care.
wRVUs have become the dominant physician productivity metric in employment contracts, propagating the procedural bias of Medicare's payment system into hospital compensation design.
The conversion factor has stagnated or declined in real terms over two decades, creating compounding financial pressure on physician practices — particularly those heavily dependent on Medicare.
The 2021 E/M code revaluation was the most significant attempt to correct cognitive-service undervaluation in RBRVS history, but its impact was limited by budget-neutrality offsets and commercial insurer non-adoption.
The RUC is a private advisory body convened by the American Medical Association. Its 32 members are drawn largely from physician specialty societies, and it recommends RVU values to CMS. A 2012 Health Affairs study found CMS agreed with about 87% of the RUC's work-value recommendations from 1994 to 2010. This structure — and the underrepresentation of primary care on the RUC — has been a major driver of the procedural payment bias in the RBRVS system.
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), which sets values unilaterally through its actuaries.
The AMA/Specialty Society Relative Value Scale Update Committee (RUC), whose recommendations CMS accepts in the large majority of cases.
The American Hospital Association (AHA), which negotiates values on behalf of hospital-based physicians.
The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission (MedPAC), which sets values through Congressional mandate.

######## value-based-care | mips-merit-based-incentive | MIPS: The Merit-Based Incentive Payment System
MIPS: The Merit-Based Incentive Payment System
Why MIPS Was Created: The Death of the SGR and the Birth of MACRA
For nearly two decades, Medicare physician payment operated under the shadow of the Sustainable Growth Rate (SGR) formula — a mechanism Congress invented in 1997 to prevent physician spending from exceeding GDP growth. The SGR failed in its purpose almost immediately. Whenever physician spending exceeded the SGR target, the formula required automatic fee cuts that Congress consistently reversed through emergency "doc fix" legislation, rather than allow payment rates to collapse. By 2015, the accumulated deficit had grown to the point where the pending automatic cut was 21.2% — an amount no one considered politically or practically possible to implement.
On April 16, 2015, President Obama signed the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act (MACRA) into law, with rare bipartisan support. MACRA permanently repealed the SGR and replaced the patchwork of overlapping quality reporting programs — the Physician Quality Reporting System (PQRS), the Value Modifier, and the Meaningful Use program for electronic health records — with a single unified framework: the Quality Payment Program (QPP). The QPP offered physicians two paths: the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) and participation in Advanced Alternative Payment Models (Advanced APMs).
MIPS launched January 1, 2017, as the default track for most Medicare-participating clinicians. It was designed to consolidate performance measurement into a single composite score, reduce administrative duplication, and begin moving physician payment toward a value orientation by adjusting fees up or down based on quality, cost, and technology adoption. For the first time, physician payment adjustments under Medicare would be explicitly tied to measured performance — not just volume.
Key Concept: MIPS (Merit-Based Incentive Payment System) is the primary track of the CMS Quality Payment Program, established by MACRA in 2015. It scores eligible clinicians on four performance categories — Quality, Cost, Promoting Interoperability, and Improvement Activities — and adjusts Medicare Part B payment rates up or down by up to ±9% based on their composite score.
CMS estimated approximately 572,000 eligible clinicians required to participate in the 2024 MIPS performance period — CMS QPP Final Rule 2024

The Four Performance Categories: What MIPS Actually Measures
MIPS organizes performance measurement into four weighted categories, each contributing a share of the 100-point composite score used to determine a clinician's payment adjustment. For 2024, the category weights are: Quality (30%), Cost (30%), Promoting Interoperability (25%), and Improvement Activities (15%). These weights represent a significant evolution from the program's early years, when Quality carried 60% of the score and Cost was minimal. The increasing weight of Cost reflects CMS's intent to hold clinicians more accountable for the total expense of the care they deliver.
The Quality category requires clinicians to report on at least six quality measures from a list of hundreds, including one outcome measure or one high-priority measure. Measures span clinical domains such as diabetes management, cancer screening, cardiovascular risk reduction, and behavioral health. Performance is benchmarked against historical rates, so a clinician who outperforms their peers on a measure earns more points in that measure's category. The Cost category, by contrast, does not require any reporting — CMS calculates it directly from Medicare claims, attributing episode and total cost of care metrics to the responsible clinician.
The Promoting Interoperability (PI) category, worth 25% of the composite score, evaluates the use of certified electronic health record technology, with measures focused on patient access to records, electronic prescribing, health information exchange, and public health reporting. The Improvement Activities category, at 15%, allows clinicians to earn points by attesting to participation in one of approximately 95 defined activities — such as care coordination, patient engagement, clinical practice improvement, or population health management — each weighted as medium or high impact.
Report at least 6 quality measures (including 1 outcome measure) via claims, registry, EHR, or QCDR submission over a 12-month performance period.
Collect Quality Data
CMS automatically calculates cost category performance from Medicare claims — no separate reporting required from the clinician.
CMS Calculates Cost
Clinicians attest to completing one or more improvement activities worth a total of at least 40 points (medium activities = 10 pts, high = 20 pts).
Attest to Improvement Activities
Clinicians report on EHR-based PI measures through their certified EHR technology for a minimum 180-day period.
Report Promoting Interoperability
CMS weights the four category scores (30/30/25/15) and sums them into a 0–100 MIPS Final Score for the performance year.
Calculate Composite Score
The composite score is compared to the performance threshold (75 points in 2024) and a payment adjustment of up to +/-9% is applied to Medicare Part B payments two years later.
Apply Payment Adjustment
How the MIPS Composite Score Is Built
Performance Thresholds, Payment Adjustments, and the 2026 Outlook
The MIPS payment adjustment applies to Medicare Part B payments in the year two years after the performance year — so 2024 performance determines 2026 payment rates. For 2024, the performance threshold is 75 points on the 100-point composite scale. Clinicians who score at or above 75 points receive a neutral or positive payment adjustment; those who score below 75 receive a negative adjustment; those below 18.75 points (the exceptional negative threshold) receive the maximum penalty of -9%.
The statutory maximum positive adjustment is also ±9%, but the actual positive adjustment is constrained by the program's budget-neutrality requirement: the total positive adjustments paid must be funded by the total negative adjustments collected. In practice, because the vast majority of MIPS-eligible clinicians score above the performance threshold, the positive adjustment pool is spread thinly across a large number of clinicians. For 2026 payments (based on 2024 performance), CMS estimated the maximum positive adjustment at only approximately +1.05% — the lowest in program history — despite the statutory maximum of +9%.
This dynamic reveals a fundamental tension in MIPS design. The program was built to create meaningful financial incentives for improvement, but budget-neutrality has compressed the actual positive adjustment to the point where it provides a weak incentive for the additional administrative burden required to optimize performance. The threat of the -9% penalty has been more behaviorally significant than the promise of a +1.05% bonus — a pattern that raises questions about whether MIPS is actually changing clinical behavior or primarily ensuring compliance.
