Who Must Participate and Who Is Exempt
Not every Medicare-participating clinician is subject to MIPS. CMS defines eligibility through a low-volume threshold: clinicians must exceed all three of the following criteria to be required to participate — billing more than $90,000 for Medicare Part B-covered services, seeing more than 200 Medicare patients, and providing more than 200 covered professional services to Part B patients in a year. Clinicians who fall below any one of these thresholds are exempt from MIPS requirements, though they may choose to voluntarily report.
Clinicians who qualify to participate in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model (Advanced APM) — such as a qualifying ACO under the Medicare Shared Savings Program, or certain CMS Innovation Center models — are exempt from MIPS and instead receive the Advanced APM incentive. Through 2022, this incentive included a 5% lump-sum bonus on Medicare Part B payments. That bonus expired at the end of 2022, creating a significant policy debate about whether the financial case for joining an Advanced APM had been sufficiently weakened to slow the transition to value-based care.
Certain other clinicians are excluded: those in their first year of Medicare participation, those enrolled in Medicare Advantage, and certain facility-based clinicians who may be scored under a facility-based scoring option. Additionally, small practices and solo practitioners — particularly those in rural or underserved areas — have historically faced disproportionate MIPS penalties, in part because they lack the administrative infrastructure to optimize reporting across four performance categories simultaneously.
MIPS adjustments apply only to Medicare Part B allowed charges — not to total revenue from all payers. A physician who earns the maximum +9% MIPS bonus still receives only a 9% increase on their Medicare-specific claims, which may represent a fraction of their overall practice revenue. The financial impact of MIPS is often smaller than it appears from the headline adjustment percentages.
Common Misconception
Administrative Burden: MIPS's Most Persistent Criticism
Since its launch, MIPS has been criticized by physician organizations, small practices, and health policy researchers for imposing substantial administrative costs that are disproportionate to the financial incentives on offer. Participating in MIPS requires clinicians to understand hundreds of quality measures, select appropriate reporting mechanisms (claims, registry, EHR, or QCDR), maintain certified EHR technology meeting PI requirements, attest to improvement activities, and monitor their performance relative to benchmarks that shift annually. For a small or solo practice, this work often requires either significant staff time or the engagement of a third-party reporting vendor.
The disproportionate impact on small practices is well-documented. According to American Medical Association data, 49% of solo physicians received MIPS payment penalties in recent performance years, compared to 29% of small practices and 18% of rural practices. Larger health systems and multispecialty group practices, with dedicated quality reporting teams and sophisticated EHR implementations, consistently outperform solo and small group practitioners on MIPS scores — not necessarily because they deliver better care, but because they have more administrative capacity to optimize the reporting process.
This critique reflects a deeper concern about MIPS as a policy instrument: it measures and rewards the ability to navigate a complex reporting system as much as it measures or rewards actual quality of care. CMS has attempted to address administrative burden through the development of MIPS Value Pathways (MVPs) — streamlined reporting pathways organized around specific specialties or clinical conditions — but adoption has been slow and the program structure remains complex for most participating clinicians.
The American Medical Association has consistently documented the administrative cost of MIPS participation. In surveys of physician practices, the AMA found that MIPS-related administrative work can consume 15 or more hours per physician per week when preparing for reporting periods, diverting clinical staff to documentation and data-entry tasks rather than patient care.
The AMA has called for fundamental MIPS reform, arguing that the program's administrative overhead exceeds its clinical benefit for the majority of participating clinicians — particularly those in independent and small-group practice settings that lack the infrastructure of large health systems.
AMA MIPS Burden Research
MIPS vs. Advanced APMs: The Two Paths of the Quality Payment Program
MACRA was designed to offer two fundamentally different paths toward value-based payment. MIPS is an incremental path — it preserves the fee-for-service payment architecture while layering on quality-and-cost measurement and a modest payment adjustment. It asks clinicians to report and be measured, but does not fundamentally change how their revenue is generated. Advanced APMs, by contrast, require clinicians to take on significant financial risk — or at minimum, meaningful quality accountability — in exchange for relief from MIPS reporting and an additional financial incentive.
Advanced APMs include the Medicare Shared Savings Program at its highest risk tracks, the ACO REACH model, certain bundled payment models, and designated CMMI Innovation models. Qualifying for the Advanced APM bonus requires that a threshold percentage of a clinician's Medicare payments or patients be tied to the qualifying Advanced APM, and that the model involve more-than-nominal financial risk or a medical home model meeting CMS criteria. For 2026, the Advanced APM incentive is now subject to policy review following the expiration of the 5% bonus at end of 2022.
The design tension between MIPS and Advanced APMs reflects a broader policy debate: should the transition to value-based care be gradual and voluntary, preserving FFS while adding quality signals, or should it require providers to take on actual financial accountability for outcomes and cost? MIPS has been criticized as a "value-based care on training wheels" approach that generates compliance activity without fundamentally realigning incentives. Advanced APMs represent the deeper structural shift, but they require data infrastructure, care redesign capabilities, and risk tolerance that many smaller practices simply do not have.
MIPS is like a performance review at work — your score affects your raise by a few percent, but your underlying job and pay structure remain the same. Advanced APMs are more like moving from a salaried role to a performance-based partnership: the risk is higher, but so is the potential reward, and the nature of your work fundamentally changes.
MIPS vs. Advanced APMs: Incremental vs. Structural Payment Reform

######## value-based-care | vbc-fundamentals-m1 | Why the Way We Pay for Healthcare Is Breaking the System — And How Paying for Value Could Fix It
Why the Way We Pay for Healthcare Is Breaking the System — And How Paying for Value Could Fix It
The Fundamental Problem: A System That Pays for Sickness, Not Health
The United States spends more on healthcare than any other nation in the world — $5.3 trillion in 2024, or $15,474 per person (CMS). And yet, by nearly every measure of population health, the country performs below its peer nations. Life expectancy in the U.S. was 78.4 years in 2023, 4.1 years shorter than the average among comparable wealthy countries. Rates of chronic disease, preventable hospitalizations, and avoidable deaths are persistently higher in the U.S. than in nations that spend far less. The paradox is stark: more spending, worse outcomes.
This paradox is not the result of incompetent physicians, inferior technology, or inadequate hospitals. On most measures of technical medical capability — cancer survival rates, cardiac intervention outcomes, cutting-edge diagnostic tools — American medicine is among the best in the world. The problem is structural. The way the United States pays for healthcare systematically rewards the wrong things: it rewards treating illness rather than preventing it, rewards individual services rather than coordinated care, and rewards volume rather than value. The payment architecture shapes the behavior of every actor in the system, and the current architecture is pointing almost everyone in the wrong direction.
Value-based care (VBC) is the policy response to this misalignment. It is a broad umbrella term for payment and care delivery approaches that tie financial incentives to quality outcomes, patient experience, and cost-efficiency — rather than to the raw count of services delivered. Understanding value-based care requires first understanding the problem it is designed to solve: the incentive structure of fee-for-service medicine and the consequences that structure produces.
Key Concept: Value-based care is a healthcare payment and delivery model in which providers are compensated based on patient health outcomes and the efficiency of care delivery — rather than on the volume of services provided. The central idea is to align financial incentives with the goal of keeping patients healthy.
CMS National Health Expenditure Report — U.S. spent $5.3 trillion on health in 2024

The Triple Aim: The Framework Behind Value-Based Care
The intellectual foundation of the value-based care movement is the Triple Aim, a framework articulated by the Institute for Healthcare Improvement (IHI) in 2008. The Triple Aim holds that health system improvement requires simultaneously pursuing three goals: improving the patient experience of care (including quality and satisfaction), improving the health of populations, and reducing the per-capita cost of healthcare. These three dimensions are not naturally in tension — indeed, the Triple Aim's central insight is that addressing all three together is both possible and necessary.
Fee-for-service medicine is structurally incapable of pursuing the Triple Aim because it optimizes only for volume — which is a proxy for neither quality nor health. A system that pays for more services will generate more services, regardless of whether those services improve the patient experience, improve population health, or reduce cost. The Triple Aim requires payment mechanisms that can reward coordination, prevention, and efficiency rather than activity.
In 2014, Thomas Bodenheimer and Christine Sinsky (Annals of Family Medicine) proposed expanding the framework to a "Quadruple Aim" that adds a fourth dimension: improving the health and well-being of the healthcare workforce. This addition acknowledges that provider burnout — driven in part by the administrative burden of documentation-heavy FFS billing and compliance programs like MIPS — is itself a systemic problem that undermines care quality. A truly value-based system should improve the experience of care for clinicians, not just patients.
The problem is not that American medicine lacks quality. The problem is that the payment system rewards the wrong quality — the quality of filling out a claim, not the quality of keeping a patient well.
The Spectrum of Value-Based Payment Models
Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a spectrum of approaches that shift incentives away from pure volume and toward quality, efficiency, and outcomes. These models vary in the degree of financial risk they impose on providers, the scope of services they cover, and the populations they address. Understanding the landscape of models is essential for anyone navigating healthcare finance and policy.
At one end of the spectrum are pay-for-performance (P4P) programs, which layer quality bonuses or penalties on top of existing FFS payments. MIPS is a prominent example: it preserves fee-for-service billing while adjusting final payments up or down based on a quality and cost score. P4P models represent the lowest-risk entry point into value-based care — they do not require providers to change their fundamental revenue model — but they also generate the least structural change in care delivery because the FFS volume incentive remains intact.
Moving up the risk spectrum, bundled payment models establish a single fixed payment for an entire episode of care — for example, a total knee replacement including surgery, inpatient stay, rehabilitation, and follow-up visits over a defined period. Providers who manage the episode below the target price retain the savings; those who exceed it share in the loss. Bundled payments create powerful incentives for care coordination across the inpatient and post-acute continuum, but they apply only to defined episodes and do not address population health or primary prevention.
Lower Risk (Closer to FFS)
Pay-for-Performance (e.g., MIPS): FFS + quality adjustment

Value-Based Payment Model Spectrum
Accountable Care Organizations: The Flagship VBC Model
Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) are the most widely deployed model of value-based care in the United States. An ACO is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other healthcare providers who agree to share accountability for the quality and total cost of care for an assigned population of patients. Rather than being paid for each individual service, ACO participants receive their FFS payments as usual — but at year's end, if the ACO's total spending for its attributed beneficiaries is below a risk-adjusted benchmark, the ACO earns a share of those savings. If spending exceeds the benchmark, the ACO may owe losses back, depending on its risk track.
The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP) is the largest ACO program in the United States. As of January 2024, 480 MSSP ACOs include more than 608,000 clinicians providing care to nearly 11 million Medicare beneficiaries. In 2023, MSSP ACOs generated $2.1 billion in net savings for Medicare — the largest in the program's more than ten-year history — while also demonstrating quality improvements in diabetes management, blood pressure control, cancer screening, and depression care.
The ACO REACH (Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health) model, administered by CMMI, tests deeper accountable care, including a Global option in which ACOs take on 100% of shared savings and losses and may elect capitated payments. In 2023, the 132 ACO REACH participants managed care for more than 2 million Medicare beneficiaries, generating $695 million in net savings. The model explicitly incorporates health equity requirements — ACOs must develop health equity plans and report on disparities for high-need populations — marking a significant expansion of the VBC framework beyond cost and quality to address systemic disparities in care access and outcomes.
In 2023, the MSSP achieved its seventh consecutive year of program-wide savings and its largest net savings total in program history: $2.1 billion returned to Medicare. ACOs in the program earned shared savings payments totaling $3.1 billion — also a record. Performance also improved on quality measures related to diabetes care, blood pressure control, colorectal and breast cancer screening, statin therapy, and depression screening.
As of January 2024, 480 ACOs participated, covering nearly 11 million beneficiaries through the work of more than 608,000 clinicians. The program demonstrates that large-scale ACO participation can simultaneously reduce Medicare spending and improve measured quality — the core promise of the Triple Aim.
Medicare Shared Savings Program — 2023 Record Results
Capitation and Global Budgets: The Deepest Form of VBC
At the far end of the value-based care spectrum are capitation and global budget models, which represent the most complete structural departure from fee-for-service. Under full capitation, a provider organization receives a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment from a payer to cover all covered services for an assigned population — regardless of how many services are actually used. The provider keeps the margin if it delivers care efficiently; it absorbs the loss if it does not. Capitation fully inverts the FFS incentive: instead of more services = more revenue, the logic becomes appropriate care = retained margin.
Global budgets extend this logic to entire health systems or regions. Rather than paying on a per-patient basis, a global budget model sets an annual spending total for a defined population and gives a delivery system or state accountability for staying within that budget while meeting quality standards. Global budgets are common in other countries — the UK's NHS operates largely on a global budget basis — but they are rare in the United States, where Maryland's hospital global budget program and Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model (2017–2025) have been the most prominent examples.
Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model, which ran from 2017 (performance years from 2018) through December 31, 2025, is particularly noteworthy because it aligned Medicare, Medicaid, and major commercial insurers under a single, statewide value-based payment framework — the first all-payer ACO model in the U.S.. The model drove significant investment in primary care infrastructure and care coordination in Vermont, and its record offers lessons for other states seeking to address both cost and health equity through payment reform.
CMS attributes Medicare beneficiaries to the ACO based on their primary care utilization — which provider they visit most for primary care.
Assign a Patient Panel
CMS calculates a risk-adjusted spending benchmark — the projected total Medicare cost for that population based on historical trends and regional factors.
Set a Benchmark
ACO clinicians deliver care under their existing FFS billing arrangements — the payment change happens at the back end, not the point of service.
Providers Deliver Care
At year-end, CMS compares actual total Medicare spending for the attributed population to the benchmark.
Compare Actual vs. Benchmark
If actual spending is below the benchmark, the ACO earns a percentage share of the savings (40–75% depending on the track). If spending exceeds the benchmark in a two-sided risk track, the ACO repays a share of the losses.
Share Savings or Losses
Savings sharing is contingent on meeting minimum quality performance requirements — ACOs that miss quality thresholds have their shared savings reduced or withheld.
Quality Gate
How Value Flows in an ACO Shared Savings Model
Why the Transition Is Hard — and Why It Is Happening Anyway
The case for value-based care is compelling in theory, and the evidence from programs like MSSP and ACO REACH is increasingly convincing in practice. Yet the transition from fee-for-service to value-based payment has been slower and more contested than reformers hoped when the ACA established CMMI in 2010. The reasons are structural, financial, and cultural. Provider organizations that built their facilities, staffed their teams, and financed their operations around FFS revenue cannot rapidly restructure without risk. A hospital that derives 40% of its margin from high-volume elective procedures does not easily absorb the shift to a model that rewards reducing utilization.
There is also the challenge of measurement. Value-based payment requires robust quality metrics, reliable patient attribution, risk adjustment that does not penalize providers caring for sicker or more complex populations, and data infrastructure that can track patients across settings and over time. Building these systems is expensive, slow, and contentious. Disputes over which quality measures are clinically meaningful, how to attribute patients to providers in a fragmented system, and how to adjust benchmarks for social determinants of health have occupied policy debates for more than a decade without full resolution.
Despite these barriers, the direction of travel is clear. CMS has set explicit goals for moving Medicare toward value-based payment, and commercial payers have followed. The combination of rising healthcare costs, aging demographics, and the documented failure of FFS to produce commensurate health outcomes has created irreversible pressure for payment reform. For healthcare professionals, administrators, and policymakers, understanding the architecture of value-based care — its models, its incentives, its measurement systems, and its limitations — is no longer optional. It is the vocabulary of the field.
Value-based care programs have documented early successes in reducing cost and improving quality metrics for defined populations — but evidence on long-term population health impact and equity outcomes is still developing. Not all VBC models reduce health disparities; some early evidence suggests that ACOs serving more advantaged populations outperform those serving high-need, low-income populations, raising important questions about how VBC design can be improved to reduce — rather than widen — health equity gaps.
Key Limitation of VBC
The U.S. spends $5.3 trillion on healthcare annually — about 2.5 times the OECD per-capita average — yet achieves below-average outcomes on most population health indicators, including life expectancy.
The core cause of this paradox is a fee-for-service payment architecture that rewards volume over value, fragmenting care and incentivizing overtreatment while under-incentivizing prevention and coordination.
Value-based care (VBC) is a broad umbrella for payment models that tie financial incentives to quality, outcomes, and cost-efficiency — the central mechanism for realigning the payment system.
The Triple Aim framework — improving patient experience, improving population health, and reducing per-capita cost — provides the conceptual foundation for VBC design.
VBC models exist on a spectrum from low-risk pay-for-performance programs (like MIPS) to full capitation and global budgets; each point on the spectrum involves different degrees of financial risk and structural change.
ACOs are the flagship VBC model in Medicare; the MSSP generated a record $2.1 billion in net savings in 2023 while improving quality metrics — the seventh consecutive year of program-wide savings.
The transition to VBC faces structural, financial, and measurement barriers — but the policy and market direction is clear, making VBC literacy an essential competency for all healthcare professionals.
Pay-for-performance programs like MIPS preserve the fee-for-service billing structure and layer quality adjustments on top — providers still earn more by delivering more services, but their final payment is modified upward or downward by a quality and cost score. Capitation replaces the per-service payment with a fixed per-member-per-month amount, fully inverting the FFS incentive: efficient, high-quality care generates margin, while unnecessary utilization erodes it.
Pay-for-performance eliminates billing entirely; capitation still requires fee-for-service billing.
Pay-for-performance adjusts FFS payments based on quality scores; capitation replaces FFS with a fixed per-member payment regardless of volume.
Capitation applies only to hospital services; pay-for-performance covers physician services only.
Both models are functionally identical — they differ only in which agency administers them.
Which of the following best describes the core structural difference between pay-for-performance models (like MIPS) and capitation models?

######## value-based-care | aco-basics | ACO Fundamentals: Attribution, Benchmarks & Shared Savings
ACO Fundamentals: Attribution, Benchmarks & Shared Savings
What Is an Accountable Care Organization?
An Accountable Care Organization (ACO) is a group of doctors, hospitals, and other health care providers who voluntarily come together to deliver coordinated, high-quality care to Medicare patients. The central premise is that when providers collaborate—rather than operate in fragmented silos—they can prevent unnecessary services, catch problems earlier, and improve outcomes, all while reducing overall spending. Unlike a health maintenance organization (HMO), patients retain full freedom to see any Medicare provider; ACO membership is invisible to the patient unless they are informed.
ACOs operate under Medicare's fee-for-service (FFS) billing system as their baseline. Providers continue to bill and receive standard FFS payments for each service they deliver. On top of that baseline, the ACO is measured against a spending benchmark and a quality scorecard. If the ACO collectively keeps spending below the benchmark and meets quality thresholds, it earns a share of the savings—known as shared savings. If spending exceeds the benchmark, some ACO tracks require the group to pay back a portion of those excess costs, a feature called downside risk or shared losses.
The legal foundation for Medicare ACOs is Section 3022 of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), which amended Title XVIII of the Social Security Act by adding Section 1899 to establish the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP). The MSSP regulations were finalized in November 2011 and became effective January 3, 2012, with the first ACO agreements starting as early as April 1, 2012.
Key Concept: An ACO is not an insurance product and does not require patients to change their behavior. It is a provider-side accountability mechanism—providers take responsibility for the cost and quality of care for a defined patient population while patients continue receiving traditional Medicare benefits.
In performance year 2024, 476 ACOs participated in the Medicare Shared Savings Program, and the highest share of ACOs since the program began earned performance payments. Source: CMS PY2024 Fact Sheet.

How Attribution Works: Assigning Patients to an ACO
Because patients do not enroll in an ACO directly, CMS uses a process called attribution—sometimes called assignment—to determine which patients "belong" to which ACO for measurement purposes. Attribution is based on where a patient receives the plurality of their primary care services. Specifically, CMS examines claims data to identify which ACO-affiliated clinician provided the most primary care evaluation and management visits to a given patient, and that ACO receives credit (and accountability) for that patient.
CMS currently offers ACOs two main attribution approaches. Under prospective attribution, patients are assigned at the start of the contract performance year based on their claims from the prior calendar year. This gives ACOs advance knowledge of their defined population, enabling proactive outreach and care management. Under retrospective attribution, patients are assigned at the end of the performance period based on services used during that year, which typically produces a larger attributed population but reduces the ACO's ability to plan ahead. A hybrid approach—preliminary prospective with retrospective reconciliation—begins with a prospective list that is updated quarterly and finalized retrospectively, balancing planning certainty with accuracy.
Attribution has important financial and clinical implications. Patients who receive no primary care visits during the year may fall out of attribution, creating gaps in accountability for high-need populations. Additionally, specialists and hospitals cannot directly attract attribution—only primary care evaluation and management services count. This design intentionally places primary care physicians at the center of ACO economics, reinforcing their role as care coordinators for the attributed population.
CMS identifies all primary care evaluation and management (E&M) visits a Medicare FFS beneficiary received during the attribution window.
Primary Care Service Check
Each visit is linked to the TIN (Tax Identification Number) of the billing practice to determine which ACO participants rendered the care.
Provider Linkage
The beneficiary is attributed to the ACO whose affiliated providers delivered the greatest share of primary care E&M services, measured in allowed charges.
Plurality Rule
CMS applies eligibility criteria—the beneficiary must be enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B, not enrolled in Medicare Advantage, and not in certain other payment models.
Eligibility Screen
ACOs receive a preliminary list of attributed beneficiaries each quarter, updated throughout the year, for care management planning purposes.
Notification

Benchmarks: Setting the Spending Target
An ACO's benchmark is the spending target against which its actual expenditures are compared at the end of each performance year. Getting the benchmark right is the single most important technical feature of the MSSP, because an inflated benchmark makes it easy to show savings without actually changing care patterns, while an overly tight benchmark can make participation financially unviable.
The historical benchmark is calculated at the start of each agreement period using the weighted average of risk-adjusted, trended per-capita spending for the ACO's attributed population across the three previous benchmark years. CMS then applies a regional adjustment: the historical benchmark is blended with the average expenditures in the ACO's regional service area, giving partial weight to regional costs. This regional component reduces the incentive to cherry-pick low-cost patients and rewards ACOs that are already efficient relative to their local market.
For new agreement periods beginning January 1, 2024, CMS introduced the Accountable Care Prospective Trend (ACPT)—a fixed projected national spending growth rate—as a third component of the benchmark update factor, creating what is now known as a three-way blended update. The ACPT is blended with actual national and regional FFS spending trends to set the annual benchmark update, reducing the volatility that occurred when benchmarks moved dramatically with pandemic-era utilization swings. Together, these adjustments are designed to make the benchmark a stable, fair, and credible target.
Key Concept: The benchmark is not simply last year's spending. It is a risk-adjusted, regionally-blended, prospectively-trended target. An ACO that starts from a high-cost baseline can earn shared savings even if costs only fall modestly, while an already-efficient ACO must work harder to stay below its benchmark.
Beating the benchmark shows spending was lower than the target—but that target is not necessarily what spending would have been without the ACO. The Congressional Budget Office's April 2024 review of research that compares ACO spending with counterfactual estimates, rather than program benchmarks, found savings concentrated in certain types of ACOs — those led by independent physician groups, with more primary care providers, and with higher baseline spending. Selection effects—ACOs attracting lower-cost practices—account for some reported savings.
Common Misconception: Beating the Benchmark ≠ Reducing Spending
Shared Savings and Shared Losses: The Risk Architecture
When an ACO's actual per-capita spending falls below its benchmark by more than the minimum savings rate (MSR), it qualifies to share in those savings with Medicare. The MSR exists to filter out random statistical variation—small ACOs have higher MSRs because random fluctuation in spending is larger in smaller populations. Conversely, ACOs in downside-risk tracks face a minimum loss rate (MLR): spending must exceed the benchmark by more than the MLR before losses are owed.
The MSSP is organized into tracks with escalating levels of financial risk and reward. The BASIC track allows new ACOs to enter a glide path, starting with upside-only risk in levels A and B, then progressing to limited two-sided risk in levels C through E. The ENHANCED track offers the highest shared savings rate (up to 75 percent of savings) but requires full two-sided risk from day one. The "Pathways to Success" redesign finalized in 2018 sharply shortened the time an ACO could remain in upside-only risk, but CMS later loosened that limit: the CY2023 Physician Fee Schedule rule let eligible ACOs stay upside-only for up to seven performance years, and in the CY2026 rulemaking CMS moved to cut the maximum back to five.
In 2024, two-thirds of MSSP ACOs were in the Level E or ENHANCED track, carrying downside risk, and they delivered more than two-thirds of all savings — $5.4 billion of $6.6 billion in gross savings, according to an Accountable for Health analysis of CMS data — a marked shift from the program's early years, when nearly all ACOs stayed in upside-only tracks. Performance in 2024 also varied by organization type: low-revenue ACOs, typically physician-led or built around FQHCs and rural health clinics, generated $319 in net per capita savings versus $180 for high-revenue, typically hospital-led ACOs, and ACOs composed predominantly of primary care clinicians generated $403 versus $224.

Quality Measurement and Its Role in ACO Economics
Shared savings payments are contingent on meeting a quality performance standard—ACOs cannot earn purely by cutting costs. CMS evaluates ACO quality using a composite score drawn from measures spanning preventive care, chronic disease management, patient experience, and care coordination. The quality score gates entry to shared savings: ACOs that fall below the quality threshold receive a reduced share of any savings earned, or may be barred from payment entirely.
In 2024, nearly every ACO in the MSSP met CMS's quality standard, continuing a multi-year trend of high marks on patient experience and preventive care measures. Among ACOs reporting through the CMS Web Interface, the mean percentage of beneficiaries with controlled high blood pressure rose from 77.80 percent in 2023 to 79.49 percent in 2024—a statistically significant improvement. Preventive measures such as influenza vaccination and colorectal cancer screening also showed strong average performance.
The quality-savings linkage is a deliberate policy design: it prevents ACOs from gaming the benchmark through under-provision of care. However, critics note that most ACO quality measures are process-based rather than outcome-based, and that near-universal quality compliance across hundreds of ACOs may reflect measure selection as much as genuine care improvement. CMS has signaled ongoing interest in transitioning toward more outcome-oriented and health-equity-sensitive quality metrics.
Think of an ACO like a restaurant group with a shared kitchen budget. Each chef (provider) still cooks individual dishes (services) and charges per plate (FFS billing). But at year-end, if the whole kitchen spent less than expected AND the food quality scores were high, the restaurant group gets a bonus. The key is that no one chef gets rewarded for cutting corners on ingredients—quality scores make sure the food stays good.
ACO shared savings: combining FFS billing with collective accountability
The ACO Landscape: MSSP, ACO REACH, and ACO PC Flex
The MSSP is the largest Medicare ACO program, but it is not the only one. The ACO Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health (REACH) model, administered by the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI), is a separate advanced alternative payment model with higher financial risk and more flexibility. ACO REACH launched in 2023, replacing the Global and Professional Direct Contracting (GPDC) model, which itself built on the Next Generation ACO (2016–2021) and Pioneer ACO (2012–2016) models. In 2023, 132 ACOs participated in ACO REACH, accounting for 23 million beneficiary-months of alignment and generating about $1.64 billion in gross savings (5.8%), of which $694.6 million (2.6%) was net savings to CMS.
The ACO Primary Care Flex (ACO PC Flex) model, launched January 1, 2025, is the newest CMMI initiative. It targets low-revenue MSSP participants—typically smaller, physician-led ACOs—by offering prospective primary care payments (up-front monthly payments rather than retrospective shared savings) to support care management infrastructure that small practices cannot easily finance. This model attempts to solve the capital problem: small practices lack the cash flow to invest in care coordinators, health coaches, and analytics platforms before receiving any savings payments.
Together, these models represent CMS's evolving strategy to move the entire Medicare FFS population—not just commercially insured patients—toward accountable care. The 2025 ACO initiatives announcements from CMS signaled the goal of having every Medicare beneficiary in an accountable care relationship by 2030, though participation remains voluntary and trajectory toward that goal requires continued growth in both ACO numbers and attributed beneficiaries.
Within the ACO REACH model, a subset of participants operates as High-Needs Population (HNP) ACOs, specifically designed to serve beneficiaries with complex chronic conditions or serious illness. In performance year 2023, HNP ACOs achieved a 13.3% net savings rate—substantially higher than Standard ACOs (2.8%) or New Entrant ACOs (4.8%).
This performance reflects the financial upside available when organizations master care management for high-cost, high-need patients. HNP ACOs use intensive care models—home visits, palliative care integration, and social needs navigation—that reduce avoidable hospitalizations and emergency department visits for patients who would otherwise drive disproportionately high Medicare expenditures. Source: CMS ACO REACH PY2023 Financial and Quality Performance Results Fact Sheet.
ACO REACH High-Needs Population ACOs
ACOs are voluntary groups of providers that accept collective accountability for the cost and quality of care for an attributed Medicare population while patients retain full freedom of choice.
Section 3022 of the Affordable Care Act created the Medicare Shared Savings Program in 2012, establishing the legal foundation for Medicare ACOs.
Attribution assigns patients to an ACO based on plurality of primary care services received, with choices between prospective, retrospective, and hybrid methods that affect both population certainty and size.
The ACO benchmark is a risk-adjusted, regionally-blended, prospectively-trended spending target—not simply prior-year spending—and beating it does not automatically mean real-world costs were reduced.
Shared savings are only paid when an ACO both beats its benchmark by more than the minimum savings rate AND meets CMS's quality performance standard, preventing savings through under-provision of care.
Two-thirds of MSSP ACOs operated under two-sided (downside) risk in 2024, delivering more than two-thirds of savings, a major shift from the program's early years, and low-revenue, physician-led ACOs continue to generate larger per capita savings than hospital-led ones.
Beyond the MSSP, CMS operates ACO REACH (for advanced risk models) and the new ACO PC Flex model (for small, physician-led ACOs), reflecting a strategy to move all Medicare FFS beneficiaries into accountable care.

######## value-based-care | aco-performance-evidence | ACO Performance: What the Evidence Shows
ACO Performance: What the Evidence Shows
The Central Question: Do ACOs Actually Save Money?
Since the first Medicare Shared Savings Program ACOs began in April 2012, a persistent and important debate has surrounded a deceptively simple question: do ACOs reduce healthcare spending, or do they merely attract providers who were already efficient? The answer matters enormously for health policy—if ACOs primarily generate shared savings by selecting favorable benchmarks and low-cost patient panels, then the program transfers money to providers without improving efficiency. If they genuinely change care patterns, they offer a scalable path to sustainable Medicare.
The evidence is nuanced and depends critically on how savings are measured. Comparing ACO spending to the program benchmark—the method CMS uses to calculate shared savings payments—consistently shows large, favorable results. But the benchmark is not necessarily what spending would have been in the absence of the ACO. A more rigorous test uses a counterfactual control group of comparable non-ACO providers to estimate the treatment effect. These counterfactual analyses yield more modest, though still generally positive, findings.
Understanding the distinction between benchmark-based and counterfactual-based measurement is essential for interpreting ACO research. This lesson reviews what the program-level data, independent research, and oversight bodies have found about ACO performance across financial outcomes, quality of care, and the variables that predict success.
Key Concept: A benchmark-based savings estimate tells you how far below target an ACO performed. A counterfactual-based estimate tells you whether the ACO changed spending compared to a world where no ACO existed. The two numbers are not the same, and conflating them overstates ACO impact.
Program-Level Results: MSSP Performance Data 2012–2024
CMS publishes annual financial and quality results for the MSSP, and these figures paint an increasingly impressive picture. In performance year 2024, 476 ACOs saved $651 per assigned beneficiary relative to their benchmarks (gross), up from $515 in 2023. After $4.1 billion in performance payments to ACOs, Medicare saved $2.5 billion — $245 per beneficiary, up from $207 — the highest savings since the program began. Since the program's inception, ACOs have generated about $35 billion in gross savings and $13.6 billion in net savings to Medicare (Accountable for Health, from CMS data).
The trajectory of program performance has improved markedly as ACOs have matured and taken on greater financial risk. In the program's early years (2012–2014), many ACOs generated little savings and a significant minority exited after failing to earn shared savings payments. By 2024, 75 percent of ACOs earned performance payments—the highest share since the program launched. ACOs in the Level E and ENHANCED tracks, which carry two-sided risk, generated $5.4 billion of the $6.6 billion in gross savings (Accountable for Health analysis of CMS data). Organization type also mattered: low-revenue ACOs, typically physician-led, generated $319 in net per capita savings versus $180 for high-revenue, typically hospital-led ACOs.
Quality performance has remained consistently high throughout the program's history. In 2024, nearly every ACO met CMS's quality standard. Mean blood pressure control rates rose from 77.80 percent to 79.49 percent year over year. Long-term trends show consistent improvements in preventive care screening rates, patient experience scores, and chronic disease management metrics. The quality-savings correlation supports the argument that ACOs are not cutting costs by under-delivering care.
Gross per capita savings relative to benchmarks across the 476 MSSP ACOs in PY2024, up from $515 in 2023. Source: CMS PY2024 MSSP Fact Sheet (updated September 2025).

The CBO and Counterfactual Challenge
In April 2024, the Congressional Budget Office published a comprehensive review of Medicare ACO program performance titled "Medicare Accountable Care Organizations: Past Performance and Future Directions." Rather than relying on CMS's benchmark comparisons, the CBO reviewed research that estimates savings against comparison groups of non-ACO providers. That research suggests ACOs have produced modest gross savings, and that net savings to Medicare — after shared-savings payments — have been smaller and less certain than benchmark-based figures imply.
The CBO found greater savings associated with specific ACO types: ACOs led by independent physician groups, ACOs with a larger proportion of primary care providers, and ACOs whose baseline spending was higher than their regional average. These characteristics align with the theoretical model of how ACOs should work — primary care-driven coordination and room to reduce excess spending. The finding that physician-led ACOs outperform hospital-system ACOs is particularly notable, given that most large integrated delivery systems initially assumed their scale would be an advantage.
Selection bias is a persistent methodological challenge in ACO research. Practices that choose to form or join ACOs may be systematically different from those that do not—they may already have better care management capabilities, lower baseline utilization, or more motivated clinical leadership. Lyu, Chernew and McWilliams (Health Affairs, 2023) documented that post-2017, MSSP composition increasingly shifted toward providers with lower pre-existing spending relative to their region, consistent with providers self-selecting into the program based on expected benchmark favorability.
ACO benchmarks are designed to accomplish multiple goals—achieving savings, ensuring ACO participation, and managing risk corridor width—and therefore diverge from a pure estimate of what spending would have been without the ACO. A 2025 Health Affairs Forefront article, "'All I Do Is Win': Why Beating Benchmarks Doesn't Mean That ACOs Are Reducing Costs," argued that beating the benchmark does not prove spending was reduced. Policymakers, analysts, and healthcare leaders should treat program-reported savings figures as performance against targets, not proof of equivalent real-world savings.
Important Caveat: Benchmark ≠ Counterfactual
What Drives ACO Success? Factors the Evidence Identifies
Across multiple studies and program evaluations, several structural and operational factors consistently predict better ACO financial and quality performance. The most robust finding is that ACOs taking on downside risk—putting their own money at risk if they overspend—significantly outperform upside-only ACOs. Financial accountability changes provider behavior in ways that the prospect of shared savings alone does not. This is why CMS's "Pathways to Success" rule accelerated the timeline for mandatory risk progression, although CMS later relaxed that timeline in its CY2023 rule.
Physician leadership is a second strong predictor. Physician-led ACOs—those not dominated by a hospital anchor—tend to generate more consistent savings and quality improvements than hospital-anchored ACOs. This may reflect the fact that hospital systems have conflicting incentives: ACO shared savings require reducing hospitalizations, yet admissions revenue is the financial backbone of hospital operations. Physician-led organizations do not face this structural tension. The CBO's 2024 review found greater savings among ACOs led by independent physician groups, and CMS's PY2024 results show low-revenue, typically physician-led ACOs saving $319 per beneficiary versus $180 for high-revenue, typically hospital-led ACOs.
Investment in care management infrastructure is a third key predictor. ACOs that deploy dedicated care coordinators, use predictive risk stratification to identify high-cost patients before crises, implement post-discharge follow-up programs, and engage community health workers to address social determinants of health consistently outperform ACOs that layer the ACO contract on top of an unchanged practice model. The evidence suggests that the ACO contract is a necessary but not sufficient condition for savings—the operational transformation matters as much as the financial structure.
Characteristics Associated with Higher ACO Savings
Downside risk accepted (two-sided tracks)
Physician-led governance—no hospital system majority
Dedicated care management and care coordination staff
Robust EHR and analytics for risk stratification

Baseline spending above the regional average
Characteristics Associated with Lower ACO Savings

ACO Performance Predictors: Higher vs. Lower Savings
ACO REACH and the Next Generation ACO: Evidence from Alternative Models
The Next Generation ACO (NGACO) model (2016–2021) was designed to test whether ACOs willing to accept full two-sided risk—including capitation-like arrangements—could generate larger net savings than MSSP ACOs. Measured against benchmarks, CMS reported that Next Generation ACOs produced net savings to Medicare of about $62 million in 2016, $185 million in 2018 and $204 million in 2019, after shared savings and losses. The model ended as scheduled after an extension through 2021 for the COVID-19 public health emergency, and its features carried into the Global and Professional Direct Contracting model and then ACO REACH.
High-risk ACO models face an important tension: higher risk levels attract providers confident in their ability to save, but generous shared savings rates can convert gross program savings into net Medicare costs. The successor ACO REACH model recalibrated this balance, keeping two-sided risk while adjusting the shared savings formula and adding an explicit health equity commitment. In 2023, ACO REACH's 132 participants generated $1.643 billion in gross savings and $694.6 million in net savings to CMS.
ACO REACH distinguished itself from MSSP through several design features: a choice of global (100%) or professional (50%) risk-sharing, a requirement that at least 75 percent of each ACO's governing body consist of participating providers (to prevent private equity capture), and explicit equity benchmarks requiring ACOs to collect and report race, ethnicity, and language data and develop health equity plans. CMS has since announced that ACO REACH will end on December 31, 2026, to be followed in January 2027 by a new 10-year accountable care model, the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model.
Aledade is one of the largest physician-focused ACO operators in the United States, providing technology, data analytics, and care management support to independent primary care practices to help them succeed in ACO models. As of 2024, Aledade had grown to support hundreds of practices across dozens of states, participating in both MSSP and ACO REACH.
Aledade's approach exemplifies the physician-led model the evidence favors: independent practices retain ownership and autonomy, while Aledade provides the risk stratification tools, care coordinator training, and claims analytics that individual practices could not afford alone. Their publicly reported results consistently show above-average shared savings rates relative to national MSSP averages, supporting the thesis that physician-led, well-supported ACOs outperform hospital-anchored counterparts. Source: Aledade company publications and NAACOS ACO data.
Aledade: A Physician-Led ACO Network
Quality Evidence: What ACOs Deliver Beyond Cost
While the financial evidence on ACOs is debated, the quality evidence is more consistently positive. Studies using Medicare claims data and CAHPS surveys show that ACO beneficiaries receive more preventive services, more follow-up care after hospitalization, and report better care coordination experiences than comparable non-ACO patients. ACO quality reporting has yielded year-over-year improvements in blood pressure control, diabetic eye exam rates, tobacco cessation counseling, and influenza vaccination rates—all clinically meaningful outcomes.
A particularly important quality finding involves potentially avoidable hospitalizations. Multiple studies have shown that ACOs reduce ambulatory care-sensitive condition hospitalizations—admissions for conditions like heart failure exacerbation, diabetic ketoacidosis, and asthma that are generally preventable with good outpatient management. Reducing these admissions is clinically valuable, represents genuine care improvement rather than cost-shifting, and aligns with the theoretical mechanism by which ACOs should improve the delivery of care.
Health equity remains a significant unresolved quality challenge. Early analyses found that ACOs were more likely to be located in higher-income, less racially diverse areas, and that attributed populations skewed toward healthier, more educated patients. CMS has responded with quality measures that explicitly stratify results by race and ethnicity, equity bonuses in ACO REACH, and data collection requirements around social risk factors. Whether ACOs can reduce disparities—not just average costs—is now one of the central quality questions in the field.
The best-performing ACOs combine financial accountability (downside risk), physician leadership, care management infrastructure, and equity-focused quality measurement. No single element alone is sufficient—all four must be present for consistently strong performance.
ACO performance data must be interpreted carefully: benchmark-based savings (what CMS reports) and counterfactual-based savings (what independent researchers measure) are different numbers, with the latter being more methodologically rigorous.
In performance year 2024, MSSP ACOs saved Medicare $2.5 billion relative to benchmarks — the highest since the program began — with 75% of ACOs earning performance payments.
The Congressional Budget Office's 2024 review of counterfactual research associated greater savings with ACOs led by independent physician groups, with more primary care providers, and with baseline spending above their regional average.
Selection bias is a persistent challenge: practices that join ACOs may already be more efficient, making it difficult to isolate the true causal effect of ACO participation on spending.
The Next Generation ACO model (2016–2021) showed CMS-reported net savings each year measured against benchmarks, and its higher-risk features carried into ACO REACH.
ACO REACH (launched 2023) addressed NGACO shortcomings with rebalanced incentives, a 75% provider governance requirement, and explicit health equity commitments, generating $694.6 million in net savings to CMS in its first year; CMS plans to replace it with the LEAD Model in 2027.
Quality evidence is more consistently positive than financial evidence: ACO beneficiaries receive more preventive care, have fewer avoidable hospitalizations, and report better care coordination than comparable non-ACO patients.
Health equity remains an unresolved quality challenge, with early evidence that ACOs disproportionately served lower-risk, more affluent populations—a gap CMS is actively trying to address through redesigned quality requirements.
The CBO's April 2024 report reviewed research that uses comparison groups of non-ACO providers to estimate the counterfactual impact of ACO participation. Savings were not universal; greater savings were associated with ACOs led by independent physician groups, with a larger share of primary care providers, and with higher baseline spending relative to their region. This is distinct from the CMS benchmark-based reports, which show large savings because benchmarks are not pure counterfactuals.
ACOs universally reduced Medicare spending by large margins across all program models.
ACOs had mixed results, with greater savings among physician-led ACOs with a high share of primary care providers.

######## value-based-care | aco-medicaid-commercial | ACOs Beyond Medicare: Medicaid and Commercial ACOs
ACOs Beyond Medicare: Medicaid and Commercial ACOs
Why ACOs Expanded Beyond Medicare
The Medicare Shared Savings Program demonstrated that the accountable care concept—providers voluntarily accepting responsibility for the cost and quality of a defined population—could work at scale in a government insurance program. That demonstration triggered rapid interest from Medicaid agencies and commercial health plans, which faced similar problems: fragmented care, avoidable hospitalizations, and payment structures that rewarded volume over value. By the mid-2010s, dozens of states were designing Medicaid ACO programs and commercial insurers were launching parallel contracts with provider networks.
Yet the translation from Medicare to Medicaid and commercial markets is not straightforward. Medicare beneficiaries are older, have stable enrollment, and interact with a single federal payer using standardized rules. Medicaid populations are younger, more diverse, often have complex social needs, and experience high coverage turnover—members can churn on and off Medicaid eligibility multiple times per year, making continuity of attribution and care management extremely difficult. Commercial ACOs face different challenges: multiple competing payers with proprietary data, less standardized quality measures, and the reality that commercial patients may have ACO-like contracts with several plans simultaneously.
Despite these structural differences, the core ACO logic transfers: if providers can reduce avoidable utilization, improve preventive care, and coordinate across settings, both Medicaid programs and commercial payers stand to gain. The mechanisms—attribution, benchmarks, shared savings or shared losses—are adapted but recognizable. This lesson examines how Medicaid and commercial ACO programs have been designed, what the evidence shows about their effectiveness, and what Vermont's own experience illustrates about state-level innovation.
Key Concept: Medicaid ACOs and commercial ACOs share the fundamental ACO architecture—attributed populations, spending benchmarks, and quality-linked payments—but operate in environments with fundamentally different patient populations, payer structures, and data availability compared to the Medicare MSSP.
Medicaid ACOs: State-by-State Innovation
Medicaid is a joint federal-state program, which means there is no single national Medicaid ACO model. Each state that creates a Medicaid ACO does so through its own design, often using Section 1115 demonstration waivers to obtain federal flexibility. States have experimented with widely varying approaches: some run voluntary programs similar to MSSP, others mandate all Medicaid managed care organizations to operate within an ACO framework, and still others create global budget models that blend ACO accountability with capitation payments.
A 2024 scoping review by Holm, Pagán and Silver in Medical Care Research and Review analyzed 32 studies on Medicaid ACO programs published between 2012 and 2023. The review found mixed evidence overall—significant improvements included more primary care visits, fewer admissions and shorter inpatient stays, but only a few studies reported cost reductions, and savings depended on how long the program had been operating and how long patients were attributed. Medicaid ACOs face unique challenges: patient populations with complex social needs, frequent eligibility turnover, and program designs that vary dramatically across states.
Gains in primary care use are meaningful for a population that has historically faced significant access barriers. Cost evidence was weaker: of the 32 studies, only three examined cost reduction at all.
A 2024 scoping review identified 32 studies of Medicaid ACOs published 2012–2023 and found mixed results: more primary care visits, fewer admissions, but few documented cost savings. Source: Holm, Pagán & Silver, Medical Care Research and Review, 2024.

Oregon's Coordinated Care Organizations: The Leading State Model
Oregon's Coordinated Care Organization (CCO) program is widely regarded as the most comprehensive and rigorously evaluated Medicaid ACO model in the United States. Launched in 2012 under an 1115 waiver with substantial initial federal funding, Oregon transformed its entire Medicaid program—the Oregon Health Plan—into a statewide network of CCOs. Each CCO is a regional entity responsible for the physical, behavioral, and oral health of its attributed Medicaid members, operating under a global budget with an annual spending growth cap.
Oregon committed to reducing its Medicaid spending growth rate from 5.4 percent annually to 3.4 percent within three years. A Health Affairs study by McConnell and colleagues (2017), comparing Oregon with Colorado, found that the CCO transformation was associated with a 7 percent relative reduction in expenditures across selected services, driven primarily by reduced inpatient utilization, along with reductions in avoidable emergency department visits; overall ED visits fell in both states, with no significant difference between them.
Oregon's distinctive design elements—mandatory Medicaid enrollment (rather than voluntary), inclusion of mental health and dental services within the global budget (rather than carving them out), community advisory councils with meaningful governance authority, and integration of social determinants of health services—are widely credited for its results. In 2020 the Oregon Health Authority began five-year (2020–2024) contracts with 15 CCOs, with contracts focusing on behavioral health, health equity, social determinants, and sustainable cost growth.
Oregon currently contracts with 15 Coordinated Care Organizations that cover OHP members across the state. Each CCO integrates physical, behavioral, and oral health services under a single global budget, which is capped at a state-specified growth rate. CCOs are governed by community advisory councils that include Medicaid members, community organizations, and local stakeholders.
The Oregon model's inclusion of dental and mental health under the global budget is a critical design feature that most other state programs omit. By integrating these services, Oregon avoids the perverse incentive of carving them out—where behavioral health crises drive hospital admissions that show up as avoidable costs in the physical health budget without accountability. Research found a 7% relative reduction in selected expenditures and fewer avoidable ED visits in the program's early years. Source: CHCS/NIH; Oregon Health Authority.
Oregon Health Plan CCOs
Massachusetts MassHealth ACOs: Scale and Integration
Massachusetts launched its Medicaid ACO program in 2018 as part of a Section 1115 demonstration waiver, becoming one of the first states to integrate ACO accountability directly into its Medicaid managed care framework. By June 2023, over 1.3 million MassHealth members—more than half of the program's 2.4 million total—were enrolled in one of 17 MassHealth ACOs. This scale makes MassHealth one of the largest Medicaid ACO programs in the country by attributed population.
An independent evaluation conducted by UMass Chan Medical School found that MassHealth's 2017–2022 Section 1115 demonstration saved Massachusetts more than $500 million over five years while maintaining near-universal health coverage and the lowest uninsurance rate among comparison states. Health outcomes improved in both physical and behavioral health domains. Hospitalization rates were 23 percent lower and emergency department visit rates 13 percent lower among members who received nutrition support services compared to eligible non-participants.
MassHealth's program design included two types of ACOs: Accountable Care Partnership Plans (ACPPs), which are fully integrated ACO-managed care plans combining an ACO with a health plan, and Primary Care ACOs (PCACOs), which are ACOs working with existing managed care organizations. The program also built in a community partner infrastructure—ACO-affiliated organizations providing community health workers, care navigators, and long-term services support—reflecting recognition that social needs are major drivers of Medicaid spending. In September 2022, CMS approved an extension of the MassHealth demonstration waiver through December 2027.
The state Medicaid agency designs attribution rules, benchmark methodology, quality measures, and shared savings/risk parameters, often with federal approval via Section 1115 waiver.

Commercial ACOs: Private-Payer Accountable Care
Commercial ACOs operate under contracts between provider organizations and private health plans—employer-sponsored insurance, individual market plans, and commercial managed care. Unlike Medicare or Medicaid ACOs, commercial ACOs are governed entirely by private contracts without a regulatory framework, meaning their design varies enormously across payers, markets, and time. The common thread is still the ACO logic: a defined provider network accepts responsibility for a population's total cost of care against a benchmark, with shared savings or shared losses tied to both spending and quality performance.
Commercial ACO growth has been driven by large employers and major health plans seeking to reduce trend growth in healthcare costs. The Health Care Payment Learning and Action Network (HCPLAN) reported that value-based arrangements across all lines of business grew from 41.3 percent of payments in 2022 to 45.2 percent in 2023. Commercial value-based arrangements specifically grew from 34.6 percent to 39.2 percent in the same period, and shared-risk arrangements across all lines of business rose from 24.5 percent to 28.5 percent of payments.
Commercial ACOs face distinctive challenges that Medicare and Medicaid ACOs do not. First, multi-payer attribution: a primary care physician attributed to a commercial ACO by one payer may simultaneously be in a Medicare ACO and a Medicaid ACO, with potentially conflicting quality targets and reporting requirements. Second, data opacity: commercial claims data is proprietary and payers often share incomplete claims information with ACO partners, hampering risk stratification. Third, shorter contract terms: commercial ACO contracts often run one to three years, which is insufficient time to see the full financial benefits of care management investments that may take several years to mature.

Medicaid ACOs vs. Commercial ACOs: Key Differences
Vermont's All-Payer Model: ACOs Across All Insurance Types
Vermont pursued one of the most ambitious ACO strategies in the United States: an all-payer accountable care model in which a single ACO—OneCare Vermont—accepted responsibility for the total cost of care for Vermonters across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance. Under the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model (VAPCOM), whose agreement CMS and Vermont signed in October 2016 and which ended in 2025, OneCare Vermont received fixed prospective payments from Medicare, Medicaid, and participating commercial payers for its attributed patients, aligning financial incentives in a way that no single-payer ACO can achieve.
The all-payer design directly solves the multi-payer attribution problem that plagues commercial ACOs. When a provider's financial incentives are aligned across all of their patients—not just their Medicare patients or their one commercial contract—clinical behavior can change more consistently and comprehensively. A primary care physician in the OneCare network had the same incentive to prevent avoidable hospitalizations for their Medicaid patient as for their Medicare patient, removing a major source of conflicting financial signals that undermines single-payer ACO models.
Vermont's model has generated considerable national attention and research interest as a proof-of-concept for all-payer ACO design. The state agreed to keep per-capita cost growth below a target rate and to meet annual quality benchmarks across the attributed population. Implementation was iterative—the model was modified through renegotiation with CMS before it ended on December 31, 2025. Vermont's experience offers important lessons about the prerequisites for all-payer ACO success: state political will, a small enough market for coordination to be feasible, and strong primary care infrastructure.
Think of multi-payer ACO fragmentation like a sports referee who has to follow different rulebooks for different players on the same field. A doctor with Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial patients effectively works under three different financial systems simultaneously. Vermont's all-payer model gave everyone the same rulebook, so the referee—and the players—could play a coherent game.
All-payer ACO design: why aligning all payers matters
Medicaid and commercial ACOs adapt the Medicare ACO model—attributed populations, spending benchmarks, and quality-linked shared savings—to their distinct payer environments, patient populations, and data constraints.
A 2024 scoping review of 32 Medicaid ACO studies found mixed evidence overall, with the clearest gains in primary care visits, admissions and inpatient stays, and few documented cost savings.
Oregon's Coordinated Care Organization program is among the best-evidenced Medicaid ACO models, with a 7% relative reduction in selected expenditures in early implementation; its design integrates behavioral, physical, and oral health under one global budget.
MassHealth (Massachusetts) enrolled over 1.3 million Medicaid members in ACOs by 2023, with an independent evaluation finding $500 million in savings over five years and improved physical and behavioral health outcomes.
Commercial ACO contracts grew significantly, with value-based arrangements representing 45.2% of all healthcare payments across insurance types in 2023, up from 41.3% in 2022, according to HCPLAN data.
Commercial ACOs face unique challenges not present in Medicare or Medicaid programs: multi-payer attribution overlap, proprietary data opacity, shorter contract terms, and the absence of a federal regulatory framework.
Vermont's all-payer ACO model (OneCare Vermont, which ended in 2025) addressed multi-payer fragmentation by applying a single global budget across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers—one of the most ambitious accountable care experiments in the U.S.
Oregon's CCO model is distinctive for its mandatory enrollment (all OHP members are enrolled), its integration of mental health and dental services under the same global budget as physical health, and its community advisory council governance. This integrated service design prevents behavioral health and dental carve-outs from undermining physical health cost management.

######## value-based-care | vbc-fundamentals-module-3-economics-pillar | Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 3: The Economics Pillar — Following the Money in Value-Based Care
Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 3: The Economics Pillar — Following the Money in Value-Based Care
Here is a question that sounds simple but is genuinely hard to answer: if a hospital successfully reduces its patients’ hospitalization rate by 15% through better care management, is that good news or bad news for the hospital’s finances? The instinctive answer is that it must be good news — fewer hospitalizations means healthier patients, which is surely the goal. But in a world where 40% of that hospital’s revenue still comes from fee-for-service Medicare and Medicaid payments, fewer hospitalizations means fewer inpatient admissions, which means fewer billed days, which means lower revenue. The hospital just cut its own income by doing its job better. This is not a hypothetical paradox — it is the central economic tension of the volume-to-value transition, experienced by virtually every health system that has seriously engaged with value-based care. Understanding this tension, and the financial mechanisms that VBC contract structures use to resolve it, is what this module is about.
The Financial Anatomy of a Shared Savings Contract
The Medicare Shared Savings Program is the most widely adopted VBC model in the United States, and shared savings is the financial mechanism at its core. Understanding how shared savings actually works — how the benchmark is set, how savings are calculated, and how they are distributed — is the foundation for understanding the economics of most VBC arrangements. The concept is straightforward: CMS calculates how much it would have expected to spend on your attributed patient population if they had remained in traditional fee-for-service Medicare, adjusted for their age, health status, and geographic cost factors. This projected spend is your “benchmark.” If your ACO’s actual spending on that population comes in below the benchmark, the difference is “savings.” You share those savings with CMS according to a pre-agreed formula — typically retaining 40–75% depending on your risk track and quality performance, with CMS keeping the remainder.
The devil, as always, is in the details. The benchmark calculation uses a three-year historical average of your patient population’s spending, adjusted upward by a national trend factor. For ACOs whose patient populations were already low-cost before joining the program, this creates an immediate structural problem: their benchmark is low, so even excellent care management produces modest absolute savings, making the shared savings payment insufficient to cover the care management infrastructure investment. This is called the “low benchmark problem,” and it is the primary reason that rural and safety-net ACOs, which often already operate lean systems with lower baseline utilization, struggle to generate shared savings large enough to justify Advanced APM participation costs. CMS has revised the benchmark methodology repeatedly in response to this problem — adding regional adjustments for agreement periods beginning in 2017, reworking them in the 2018 Pathways to Success rule, and, in the CY2023 Physician Fee Schedule rule, adding a prior-savings adjustment and an administratively set growth factor (the Accountable Care Prospective Trend) to blunt the ratchet effect — but the fundamental tension between historical benchmarking and equitable VBC participation for already-efficient providers remains unresolved.
Upside-Only vs. Two-Sided Risk: The Decision That Changes Everything
One of the most consequential decisions a provider organization makes when entering a shared savings arrangement is whether to accept only upside risk — where you share in savings if you beat the benchmark but owe nothing if you miss it — or two-sided risk, where you both share savings and repay losses if spending exceeds the benchmark. This choice has profound implications for the financial planning, working capital requirements, and organizational risk appetite of the participating entity. Upside-only arrangements (MSSP Track 1 and its successors) are appropriate for organizations beginning their VBC journey: they provide financial experience with population cost management without the catastrophic downside scenario of a major loss repayment obligation. Two-sided arrangements (the MSSP ENHANCED Track, and CMMI’s ACO REACH Model — the 2023 successor to Global and Professional Direct Contracting, which runs through December 31, 2026 and is to be succeeded by the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model from January 1, 2027) offer higher shared savings percentages — sometimes up to 80% of savings — but require the organization to maintain actuarial reserves sufficient to cover a loss scenario, typically modeled at 1–3% of benchmark spending.
