Shared Savings Contract Economics: MSSP Track Comparison for a Hypothetical 5,000-Beneficiary ACO
The financial model in the table above illustrates why Two-Sided and Full-Risk tracks are substantially more attractive in their best-case financial outcome — but also why the actuarial reserve requirement creates a genuine barrier to entry for organizations operating at thin margins. For a health system with $30 million in unrestricted net assets, maintaining a $2.5 million actuarial reserve for ACO REACH participation represents a 8.3% allocation of available capital to a risk management buffer — a rational investment if leadership has high confidence in the organization’s ability to manage population cost, but a significant commitment that requires board-level approval and careful opportunity cost analysis against other capital needs.
Bundled Payments: When a Single Price Covers an Entire Episode of Care
Bundled payment models take a different economic approach to aligning incentives than shared savings. Rather than holding a provider accountable for the total cost of care across an entire attributed population, bundled payments establish a single target price for all the care associated with a specific clinical episode — typically defined as a procedure or hospitalization plus 90 days of post-acute care. If the sum of all actual payments during the episode falls below the target price, the lead provider (typically the hospital or physician group that performed the primary procedure) retains the difference. If actual costs exceed the target, the lead provider repays the excess. The economic logic is straightforward: bundled payments create a direct financial incentive for the hospital performing a hip replacement to care about which skilled nursing facility the patient is discharged to, how long they stay there, and whether they end up readmitted — because all of those costs are included in the bundle.
BPCI Advanced, CMS’s voluntary bundled payment model, ran from October 1, 2018 through December 31, 2025, with 29 inpatient and 3 outpatient clinical episode categories at launch, ranging from major joint replacement and cardiac procedures to pneumonia and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease hospitalizations. Its final evaluation (The Lewin Group for CMS, August 2026) found that participants reduced Medicare episode payments in every model year — by $743 per episode on average in Model Years 1 and 2 and by about $1,000 per episode in Model Years 3 through 6 — and that the model produced about $800 million in net Medicare savings across its eight model years: net losses in Model Years 1–3, when reconciliation payments to participants exceeded the spending reductions, were outweighed by net savings once CMS redesigned target pricing in Model Year 4 (2021). Readmission rates were similar to the comparison group, although patients in Model Years 7–8 reported less favorable changes in functional status. Critically, the savings came primarily from post-acute care — fewer patients discharged to skilled nursing or inpatient rehabilitation facilities, skilled nursing stays about three days shorter, and skilled nursing payments about $500 lower per episode — rather than from reductions in the procedural care itself, confirming the bundled payment hypothesis that the primary driver of unnecessary cost in high-volume episodes is the post-acute care tail, not the procedure. CMS concluded that BPCI Advanced did not meet its criteria for expansion, and carried its lessons into the mandatory Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), which began January 1, 2026.
The bundled payment evidence for joint replacement is about as clean as healthcare economics gets: when you make the hospital financially responsible for what happens after the patient leaves, patients spend less time in nursing homes, without more complications or readmissions, and cost Medicare less money. The same logic applies to any high-volume procedure with a predictable post-acute care pattern. The challenge is applying it to medical conditions where the post-acute trajectory is far less predictable.
Capitation: The Most Advanced — and Most Misunderstood — VBC Model
Capitation is the payment model that most completely aligns provider incentives with patient health outcomes, and the one that generates the most anxiety among providers who have not operated under it before. Under capitation, a provider or provider organization receives a fixed payment per enrolled member per month — the “PMPM” rate — and is responsible for delivering or arranging all covered healthcare services for that member, regardless of how much care they actually use. If the member uses more care than the PMPM covers, the provider absorbs the loss. If the member uses less, the provider retains the surplus. This structure creates the strongest possible financial incentive for prevention, care coordination, and early intervention — because every avoided hospitalization translates directly into retained revenue rather than lost fee-for-service income.
The anxiety around capitation is understandable but often misdirected. The concern most commonly expressed is that capitation incentivizes providers to withhold necessary care — to under-treat rather than over-treat. This concern is real and has historical basis: the managed care capitation models of the 1990s were frequently criticized for exactly this failure, and some HMO capitation arrangements did produce documented under-treatment in specific service categories. But the lesson of the 1990s HMO experience is not that capitation is inherently dangerous. It is that capitation without robust quality measurement, meaningful patient choice, and strong external accountability produces dangerous incentives. Modern capitation models — including Medicare Advantage plans and CMS’s ACO REACH program — include comprehensive quality metric frameworks with financial consequences for poor performance, minimum coverage requirements that prevent service restriction below evidence-based thresholds, and beneficiary rights to seek care outside the network when needed. The capitation model that exists in 2026 is substantively different from the managed care capitation of 1996.
How PMPM Rates Are Set: The Actuarial Core of Capitation
The financial success or failure of a capitation arrangement is largely determined before any patient is seen, at the point where the PMPM rate is negotiated or set. If the rate is set too low relative to the actual cost of providing care to the enrolled population, no amount of care management efficiency will produce a viable financial model. If the rate is set appropriately — reflecting the health acuity, demographic profile, and social complexity of the enrolled population — a well-managed capitated provider can generate a positive margin while delivering better-coordinated, lower-cost care than the fee-for-service alternative. The actuarial process of setting a PMPM rate involves risk adjustment models that account for enrollee diagnoses, functional status, and social determinants of health, applied to utilization cost data from comparable populations. For Medicare Advantage plans, CMS sets the base rate using the county-level fee-for-service benchmark and adjusts it upward or downward based on each enrollee’s Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) risk score, a diagnosis-based model that attempts to predict expected healthcare utilization for that individual in the coming year.
The Volume-to-Value Transition: Why the Math Gets Hard Before It Gets Easy
The single most common financial mistake health systems make in VBC transitions is underestimating the revenue disruption of the transition period — the window, typically 18 to 36 months, during which care management investments have begun reducing utilization but VBC contract revenue has not yet scaled to replace the lost fee-for-service volume. Consider a regional health system generating $400 million in annual net patient revenue, with 30% of that revenue from inpatient admissions billed on a fee-for-service basis. The system joins MSSP and invests $2 million in care management infrastructure — care coordinators, a risk stratification platform, a post-discharge follow-up program — that begins generating measurable results in year one, reducing its attributed Medicare population’s hospitalization rate by 12%. That 12% reduction represents approximately 240 avoided admissions. At an average net revenue of $8,500 per admission, it also represents a $2.04 million reduction in fee-for-service inpatient revenue. The system’s MSSP shared savings payment for year one, based on total population savings, might be $1.4 million. Net financial impact of year one VBC investment: negative $640,000.
This math is not an argument against VBC. It is an argument for understanding VBC as a multi-year financial investment with a specific payback horizon, rather than a year-one revenue enhancement strategy. CMS’s own results show what is achievable at scale: in Performance Year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated gross savings of $651 per assigned beneficiary (shared between ACOs and Medicare) and net Medicare savings of $245, and 75% of the 476 participating ACOs earned performance payments. CMS publishes no standard figure for what ACOs spend on care management infrastructure, so the return on that investment has to be modeled from each organization’s own cost base. The problem is that most health system financial planning cycles operate on one-to-three year horizons, which are too short to capture the full economic benefit of VBC investment. Organizations that have successfully navigated the volume-to-value transition have done so by securing board approval for a five-to-seven year VBC investment thesis with explicit transition period loss projections, rather than attempting to justify each year’s VBC expenditure against that same year’s VBC revenue.
For CFOs and Finance Leaders: If your organization is evaluating ACO or Advanced APM participation, your financial model must explicitly project the transition period revenue displacement — the reduction in fee-for-service inpatient and ED revenue that will occur as care management succeeds. An ACO financial model that shows positive net revenue in year one almost certainly has a methodology error, either in the care management cost estimates or in the assumed savings rate. Realistic five-year models typically show a cumulative loss in years one and two, breakeven in year three, and meaningful positive return in years four and five. Present this model honestly to your board, or the VBC investment will be defunded the first time a quarterly loss appears.
Primary Care Investment as Economic Infrastructure
One of the most powerful and counterintuitive findings in health economics is that investment in primary care produces returns that are comparable to, and in many cases superior to, investment in specialty care infrastructure — not in terms of individual clinical case intensity, but in terms of total population health spending and outcomes. The economic mechanism is straightforward once articulated: primary care reduces the incidence of the expensive downstream events — hospitalizations, emergency visits, specialist procedures, complications of uncontrolled chronic disease — that account for the vast majority of total healthcare spending. The evidence is strongest on outcomes and quality: Baicker and Chandra (Health Affairs, 2004) found that states with more general practitioners per capita delivered higher-quality care to Medicare beneficiaries at lower spending, while states with more specialists spent more for lower quality; and Basu and colleagues (JAMA Internal Medicine, 2019) found that every 10 additional primary care physicians per 100,000 people was associated with a 51.5-day increase in life expectancy. Supply alone is not a cost-control lever, however — a 2009 Health Affairs analysis found that simply having more primary care physicians did not slow spending growth — which is why payment models that reward primary care for total cost matter.
The economic return on primary care investment is particularly relevant for value-based care organizations making resource allocation decisions. Under fee-for-service, a hospital has limited financial incentive to invest in expanding primary care capacity in its community — more primary care visits may mean fewer specialist referrals and fewer hospitalizations, which means less hospital revenue. Under a capitated or shared savings VBC model, the same investment in primary care capacity is a direct cost reduction strategy: every diabetic patient who sees their primary care provider quarterly and maintains target HbA1c levels is a patient less likely to generate a costly admission for a diabetic complication. The VBC payment model converts primary care from a cost center competing with hospital services for capital allocation into a return-generating infrastructure investment — which is the single most important realignment that value-based payment architecture produces.

Care Management Interventions: What the Published Evaluations Found
The evidence in the table above carries an important lesson: the interventions that paid for themselves in trials were targeted ones — transition coaching for patients leaving the hospital, community health workers for patients with documented unmet social needs — while broad primary care payment models that spread enhanced payments across whole practice panels reduced hospital use without producing net Medicare savings. An organization implementing a care coordinator program without a functioning risk stratification system to identify which patients the coordinator should prioritize will see substantially lower returns — because care management applied uniformly across a population is far less efficient than care management targeted to the patients most likely to have high-cost events in the next 12 months. The technology readiness discussion in Module 4 is therefore directly connected to the economics of VBC investment: organizations that build population health data infrastructure before scaling care management programs generate significantly better returns than those that sequence these investments in reverse order.
Care coordination works when it is aimed at the right patients: its effectiveness depends on a functioning risk stratification system that identifies which patients are genuinely high-risk, not just high-cost in the prior year.
Post-discharge transition support has some of the strongest trial evidence in care management: in Coleman’s randomized trial of 750 older adults, transition coaching cut 30-day rehospitalizations from 11.9% to 8.3% and lowered six-month hospital costs, because the cost of coaching is small relative to the cost of a readmission.
Community health worker programs are the intervention most directly connected to social determinants of health — addressing food insecurity, housing instability, and transportation barriers that drive utilization patterns that clinical care alone cannot change — and Penn’s IMPaCT program returned $2.47 to Medicaid for every dollar invested, within a single fiscal year.
Advanced primary care transformation is the most comprehensive intervention, but the federal evidence is sobering: neither CPC+ nor Primary Care First produced net Medicare savings once their enhanced payments were counted, and CPC+ practices with incentives to control total cost of care, such as Shared Savings Program participants, did better at lowering costs — which is why primary care investment pays off most reliably inside a total-cost-of-care arrangement rather than as a stand-alone add-on.
The organizations that are winning in value-based care are not winning because they have better doctors or better patients. They are winning because they have better data, better targeting, and better financial discipline about which interventions they invest in and for which patient populations. VBC is fundamentally an information business with a clinical delivery layer on top.
Module 3 Summary: The Economics of VBC Reward Patience, Infrastructure, and Precision
The economics of value-based care are not complicated in their logic, but they are frequently misunderstood in their timing and their requirements. Shared savings arrangements reward population cost management, but only after a benchmark has been established and a minimum savings threshold has been crossed. Bundled payments reward episode cost efficiency, but require investment in post-acute care coordination infrastructure that most hospitals have historically not needed. Capitation rewards comprehensive population health management, but requires actuarial sophistication, quality measurement capability, and working capital reserves that are significant organizational commitments. All three model types have in common a multi-year investment horizon that is at odds with annual budget cycles, and a data infrastructure dependency that is at odds with the technology readiness of many rural and safety-net providers.
The economic case for making these investments nonetheless is visible in CMS’s own results: in Performance Year 2024, Shared Savings Program ACOs generated gross savings of $651 per assigned beneficiary and net Medicare savings of $245, with physician-led, low-revenue ACOs outperforming hospital-led ones ($319 versus $180 net per beneficiary) — returns that depend on care management infrastructure maturing and on the organization’s ability to identify and target high-risk patients. The organizations that have reached this performance level did not arrive there by treating VBC as a compliance exercise or a contract opportunity. They treated it as a fundamental redesign of how they organize and deliver care, supported by a financial model that explicitly anticipated and planned for the transition period losses that are the unavoidable cost of that redesign. Module 4 examines the technology infrastructure that makes this financial performance possible.
Review your organization’s current VBC contract portfolio and categorize each contract by model type: shared savings (upside only or two-sided), bundled payment, or capitation. For each contract, identify whether you have a financial model projecting per-beneficiary investment cost, expected savings rate, and net financial benefit over a five-year horizon.
Ask your CFO to quantify the annual fee-for-service revenue at risk from your care management programs — the inpatient admissions and emergency visits that your VBC interventions are intended to prevent, translated into net revenue impact. Compare this to your projected shared savings or capitation savings. If the net is negative, verify your model is using a five-year, not a one-year, planning horizon.
Review the evidence in the care management intervention table in this module and identify which intervention types your organization is currently investing in. For each intervention, assess whether you have a functioning risk stratification system that targets the intervention to high-risk patients rather than applying it uniformly across your attributed population.
Assess your organization’s actuarial reserve capacity for two-sided risk participation. If your unrestricted net assets are below $15 million, upside-only MSSP participation is the appropriate starting point. If your unrestricted net assets exceed $30 million and you have three or more years of MSSP experience, a formal analysis of ENHANCED track participation, or of CMMI’s LEAD Model (the ACO REACH successor beginning January 1, 2027), is warranted.
Module 3 Key Takeaway: The economics of value-based care favor organizations that plan in five-year cycles, invest in care management infrastructure before scaling VBC contract volume, and understand the specific financial mechanics of their contract type at the level of the benchmark calculation and the savings distribution formula. VBC is not a revenue strategy for the next fiscal year. It is a business model for the next decade — one that rewards the organizations that build the infrastructure, accept the transition period losses, and stay the course long enough for the compounding returns of mature care management to materialize.
Module 3 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the financial mechanics of value-based care from first principles. It explains, in plain language, how money actually flows in the major VBC contract structures — shared savings, bundled payments, and capitation — how providers calculate whether a VBC arrangement is financially rational for their organization, what the volume-to-value transition problem means in practice for health system balance sheets, and what the economic evidence says about which VBC models generate durable savings versus which ones simply shift cost without reducing it. Learners will leave this module able to evaluate a VBC contract term sheet, identify the key actuarial concepts their finance teams are using, and understand the economic case for primary care investment as the highest-return infrastructure spend in healthcare.
######## value-based-care | bundled-payment-mechanics | Episode-Based Bundled Payments: How They Work
Episode-Based Bundled Payments: How They Work
What Is an Episode-Based Bundled Payment?
A bundled payment — also called an episode-based payment — collapses the dozens of separate claims that Medicare or a commercial payer would ordinarily process for a single clinical event into one aggregated target price. Instead of a hospital billing for the inpatient stay, a surgeon billing separately for the procedure, a post-acute facility billing for its days, and a home health agency billing for visits, the payer holds all of those costs up against a single benchmark. If the team delivers the episode for less, providers share in the savings; if spending exceeds the target, they owe the difference back.
The logic is straightforward: fee-for-service rewards doing more — more tests, longer stays, more specialist consults — because each service generates a separate payment. Bundling inverts that incentive. A provider who reduces an unnecessary post-acute day or avoids a preventable readmission keeps part of the savings rather than losing revenue. Quality guardrails prevent providers from cutting corners to hit their target: readmission rates, mortality, and patient-experience scores are tracked, and poor quality can disqualify a participant from receiving any reconciliation payment.
Bundled payments sit in the middle of the value-based care spectrum. They are more aggressive than pay-for-performance bonuses, which layer small incentives onto an otherwise unchanged fee-for-service chassis, but less comprehensive than capitation, which hands a provider a fixed monthly sum to cover all care. Bundles concentrate accountability on a defined clinical episode — a joint replacement, a cardiac procedure, a chemotherapy course — making them easier to attribute to specific providers and easier to price than a full-population capitation arrangement.
An episode of care is a clinically meaningful window of time tied to a specific health event — typically an inpatient anchor stay or a qualifying outpatient procedure, plus a defined follow-up period (most commonly 90 days) during which related care is included in the bundle.

The Mechanics: How a Bundle Is Structured
Every bundled payment model defines three core elements: the anchor event that starts the clock, the episode window, and the care that is included or excluded. In the CMS Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced (BPCI Advanced) model — the largest federal voluntary bundled payment program, which ran from 2018 until it ended on December 31, 2025 — an episode begins either with an inpatient admission identified by a Medicare Severity-Diagnosis Related Group (MS-DRG) code, called the Anchor Stay, or with a qualifying outpatient procedure in a hospital outpatient department, called the Anchor Procedure. The episode ends 90 days after the patient is discharged or the procedure is completed.
The financial engine is retrospective reconciliation. Medicare continues to pay providers their ordinary fee-for-service claims throughout the episode — nobody waits for a single check. At the end of each six-month performance period, CMS totals all non-excluded Medicare claims for each participant's episodes and compares that aggregate with the pre-set target price. If spending is below the target, the participant earns a reconciliation payment (shared savings). If spending exceeds the target, the participant owes a repayment amount. CMS provides preliminary target prices before each model year begins so participants can plan care-delivery changes in advance.
Target prices are calculated from historical Medicare claims data for that clinical episode type in the participant's market, risk-adjusted for patient complexity, and trended forward with a discount rate (the "haircut") that represents the savings Medicare expects to achieve. The haircut ensures the program generates net savings for the federal government even after reconciliation payments are made to high-performing participants.
Patient is admitted for an inpatient stay (Anchor Stay) or undergoes a qualifying outpatient procedure (Anchor Procedure) at a participating hospital or physician group practice.
Anchor Event
CMS begins tracking all Medicare FFS claims for care related to the clinical episode — hospital, physician, post-acute, home health, readmissions, and outpatient visits.
Episode Opens
The episode window covers the anchor event plus 90 days. Excluded services (e.g., trauma, unrelated hospitalizations) are carved out of the bundle per CMS rules.
90-Day Follow-Up
Twice a year (Jan–Jun and Jul–Dec), CMS tallies aggregate FFS payments for all episodes and compares them to aggregate target prices across the participant's portfolio.
Performance Period Ends
If aggregate spending is below the target price, the participant receives a reconciliation payment. If above, the participant owes a repayment. Quality thresholds must be met to receive any payment.
Reconciliation
How a BPCI Advanced Episode Flows
Who Participates and What They Are Accountable For
Under BPCI Advanced, two entity types could participate: acute care hospitals (ACHs) and physician group practices (PGPs). A hospital participating as an ACH is accountable for the full 90-day episode cost for every eligible patient admitted. A PGP participates as an episode initiator — responsible for managing costs during the episode triggered by the group's physicians. This distinction matters: hospitals have more leverage over post-acute placement, while physician groups have more direct influence over care protocols and follow-up intensity.
The 35 BPCI Advanced clinical episodes span eight clinical service line groups: cardiac care, cardiac procedures, gastrointestinal surgery, gastrointestinal care, neurological care, medical and critical care, spinal procedures, and orthopedics. Participants do not have to take on all 35 — they can select the episode types where they have the most clinical volume, existing care-coordination infrastructure, and confidence in their ability to manage costs. This flexibility encourages participation but also creates selection effects: hospitals tend to choose episode types where they already perform well.
Quality measurement is built into the financial settlement. BPCI Advanced tracks Medicare Spending per Beneficiary (MSPB) composite quality scores and requires participants to submit quality data. Low quality scores can reduce or eliminate reconciliation payments, ensuring that cost-cutting does not come at the expense of patient safety. Participants are also encouraged — but not required — to engage post-acute providers (skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies) as downstream episode partners who share in savings and absorb a portion of any penalties.

Voluntary vs. Mandatory Bundled Payment Models
The Target Price: How CMS Sets the Benchmark
Setting an accurate target price is the most technically demanding element of any bundled payment program. If the target is too high, providers collect windfall payments without changing behavior. If it is too low, providers lose money on every episode regardless of efficiency gains, and they exit the program. CMS attempts to thread this needle by using three to five years of historical fee-for-service claims for the specific episode type in the participant's region, then applying risk adjustments and a discount that ensures the government retains savings.
The target price methodology for BPCI Advanced uses a blend of national and regional data, adjusted for the case-mix complexity of the participant's patient population using hierarchical condition categories (HCCs). High-severity patients receive higher target prices; straightforward cases receive lower ones. CMS also applies a "stop-loss" and "stop-gain" corridor: no single episode can swing the reconciliation more than a defined dollar cap in either direction, protecting both participants and Medicare from extreme outlier cases.
Because target prices are anchored to historical spending, participants who have already reduced episode costs through prior efficiency work start with a lower baseline — a phenomenon sometimes called the "ratchet effect." As participants reduce costs over time, CMS lowers the target price in subsequent model years, requiring continuous improvement just to maintain savings. This dynamic has led some high-performing participants to exit voluntary programs voluntarily once their baseline is compressed, a structural tension that mandatory models are designed to overcome.
Think of the target price like a par score in golf: it is based on what a skilled player should need to complete the hole, adjusted for the difficulty of the terrain (patient complexity). Finishing under par earns savings; going over means you owe the difference. And once you consistently shoot par, the course committee lowers the expected score next season.
Bundled Payment Target Price Mechanics
Care Transformation: What Providers Actually Change
The practical care changes driven by bundled payments cluster around three levers: post-acute placement, length of stay, and readmission reduction. Post-acute care — skilled nursing facilities, inpatient rehabilitation, home health — is the single largest driver of episode cost variation for surgical procedures. A hip replacement patient discharged to a skilled nursing facility costs Medicare roughly twice as much over 90 days as the same patient discharged directly home with home health support. Bundled payment participants therefore invest heavily in standardized discharge criteria, preferred SNF networks, and home health partnerships.
Clinical pathway standardization is the second major lever. When a hospital takes on risk for a hip replacement episode, it has a powerful financial incentive to create and enforce a standard care protocol: pre-operative patient optimization (weight, hemoglobin, diabetes control), standardized implant selection, evidence-based rehabilitation protocols, and scheduled follow-up calls. These protocols reduce variance — the expensive outlier cases that blow up episode budgets — and often improve clinical outcomes simultaneously.
Readmission prevention rounds out the triad. A 90-day episode means that any readmission within three months of the initial procedure falls inside the bundle and adds directly to the participant's cost. Participants invest in post-discharge nurse navigator programs, 24/7 patient hotlines, medication reconciliation, and remote monitoring to catch warning signs before they become emergency department visits. These infrastructure investments require upfront capital, which is part of why BPCI Advanced pays preliminary reconciliation payments — to fund the care-coordination capabilities that drive savings.
Analyses of BPCI Advanced performance in lower-extremity joint replacement (one of the highest-volume episodes in the model) are a large part of why the model as a whole saved Medicare an estimated net $344 million in Model Year 5 (about $800 million net across all eight model years, per the 2026 final evaluation). Quality metrics including readmission and mortality rates remained stable, indicating that cost reductions were achieved without compromising patient safety.
Participants who succeeded shared common characteristics: strong surgeon engagement, standardized implant formularies, disciplined SNF referral networks, and nurse navigator programs for post-discharge monitoring. Hospitals that treated bundled payments as a physician engagement strategy — rather than a finance department exercise — consistently outperformed those that did not.
Bundled Payments for Care Improvement Advanced — Orthopedic Episode Results
The Future of Bundled Payments: From Voluntary to Mandatory
CMS has moved decisively toward mandatory bundled payment models after learning that voluntary programs attract a self-selected group of already-efficient providers. The Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model — launched in 2016 as a mandatory program in randomly selected metropolitan statistical areas — was the first federal mandatory bundle and provided critical evidence that bundles can generate savings at scale without quality deterioration. CJR saved Medicare an estimated $63 million between 2016 and 2018.
The next generation mandatory model is the Transforming Episode Accountability Model (TEAM), which CMS launched on January 1, 2026, to run through December 31, 2030. TEAM requires approximately 741 acute care hospitals in selected Core-Based Statistical Areas to accept financial risk for five surgical episode types: lower extremity joint replacement, surgical hip femur fracture treatment, spinal fusion, coronary artery bypass graft, and major bowel procedure. Unlike BPCI Advanced's 90-day window, TEAM episodes end 30 days after discharge, reflecting a sharper focus on the immediate post-acute transition.
Commercial payers have also accelerated their own bundled payment programs independently of CMS. Large self-insured employers — working through coalitions like the Pacific Business Group on Health — negotiate direct bundle contracts with hospital systems for high-volume procedures. The multi-payer environment creates both opportunity (providers can amortize care-coordination infrastructure across multiple payers) and complexity (different episode definitions, target price methodologies, and quality metrics across each payer relationship). Standardization of episode definitions across payers remains one of the field's central operational challenges.
Bundled payments cover a specific clinical episode, not a patient's entire care. A patient under a bundled payment arrangement for a knee replacement still receives fee-for-service payment for unrelated conditions like diabetes management or a subsequent cardiac event. Do not confuse episode-based bundles with full-risk capitation or population-based payment models, which cover all care for a defined patient population.
Bundled Payments vs. Global Capitation
A bundled payment collapses all claims for a defined clinical episode into a single target price, aligning provider incentives around efficiency and quality rather than volume.

######## value-based-care | bundled-payment-evidence | Bundled Payment Evidence: What the Research Shows
Bundled Payment Evidence: What the Research Shows
Reading the Evidence: What "Success" Means in Bundled Payment Research
Evaluating bundled payment programs is harder than it appears. The central question — "do bundles save money and improve care?" — demands three separate answers: Do they reduce total episode spending? Do they reduce spending in a way that generates net savings to Medicare after reconciliation payments? And do they maintain or improve the quality of care delivered? These are distinct tests, and a program can pass one while failing another. Most rigorous research now distinguishes between gross episode savings (reductions in FFS claims) and net Medicare savings (what remains after reconciliation bonuses are subtracted).
The methodological challenge is defining the counterfactual. What would those patients have cost if the bundle had never existed? Researchers typically compare bundle participants to matched comparison hospitals or use difference-in-differences designs that control for pre-existing trends. Both approaches can be confounded by the selection effect: providers who voluntarily enter bundled payment programs are not a random sample — they tend to be larger, more integrated, and already more cost-efficient than non-participants. Any evaluation that does not rigorously account for this self-selection risk will overstate the program's causal impact.
With those caveats in mind, the body of evidence on bundled payments is substantial and growing. The strongest evidence comes from surgical episodes — joint replacements, spine procedures, cardiac procedures — where episode costs are large, post-acute care is a known driver of variation, and the bundle gives providers a clear lever to pull. Evidence for medical episodes (pneumonia, heart failure, sepsis) is much weaker and in some cases negative, reflecting the inherent difficulty of coordinating care for patients with complex, unpredictable trajectories.
Net Medicare savings = gross episode spending reduction minus reconciliation payments made to participants. A model can achieve gross savings (claims go down) while generating net losses (bonuses paid out exceed the savings). Evaluations that report only gross savings overstate program value to the federal government.
Surgical Episodes: Where Bundles Work Best
The most consistent evidence for bundled payment effectiveness comes from lower-extremity joint replacement — hip and knee arthroplasty. Multiple independent studies evaluating BPCI and the mandatory Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model found that participation was associated with significant reductions in episode spending, driven primarily by shifts in post-acute care utilization: fewer discharges to skilled nursing facilities and inpatient rehabilitation, shorter SNF stays when they do occur, and lower readmission rates.
A landmark NEJM study evaluating the first two years of the CJR mandatory model found statistically significant episode cost reductions without deterioration in mortality, readmission, or patient-reported function. Analyses of BPCI orthopedic episodes found per-episode spending declines averaging roughly $1,166, with the reductions concentrated in SNF costs. Importantly, these quality-neutral cost reductions suggest that prior fee-for-service spending included avoidable post-acute utilization that could be eliminated without harming patients.
Cardiac procedures show similarly strong results. Bundled payment programs for coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) and percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) have demonstrated cost reductions through shorter ICU stays, earlier extubation protocols, and standardized cardiac rehabilitation pathways. The BPCI program for major cardiac procedures generated savings across participating sites, with the highest-performing hospitals combining aggressive clinical protocol standardization with strong post-discharge follow-up programs.

Medical Episodes: The Mixed and Negative Evidence
The picture for medical episode bundles — heart failure, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, sepsis — is considerably less encouraging. A 2024 study published in JAMA Cardiology evaluating BPCI Model 2 participation for heart failure (18 BPCI hospitals versus 211 comparison hospitals) found that hospital participation was not associated with improvement in process-of-care quality measures, nor with reductions in 30-day or 90-day risk-adjusted all-cause mortality or readmission rates. In other words, the bundle had no detectable effect on quality or outcomes for this high-volume condition.
Why do medical episodes respond so differently? Several structural factors explain the divergence. First, medical episodes have much higher cost variance — a heart failure patient can cost $8,000 or $80,000 depending on comorbidities and complications that are difficult to predict or control at admission. Surgical episodes have more predictable cost trajectories, making target prices more accurate and financial risk more manageable. Second, post-acute care is a less dominant cost driver for medical episodes, meaning providers have fewer high-leverage levers to pull to reduce spending.
Third, medical episodes require cross-specialty coordination that is structurally harder to achieve. A joint replacement bundle centers on an orthopedic surgeon who acts as the natural care captain. A heart failure bundle involves hospitalists, cardiologists, primary care physicians, pharmacists, and home health agencies — all of whom need to function as a coordinated team across settings they have historically operated in silos. Building those relationships requires organizational trust and shared workflows that take years to develop and are not financially motivated by the bundle alone.
A study published in JAMA Cardiology in early 2024 analyzing BPCI participation for heart failure episodes found that bundled payment participation was not associated with improved quality performance or outcomes on key measures including 30-day and 90-day readmission and mortality rates. The researchers concluded that bundled payment models may be most effective for surgical and procedural conditions where post-acute care costs are predictable and reducible, rather than complex medical conditions with highly variable trajectories.
This evidence is consistent with CMS's own evaluation findings and has informed the design of subsequent models, which have increasingly focused on high-cost surgical procedure types with clearer care pathways and more concentrated provider accountability.
BPCI Heart Failure Episode — PubMed Study (2024)
BPCI Advanced: Evaluation Findings Across Five Model Years
CMS has published multiple annual evaluation reports for BPCI Advanced, providing the most detailed longitudinal evidence available on a voluntary federal bundled payment program. In Model Year 5 (2022), BPCI Advanced generated approximately $344 million in net Medicare savings — a roughly 4% reduction in episode spending compared to the risk-adjusted target price benchmark. The model ended on December 31, 2025, and its final evaluation (August 2026) put net Medicare savings at about $800 million across all eight model years, after net losses in Model Years 1–3. Readmission and mortality rates remained stable, satisfying the quality non-inferiority threshold built into the model.
Participation patterns in BPCI Advanced reveal the selection dynamics that complicate evaluation. The model consistently attracted high-volume orthopedic and cardiac programs at large academic medical centers and community hospitals with strong surgical volumes. These institutions already invested in care coordination prior to joining the program and were better positioned to achieve savings from day one. The Penn LDI evaluation noted that physician group practice participation in BPCI Advanced was lower than hospital participation, and that future models need to better engage PGPs if savings are to be extended to the physician setting.
The fourth annual CMS evaluation report (2023) confirmed that savings persisted through the later model years but that per-episode savings rates were compressing over time — consistent with the "ratchet effect" where target prices are adjusted downward as participants demonstrate efficiency. High-performing participants reported that maintaining savings required continuous investment in care coordination and protocol improvement, not a one-time transformation. This finding has important implications for program sustainability and the transition from voluntary to mandatory models.
Surgical Episodes (Strong Evidence)

What the Evidence Shows: Surgical vs. Medical Episode Bundles
What Predicts Success in a Bundled Payment Program?
Research consistently identifies a cluster of organizational characteristics that distinguish high-performing bundled payment participants from those who exit or underperform. Surgeon or specialist engagement is the single most consistent predictor of success. When the physician who performs the procedure is an active partner in designing the episode care pathway — not merely a recipient of hospital-imposed protocols — adoption is faster, variance is lower, and cost reductions are more durable. Programs that treat bundled payment as a finance problem rather than a clinical quality initiative rarely succeed.
Strong post-acute networks are the second predictor. High performers develop preferred relationships with a small set of SNFs and home health agencies, share patient-level data with those partners, and create clear discharge criteria that minimize unnecessary institutional post-acute stays. Facilities that discharge patients to a broad, undifferentiated network of post-acute providers lose the ability to standardize care in the 90-day tail of the episode — where cost variation is highest and provider accountability is most diffuse.
Data infrastructure matters more than most institutions anticipate before joining a bundle. Participants need near-real-time visibility into their episode claims to identify which patients are generating outlier costs and why. Providers who wait for quarterly claims reports to understand their performance cannot make mid-episode course corrections. Successful participants invest in analytics platforms that flag high-cost patterns early — unexpected readmissions, unusually long SNF stays, duplicate imaging — so care managers can intervene before costs accumulate beyond the target.
Involve proceduralists in episode pathway design from the start. Surgeon buy-in drives protocol adoption and reduces implant and care variation.
Engage Surgeons as Co-Owners
Concentrate referrals to a small set of SNFs and home health agencies with shared data access, standardized handoff protocols, and aligned incentives.
Build a Preferred Post-Acute Network
Assign dedicated nurse navigators to high-risk bundle patients for proactive post-discharge follow-up, medication reconciliation, and early readmission interception.
Create a Nurse Navigator Function
Use near-real-time claims analytics to track episode performance by patient, provider, and clinical pathway — not quarterly reports that arrive too late to act on.
Invest in Episode Analytics
In surgical bundles, implant costs are a controllable variable. Formulary standardization reduces materials costs without affecting clinical outcomes.
Standardize Implant Selection
What High-Performing Bundled Payment Participants Do Differently
Limitations and Open Questions in the Field
Despite the growing body of evidence, several important questions remain unresolved. The most significant is generalizability: can the savings demonstrated by self-selected high performers in voluntary programs be replicated across a broader, less-selected population of hospitals forced to participate in mandatory models? Early evidence from the CJR mandatory model is cautiously optimistic — savings were achieved across a heterogeneous set of hospitals — but TEAM's mandatory extension to five episode types beginning in 2026 will provide the most definitive test yet.
Equity concerns are a second open question. Research has found that bundled payment programs may inadvertently disadvantage safety-net hospitals that serve higher proportions of low-income patients with complex social needs. These patients have higher post-acute care needs and face barriers — transportation, housing instability, medication access — that make care coordination harder and episode costs higher. Standard risk adjustment does not fully account for social determinants of health, potentially making target prices systematically under-set for safety-net populations.
The interaction between bundles and other value-based care models is also poorly understood. A hospital simultaneously participating in an ACO and BPCI Advanced for overlapping patient populations faces complex attribution rules and potentially conflicting incentives. CMS has worked to align these models, but providers operating in multiple value-based contracts simultaneously need sophisticated analytics to understand how their performance in one program affects their financial exposure in another. As the value-based care ecosystem matures, managing this portfolio complexity will become a core healthcare administration competency.
Many news reports and even some policy briefs describe bundled payment "savings" without clarifying whether those figures are gross (before reconciliation payments to providers) or net (after payments). Programs that reduced episode claims but paid out bonuses exceeding the reduction — as was the case in some early BPCI surgical episodes — technically lost money for Medicare even while appearing successful. Always ask: savings to whom, measured how?
Gross Savings Are Not Net Savings

Medical episode bundles for conditions like heart failure have shown limited or no impact on quality or cost, reflecting higher cost variance and more complex multi-specialty coordination needs.

######## value-based-care | oncology-care-model | The Oncology Care Model: VBC in Cancer Care
The Oncology Care Model: VBC in Cancer Care
Why Cancer Care Needed Its Own Value-Based Model
Cancer care sits at the intersection of several cost crises in American healthcare. Chemotherapy drug prices have risen dramatically — targeted therapies can cost $100,000 or more per patient per year — and utilization is intensive, with patients receiving not just drugs but frequent lab work, imaging, supportive care, and hospitalizations for complications. Yet the fee-for-service system that governed oncology for decades provided no mechanism to reward coordination, reduce emergency visits, or guide patients toward evidence-based regimens. Oncologists were paid for administering drugs (via the buy-and-bill system), not for managing the comprehensive trajectory of a patient's cancer care.
The fragmentation problem in oncology is acute. A Medicare beneficiary receiving chemotherapy may interact with a medical oncologist, a radiation oncologist, a surgeon, a hospitalist, a palliative care team, social workers, and home health aides — often in separate organizations with no shared data, no common care plan, and no financial incentive to reduce unnecessary emergency department visits or duplicative imaging. When a patient calls at 2 a.m. with fever and chills during neutropenia, the default in a fragmented system is to send them to the ER for a costly workup, even when a phone triage protocol with a nurse practitioner might safely manage the situation.
CMS recognized this problem and launched the Oncology Care Model (OCM) in 2016 as the first cancer-focused alternative payment model in the federal portfolio. OCM ran through June 30, 2022, involving 122 oncology practices and five commercial payer partners. It was succeeded by the Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM), which launched July 1, 2023, with a refined episode structure and narrower scope focused on seven high-cost cancer types. Both models used a common architecture: a six-month chemotherapy episode triggered by the start of systemic treatment, a monthly enhanced payment to fund care coordination, and a performance-based payment tied to end-of-episode cost and quality.
The Oncology Care Model was the first alternative payment model specifically designed for cancer care. It ran from 2016 to 2022, covering chemotherapy episodes for any cancer type treated at participating practices, and served as the proof-of-concept for the successor Enhancing Oncology Model launched in 2023.

The OCM Episode: Structure and Payment Architecture
An OCM episode is triggered when a Medicare beneficiary begins a course of systemic chemotherapy at a participating practice. The episode lasts six months from the date of the first chemotherapy claim. Unlike a surgical bundle anchored to a single procedure, a six-month oncology episode encompasses a dynamic, evolving clinical situation: cycles of chemotherapy, supportive care, scans to assess treatment response, management of side effects, and potentially a treatment switch if the first regimen fails. The breadth of included services reflects both the comprehensiveness of cancer care and the challenge of attributing costs to any single responsible clinician.
The OCM payment structure had two components. First, the monthly enhanced oncology services (MEOS) payment: $160 per beneficiary per month for each month of the six-month episode, regardless of outcomes. The MEOS was explicitly designed as an upfront investment — an infrastructure subsidy to pay for the care coordination staff, extended hours access, and data reporting requirements that CMS required all participating practices to implement. Over a full six-month episode, a single patient generated $960 in MEOS payments to the practice.
The second component was performance-based payments (PBPs): additional payments made retrospectively if a practice's actual episode spending fell below a risk-adjusted benchmark price and the practice met quality thresholds. PBPs were available only to practices that achieved both cost and quality targets, ensuring that cost reductions did not come at the expense of care quality. Practices that generated excess costs above the benchmark owed a repayment in the model's two-sided risk phase — a key distinction from programs that offer upside-only participation.
Medicare beneficiary starts chemotherapy at a participating oncology practice. A new six-month episode clock begins.

MEOS Payments
Practice must provide 24/7 patient access, care coordination, evidence-based treatment planning, electronic care plans, and patient navigation as conditions of MEOS receipt.
Enhanced Services Delivered
At the end of six months, the episode closes. CMS tallies all Medicare claims for the patient during the episode.
Episode Closes
CMS compares actual episode spending to the risk-adjusted benchmark. If below benchmark and quality thresholds met, practice receives a performance-based payment. If above, repayment may be owed (in two-sided risk phase).
Reconciliation
OCM Episode Payment Flow
What OCM Required Practices to Do
Participation in OCM was not simply a financial arrangement — it required oncology practices to undergo substantive operational transformation. CMS specified six practice redesign activities that all participating practices had to implement: (1) 24/7 patient access to an appropriate clinician with real-time access to the practice's medical records; (2) the core functions of patient navigation — helping patients understand their diagnoses, manage treatment side effects, and navigate the healthcare system; (3) a documented care plan for each patient containing the 13 components of the Institute of Medicine Care Management Plan; (4) treatment with therapies consistent with nationally recognized clinical guidelines; (5) use of certified electronic health record technology; and (6) use of data for continuous quality improvement, including clinical and quality data reported to CMS.
The 24/7 access requirement was among the most impactful changes. Oncology practices accustomed to referring after-hours patients to the emergency department had to establish structured telephone triage protocols staffed by oncology-trained nurses. The goal was to keep patients with manageable symptoms — fever, nausea, pain — out of the emergency department when they did not need hospital-level care; the final evaluation found, however, that OCM did not change the likelihood of ED visits relative to comparison practices. The MEOS payment was intended to cover the staffing cost of this function.
Patient navigation deserves special attention as a care delivery innovation. An oncology navigator — typically a nurse or social worker — acts as the patient's guide and advocate throughout the treatment course. Navigators schedule and track appointments, coordinate transportation, connect patients with financial assistance programs, manage prescription adherence, and serve as the first point of contact when something goes wrong. Research consistently shows that navigation programs reduce treatment delays, improve adherence, and decrease emergency utilization, particularly for patients from low-income or underserved communities who face the greatest structural barriers.
The University of Alabama at Birmingham's Patient Care Connect Program, funded by a CMS Innovation Center award, placed lay navigators — community hires with bachelor's degrees, not licensed clinicians — across 2 academic and 10 community cancer centers in five Southeastern states to support older patients from diagnosis through survivorship or end of life.
A propensity-matched study of Medicare beneficiaries from 2012 to 2015 (Rocque et al., JAMA Oncology, 2017) found that, compared with non-navigated patients, navigated patients' costs fell by $781 more per quarter, with larger quarterly declines in ED visits (6.0%), hospitalizations (7.9%), and ICU admissions (10.6%). The program was not part of OCM, but it shows the kind of navigation infrastructure OCM's requirements were meant to fund.
UAB Patient Care Connect — Lay Navigation in Practice
What the OCM Evaluation Found: Savings, Losses, and Quality
The final OCM evaluation (Abt Global, May 2024), covering all 11 performance periods through the model's June 2022 conclusion, revealed a complex picture of modest relative savings overwhelmed by incentive payments. Total episode payments rose $616 less in OCM episodes than in comparison episodes — a 2.1 percent relative reduction. The reductions came mainly from more cost-conscious use of supportive care drugs in higher-risk cancers. This looks like success on its face, but the MEOS payments alone could reach $960 per six-month episode, and they were paid whether or not a practice met its benchmark.
When MEOS payments and performance-based payments were included in the net calculation, the OCM program resulted in an estimated net loss to Medicare of $639 million over its six years of operation. The program reduced FFS claims but paid out more in MEOS and PBP payments than it recovered in savings. This is the core tension in oncology value-based care: the coordination infrastructure needed to improve care is expensive, and the savings it generated — in OCM, mostly from more cost-conscious use of supportive care drugs rather than from avoided hospital care — may not be large enough to offset the infrastructure investment at scale.
Quality results were mixed. The evaluation found no significant changes, either positive or negative, in hospitalizations, emergency department visits, or measured quality outcomes for the overall OCM patient population. However, one positive finding emerged in equity: while OCM did not improve adherence to oral cancer treatment overall, it was associated with significantly improved adherence for patients who were Black, Hispanic, or dually eligible for Medicaid — populations that historically received less aggressive or guideline-concordant treatment. This represents a meaningful equity improvement and aligns with one of the model's explicit goals of reducing treatment disparities.

The Enhancing Oncology Model: Lessons Applied
CMS launched the Enhancing Oncology Model (EOM) on July 1, 2023, incorporating lessons from the OCM evaluation. The most consequential design change was the shift from a universal chemotherapy trigger to a narrow focus on seven high-cost, high-volume cancer types: high-risk breast cancer, lung cancer, chronic leukemia (CLL), small intestine/colorectal cancer, lymphoma, multiple myeloma, and high-risk prostate cancer. These conditions were selected because OCM data showed they had the highest episode costs, the highest variation in spending, and therefore the greatest potential for achievable savings.
EOM retained the six-month episode structure and the Monthly Enhanced Oncology Services (MEOS) payment, but cut it to $70 per beneficiary per month at launch ($100 for beneficiaries dually eligible for Medicaid), down from OCM's $160, to improve net savings potential. CMS raised it to $110 ($140 for dual-eligible beneficiaries) effective January 1, 2025. EOM also requires practices to take on two-sided financial risk from the start of the model — unlike OCM, which phased practices into downside risk gradually. This faster risk exposure is intended to sharpen the financial incentives for cost management and distinguish practices willing to commit to the model from those testing the waters for upside-only payments.
EOM launched with stronger health equity requirements than OCM: practices had to screen beneficiaries for health-related social needs, collect and report sociodemographic data, and develop a health equity plan. Those elements did not last. In 2025 CMS amended EOM agreements, citing executive orders effective January 20, 2025: it stopped requiring or accepting health equity plans and changed the social-needs data collection requirements. A second cohort of EOM participants launched July 1, 2025, indicating continued CMS commitment to the oncology VBC program.
Running an OCM practice is like running a restaurant that charges a fixed price for a full meal, no matter what courses the diner orders. The $160 MEOS payment per month is the fixed cover charge — it pays for the kitchen staff and service setup. The performance-based payment is like a tip only given if the diner leaves satisfied and the total cost to the house stays under budget. If the kitchen spends more on ingredients than the cover charge brings in, the restaurant loses money — which is exactly what happened to Medicare net of MEOS payments in the OCM.
Oncology Care Model Payment Architecture
Implications for the Future of Specialty Value-Based Care
The OCM and EOM experience holds lessons that extend well beyond oncology. They demonstrate that applying VBC principles to specialty care is structurally harder than applying them to surgical episodes, because the episode cost structure is more complex, the patient population is more fragile, and the care coordination demands are higher. The oncology experience has also highlighted the fundamental tension in alternative payment model design: the coordination infrastructure needed to improve care requires upfront investment, and those investments must generate sufficient downstream savings to justify their cost to the payer.
The models also show the importance of data infrastructure. Managing a six-month episode means tracking episode spending, identifying high-cost patients early in the episode, and monitoring care plan adherence — and quarterly claims reports arrive too late to guide clinical interventions. The lesson generalizes: VBC success is a data analytics challenge as much as a clinical care challenge.
Finally, the oncology VBC experience raises profound questions about the appropriate boundary of value-based accountability in end-of-life care. Patients with metastatic disease receiving chemotherapy near the end of life generate very high episode costs, and those costs are largely driven by clinical and patient preferences about aggressive versus palliative treatment rather than by efficiency failures. Any model that holds practices financially accountable for total episode cost must grapple with the risk that financial incentives inadvertently discourage appropriate aggressive treatment for patients who want it, or conversely, encourage premature transitions to hospice for financial reasons. This ethical dimension requires ongoing vigilance in model design and evaluation.
The OCM's estimated $639 million net loss to Medicare reflects a payment design issue — the $160 MEOS was set too high relative to achievable savings — not a failure of the care coordination concept. The equity improvements and coordination infrastructure built by participating practices have lasting value beyond the financial reconciliation. EOM's reduced monthly payment and narrower episode focus are direct responses to this design lesson.
Net Loss Does Not Mean the Model Failed
