######## value-based-care | vbc-quality-measures-hedis-ecqm | HEDIS, eCQMs & the Quality Measurement Ecosystem
HEDIS, eCQMs and the Quality Measurement Ecosystem
American healthcare has invested billions of dollars in quality measurement infrastructure over the past three decades. The result is an ecosystem of extraordinary complexity: hundreds of individual measures, maintained by multiple private organizations and government agencies, collected through administrative claims, hybrid abstraction methods, and electronic health records, reported to dozens of programs across CMS, commercial insurers, state agencies, and accreditation bodies. Any serious practitioner of value-based care must understand this ecosystem — not just which measures exist, but how they are constructed, how they are collected, what they actually measure, and why the ecosystem has failed to produce the reliable, actionable quality intelligence its architects envisioned.
NCQA and HEDIS: The Dominant Commercial Quality Framework
The Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set (HEDIS) is maintained by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) and represents the most widely used quality measurement framework in American healthcare. HEDIS comprises approximately 90 measures across 6 domains: effectiveness of care, access and availability of care, patient experience, utilization, health plan descriptive information, and measures reported using Electronic Clinical Data Systems (ECDS). HEDIS measures are used in NCQA health plan accreditation, Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, Medicaid managed care quality requirements, and commercial health plan quality reporting to employers and consumers.
HEDIS measures are constructed from three data sources, each with different characteristics. Administrative data (claims-based) uses medical and pharmacy claims to identify patients who received or failed to receive a specified service. Administrative data has 100% population coverage and low collection cost but is subject to coding completeness variations and cannot capture clinical nuances not reflected in billing codes. Medical record review (abstraction) supplements claims with chart review to identify services not captured in claims — particularly lab values, clinical findings, and services delivered but not billed. Hybrid measures combine claims and medical record data for higher precision at higher collection cost.
Electronic HEDIS (eHEDIS) and EHR Data Submission
NCQA has been progressively expanding electronic HEDIS (eHEDIS) — versions of HEDIS measures calculated directly from structured EHR data rather than claims or medical record abstraction. eHEDIS has the potential to reduce the administrative burden of HEDIS collection while improving data accuracy, since clinical values like HbA1c results and blood pressure readings can be captured directly rather than inferred from billing codes. However, eHEDIS implementation requires standardized data extraction from EHR systems, which remains technically challenging given the diversity of EHR platforms and the inconsistency of structured data entry across clinical workflows.
Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs) and the CMS Quality Framework
Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs) are a parallel quality measure infrastructure developed by CMS and the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) specifically for use with certified EHR technology. eCQMs are specified in Health Quality Measure Format (HQMF), with measure logic written in Clinical Quality Language (CQL) since the 2019 reporting period — a machine-readable specification that allows EHR systems to calculate measure results automatically from structured clinical data. CMS uses eCQMs in multiple quality reporting programs including the Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) program for hospitals, the Outpatient Quality Reporting (OQR) program, and the MIPS quality category.
The FHIR plumbing that digital measurement depends on is being laid by two 2020 rules: the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access final rule, which required CMS-regulated payers (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP and federal-exchange plans) to offer FHIR-based Patient Access APIs, and the ONC Cures Act final rule, which required certified EHRs to support standardized FHIR APIs. NCQA's shift of HEDIS measures to Electronic Clinical Data Systems (ECDS) reporting, which draws on EHR, registry and HIE data rather than claims alone, represents the convergence of the HEDIS and eCQM frameworks toward a common digital infrastructure.
CMS Core Measure Sets: Inpatient, Outpatient, and Primary Care
CMS maintains Core Measure Sets for different care settings that serve as the quality reporting basis for hospital and physician payment programs. The Hospital Inpatient Core Measure Set covers domains including heart failure, pneumonia, venous thromboembolism prevention, stroke care, and perinatal care. The Hospital Outpatient Core Measure Set covers cataract surgery, colonoscopy, and emergency department throughput. The Clinician and Group Core Measure Set covers primary care quality domains including preventive care, chronic disease management (diabetes, cardiovascular disease, depression), and care coordination.
CMS aligns these core measure sets with HEDIS and endorsed measures (formerly NQF-endorsed, now endorsed through CMS's consensus-based entity) to the extent possible, but alignment across programs is imperfect. A health system reporting quality to CMS under IQR, to NCQA for health plan accreditation, to commercial payers for VBC contracts, and to state agencies for Medicaid managed care quality requirements may be reporting on dozens of overlapping but non-identical measures to multiple audiences simultaneously — a duplication problem that consumes significant resources without proportionate insight.
Measure Endorsement: The Scientific Legitimacy Process
For two decades the National Quality Forum (NQF), a nonprofit, ran the consensus-based endorsement process that federal programs relied on. Since 2023, CMS's consensus-based entity (CBE) contract has been held by Battelle, which runs measure endorsement and pre-rulemaking review through the Partnership for Quality Measurement (PQM). Endorsement signals that a measure meets standards for importance, scientific acceptability, usability, and feasibility; endorsed measures carry a CBE number (legacy NQF numbers were kept), and CMS gives weight to endorsement when selecting measures for its quality reporting and payment programs.
Endorsement involves technical expert panels, public comment, and committee review — a rigorous procedure that has historically taken a year or more per measure. This thoroughness ensures scientific quality but also slows the introduction of new measures in rapidly evolving clinical areas. The process has also been criticized for favoring measures with strong specialty society backing over measures that might be more clinically important but lack organized constituency support.
Process, Outcome, and Structural Measures: The Quality Hierarchy
Quality measures fall into three categories with different strengths and limitations. Process measures assess whether a specific evidence-based clinical action was taken — for example, whether a diabetic patient received an HbA1c test within the measurement year. Process measures are actionable (clinicians know exactly what to do to improve them) and relatively easy to collect, but they measure inputs rather than outcomes and can be gamed by performing the measured process without the broader clinical context that makes it beneficial.
Outcome measures assess whether patients achieved a desired health state — for example, whether a diabetic patient achieved HbA1c control below 8%. Outcome measures reflect what patients actually care about but are influenced by factors outside the provider's control including patient adherence, social determinants, and biological factors. Structural measures assess whether an organization has the infrastructure or capabilities associated with quality care — for example, whether a practice uses an electronic health record or has a formal chronic disease management program.
The quality measurement field has been moving toward outcome measures for two decades, reflecting the recognition that process compliance does not guarantee outcomes. MIPS requires clinicians to report at least one outcome measure (or another high-priority measure if no outcome measure applies), and the Medicare Advantage Star Ratings weight outcome measures three times as heavily as process measures. However, outcome measures require larger sample sizes for reliable measurement, are more sensitive to case mix and social risk, and demand more sophisticated risk adjustment — creating a tension between measurement validity and operational feasibility.
The Measure Proliferation Problem
The quality measurement ecosystem has grown without systematic coordination, resulting in measure proliferation that burdens providers without proportionate information value. A 2016 Health Affairs study (Casalino et al.) estimated that US physician practices spend more than $15.4 billion a year, about 785 hours per physician, reporting quality measures to CMS and commercial payers. Many of these measures are similar but not identical — measuring hemoglobin A1c with slightly different age cutoffs or different denominator specifications across programs — requiring separate data collection and reporting workflows for technically similar clinical concepts.
The Core Quality Measures Collaborative (CQMC) was established by CMS and major commercial payers to develop aligned measure sets for specific clinical conditions, reducing the measure burden on providers through cross-payer alignment. The CQMC has made progress in aligning measures for oncology, cardiovascular care, and behavioral health, but alignment remains incomplete. The fundamental problem is that each payer has incentive to use measures that reflect well on its plan's enrolled population or that align with its specific quality improvement priorities — creating centrifugal pressure toward differentiation that multi-stakeholder alignment efforts must continuously counteract.
Digital Quality Measures: The Next Generation
CMS and NCQA have both committed to transitioning quality measurement to a fully digital infrastructure — digital quality measures (dQMs) — that would replace claims-based and hybrid collection methods with structured EHR and health information exchange data. A fully digital measure infrastructure would dramatically reduce collection costs, increase measurement frequency from annual to near-real-time, and enable more granular analysis of care patterns than claims-based approaches allow.
The transition to dQMs requires three preconditions that are not yet universally met: standardized structured data entry in EHRs (particularly for clinical values like vital signs, lab results, and medication records), standardized FHIR-based data exchange APIs across all EHR platforms, and quality measure logic expressed in CQL (Clinical Quality Language) that can run against standardized FHIR data models. Progress on all three fronts has been substantial since the 21st Century Cures Act's interoperability provisions took effect, but the transition from a claims-based to a digital quality measurement ecosystem will take years and significant investment to complete.
Equity Stratification: The Missing Dimension
One of the most significant evolution in quality measurement over the past five years has been the growing imperative to stratify quality data by race, ethnicity, language, income, and disability status. Aggregate quality scores can conceal dramatic disparities: a health plan that achieves the 75th percentile on overall HbA1c control may have excellent performance for white, commercially insured members and significantly lower performance for Black, Hispanic, or Medicaid-enrolled members. Without stratified data, these disparities are invisible and therefore unaddressable.
NCQA introduced the Health Equity Accreditation program in 2021 and has been adding race and ethnicity stratification to HEDIS measures. CMS finalized a Health Equity Index reward for the Medicare Advantage Star Ratings (later renamed Excellent Health Outcomes for All), then cancelled it in the CY2027 final rule of April 2026 and kept the historical reward factor, a reminder that equity incentives in federal programs remain politically contingent. The Enhancing Oncology Model launched in 2023 requiring participants to screen for health-related social needs, collect sociodemographic data and submit health equity plans; a 2025 amendment dropped the equity plan requirement. The field is moving from measuring average quality to measuring the distribution of quality across demographic groups, which is a more demanding and more informative standard.
The quality measurement ecosystem is both indispensable and dysfunctional. It is indispensable because without standardized, systematically collected quality data, there is no objective basis for value-based care payment, quality improvement, or consumer choice. It is dysfunctional because measure proliferation, data collection burden, gaming risk, and equity gaps have made it expensive, administratively burdensome, and only partially informative. The transition to digital quality measures represents the most promising path forward — enabling richer, more frequent, more equitable quality intelligence at lower operational cost — but requires sustained investment in health information infrastructure and regulatory alignment that the market alone will not produce.
The American quality measurement ecosystem comprises hundreds of measures maintained by dozens of organizations, collected through multiple data streams, and applied inconsistently across payers and programs. This lesson provides a comprehensive map of the ecosystem: HEDIS and the NCQA, electronic Clinical Quality Measures and their EHR infrastructure, the NQF endorsement process, the progression from process to outcome measures, the measure proliferation problem, the emerging shift toward digital quality measures, and the growing imperative to stratify quality data by equity dimensions.
######## value-based-care | vbc-patient-reported-outcomes | Patient-Reported Outcomes: Measuring What Patients Care About
Patient-Reported Outcomes: Measuring What Patients Care About
For most of quality measurement's history, the question of whether healthcare was working was answered by providers: Did the doctor prescribe the right medication? Was the correct procedure performed? Was the HbA1c checked? These process and surrogate outcome measures tell us whether clinical activities occurred, but they do not tell us whether the patient experienced less pain, returned to work, felt better, or found their treatment worthwhile. Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) — structured, standardized measurements of how patients feel and function, collected directly from patients rather than abstracted from charts — address this fundamental gap. They are the most patient-centered form of quality evidence available, and their use in value-based care is expanding rapidly.
What Patient-Reported Outcomes Are and Why They Matter
A patient-reported outcome is any report of the status of a patient's health condition or health behavior that comes directly from the patient, without interpretation by a clinician or anyone else. PROs can cover a wide range of health domains: symptoms (pain intensity, fatigue severity, dyspnea), function (physical function, cognitive function, social functioning), mental health (depression, anxiety, emotional well-being), treatment adherence and side effects, health-related quality of life, and patient satisfaction with care.
PROs matter for value-based care for several interconnected reasons. First, they measure outcomes that patients actually care about — the FDA increasingly asks oncology drug sponsors to collect core PRO data (symptoms, symptomatic side effects and physical function) alongside tumor response, as set out in its June 2021 draft guidance on core patient-reported outcomes in cancer clinical trials. Second, they capture dimensions of health that are invisible to clinical observation: a patient who presents to clinic appearing well but reporting severe fatigue and poor function is a different clinical picture than a patient whose vital signs and lab values are all normal. Third, they enable comparison across interventions, clinicians, and healthcare systems on grounds that patients find meaningful, not just grounds that are administratively convenient.
PROMIS: The Patient-Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System
PROMIS, developed by the NIH beginning in 2004 and now maintained by Northwestern University's Health Measures organization, is the most comprehensive and methodologically rigorous PRO instrument system available in American healthcare. PROMIS was designed to solve several problems with legacy PRO instruments: they were condition-specific (requiring different instruments for different diseases), they used arbitrary scoring systems that did not allow cross-condition comparison, they were paper-based and administratively cumbersome, and they were developed with limited psychometric rigor.
PROMIS achieves its goals through three key design features. First, it is built on Item Response Theory (IRT) — a psychometric framework that calibrates each individual survey question on a continuous scale, allowing scores from different combinations of questions to be placed on a common metric. Second, it uses Item Banks — large pools of calibrated questions for each health domain — that allow flexible measurement. Third, it implements Computerized Adaptive Testing (CAT), where an algorithm selects the most informative questions from the item bank based on the patient's answers to previous questions, achieving precise measurement with typically 4 to 12 questions per domain, fewer than traditional fixed-length instruments require.
PROMIS is normed to the US general population with a mean T-score of 50 and standard deviation of 10, meaning a patient with a PROMIS Physical Function score of 40 is approximately one standard deviation below the population mean. This general-population norming allows direct comparison across conditions: a patient with knee osteoarthritis who scores 35 on physical function can be compared to a patient with heart failure or multiple sclerosis on the same scale, enabling cross-condition burden measurement that condition-specific instruments cannot provide.
PROMIS Domains and Clinical Applications
PROMIS maintains validated item banks and short-form instruments across physical, mental, and social health. The most commonly used domains in clinical practice include: Physical Function (assessment of physical activities of daily living and higher-level physical activity); Pain Interference (the degree to which pain disrupts daily activities and participation); Fatigue (the subjective experience of tiredness, weakness, and lack of energy); Depression (mood, affect, and somatic symptoms associated with depressive disorders); Anxiety (subjective fear, apprehension, and tension); and Social Function (ability to participate in social activities and roles).
PROMIS also includes pediatric versions and proxy-report versions (completed by caregivers for patients who cannot self-report), extending its applicability across age groups and clinical populations. Global Health short forms — a 10-item instrument covering physical and mental health global assessments — provide a rapid screening tool that is widely used in population health management contexts.
Condition-Specific PRO Instruments: Complementing PROMIS
While PROMIS provides a universal, comparable measurement framework, condition-specific PRO instruments capture clinical details relevant to specific diseases that generic instruments miss. The Hip disability and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (HOOS) and Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS) are widely used in orthopedic value-based care programs and bundled payment models. Their short forms, the HOOS JR and KOOS JR, are the instruments behind CMS's hip and knee replacement PRO measures: voluntary PRO data submission in the Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement (CJR) model since 2016, and the Hospital IQR Program's THA/TKA patient-reported outcome performance measure. The PROMIS CAT for Physical Function and the KOOS/HOOS complement each other: PROMIS provides population-comparable scores; KOOS/HOOS captures joint-specific function details that matter for orthopedic management.
In oncology, condition-specific and symptom-specific PRO instruments are essential because cancer treatments produce unique symptom profiles not captured by generic instruments. The FACT-G (Functional Assessment of Cancer Therapy - General) and disease-specific variants (FACT-B for breast cancer, FACT-L for lung cancer) are standard in oncology clinical trials and increasingly in routine clinical practice. The FDA's June 2021 draft guidance on core patient-reported outcomes in cancer clinical trials set out which PRO domains sponsors should collect, signaling that PROs are becoming a permanent component of oncology evidence.
PRO Performance Measures: From Research to Accountability
A PRO Performance Measure (PRO-PM) is a standardized quality measure based on PRO data that is used to evaluate and compare the performance of healthcare providers or health plans. PRO-PMs move PRO data from individual clinical use (informing care for individual patients) to accountability use (comparing providers or programs). The development of valid, reliable PRO-PMs requires: adequate sample sizes for reliable provider-level measurement, appropriate risk adjustment for case mix (sicker patients report worse outcomes), standardized data collection protocols, and infrastructure for systematic PRO administration and reporting.
CMS has included PRO-PMs in several APM quality frameworks. The CJR bundled payment model rewarded hospitals for voluntarily submitting HOOS JR and KOOS JR data for hip and knee replacement beginning in 2016, and the Hospital IQR Program has since adopted a THA/TKA PRO performance measure built on the same instruments. The Enhancing Oncology Model (2023) requires participating practices to implement electronic PRO collection for symptom monitoring. These CMS decisions signal that PROs will become a standard component of quality measurement in APMs, though the infrastructure for systematic collection and reporting is still being built.
Digital Health and Real-Time PRO Collection
Digital health technology has dramatically expanded the practical feasibility of PRO collection. Patient portals, smartphone applications, SMS-based surveys, and tablet-based collection in waiting rooms allow PROs to be collected at scale without the paper burden that made systematic collection impractical in busy clinical settings. EHR integration platforms — including APIs connecting PROMIS assessment tools with Epic, Cerner, and other EHR systems — allow PRO results to flow directly into the patient's chart and appear as structured data available for quality measurement and care management.
The most clinically impactful application of digital PRO collection is real-time symptom monitoring in oncology. A randomized trial by Ethan Basch and colleagues, published in the Journal of Clinical Oncology (2016) with survival results in JAMA (2017), demonstrated that weekly web-based symptom monitoring — where patients report symptoms between clinic visits and clinicians receive alerts for concerning symptom escalation — reduced emergency department visits, improved quality of life, and extended overall survival in cancer patients receiving systemic treatment. These results, replicated in multiple studies, have made digital PRO collection a clinical best practice recommendation in oncology, not just a research tool.
Implementation Barriers: Burden, EHR Integration, and Workflow
Despite their clinical and policy value, PROs face significant implementation barriers in routine practice. Patient burden is the most commonly cited: completing multiple PRO instruments at each visit, particularly for patients with multiple chronic conditions who may be asked to complete instruments by multiple providers, creates fatigue and declining response rates over time. Survey optimization — using adaptive testing to minimize questions, selecting domain-specific measures rather than comprehensive batteries, and deploying instruments at clinically appropriate time points — can reduce burden significantly.
EHR integration remains technically challenging despite improvements in interoperability standards. Most EHR systems do not natively display PRO trends in clinically actionable formats — instead, PRO scores appear as discrete data elements or notes that require manual review, rather than trend graphs that show longitudinal change relative to population norms. Workflow integration requires deliberate clinical process design: specifying when PROs are administered, who reviews them, what the clinical response protocol is for concerning scores, and how PRO data informs treatment decision conversations.
Equity Concerns in PRO Collection and Interpretation
PRO collection raises equity concerns that must be addressed for the data to be valid and actionable across diverse populations. Digital PRO collection platforms assume smartphone access, digital literacy, and English proficiency that is not universal. Patients with limited English proficiency, lower digital literacy, or lack of smartphone access systematically have lower PRO completion rates, creating selection bias in the resulting data that may obscure the populations with highest clinical need. PROMIS instruments have been translated and validated in Spanish and several other languages, and some instruments have been validated in low-literacy versions, but coverage across all relevant languages and literacy levels remains incomplete.
Population-level PRO benchmarks may also reflect underlying social inequity rather than provider performance. If a safety-net hospital's patient population reports higher pain scores and lower physical function than a tertiary academic medical center's population, this difference likely reflects socioeconomic and health status differences between populations rather than quality differences between providers. Using unadjusted PRO data for provider accountability without social risk adjustment risks misattributing population health burden to provider quality — the same problem that affects risk adjustment for financial accountability in ACOs.
Patient-reported outcomes represent the most direct measurement of whether healthcare is achieving what patients come to clinicians for: less pain, better function, improved quality of life, and the ability to live according to their values. The methodological infrastructure for valid, reliable PRO collection exists in PROMIS and the growing ecosystem of validated instruments. The digital infrastructure for scalable collection is increasingly available. What remains is the harder work of building clinical workflows that use PRO data in real time, equity-aware collection protocols that serve all patients, and accountability frameworks that use PRO data in ways that improve care rather than creating gaming incentives. PROs are moving from research instrument to clinical standard — the question is how quickly the healthcare system can build the infrastructure to use them well.
Patient-reported outcomes (PROs) capture what patients themselves experience — pain, function, fatigue, mental health, quality of life — offering a fundamentally different quality signal than clinician-observed outcomes or administrative measures. This lesson covers PROMIS and its computerized adaptive testing approach, condition-specific PRO instruments, the CMS framework for PRO performance measures, digital health opportunities and barriers, equity concerns in PRO collection, and the emerging use of real-time PRO data in care management.
######## value-based-care | risk-adjustment-hcc | Risk Adjustment & HCC Scores: Leveling the Playing Field
Risk Adjustment & HCC Scores: Leveling the Playing Field
What Is Risk Adjustment and Why Does It Exist?
When Medicare pays a private health plan to cover a beneficiary, it faces a fundamental problem: sicker patients cost more. Without correction, plans would compete by cherry-picking healthy enrollees — a practice called "favorable selection" — leaving the sickest patients with fewer options and worse care. Risk adjustment is the statistical mechanism that corrects this distortion by modifying per-member payments to reflect the expected health costs of each enrollee.
The core logic is straightforward. A Medicare Advantage plan enrolling a 70-year-old with diabetes, heart failure, and chronic kidney disease should receive substantially more per month than a plan enrolling a healthy 65-year-old. Without that adjustment, the plan covering the sicker patient would face a financial loss — creating pressure to cut services, narrow networks, or exit the market. Risk adjustment removes that incentive by making the financial playing field level regardless of who enrolls.
CMS has used the CMS-HCC risk adjustment model in Medicare Advantage since 2004. The model inputs demographic characteristics (age, sex, Medicaid dual-eligibility status, disability status) and diagnosed health conditions into a predictive formula. The output is a risk score — a number expressing how expensive a patient is expected to be relative to the average Medicare beneficiary, who has a risk score of 1.0. A score of 1.4 means the plan receives 40 percent more per month than average; a score of 0.7 means 30 percent less.
Risk adjustment transforms capitated payments from flat per-member amounts into condition-adjusted amounts, ensuring that plans covering sicker populations are adequately compensated and have no financial motive to avoid high-need patients.
A score of 1.0 represents the average Medicare beneficiary cost baseline — Source: CMS

How Hierarchical Condition Categories Work
The CMS-HCC (Hierarchical Condition Category) model is the actuarial engine behind Medicare Advantage risk adjustment. It assigns ICD-10 diagnosis codes to condition categories that have been grouped by clinical and cost similarity. Each category carries an additive risk score coefficient — a number calibrated from fee-for-service Medicare claims data showing how much that condition, on average, raises expected annual costs above baseline.
The word "hierarchical" reflects an important design choice: when multiple conditions in the same disease family are present, only the most severe applies. A patient diagnosed with both "Type 2 diabetes without complications" and "Type 2 diabetes with chronic kidney disease" counts only in the more severe CKD category, not in both. This prevents double-counting within a clinical hierarchy while still allowing additive scoring across unrelated disease categories. A patient with diabetes, heart failure, and cancer would receive coefficients for all three separate disease groups.
Demographic factors are also built into the model. Age and sex interact with conditions — the same diabetes diagnosis carries different coefficients for a 68-year-old versus a 78-year-old, reflecting different baseline risk levels. Dual-eligibility status (being enrolled in both Medicare and Medicaid) and disability status add further adjustments, because low-income and disabled beneficiaries tend to have higher healthcare utilization even controlling for diagnosed conditions.
Medicare Advantage plans submit ICD-10 diagnosis codes gathered from all encounters, hospitalizations, and health assessments during the prior calendar year.
Diagnoses Submitted
CMS maps each submitted ICD-10 code to one of the HCC categories using a published crosswalk table. Not all diagnosis codes map to an HCC — roughly 7,770 of the roughly 75,000 ICD-10 codes map under the current V28 model.
Mapping to HCCs
Within each disease family, the hierarchy rule is applied — only the most severe condition category is retained when multiple related diagnoses are present.
Hierarchies Applied
Each applicable HCC coefficient is added together along with demographic coefficients (age/sex, dual status, disability) to produce the final risk score.
Coefficients Summed
The risk score is multiplied by the county-level benchmark rate set by CMS to produce the monthly capitated payment to the plan.
Payment Calculated
How a Risk Score Is Calculated
Model V28: The 2024 Overhaul
CMS substantially revised the HCC model beginning in 2024 with the introduction of Version 28 (V28), which replaced the longstanding Version 24 (V24). The transition was phased over three years: V28 applied to 33 percent of payment in 2024, 67 percent in 2025, and 100 percent beginning January 1, 2026. V28 expanded the number of condition categories from 86 to 115, reflecting advances in clinical knowledge and updated cost data from more recent Medicare claims.
One major change was the removal of several diagnosis codes that had been subject to widespread manipulation. V28 reduced the number of valid ICD-10 codes that map to HCCs from 9,797 under V24 to 7,770 under V28 — a reduction of over 2,000 mappable codes. CMS determined that many of these removed codes lacked strong predictive power for future costs or were being entered on risk-adjustment-specific encounters rather than as genuine clinical findings. The net effect of V28 is projected to reduce average Medicare Advantage risk scores by approximately 3.12 percent.
The model recalibration matters enormously for plan finances. A 3 percent reduction in average risk scores across the entire Medicare Advantage program — which covers over 33 million beneficiaries — translates to billions of dollars in reduced annual payments. Plans with the highest concentrations of previously-manipulated diagnoses face the steepest payment reductions, creating strong financial pressure to improve the integrity of their coding practices.
Under the old V24 model, certain conditions like "atherosclerosis of the extremities with intermittent claudication" and "angina pectoris" mapped to HCCs that contributed meaningfully to risk scores. Under V28, these and hundreds of similar codes were removed or recategorized because they showed weak predictive validity in claims data analysis.
Plans that had been aggressively coding these conditions through in-home health risk assessments saw the largest payment reductions. CMS structured the 3-year phase-in specifically to allow time for plans to adjust their clinical documentation workflows rather than face an immediate financial cliff.
CMS-HCC V28 Transition Impact
Under the risk adjustment rules, diagnoses must come from a physician, nonphysician practitioner, or facility encounter — and must be documented in the medical record. Diagnoses captured only on health risk assessments without supporting clinical documentation do not qualify under RADV audit standards, even if they were accepted for payment.
Not All Diagnosis Sources Are Equal
The Upcoding Problem and Federal Oversight
Risk adjustment creates a perverse financial incentive: the more diagnoses a plan documents, the more money it receives. Plans discovered that aggressive diagnosis capture — particularly through in-home health risk assessments (HRAs) conducted by plan-employed vendors — could substantially boost risk scores without corresponding increases in actual care delivered. The OIG and MedPAC have documented this "coding intensity" problem for over a decade.
In October 2024, HHS OIG published a report estimating that diagnoses reported only on HRAs and HRA-linked chart reviews — and not on any other service records — resulted in approximately $7.5 billion in risk-adjusted payments for 2023 that lacked adequate clinical documentation support. Nearly two-thirds of that total came from in-home HRAs and HRA-linked chart reviews, often administered by MA companies or their vendors, and just 20 MA companies drove 80 percent of it. OIG recommended that CMS restrict the use of diagnoses reported only on in-home HRAs, audit HRA-only diagnoses, and examine the conditions most susceptible to misuse.
CMS conducts Risk Adjustment Data Validation (RADV) audits to verify that submitted diagnoses are supported by medical record documentation. In 2023, CMS finalized updated RADV audit methodology that significantly strengthened the extrapolation approach — meaning that if an audit finds a certain percentage of diagnoses are unsupported, CMS can recover overpayments estimated across the plan's entire enrolled population, not just the audited sample. Humana challenged the rule, and in September 2025 a federal district court in Texas vacated it; CMS appealed in November 2025.

Think of HCC upcoding like a car insurance company that always finds a reason to label your car as a "high-performance sports model" because sports cars get higher premiums — even when your car is a standard sedan. The risk adjustment system needs accurate diagnosis data the way insurance needs accurate vehicle classifications.
HCC Coding Integrity and Risk Adjustment Manipulation
Risk Adjustment in Other Value-Based Programs
HCC-based risk adjustment is not limited to capitated Medicare Advantage payments. Risk scores are used across a wide range of value-based programs to ensure that providers caring for sicker patient panels are not unfairly penalized in quality and cost comparisons. In the Medicare Shared Savings Program, ACO benchmark calculations are risk-adjusted to reflect the clinical complexity of assigned beneficiaries. Without this adjustment, ACOs serving rural or low-income populations with higher burdens of chronic disease would systematically appear to perform worse than those serving healthy suburban populations.
The ACA's individual market also uses a separate risk adjustment program (not HCC-based) administered by CMS to redistribute funds among insurers on the exchanges, compensating plans that enroll sicker populations at the expense of those that enroll healthier ones. This prevents the "death spiral" dynamic in which sick individuals cluster in high-premium plans while healthy individuals opt out, destabilizing the market.
Despite these protections, risk adjustment remains an imperfect science. The model predicts expected costs from prior-year diagnoses, but health status can change rapidly. Newly diagnosed conditions mid-year are not captured until the next payment cycle. The model also underpredicts costs for some high-cost outlier patients and overpredicts for others. These limitations mean that even a well-designed risk adjustment system will produce some payment inaccuracies — the goal is minimizing systematic bias, not achieving perfection.
What Risk Adjustment Achieves
Compensates plans for sicker enrolled populations
Removes financial incentive to avoid high-need patients
Enables fair performance comparisons across unlike populations
Reduces incentive for favorable selection in competitive markets
Limitations of Risk Adjustment
Cannot adjust for diagnoses not documented in the prior year
Creates financial incentive for aggressive (and fraudulent) coding
Does not capture social risk factors like poverty or housing instability
Model accuracy degrades for extreme outlier patients
Risk Adjustment: What It Does vs. What It Cannot Do
Risk adjustment modifies capitated payments based on expected health costs, removing the financial incentive for plans to avoid enrolling sick patients.
The CMS-HCC model maps ICD-10 diagnosis codes to condition categories, each carrying an additive cost coefficient calibrated from fee-for-service Medicare claims data.
The "hierarchical" principle means only the most severe condition within a disease family counts, preventing double-counting while allowing additive scoring across unrelated diseases.

Risk adjustment is used beyond Medicare Advantage in ACO benchmarking, individual market programs, and other value-based arrangements to ensure fair comparisons across unlike patient populations.
The fundamental tension in risk adjustment is that accurate coding is essential for fair payment, but the financial incentive to maximize diagnoses creates persistent pressure toward upcoding and fraud.

######## value-based-care | social-risk-adjustment | Social Risk in Risk Adjustment: Should We Adjust for Poverty?
Social Risk in Risk Adjustment: Should We Adjust for Poverty?
The Question at the Heart of the Debate
Should a hospital be held to the same quality standard if half its patients live in poverty as a hospital whose patients are predominantly middle-class? Should a primary care practice treating a community with high rates of food insecurity, unstable housing, and limited transportation be judged on the same readmission rate curve as a practice in a wealthy suburb? These are not rhetorical questions. They are policy choices embedded in every value-based payment program — and the answer determines whether those programs help or harm the safety-net providers that serve America's most vulnerable patients.
Social risk adjustment refers to the practice of modifying quality and cost benchmarks — or risk scores — to account for patients' social and economic circumstances that are unrelated to the quality of clinical care. When a patient is readmitted to the hospital partly because she has no transportation to her follow-up appointment, no refrigerator for her medications, and no one at home to monitor her condition, that readmission reflects her social circumstances — not her provider's clinical competence. The debate is whether the payment system should account for that reality.
The stakes are enormous. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing Program, the Merit-Based Incentive Payment System, and the Shared Savings Program all use outcome and quality metrics that are sensitive to patients' socioeconomic status. Safety-net hospitals and practices that disproportionately serve low-income and disabled populations have argued for years that these programs systematically penalize them — not for delivering poor care, but for serving poor patients.
Social risk factors — including income level, housing stability, food security, education, transportation access, and social support — are estimated to influence up to 80 percent of health outcomes. Yet most value-based payment programs historically adjusted only for clinical diagnoses, not for these upstream determinants.
The NQF and the Evidence Base
The National Quality Forum (NQF) established an expert panel in 2014 to examine whether quality measures should be adjusted for social risk factors. The panel's report called for adjustment "under a defined set of circumstances," concluding that failing to adjust might worsen health disparities by creating systematic financial pressure on providers who serve disadvantaged populations. This finding sparked a multi-year policy debate involving CMS, MedPAC, the National Academy of Medicine, and Congress.
In 2017, the NQF completed a multi-stakeholder trial that tested social risk adjustment across multiple quality measures. The trial found that incorporating social risk factors into performance measurement was feasible — though challenging — and that social risk factors were statistically significant predictors of outcomes on many measures. The study documented clear performance disparities between providers serving high-social-risk versus low-social-risk populations, validating concerns that unadjusted comparisons were systematically misleading.
Research has consistently shown that dual-eligible beneficiaries (those who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid) and low-income subsidy recipients in Medicare Advantage perform worse on clinical quality measures, have higher readmission rates, and score lower on patient experience surveys — even when controlling for clinical diagnoses. These patterns persist across different geographic regions, health systems, and care settings, suggesting that the disparity is driven by social circumstances rather than differences in clinical care quality.
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), created by the ACA in 2010 with penalties beginning in fiscal year 2013, penalizes hospitals with higher-than-expected 30-day readmissions for conditions including heart failure, pneumonia, and hip/knee replacement. Safety-net hospitals — which serve disproportionately high shares of low-income and uninsured patients — have consistently received higher penalties under HRRP.
Critics argued that much of the gap reflected patients' social circumstances rather than poor hospital care. Congress partially addressed this in the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which required a peer-grouping system — applied from fiscal year 2019 — that compares hospitals to others with similar shares of low-income patients — a form of social risk adjustment for HRRP.
Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program and Safety-Net Hospitals
The Two Sides of the Policy Debate
The case for social risk adjustment rests on fairness and access. If safety-net providers are systematically penalized in value-based programs because of who their patients are rather than how well they perform clinically, the programs create a perverse incentive to avoid serving vulnerable populations. Over time, financial penalties can reduce resources available for quality improvement, drive providers to exit the market, or create pressure to limit services to high-risk patients. The ultimate losers are the patients who most depend on those providers.
The case against social risk adjustment is also grounded in legitimate policy concerns. Critics argue that adjusting outcome measures for patients' social circumstances could mask genuine disparities in the quality of care delivered to low-income patients. If a hospital serving mostly poor patients actually does deliver inferior care, adjusting the benchmark to account for poverty could obscure that reality and remove the accountability pressure that drives improvement. From this perspective, social risk adjustment could become a tool for excusing poor performance rather than addressing its root causes.
A third position — increasingly adopted by CMS — attempts to split the difference. Rather than adjusting outcome benchmarks for social risk, this approach focuses on measuring and rewarding active interventions to address social needs: screening patients for SDOH, connecting them to community resources, reducing disparities in performance within a provider's own patient population. This "stratification and accountability" approach holds that providers should not be rewarded merely for serving a disadvantaged population, but should be rewarded for actively reducing disparities within that population.
Arguments For Adjustment
Prevents systematic financial penalties on safety-net providers
Removes incentive to avoid enrolling or treating vulnerable patients
Reflects reality that social factors drive outcomes beyond providers' control
Supported by NQF, National Academy of Medicine, and safety-net advocates
Arguments Against Adjustment
Could mask genuine disparities in care quality for low-income patients
Removes accountability pressure to improve outcomes for disadvantaged populations
May create perverse incentive to label patients as socially disadvantaged
Difficult to implement consistently without reliable standardized SDOH data
Social Risk Adjustment: The Core Policy Debate
What CMS Has Actually Done
CMS has moved incrementally toward incorporating social risk into payment programs, though it has not adopted comprehensive social risk adjustment for most quality measures. The most significant step was the peer-grouping adjustment for HRRP, enacted in the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 and applied from fiscal year 2019, which compares hospitals' readmission rates to peers with similar socioeconomic patient mixes rather than to the national average. This approach acknowledges that different hospitals operate in structurally different environments without fully excusing poor performance.
In 2024, CMS issued regulations requiring hospitals participating in federal payment programs to screen all patients for five social determinants: food insecurity, housing instability, transportation needs, utility difficulties, and interpersonal safety. These screening requirements create a standardized data foundation that could eventually support more rigorous social risk adjustment. CMS also established billing codes for Social Determinants of Health Risk Assessments, Community Health Integration services, and Principal Illness Navigation — creating reimbursement pathways for directly addressing social needs.
For Medicare Advantage, CMS introduced the Health Equity Index (HEI) as part of the Star Ratings system, taking effect for 2027 star ratings based on 2024–2025 performance data. The HEI rewards plans that achieve high performance specifically among enrollees with social risk factors — dual-eligible beneficiaries, low-income subsidy recipients, and disability-status enrollees. Rather than adjusting benchmarks downward, the HEI adds bonus points for demonstrating equitable outcomes across all enrolled populations.
Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program launches with no social risk adjustment, immediately triggering criticism from safety-net hospitals that face disproportionate penalties.

CMS Timeline: Social Risk in Payment Programs
The Data Problem and the Path Forward
The most practical obstacle to comprehensive social risk adjustment is data. Unlike clinical diagnoses, which are captured through standardized ICD-10 codes in medical claims, social risk factors are inconsistently documented across health systems, insurers, and geographic regions. Poverty is not an ICD-10 code. Housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers are documented in some EHR systems but not others, and the definitions and screening tools vary widely.
The 2024 SDOH screening mandates represent an attempt to solve this data problem at the population level by requiring consistent, standardized screening across all Medicare- and Medicaid-participating hospitals. Over time, if these requirements are enforced and data is aggregated at the CMS level, it becomes possible to construct reliable patient-level social risk profiles that could support more refined payment adjustments. Several states — including Massachusetts, New York, and California — have moved faster than federal policy by requiring SDOH documentation in Medicaid managed care contracts.
The Vermont Blueprint for Health offers an instructive model. Vermont has integrated social risk data collection into its community health team model, using standardized SDOH screening across all primary care practices. This data informs both population health interventions and, increasingly, payment arrangements that account for the social complexity of a practice's attributed population. Vermont's approach suggests that social risk adjustment is not just technically feasible but operationally achievable when built systematically into care delivery infrastructure from the ground up.
The emerging CMS framework distinguishes between "adjusting for" social risk (lowering benchmarks for disadvantaged populations) and "rewarding action on" social risk (paying for SDOH screening, community health integration, and demonstrated disparity reduction). Both approaches are moving forward simultaneously in different programs.
Social risk adjustment modifies quality and cost benchmarks to account for patients' social and economic circumstances — income, housing, food security — that drive outcomes beyond providers' clinical control.
The NQF's 2014 expert panel endorsed social risk adjustment under defined circumstances, and a 2017 multi-stakeholder trial confirmed it is feasible and that social factors are significant predictors of outcomes.
The core policy debate pits fairness concerns (safety-net providers are unfairly penalized) against accountability concerns (adjustment could mask genuine care quality disparities for low-income patients).
Congress partially adopted social risk adjustment for the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program in the 21st Century Cures Act (2016) by creating socioeconomic peer groups rather than comparing all hospitals to a single national benchmark.
CMS's 2024 SDOH screening mandate requires hospitals to screen patients for five social domains, building the data infrastructure needed for more systematic social risk adjustment in the future.
The CMS Health Equity Index, effective for 2027 Star Ratings, rewards Medicare Advantage plans for achieving equitable outcomes across social risk subgroups — an "accountability for equity" approach rather than benchmark adjustment.
The absence of standardized, reliable social risk data remains the primary technical barrier to comprehensive social risk adjustment in federal value-based payment programs.
The 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 required peer groups within HRRP (applied from fiscal year 2019) based on hospitals' shares of dual-eligible beneficiaries, so each hospital is compared to peers serving similar proportions of low-income patients rather than the national average. This is a form of social risk adjustment that acknowledges structural differences in operating environments without fully eliminating accountability for readmission performance.

######## value-based-care | medicare-star-ratings | Medicare Advantage Star Ratings: Formula, Stakes & Strategy
Medicare Advantage Star Ratings: Formula, Stakes & Strategy
Why Star Ratings Exist
Medicare Advantage is a consumer marketplace. Unlike traditional Medicare — which is run by the federal government and is largely standardized — Medicare Advantage is delivered by private insurance companies that must compete for enrollees. From the beginning, policymakers recognized that consumers needed a standardized, publicly available signal of plan quality to make informed choices. The Star Ratings system, formally established under the Medicare Modernization Act and expanded significantly by the ACA, provides that signal on a scale of 1 to 5 stars.
The Star Ratings system serves two distinct purposes that are sometimes in tension. First, it is a consumer information tool: the ratings are published on Medicare Plan Finder, and research shows that beneficiaries use star ratings when selecting plans — higher-rated plans attract more enrollees. Second, it is a financial incentive mechanism: plans with 4 or more stars receive quality bonus payments that can total hundreds of millions of dollars annually for large insurers. Both functions are served by the same set of measures, which creates pressure to optimize for measured metrics at the expense of unmeasured aspects of care.
The Star Ratings program has evolved substantially since its inception. CMS has progressively raised performance thresholds, added new measures, introduced methodological improvements like outlier deletion, and incorporated new domains such as health equity. Each annual cycle of measure updates and cut-point changes produces winners and losers among the nation's more than 700 Medicare Advantage contracts — and the financial consequences can run into the hundreds of millions of dollars per percentage point of star rating change.
Medicare Advantage Star Ratings simultaneously function as a consumer choice signal published on Medicare Plan Finder and as a financial incentive mechanism that awards billions of dollars in quality bonus payments to plans achieving 4 or more stars.
The Nine Domains and Forty-Plus Measures
The overall star rating for a Medicare Advantage Prescription Drug (MA-PD) plan is computed from performance across nine domains, with a maximum of 42 individual measures (40 unique measures, with 2 duplicated across Part C and Part D calculations). The nine domains span both clinical quality and member experience: Staying Healthy (screenings and vaccines), Managing Chronic Conditions (disease-specific clinical outcomes), Plan Responsiveness and Care (access and appeals), Member Complaints and Changes (grievances and disenrollment), and Drug Pricing and Patient Safety (Part D-specific).
Not all measures carry equal weight in the final star rating calculation. CMS applies a triple-weight to measures it considers highest-priority: patient experience surveys (Health Outcomes Survey and Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems, known as CAHPS), care coordination measures, and medication adherence measures. Double-weighted measures include preventive care screenings and chronic disease management. Single-weighted measures include administrative outcomes like complaint rates. This weighting structure means that member experience and care coordination dominate the overall rating in a way that the raw count of measures does not suggest.
Cut points — the thresholds separating 1-star from 2-star, 2-star from 3-star, and so on — are recalculated each year based on the distribution of plan performance during the measurement period. This means that achieving a 4-star rating requires hitting a different absolute performance threshold each year, depending on how the industry as a whole performed. In a year when most plans improved, cut points shift upward, and a plan that maintained the same absolute score might drop from 4 to 3 stars. This relative performance architecture creates both competitive pressure and financial instability.

Medicare Advantage Star Rating Domains
The Quality Bonus Payment Formula
The financial stakes of star ratings are substantial. Plans that achieve at least 4 stars receive a quality bonus payment (QBP) that increases their county-level benchmark rate by 5 percentage points. This benchmark increase translates directly into higher capitated payments per enrollee. For a large Medicare Advantage plan enrolling hundreds of thousands of beneficiaries, a 5-percentage-point benchmark increase can mean hundreds of millions of dollars in additional annual revenue — the difference between profitability and loss in many markets.
The QBP formula also affects how plans share their rebate — the amount by which their bid falls below the quality-adjusted benchmark. Plans with 3 stars or below retain 50 percent of the rebate to fund additional benefits. Plans with 3.5 to 4 stars retain 65 percent. Plans with 4.5 or 5 stars retain 70 percent. The retained rebate is used to fund supplemental benefits (dental, vision, hearing, transportation, meals) that differentiate plans in the consumer market. Higher-rated plans therefore have both higher benchmarks and higher rebate retention — a compounding financial advantage that makes the 4-star threshold the most consequential boundary in Medicare Advantage finance.
Medicare Advantage quality bonus payments reached at least $11.8 billion in 2024 and are projected to total at least $12.7 billion in 2025, according to KFF analysis. These amounts represent a substantial subsidy embedded within the Medicare Advantage program. Critics argue that the bonus program pays out regardless of whether quality improvements are clinically meaningful or whether they produce better health outcomes — inflating spending without proportionate benefit to beneficiaries.

5-Star Plans in 2025
The 2025 Ratings Shock and the Tukey Method
The 2025 Medicare Advantage Star Ratings, released in October 2024, produced a striking decline across the industry. The average plan star rating fell from 4.07 in 2024 to 3.92 in 2025 — the first time the average had fallen below 4.0 since the early years of the program. More dramatically, only 7 plans achieved a 5-star rating in 2025, compared with 38 in 2024. The share of MA prescription drug plans achieving 4 or more stars dropped from 43 percent to 40 percent.
The primary driver of this decline was CMS's introduction of the Tukey Outlier Deletion Method for calculating cut points. This statistical technique removes extreme outliers from the performance distribution before calculating the thresholds between star levels. When outliers at the low end of performance are removed, the distribution shifts upward — and so do the cut points. The result is that a plan must now achieve higher absolute performance to earn the same star rating. CMS argued that the Tukey method produces more accurate cut points that better represent the typical range of plan performance.
The industry reacted with significant alarm. Plans that had maintained 4-star status for multiple years suddenly found themselves at 3.5 or 3 stars — with all the financial consequences that implies. Several large insurers, including UnitedHealth Group and Humana, disclosed that the rating declines would cost them hundreds of millions of dollars in reduced bonus payments. CMS received significant industry pushback and litigation, arguing that the methodology changes were insufficiently explained and implemented too abruptly.
Plan strategies to improve star ratings can include genuine quality improvements — better care coordination, more effective disease management — or gaming behaviors that improve measured scores without improving underlying care. Examples of the latter include aggressive outreach to complete HEDIS chart reviews without changing clinical processes, or narrowing supplemental benefits to lower the denominator of certain denominators. CMS periodically audits for gaming and adjusts measure specifications to reduce these opportunities.
Gaming vs. Genuine Improvement
Strategic Implications for Health Plans
Achieving and maintaining 4-star status has become one of the highest-priority strategic objectives for Medicare Advantage plans. Plans invest heavily in star ratings improvement programs: dedicated care management teams focused on HEDIS measure gaps, CAHPS survey outreach to improve member experience scores, pharmacy programs to improve medication adherence measures, and data analytics platforms that identify at-risk members before they miss screenings or fall out of compliance on chronic disease measures.
The CAHPS survey — which asks members to rate their experience with the plan, providers, and customer service — is particularly important given its triple weighting. Plans invest in member engagement programs, simplified appeals processes, and provider network management specifically to drive up CAHPS scores. The challenge is that CAHPS measures member perceptions, which are influenced by factors ranging from genuine care quality to marketing messaging and member demographics — making them both important outcome signals and susceptible to perception management.
Plans also monitor their performance within the Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI) — a CMS mechanism that adjusts star ratings upward for plans with high shares of dual-eligible and low-income subsidy beneficiaries. The CAI is discussed in detail in the next lesson on equity and the LIS problem, but for strategic purposes, it means that plans enrolling high shares of low-income beneficiaries receive partially offsetting adjustments to their star rating that help account for the expected performance challenges associated with serving socially disadvantaged populations.
Think of the Medicare Advantage Star Ratings system as a restaurant inspection score that directly determines how much your supplier will charge you for ingredients. A restaurant that falls from an A to a B doesn't just lose some customers — it also faces higher wholesale prices for everything it buys. The inspection criteria change every year, and a new scoring method might drop dozens of A-rated restaurants to B overnight. That is essentially what happened to Medicare Advantage plans in 2025.
The Financial Stakes of Medicare Advantage Star Ratings

######## value-based-care | star-ratings-equity-critique | Star Ratings & Equity: The Low-Income Subsidy Problem
Star Ratings & Equity: The Low-Income Subsidy Problem
The Low-Income Subsidy and Who It Represents
Within Medicare Advantage, no group of beneficiaries is more politically and programmatically complex than those who receive the Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) — also called Extra Help. The LIS program subsidizes Part D prescription drug costs for Medicare beneficiaries with limited income and resources, reducing or eliminating premiums, deductibles, and copayments for eligible enrollees. In 2024, about 13.7 million Medicare beneficiaries received the low-income subsidy — roughly a quarter of the 53 million Part D enrollees.
LIS beneficiaries are disproportionately represented in certain Medicare Advantage plans — particularly dual-eligible special needs plans (D-SNPs) that specialize in serving people who qualify for both Medicare and Medicaid. These beneficiaries carry significant social complexity: they are more likely to have multiple chronic conditions, unstable housing, food insecurity, limited health literacy, and barriers to transportation. They are also more likely to miss appointments, have lower medication adherence rates, and score lower on patient experience surveys — through no fault of the plans that serve them.
The Star Ratings system was designed when Medicare Advantage enrollment was dominated by relatively affluent, healthy seniors. As D-SNPs and LIS-serving plans have grown — driven by CMS policy and market dynamics — the system has had to grapple with a fundamental design tension: should plans serving the most complex, socially disadvantaged populations be held to identical performance standards as plans serving predominantly healthy, high-income beneficiaries?
Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries — also called Extra Help recipients — are Medicare Part D enrollees with limited income and resources who receive federal subsidies for prescription drug costs. Plans serving high LIS concentrations consistently face structural performance disadvantages in the Star Ratings system that are only partially offset by existing adjustments.
How the Star Ratings System Disadvantages LIS-Heavy Plans
The Star Ratings system measures performance on approximately 42 metrics, and LIS status correlates negatively with performance on a wide range of them. Medication adherence measures — which are triple-weighted in the Part D domain — show consistent LIS gaps. Research across multiple years of CMS data shows that LIS beneficiaries are significantly less likely to adhere to statins, ACE inhibitors/ARBs, and oral diabetic medications, even when controlling for demographics and clinical diagnoses. The reasons are structural: cost-sharing (even if subsidized), transportation barriers, social instability, and limited pharmacy access in low-income neighborhoods.
CAHPS patient experience scores — weighted four times as heavily as process measures in the 2023–2025 Star Ratings, and twice as heavily from 2026 — also show systematic LIS disadvantages. LIS beneficiaries report lower satisfaction with their health plan and care experience across multiple CAHPS domains, including communication with providers, coordination of care, and plan responsiveness. Research has found that these lower CAHPS scores reflect real experience differences driven by factors including neighborhood poverty, language barriers, and concentration of LIS beneficiaries in plans with less administrative capacity — but they are partially attributable to social circumstances rather than plan performance.
The cumulative effect is that plans serving high concentrations of LIS beneficiaries face a structural performance headwind on multiple high-weight measures simultaneously. A plan serving 60 percent LIS beneficiaries competing against a plan serving 15 percent LIS beneficiaries for the same star rating faces a mathematically different challenge. This creates an equity paradox: the plans most committed to serving America's most vulnerable Medicare beneficiaries are the plans most financially penalized by the quality measurement system.
Dual Eligible Special Needs Plans (D-SNPs) enroll beneficiaries who are simultaneously eligible for Medicare and Medicaid — the highest-complexity, most socially disadvantaged subset of Medicare beneficiaries. D-SNPs typically report lower star ratings than non-SNP Medicare Advantage plans, even when delivering care that health equity advocates consider high quality.
D-SNPs disproportionately serve beneficiaries with mental illness, substance use disorders, housing instability, and multiple chronic conditions — all characteristics associated with lower measured performance on star rating metrics. Despite serving arguably the most important population in Medicare, D-SNPs are persistently disadvantaged in the quality bonus payment system.
D-SNPs and the LIS Performance Gap
The Categorical Adjustment Index: A Partial Solution
CMS has been aware of the LIS performance gap for years and has responded with the Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI). The CAI adds points to a contract's overall star rating to adjust for the mean within-contract performance disparity associated with its percentage of enrollees receiving the Part D low-income subsidy or dual eligibility and those who are disabled. The adjustment is applied at the contract level, not the measure level, and it primarily benefits contracts with high LIS/dual-eligible enrollment.
The CAI works by estimating, across all contracts, the average within-contract gap between LIS/dual-eligible or disabled beneficiaries and other beneficiaries on selected measures. Each contract is then placed in an adjustment category by its share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees, and a factor is added to (or subtracted from) its rating; contracts with larger shares receive larger positive adjustments. The goal is to ensure that such contracts' performance is not understated solely because of the composition of their enrolled population.
The CAI has limitations, however. Critics argue that it is insufficiently generous to fully offset the performance disadvantage facing heavily LIS-concentrated plans, and that the within-contract comparison methodology misses much of the structural disadvantage these plans face. Plans serving 80 percent LIS beneficiaries cannot simply be compared to themselves — they need comparison against the very different standard that applies to plans serving mostly healthy, wealthy seniors. The CAI represents an incremental accommodation rather than a fundamental redesign of the measurement framework.
Current CMS Approach (CAI)
Adjusts the overall rating by the contract's share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees
Primarily benefits plans with high LIS/dual-eligible concentrations
Adjusts the final star rating score, not individual measure cut points
Criticized as insufficient to fully offset LIS structural disadvantages
Proposed Alternative Approaches
Separate performance benchmarks for LIS-concentrated plans (peer grouping)
Social risk adjustment of individual measure cut points
Distinct rating tracks for D-SNPs and non-SNP plans
Outcome measures specifically designed for socially complex populations
Star Ratings Equity Mechanisms: Existing vs. Proposed
The Health Equity Index: A Framework Withdrawn
CMS introduced a new mechanism — the Health Equity Index (HEI) — as part of a broader effort to align Medicare Advantage incentives with health equity goals. Unlike the CAI, which adjusts for the penalty associated with having many LIS beneficiaries, the HEI is designed to reward plans that actively improve outcomes specifically for their most disadvantaged enrollees. CMS finalized the HEI in April 2023 to take effect for 2027 Star Ratings, using 2024 and 2025 performance data. In its CY2027 final rule (April 2026), CMS removed the HEI reward — by then renamed Excellent Health Outcomes for All — before it ever took effect, and kept the historical reward factor instead.
As designed, the HEI would have replaced the existing reward factor in the star ratings program. Plans would have earned HEI points based on their performance on specific quality measures among their Social Risk Factor (SRF) population — defined as enrollees receiving Extra Help/LIS, dual-eligible beneficiaries, and disability-status enrollees. Contracts meeting minimum SRF enrollment thresholds could have earned up to 0.4 points added to their unrounded star rating.
The HEI would have marked a philosophical shift from the CAI. Rather than simply adjusting for the negative performance effect of having many LIS beneficiaries, the HEI was designed to create a positive incentive for achieving high quality specifically among LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries. A plan that served many LIS enrollees but did not improve their outcomes would have received no HEI reward. A plan that actively closed care gaps, improved medication adherence, and achieved high CAHPS scores among its LIS population would have earned a meaningful star rating bonus. It would have shifted the frame from "compensation for disadvantage" to "reward for demonstrated equity."
All Medicare Advantage plans were measured against the same cut points with no adjustment for LIS concentration or social risk, creating systematic disadvantages for safety-net plans.
Pre-2012: No Equity Adjustment
CMS introduced a small reward factor for contracts with consistently high and stable performance across measures — but this primarily benefited already-high-performing plans, not LIS-heavy ones.
2012: Reward Factor
The Categorical Adjustment Index began adjusting final star ratings by each contract's share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees, as an interim fix for the average within-contract disparity.
2017: CAI Introduced
CMS finalized the Health Equity Index in April 2023; plan performance in 2024–2025 was to set the first HEI rewards for 2027 Star Ratings.
2023: HEI Finalized
In its CY2027 final rule (April 2026), CMS removed the HEI reward (renamed Excellent Health Outcomes for All) before it took effect and kept the historical reward factor.
2026: HEI Withdrawn
The Evolution of Equity Adjustments in Star Ratings
What These Changes Mean for Policy and Practice
The CAI represents genuine but partial progress toward a more equitable Medicare Advantage quality measurement system, and with the HEI withdrawn it remains the main equity mechanism — substantial structural problems remain. The core measurement framework still compares all plans on the same absolute performance thresholds using annually-shifted cut points that do not distinguish between plans serving 10 percent LIS beneficiaries and plans serving 80 percent LIS beneficiaries. Until CMS adopts either separate rating tracks for D-SNPs or individual measure-level social risk adjustment, the most vulnerable beneficiaries will continue to be served by plans that are disproportionately penalized in the quality bonus payment system.
Even without the HEI, the strategic lesson for plans holds. Plans need to identify their SRF population, track measure performance specifically within that subgroup, and build targeted interventions to close equity gaps — not just overall performance gaps. This requires more granular data infrastructure than most plans have historically maintained, and it requires care management programs that are designed specifically for the social complexity of LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries rather than programs designed for the general MA population and then applied to SRF members by default.
The broader policy implication is that the link between health equity and Medicare Advantage financial performance remains politically contingent. The HEI would have stopped rewarding a plan that achieves high average star ratings by serving predominantly healthy, wealthy seniors while its LIS minority underperforms on the same terms as a plan with equitable outcomes across its full enrolled population. With the HEI withdrawn before its first ratings, whether a dedicated equity reward could have offset the structural disadvantages of the most LIS-concentrated plans remains untested.
CMS removed the Health Equity Index in its CY2027 final rule (April 2026), before its first ratings, and kept the historical reward factor. Plans still benefit from care management programs designed for their Social Risk Factor population — LIS recipients, dual-eligible beneficiaries, and disabled enrollees — because gaps among those members still pull down heavily weighted adherence and patient-experience measures.
Low-Income Subsidy (LIS) beneficiaries — about 13.7 million enrollees in 2024 — consistently score lower on Medicare Advantage star rating measures due to social and economic barriers that are structurally distinct from clinical care quality.
Plans serving high concentrations of LIS and dual-eligible beneficiaries face systematic performance disadvantages on the most heavily weighted star rating measures, including medication adherence (triple-weighted) and CAHPS patient experience surveys (weighted 4x in 2023–2025, 2x from 2026).
The Categorical Adjustment Index (CAI) partially offsets this disadvantage by adjusting final star ratings according to each contract's share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees — but critics argue it is insufficient.
The Health Equity Index (HEI), finalized in 2023 for 2027 Star Ratings, would have replaced the old reward factor with a reward for high performance among each plan's Social Risk Factor population — but CMS removed it in its CY2027 final rule (April 2026) and kept the historical reward factor.
The HEI would have marked a philosophical shift from compensating for having disadvantaged enrollees to rewarding actively improving outcomes for them — changing the incentive from enrollment composition to care delivery equity.
As designed, contracts meeting minimum SRF enrollment thresholds could have earned up to 0.4 additional star rating points from the HEI for high SRF-specific performance.
Comprehensive reform of the star ratings system for equity — including separate D-SNP rating tracks or individual measure-level social risk adjustment — remains a pending policy challenge, and the HEI's withdrawal leaves the CAI as the only equity-specific adjustment.
The CAI is a defensive adjustment that partially compensates plans for the performance penalty associated with enrolling many LIS/dual-eligible beneficiaries — it adjusts ratings according to the contract's share of LIS/dual-eligible and disabled enrollees. The HEI, as designed, was an offensive reward that would have required plans to demonstrate high performance specifically among their SRF population to earn bonus points (CMS withdrew it in April 2026 before it took effect). One adjusts for disadvantage; the other would have rewarded demonstrated equity in care delivery.
The CAI applies to Part D measures only, while the HEI applies to Part C measures only
The CAI adjusts ratings upward for having many LIS enrollees, while the HEI was designed to reward plans for actively achieving high performance among their LIS and dual-eligible members
The CAI is used only for 5-star plans, while the HEI applies to all plans regardless of rating
The CAI is a financial bonus payment, while the HEI is a star rating adjustment
