######## value-based-care | vbc-future-directions | Where VBC Is Heading: Primary Care, Equity & Scale
Where Value-Based Care Is Heading: Primary Care, Risk & the Next Decade
A Field at an Inflection Point
Value-based care is no longer an experiment at the margins of American healthcare — it is the explicit direction of federal policy. But "the future of VBC" is not a smooth, predictable curve. The years 2025 and 2026 brought one of the sharpest strategic pivots in the history of the CMS Innovation Center (CMMI), the federal body that designs and tests new payment models. Understanding where VBC is heading means understanding both the durable trends and the recent reset that reshaped them.
On May 13, 2025, CMMI launched a new strategy organized around three pillars: promoting evidence-based prevention, empowering people to achieve their health goals, and driving choice and competition. All three sit on a single foundational principle the Center repeated insistently — protecting the federal taxpayer. The Innovation Center declared it would focus on the models that show the greatest promise for generating savings while improving quality, signaling a smaller, more demanding portfolio than the sprawling set of demonstrations that came before.
This matters because it changes what "value" is being optimized for. The previous era emphasized broad participation and equity-focused expansion. The current era emphasizes demonstrable financial performance, downside risk, prevention built into every model, and competition among providers. The destination — paying for outcomes instead of volume — is unchanged. The route, the guardrails, and the rhetoric have shifted considerably.
Key Concept: The CMS Innovation Center (CMMI) is the federal "laboratory" for payment reform. Its strategy determines which value-based models exist, who can join them, and how much financial risk providers must bear — making CMMI’s direction the single best predictor of where VBC is heading.
Prevention, empowering people, and choice & competition — all anchored to protecting the taxpayer — launched May 13, 2025 (CMS Innovation Center)
CMMI 2025 Strategy
3 pillars
The Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model is a 10-year initiative beginning January 1, 2027 (CMS)
LEAD Model Lifespan
10 years
The Portfolio Reset: What Ended and Why
The clearest signal of the new direction was what CMMI chose to stop doing. In 2025 the Innovation Center terminated several models before their originally scheduled end dates — most notably Primary Care First (PCF) and Making Care Primary (MCP). On its face, ending primary-care models looks like a retreat from primary care. CMMI framed it as the opposite: a way to move beneficiaries into more permanent, scalable programs — above all the Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), the agency’s flagship and permanent accountable care initiative.
The logic of the reset is that CMMI will narrow its portfolio to models with clearer savings logic, more defined provider obligations, and cleaner policy goals, while keeping primary care and accountable care as the foundation. Future models will place greater weight on downside financial risk — meaning providers can lose money, not just share in savings — and on measurable reductions in unnecessary utilization. The result is a smaller portfolio that asks more of the participants who remain.
The earlier ambition to place essentially all Traditional Medicare beneficiaries (and the vast majority of Medicaid beneficiaries) in accountable care relationships by 2030 has not been restated under the 2025 strategy. The emphasis shifted from maximizing participation to demonstrating savings — a meaningful change in how success is defined.
A Notable Absence: The 2030 Goal
For providers, the reset created real disruption. Organizations built around models that were terminated early had to find a new home, typically MSSP or a successor demonstration. This is the recurring tension of payment reform: the very experimentation that drives progress also creates instability for the practices that bet on a given model. Reading CMMI’s strategy is therefore not academic — it directly determines which contracts a health system can sign next year.
From ACO REACH to LEAD: The Next Generation of Risk
No transition better illustrates the new era than the end of ACO REACH and the rise of its successor. The ACO REACH (Realizing Equity, Access, and Community Health) Model, launched in 2023, was the most advanced risk-bearing accountable care model in Traditional Medicare: it paired prospective, population-based payments with two-sided financial risk and provider-led governance. It will run for four performance years — 2023 through 2026 — and then conclude on December 31, 2026.
In its place, CMMI announced the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model, a 10-year initiative with Performance Year 1 beginning January 1, 2027. The unusually long time horizon is itself the point: it signals that CMMI wants stable, durable risk arrangements rather than short demonstrations that expire and strand their participants. The obvious candidates for LEAD are the organizations already in ACO REACH — they have the risk experience, the contracts, and an existing model ending exactly when LEAD begins. REACH organizations that do not move into LEAD would revert to MSSP or to fee-for-service.
The model concludes on December 31, 2026 after its final performance year — it does not continue in any form.
ACO REACH ends
The 10-year Long-term Enhanced ACO Design Model starts January 1, 2027, designed as the durable successor for risk-bearing ACOs.
LEAD begins
Experienced REACH ACOs can apply to LEAD; those that do not must fall back to MSSP or to traditional fee-for-service.
Organizations choose a path
Even before sunset, PY2026 REACH introduced caps on risk-score growth and reduced the weight of the regional benchmark — previewing the more demanding LEAD era.
Tighter guardrails apply
How the REACH-to-LEAD Transition Works
The 2026 updates to REACH preview the direction LEAD will extend. CMS added a 3% cap on Standard ACOs' cumulative risk-score growth from 2019 through 2026 (High Needs ACOs face an asymmetric 8% cap on 2023–2026 growth for newly voluntarily aligned beneficiaries), and it reduced the weight of the regional benchmark — shifting Standard ACOs toward a 60/40 blend favoring historical baselines. CMS’s financial operating guides now call the model’s Health Equity Benchmark Adjustment the "Population Adjustment"; for PY2026 it combines a new Community Deprivation Index with beneficiaries’ dual-eligibility and Part D Low-Income Subsidy status.
Prevention, Patient Empowerment, and Competition
The three pillars of the 2025 strategy are not slogans — each carries concrete design commitments that will shape the models providers actually operate under. The most striking is the prevention pillar: CMMI promised that prevention will be part of every model it tests, with mechanisms for providers to offer services such as exercise and nutritional support that promote healthier lifestyles. This embeds population health and upstream intervention into the structure of payment, rather than treating it as an optional add-on.
The empowerment pillar centers on data and incentives: models are expected to better connect people to their own health data, unlock data access across all models, and align financial incentives so patients are active participants rather than passive recipients. The choice-and-competition pillar aims to broaden participation in alternative payment models — with explicit attention to independent and rural providers, the practices most at risk of being squeezed out of a market dominated by large consolidated systems.

Maximize participation in accountable care
Broad equity-focused expansion goals
Many parallel demonstration models
Upside-heavy, lower-risk on-ramps

2025–2026 CMMI Emphasis
Demonstrate measurable savings to taxpayers
Prevention built into every model
Smaller, more demanding portfolio
Greater weight on downside financial risk
No restated 2030 universal-participation target
How the Emphasis Shifted
What This Means for the Decade Ahead
Pulling the threads together, several durable trends emerge from the noise of any single administration’s rebranding. First, risk is going up. The trajectory from shared-savings-only arrangements toward two-sided risk and long-horizon models like LEAD is consistent across strategies — providers will increasingly be accountable for total cost and outcomes, not merely rewarded for bonus performance. Second, primary care and accountable care remain the foundation even as the specific models churn; the MSSP, as a permanent program, is the stable anchor toward which beneficiaries are repeatedly funneled.
Third, prevention and patient-reported data are moving from periphery to core. A strategy that puts prevention in every model, combined with the strategy’s push to connect people to their own health data, means the definition of "value" is broadening beyond cost and clinical metrics to include what patients experience and whether illness is avoided in the first place. Fourth, the politics of value-based care are real and consequential: strategies, model names, and benchmarks change with administrations, and successful organizations build the underlying capabilities — risk management, data infrastructure, care coordination — that transfer across whatever model is in vogue.
Chasing individual payment models is like trying to catch each wave at the beach — exhausting and unpredictable, because waves come and go. Building core value-based capabilities is like learning to swim: once you can manage financial risk, use your data, and coordinate care, you stay afloat no matter which wave (REACH, LEAD, MSSP, the next acronym) arrives.
Adapting to a changing VBC model landscape
For a state like Vermont — which has pursued some of the nation’s most ambitious payment reform through all-payer accountable care — these federal currents are not abstract. The fate of national models, the rise of long-horizon designs like LEAD, and the prevention-first framing all shape what is possible at the state level. The organizations that will thrive are not those that guess the next model correctly, but those that build the durable muscle of taking accountability for a population’s health and cost — the one capability every version of value-based care demands.

######## value-based-care | global-budgets-hospital-finance | Global Budgets for Hospitals: Maryland & Beyond
Global Budgets for Hospitals: Maryland, Vermont & the AHEAD Model
The Most Radical Idea in Hospital Payment
Almost every payment reform discussed in value-based care leaves one thing intact: the hospital still gets paid more when it does more. Shared savings, bundled payments, and pay-for-performance all sit on top of an underlying fee-for-service chassis. A global budget throws that chassis out. Under a global budget, a hospital is given a fixed amount of revenue, set in advance, to cover its inpatient and hospital-based outpatient services for the year — regardless of how many admissions, procedures, or tests it performs.
This single change inverts the hospital’s financial incentives. Under fee-for-service, an empty bed is lost revenue. Under a global budget, an empty bed is money saved — because the revenue is guaranteed either way. Suddenly the hospital has a powerful reason to prevent admissions, reduce avoidable emergency visits, invest in care coordination, and keep its community healthy enough to stay out of the building. Revenue is decoupled from volume, and population health becomes a business strategy rather than a charitable afterthought.
Global budgets are not theoretical. They have been operating at the level of entire states for over a decade, producing some of the strongest evidence in all of payment reform — and they are now expanding through a federal model that includes Vermont. Understanding global budgets means understanding both how the mechanism works and what happened when real states tried it.
Key Concept: A global budget is a fixed, prospectively set amount of revenue a hospital receives to cover its services for a defined period — typically a year. It decouples hospital revenue from the volume of care delivered, reversing the core fee-for-service incentive.
Net savings to Medicare over the first three years of the Maryland Total Cost of Care Model, 2019–2021 (CMS)
Maryland Medicare Net Savings

How a Global Budget Actually Works
The mechanics are conceptually simple but operationally demanding. A regulator or payer sets each hospital’s budget prospectively — before the year begins — based primarily on the hospital’s historical net revenue for inpatient and outpatient hospital-based services. That budget is then adjusted year to year for factors like inflation, population changes, quality performance, and shifts in the services the hospital provides. The hospital knows, on day one, roughly what it will earn for the entire year.
The defining feature is that this is an all-payer arrangement in its strongest forms: the budget applies across payers rather than just for Medicare, which prevents hospitals from simply shifting costs onto private insurers to make up for constrained public revenue. Within the budget, the hospital adjusts its prices (unit rates) during the year so that total revenue lands on target. If volume falls, rates can rise to hit the budget; if volume surges, rates fall. The budget — not the visit count — is the anchor.
A hospital’s revenue for the year is fixed in advance, based largely on its historical net revenue for hospital-based services.
Set the budget prospectively
Because the total is fixed, an extra admission no longer means extra revenue — and a prevented admission no longer means lost revenue.
Decouple revenue from volume
The hospital now profits by keeping people healthy and out of the building: fewer avoidable admissions, fewer ED visits, more coordination.
Flip the incentive toward prevention
Unit prices are trued up during the year so total revenue lands on the budgeted amount regardless of how volume moves.
Adjust rates to hit the target
The Logic Chain of a Global Budget
A global budget that applies to only one payer (e.g., Medicare) invites cost-shifting — the hospital simply bills private insurers more to offset constrained public revenue. The strongest global budget models, like Maryland’s, are all-payer: every payer’s rates are regulated, closing the cost-shift loophole.
Why the "All-Payer" Part Matters
Maryland: The Proof of Concept
No state has gone further than Maryland, which has regulated hospital rates since the 1970s and in 2014 launched an all-payer hospital global budget under its All-Payer Model. In 2019 it expanded into the Maryland Total Cost of Care (TCOC) Model, which built on the global budgets by adding incentives for providers across the system — not just hospitals — to coordinate care and manage the total cost of a patient’s care, including outside the hospital walls.
The results make Maryland the strongest real-world case for global budgets. The global budget approach generated $689 million in net savings to Medicare over the first three years of the TCOC Model (2019–2021). Over the first four years (2019–2022), total Medicare spending for Part A and Part B declined by an average of $292 per beneficiary per year, or 2.1%. On utilization, the model cut hospital spending by 6.1%, hospital admissions by 16.2%, outpatient emergency department visits by 5.9%, and preventable admissions by 16.8% — exactly the pattern the incentive design predicts.
Maryland’s model demonstrated that a state could hold hospital revenue growth to a fixed budget while improving quality — saving Medicare hundreds of millions of dollars and sharply reducing avoidable hospital use.

Its success directly shaped federal policy. Rather than letting the approach expire, CMS announced the Maryland TCOC Model would end December 31, 2025, and Maryland signed a new long-term agreement to continue an all-payer total-cost-of-care approach under the federal AHEAD Model — extending the experiment into a multi-state framework.
Maryland Total Cost of Care Model (2019–2025)
Beyond Maryland: Rural Hospitals and the Spread of the Idea
Maryland proved global budgets work at scale, but a different problem made them attractive elsewhere: the financial fragility of rural hospitals. Rural hospitals with low patient volumes are devastated by fee-for-service, where revenue depends on filling beds that are often empty. A global budget guarantees their revenue regardless of volume — a lifeline that can keep the doors open in communities that would otherwise lose access entirely.
Pennsylvania tested this directly. The Pennsylvania Rural Health Model (PRHM), which ran from 2019 to 2024, gave participating rural hospitals prospective all-payer global budgets based primarily on their historical net revenue, aiming to stabilize their finances and improve population health. The evidence was genuinely mixed: the model delivered meaningful financial stability for fragile rural hospitals, but its impact on quality outcomes was less clear — a reminder that guaranteeing revenue solves the solvency problem without automatically transforming the quality of care.
Fee-for-Service Hospital
Empty bed = lost revenue
Financial reward for more admissions and procedures
Prevention reduces income
Rural low-volume hospitals are financially fragile
Revenue rises with utilization
Global Budget Hospital
Empty bed = money saved against a fixed budget
Financial reward for avoiding unnecessary care
Prevention protects the bottom line
Rural hospitals get predictable, guaranteed revenue
Revenue is fixed regardless of utilization
Hospital Incentives: Fee-for-Service vs. Global Budget
The AHEAD Model and Vermont’s Path
The federal government is now scaling the global-budget concept across multiple states through the AHEAD Model — States Advancing All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development (also rendered "Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design"). AHEAD is a state-based total-cost-of-care model that includes global budgets for participating hospitals and holds participating states accountable for controlling overall growth in healthcare spending while improving population health. CMS issues an agreement to each participating state, which can receive up to $12 million in funding to build the infrastructure, and the model is designed as a long-term effort running through December 31, 2035.
Vermont signed on to AHEAD in January 2025 — a natural step given its history. For eight years, Vermont ran the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model (VTAPM), a state-led accountable care experiment operated largely through the accountable care organization OneCare Vermont. That model sunset at the end of 2025, and OneCare Vermont announced it would wind down operations at the conclusion of 2025, closing one chapter of the state’s reform story. AHEAD, with its hospital global budgets, was meant to be the next chapter — but after CMS capped the expected additional federal funding near $10 million (from roughly $138 million), Vermont withdrew in July 2026, and its move toward hospital global budgets now rests on state law (Act 68 of 2025) rather than the federal model.
AHEAD’s rollout is staged across cohorts, with performance periods phased in over the following years so that states have time to build the regulatory and data infrastructure global budgets require. Vermont’s transition illustrates both the promise and the difficulty of this work: the VTAPM faced real challenges, including the withdrawal of major insurers and persistent questions about cost control and quality, even as it advanced the state’s reform agenda. Global budgets do not erase those challenges — they restructure the incentives within which a state must still do the hard operational work.
Fee-for-service pays a hospital like a taxi meter — every additional mile (admission, test, procedure) adds to the fare, so there’s no reason to take the shortest route. A global budget pays like a monthly transit pass: the cost is fixed up front, so the operator’s incentive flips entirely toward moving people efficiently and avoiding unnecessary trips.
Global budgets vs. fee-for-service hospital payment
Promise, Limits, and What It Takes
Global budgets are among the most powerful tools in value-based care precisely because they attack the root of the volume problem rather than layering incentives on top of it. The Maryland evidence — real Medicare savings alongside large reductions in admissions and preventable hospitalizations — is some of the most compelling in the field. For rural hospitals, global budgets can be the difference between survival and closure.
But the model is demanding and not a cure-all. It requires a strong rate-setting authority or regulator capable of setting and adjusting budgets fairly, robust all-payer data systems, and trust among hospitals, payers, and the state. Pennsylvania’s experience showed that financial stabilization can outpace quality improvement, and Vermont’s showed that even a committed state can struggle with insurer participation and measurable cost control. Global budgets change what a hospital is rewarded for; they do not, by themselves, build the care-coordination capacity needed to act on that incentive.
The trajectory, though, is unmistakable. From Maryland’s decade-long proof of concept, to Pennsylvania’s rural lifeline, to the multi-state AHEAD Model — with Maryland in performance since 2026 and Connecticut, Hawaii, Rhode Island and downstate New York slated to follow, through 2035 — global budgets have moved from a regulatory curiosity to a central instrument of national payment reform. For students of value-based care, they represent the clearest answer yet to the field’s founding question: what happens when you simply stop paying hospitals more for doing more?
A global budget is a fixed amount of revenue, set in advance, that covers a hospital’s inpatient and hospital-based outpatient services for the year — decoupling revenue from the volume of care delivered.
By making revenue fixed, global budgets reverse the fee-for-service incentive: a prevented admission saves money rather than losing it, turning population health and prevention into a financial strategy.
The strongest models are all-payer, applying regulated rates across all payers to close the cost-shifting loophole that undermines single-payer budgets.
Maryland is the leading proof of concept: its Total Cost of Care Model generated $689 million in net Medicare savings (2019–2021), cut Medicare per-beneficiary spending 2.1% (~$292/year, 2019–2022), and reduced hospital admissions 16.2% and preventable admissions 16.8% over four years.
Maryland’s TCOC Model ended December 31, 2025, with the state continuing an all-payer total-cost-of-care approach under the federal AHEAD Model.
The Pennsylvania Rural Health Model (2019–2024) used global budgets to stabilize fragile rural hospitals’ finances, though its effect on quality outcomes was mixed — financial fix, quality flaw.
The federal AHEAD Model is scaling global budgets and total-cost-of-care accountability across multiple states, offering up to $12 million per state and running through December 31, 2035.
Vermont, after running the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model through 2025 (with OneCare Vermont winding down at the end of 2025), signed on to AHEAD in January 2025 but withdrew in July 2026; its hospital global budgets now proceed under state law (Act 68).

######## value-based-care | vbc-clinical-m5 | From Volume to Value at the Bedside: How Value-Based Care Transforms Clinical Practice
From Volume to Value at the Bedside: How Value-Based Care Transforms Clinical Practice
Picture a primary care physician seeing 24 patients in a day. Under fee-for-service, she is rewarded for each visit, each test ordered, each referral made. Under value-based care, she is rewarded for something harder to measure but far more important: whether her patients are actually healthier. That shift in incentives changes everything that happens in the exam room.
This module is about the clinical side of the VBC transformation. It is not abstract. The shift shows up in care team huddles, in how discharge plans are written, in how nurses manage phone calls with patients just released from the hospital, and in how a physician spends the last five minutes of every appointment. Understanding these changes is essential for anyone who works in, manages, or influences clinical care.
In 2017, 3.5 million potentially preventable adult hospital stays — 12.9% of all nonobstetric adult stays — cost $33.7 billion; heart failure was the most common reason. Source: AHRQ HCUP Statistical Brief #259.

In 2003–04, 19.6% of Medicare beneficiaries discharged from a hospital were readmitted within 30 days — the finding that helped prompt the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program. Source: Jencks, Williams & Coleman, New England Journal of Medicine, 2009.

Why Clinical Practice Must Change
How Payment Models Shape Clinical Decisions
Clinicians do not consciously think 'I am going to order this test because I will get paid for it.' But payment systems create incentive structures that shape behavior in powerful ways. Under fee-for-service, a busy practice survives by filling the schedule. Under value-based care, a practice is rewarded for keeping patients healthy enough that they do not need to come back as often.
Think about two gyms. The first gym charges you every time you visit — the more you visit, the more they earn. They are motivated to have you come back constantly. The second gym charges a flat monthly fee — they earn the same whether you come twice a week or never. But if you quit because you are not getting healthier, they lose your membership. That gym is motivated to actually get you fit.
Fee-for-service is the first gym — providers earn more when you come back. Value-based care is the second gym — providers earn more when you stay healthy and do not need to come back. The incentives point in opposite directions, and that shapes clinical practice in profound ways.

Clinical Practice: Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Care
These differences are not just philosophical. They have real operational consequences. A practice moving to value-based contracts must restructure its workflows, hire different staff — care coordinators, community health workers, data analysts — and invest in systems that identify which patients are at risk before they land in the emergency room.
Quality Measures: How Clinical Performance Is Evaluated
In value-based care, clinicians and practices are evaluated on a structured set of quality measures — standardized metrics that assess whether patients are receiving evidence-based care and achieving good outcomes. These come from several sources: the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, the National Committee for Quality Assurance, and the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality.
Quality Measure: A standardized, evidence-based metric used to assess whether patients receive recommended care. Examples: the percentage of diabetic patients with HbA1c under 8.0%, the percentage of patients with hypertension whose blood pressure is controlled, or the percentage of eligible patients who received a colorectal cancer screening.
There are hundreds of quality measures in use across the US healthcare system. For primary care practices in most VBC contracts, a core set of 10 to 20 measures typically drives the bulk of performance-based bonuses or penalties. The most important fall into four categories.
Did patients receive recommended screenings and immunizations? Examples: mammography rates, colorectal cancer screening, flu vaccine administration, pediatric well-child visits. These measures track whether clinicians are proactively catching problems early.
Preventive Care
Are patients with ongoing conditions managed to target levels? Examples: HbA1c control for diabetics, blood pressure control for hypertension patients, statin therapy for cardiovascular patients. These measures track whether care prevents deterioration.
Chronic Disease Management
Do patients feel heard, respected, and well-informed? Measured via standardized CAHPS surveys. Tracks communication quality, care coordination experience, and overall satisfaction. Poor scores often signal care gaps.
Patient Experience
Are patients using the ER and hospital for things that could be handled in outpatient settings? Examples: ED visit rate for ambulatory care-sensitive conditions, 30-day readmission rate, potentially preventable admissions. High rates signal gaps in primary care access or management.
Avoidable Utilization
The Four Domains of Clinical Quality in Value-Based Care
Quality measures are just bureaucratic checkboxes that distract from real clinical care.
Well-designed quality measures are derived from clinical evidence. A practice that achieves high HbA1c control rates has fewer diabetic patients with amputations, kidney failure, and blindness. The measures exist because doing them consistently saves lives. The legitimate concern is ensuring that measures focus on the right things — and that they do not create perverse incentives of their own.
The most sophisticated VBC programs now move beyond process measures — did we do the right thing? — toward outcome measures: did the patient get better? Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model (2017–2025) tracked outcomes like population-level diabetes prevalence trends and preventable hospitalization rates, not just whether a doctor ordered a hemoglobin A1c test.
Population Health Management: Responsibility Beyond the Appointment
One of the most fundamental shifts in value-based care is moving from patient-by-patient thinking to population-level thinking. Under fee-for-service, a physician's responsibility begins when a patient walks through the door and ends when they leave. Under VBC, a care team is responsible for the health of an entire attributed patient panel — including the people who are not coming in.
A school principal does not just react to students who show up in her office with problems. She monitors attendance rates, tracks which students are falling behind, identifies patterns of absenteeism, and proactively reaches out to struggling families before a student drops out. She manages the entire school population — not just the ones who knock on her door.
Population health management works the same way. A VBC practice does not just treat patients who schedule appointments. It monitors the health status of its entire panel — flagging patients overdue for a screening, whose blood pressure has not been checked in 18 months, or whose recent ER visits suggest they are struggling to manage a chronic condition at home.
Population health management
Population health management requires three things fee-for-service practices rarely had: data, staff, and proactive processes. The data comes from electronic health records and claims. The staff — care managers or medical assistants in expanded roles — conduct outreach to patients who need follow-up. The processes include monthly panel reviews, risk stratification algorithms, and care gap closure protocols.
Consistently, the sickest 5% of patients account for roughly 50% of total healthcare spending. VBC practices identify and intensively manage this group. Source: AHRQ.

Population Health by the Numbers
Risk stratification is the engine of population health management. Practices use algorithms — built into EHR systems or analytics platforms — to sort patients into tiers based on their likelihood of a high-cost clinical event in the next 6 to 12 months. High-risk patients get intensive care management: regular check-ins, home visits, medication reconciliation. Low-risk patients get preventive outreach: reminders for annual wellness visits and screenings.
ChenMed operates primary care centers designed for older, lower-income Medicare Advantage patients with complex chronic illness. Its model inverts the usual primary care formula: physicians carry small patient panels, see patients far more often, and spend more face-to-face time with them, supported by on-site care teams and transportation to appointments.
Real-World Example
In a matched comparison of 5,695 patients from each model, ChenMed's 'high-touch' patients averaged 8.7 primary care visits a year versus 3.8 under standard care, had 50% fewer hospital admissions, and cost 28% less. The study was led by ChenMed clinicians with University of Miami co-investigators, so it is not independent.
Ghany R et al., 'High-Touch Care Leads to Better Outcomes and Lower Costs in a Senior Population,' American Journal of Managed Care, September 2018

Care Coordination: The Connective Tissue of Value-Based Care
The US healthcare system was built around specialization. Cardiologists manage hearts. Endocrinologists manage diabetes. Orthopedic surgeons manage joints. This works extraordinarily well for complex procedures and rare conditions. It works catastrophically poorly for the average Medicare patient with five chronic conditions who sees seven different specialists — none of whom talk to each other.
Care Coordination: The deliberate organization of patient care activities and the sharing of information among all participants to achieve safer, more effective care. It includes communication between providers, follow-up after transitions, medication reconciliation, and ensuring patients understand their care plan.
Poor care coordination is expensive and dangerous. When a cardiologist adds a new medication and does not know the patient's nephrologist recently changed a kidney medication, the combination can cause serious harm. When a hospital discharges a patient with instructions to 'schedule a follow-up within a week' but does not help make that appointment, the patient often does not go — and ends up back in the ER within 30 days.
Failures of care coordination — duplicated tests, missed follow-ups, avoidable complications after transitions — waste an estimated $27.2 billion to $78.2 billion a year. Source: Shrank, Rogstad & Parekh, JAMA, 2019.

In 2023, 51.4% of US adults — about 130 million people — reported multiple chronic conditions, including 78.8% of adults 65 and older, requiring active coordination among multiple providers. Source: CDC, Preventing Chronic Disease, 2025 (BRFSS 2013–2023).

The Cost of Poor Care Coordination
Value-based care fixes this by making coordination an explicit responsibility with a named owner. The care coordinator — often a registered nurse, social worker, or medical assistant in an extended role — serves as the connective tissue between providers, between hospital and home, and between patient and care plan. Their job is to make sure nothing falls through the cracks.
Weekly review of the patient panel with the care team. Flag patients overdue for follow-up, those who had a recent hospitalization, or whose risk score changed in the EHR. Decide who gets a proactive outreach call this week.
Panel Review
When a patient is discharged from the hospital, the coordinator calls within 48 to 72 hours: Did you fill your medications? Do you understand your discharge instructions? Is your follow-up appointment scheduled? Can you get there?
Transition Management
Ensure that specialist visit notes are shared with the primary care team. Follow up to confirm referrals were completed. Flag conflicting medication orders for physician review.
Specialist Coordination
At every transition point — admission, discharge, specialist visit — reconcile the patient's complete medication list. Polypharmacy is a leading cause of preventable harm, especially in older adults.
Medication Reconciliation
Help patients understand their care plan, set personal health goals, and navigate the health system. Activated patients — those who feel confident managing their own health — have significantly better outcomes and lower costs.
Patient Activation
What a Care Coordinator Does in a VBC Practice
Vermont's Blueprint for Health embeds Community Health Teams in primary care practices across the state. Each CHT includes nurses, social workers, dietitians, and community health workers co-located with or closely partnered with primary care practices. When a practice flags a high-risk patient — perhaps a diabetic with three recent ER visits — the CHT mobilizes. They assess barriers such as no transportation, food insecurity, or depression, connect patients to community resources, and manage follow-up.
Case Study
Blueprint practices with active CHT partnerships have shown significant reductions in preventable hospitalization rates and improvements in chronic disease management scores compared to non-Blueprint practices. Source: Vermont DVHA Blueprint evaluation reports.
Vermont Department of Vermont Health Access, Blueprint for Health Annual Reports

Reducing Preventable Hospitalizations and Readmissions
Hospitalizations are the single largest driver of healthcare costs. A single inpatient stay for a Medicare patient costs, on average, more than $13,000. Many of those hospitalizations are for conditions that, if managed properly in an outpatient setting, should never have required a hospital bed. These are called ambulatory care-sensitive conditions — uncontrolled diabetes, COPD exacerbations, congestive heart failure, urinary tract infections.
Ambulatory Care-Sensitive Conditions (ACSCs): Medical conditions for which timely and appropriate outpatient care can prevent hospitalization. They include asthma, COPD, congestive heart failure, diabetes complications, and hypertension. High ACSC hospitalization rates signal that primary care access or quality is failing.
Value-based care contracts explicitly target ACSC hospitalization rates as a key performance indicator. A practice with a high ACSC rate is leaving money on the table — and more importantly, leaving patients in harm's way. Hospitalizations carry real clinical risk: hospital-acquired infections, medication errors, delirium in elderly patients, and the deconditioning from days of bed rest.
Keeping patients out of the hospital means denying them care they need.
Reducing avoidable hospitalizations is about providing better care earlier — not rationing. A patient with COPD who sees their care coordinator monthly, has a written action plan for exacerbations, and can reach a nurse by phone when their breathing worsens is receiving better care than a patient who sees their doctor twice a year and lands in the hospital every winter. The goal is the right care in the right setting.
Readmissions are a related but distinct problem. A readmission occurs when a patient returns to the hospital within 30 days of discharge. The national Medicare readmission rate hovers around 15 to 20 percent. CMS began financially penalizing hospitals for excess readmissions in 2013 under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program. Since then, rates have declined — but remain stubbornly high.
Use a standardized discharge checklist: review medications, schedule follow-up before discharge, provide written instructions in plain language at a 6th-grade reading level, confirm patient understanding via teach-back method.
Structured Discharge Planning
A nurse or care coordinator calls within 2 to 3 days of discharge. Confirm the patient is taking medications correctly, understands warning signs, and has a follow-up appointment. Early problem identification prevents crisis.
48 to 72 Hour Post-Discharge Call
Patients seen by their primary care provider within 7 days of discharge have significantly lower readmission rates. Schedule this before the patient leaves the hospital whenever possible.
Rapid Follow-Up Appointment
Medication errors during care transitions are extremely common. Pharmacist-led or nurse-led reconciliation at discharge — comparing the inpatient list to what the patient took before admission — catches dangerous discrepancies.
Medication Reconciliation
Many readmissions are driven by social factors: no food at home, no transportation to the pharmacy, social isolation causing non-adherence. Transitional care programs that screen for social needs and connect patients to community resources see the largest readmission reductions.
Address Social Needs
Evidence-Based Interventions That Reduce Readmissions
Under a VBC contract, this patient represents an open care gap. The practice is responsible for her health outcomes even when she is not actively seeking care. The right response is proactive outreach: a care coordinator calls or sends a letter, offers scheduling assistance including transportation help if needed, and flags her for the team's panel review. If she has barriers to care — cost, transportation, work schedule — the team works to address them. Waiting for her to call is no longer acceptable practice.
Think about what 'population health management' means — and who is responsible for patients who are NOT in the office.
A patient with type 2 diabetes and hypertension has not been seen in your practice in 14 months. Her last HbA1c was 9.2 — well above the target of 8.0. She is not scheduled for an upcoming appointment. Under a value-based care contract, what should happen?
The New Clinical Team: Roles That Value-Based Care Built
Value-based care has not replaced physicians. But it has radically expanded the clinical team around them. In a well-functioning VBC practice, the physician is the expert clinician and diagnostic mind — supported by a team that handles much of what was once shoved into a 15-minute visit or never done at all.

The Care Team: Traditional vs. Value-Based
Advanced Practice Providers — nurse practitioners and physician assistants — play an expanded role in VBC models, often managing the bulk of stable chronic disease visits and wellness exams while physicians focus on complex diagnostic cases. This is team-based care: the right person, for the right patient, at the right time.
Vermont Clinical Programs: Value-Based Care in Action
Vermont is not just talking about value-based clinical care — it has been running the experiment for over a decade. The Blueprint for Health, launched in 2006, was one of the first statewide primary care transformation programs in the country. Every participating practice has undergone a formal practice transformation process: team-based care, patient registries, care coordination, and quality measurement.
Vermont's All-Payer ACO Model, which ran from 2017 through December 31, 2025, took this further. OneCare Vermont — the state's accountable care organization until it wound down at the end of 2025 — held a global budget covering roughly a third of Vermont residents. Practices within OneCare were responsible for the total cost of care for their attributed population. Every preventable hospitalization and readmission is a financial signal that something in the clinical model needs to change.
Copley Hospital is a 25-bed critical access hospital in Morrisville serving a largely rural population. In its 2018 community health needs assessment progress report, filed with the Green Mountain Care Board, Copley described two concrete steps to cut 30-day all-cause readmissions: arranging follow-up with a primary care provider within 7 days of discharge, and reviewing each inpatient readmission in real time to find what went wrong.
Vermont in Focus
Copley reported 30-day all-cause readmission rates of 4.4%–17.0% across January–September 2017 (Vermont critical access hospitals: 8.7%–16.8%) and 6.92% for January–April 2018 — below or on par with its critical access peers, showing that a small rural hospital can move the measures VBC contracts reward with simple, disciplined transition steps.
Copley Hospital, Community Health Needs Assessment Progress Report 2018 (Green Mountain Care Board hospital budget filing B19H31)

The Clinical Case for Value-Based Care
For many clinicians, the shift to value-based care feels like an administrative imposition — more metrics to track, more documentation requirements, more meetings. That is a legitimate concern, and it reflects real transition pain. But the underlying logic of VBC aligns more closely with why most clinicians entered medicine than fee-for-service ever did.
Fee-for-service rewarded doing more. It paid well for procedures and poorly for conversations, care coordination, and prevention. It created a system where a physician who spent 45 minutes with a complex elderly patient on 12 medications was paid the same as a physician who spent 10 minutes. It created burnout among clinicians who wanted to practice relationship-based medicine but were trapped on a volume treadmill.
Physician burnout peaked at 62.8% in 2021 and, though it has eased since — 43.2% of physicians reported at least one symptom in 2024 — it remains high, with administrative burden a leading driver. VBC, done well, can restore what drew clinicians to medicine: time with patients, team support, and a payment system that rewards doing what is actually right for the patient. Source: American Medical Association national burnout survey data, 2021–2024.
A preventable hospitalization (ambulatory care-sensitive admission) is a hospital stay that could have been avoided with timely outpatient care — like a COPD patient hospitalized for an exacerbation that could have been managed in the clinic with proper monitoring and medication adjustment. A readmission occurs when a patient returns to the hospital within 30 days of being discharged. Both matter under VBC because they represent clinical failures where the care system fell short. Both carry financial consequences: preventable admissions represent waste, and readmissions trigger CMS penalties under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program.
Think about timing — one happens before the hospital stay, one happens after.
What is the difference between a 'preventable hospitalization' and a '30-day readmission,' and why do both matter under VBC contracts?
Fee-for-service pays for volume; value-based care pays for outcomes — this distinction reshapes every clinical workflow.
Quality measures in VBC track preventive care, chronic disease management, patient experience, and avoidable utilization.
Population health management means taking responsibility for patients who are NOT in the office — not just those who show up.
Care coordination is a clinical skill and a team function — it prevents the gaps between providers that cause harm and cost.
Preventable hospitalizations and readmissions are the most visible signals of clinical model failure — and the primary financial targets in VBC contracts.
Vermont's Blueprint for Health and its All-Payer ACO Model (2017–2025) demonstrate that statewide clinical transformation is achievable with measurable results.
Value-based care, done well, can restore the relationship-centered practice that most clinicians entered medicine to provide.
Key Takeaways — Clinical Practice Under Value-Based Care
Value-based care is not just a billing change — it reshapes what happens in every exam room, every hospital ward, and every care team huddle. This module explores how the shift from fee-for-service to value changes clinical workflows, team structures, quality measurement, population health management, and care coordination. If you practice, manage, or support clinical care in any setting, this module explains why the ground is shifting beneath your feet — and what to do about it.
######## value-based-care | vbc-equity-m6 | Who Gets Left Behind: Health Equity, Social Determinants, and Building a VBC System That Works for Everyone
Who Gets Left Behind: Health Equity, Social Determinants, and Building a VBC System That Works for Everyone
The Equity Gap That Value-Based Care Must Confront
Value-based care was designed to improve quality while reducing costs — a goal that sounds universal but has been implemented in ways that systematically exclude or disadvantage the people who most need better care. The promise of VBC is that if we pay for outcomes rather than volume, the entire health system will orient toward keeping people healthy and intervening effectively when they get sick. But that promise breaks down when the populations most likely to get sick are also the populations whose providers are most financially penalized for serving them, and whose social circumstances make achieving measured outcomes hardest.
Health disparities in the United States are pervasive, well-documented, and stubbornly persistent. Black Americans have shorter life expectancies than white Americans, higher rates of preventable hospitalizations, worse outcomes for nearly every major chronic disease, and less access to high-quality specialty care. Hispanic Americans face systematic barriers to accessing care due to language, immigration status, and geographic concentration in underserved communities. Rural Americans — regardless of race — face provider shortages, longer travel distances to specialists, and hospital closures that have accelerated over the past decade. These are not statistical abstractions; they are the lived experiences of tens of millions of Americans who depend on a healthcare system that was not designed with them in mind.
An analysis of U.S. county data (Hood et al., American Journal of Preventive Medicine, 2016) estimated that socioeconomic factors — income, education, employment, family and social support, community safety — account for about 47 percent of modifiable health outcomes, health behaviors for 34 percent, and clinical care for only 16 percent. This means that value-based programs focused exclusively on clinical quality metrics are, at best, optimizing a minority of the drivers of health. A VBC system that ignores social determinants is like a building code that focuses only on the foundation while ignoring whether the occupants have heat, water, and a safe neighborhood.
Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, transportation, and neighborhood safety — together with health behaviors, account for roughly 80% of modifiable health outcomes, while clinical care accounts for about 16% (Hood et al., 2016). A value-based care system that ignores these upstream factors cannot achieve equitable health improvement, regardless of how well it optimizes clinical delivery.
Socioeconomic factors (47%) and health behaviors (34%) together account for about 80% of modifiable health outcomes; clinical care 16% — Hood et al., Am J Prev Med 2016
Outcomes from Non-Clinical Factors
80%
Black Americans' life expectancy (74.0 years) trailed White Americans' (78.4) by 4.4 years in 2023 — KFF analysis of NCHS U.S. Life Tables, 2023
Black-White Life Expectancy Gap
4.4 Years
How Current VBC Design Can Worsen Disparities
The architecture of most value-based payment programs contains features that can actively worsen health disparities, even when the programs' intentions are positive. The clearest example is financial benchmarking based on historical costs. When ACOs or hospitals have their savings targets set relative to their own historical spending, providers who historically underserved low-income populations — spending less not because of efficiency but because patients couldn't afford care — will have lower baselines and therefore must improve more to earn bonuses. Conversely, providers who historically overspent may generate "savings" simply by stopping unnecessary high-cost care, even without improving outcomes.
Quality metrics in VBC programs are similarly biased by the populations they measure. Preventive care rates, disease management outcomes, and patient experience scores are all sensitive to social determinants that providers cannot control. A physician practicing in a food desert who consistently struggles to improve her patients' HbA1c levels despite excellent clinical care faces the same performance benchmark as a physician in an affluent community where patients can afford fresh food, have stable employment, and can take time off to manage their chronic conditions. Without social risk adjustment, the quality measurement system punishes the former and rewards the latter.
Provider network and geographic access issues compound these problems. VBC programs are most effective when patients have consistent, ongoing relationships with their primary care providers — the foundation of care coordination and preventive care. But underserved communities have higher rates of safety-net provider dependence, federally qualified health center (FQHC) utilization, and emergency department use as primary care. These non-standard care patterns make attribution difficult in ACO models and reduce the effectiveness of care coordination interventions designed around assumptions of regular primary care visits.
Value-based care programs that penalize providers for serving disadvantaged populations create incentives for "cream skimming" — the strategic avoidance of high-risk, high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients in favor of healthier, wealthier ones. When financial models reward efficiency over equity, providers who serve the most vulnerable patients can face the steepest penalties, creating pressure to deprioritize or exclude these populations from VBC arrangements.
The "Cream Skimming" Risk
The Social Determinants Framework in Practice
Addressing social determinants within a VBC framework requires moving beyond clinical-only interventions. Several models have demonstrated that systematic SDOH screening and community-based intervention — when integrated with clinical care delivery — can improve both health outcomes and financial performance. The logic is compelling: a patient who loses her apartment will generate emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and uncontrolled chronic disease management costs that dwarf the cost of housing support. If the VBC arrangement captures the savings from those avoided costs, investing in housing support can be financially rational, not just compassionate.
The Camden Coalition of Healthcare Providers in Camden, New Jersey pioneered the concept of "hotspotting" — identifying the highest-cost, most frequently hospitalized patients and providing intensive community-based support to address both clinical and social needs. Its wraparound services included housing assistance, transportation, medication management, and care coordination. When the approach was tested rigorously, however, the result was sobering: a randomized trial of the Coalition's care-transitions program (Finkelstein et al., New England Journal of Medicine, 2020) found 180-day readmission rates of 62.3 percent among enrolled patients versus 61.7 percent under usual care — no significant difference. The model still shaped complex care management nationally, and the trial is a standing lesson that promising before-and-after results need controlled evaluation.
The Vermont Blueprint for Health, whose multi-payer community health teams began in pilot communities in 2008, integrates community health teams — social workers, care coordinators, community health workers — with primary care practices. These teams address social needs alongside clinical needs. A peer-reviewed analysis of six years of Vermont all-payer claims (Jones et al., Population Health Management, 2016) associated the Blueprint's community-oriented medical-home model with lower expenditures and utilization while maintaining quality — one of the longest-running statewide examples of linking community supports to primary care.
The Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model, launched by CMMI in 2017, tested whether systematically identifying and addressing health-related social needs — through screening, referral, and community navigation — could reduce Medicare and Medicaid utilization and costs.
Twenty-eight bridge organizations screened more than 1 million Medicaid and Medicare beneficiaries for five core needs: housing instability, food insecurity, transportation problems, utility difficulties, and interpersonal violence. In the Assistance Track, navigation-eligible beneficiaries (at least one need plus two or more ED visits in the prior year) were randomized to referral information alone or referral plus an offer of navigation; the Alignment Track was not randomized. CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures — with fewer inpatient admissions and readmissions among Medicaid beneficiaries and fewer ED visits and ambulatory-care-sensitive admissions among fee-for-service Medicare beneficiaries — even though rates of need resolution were similar to the control group.
CMS Accountable Health Communities Model
What an Equity-Centered VBC System Looks Like
Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires changes at multiple levels: the data infrastructure for measuring equity, the payment architecture that removes penalties for serving disadvantaged populations, the workforce that can address social and clinical needs together, and the community partnerships that connect healthcare systems to social services. None of these changes is simple, and all of them require sustained policy commitment across multiple administrations.
On measurement, equity-centered VBC requires stratifying all quality measures by race, ethnicity, income, disability status, and social risk factor status — and holding providers accountable for reducing within-panel disparities, not just improving average performance. CMS moved in this direction in 2023, finalizing a Health Equity Index reward for Medicare Advantage Star Ratings and a health equity adjustment for the Hospital Value-Based Purchasing program, but reversed both in 2025: the FY2026 inpatient rule removed the hospital adjustment, and the CY2027 Medicare Advantage rule did not implement the reward. But the data infrastructure for consistent race and ethnicity reporting in healthcare claims remains incomplete, and many providers cannot accurately stratify their own quality data by social characteristics.
On workforce, community health workers (CHWs) have emerged as one of the highest-value tools for bridging clinical care and social needs. CHWs are trusted community members who provide health education, navigation, care coordination, and social support — often in patients' homes and in community settings rather than clinical offices. In the CY2024 Physician Fee Schedule, CMS created Medicare's first Community Health Integration codes (G0019, G0022) for CHW services furnished under a billing practitioner's supervision; Medicaid coverage of CHW services remains a state option; in KFF's 2022 survey, 29 of 48 responding states reported allowing Medicaid payment for CHW services. This represents a significant structural change that could enable systematic SDOH intervention at scale.
Require all quality metrics to be reported and benchmarked by race, ethnicity, income, and social risk factor status — rewarding disparity reduction, not just average performance improvement.
Stratified Quality Measurement
Adjust payment benchmarks and quality thresholds to account for patients' social circumstances, removing the financial penalty for serving disadvantaged populations.
Social Risk Adjustment
Require systematic screening for social determinants across all care settings, using standardized tools and coding systems to create consistent, actionable social risk data.
Universal SDOH Screening
Fund community health workers, care coordinators, and social workers embedded in clinical practices or operating as shared community resources accessible to VBC participants.
Community Health Integration
Create financial mechanisms for healthcare systems to partner with housing agencies, food banks, transportation providers, and workforce development programs to address identified social needs.
Cross-Sector Partnerships
Hold VBC participants accountable not just for clinical quality averages but for demonstrated reduction in health disparities within their attributed populations.
Outcome Accountability
Components of an Equity-Centered VBC System
The Policy Landscape and What Remains Unresolved
CMS has articulated a health equity commitment across multiple programs and policy documents, but translating that commitment into payment design that meaningfully advances equity is a work in progress. The Innovation Center's October 2021 Strategy Refresh named health equity a strategic objective, committing to embed it in every model. The AHC model, the Making Care Primary model, and ACO REACH all included equity-specific requirements or payment adjustments. Yet in March 2025 CMMI announced the early termination of four models — Making Care Primary among them — raising uncertainty about the long-term trajectory of equity-focused innovation.
Medicaid is potentially a more powerful lever for health equity in VBC than Medicare, because Medicaid disproportionately serves the populations with the most pronounced health disparities — low-income adults, children, people with disabilities, and pregnant women. Several states have moved aggressively to incorporate SDOH into Medicaid managed care contracts: North Carolina's Healthy Opportunities Pilots — described by the state as the nation's first comprehensive program to test evidence-based non-medical interventions for high-needs Medicaid enrollees — tested whether braiding healthcare and social service funding could improve outcomes for the most complex enrollees; services stopped on July 1, 2025, when state funding lapsed. Massachusetts, Oregon, and California have implemented similar Medicaid innovations.
The fundamental unresolved tension is between universalism and targeting. A truly equitable VBC system would require different standards, different investments, and different timelines for providers and populations at different starting points — a form of affirmative payment design that explicitly prioritizes closing gaps rather than maximizing average performance. American health policy has historically struggled with this kind of targeted approach, preferring universal standards that appear fair on paper but embed structural inequities in practice. Resolving that tension — acknowledging that equity sometimes requires differential treatment — is the defining political and policy challenge for the next generation of value-based care design.
A school system that grades every student on the same curve regardless of whether they had tutors, stable housing, and enough food is not measuring academic achievement — it is measuring socioeconomic advantage. Value-based care faces the same problem: measuring health outcomes on a single universal scale when the determinants of those outcomes are profoundly unequal.
Health Equity and VBC Performance Measurement
Social determinants of health — income, housing, education, food security, and transportation — together with health behaviors, drive roughly 80 percent of modifiable health outcomes, meaning VBC programs focused only on clinical quality metrics are optimizing a minority of what actually drives health.
Current VBC program design can worsen disparities through historical cost benchmarking, unadjusted quality metrics, and financial penalties that disproportionately fall on safety-net providers serving the most disadvantaged populations.
The "cream skimming" risk — providers strategically avoiding high-complexity, socially disadvantaged patients — is a real consequence of VBC financial models that penalize rather than reward serving vulnerable populations.
Community health workers, SDOH screening programs, and cross-sector partnerships between healthcare and social services represent promising operational strategies for addressing social determinants within VBC arrangements.
The Vermont Blueprint for Health and CMS Accountable Health Communities Model provide real-world evidence that linking community supports to primary care, and social-needs screening to navigation, can lower spending and hospital-based use.
CMS made health equity a design objective for Innovation Center models in 2021 and created Medicare billing codes for community health integration and SDOH risk assessment in 2024 — but in 2025 it rolled back several equity provisions, so equity-adjusted payment design remains unsettled.
Building a VBC system that works for everyone requires stratified quality measurement, social risk adjustment, universal SDOH screening, community health integration, and outcome accountability for demonstrated disparity reduction — not just average performance improvement.
The AHC Model specifically tested the clinical and financial impact of screening beneficiaries for five health-related social needs — housing instability, food insecurity, transportation, utilities, and interpersonal safety — and then providing community navigation to connect them with social services. CMS's final evaluation found that navigation lowered total health care expenditures and hospital-based use among navigation-eligible beneficiaries (fewer inpatient admissions for Medicaid enrollees, fewer ED visits for fee-for-service Medicare enrollees), supporting the premise that addressing social needs can reduce utilization and cost.

######## value-based-care | vbc-fundamentals-module-2-policy-pillar | Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 2: The Policy Pillar — Laws, Rules, and the Regulatory Architecture That Makes (or Breaks) Value-Based Care
Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 2: The Policy Pillar — Laws, Rules, and the Regulatory Architecture That Makes (or Breaks) Value-Based Care
Imagine you want to start a new kind of restaurant — one that charges customers a flat monthly fee to eat as many healthy meals as they need, rather than charging per dish. The idea makes sense nutritionally and economically. But before you open, you discover that local zoning laws require all food establishments to post per-item prices. The health department’s inspection checklist was designed for traditional menus. Your liquor license application has no category for subscription dining. None of these rules were written to block your idea — they were simply written when your idea did not exist. This is precisely the situation that value-based care innovators face in the American healthcare regulatory environment. The laws, billing codes, anti-kickback rules, and licensure frameworks that govern U.S. healthcare were almost entirely written for a fee-for-service world. Navigating, modifying, and sometimes working around them is not a bureaucratic inconvenience for VBC implementation — it is one of its defining challenges.
Why Policy Is a Pillar, Not Just a Background Condition
Healthcare is one of the most heavily regulated industries in the United States, and for good reason: the decisions made in healthcare settings involve life and death, profound information asymmetry between providers and patients, and the expenditure of trillions of dollars of public funds. The regulatory architecture that governs healthcare payment — Medicare and Medicaid rules, anti-kickback statutes, the Stark Law governing physician self-referral, state insurance laws, and HIPAA privacy regulations — was built incrementally over six decades, each layer added in response to a specific problem or abuse. The result is a regulatory environment of extraordinary complexity that can simultaneously protect patients and obstruct innovation, often in the same rule. For value-based care specifically, the policy environment matters in three distinct ways: it determines which VBC models are legally permissible, it shapes the financial terms under which VBC contracts can operate, and it establishes the data sharing authorities that VBC’s information infrastructure depends upon.
The good news for learners approaching this material is that you do not need to become a healthcare attorney to understand the policy landscape for VBC. What you do need is a working knowledge of four things: the major federal legislation that authorized and funds VBC programs, the agency — CMS and its Innovation Center — that designs and operates most federal VBC models, the specific legal waivers that allow VBC arrangements to operate outside standard fee-for-service rules, and the state-level Medicaid policy environment that governs VBC adoption for the Medicaid population, which accounts for about 18% of all U.S. healthcare spending and the majority of payer mix for rural and safety-net hospitals. This module covers all four in sequence, with enough practical depth that you can apply the concepts to your organization’s specific situation.
The ACA’s Innovation Center: The Engine of U.S. VBC Development
The Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation, universally known as CMMI, was established by Section 3021 of the Affordable Care Act in 2010 with a mandatory appropriation of $10 billion over ten years and a statutory mission to test, evaluate, and scale new payment and delivery models that reduce spending while preserving or improving quality. CMMI’s legal authority is significant: it can implement new payment models for Medicare and Medicaid without going through the standard notice-and-comment rulemaking process that governs most federal regulation, as long as the model operates within specific statutory parameters; expanding a model nationally additionally requires the CMS Chief Actuary to certify that expansion would not increase net program spending. This streamlined authority was deliberately designed to allow rapid policy experimentation — the legislative drafters recognized that VBC model design requires iteration and learning, and that subjecting every model modification to a 12-month rulemaking cycle would make meaningful innovation impossible.
Since 2011, CMMI has launched more than 50 distinct payment model pilots across Medicare and Medicaid, covering primary care transformation, specialty care bundling, accountable care organizations, direct contracting, and state-level all-payer models. The budget allocated per model varies enormously — from small demonstration projects covering a few thousand beneficiaries to large-scale national programs like the Medicare Shared Savings Program, which enrolled 11.2 million beneficiaries by 2025. CMMI’s mandate requires it to demonstrate that each model either reduces net Medicare spending, improves quality without increasing spending, or both. Models that fail to meet these thresholds can be modified or terminated. CMMI's own 2021 strategy review found that only six of its more than 50 models had produced statistically significant savings, and in March 2025 it announced it would end four models early, effective December 31, 2025 — Primary Care First, Making Care Primary, ESRD Treatment Choices, and the Maryland Total Cost of Care Model — citing evaluations and forecasts of increased spending; it is a record that reflects honest evaluation but has also drawn criticism from providers who invested substantially in model infrastructure before termination decisions.
CMMI’s authority to move faster than the standard rulemaking process is its most valuable feature and its most politically contested one. Every model CMMI launches is a hypothesis about how to organize care better. Some hypotheses are wrong. The question is whether the system is learning fast enough from both successes and failures.
MACRA: The Law That Made VBC Participation Effectively Mandatory for Physicians
If CMMI is the engine of federal VBC development, the Medicare Access and CHIP Reauthorization Act of 2015 — universally known as MACRA — is the law that turned VBC from an optional experiment into the default trajectory for physician payment in Medicare. MACRA was passed with rare bipartisan consensus, repealing the deeply unpopular Sustainable Growth Rate formula that had governed Medicare physician payments since 1997 and replacing it with a two-track system that explicitly links physician payment updates to VBC participation. Understanding MACRA’s structure is essential for any clinical or administrative leader whose organization bills Medicare for physician services, because it directly determines how physicians are paid and how much.
MACRA’s two tracks work as follows. Physicians who remain in traditional fee-for-service Medicare participate in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System, or MIPS, which adjusts their annual Medicare payments up or down by up to 9% based on performance across four categories: quality (30% weight), cost (30%), promoting interoperability (25%), and improvement activities (15%) — the weights in effect since the 2022 performance year. MIPS is designed as a transitional step — it maintains the fee-for-service base payment structure while adding a performance overlay that rewards quality and penalizes inefficiency. The alternative track, and the one that MACRA’s architects intended as the destination, is participation in an Advanced Alternative Payment Model, or APM, which includes CMS-approved VBC arrangements that meet specific risk and quality criteria. Physicians who generate a sufficient share of their Medicare revenue through APM participation become Qualifying APM Participants — originally earning a 5% lump-sum bonus (since reduced and, for 2025 performance onward, lapsed) and a higher fee-schedule update — and are exempt from MIPS reporting requirements — a substantial financial incentive to move toward more advanced VBC structures.
The MIPS-to-APM Progression: What It Looks Like in Practice
The practical effect of MACRA’s two-track architecture is to create a structured pathway from fee-for-service through MIPS participation toward Advanced APM engagement, with financial incentives escalating at each stage. A solo primary care physician in rural Wyoming who bills Medicare exclusively on a fee-for-service basis is automatically enrolled in MIPS and will receive payment adjustments — upward or downward — based on their quality reporting, EHR utilization, and cost performance. The same physician who joins an Advanced APM, such as a two-sided Medicare ACO, and receives at least 75% of their Medicare Part B payments (or sees 50% of their Medicare patients) through it qualifies as an Advanced APM participant, earns the higher QP fee-schedule update (the original 5% lump-sum bonus lapsed after the 2024 performance year), and escapes the MIPS reporting burden. MACRA’s architecture was designed to make this progression financially attractive enough that providers would voluntarily move toward advanced VBC structures over time, without the political controversy of making VBC participation legally mandatory.
