MACRA Payment Track Comparison: MIPS vs. Advanced APM Participation, 2026
Policy Insight for Practice Leaders: If your organization’s physicians are currently in MIPS and scoring below 75, you are almost certainly paying more in administrative reporting costs than you are receiving in payment bonuses. A 2021 study of independent practices by Khullar and colleagues (JAMA Health Forum) put the cost of MIPS participation at $12,811 per physician per year in 2019, driven by about 200 hours of physician and staff time. Joining an ACO or Advanced APM eliminates this burden while generating shared savings upside. The question is not whether to make the move — it is when your organization has the infrastructure to do it responsibly.
The Stark Law and Anti-Kickback Statute: The Rules VBC Had to Work Around
Two of the most significant legal barriers to value-based care adoption are laws that were designed to protect patients from fraud: the Stark Law, which prohibits physician self-referral for designated health services when a financial relationship exists between the physician and the referred entity, and the Federal Anti-Kickback Statute, which prohibits offering or receiving anything of value to induce referrals of federal healthcare program business. Both laws were enacted in the 1980s and 1990s to address genuine abuses in fee-for-service medicine — physicians referring patients to laboratories or imaging centers they owned, and pharmaceutical companies paying physicians to prescribe specific drugs. They are important protections. They are also written in a way that, on their face, makes many value-based care arrangements technically illegal.
Consider a simple VBC arrangement: a hospital wants to share a portion of the savings generated by an ACO with the primary care physicians who successfully manage their attributed patient panels and reduce unnecessary hospitalizations. Under a strict reading of the Anti-Kickback Statute, this payment could be characterized as remuneration to physicians for reducing referrals to the hospital — which is exactly what the statute was written to prohibit when the financial relationship runs in the other direction. In November 2020, CMS (for the Stark Law) and the HHS Office of Inspector General (for the Anti-Kickback Statute) simultaneously published new rules — commonly called the Stark Law and AKS VBC Exceptions — that created explicit regulatory safe harbors for value-based arrangements meeting specific criteria. These exceptions are the legal foundation on which most current VBC contract structures rest, and understanding their existence (if not their full technical detail) is important context for any leader involved in VBC contract negotiation.
What the 2020 VBC Exceptions Actually Allow
The 2020 Stark Law and AKS VBC exceptions created three tiers of safe harbor protection based on the level of financial risk the arrangement assumes. The first tier, the “care coordination arrangement” exception, covers low-risk VBC arrangements where physicians and hospitals share non-monetary resources — care coordinators, technology platforms, data analytics tools — without direct financial remuneration flowing between them. The second tier covers arrangements where the parties share substantial downside financial risk, defined as the physician group being responsible for a meaningful share of losses if spending targets are not met. The third and most protective tier applies to arrangements where a physician entity is “fully at risk” — accepting capitation-level accountability for a defined patient population. The practical effect of this tiered structure is that more financially protective exceptions are available to VBC arrangements that accept more financial risk — a policy design that explicitly incentivizes providers to move toward more advanced VBC models in exchange for greater legal certainty.
State Medicaid Policy: Where VBC Gets Complicated Fast
Medicaid, the joint federal-state health insurance program for low-income Americans, covered about 76 million people together with CHIP at the end of 2025 and accounts for about 18% of all U.S. healthcare spending. For rural and safety-net hospitals, Medicaid is often the dominant payer — in some Critical Access Hospitals, Medicaid accounts for more than 40% of patient volume. Any serious discussion of VBC adoption must therefore grapple with Medicaid policy, and Medicaid policy is, by design, a state-level affair. Under the Social Security Act, the federal government sets minimum Medicaid standards and matches state spending at a regular rate (FMAP) that runs from a 50% floor to about 77% depending on state per-capita income, with a separate 90% match for the ACA expansion population — but states have substantial flexibility in how they design their Medicaid programs, including how they pay providers. This flexibility has produced a 50-state patchwork of Medicaid VBC approaches that range from nationally leading to years behind, often with little correlation to state wealth or healthcare system capacity.
States access this flexibility primarily through two mechanisms: Section 1115 waivers, which allow states to use Medicaid funds in ways not otherwise permitted by federal statute in exchange for CMS approval of a formal waiver application and evaluation framework, and Section 1915 waivers, which allow states to require Medicaid beneficiaries to enroll in managed care organizations rather than traditional fee-for-service Medicaid. As of 2025, 41 states (including DC) contract with comprehensive Medicaid managed care organizations, and many states use Section 1115 waivers to add VBC-oriented payment reform components. The remaining states continue to operate primarily fee-for-service Medicaid programs, creating a two-tier national Medicaid environment where the VBC infrastructure, data systems, and provider capabilities in a given state depend heavily on decisions made by state legislatures and Medicaid agencies that most healthcare professionals are only vaguely aware of.

State Medicaid VBC Adoption Landscape: Selected State Comparisons, 2025
The state variation in Medicaid VBC adoption documented in the table above is not simply a story of some states moving faster than others. It reflects fundamentally different political economies, administrative capacities, and provider infrastructure realities. Massachusetts’ MassHealth ACO Program, which by June 2023 enrolled more than 1.3 million members — over half of all MassHealth members — in its ACOs, required a decade of incremental managed care development, a sophisticated state health information exchange, and a robust community health worker infrastructure before global budgets were feasible. Mississippi, where about 65% of Medicaid beneficiaries are in MississippiCAN managed care and the rest remain in fee-for-service (Division of Medicaid 2024 Annual Report), faces not just a political environment less favorable to managed care but a provider infrastructure so financially fragile — as examined in the DSH module — that asking rural hospitals to accept downside financial risk before their basic solvency is secured would be policy malpractice. Understanding this context prevents the common mistake of treating state VBC laggards as simply lacking political will, when the more accurate diagnosis is often a missing infrastructure foundation.
The AHEAD Model: The Boldest Current Federal VBC Policy Experiment
The CMS AHEAD Model — announced in 2023 as the States Advancing All-Payer Health Equity Approaches and Development Model and renamed Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design after CMS redesigned it in September 2025 — is one of the most ambitious federal VBC policy experiments currently active in the United States. AHEAD is fundamentally different from previous CMS models in one critical way: it operates across all payers simultaneously, not just Medicare. In the participating states — Maryland, Connecticut, Hawaii, Rhode Island, and downstate New York (Vermont signed in January 2025 but withdrew in July 2026) — CMS is working with state governments and commercial insurers to establish coordinated spending targets that apply to Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial insurance simultaneously. The goal is to eliminate the perverse incentive created by single-payer VBC models, where a provider that successfully reduces costs for its Medicare ACO population may simply shift utilization to its commercially insured population, producing savings for Medicare at the expense of commercial payer spending.
AHEAD’s architecture has three components that build on each other. Hospital Global Budgets establish annual spending targets for inpatient and outpatient hospital care, similar to the all-payer hospital global budgets Maryland has operated statewide since 2014, built on the all-payer rate-setting system it has run under a Medicare waiver since 1977. Primary Care Investment establishes a per-capita funding floor for primary care services in each participating state, addressing the underfunding of primary care that Module 1 identified as a structural driver of the U.S. spending-outcomes gap. And population health accountability — originally a state Health Equity Plan with disparity-reduction goals — was replaced in CMS's September 2025 redesign by statewide and hospital Population Health Accountability Plans focused on preventive care and chronic disease prevention, while the requirements to report quality by race and ethnicity and to submit demographic data were dropped and states must now adopt at least two policies promoting choice and competition. AHEAD’s results will not be statistically meaningful for several years — Cohorts 2 and 3 begin performance only in January 2028 — but its structural design is one of the most coherent attempts yet to address the whole-system payment reform that health economists have argued is necessary for genuine transformation.
The AHEAD Model is not a pilot. It is a policy architecture for what the American healthcare payment system could look like at scale — one where no payer is an island, where primary care is funded as infrastructure rather than as a commodity, and where population health is a contractual obligation rather than an aspiration. Whether it works depends entirely on whether the participating states build the administrative and data infrastructure to make the targets meaningful.
Reading Policy Signals: How to Know What’s Coming Before It Arrives
One of the most practical skills a healthcare leader can develop is the ability to read federal policy signals early — to understand what CMS, Congress, and state Medicaid agencies are signaling about the future direction of payment policy before new rules take effect. This skill is valuable because VBC model participation requires organizational investment — in data systems, care management staffing, and actuarial capabilities — that takes 18 to 36 months to build. Organizations that wait until a rule is finalized to begin building readiness will always be behind. The following framework identifies the primary signals that healthcare leaders should monitor continuously as leading indicators of VBC policy direction.
CMS Requests for Information (RFIs) are formal public notices in which CMS invites stakeholder comment on a policy concept before publishing a proposed rule. An RFI on a new payment model concept typically precedes a proposed rule by 12–18 months, giving organizations that monitor them a substantial head start on understanding what is coming and beginning internal readiness assessments.
The Annual Physician Fee Schedule Proposed Rule, published every July for the following calendar year, contains the annual MIPS threshold adjustments, quality measure updates, and any modifications to Advanced APM qualifying criteria. Reading the proposed rule summary — not the full document, which runs to thousands of pages — each July is the single most efficient way to stay current on federal physician payment policy.
CMMI Model Termination Notices are official signals that a payment model has not met its statutory savings or quality thresholds. When CMMI terminates a model, it typically publishes evaluation findings that explain why. Reading these findings is often more instructive than reading the original model design documents, because they identify the specific infrastructure gaps, attribution problems, or market conditions that prevented the model from working — lessons directly applicable to understanding what makes other VBC models succeed.
State Medicaid Managed Care Request for Proposals are published by state Medicaid agencies when they are procuring new managed care contracts, typically on three-to-five year cycles. These documents specify the quality metrics, VBC incentive structures, SDOH screening requirements, and health equity goals that Medicaid managed care organizations and their provider networks will be held to. Organizations that serve Medicaid populations should read their state’s current managed care RFP as a direct statement of the performance expectations they will face in the next contract cycle.
Module 2 Summary: The Policy Environment Is Not Your Enemy — But You Must Understand It
The policy architecture governing value-based care in the United States is complex, layered, and still evolving — but it is not impenetrable to practitioners willing to invest in understanding its structure. The key institutions are CMS and its Innovation Center, which design and operate most federal VBC models; Congress, which authorizes and funds VBC infrastructure through legislation like MACRA and the ACA; and state Medicaid agencies, which determine how value-based principles are applied to the Medicaid population that drives solvency for most safety-net and rural providers. The key legal frameworks are MACRA’s two-track physician payment architecture, the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions, and the Section 1115 and 1915 waiver authorities that give states flexibility to innovate within federal Medicaid rules.
The most important single insight from this module is that policy does not just regulate VBC — it enables it. The shared savings that MSSP ACOs distribute to physicians are legal because of CMMI’s model authority and the AKS safe harbor. The global budgets that Maryland hospitals operate under rest on the state’s all-payer rate-setting authority, first granted by a Medicare waiver in 1977 and continued today under its AHEAD agreement. The care coordination resources that a hospital shares with its independent physician partners are legally protected because of the 2020 VBC exceptions. Every advanced VBC arrangement you will encounter in your career rests on a specific legal and regulatory foundation. Understanding that foundation — at least at the level of knowing which questions to ask your legal team — is not optional for any leader who wants to move their organization toward value.
Identify your organization’s current MACRA track: are your physicians primarily in MIPS, in an Advanced APM, or in both? If primarily MIPS, what is the organization’s target timeline for APM qualification, and what infrastructure gaps stand between you and that threshold?
Review your state’s current Medicaid managed care contract or RFP. Identify the three quality metrics with the highest incentive weight and assess your organization’s current performance on each. The gap between your current performance and the contract’s quality bonus threshold is a direct measure of revenue at risk.
Determine whether your state is an AHEAD Model participant. If yes, begin engaging your state hospital association and state health department about the hospital global budget timeline and what data your organization will need to submit. If no, note that CMS's September 2025 redesign of AHEAD offered an opportunity for two additional states to participate starting in 2028 and/or 2029; all cohorts now run through December 31, 2035.
Schedule a conversation with your legal or compliance team specifically about the 2020 Stark Law and Anti-Kickback VBC exceptions. Ask them to identify any current or planned VBC arrangements at your organization that rely on these exceptions, and to confirm that the arrangements are structured to satisfy the applicable safe harbor criteria.
Module 2 Key Takeaway: The U.S. healthcare policy environment was built for fee-for-service, but it has been systematically modified over the past 15 years to enable value-based care. CMMI’s model authority, MACRA’s APM incentive structure, the 2020 VBC legal exceptions, and state Medicaid waiver programs together constitute a policy architecture that makes advanced VBC legally and financially feasible for most U.S. healthcare organizations. The organizations that understand this architecture and align their strategy to it are the ones that will be best positioned as CMS accelerates its stated goal of having 100% of Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship by 2030.

Module 2 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the federal and state policy architecture that governs value-based care adoption in the United States. Building on Module 1’s conceptual foundation, this module explains in plain language how MACRA, the ACA’s Innovation Center, and state Medicaid waiver programs create the legal and financial scaffolding for VBC models, identifies the regulatory barriers that slow adoption for rural and safety-net providers, and equips learners to read and interpret the policy signals that will shape their organization’s VBC strategy through 2030. ######## value-based-care | vbc-fundamentals-module-4-technology-pillar | Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 4: The Technology Pillar — Data, AI, and the Digital Infrastructure That Makes VBC Work
Value-Based Care Fundamentals — Module 4: The Technology Pillar — Data, AI, and the Digital Infrastructure That Makes VBC Work
Imagine trying to run a nationwide airline reservation system where every airport kept its flight records on paper, no two airports used the same form, and sharing records between airports required a fax machine and a three-day waiting period. Connecting passengers to flights would be technically possible but operationally chaotic — delays, lost records, missed connections, and dangerous errors would be routine, not exceptional. This is, only slightly exaggerated, the state of health information exchange in the United States as recently as 2019, and in many rural markets as recently as 2024. Value-based care requires something that American healthcare has never had at scale: a reliable, real-time, standards-based system for sharing patient health information across organizational boundaries. Without it, an Accountable Care Organization cannot know that its attributed Medicare patient was admitted to a hospital outside the network last Tuesday. A care coordinator cannot know that a high-risk patient missed their primary care appointment. A risk stratification algorithm cannot identify a patient approaching a high-cost event without complete longitudinal data about their diagnosis history, medication adherence, and recent utilization. Technology is not a nice-to-have for advanced VBC. It is the operating system on which the entire model runs.
The Three Technology Layers VBC Requires
The technology infrastructure that supports effective value-based care can be understood as three interdependent layers, each building on the one below it. The foundation layer is clinical data capture: the electronic health record system that documents every patient encounter, diagnosis, medication, order, and result in a structured, machine-readable format. The second layer is data integration and exchange: the health information exchange infrastructure that connects EHR systems across organizations so that complete patient data is available regardless of where care was delivered. The third layer is analytics and intelligence: the population health management platforms, risk stratification tools, and increasingly AI-powered predictive models that transform raw clinical data into actionable care management intelligence — identifying which patients are at highest risk of imminent high-cost events, which chronic disease patients are overdue for interventions, and which populations are generating the most preventable utilization. Each layer is necessary but not sufficient. Strong EHR implementation without HIE connectivity produces siloed data. HIE connectivity without analytics produces data that no one has the capacity to act on. Analytics without high-quality underlying data produces predictions that are wrong in ways that are hard to detect until they cause harm.
Electronic Health Records: The Foundation Layer
The United States made a massive federal investment in EHR adoption through the HITECH Act of 2009, which appropriated $27 billion in Medicare and Medicaid incentive payments to encourage providers to implement certified EHR systems and demonstrate “meaningful use” — a defined set of capabilities including electronic prescribing, clinical decision support, and patient portal access. Certified EHR adoption among non-federal acute-care hospitals rose from roughly 10% in 2008 to about 96% by 2021 (Health Affairs; ONC), one of the most rapid technology adoption curves in any industry, and it created the clinical data foundation that value-based care analytics requires. However, adoption rates mask significant quality variation that is directly relevant to VBC capability. Having a certified EHR does not mean having a fully configured, fully utilized EHR that generates high-quality structured data. Many providers, particularly smaller rural practices and critical access hospitals, implemented EHR systems at the minimum level required to qualify for HITECH incentive payments, resulting in installations that function primarily as billing and documentation tools rather than population health data platforms.
The VBC-relevant EHR capabilities that matter most are not the basic documentation features that HITECH required, but the advanced data quality and interoperability features that turn an EHR from a digital chart room into a population health intelligence system. These include structured problem lists and medication lists that use standardized coding (ICD-10 for diagnoses, RxNorm for medications, SNOMED CT for clinical concepts) rather than free-text notes; care gap reporting that identifies patients overdue for preventive services or chronic disease monitoring; patient panel management tools that allow care coordinators to view their entire assigned patient population sorted by risk level; and FHIR API connectivity that allows the EHR to exchange data with external systems using the standardized data format that the 21st Century Cures Act mandated in 2020. Federal data show the gap is real: in 2023, 70% of non-federal acute care hospitals engaged in all four domains of interoperable exchange (sending, receiving, finding, and integrating patient data), but only 43% did so routinely, and small, rural, critical access, and independent hospitals engaged less often than better-resourced hospitals (ONC Data Brief No. 71, 2024).
The 21st Century Cures Act: The Law That Changed EHR Interoperability Requirements
The 21st Century Cures Act, enacted in December 2016 with its implementing regulations finalized in 2020, made two changes to the EHR landscape that are directly relevant to VBC technology readiness. First, it prohibited “information blocking” — defined as any practice that unreasonably restricts the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information — and established civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers, networks, and exchanges that engage in information blocking. This provision was specifically designed to address a well-documented pattern in which EHR vendors and some health systems restricted data sharing with competitors or external partners, creating artificial data silos that served commercial interests at the expense of care coordination. Second, it mandated that all certified EHR systems implement standardized FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) application programming interfaces by 2022, enabling third-party developers to build population health applications that connect directly to EHR data without requiring custom integrations. The FHIR mandate is the technical foundation of the modern population health analytics market, as it allows risk stratification platforms, care gap tools, and quality reporting systems to access EHR data through a single standardized connection rather than a patchwork of proprietary integrations.
The 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition changed the competitive dynamics of health IT in a way that CMS’s interoperability rules alone could not have. When health IT developers and exchanges face penalties of up to $1 million per violation for restricting data access, and providers face their own federal disincentives, the legal calculus of data hoarding changes overnight. The challenge now is not permission — it is infrastructure. Building the pipes to carry the data that is now legally required to flow is the work of this decade.
Health Information Exchange: The Data Sharing Layer
Health information exchange (HIE) refers to the electronic sharing of patient health information across organizational boundaries — between hospitals, physician practices, laboratories, pharmacies, and post-acute care providers that may use different EHR systems and operate in different ownership structures. For value-based care, HIE is not optional infrastructure. An ACO that cannot receive notifications when its attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any hospital in its market cannot manage post-discharge follow-up effectively. A care coordinator who cannot see a patient’s complete medication list across all prescribers cannot identify dangerous drug interactions or medication non-adherence. A risk stratification algorithm that only has access to the patient’s encounters at one health system is working from an incomplete and potentially misleading clinical picture. The importance of HIE to VBC has been recognized in federal policy through TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — which ONC published in January 2022 as the national framework for interoperable health information exchange.
TEFCA establishes a set of technical and legal standards that health information networks must meet to become Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs), and creates a framework under which QHINs are required to share data with each other upon request, effectively creating a nationwide health information exchange network for the first time. By early 2026, eleven networks had been designated as QHINs — eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, Health Gorilla, KONZA National Network, and MedAllies (December 2023); CommonWell Health Alliance and Kno2 (February 2024); Netsmart; eClinicalWorks; Surescripts; and Oracle Health Information Network (November 2025). The coverage of these networks is extensive in urban and suburban markets but remains uneven in rural areas, where the combination of fewer participating providers, older EHR systems, and limited broadband infrastructure creates connectivity gaps that directly limit rural ACO and VBC participants’ ability to receive real-time patient data from non-network sources. The FCC’s Rural Health Care Program (including its Healthcare Connect Fund) and USDA’s ReConnect Program are the primary federal mechanisms for addressing rural broadband gaps, and rural providers’ requests to the FCC program routinely exceed its annual funding cap.
The capability gap between lower-resourced rural hospitals and better-resourced systems represents a structural VBC readiness disparity that policy interventions alone cannot close without significant capital investment. A rural Critical Access Hospital that lacks FHIR R4 API implementation, state HIE connectivity, and a population health platform is not technically capable of the patient data workflows that MSSP ACO participation requires — not because of organizational will or leadership quality, but because the digital infrastructure that enables those workflows has not been built. The federal programs designed to address this gap — including the FCC’s Rural Health Care Program, capped at about $724 million for funding year 2025, ONC’s Health IT Certification Program, and HRSA’s Rural Health Information Technology funding stream — are necessary but insufficient at their current funding levels to close the rural-urban technology gap within a policy-relevant timeframe.
AI and Risk Stratification: The Intelligence Layer
Risk stratification — the process of identifying which patients within a large population are at highest risk of future high-cost health events — is the intelligence function that turns population health data into actionable care management priorities. In a VBC model managing 10,000 attributed patients, a care management team cannot proactively reach out to every patient every month. They need a system that identifies the 300 or 400 patients most likely to have a preventable hospital admission, emergency department visit, or serious clinical deterioration in the next 90 days, so that care coordination resources can be concentrated where they will have the greatest impact. Traditional risk stratification relied on simple actuarial models — patients with the highest total spending in the prior year were assumed to be the highest risk in the coming year. These models are easy to implement but systematically misdirected: they identify patients who were recently sick rather than patients who are about to become sick, missing the early intervention window where care management is most effective and most cost-efficient.
Modern AI-powered risk stratification uses machine learning models trained on large clinical datasets to predict future utilization risk based on a much richer set of signals than historical spending alone. These models incorporate diagnosis trajectories (the sequence and pattern of diagnoses over time, not just their presence or absence), medication adherence signals derived from pharmacy data and EHR medication reconciliation records, laboratory value trends (a gradually rising HbA1c over three visits is a stronger predictor of near-term hospitalization than a single elevated value), social determinants of health flags derived from screening questionnaires and zip-code-level data, and behavioral health diagnoses and substance use disorder flags that are strongly predictive of high-cost medical utilization. Predictive accuracy is usually reported as the C-statistic — the probability that the model ranks a patient who will be hospitalized above one who will not — and models that add clinical EHR data to claims generally discriminate better than claims-only models, though published gains vary widely by population and outcome and should be validated locally before they drive care coordinator workloads.
The AI Bias Problem: When Risk Stratification Perpetuates Inequity
AI risk stratification tools carry a well-documented and serious equity risk: because they are trained on historical healthcare utilization data, they tend to encode the biases present in that data. A landmark 2019 study published in Science by Obermeyer et al. found that a widely used commercial risk stratification algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients because it used healthcare costs as a proxy for health need — and because Black patients historically had lower healthcare costs not because they were healthier, but because structural barriers limited their access to care. The algorithm learned that low-cost patients were low-need patients, a correlation that held for white patients but produced systematic underestimation of Black patients’ clinical risk. The practical consequence was that Black patients were significantly less likely to be identified for high-intensity care management programs, perpetuating the very care access disparities that VBC is intended to address. This finding has been replicated for other demographic groups and other algorithm types, establishing AI bias as a genuine and important equity challenge in VBC technology deployment.
Algorithmic bias in risk stratification is a documented, real-world problem. Obermeyer and colleagues (Science, 2019) showed that a widely used commercial risk-prediction algorithm systematically underestimated the health needs of Black patients, because it was trained on historical cost data shaped by unequal access — the model learned to encode access barriers as lower predicted need. The lesson for VBC: a risk model trained on fee-for-service utilization in a world with documented access barriers will reproduce those barriers unless it is explicitly audited and recalibrated for equity.
Technology Governance Requirement: Any healthcare organization deploying an AI risk stratification tool in a VBC context has an ethical and, increasingly, a legal obligation to audit the tool for demographic performance disparities before deployment and on a regular basis thereafter. The audit should examine whether the model’s sensitivity and specificity — its ability to correctly identify high-risk and low-risk patients — varies significantly across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic subgroups. If it does, the organization must either select a different model, recalibrate the existing model for its specific population, or supplement algorithmic risk scoring with clinical and social worker judgment for populations where the algorithm performs poorly.
Telehealth as a VBC Enabler: The COVID Legacy
The COVID-19 pandemic produced one technology outcome that has proven durably beneficial for value-based care: the rapid normalization of telehealth as a routine care delivery modality. Between March and June 2020, CMS issued emergency waivers that allowed Medicare to reimburse telehealth visits at parity with in-person visits, removed geographic restrictions that had historically limited telehealth to rural areas, and authorized audio-only visits for patients without video capability. Telehealth surged from about 0.2% of outpatient evaluation-and-management visits in February 2020 to a peak of roughly 50.7% in April 2020 — on the order of 78 times the pre-pandemic level (CDC MMWR; HHS ASPE) — demonstrating both latent demand and the clinical feasibility of delivering much of primary care and chronic disease management by video or phone. For value-based care organizations, telehealth is a care management efficiency multiplier: it lets care coordinators and physicians conduct follow-ups, medication reviews, and chronic disease check-ins at a fraction of the cost and scheduling friction of in-person visits, enabling more frequent contact with high-risk patients than a purely in-person model allows.
The scale of Medicare adoption is documented: the HHS Office of Inspector General found that more than 28 million Medicare beneficiaries — over 2 in 5 — used telehealth in the first year of the pandemic, using 88 times more telehealth services than the year before, with office visits making up just under half of that use. The same review found urban beneficiaries more likely than rural ones to use telehealth — a reminder that the rural populations with the most to gain also face the broadband and device barriers that limit uptake.
The policy question that followed the pandemic’s emergency waivers was whether CMS would make the telehealth flexibilities permanent. Congress answered with a series of short-term extensions rather than a permanent fix: the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 carried the flexibilities through 2024, later stopgap bills carried them into 2025, they briefly lapsed during the funding gaps of late 2025 and January 31, 2026, and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2026 (H.R. 7148, enacted February 2026) extended them — including home as an originating site, audio-only visits, and FQHC/RHC distant-site services — through December 31, 2027. For rural VBC providers, the permanence of these telehealth payment rules is not a convenience issue — it is a care model viability issue. An ACO serving a rural population where 40% of attributed patients live more than 30 miles from the nearest primary care office cannot achieve the visit frequency that effective chronic disease management requires without telehealth as a structural component of its care model.
Building Technology Readiness: The Sequenced Investment Roadmap
For healthcare leaders assessing their organization’s VBC technology readiness, the most common mistake is attempting to deploy advanced analytics capabilities before the foundational data quality and connectivity infrastructure is in place. A population health platform fed by an EHR with poorly configured structured data will generate inaccurate risk scores. A care gap reporting system connected to an EHR that does not have standardized problem list coding will miss a significant proportion of the gaps it is supposed to identify. Technology investment in VBC should follow a deliberate sequence, with each layer validated before the next is added.
Phase 1 — Data Foundation (Months 1–6): Audit your EHR’s structured data quality. Assess the completeness and accuracy of your problem list, medication list, and care gap documentation. Implement standardized coding for diagnoses (ICD-10), medications (RxNorm), and procedures (CPT). This phase produces no new technology capability but is the single most important determinant of all subsequent analytics quality.
Phase 2 — Connectivity (Months 4–12): Activate your state HIE connection and configure admission-discharge-transfer (ADT) alert feeds so that care coordinators receive real-time notifications when attributed patients are admitted to or discharged from any participating hospital in your market. This is the highest-ROI single connectivity investment for ACO care management.
Phase 3 — Panel Management (Months 9–18): Implement a population health management platform that allows care coordinators to view and filter their attributed patient panel by risk level, care gap status, and recent utilization events. At this stage, risk stratification can be claims-based or simple rules-based — AI is not required for effective panel management at this phase.
Phase 4 — Predictive Intelligence (Months 18–36): Implement AI-powered risk stratification once your EHR data quality and HIE connectivity are sufficient to feed the model with the multi-modal data it requires for accurate predictions. Conduct a demographic equity audit of the model before deployment. Begin using model outputs to prioritize care coordinator outreach and track whether high-model-score patients who receive outreach have lower subsequent hospitalization rates than comparable patients who do not.
Phase 5 — Continuous Improvement (Ongoing): Establish a quarterly data quality review cycle that monitors EHR documentation completeness, risk model accuracy, care gap closure rates, and population health outcome trends. Use this data to identify where the care management workflow is breaking down — whether the issue is risk score accuracy, care coordinator capacity, patient engagement, or post-acute care coordination — and address the root cause rather than adjusting the technology.
Module 4 Summary: Technology Is the Operating System of Value-Based Care
The technology infrastructure required for effective value-based care is not exotic or cutting-edge by the standards of other industries. What VBC requires is reliable clinical data capture, standards-based data exchange, and analytics capable of turning population data into actionable care management intelligence. These are not science-fiction capabilities. They exist today in mature form at health systems like Kaiser Permanente, Intermountain Healthcare, and Geisinger. The challenge is not invention — it is diffusion. The rural Critical Access Hospitals that lack the foundational technology capabilities for advanced VBC participation are not being held back by the absence of technology. They are being held back by the absence of capital, broadband infrastructure, and technical implementation support that would allow them to deploy technology that already exists.
The federal investment framework for closing this gap — TEFCA for interoperability standards, the 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition and FHIR mandate, the FCC’s Healthcare Connect Fund for rural broadband, ONC’s certification program for EHR capabilities, and HRSA’s rural health IT funding stream — represents the most coherent federal technology infrastructure investment in healthcare history. Whether it is sufficient to close the rural-urban VBC readiness gap within a policy-relevant timeframe is an open question that depends on appropriations decisions, state implementation capacity, and vendor market dynamics that are outside any single organization’s control. What is within your organization’s control is the sequenced technology investment roadmap described in this module, and the commitment to building VBC data infrastructure as a strategic priority rather than an IT project.
VBC technology infrastructure has three interdependent layers: clinical data capture (EHR), data integration and exchange (HIE and FHIR), and analytics and intelligence (population health platforms and AI risk stratification). Each layer depends on the quality of the layer below it, making data foundation investment the highest-priority first step.
The 21st Century Cures Act’s information blocking prohibition and FHIR API mandate are the legal and technical foundations of modern health IT interoperability. Health IT developers, health information exchanges, and networks that engage in information blocking face civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation; health care providers face separate federal disincentives, such as losing Promoting Interoperability credit under MIPS, under a 2024 HHS rule.
AI risk stratification tools improve high-risk patient identification accuracy significantly compared to claims-based models, but carry documented equity risks from training data bias that require formal demographic audit before deployment and on an ongoing basis.
Telehealth is a structural care model component for rural VBC providers serving populations where in-person visit frequency sufficient for effective chronic disease management is geographically and logistically impossible. The permanence of post-pandemic telehealth reimbursement parity is a VBC infrastructure issue, not simply a convenience policy question.
Module 4 Key Takeaway: Technology readiness is the most concrete and actionable dimension of VBC preparation because it can be assessed objectively, sequenced rationally, and funded through a combination of organizational capital and federal programs. Before your organization takes on additional VBC financial risk, conduct a structured technology readiness assessment using the capability gap framework from this module and identify which phase of the five-phase roadmap you are currently in. Attempting to manage population cost without the data infrastructure to know who your highest-risk patients are and what is happening to them across the care continuum is the most common cause of VBC financial underperformance — and the most preventable.
Module 4 of the HTR Academy Value-Based Care Fundamentals course examines the technology infrastructure that value-based care requires to function — and what happens when that infrastructure is missing. This module explains, in plain language, what interoperable electronic health records, health information exchange, and AI-powered risk stratification tools actually do in a VBC context, why many rural Critical Access Hospitals remain technology-unready for advanced VBC participation, and how the federal interoperability agenda — including the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability Rule, and the TEFCA framework — is building the data infrastructure that VBC depends upon. By the end of this module, learners will understand the specific technology capabilities that VBC models require, the sequence in which they should be built, and the federal programs that fund them.
######## hospital-finance | hospital-business-model | The Hospital Business Model
The Hospital Business Model: How Hospitals Actually Make Money
A Business That Doesn’t Behave Like One
A hospital is one of the strangest businesses in the American economy. It often cannot tell a patient the price before delivering the service, gets paid different amounts by different customers for the identical procedure, is frequently legally barred from turning anyone away in an emergency, and — in the majority of cases — is not even trying to earn a profit in the conventional sense. Yet a hospital must still bring in more money than it spends, or it closes. Understanding how it does that is the foundation of everything else in hospital finance.
The single most important fact about the hospital business model is where the money comes from. Net patient revenue — the money a hospital actually collects for treating patients, after discounts and adjustments — accounts for an average of roughly 90.9% of total hospital revenue. The rest comes from non-patient sources: investment income, philanthropy, grants, and ancillary operations like parking, cafeterias, and retail pharmacy. For most hospitals, the business is overwhelmingly the business of getting paid for patient care.
But "getting paid for patient care" hides enormous complexity. A hospital does not have one customer paying one price; it has a portfolio of payers — Medicare, Medicaid, commercial insurers, and patients themselves — each paying a different rate, set by a different mechanism, for the same bed and the same surgeon. The mix of those payers, and how much each pays, largely determines whether the hospital thrives or struggles.
Key Concept: Net patient revenue is the cash a hospital actually collects for patient care after contractual discounts, charity care, and bad debt are subtracted from its billed charges. It is the engine of the hospital business model — averaging about 90.9% of total hospital revenue.
Net patient revenue as an average share of total hospital revenue; the rest comes from investments, philanthropy, and ancillary operations (Trilliant Health)
Revenue From Patient Care

The Payer Mix: Many Customers, Many Prices
The defining feature of hospital revenue is that the same service generates wildly different payments depending on who is paying. A hospital’s payer mix — the proportion of its revenue coming from each type of payer — is therefore one of the most consequential numbers in its finances. In Definitive Healthcare's 2024 analysis of more than 5,700 hospitals, commercial, private, self-pay, and other payers account for about 70.7% of net patient revenue, Medicare about 14.4%, and Medicaid about 14.8% — even though, by the AHA's count, Medicare and Medicaid pay for more than 70% of hospital inpatient days.
These payers do not pay equally well. Commercial insurers generally pay rates well above the hospital’s cost. Government payers pay less — often below cost. In 2023, Medicare paid hospitals roughly 83 cents for every dollar of cost, and Medicare and Medicaid underpayments together totaled about $130 billion, according to the AHA. Medicaid frequently pays even less. The practical consequence is that a hospital’s financial health depends heavily on how many commercially insured patients it serves relative to Medicare and Medicaid patients.
Commercial / Private Insurance
Largest share of net patient revenue (~70.7% with self-pay and other)
Negotiated rates generally above cost
Effectively subsidizes underpaying payers
A favorable payer mix strengthens margins
Government Payers (Medicare/Medicaid)
Medicare ~14.4%, Medicaid ~14.8% of revenue, but over 70% of inpatient days

A high government mix pressures margins
How Different Payers Treat the Same Service
This dynamic produces one of the most important and least understood phenomena in hospital finance: the cross-subsidy. Because government payers often pay below cost, hospitals rely on higher commercial payments to make up the difference. In effect, privately insured patients (and their employers) subsidize the care of Medicare and Medicaid patients. This is why two hospitals with identical clinical operations can have opposite financial fates simply because one sits in a wealthy area with many commercially insured patients and the other serves a low-income community dependent on Medicaid.
The Cost Side: Where the Money Goes
If revenue is complicated, expenses are comparatively straightforward — and dominated by one category. Total compensation and related expenses account for roughly 56% to 60% of total hospital costs. A hospital is, financially, a labor business: physicians, nurses, technicians, and support staff are the overwhelming majority of what it spends. This is why workforce shortages and wage inflation hit hospital finances so hard, and why the contract-labor surge during and after the pandemic was financially devastating.
The remaining expenses fall into supplies and drugs (which have risen sharply with pharmaceutical prices), capital and facilities (the enormous cost of buildings and equipment), and administrative overhead (billing, compliance, IT, and the machinery required to navigate the multi-payer system described above). Because labor is such a large and relatively fixed cost, hospitals have limited ability to quickly cut expenses when revenue falls — a key reason hospital margins are so sensitive to volume and payer mix.
In 2024, hospitals saw a meaningful financial recovery — Kaufman Hall's national operating margin index, a median across U.S. hospitals, reached about 5% for the calendar year, and Fitch noted nonprofit margins flipped positive (a median around 1.2% for early-fiscal-year reporters, up from -0.5% the prior year).

Even so, a 1–5% operating margin is razor-thin for an organization with massive fixed labor and facility costs. A bad flu season, a payer-mix shift toward Medicaid, or a wage spike can erase it. This is why hospital finance treats even profitable years as fragile.
Why a "Good Year" Is Still a Thin Year
Nonprofit vs. For-Profit: Two Different Models
American hospitals come in two broad financial species, and the difference is not cosmetic. For-profit hospitals (such as HCA Healthcare and Tenet Healthcare) are owned by shareholders and exist to generate returns; their margins reflect it. In Q2 2024, HCA posted roughly a 12.8% operating margin and Tenet roughly 14.9% — multiples of the nonprofit median. For-profit systems tend to be disciplined about payer mix, service-line profitability, and cost control because investors demand it.
Nonprofit hospitals — the majority of U.S. hospitals — operate under a fundamentally different bargain. They are exempt from federal income, state, and local property taxes, an exemption KFF valued at about $28.1 billion in 2020 ($14.4 billion federal and $13.7 billion state and local) in foregone revenue. In exchange, they must satisfy the community benefit standard: under IRS Revenue Ruling 69-545 and the Affordable Care Act’s IRC Section 501(r), a nonprofit hospital must demonstrate that it benefits the community rather than private individuals — through charity care, unreimbursed Medicaid, community health programs, education, research, and subsidized services.
A nonprofit hospital still must earn a surplus (revenue above expenses) to fund equipment, buildings, and reserves — it simply reinvests that surplus rather than distributing it to shareholders. The label refers to who owns the profit, not whether the hospital tries to be financially sound. Both species must out-earn their costs to survive.
“Nonprofit” Does Not Mean “No Margin”
This bargain is increasingly contested. Critics note that "community benefit" has no precise federal statutory definition, enforcement is weak, and some nonprofit hospitals provide less charity care than the value of their tax exemption. The federal revenue loss from the exemption is projected at roughly $260 billion over 2025–2034. For anyone studying hospital finance, the lesson is that a nonprofit hospital’s tax status is not a given — it is a conditional privilege tied to obligations that regulators and the public are scrutinizing more closely.
Putting It Together: The Hospital as a System
Once the pieces are assembled, the hospital business model resolves into a clear logic. Revenue is overwhelmingly patient revenue, collected from a mix of payers who pay very different amounts; the favorable commercial payments cross-subsidize the below-cost government payments. Expenses are dominated by labor and are largely fixed in the short run. The gap between the two — the operating margin — is typically thin, often in the low single digits for nonprofits, leaving little cushion against shocks.
A hospital’s finances work like a restaurant where the menu has one price, but the city forces you to charge regulars (Medicare and Medicaid) less than the food costs, while tourists (commercial insurers) pay a premium that keeps the kitchen open. Most of your spending is the cooks’ and servers’ wages, which you can’t cut overnight. If too many regulars show up and too few tourists, you lose money even with a full dining room.
Payer mix, cross-subsidy, and fixed labor costs
This is why so much of hospital strategy reduces to a few levers: improving the payer mix, negotiating better commercial rates, controlling labor costs, growing profitable service lines, and — increasingly — accepting value-based contracts that pay for keeping people healthy rather than for volume. Every topic that follows in hospital finance, from reading the financial statements to capital budgeting to value-based payment, is ultimately about managing the tension this business model creates: a mission to care for everyone, funded by a payment system that pays unevenly and a cost structure that rarely bends.
For the value-based-care era, the model carries a final implication. A business that earns thin margins by filling beds is structurally fragile and misaligned with population health. The shift toward paying hospitals for outcomes — through shared savings, bundled payments, and global budgets — is, at its core, an attempt to rewire this business model so that a healthy community is a financial asset rather than an empty-bed liability.
Net patient revenue — money collected for patient care after discounts and adjustments — averages about 90.9% of total hospital revenue, making the hospital fundamentally a patient-care business supplemented by investment income and philanthropy.
A hospital has many payers paying different prices for the same service; by net patient revenue, payer mix is roughly 70.7% commercial/private/self-pay/other, 14.4% Medicare, and 14.8% Medicaid (Definitive Healthcare, 2024), though Medicare and Medicaid pay for over 70% of inpatient days.
Government payers often pay below cost — Medicare paid roughly 83 cents per dollar of cost in 2023, and Medicare plus Medicaid underpayments reached about $130 billion — forcing hospitals to rely on a cross-subsidy from higher commercial payments.
Expenses are dominated by labor: total compensation accounts for roughly 56–60% of hospital costs and is largely fixed in the short term, making margins highly sensitive to volume and payer mix.
Operating margins are typically thin; even in the recovered year of 2024, medians ran from about 1.2% for nonprofits (Fitch early reporters) to about 5% across all hospitals (Kaufman Hall), versus 12–15% for large for-profit systems like HCA and Tenet.
Nonprofit hospitals are exempt from income, property, and other taxes (worth about $28 billion in 2020, per KFF) in exchange for meeting the community benefit standard under IRS Revenue Ruling 69-545 and ACA Section 501(r).
"Nonprofit" describes who owns the surplus, not whether the hospital seeks one — every hospital must earn more than it spends to fund equipment, facilities, and reserves and to survive.
The thin-margin, volume-dependent business model is structurally misaligned with population health, which is precisely why value-based payment seeks to rewire it so that a healthy community becomes a financial asset rather than a liability.

######## hospital-finance | reading-hospital-financial-statements | Reading a Hospital Financial Statement
Reading a Hospital Financial Statement: The Three Core Reports
Three Documents That Tell the Whole Story
Every hospital, whether a rural critical-access facility or a multibillion-dollar academic system, tells its financial story through the same three core documents: the income statement, the balance sheet, and the cash flow statement. Together with the footnotes to the audited financials, these reports answer three different but related questions: Did the hospital make money this year? What does it own and owe right now? And where did its cash actually come from and go? Learning to read them is the single most transferable skill in hospital finance.
A crucial wrinkle is that the names change depending on who owns the hospital. Because most U.S. hospitals are nonprofit, their statements often carry nonprofit terminology: the income statement becomes the "statement of operations" or "statement of activities," and what a for-profit calls "equity" a nonprofit calls "net assets." The concepts underneath are nearly identical — only the labels differ. This lesson uses both names so you can read either kind of statement with confidence.
The goal is not to become an accountant. It is to be able to pick up a hospital’s financials and quickly form a judgment: Is this organization profitable, liquid, and solvent — or is it heading for trouble? Each of the three statements illuminates one of those three dimensions, and together they reveal far more than any single number like "revenue" or "margin" ever could.
Key Concept: The income statement shows profitability (a flow over time), the balance sheet shows financial position (a snapshot at a moment), and the cash flow statement shows liquidity (where cash actually moved). Reading all three together prevents the mistakes that come from looking at any one alone.
The Income Statement: Did the Hospital Make Money?
The income statement — the statement of operations for a nonprofit — measures financial performance over a period, usually a fiscal year. It starts with revenue and subtracts expenses to arrive at the bottom line. At the top sits the hospital’s lifeblood: net patient service revenue (NPSR), the revenue a hospital expects to collect for services provided after subtracting contractual allowances (the negotiated discounts off its list prices). NPSR is the primary source of revenue for nearly every hospital.
The most important structural feature of a hospital income statement is the split between operating and non-operating items. Transactions that management deems ongoing, major, or central to providing health care — patient revenue and the expenses to deliver care — are reported as operating revenue and expenses. Everything else, most notably investment income from the hospital’s reserves and endowment, is reported as non-operating. This distinction is why a hospital can post a positive bottom line while losing money on actual patient care: strong investment returns can mask a negative operating margin.
The core revenue from patient care after contractual allowances — the engine of the business.
Start with net patient service revenue
Grants, program fees, and other revenue central to operations.
Add other operating revenue
Salaries and benefits (the largest line), supplies, drugs, depreciation, and overhead.
Subtract operating expenses
Operating revenue minus operating expenses — the truest measure of whether core care delivery is sustainable.
Find operating income (or loss)
Investment income and other non-core gains/losses produce the final excess of revenue over expenses (the "bottom line").
Add non-operating items
Reading an Income Statement From Top to Bottom
Always separate operating income from the bottom line. A hospital with a positive overall result but a negative operating margin is losing money on its core mission and surviving on investment returns — a fragile position that the headline "profit" number hides.
Operating Income Is the Number That Matters Most
The Balance Sheet: What Does the Hospital Own and Owe?
The balance sheet — the statement of financial position — is a snapshot at a single moment in time, built on one unbreakable equation: assets equal liabilities plus net assets (equity). Assets are what the hospital owns; liabilities are what it owes; net assets are what would be left over if it paid off everything. The two sides always balance, which is the origin of the name.
Assets divide into current assets — cash, short-term investments, and accounts receivable (money owed by payers for care already delivered) — and non-current assets, dominated by property, plant, and equipment (PP&E): the buildings, MRI machines, and infrastructure that make a hospital so capital-intensive. Liabilities divide the same way: current liabilities like accounts payable and short-term debt, and long-term liabilities like bonds payable and pension obligations. The gap between what a hospital owns and owes — its net assets — reflects its accumulated financial strength and its capacity to reinvest and to borrow.
For nonprofit hospitals, the equity section uses distinctive language. Following FASB ASU 2016-14 (effective 2018), net assets are reported in two categories: net assets without donor restrictions (formerly "unrestricted") and net assets with donor restrictions (formerly "restricted"). Net assets without donor restrictions can be used for any purpose advancing the mission, while restricted net assets carry conditions set by the donor. When analysts assess a nonprofit hospital’s financial cushion, they focus on the unrestricted portion, because that is the money truly available to absorb shocks.
Imagine two hospitals that both report a 3% operating margin this year — identical on the income statement.

Hospital A has months of cash in reserve, modest debt, and strong unrestricted net assets. Hospital B has nearly drained its cash, carries heavy bond debt, and has thin net assets. The income statement says they are equally healthy; the balance sheet reveals that Hospital B is one bad quarter from a crisis. This is why no one judges a hospital on profitability alone.
Why the Balance Sheet Catches What the Income Statement Misses
The Cash Flow Statement: Where Did the Cash Go?
Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact. The income statement is built on accrual accounting, recording revenue when care is delivered — even if the payer takes months to pay. A hospital can report healthy "profit" while its bank account drains, because reported revenue is not the same as collected cash. The cash flow statement closes this gap by tracking the actual movement of money, organized into three activities: operating, investing, and financing.
Cash from operating activities shows whether day-to-day care generates real cash — the most important section for judging sustainability. Cash from investing activities captures purchases and sales of long-term assets, such as buying a new surgical robot or building a wing (large negative numbers here are normal and often healthy, signaling reinvestment). Cash from financing activities reflects borrowing and repaying debt and changes in long-term financing. Reading the three together shows not just whether a hospital made money, but whether that money is real and where it is being deployed.
The three statements are like a fitness assessment. The income statement is your weight change over the year (did you gain or lose?). The balance sheet is a snapshot of your body composition today (muscle vs. fat, strength vs. fragility). The cash flow statement is your actual heartbeat — the real-time circulation that keeps you alive regardless of what the scale says. A good doctor looks at all three; so does a good analyst.
How the three financial statements work together
The First Numbers an Analyst Looks For
Once you can navigate the three statements, a handful of figures give a fast read on a hospital’s health. The most famous is days cash on hand (DCOH) — how many days the hospital could keep operating using only its available cash if all revenue stopped. It is calculated as cash plus cash equivalents plus short-term investments, divided by average daily operating expenses (total expenses minus depreciation and amortization, divided by the days in the period). DCOH draws on both the balance sheet (cash) and the income statement (expenses), which is why it requires reading the statements together.
Benchmarks give the number meaning. Strong liquidity is generally considered to be roughly 150–205 days of cash on hand, with the exact target varying by hospital size, location, and ownership. A hospital with 200 days of cash has a deep cushion; one with 30 days is in danger. Alongside DCOH, analysts check the current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities; 1.0 or higher means short-term obligations are covered) and days in accounts receivable (how long, on average, it takes to collect payment — where a rising number means cash is stuck in unpaid claims).
These metrics are the bridge to the next lesson on financial ratios, but the point here is structural: each ratio pulls data from one or more of the three core statements. You cannot compute days cash on hand without the balance sheet and income statement; you cannot judge collection efficiency without net patient revenue and accounts receivable. Mastering the statements is the prerequisite for every ratio, dashboard, and bond rating that follows — and for forming an honest judgment about whether a hospital is built to last.
Hospitals report through three core statements — the income statement (profitability over time), the balance sheet (financial position at a moment), and the cash flow statement (actual movement of cash) — plus footnotes to the audited financials.
Nonprofit hospitals use different labels: the income statement is the "statement of operations/activities" and "equity" is called "net assets," but the underlying concepts are essentially the same.
Net patient service revenue (NPSR) — revenue expected after contractual allowances — sits at the top of the income statement and is the primary revenue source for nearly every hospital.
Always separate operating income from the bottom line: a hospital can show overall "profit" while losing money on patient care, propped up by non-operating investment income.
The balance sheet rests on assets = liabilities + net assets; for nonprofits, FASB ASU 2016-14 splits net assets into "without donor restrictions" (formerly unrestricted) and "with donor restrictions" (formerly restricted).
The cash flow statement reconciles accrual "profit" with real cash, separating operating, investing, and financing activities — and cash from operations is the truest test of sustainability.
Days cash on hand (DCOH) measures how long a hospital could operate on existing cash; strong levels run roughly 150–205 days, drawing on both the balance sheet and income statement.
Every financial ratio pulls from one or more of the three statements, so mastering the statements is the prerequisite for ratios, dashboards, and bond ratings.

######## hospital-finance | hospital-financial-ratios | Key Financial Ratios for Hospitals
Key Financial Ratios for Hospitals: Reading Health in Five Numbers
Why Raw Numbers Lie and Ratios Tell the Truth
A hospital reporting $50 million in profit sounds healthy — until you learn it has $5 billion in revenue, making that "huge" profit a razor-thin 1% margin. Raw dollar figures are nearly meaningless in isolation because hospitals vary so enormously in size. Financial ratios solve this by expressing each number as a relationship — profit relative to revenue, cash relative to expenses, debt relative to capital — so that a 25-bed rural hospital and a 1,200-bed academic system can be compared on the same scale.
Ratios are also how the people who hold real power over hospitals make decisions. Bond rating agencies, lenders, boards, and state regulators all judge a hospital through ratios and against published benchmark medians, such as those compiled by the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA). A hospital’s ratios determine its credit rating, its borrowing cost, and sometimes its survival. Learning to read them is learning the language in which a hospital’s fate is actually decided.
Hospital financial ratios are conventionally grouped into five categories: profitability, liquidity, capital structure, asset efficiency, and a catch-all "other." Each category answers a different question. Together, they form a complete diagnostic — the financial equivalent of checking vital signs across multiple organ systems rather than taking a single temperature.
Key Concept: A financial ratio expresses one financial figure as a proportion of another, neutralizing differences in size so hospitals can be compared to each other and to benchmark medians. Ratios fall into five families: profitability, liquidity, capital structure, asset efficiency, and other.
Recent national hospital operating-margin medians ran roughly 1–2% in 2024–2025 — profitable but very thin (HFMA / Fitch)
Median Operating Margin
~1–2%
Median days cash on hand ran roughly 215–220 days in fiscal 2024, a favorable liquidity cushion versus history (Fitch)
Days Cash on Hand
~215–220 days
Profitability: Is the Hospital Earning a Surplus?
Profitability ratios measure whether an organization can produce a surplus of revenue over expenses. The two headline measures are operating margin and total margin. Operating margin is operating income divided by operating revenue — it isolates whether the core business of delivering care is sustainable. Total margin is the bottom line (including non-operating items like investment income) divided by total revenue. The gap between them reveals how much a hospital leans on investment returns rather than patient care to stay in the black.
The numbers are sobering. Recent medians put hospital operating margins around 1–2%, and Fitch reported its rated-credit median operating margin rising from roughly 0.2% in 2022 to about 1.1% in 2024 and 1.5% in 2025. These are slim figures for organizations carrying enormous fixed costs. A 1–2% operating margin means that a modest shift in payer mix, a wage spike, or a soft quarter of volume can tip a hospital from surplus to loss.
If a hospital’s total margin is strongly positive but its operating margin is near zero or negative, the institution is being kept afloat by investment income, not by patient care. That is a structurally fragile position, because investment returns are volatile and outside the hospital’s control.
Operating Margin vs. Total Margin: Mind the Gap
Liquidity: Can the Hospital Pay Its Bills?
Liquidity ratios measure the ability to meet short-term obligations, collect what is owed, and maintain a cash position. The most watched is days cash on hand (DCOH) — how many days the hospital could keep operating on existing cash if revenue stopped — calculated from cash and investments divided by average daily operating expenses (excluding depreciation). Recent medians around 215–220 days represent a strong cushion; a hospital below 50 days is in genuine danger.
Two other liquidity measures matter. The current ratio (current assets divided by current liabilities) tests whether short-term obligations are covered; a value of 1.0 or higher means current assets are sufficient to pay current liabilities. Days in accounts receivable measures the average collection period — net patient receivables divided by average daily net patient revenue. A rising number is a warning: it means cash is trapped in unpaid claims, often signaling billing problems, denials, or payer slow-walking that starve operations of working capital.
How long could the hospital survive with no incoming revenue? Strong is roughly 150–220+ days.
Days cash on hand
Are short-term assets enough to cover short-term debts? 1.0 or higher is the floor.
Current ratio
How fast does the hospital collect? Lower is better; a rising trend signals trapped cash.
Days in accounts receivable
How much cash backs the debt? Recent medians around 170–178% indicate flexibility.

The Liquidity Quick-Check
Capital Structure and Asset Efficiency: Built to Last?
Capital structure ratios measure how a hospital’s assets are financed and its capacity to take on new debt — the questions a bond rating agency cares about most. Equity financing (total net assets divided by total assets) shows how much of the hospital is funded by its own resources versus debt; a higher value means more room to borrow. Debt service coverage measures whether the hospital generates enough cash to cover its debt payments (principal, interest, and leases); a ratio below 1.0 means it is not generating enough to meet obligations — a serious red flag for lenders.
Asset efficiency ratios relate revenue to the assets used to generate it, and one deserves special attention: average age of plant. Despite its name, it is a financial ratio, not a literal measurement — calculated as accumulated depreciation divided by annual depreciation expense. It approximates how "old" a hospital’s buildings and equipment are in financial terms. A rising average age of plant signals deferred investment and a looming need for capital: the hospital is running on aging infrastructure that will soon demand expensive replacement.
When Fitch or Moody’s rates a hospital’s bonds, no single ratio decides the grade. A strong analyst reads the set: an operating margin around 1–2%, days cash on hand near 200, cash-to-debt above 170%, debt service coverage comfortably above 1.0, and an average age of plant that is not creeping upward.

A hospital strong on profitability but weak on liquidity, or flush with cash but carrying an aging plant and thin debt coverage, will be rated and priced accordingly. The rating then determines the interest rate the hospital pays to borrow — turning these ratios directly into millions of dollars of cost.
How Rating Agencies Read These Ratios Together
Using Ratios Wisely: Trends, Benchmarks, and Context
A ratio in isolation is only a starting point; its meaning comes from comparison. Two comparisons matter most. First, benchmarking: how does the hospital compare to the median for similar hospitals, using sources like HFMA’s published ratio medians? A current ratio of 1.5 means little until you know peers run at 2.0. Second, trending: which direction is the ratio moving over several years? A days-cash-on-hand figure of 120 is reassuring if it rose from 80, and alarming if it fell from 200. The trajectory often matters more than the snapshot.
Financial ratios are like a patient’s vital signs. No single vital — heart rate, blood pressure, temperature, oxygen — tells you whether someone is healthy; a clinician reads them as a set and watches how they change over time. A hospital with a great profitability "pulse" but a dangerously low liquidity "blood pressure" is no healthier than a patient with one perfect vital and one in crisis.
Reading financial ratios as a complete diagnostic
Ratios also have limits that a careful analyst respects. They can be distorted by one-time events (a large gift, a lawsuit, an asset sale), by accounting choices, and by differences between hospital types — a critical-access rural hospital and an urban academic medical center should not be held to identical targets. Days cash on hand, in particular, does not capture access to lines of credit or the timing of large obligations, so even a favorable number can hide a coming squeeze. Ratios are a powerful lens, not a verdict.
Put together, the five categories give a hospital’s complete financial picture: Is it profitable (profitability)? Can it pay its bills (liquidity)? Is it financed sustainably and able to borrow (capital structure)? Is it using its assets efficiently and keeping them current (asset efficiency)? For everyone from a board member to a state regulator to a value-based-care strategist, fluency in these ratios is the difference between reacting to last year’s crisis and seeing next year’s coming.
Financial ratios express one figure as a proportion of another, neutralizing size differences so hospitals can be compared to peers and to benchmark medians (e.g., HFMA), and they drive bond ratings, borrowing costs, and regulatory judgments.
Hospital ratios fall into five categories: profitability, liquidity, capital structure, asset efficiency, and other — each answering a different diagnostic question.
Operating margin (operating income ÷ operating revenue) isolates core care sustainability; total margin includes non-operating income — a large gap between them signals reliance on investment returns rather than patient care.
Recent operating-margin medians run roughly 1–2% (Fitch rated-credit median ~1.1% in 2024 and ~1.5% in 2025), leaving little cushion against shocks.
Key liquidity ratios are days cash on hand (recent medians ~215–220 days), the current ratio (≥1.0 floor), days in accounts receivable (lower is better), and cash-to-debt (~170–178%).
Capital structure ratios — equity financing and debt service coverage (a ratio below 1.0 means the hospital cannot cover its debt payments) — measure financing sustainability and borrowing capacity.
Average age of plant (accumulated depreciation ÷ depreciation expense) is a financial, not physical, measure; a rising value warns of deferred investment and a looming need for capital.
Ratios gain meaning only through benchmarking against peers and trending over time, and they have real limits — distorted by one-time events, accounting choices, and hospital-type differences — so they inform judgment rather than replace it.
