######## hospital-finance | payer-mix-revenue | Payer Mix and Its Impact on Revenue
Payer Mix and Its Impact on Hospital Revenue
The Most Important Number You’ve Never Heard Of
Ask a hospital CFO what keeps them up at night, and "payer mix" will be near the top of the list. Payer mix is the proportion of a hospital’s patients — or revenue — coming from each type of payer: commercial insurers, Medicare, Medicaid, and the uninsured (self-pay). It is one of the single most powerful determinants of whether a hospital thrives or struggles, because the same exact service generates dramatically different payment depending on who is footing the bill.
The reason payer mix matters so much is a structural quirk of American healthcare: government payers reimburse hospitals below the cost of providing care, while commercial insurers pay well above it. A hospital does not control its prices the way an ordinary business does; instead, its revenue is dictated by the blend of payers walking through its doors. Two hospitals delivering identical care can have completely different financial fates simply because one serves more commercially insured patients and the other more Medicaid patients.
This lesson unpacks how payer mix works, why the gap between payers is so large, how it produces the cross-subsidy that holds American hospital finance together, and why a single policy change — like the long-scheduled Medicaid DSH cuts — can threaten the survival of the hospitals serving the most vulnerable communities.
Key Concept: Payer mix is the distribution of a hospital’s patients or revenue across payer types (commercial, Medicare, Medicaid, self-pay). Because each payer reimburses at a very different rate, payer mix is a primary driver of a hospital’s financial health.
In 2022, private insurers paid hospitals on average 254% of what Medicare would pay for the same services — up from 224% in 2020 (RAND, 2024)
Commercial vs. Medicare Prices
254%
MedPAC put hospitals' overall fee-for-service Medicare margin at -13% in 2023 and projects about -13% for 2025 — paid below the cost of care (MedPAC, March 2025)
Medicare FFS Margin (2023)
-13%
The Volume–Revenue Paradox
The most revealing fact about payer mix is that patient volume and revenue do not line up. Medicare and Medicaid together accounted for about two-thirds (67%) of all hospital discharges in 2023 — Medicare nearly half (46%) and Medicaid more than a fifth (21%) — while private insurance covered just 24% of discharges and self-pay 4%. Yet when you look at revenue, the picture inverts: commercial, private, self-pay, and other payers together generate roughly 70.7% of hospital net patient revenue, while Medicare contributes about 14.4% and Medicaid about 14.8% (Definitive Healthcare, 2024).
Read those two sets of numbers side by side and the paradox is stark. Government payers fill most of the beds but provide less than half the money; commercial payers fill a minority of beds but provide the lion’s share of revenue. A bed occupied by a commercially insured patient is worth far more to the hospital’s bottom line than the same bed occupied by a Medicaid patient — even though the care delivered is identical.
Share of Discharges (Volume)
Medicare ~46% of discharges
Medicaid ~21% of discharges
Private insurance ~24% of discharges
Self-pay ~4% of discharges
Government payers fill ~67% of beds
Share of Net Revenue (Money)
Commercial/private/self-pay/other ~70.7%
Medicare ~14.4%
Medicaid ~14.8%
Government payers provide <50% of revenue
Commercial dollars dominate the bottom line
Discharges vs. Revenue: The Inversion
A hospital can run at full occupancy and still lose money if too many of those patients are covered by below-cost government payers. Volume alone says nothing about financial health — payer mix is what turns volume into solvency or into deeper losses.
Why "Filling Beds" Is Not the Same as "Making Money"
Why the Payment Gap Is So Large
The chasm between what commercial and government payers pay is not subtle. The RAND Corporation, analyzing billions of dollars in claims across thousands of hospitals, found that in 2022 employers and private insurers paid on average 254% of what Medicare would have paid for the same services at the same facilities — a figure that has climbed from 224% in 2020 and 247% in 2018. In some states, commercial prices averaged above 300% of Medicare. Meanwhile, MedPAC put hospitals' fee-for-service Medicare margin at -13% in 2023, and Medicaid often pays even less.
These divergent trajectories compound over time. Inpatient hospital prices paid by private insurers rose about 50% from mid-2014 to late 2024 — twice the 25% growth in Medicare inpatient prices and more than twice the 19% growth in Medicaid prices over the same span. Government rates are administratively set and grow slowly; commercial rates are negotiated and have escalated rapidly. The result is an ever-widening gap that makes commercial patients increasingly valuable and government patients increasingly costly to serve.
This gap is the engine behind the cross-subsidy that defines hospital finance. Because Medicare and Medicaid pay below cost, hospitals depend on commercial payments above cost to cover the shortfall. In effect, privately insured patients and their employers subsidize the care of government-insured patients. A hospital with a rich commercial payer mix has a built-in cushion; a hospital dependent on Medicaid and the uninsured has none.
Safety-Net Hospitals and the Limits of Cost-Shifting
The cross-subsidy mechanism has a brutal corollary: it only works if you have commercial patients to shift costs onto. Safety-net hospitals — those serving large numbers of Medicaid and uninsured patients — usually have a low percentage of commercially insured patients, which means they cannot cost-shift their losses to private insurers. They are squeezed from both sides: more below-cost patients, fewer above-cost patients to make up the difference.
To keep these essential hospitals afloat, federal law requires states to make Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) payments — supplemental funding to hospitals that serve a disproportionate share of low-income, uninsured, and Medicaid patients. DSH payments help offset the cost of uncompensated care and, for many safety-net and teaching hospitals, constitute a significant portion of total revenue. DSH is, in essence, the government’s acknowledgment that its own below-cost payments would otherwise bankrupt the hospitals serving the neediest patients.
Medicaid DSH payment cuts, enacted in the ACA and delayed repeatedly for more than a decade, were scheduled to take effect on October 1, 2025, at $8 billion a year for FY 2026–2028. Congress delayed them again in a November 2025 continuing resolution, and the funding package signed on February 3, 2026 eliminated the FY 2026 and FY 2027 reductions — leaving one year, about $8 billion, still scheduled for FY 2028.

For safety-net hospitals, the near-miss is itself the lesson: because they cannot cost-shift to commercial payers, a supplemental payment stream that Congress must keep rescuing at the last minute can make or break their budgets — and the remaining cut is scheduled to arrive as tightened Medicaid eligibility is projected to increase the number of uninsured patients. It is a textbook illustration of how a payer-mix-dependent hospital lives or dies by policy decisions it does not control.
The Medicaid DSH Cuts: Scheduled, Delayed, Partly Eliminated
Managing Payer Mix: Strategy and Its Ethical Edge
Because payer mix is so consequential, hospitals actively try to influence it — and here the financial logic collides with the mission. Strategies to improve payer mix include locating new facilities and service lines in commercially insured areas, marketing profitable elective services (orthopedics, cardiology) that attract well-insured patients, negotiating harder with commercial payers, and improving the revenue cycle so that more of what is billed is actually collected. Each of these can shift the blend toward higher-paying payers.
Payer mix works like a restaurant whose city mandates that it serve some customers at a loss. The restaurant survives only by attracting enough full-price diners to subsidize the discounted ones. A bistro in a wealthy neighborhood manages easily; one required to serve mostly discounted customers, with few full-price diners nearby, slowly bleeds out — no matter how good its food. DSH payments are the city’s subsidy to keep that second restaurant’s doors open.
How payer mix and the cross-subsidy work
But payer-mix management has a sharp ethical edge. Strategies that optimize the payer mix can shade into "payer-mix avoidance" — quietly steering away from Medicaid and uninsured patients toward commercially insured ones. Taken too far, this undermines access for vulnerable populations and, for nonprofit hospitals, conflicts directly with the community-benefit obligations that justify their tax exemption. The tension between financial survival (which rewards a commercial-heavy mix) and mission (which demands serving everyone) is one of the defining dilemmas of hospital management.
This tension is also a central argument for value-based care and global budgets. As long as hospitals are paid per service, payer mix dictates their fate and rewards them for chasing well-insured patients. Models that pay for keeping a defined population healthy — regardless of each patient’s insurance — begin to loosen the grip of payer mix on hospital strategy. Understanding payer mix is therefore not just an accounting exercise; it is the key to understanding why American hospitals behave the way they do, and why reformers are so determined to change how they are paid.
Payer mix — the distribution of a hospital’s patients or revenue across commercial, Medicare, Medicaid, and self-pay — is a primary driver of financial health because each payer reimburses at very different rates.
Volume and revenue diverge sharply: Medicare and Medicaid filled about 67% of discharges in 2023 but provided under half of revenue, while commercial/private/self-pay generated roughly 70.7% of net patient revenue from only ~28% of discharges.
Government payers reimburse below cost (MedPAC put hospitals' Medicare fee-for-service margin at -13% in 2023), while commercial payers pay well above it — RAND found private plans paid 254% of Medicare rates in 2022.
The payment gap is widening: private inpatient prices rose ~50% from 2014–2024 versus 25% for Medicare and 19% for Medicaid, deepening the cross-subsidy in which commercial payments cover below-cost government care.
Safety-net hospitals serve many Medicaid and uninsured patients but have few commercial patients, so they cannot cost-shift losses — making them structurally vulnerable.
Disproportionate Share Hospital (DSH) payments are federally required supplemental funds that help safety-net hospitals offset uncompensated care, often forming a significant share of their revenue.
Medicaid DSH cuts of $8 billion a year were scheduled to begin October 1, 2025; after short-term delays, a February 2026 funding law eliminated the FY 2026 and FY 2027 cuts, leaving about $8 billion scheduled for FY 2028 — just as tightened eligibility threatens to raise uncompensated care.
Hospitals actively manage payer mix through facility location, service-line strategy, and payer negotiation — but pushing toward "payer-mix avoidance" of Medicaid/uninsured patients conflicts with access and nonprofit community-benefit obligations, a core argument for value-based payment.

######## hospital-finance | chargemaster-gross-net-revenue | Chargemaster and Gross vs Net Revenue
The Chargemaster and Gross vs. Net Revenue: Why Hospital Prices Are Fiction
The $5,000 MRI That Nobody Pays $5,000 For
A hospital lists an MRI at $5,000. A commercial insurer pays $1,200 for it. Medicare pays perhaps $500. A cash-paying patient might be quoted $3,200. The uninsured patient who never negotiates gets billed the full $5,000. Same machine, same scan, same hospital — four wildly different prices, none of which has much to do with what the scan actually costs to perform. Welcome to the strangest pricing system in the American economy, governed by a document called the chargemaster.
The chargemaster — formally the charge description master (CDM) — is a comprehensive listing of every billable item and service a hospital offers, each paired with a price and standardized billing codes. Every blood test, surgical supply, medication dose, room-day, and procedure has its own line item, and a large hospital’s chargemaster can contain tens of thousands of entries. The price attached to each item is called the gross charge or "list price."
Understanding the chargemaster is the key to one of hospital finance’s most important distinctions: the difference between what a hospital charges (gross revenue) and what it actually collects (net revenue). Confusing the two leads to wildly wrong conclusions about hospital finances — and the gap between them is where almost all the action in hospital revenue lives.
Key Concept: The chargemaster (CDM) is a hospital’s master list of every billable item and its gross charge (list price). Gross charges are the starting point for billing, but they are not what the hospital actually collects — net revenue is.
The average hospital’s charges are about 3.4 times the actual cost of providing care, with some exceeding a 10x charge-to-cost ratio (Health Affairs / NIH studies)
Charges vs. Actual Cost
~3.4x
Hospitals’ chargemaster list prices are on average about 164% higher than negotiated prices for the same services (Health Affairs)
List Price Over Negotiated
164%
Gross Revenue, Contractual Allowances, and Net Revenue
The relationship among the key terms is best understood as a subtraction. Gross revenue (or gross charges) is the total amount a hospital bills for its services during a period, calculated at full chargemaster prices. But almost no one pays full chargemaster prices. Each insurer has a negotiated rate — the contractually agreed amount it will actually pay — that is far lower. The difference between the gross charge and what is contractually allowed is called the contractual allowance.
Net patient revenue is what remains after subtracting contractual allowances, charity care, and bad debt from gross charges. It is the money the hospital actually expects to collect — and it is dramatically lower than gross revenue. Using the earlier example: a $5,000 chargemaster MRI with an insurer’s $1,200 negotiated rate generates a $3,800 contractual allowance and just $1,200 in net revenue. The $5,000 gross charge is essentially a fiction; the $1,200 is the financial reality.
The full chargemaster list price for every item billed — e.g., $5,000 for an MRI.
Start with the gross charge
The difference between the list price and the payer’s negotiated rate — the discount the hospital agreed to.
Subtract contractual allowances
Care provided free to those who qualify, plus bills that go uncollected.
Subtract charity care and bad debt
What the hospital actually expects to collect — the only revenue figure that reflects financial reality.
Arrive at net patient revenue
From Gross Charge to Net Revenue
Gross revenue figures are inflated by chargemaster fiction and can be several times higher than net revenue. Headlines about hospitals "charging" enormous sums almost always cite gross charges. The number that matters for solvency, margins, and analysis is net patient revenue.
Never Judge a Hospital by Gross Charges
Why Chargemaster Prices Are So High — and So Meaningless
If almost no one pays them, why are chargemaster prices set so absurdly high? The answer is a self-reinforcing cycle that has little to do with cost. Hospitals inflate chargemaster prices because insurers negotiate discounts off the list price; insurers then demand steeper discounts as prices rise; and hospitals raise list prices further to preserve revenue after those discounts. Over time this ratchet detaches list prices from any rational basis. Between 1996 and 2017, chargemaster markups increased by an average of 155% across more than 3,400 acute-care hospitals.
The result is markups that strain belief. The average hospital’s charges run about 3.4 times the actual cost of care, and the average charge-to-cost ratio across patient-care departments has been measured anywhere from 1.8 to 28.5, with for-profit hospitals carrying notably higher ratios than government hospitals. Researchers have found that both cash prices and commercial negotiated rates are typically set as a consistent percentage discount off the chargemaster — cash prices averaging around 64% and commercial negotiated rates around 58% of chargemaster prices — which is why the inflated list price still influences what real payers pay.
The chargemaster works like the "manufacturer’s suggested retail price" on a car windshield that no one actually pays. The sticker says $50,000; the dealer expects to negotiate down to $38,000; a savvy buyer pays $35,000; and only the customer who walks in and pays the sticker without haggling gets soaked. The sticker exists mainly to anchor the negotiation — and in hospitals, the uninsured are the ones most likely to be billed the sticker.
Chargemaster list prices vs. negotiated rates
This is why chargemaster prices are described as essentially meaningless as a measure of value, yet harmful in practice. They are meaningless because they reflect a negotiating posture rather than cost or quality. They are harmful because the people least able to negotiate — the uninsured and out-of-network patients — are precisely those most likely to be charged the full, inflated list price, turning the chargemaster into a regressive engine of medical debt.
Price Transparency: Forcing the Fiction Into the Open
For decades, chargemaster prices and negotiated rates were closely guarded secrets, making it impossible for patients to shop or for researchers to compare. Federal hospital price transparency rules changed that. Hospitals are now required to publish a machine-readable file disclosing five standard charges for their items and services: the gross chargemaster charge, the discounted cash price, the payer-specific negotiated charge, and the de-identified minimum and maximum negotiated charges.
CMS has steadily tightened the requirements. Starting in July 2024, hospitals must use a standardized CMS template in a non-proprietary format (CSV or JSON), making the data far more usable. Enforcement carries teeth: CMS can levy fines of up to $5,500 per day for non-compliance at hospitals with 30 or more beds. As of late 2024, roughly 70% of hospitals were substantially compliant with all five required data elements, about 15% posted partial files (often missing payer-specific negotiated rates), and about 15% remained non-compliant.
Compliance has been uneven. A 2024 HHS Office of Inspector General audit of 100 hospitals found 37 failed to meet key price-transparency requirements, with 34 not complying with the machine-readable file rules — yet by September 2024 CMS had issued only 14 civil monetary penalties nationwide, totaling about $4 million.

In February 2025, a federal executive order directed agencies to ramp up enforcement of price transparency within 90 days, signaling that the era of lax enforcement may be ending. For hospital finance teams, transparency has shifted from a back-office compliance task to a strategic exposure: published negotiated rates can now be seen by competitors, employers, and the insurers across the negotiating table.
Transparency Meets Enforcement (2024–2025)
Why This Matters Beyond the Billing Office
The chargemaster is not just an administrative artifact; it sits at the center of how hospitals manage revenue. The chargemaster team must keep tens of thousands of codes and prices accurate and current — an error in a single high-volume code can cost or expose the hospital to millions. Because cash prices and negotiated rates are often calculated as percentages of chargemaster prices, the list price still cascades into real collections, which is why hospitals continue to maintain and update it even as everyone acknowledges it is largely fiction.
For patients, the gross-versus-net gap is the source of enormous confusion and harm. A patient who receives a bill at full chargemaster rates is seeing a number almost no insured person would ever pay. Understanding that gross charges are negotiable — and that hospitals routinely collect a fraction of them — is the foundation of medical-bill advocacy and of the charity-care and financial-assistance policies that nonprofit hospitals are obligated to offer.
Finally, the chargemaster illustrates exactly why value-based care exists. A payment system built on inflated, arbitrary list prices and opaque negotiated discounts is the antithesis of paying for value. The push toward transparency, reference pricing, and ultimately models that pay for outcomes rather than line-item charges is, in large part, an effort to escape the distorting gravity of the chargemaster. To understand hospital revenue, you must first understand that the prices are not real — and then understand the elaborate machinery that turns those fictional prices into the very real dollars a hospital lives on.
The chargemaster (charge description master, or CDM) is a hospital’s master list of every billable item and its gross charge (list price), often containing tens of thousands of entries.
Gross revenue is what a hospital bills at full chargemaster prices; net patient revenue is what it actually collects after subtracting contractual allowances, charity care, and bad debt — and it is far lower.
A contractual allowance is the difference between the chargemaster price and a payer’s negotiated rate; it represents the discount the hospital agreed to and is not real revenue.
Chargemaster prices are extremely inflated — averaging about 3.4 times actual cost and roughly 164% above negotiated prices — because of a self-reinforcing cycle of list-price inflation and insurer discounting, not because of cost.
List prices are largely meaningless as a measure of value but harmful in practice, because the uninsured and out-of-network patients are the ones most likely to be billed the full inflated charge.

Enforcement is tightening: fines reach up to $5,500/day for larger non-compliant hospitals; ~70% were substantially compliant by late 2024, and a February 2025 executive order directed stronger enforcement.
Because cash prices and negotiated rates are often set as percentages of chargemaster prices, the fictional list price still cascades into real collections — and the whole distorted system is a core argument for value-based payment.

######## hospital-finance | contractual-adjustments-charity | Contractual Adjustments, Charity Care, and Bad Debt
Contractual Adjustments, Charity Care, and Bad Debt: The Three Ways Hospitals Don't Get Paid
The Gap Between Billed and Collected
In the previous lesson, we saw that a hospital’s gross charges (what it bills at chargemaster prices) are far higher than its net revenue (what it actually collects). This lesson dissects exactly where that money goes. The difference between what a hospital bills and what it keeps is not one thing — it is three distinct categories, each with its own cause, accounting treatment, and policy significance: contractual adjustments, charity care, and bad debt.
Confusing these three is one of the most common errors in hospital finance, and it leads to badly wrong conclusions. A contractual adjustment is a planned discount the hospital agreed to. Charity care is care the hospital chose to give away to those who cannot pay. Bad debt is money the hospital expected to collect but never received. They look similar on a statement — all three reduce gross charges down toward net revenue — but they mean completely different things about the hospital and its patients.
Getting the distinctions right matters enormously. They determine how a hospital reports its finances, whether a nonprofit meets its community-benefit obligations, how much "uncompensated care" the sector claims, and how aggressively a hospital pursues patients for unpaid bills. This is where hospital finance, tax law, and medical-debt policy all intersect.
Key Concept: Three different write-downs separate gross charges from net revenue. Contractual adjustments are agreed payer discounts (not uncompensated care). Charity care is free/discounted care for those who cannot pay. Bad debt is expected payment that was never received. Charity care + bad debt = uncompensated care.
U.S. hospitals provided almost $745 billion in uncompensated care between 2000 and 2020 (American Hospital Association)
Uncompensated Care, 2000–2020
~$745B
Charity care plus bad debt, measured at cost, in a single year (American Hospital Association, 2022 fact sheet)
Uncompensated Care in 2020
$42.7B
Contractual Adjustments: The Discount You Agreed To
A contractual adjustment (or contractual allowance) is the difference between a hospital’s gross charge and the amount a payer is contractually obligated to pay under its negotiated rate. If a hospital bills $5,000 for a procedure and the insurer’s contract says it will pay $1,200, the $3,800 difference is a contractual adjustment. Crucially, this is not money the hospital ever expected to receive — it is the discount baked into the contract the hospital signed.
This is the single most important point about contractual adjustments: they are not uncompensated care. The IRS is explicit that charity care excludes contractual adjustments with third-party payors, self-pay or prompt-pay discounts, and the gap between Medicare/Medicaid revenue and cost. A contractual adjustment simply reflects the reality that chargemaster prices are fiction and negotiated rates are the truth. By far the largest portion of the gap between gross and net revenue is contractual adjustments — and it represents a planned discount, not a loss or a charitable act.
Hospitals (and headlines) sometimes describe the gap between inflated chargemaster prices and negotiated payments as money "lost" or "given away." It is neither. A contractual adjustment is a discount off a fictional list price the hospital itself set artificially high — not a charitable contribution and not uncompensated care.
Contractual Adjustments Are Not "Losses"
Charity Care vs. Bad Debt: Intent Is the Dividing Line
Once contractual adjustments are set aside, the remaining unpaid amounts fall into two categories that look identical on a balance sheet but differ entirely in meaning. The dividing line is intent and expectation. Charity care is free or discounted care provided to patients who are unable to pay and who meet the hospital’s specified income and asset criteria. The hospital never expected payment — it deliberately provided the care for free or at a reduced cost to those in need.
Bad debt is the opposite: it represents services for which the hospital expected payment but never received it. Bad debt arises when patients who could potentially pay — or who never applied for financial assistance — simply do not pay their bills, whether because they cannot, will not, or never engaged with the billing process. The same unpaid $2,000 hospital bill is charity care if the patient qualified for and received financial assistance, but bad debt if the patient simply never paid and never applied.
Charity Care
Hospital never expected payment
Patient qualifies under income/asset criteria
Deliberately provided free or discounted
Counts toward nonprofit community benefit
Reflects the hospital’s charitable mission
Bad Debt
Hospital expected payment but did not collect
Patient may not have applied for assistance
Results from non-payment, not a granted discount
Treated as a credit loss, not charity
Often reflects gaps in screening or collections
Charity Care vs. Bad Debt
Together, charity care and bad debt make up uncompensated care — the overall measure of hospital care for which no payment was received from patient or insurer. This is the number the hospital industry cites to demonstrate the burden of serving the uninsured and underinsured. Note what it excludes: contractual adjustments and the Medicare/Medicaid shortfall are not part of uncompensated care, which is why precise definitions matter so much in debates about hospital finances.
Why the Distinction Has Legal Teeth: Section 501(r)
For nonprofit hospitals, the line between charity care and bad debt is not just an accounting nicety — it is a legal obligation tied to their tax exemption. Under Internal Revenue Code Section 501(r), enacted as part of the Affordable Care Act, tax-exempt hospitals must establish a written financial assistance policy (FAP) and a separate written policy for emergency medical care. The FAP must spell out the eligibility criteria for charity care, how patients apply, and how the hospital distinguishes charity care from bad debt.
Section 501(r) goes further, imposing concrete patient protections. It limits the amounts a hospital can charge financial-assistance-eligible patients for emergency or medically necessary care (they cannot be billed more than the amounts generally billed to insured patients), and it restricts "extraordinary collection actions" — such as lawsuits, wage garnishment, or reporting to credit agencies — until the hospital has made reasonable efforts to determine whether the patient qualifies for financial assistance. A hospital that fails these requirements risks its tax-exempt status.
Imagine a uninsured patient treated in the ER who never fills out a financial-assistance application. If the hospital simply sends the bill to collections, the unpaid amount becomes bad debt — and the patient may face aggressive collection actions.

If instead the hospital screens the patient and determines they would have qualified for financial assistance (sometimes called "presumptive eligibility"), the same care is reclassified as charity care. The dollars written off are similar, but the meaning is opposite: one is a failure of process that harms a vulnerable patient and inflates bad debt; the other fulfills the hospital’s charitable mission and its 501(r) obligations. This is why screening patients for assistance is both an ethical and a financial priority.
Why "Presumptive Charity" Matters
The Bigger Picture: A Rising Burden
These categories are not static — they move with the economy and with policy. Uncompensated care has been an enormous and growing burden: U.S. hospitals provided almost $745 billion in uncompensated care between 2000 and 2020, including $42.7 billion in 2020 alone (AHA). And it moves with coverage: when pandemic-era Medicaid continuous-enrollment protections unwound in 2023 and more patients lost insurance, hospitals faced more uninsured patients and more unpaid bills.
The strain falls unevenly. Rural and safety-net hospitals, which serve disproportionate numbers of uninsured and low-income patients, absorb the most uncompensated care while having the fewest commercial patients to offset it. As uncompensated care rises, these facilities are forced to cut services, delay investments, or close — exactly the institutions whose communities can least afford to lose them. The scheduled Medicaid DSH cuts, discussed in the payer-mix lesson, threaten to land on top of this rising uncompensated-care burden.
Think of a hospital’s billed charges as a restaurant tab. The contractual adjustment is the standing discount the regular customer’s membership card always applies — expected and agreed. Charity care is the meal the owner deliberately comps for someone who clearly can’t pay. Bad debt is the diner who quietly walks out without paying a bill the owner fully expected to collect. All three reduce the till, but only a careless bookkeeper would record them the same way.
Contractual adjustments vs. charity care vs. bad debt
For the student of hospital finance, the lesson is precision. When you see that a hospital "wrote off" a large sum, the first question is always: which kind of write-off? A mountain of contractual adjustments is normal and meaningless as a measure of charity. A large charity-care figure may reflect genuine community benefit. A swelling bad-debt figure may signal a broken financial-assistance process or a community losing insurance. Three numbers that look alike tell three completely different stories — and knowing which is which is the mark of someone who actually understands how hospitals get paid, and how they don’t.
The gap between a hospital’s gross charges and net revenue comes from three distinct categories: contractual adjustments, charity care, and bad debt — each with a different cause and meaning.
A contractual adjustment is the agreed difference between the chargemaster price and a payer’s negotiated rate; it is a planned discount, NOT uncompensated care and NOT a loss.
Charity care is care the hospital never expected to be paid for, provided free or discounted to patients who meet income/asset criteria; bad debt is care the hospital expected payment for but never received.
The dividing line between charity care and bad debt is intent and expectation — the same unpaid bill can be either, depending on whether the patient qualified for and received financial assistance.
Charity care plus bad debt equals uncompensated care; this measure excludes contractual adjustments and the Medicare/Medicaid payment shortfall.
IRC Section 501(r) requires tax-exempt hospitals to maintain a written financial assistance policy (FAP), limit charges to FAP-eligible patients, and restrict extraordinary collection actions until they determine assistance eligibility.
Screening patients for assistance ("presumptive eligibility") can reclassify bad debt as charity care — fulfilling the charitable mission and 501(r) obligations rather than subjecting vulnerable patients to aggressive collections.
Uncompensated care is large and rising — almost $745 billion from 2000–2020, and $42.7 billion in 2020 alone — and it falls hardest on rural and safety-net hospitals.

######## hospital-finance | direct-indirect-costs | Direct vs Indirect Costs in Healthcare
Direct vs. Indirect Costs in Healthcare: What Care Actually Costs
The Deceptively Hard Question: What Does It Cost?
Ask what a hospital charges for an appendectomy and you can look it up on the chargemaster. Ask what an appendectomy actually costs the hospital to perform, and you have entered one of the hardest problems in all of finance. The surgeon’s time and the sutures are easy. But what about the hospital’s electricity, the billing department, the CEO’s salary, the parking garage, the IT systems, the housekeeping staff who clean the operating room between cases? All of these are part of the true cost — but none of them belongs to that single surgery in any obvious way.
Cost accounting is the discipline that answers this question, and it begins with a single foundational distinction: the difference between direct costs and indirect costs. Direct costs can be traced to a specific patient, service, or department. Indirect costs — also called overhead — support the whole organization and cannot be tied to any one service without a deliberate allocation method. Getting this distinction right is the prerequisite for nearly everything else hospitals do with money: setting prices, evaluating service lines, negotiating contracts, and deciding whether a given payment actually covers the cost of care.
This matters more than ever under value-based care. When a hospital accepts a fixed payment for an episode or a population, it can no longer simply bill for more services to cover its costs — it must actually know what its costs are. A hospital that cannot accurately cost its care is flying blind into financial risk.
Key Concept: Direct costs are traceable to a specific patient, service, or department (e.g., a drug given to a patient). Indirect costs (overhead) support the whole organization and cannot be tied to one service without allocation (e.g., administration, utilities, housekeeping).
Direct Costs: Traceable to the Care Itself
Direct costs are those directly attributable to patient care — the costs that exist because a specific service was delivered. Classic examples include nursing services, drugs, medical supplies, diagnostic imaging, rehabilitation, and food services. In hospital accounting, the departments that directly provide services to patients — radiology, the operating room, the laboratory — are called direct cost centers (or revenue-producing departments), and the costs they incur are direct costs.
A practical test cuts through the ambiguity: if the operating unit did not exist, would this cost also disappear? If a hospital closed its radiology department, the radiologists’ salaries, the contrast dye, and the imaging supplies would vanish — those are direct costs of radiology. The test ties a cost to the specific activity that causes it. Because direct costs can be traced, they are the easier half of the problem; the hard part is everything that supports those departments without belonging to any one of them.
Indirect Costs: The Overhead That Touches Everything
Indirect costs, also known as overhead, are incurred for the overall operation and not for any single unit. They are borne by all departments because they are not unique to any one. The overhead departments — administration, human resources, finance and billing, housekeeping, plant and maintenance, utilities, information technology — are called indirect cost centers. They generate no patient revenue themselves, yet no patient care could happen without them. The CEO’s salary, the electric bill, and the cost of the medical-records system are all indirect costs.
The challenge is that a patient never receives a "housekeeping service" as a discrete, billable event, yet a clean operating room is essential to their surgery. To know the full cost of that surgery, the hospital must somehow assign a share of housekeeping, administration, and utilities to it. This is the central problem of cost accounting: indirect costs are real and large, but they have to be spread across services using a deliberate, defensible method rather than direct measurement.
Direct Costs
Traceable to a specific service or department
Examples: drugs, supplies, nursing, imaging
Incurred by revenue-producing departments
Disappear if that department/service ends
Relatively easy to measure and assign
Indirect Costs (Overhead)
Support the whole organization, not one unit
Examples: administration, utilities, housekeeping, IT
Incurred by overhead (non-revenue) departments
Persist regardless of any single service
Must be allocated, not directly measured
Direct vs. Indirect Costs
A Second Dimension: Fixed vs. Variable
Direct-versus-indirect is not the only way costs are classified. A second, equally important dimension is how a cost behaves when patient volume changes: fixed versus variable. Variable costs rise and fall with the number of patients treated — the more surgeries performed, the more sutures, anesthesia, and supplies consumed. Fixed costs stay roughly constant regardless of volume over the short term — the mortgage on the building, the depreciation on the MRI machine, and much of the administrative salary base do not change whether the hospital treats 100 or 1,000 patients this month.
These two dimensions combine. A cost can be direct and variable (drugs given to a patient), direct and fixed (the salary of a department manager who is needed regardless of patient count), or indirect and fixed (the facilities and utilities base). Many real-world costs are semi-variable — partly fixed, partly variable — like staffing that has a baseline crew plus extra hours called in as volume rises. Understanding cost behavior is what lets a hospital predict how its costs will change if it grows a service line, loses volume, or takes on a capitated population.
Because hospitals carry enormous fixed costs (buildings, equipment, core staff), a drop in patient volume cannot be matched by an equal drop in costs. Revenue falls faster than expenses, so margins collapse quickly — one reason a soft quarter or a payer-mix shift can tip a hospital from surplus to loss.
Why Fixed Costs Make Hospitals Fragile
Allocation: Spreading Overhead to Find the Full Cost
The reason direct and indirect costs matter so much is that hospitals need to know the full cost of producing each patient service — including its fair share of overhead — to judge whether a payment is adequate. Cost allocation is the process of distributing the indirect costs of overhead departments to the patient-service departments. It relies on two building blocks: a cost pool (a grouping of costs to be allocated, such as total housekeeping cost) and a base or cost driver (the criterion used to spread it, such as square footage cleaned). Together they yield an application rate that assigns overhead to each department.
Group the indirect costs to be allocated — e.g., the total cost of the housekeeping department.
Identify the cost pool
Pick a sensible basis for spreading it — e.g., square footage for housekeeping, or number of employees for HR.
Choose a cost driver (base)
Divide the cost pool by the total base to get a rate (e.g., dollars of housekeeping cost per square foot).
Compute an application rate
Apply the rate to each revenue-producing department to load its share of overhead onto its direct costs.
Assign overhead to departments
How Cost Allocation Works
The most common allocation technique is the step-down method, which distributes overhead sequentially — from the higher-level cost centers down to lower ones in a ranked order — so that, for example, administration’s costs are spread first, then housekeeping’s, and so on, until all overhead lands on the revenue-producing departments. Its limitation is that it does not capture reciprocal relationships (housekeeping serves administration, but administration also serves housekeeping). More advanced reciprocal allocation methods use simultaneous equations to handle that two-way flow, at the cost of greater complexity.
Allocating overhead is like splitting the rent and utilities in a shared house among roommates. Each person’s own groceries are a "direct cost" — easy to assign. But the heating bill, the Wi-Fi, and the cleaning supplies benefit everyone, so you need a fair rule to divide them: maybe by bedroom size, maybe evenly. The rule you choose (the cost driver) changes what each roommate "owes" — just as a hospital’s allocation choices change what each department appears to cost.
How indirect cost allocation works
This last point is the crucial one: allocation is judgment, not measurement. The choice of cost driver materially changes how much overhead each service appears to bear, which in turn changes whether that service looks profitable or unprofitable. Two hospitals with identical real costs can report very different service-line margins depending on how they allocate overhead. That is precisely why more sophisticated costing methods — cost-per-case analysis and activity-based costing, covered in the next lessons — were developed: to allocate overhead more accurately and give leaders a truer picture of what their care actually costs.
Cost accounting answers what care actually costs, starting with the distinction between direct costs (traceable to a specific service or department) and indirect costs/overhead (supporting the whole organization).
Direct costs are incurred by revenue-producing departments (radiology, OR, lab) and include nursing, drugs, supplies, and imaging; a practical test is whether the cost would disappear if that department ceased to exist.
Indirect costs are incurred by overhead departments (administration, housekeeping, IT, utilities) that generate no patient revenue but are essential, and they must be spread across services through allocation.
A second dimension classifies costs by behavior: variable costs change with patient volume, fixed costs stay roughly constant in the short term, and many costs are semi-variable (a fixed base plus a variable component).
Heavy fixed costs make hospitals financially fragile, because when volume drops, revenue falls faster than costs and margins collapse quickly.
Cost allocation distributes overhead to patient-service departments using a cost pool (the costs to allocate) and a cost driver/base (the criterion for spreading them) to compute an application rate.
The step-down method allocates overhead sequentially from higher to lower cost centers but ignores reciprocal (two-way) relationships; reciprocal allocation uses simultaneous equations to capture them more accurately.
Allocation is judgment, not measurement — the choice of cost driver changes which services appear profitable, which is why more accurate methods like cost-per-case and activity-based costing were developed.

[2] PatientBetter Glossary: "What Are Direct Costs In Healthcare?" — https://patientbetter.com/glossary/direct-costs/ — direct costs as those directly attributable to patient care (nursing, drugs, supplies, imaging, rehab, food).

######## hospital-finance | cost-per-case-service-line | Cost Per Case and Service Line Analysis
Cost Per Case and Service Line Analysis: Finding the Money in the Mix
From "What Does Care Cost?" to "Which Care Makes Money?"
The previous lesson established that hospitals must allocate overhead to know the full cost of care. This lesson takes the next step: using cost information to answer the questions that actually drive hospital strategy. What does a single case — one knee replacement, one heart catheterization, one delivery — cost the hospital? And which clinical service lines are financially carrying the institution versus quietly draining it? These are the questions that determine where a hospital invests, what it markets, and sometimes what it stops doing altogether.
Two analytical tools answer them. Cost-per-case analysis estimates the cost of treating an individual patient or procedure. Service-line analysis aggregates those cases into clinical lines — cardiology, orthopedics, obstetrics, oncology — and measures the financial contribution of each. Together they turn the abstract idea of "cost" into concrete management decisions, and they reveal a truth that surprises many: a hospital’s busiest services are not always its most profitable, and its profitable services are not always the ones it promotes.
Key Concept: Cost-per-case analysis estimates what treating one patient or procedure costs the hospital. Service-line analysis aggregates cases into clinical lines (e.g., cardiology) to measure each line’s financial contribution — guiding investment, growth, and divestment decisions.
Orthopedic surgeons generate an average of roughly $3.3 million in annual revenue for their affiliated hospitals — among the highest of any specialty (Merritt Hawkins 2019 survey)
Orthopedic Surgeon Hospital Revenue
~$3.3M
Contribution margins for total hip replacement ran about $5,889 higher in concentrated hospital markets than in competitive ones (AJMC, Robinson)
Hip Replacement Margin Gap
$5,889
How Hospitals Estimate Cost Per Case
There is no single perfect way to cost an individual case; hospitals use several methods that trade accuracy against effort. The simplest is the ratio of cost to charges (RCC): a department divides its total cost by its total charges to get a ratio (say, $40 million in cost against $100 million in charges equals 0.4), then multiplies a case’s charges by that ratio to estimate its cost. RCC is fast and useful for high-level departmental monitoring, but because it applies a single average ratio to every case, it is unreliable for individual case-level decisions.
A more refined approach is RVU-based costing, which uses relative value units — standardized measures of the resources (physician time, staff time, equipment, supplies) a procedure consumes. The hospital divides total expenses by total RVUs to get a cost per RVU, then multiplies by the RVUs assigned to a given procedure. This better reflects relative resource intensity, though it can misstate cost when local workflows or patient mix differ from the national averages embedded in the RVU scale. The most precise (and most labor-intensive) method is microcosting, which tallies the actual individual resources consumed by a specific case.
Multiply a case’s charges by the department’s cost-to-charge ratio. Fast and good for high-level monitoring; too crude for case-level decisions.
Ratio of cost to charges (RCC)
Divide total expenses by total RVUs to get cost per RVU, then multiply by a procedure’s RVUs. Reflects relative resource intensity.
RVU-based costing
Tally the actual resources a specific case consumes. Most accurate, most labor-intensive — reserved for high-value analyses.
Microcosting
Three Common Cost-Per-Case Methods
RCC and similar average-based methods apply one ratio across every case, masking the real variation in resource use. They are fine for monitoring trends but dangerous for deciding whether a specific procedure or contract is profitable — that requires methods that reflect actual case-level resources.
Don’t Use Average Ratios for Specific Decisions
Contribution Margin: The Service-Line Workhorse
Once cases can be costed, the central tool for comparing them is contribution margin. Contribution margin measures the profitability of a case or service exclusive of indirect costs — that is, revenue minus the variable (direct) costs of providing the care, before subtracting overhead like administration, capital depreciation, and the cost of charity care. For a hospital paid a fixed amount per DRG (diagnosis-related group), contribution margin is calculated by comparing the case-related variable costs against the DRG payment for that case.
The reason contribution margin, rather than full cost, is the preferred tool for comparing treatments within a service line is subtle but important. Overhead is largely fixed and will be incurred whether or not a particular case is performed. So when deciding whether one more procedure is worth doing — or which procedures to grow — what matters is whether its revenue exceeds the additional variable cost it triggers. A procedure with a positive contribution margin helps cover the hospital’s fixed overhead even if, after full overhead allocation, it appears only marginally profitable.
The numbers vary enormously by procedure and market. One analysis found contribution margins running thousands of dollars higher in concentrated (less competitive) hospital markets — about $5,259 higher for angioplasty, $4,123 for total knee replacement, $5,889 for total hip replacement, and $7,931 for lumbar spine fusion — than in competitive markets, reflecting the pricing power that comes with market concentration. The same procedure can be a financial winner or a loser depending on the payment rate, the patient’s payer, and the hospital’s cost structure.
Which Service Lines Carry the Hospital?
Aggregate the contribution margins across a clinical line and you get service-line profitability — the financial scorecard hospital executives live by. The pattern is consistent across American hospitals: procedure-heavy specialties such as cardiovascular surgery, interventional cardiology, orthopedics, and neurosurgery consistently rank among the most profitable, while services like primary care, behavioral health, and obstetrics often run thin or negative margins despite being essential. An orthopedic surgeon generating around $3.3 million in annual hospital revenue (Merritt Hawkins, 2019) illustrates why these lines command so much strategic attention.
This profitability is exactly what funds the rest of the hospital. Positive contribution margins on orthopedic and cardiac procedures — especially for privately insured patients — are used to subsidize less remunerative procedures and patient groups, from money-losing behavioral health to charity care. Service-line analysis thus reveals the internal cross-subsidy that mirrors the payer-mix cross-subsidy: a handful of profitable lines keep the doors open for the mission-driven but unprofitable ones.
A community hospital might assume its high-volume emergency department or its busy primary care clinics are financial pillars, simply because they are always full.

Service-line profitability reporting often overturns that assumption: those high-activity areas may carry thin or negative margins, while a lower-volume cardiac or orthopedic line quietly generates most of the contribution to margin. Leaders who assume a service line is profitable based on volume, referrals, or "downstream revenue" frequently find those assumptions don’t survive scrutiny — high activity does not guarantee positive margin. This is why CFOs insist on actual margin data rather than volume as the basis for strategy.
Why Volume Can Deceive
Turning Analysis Into Strategy — Carefully
With reliable cost-per-case and service-line data, leadership can make deliberate choices: grow the service lines with strong margins, invest in the staff and equipment that expand them, scrutinize lines that consume heavy resources for little contribution, and renegotiate or restructure money-losing arrangements. The purest financial logic says concentrate on the profitable lines and shed the unprofitable ones. Many hospital strategies — the marketing push behind a new orthopedic institute, the expansion of a cardiac program — flow directly from this analysis.
A hospital’s service lines are like a grocery store’s departments. The store may sell mountains of low-margin staples like milk and bread (the high-volume ED and primary care), but it earns its real profit on the prepared foods and specialty items (cardiac and orthopedic procedures). A manager who judged each department only by how many customers it served would mismanage the store; the one who tracks margin by department knows which aisles fund the rest — and which loss leaders are worth keeping anyway.
Service-line profitability analysis
But pure financial logic runs straight into the hospital’s mission and obligations. The unprofitable service lines — behavioral health, obstetrics in rural areas, primary care, charity care — are often the ones a community most needs and, for nonprofit hospitals, the ones their tax-exempt community-benefit obligations require. A hospital that shed every money-losing line would betray its purpose and likely its legal standing. Service-line analysis must therefore inform strategy without dictating it; the goal is a sustainable portfolio, not the elimination of everything that loses money.
There is also a methodological humility required. As the previous lesson showed, overhead allocation is judgment, so a line’s "profitability" depends partly on how costs were assigned. Good analysts distinguish contribution margin (clean, based on variable costs) from fully allocated margin (which carries allocation assumptions), and they incorporate downstream and total-cost-of-care effects rather than viewing each line in isolation. Done well, cost-per-case and service-line analysis are among the most powerful tools in hospital finance. Done carelessly, they can justify abandoning exactly the care a community depends on — which is why the numbers must always be read alongside the mission.
Cost-per-case analysis estimates what treating one patient or procedure costs; service-line analysis aggregates cases into clinical lines to measure each line’s financial contribution and guide strategy.

######## hospital-finance | activity-based-costing | Activity-Based Costing in Hospitals
Activity-Based Costing in Hospitals: Following the Patient to Find the Cost
The Problem With Spreading Overhead by Formula
The traditional cost-allocation methods covered earlier — step-down allocation, ratios of cost to charges — share a common weakness: they spread overhead using broad averages and formulas rather than tracing it to what actually drives it. They answer "what share of administration should radiology bear?" with a tidy ratio, but that ratio may bear little relation to how much administrative work radiology truly causes. For decades this was good enough, because hospitals were paid for volume and didn’t urgently need precise costs. Value-based care changed that calculus entirely.
Activity-based costing (ABC) is the response. ABC is an approach to costing that traces resource consumption to activities, and activities to cost objects (such as a patient, a procedure, or a service). Instead of assuming overhead spreads evenly, ABC asks what activities a service actually requires — scheduling, registration, the procedure itself, recovery, billing — and assigns the cost of each activity based on how much of it the service consumes. The result is a far more accurate picture of what a given episode of care truly costs.
The most influential refinement, designed specifically to make ABC practical in healthcare, is time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC). It has become the leading method for answering the question that value-based care makes unavoidable: when a hospital is paid a single bundled or capitated amount, does that payment actually cover the cost of delivering the care?
Key Concept: Activity-based costing (ABC) traces resource use to specific activities and then to cost objects (patients, procedures), rather than spreading overhead by broad averages. Time-driven ABC (TDABC) simplifies this by costing the actual time each step of care consumes.
How Activity-Based Costing Works
The core idea of ABC is that activities, not departments, consume resources — and products or services consume activities. Rather than asking "how much did the radiology department spend?", ABC asks "what activities happen in radiology, what does each cost, and how many of each does a given patient require?" A chest X-ray and a complex interventional procedure may occur in the same department, but they consume vastly different activities; ABC captures that difference where average-based methods blur it.
Traditional ABC, however, earned a reputation for being expensive, slow, and hard to maintain. Mapping every activity and continuously surveying staff about how they spend their time proved impractical for organizations as complex as hospitals. This implementation burden is precisely why the original ABC method, despite its conceptual appeal, was adopted unevenly — it was more commonly used in narrower settings like laboratories than across whole hospitals.
Classic activity-based costing is conceptually superior to formula-based allocation but notoriously resource-intensive to build and maintain — requiring detailed activity mapping and ongoing staff time surveys. That practical burden, not a flaw in the logic, limited its spread in healthcare and motivated the time-driven version.
ABC’s Accuracy Came at a Cost
Time-Driven ABC: The Healthcare Breakthrough
Time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC) was created by Robert Kaplan and Steven Anderson at Harvard Business School to simplify and modernize ABC, and it was brought squarely into healthcare when Kaplan and Michael Porter laid out a seven-step approach for applying it in clinical settings in 2011. TDABC’s elegance is that it reduces the entire costing problem to just two parameters: the capacity cost rate (the cost per unit of time for a given resource — a nurse, an operating room, an MRI) and the time each activity in the care pathway requires.
In practice, a multidisciplinary team builds a process map that follows the patient through the complete care cycle — from scheduling and check-in, through the procedure and recovery, to follow-up and billing. For each step, they estimate the time consumed and multiply it by the capacity cost rate of the resources used. Summing across all steps yields the total cost of treating that patient for that condition. By prioritizing accuracy over false precision and requiring far fewer resources than classic ABC, TDABC made activity-based costing finally feasible at the scale of a hospital.
A multidisciplinary team traces every step a patient goes through for a condition or procedure, from scheduling to follow-up.
Map the care pathway
For each activity, estimate how much time each resource (clinician, room, equipment) is used.
Estimate time per step
Determine the cost per minute for each resource — its total cost divided by its available capacity.
Calculate capacity cost rates
Multiply time by capacity cost rate at each step and add them up to get the true cost of the full care cycle.
Multiply and sum
The Logic of Time-Driven ABC
TDABC has now been applied across the full range of care — primary, secondary, acute, tertiary, and long-term — and to procedures as varied as colonoscopy, aortic valve replacement, and carpal tunnel release. Because it produces patient-specific, activity-level costs, it gives leaders something formula-based allocation never could: a defensible, granular answer to what each step of care actually costs, and where in the pathway the money is going.
Why It Matters for Value-Based Care
The rise of TDABC in healthcare is inseparable from the rise of value-based care. Implementing value-based initiatives depends on cost-assessment methods that produce high-quality cost information, and TDABC is increasingly used to fill that cost-information gap. When a hospital accepts a bundled payment for a joint replacement or a capitated rate for a population, it can no longer hide imprecise costing behind fee-for-service billing — it must know, step by step, what the care costs to know whether the payment is sustainable.
TDABC also does something subtler: it turns costing into an improvement tool. By revealing the time and cost of each step in a care pathway, it exposes waste — idle equipment, redundant steps, bottlenecks — that can be removed without harming patients. A systematic review found that TDABC contributed to value-based initiatives, especially through cost-saving findings, in the studies that applied it for that purpose. One published example used TDABC specifically to reduce idle time in an interventional radiology suite, converting cost transparency directly into efficiency.
In a pilot analyzing colonoscopy, aortic valve replacement, and carpal tunnel release, clinicians used TDABC to map the true cost of each procedure’s full care cycle.

The value of the exercise was not just a more accurate number — it was visibility. Seeing exactly where time and money were consumed let teams identify steps that added cost without adding value, compare their costs against the bundled payments they received, and target specific improvements. This is the core promise of TDABC for value-based care: it measures the denominator (cost) in the value equation of outcomes-over-cost, making true value measurable for the first time.
TDABC as a Value Platform
The Barriers — and the Honest Verdict
Despite its promise, TDABC is far from universally adopted, and the reasons are instructive. Resource and operational constraints loom large: hospitals facing unpredictable payment environments and competing priorities (like major electronic-health-record implementations) struggle to invest in building costing systems. Organizational barriers — resistance to change, the difficulty of collecting accurate data, and the need for continuous training — slow adoption further. And methodological gaps remain: TDABC still struggles with allocating shared support-department costs, and its ability to directly inform bundled-payment rates is not yet well established.
Even the seemingly simple step of estimating staff time at each point in the process map remains resource-intensive in practice. These are not reasons to dismiss TDABC, but they explain why a method praised in the literature for two decades is still spreading unevenly across real hospitals. The path forward, researchers agree, requires further methodological standardization, genuine workforce engagement, and tighter integration with the decisions hospitals actually make.
Traditional cost allocation is like splitting a group restaurant bill evenly regardless of what each person ordered — fast, but unfair to the person who had only a salad. Time-driven activity-based costing is like an itemized receipt that follows each diner’s actual order. It takes more effort to produce, but it finally shows who truly cost what — which is exactly what you need when someone else (a bundled payer) is paying a fixed amount for the whole table.
TDABC vs. formula-based cost allocation
The honest verdict is that activity-based costing, and TDABC in particular, represents the most accurate available answer to hospital finance’s hardest question — what does care actually cost? — while remaining genuinely difficult to implement well. For a hospital moving into value-based contracts, that trade-off increasingly tilts toward adoption: the cost of not knowing your costs rises sharply the moment your revenue is fixed. Understanding ABC and TDABC is therefore understanding both the destination of hospital cost accounting and the real-world friction on the road to it.
Activity-based costing (ABC) traces resource consumption to specific activities and then to cost objects (patients, procedures), giving far more accurate costs than formula-based methods like step-down allocation or cost-to-charge ratios.
Classic ABC is conceptually superior but notoriously expensive, slow, and hard to maintain, which limited its adoption in healthcare to narrower settings like laboratories.
Time-driven activity-based costing (TDABC), created by Kaplan and Anderson and brought into healthcare via Kaplan and Porter’s 2011 seven-step approach, simplifies ABC using just two parameters: the capacity cost rate and the time each activity requires.
TDABC works by mapping the full patient care pathway, estimating the time each step consumes, and multiplying by each resource’s capacity cost rate to produce a patient-specific, activity-level cost.
TDABC has been applied across all care settings and many procedures (colonoscopy, aortic valve replacement, carpal tunnel release), giving leaders a defensible answer to what each step of care truly costs.
TDABC is central to value-based care because fixed payments (bundles, capitation) require knowing true costs, and it doubles as an improvement tool by exposing waste and idle capacity in care pathways.
Adoption barriers are real: resource and operational constraints, resistance to change, data-collection difficulty, unresolved support-cost allocation, and resource-intensive staff-time estimation.
The honest verdict is that ABC/TDABC offers the most accurate answer to what care costs but remains hard to implement — and the cost of not knowing your costs rises sharply once revenue is fixed under value-based contracts.

######## hospital-finance | operating-vs-capital-budget | Operating Budget vs Capital Budget
Operating Budget vs. Capital Budget: Two Plans, Two Time Horizons
Two Budgets, Two Fundamentally Different Questions
Every hospital builds two distinct budgets each year, and confusing them is a recipe for financial trouble. The operating budget answers the question: "What will it cost to run the hospital day to day this year, and what revenue will those operations bring in?" The capital budget answers a different question entirely: "What major, long-lived assets should we invest in to keep the hospital functioning and competitive for years to come?" One is about keeping the lights on this year; the other is about buying the building the lights hang in.
The distinction tracks the difference between operating expenses (OpEx) and capital expenditures (CapEx). An operating budget covers personnel salaries, supplies and materials, drugs, and administrative overhead — the recurring costs consumed within the year. A capital budget covers durable goods and long-term assets: imaging machines, surgical robots, beds, building renovations, and new facilities — items that deliver value over many years. The accounting, the approval process, and the strategic stakes differ for each.
Though separate, the two budgets are deeply intertwined. A capital decision made this year — buying a new surgical robot — drives operating costs for years afterward through maintenance, supplies, staffing, and the depreciation that flows back onto the income statement. Understanding how the two budgets relate is essential to grasping how hospitals actually plan and fund their futures.
Key Concept: The operating budget plans recurring annual revenue and expenses (salaries, supplies, overhead). The capital budget plans investments in long-lived assets (equipment, buildings) that provide value beyond one year. They are separate documents but each shapes the other.
Capital assets are property, plant, and equipment with useful lives spanning more than one year — the dividing line from operating expenses (HFM Magazine)
Capital Asset Test
>1 year
Hospital capital expenditures rose to a median of 123.4% of depreciation expense in FY24 — the highest since 2013, signaling renewed investment in aging facilities (Fitch)
CapEx vs. Depreciation (FY24)
123.4%
The Operating Budget: Running the Hospital This Year
The operating budget is the financial plan for the hospital’s ongoing operations over the coming fiscal year. On the expense side it includes personnel salaries and benefits (the largest component, as the cost-accounting lessons established), medical and surgical supplies, pharmaceuticals, utilities, and administrative overhead. On the revenue side it projects net patient revenue based on expected volumes and payer mix, plus other operating revenue. The difference between projected operating revenue and operating expense is the budgeted operating margin.
Building the operating budget is fundamentally an exercise in forecasting: how many patients will the hospital treat, in what mix of services, paid by which payers, at what cost? Hospitals approach this in different ways. Incremental budgeting starts from last year’s budget and adjusts for expected changes — simpler but prone to perpetuating old inefficiencies. Zero-based budgeting builds the budget from scratch each year, justifying every expense — more rigorous and more revealing, but far more labor-intensive. Most hospitals land somewhere in between.
Because the operating budget governs the recurring money that keeps care flowing, it is the document most departments interact with daily. Variances — the gaps between budgeted and actual results — are tracked monthly, and managers are held accountable for explaining and correcting them. The operating budget is, in effect, the hospital’s financial steering wheel for the year.
The Capital Budget: Investing in the Long Term
The capital budget allocates funding to the purchase of durable, long-lived assets — and the stakes per decision are far higher. A single capital request might be a robotic surgical system, a CT or MRI machine, a building renovation, or an entirely new off-site clinic. What makes something "capital" rather than "operating" is defined by the organization’s written capitalization policy, which sets a minimum dollar threshold and an expected service life (more than one year) for an item to be treated as a capital asset. There is no universal dollar figure; each hospital sets its own threshold.
Capital assets are accounted for differently from operating expenses, and this is where the two budgets connect on the financial statements. Rather than being expensed all at once, a capital asset’s cost is spread across its useful life through depreciation — the periodic charge reflecting the gradual consumption of the asset, most commonly spread evenly (straight-line) over its estimated life. So the MRI machine bought from the capital budget shows up year after year as depreciation in the operating budget, quietly linking a one-time capital decision to ongoing operating costs.
Whether a purchase hits the capital budget or the operating budget depends on the hospital’s capitalization threshold. A $400 piece of equipment is an operating expense; a $400,000 imaging system is a capital asset depreciated over years. Misclassifying items distorts both budgets and the financial statements — which is why a clear written capitalization policy matters.
Capitalize or Expense? The Threshold Decides
Hospitals also plan how to fund capital. One important mechanism is funded depreciation — a designated financial account a hospital builds up specifically to fund future debt service and capital expenditures. Setting aside funds as assets depreciate helps ensure money is available to replace them when they wear out, rather than scrambling for financing at the moment of need.
How Capital Decisions Actually Get Made
The defining reality of capital budgeting is scarcity: hospitals operate with a fixed annual capital budget, so every approved request competes with every other department’s needs. Radiology’s new scanner competes with cardiology’s catheterization lab, with the roof that needs replacing, with the electronic health record upgrade. Unlike operating costs that recur predictably, capital requests are discrete, large, and mutually exclusive — approving one often means denying another.
The process typically begins when a clinical department identifies a need and submits a capital request that includes the clinical justification, estimated cost, and expected return. Decision-makers then weigh these requests against one another using criteria such as essential service needs, regulatory and safety requirements, alignment with strategic priorities, historical budgets, and the organization’s overall financial position. The strategic planning process serves to assess and prioritize future capital goals against the hard limits of financial reality.
Clinical or operational staff submit a capital request with justification, estimated cost, and expected return.
A department identifies a need
All requests across the organization compete for a single fixed capital budget.
Requests are pooled and compared
Decision-makers weigh clinical necessity, safety/regulatory requirements, strategic fit, ROI, and financial capacity.
Leadership prioritizes
Selected projects are funded; the rest are deferred to future years or rejected, and operating-cost impacts are planned for.
Funded items are approved
The Capital Budgeting Process
Why the Two Budgets Must Be Read Together
The deepest insight of this lesson is that the operating and capital budgets cannot be managed in isolation, because each shapes the other. Capital investments drive future operating costs: a new facility requires staff, supplies, utilities, and maintenance; a new technology requires trained operators and service contracts. A hospital that approves a gleaming new surgical wing without budgeting for the operating costs to run it has set a trap for its future self. Conversely, funding for capital purchases may need to come from operating surplus, so a thin operating margin directly constrains the capital a hospital can afford.
The two budgets are like a household’s monthly budget versus its decision to buy a house. The monthly budget covers groceries, utilities, and gas — recurring and adjustable. Buying a house is a capital decision: a large, long-lived asset paid for over time, which then locks in years of mortgage payments, property taxes, and upkeep that reappear in every future monthly budget. Smart families plan both together; so do smart hospitals.
Operating budget vs. capital budget
Recent trends make capital planning especially pressing. Fitch reported that hospital capital expenditures rose to a median of 123.4% of depreciation expense in FY24 — up from 109.1% the prior year and the highest level since 2013. Spending above 100% of depreciation means hospitals are reinvesting faster than their assets are wearing out, a healthy sign after years of deferred investment, but one that depends on operating margins strong enough to fund it. The average-age-of-plant ratio from the financial-ratios lesson is the warning gauge here: aging facilities eventually force capital spending whether or not the operating budget can comfortably support it.
For anyone learning hospital finance, the takeaway is to always ask which budget a decision lives in and how it ripples into the other. A supply cost is operating; a building is capital; but the building generates operating costs forever after. The most consequential financial decisions a hospital makes — whether to build, what technology to buy, how to fund it — happen in the capital budget, while the operating budget determines whether the hospital can keep those promises year after year. Mastering the relationship between the two is mastering how a hospital plans to survive both this year and the next decade.

######## hospital-finance | capital-planning | Capital Planning: CON, ROI, and Prioritization
Capital Planning: Certificate of Need, ROI, and Prioritization
Deciding What to Build and What to Buy
The previous lesson established that hospitals plan major investments through a fixed capital budget, where every department’s request competes for limited dollars. This lesson is about how those decisions actually get made — and constrained. Capital planning sits at the intersection of three forces: the financial analysis that tells a hospital whether an investment will pay off, the strategic judgment about what the institution needs to fulfill its mission, and the government regulation that, in many states, determines whether the hospital is even allowed to make the investment at all.
These three forces pull in different directions. Pure financial analysis favors the projects with the best returns. Strategic and mission considerations may favor projects with modest financial returns but high community value. And in much of the country, a state regulator wielding "certificate of need" authority can block a project entirely, regardless of how attractive it looks on the hospital’s spreadsheet. Capital planning is the discipline of navigating all three.
Key Concept: Capital planning combines financial analysis (NPV, IRR, payback, profitability index), strategic and mission-driven prioritization, and — in many states — Certificate of Need (CON) regulatory approval to decide which long-term investments a hospital pursues.
Thirty-five states and Washington, D.C. operate certificate-of-need programs regulating major health facility investments (NCSL)
Operate CON Programs
