Capital thresholds that trigger CON review vary enormously by state — e.g., ~$1.5M in Iowa versus $30M for general hospitals in New York (NCSL / NY DOH)
CON Trigger Thresholds
$1.5M–$30M
Certificate of Need: The Regulatory Gatekeeper
Certificate of Need (CON) programs are state laws that require health care providers to obtain government approval before making major capital investments — building or expanding facilities, adding beds, or acquiring expensive equipment. Their stated purpose is to restrain health care facility costs and allow coordinated planning of new services and construction, on the theory that unchecked duplication of expensive services (every hospital buying its own proton-beam machine) drives up total spending. Currently, 35 states and Washington, D.C. operate CON programs, with enormous variation among them.
The dollar threshold that triggers CON review reveals how differently states approach this. In New York, projects by general hospitals exceeding $30 million require a CON; in Iowa, projects over just $1.5 million do. Thresholds are typically lower for non-hospital providers like ambulatory surgery centers than for hospitals. The practical effect is that the same capital project — say, a new surgery center — might sail through unregulated in one state and require a months-long, contestable approval process in another.
CON laws are genuinely controversial, and the evidence is mixed and politically charged. Critics point to research suggesting hospital charges are about 5.5% lower five years after a state repeals CON, and that per-capita hospital expenditures run about 20.6% higher in CON states — arguing the laws protect incumbents and stifle competition. Defenders argue CON prevents wasteful duplication and protects rural and safety-net providers from being undercut. The result is an active reform landscape: in 2024, Georgia advanced reforms exempting certain single-specialty ASCs from review, and New York proposed raising its hospital CON threshold from $15 million to $30 million.
In a CON state, a hospital cannot simply decide to build based on financial merit. It must first determine whether the project triggers CON review and, if so, win regulatory approval — a process competitors can oppose. A capital plan that ignores CON can be dead on arrival no matter how strong its projected return.
CON Is the First Question, Not an Afterthought
The Financial Analysis: Will the Investment Pay Off?
For projects that clear regulatory hurdles, hospitals apply rigorous capital-budgeting techniques to judge financial merit. The most important is net present value (NPV), which measures the dollar profitability of a project by discounting its expected future cash flows back to today’s dollars and subtracting the initial investment. A positive NPV means the project is expected to create value after accounting for the time value of money; a negative NPV means it destroys value. NPV is the gold standard because it answers the question that matters: will this investment make the hospital better off in real terms?
Several companion metrics fill out the picture. Internal rate of return (IRR) expresses a project’s return as a percentage, making it easy to compare against the hospital’s cost of capital. Payback period measures how long it takes to recoup the original investment — intuitive and useful for gauging risk, but flawed because it ignores both long-term profitability and the time value of money. Profitability index (PI) measures return per dollar invested, which is especially valuable when capital is scarce because it ranks projects by efficiency of capital use, not just total return.
Discounts future cash flows to today and subtracts the cost; positive NPV creates value. The primary decision metric.
Net present value (NPV)
The percentage return a project earns; compared against the hospital’s cost of capital.
Internal rate of return (IRR)
How long to recoup the investment; simple risk gauge, but ignores time value of money and long-term returns.
Payback period
Return per dollar invested; ideal for ranking projects when capital is limited.
Profitability index (PI)
Core Capital-Investment Metrics
Beyond the Numbers: Strategic and Mission Scoring
If hospitals funded only the highest-NPV projects, they would look very different — and would likely violate their missions and obligations. Many essential investments have modest or even negative financial returns: replacing a failing fire-safety system, meeting a new regulatory mandate, building behavioral health capacity, or upgrading the electronic health record. A purely financial ranking would starve these in favor of profitable service-line expansions. So hospitals deliberately incorporate non-financial criteria into capital decisions.
The standard tool is project scoring — a ranking technique that combines financial metrics with non-financial factors such as patient safety, regulatory compliance, quality improvement, strategic alignment, and community need. Each request is scored across these dimensions, allowing a high-need safety project with poor financials to compete fairly against a high-return revenue project. This is how hospitals reconcile the spreadsheet with the mission: the NPV matters, but it is one input among several, not the sole verdict.
Imagine a hospital weighing two capital requests of equal cost. Project A is a new orthopedic suite with a strong positive NPV and a three-year payback. Project B is a replacement HVAC and electrical system with no revenue at all — pure cost.

On financial metrics alone, Project A wins easily. But a scoring model that weights safety, regulatory compliance, and operational risk will likely rank Project B higher, because a failing electrical system threatens the entire facility. The orthopedic suite generates money; the infrastructure keeps the hospital legally open and physically safe. Good capital planning funds both in the right order — and project scoring is how that judgment is made explicit and defensible.
How Two Requests Compete
Putting Capital Planning Together
Effective capital planning braids the three strands into a single disciplined process. First, the regulatory screen: does the project trigger CON review in this state, and can approval be won? Second, the financial analysis: what are the NPV, IRR, payback, and profitability index, and how do they compare to other requests competing for the same limited budget? Third, the strategic and mission scoring: how does the project rank on safety, compliance, quality, community need, and strategic fit? Only a project that survives all three screens — or is deliberately funded despite weak financials for strategic reasons — earns a place in the capital budget.
Capital planning is like a family deciding on a major home investment. First they check whether local zoning even permits it (the CON regulatory screen). Then they run the numbers — will the addition raise the home’s value more than it costs (NPV)? Finally they weigh things money can’t capture: a wheelchair ramp for an aging parent may have terrible "ROI" but tops the list because the need is real. Hospitals do exactly this, just with stakes in the tens of millions.
The three screens of capital planning
The discipline matters because capital decisions are largely irreversible and shape a hospital for decades. A building, once built, must be staffed and maintained for its lifetime; a technology, once bought, locks in service contracts and training. As the prior lesson showed, these capital choices flow into the operating budget as depreciation and operating costs for years. A hospital that chases high-NPV projects while neglecting infrastructure, or that lets mission override financial reality entirely, will eventually find its capital decisions undermining its solvency.
In the value-based-care era, capital planning is also shifting. Investments increasingly favor projects that support population health, care coordination, data infrastructure, and outpatient and community settings — rather than simply adding inpatient beds and procedure rooms. The metrics stay the same, but the strategic scoring evolves: a project that lowers total cost of care and keeps patients healthy may rank higher than a revenue-maximizing inpatient expansion that a fee-for-service hospital would have prized. Understanding capital planning means understanding not just the tools, but how a changing payment landscape changes what a hospital should choose to build.
Capital planning combines three forces: regulatory approval (Certificate of Need), financial analysis (NPV, IRR, payback, profitability index), and strategic/mission-driven prioritization.
Certificate of Need (CON) laws require government approval before major health-facility investments; 35 states and DC operate CON programs, intended to restrain costs and coordinate planning.

Companion metrics include IRR (percentage return vs. cost of capital), payback period (simple but ignores time value of money), and profitability index (return per dollar, ideal when capital is scarce).

######## hospital-finance | debt-financing | Debt Financing: Bonds, Credit Ratings, and Covenants
Debt Financing: Bonds, Credit Ratings, and Covenants
How Hospitals Pay for the Big Things
A new hospital tower can cost hundreds of millions of dollars. A major system-wide electronic health record can run into the billions. No hospital pays for investments of this scale out of its annual operating surplus — the thin margins covered in earlier lessons make that impossible. Instead, hospitals borrow, and the dominant way they borrow is by issuing bonds. Understanding debt financing — how hospitals issue bonds, how credit ratings determine what they pay, and how covenants constrain what they do afterward — is essential to understanding how hospitals fund their futures.
For nonprofit hospitals, debt financing comes with a powerful advantage rooted in their tax status. Because they are 501(c)(3) charitable organizations, they can issue tax-exempt (municipal) debt — bonds whose interest is exempt from federal (and often state) income tax for the investor. That tax exemption lets investors accept a lower interest rate, and nonprofit hospital borrowers save, on average, an estimated 2 percentage points on their borrowing compared to taxable bonds or bank financing. On a $300 million bond, two points is enormous, and those savings ultimately lower the cost of care.
But borrowing at attractive rates is not automatic. A hospital must convince investors it will repay, and the entire machinery of credit ratings and bond covenants exists to price and police that risk. The story of hospital debt financing is the story of how a hospital’s financial health — the ratios from earlier lessons — translates directly into the cost and availability of the capital it needs to survive.
Key Concept: Nonprofit hospitals fund major investments primarily by issuing tax-exempt (municipal) bonds, saving roughly 2 percentage points versus taxable financing. Credit ratings determine the interest rate they pay, and bond covenants impose ongoing financial requirements they must meet.
Nonprofit hospitals save an estimated 2 percentage points on borrowing by issuing tax-exempt bonds versus taxable debt — savings that lower the cost of care (industry analyses)
Tax-Exempt Borrowing Savings
~2 pts
Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch collectively issued 95 hospital downgrades against 37 upgrades in 2024, reflecting ongoing expense pressure (Fierce Healthcare)
Downgrades vs. Upgrades (2024)
95 vs 37
Tax-Exempt Bonds: The Workhorse of Hospital Capital
When a nonprofit hospital issues a bond, it is borrowing from investors who buy the bonds and receive interest payments over time, with the principal repaid at maturity. These are typically issued through a state or local financing authority, which is what gives them their tax-exempt, "municipal" character. The proceeds fund capital projects — and in recent years, new issuance has gone primarily toward renovation and expansion of existing facilities and growth opportunities, especially ambulatory (outpatient) expansion that reflects care moving out of inpatient settings.
The municipal hospital bond market is cyclical and revealing. After three years of declining volume, 2024 saw a large rebound, with healthcare bond issuance jumping more than 100% year over year as hospitals returned to the capital markets to fund delayed projects. This rebound signals both pent-up capital needs from years of deferred investment and enough financial recovery for hospitals to take on new debt — connecting directly to the rising capital-expenditure trends discussed in the budgeting lessons.
Credit Ratings: The Price of Trust
Before a hospital can sell bonds at a good rate, it must be rated. The three major credit rating agencies — Moody’s, Standard & Poor’s (S&P), and Fitch — evaluate a hospital based on the likelihood that it will default on its debt, examining metrics like its cost structure, local demographics, and payer mix, alongside the financial ratios covered earlier (operating margin, days cash on hand, debt service coverage). The rating they assign is a letter grade that investors use to judge risk.
The most important dividing line is investment grade. Bonds rated BBB- or higher by S&P and Fitch, or Baa3 or higher by Moody’s, are investment grade; anything below is "speculative" or "junk." This line matters enormously because many institutional investors are restricted to investment-grade securities, so a hospital that falls below it loses access to a huge pool of buyers. The rating directly sets the interest rate: a higher rating signals lower risk, so investors accept lower returns, and the hospital borrows more cheaply.
Ratings move, and the direction has been worrying. In 2024, the three agencies collectively issued 95 downgrades against just 37 upgrades — an improvement over 2023’s 116 downgrades and 33 upgrades, but still a lopsided picture. Many downgrades reflected ongoing expense pressure that outpaced revenue growth, even as patient volumes recovered and reliance on contract labor declined. Each downgrade is more than a label: it tangibly raises the hospital’s future borrowing costs and signals deteriorating financial health to the entire market.
When a hospital’s rating falls, investors demand more return for the added perceived risk, pushing up interest rates on new debt, widening spreads, and triggering more restrictive terms and reserve requirements. A drop below investment grade can be severely detrimental — sharply limiting access to capital and harming even existing bondholders.
A Downgrade Is Expensive — Especially Below Investment Grade
Covenants: The Strings Attached to Borrowing
Lending a hospital hundreds of millions of dollars is risky, so bondholders protect themselves with covenants — contractual promises the hospital must keep for as long as the bonds are outstanding. The two most common financial covenants come straight from the ratios covered earlier. A debt service coverage ratio (DSCR) covenant requires the hospital to maintain enough cash flow to cover its principal and interest payments, with minimums often ranging from 1.10 to 1.25. A days cash on hand covenant requires the hospital to keep a minimum liquidity cushion, often in the range of 40 to 80 days.
These covenants are typically consolidated through a master trust indenture, a financing structure that pools the credit of multiple nonprofit entities into an "obligated group" and consolidates all financial covenants into a single document used across the system’s bond issues. The structure lets a health system borrow on the combined strength of its members. Privately placed bonds held by banks often carry more stringent covenants than publicly issued bonds under a master indenture — but they offer the flexibility of negotiating directly with the lender if trouble arises.
Maintain cash flow sufficient to cover debt payments — minimums often 1.10 to 1.25.
Debt service coverage ratio
Keep a minimum liquidity cushion — often 40 to 80 days of operating expenses.
Days cash on hand
Demonstrate financial capacity before issuing more debt, protecting existing bondholders.
Additional bonds test
Provide regular financial statements and certify covenant compliance to bondholders.
Reporting and compliance
Common Hospital Bond Covenants
Breaching a covenant is serious. A covenant default can trigger remedies ranging from penalty rates to, in the worst case, acceleration — the lender demanding immediate repayment of the entire balance. Because the consequences are so severe, hospitals approaching a covenant breach must take aggressive early action: cutting costs, raising liquidity, or negotiating waivers and amendments with bondholders or banks before the breach occurs. Covenant management is a core discipline of hospital treasury operations, not a back-office afterthought.
Why Debt Financing Ties the Whole Course Together
Debt financing is where nearly every concept in hospital finance converges. The financial ratios from Module 1 are not academic — they are literally the inputs rating agencies use and the thresholds covenants enforce. A hospital’s payer mix and operating margin shape its rating; its days cash on hand is both a liquidity measure and a covenant requirement; its debt service coverage determines whether it can borrow more. The abstract idea of "financial health" becomes concrete the moment a hospital tries to raise capital.
A hospital borrowing through bonds is like a homebuyer getting a mortgage. The credit rating is the credit score: a better score means a lower interest rate and access to more lenders. The tax exemption is like a special low-rate program only certain buyers qualify for. The covenants are the mortgage terms — keep your income above a threshold, maintain insurance — and breaking them can let the bank call the loan. Just as a homebuyer’s whole financial life shapes their mortgage, a hospital’s entire financial profile shapes its access to capital.
Hospital bonds, ratings, and covenants
This convergence creates a powerful feedback loop, for better or worse. A financially strong hospital earns a high rating, borrows cheaply, invests in facilities and technology that strengthen it further, and easily meets its covenants. A struggling hospital gets downgraded, borrows expensively (if at all), cannot fund the investments that would improve its position, and risks breaching covenants — accelerating its decline. Debt financing can be a ladder up or a spiral down, and which one depends on the fundamentals built in every prior lesson.
For the student of hospital finance, debt financing is the capstone of the capital side of the field. It shows why margins, liquidity, and coverage ratios matter beyond the financial statements: they determine whether a hospital can afford to build, expand, and modernize — or whether it is locked out of the capital markets precisely when it most needs them. Mastering bonds, ratings, and covenants means seeing how a hospital’s past financial performance becomes the constraint and the engine of its future.
Hospitals fund large capital investments primarily by issuing bonds; nonprofit (501(c)(3)) hospitals can issue tax-exempt municipal bonds, saving roughly 2 percentage points versus taxable financing.
Healthcare bond issuance rebounded sharply in 2024 (up more than 100% year over year), with proceeds going largely to renovation, expansion, and ambulatory (outpatient) growth.
The three major rating agencies — Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch — assess default risk using cost structure, demographics, payer mix, and financial ratios, assigning a credit rating that sets the hospital’s borrowing cost.
Investment grade (BBB-/Baa3 or higher) is the critical threshold; falling below it cuts off access to many institutional investors and sharply raises borrowing costs.
Rating trends have been negative: agencies issued 95 downgrades versus 37 upgrades in 2024, driven by expenses outpacing revenue, and each downgrade raises future borrowing costs.
Bond covenants impose ongoing requirements — commonly a debt service coverage ratio (often 1.10–1.25 minimum) and days cash on hand (often 40–80 days) — frequently consolidated via a master trust indenture and obligated group.
Breaching a covenant can trigger penalty rates or acceleration (demand for immediate full repayment), so hospitals must act aggressively and early to cut costs, raise liquidity, or negotiate waivers.
Debt financing ties the whole course together: the financial ratios are the very inputs rating agencies use and covenants enforce, creating a feedback loop that can be a ladder up or a spiral down.

######## hospital-finance | volume-to-value-financial-implications | Transitioning from Volume to Value: Financial Implications
Transitioning from Volume to Value: The Financial Implications
When Doing the Right Thing Costs You Money
Imagine a hospital that runs a brilliant program to keep heart-failure patients healthy at home. The program works: admissions for those patients drop sharply. Under fee-for-service, this clinical triumph is a financial disaster — every avoided admission is lost revenue, while the hospital’s fixed costs (the building, the staff, the equipment) remain. The hospital did exactly what good medicine demands and was punished for it by its own payment system. This is the central, uncomfortable truth of the volume-to-value transition, and it is the reason that transition is so financially treacherous.
Value-based care asks hospitals to deliver less of the high-margin, volume-driven care that fee-for-service rewards — fewer admissions, fewer readmissions, fewer unnecessary procedures — in exchange for payments tied to keeping populations healthy. But the shift does not happen overnight, and during the long in-between, hospitals must operate under two contradictory payment logics at once. The financial implications of that contradiction are the subject of this lesson.
This is not abstract. It determines whether a hospital can afford to pursue value-based contracts, how fast it can move, and whether its mission to improve health aligns with or fights against its need to stay solvent. For a field built on the promise of paying for outcomes instead of volume, the messy economics of getting there are where most hospitals actually live.
Key Concept: Under fee-for-service, reducing unnecessary care reduces revenue while fixed costs remain — so a hospital succeeding at value-based care can lose money on the very utilization it eliminated. Managing this contradiction during the transition is the core financial challenge of moving from volume to value.
Inpatient primary knee replacements dropped 21.2% year-over-year as procedures shifted to outpatient settings — a volume-to-value migration of revenue (Strata Decision Technology)
Inpatient Knee Replacements
-21.2%
Hospitals can lose up to 3% of Medicare payments under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program — paying for the volume they fail to prevent (CMS)
Medicare Readmission Penalty
Up to 3%
The Two Canoes Problem
The transition’s defining metaphor is the "two canoes" problem: a hospital stands with one foot in the fee-for-service canoe and one foot in the value-based-care canoe, and the two canoes are drifting apart because their incentives point in opposite directions. Value-based contracts demand very different business and clinical practices than those that maximize fee-for-service revenue — yet with most income still anchored to volume, hospitals often cannot afford a wholesale pivot to cost-conscious care. They must straddle both worlds, and straddling is precarious.
The financial mechanics of the straddle are genuinely hard to model. A health system CFO asked "what is the financial impact of reducing chronic-disease admissions by 25%?" faces a brutal calculation: the saved direct care costs are real, but so is the lost reimbursement, and the overhead that those admissions used to cover does not disappear. The published research is blunt about the consequence — because preventing a hospitalization leaves overhead costs uncovered, the loss of reimbursement revenue can actually mitigate a hospital’s incentive to reduce readmissions in the first place. The payment system fights the clinical goal.
Value-based contracts return a portion of the savings a hospital generates — but that share frequently does not fully offset the fee-for-service revenue lost when admissions and procedures fall. A hospital can improve care, generate system-wide savings, and still come out behind financially if it has not shifted enough of its revenue to value-based payment.
Shared Savings Often Don’t Cover the Loss
Where the Revenue Goes: The Migration of Care
The volume-to-value shift is not only about eliminating care — it is also about moving it. Procedures that once required expensive inpatient stays are migrating to lower-cost outpatient settings, and the financial footprint follows. Inpatient primary knee replacements fell 21.2% year over year as those cases moved to outpatient sites. Each of these shifts trims the high-revenue inpatient business that hospitals were built around, even when overall volumes remain healthy.
Paradoxically, this is happening during a period of strong hospital revenue. Through 2024, hospitals posted 20 consecutive months of year-over-year revenue increases, with outpatient revenue up 8.0% — outpacing inpatient growth of 6.1% — and full-year median operating margins holding above 4.5% and reaching 6% by December. The headline numbers look healthy, but underneath them the revenue base is migrating from inpatient to outpatient and from volume toward value, reshaping where and how hospitals earn their money.
A teaching hospital invests in a care-transitions program that successfully prevents readmissions. Clinically and ethically, this is unambiguously good — and under the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program, avoiding readmissions also dodges penalties of up to 3% of Medicare payments.

But under fee-for-service, each prevented readmission is also a lost admission: revenue the hospital would have collected, gone, while the fixed overhead remains. Whether the program helps or hurts the hospital financially depends entirely on its payment mix — how much of its revenue is value-based (rewarding the prevention) versus fee-for-service (penalizing the lost volume). The same clinical action is a financial win or loss depending on which canoe carries more of the hospital’s weight.
The Avoided Readmission Paradox
Managing the Straddle: Tipping Points and Bridges
If straddling two canoes is dangerous, how do hospitals survive it? The strategic answer centers on the concept of a tipping point: the share of revenue under value-based contracts at which it becomes financially rational to fully embrace cost-conscious care. Below that threshold, a hospital that aggressively cuts volume bleeds fee-for-service revenue faster than its value-based payments grow. Above it, reducing unnecessary utilization finally rewards the hospital more than it costs. Much of value-based strategy is about deliberately managing the pace of the shift so the two sides cross over without the hospital capsizing in between.
Hospitals use several bridges to tie the canoes closer together during the crossing. Expanded fee-for-service reimbursement — new billing codes for care coordination, remote patient monitoring, and chronic-care management — lets a hospital get paid for value-promoting activities even while still in the fee-for-service world, acting like bungee cords that keep the canoes from drifting too far apart. Hospitals also sequence their risk-taking, starting with upside-only shared savings before accepting downside risk, and concentrate value-based efforts on the populations and service lines where they can succeed first.
Determine what share of revenue is fee-for-service versus value-based — the position between the two canoes.
Assess the payment mix
Bill new care-coordination and monitoring codes to get paid for value activities while still in fee-for-service.
Use transitional bridges
Move from upside-only shared savings toward two-sided risk as value-based revenue grows.
Sequence the risk
Pace the shift so value-based payments grow fast enough to offset declining fee-for-service volume.
Manage toward the tipping point
Navigating the Volume-to-Value Transition
Why This Is the Hardest Problem in Hospital Finance
The volume-to-value transition is uniquely difficult because it asks an organization to undermine its current business model in order to build its future one — while keeping the lights on throughout. Every other industry that has been disrupted got to fail and be replaced; hospitals must transform themselves without interruption, because the community cannot go without a hospital while it figures out its finances. The two-canoes problem is not a temporary inconvenience but a structural feature of a decades-long, incomplete transition.
Moving from volume to value is like a store that earns most of its money selling cigarettes being told its future is selling gym memberships. As long as cigarettes pay the bills, every successful fitness program cannibalizes the store’s own revenue. It cannot simply stop selling cigarettes (it would go bankrupt) nor ignore the future (memberships are where the market is going). It has to grow the new business fast enough to replace the old one before the old one is taken away — exactly the tightrope hospitals walk.
The volume-to-value financial transition
External pressure is compressing the timeline. Hospitals are bracing for major revenue hits beginning in 2027 from provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA), pushing many to cut expenses and rethink their revenue base now. As fee-for-service reimbursement grows less sustainable and government payments tighten, the calculus increasingly favors moving toward value — not because value-based contracts are lucrative, but because the volume-based alternative is eroding. The two canoes are being pulled toward the value side whether hospitals are ready or not.
For the student of hospital finance, this lesson reframes everything that came before. Payer mix, margins, cost accounting, and capital structure all take on new meaning when revenue can be reduced by success rather than failure. The hospitals that navigate the transition will be those that understand their cost structure precisely (hence the emphasis on activity-based costing), manage the pace of risk deliberately, and build the population-health capabilities that make value-based payment a strength rather than a threat. The next lessons — on shared savings and risk, and on the business case for population health — are about exactly how to do that.
Under fee-for-service, reducing unnecessary care (admissions, readmissions, procedures) cuts revenue while fixed overhead remains — so a hospital can succeed clinically at value-based care and lose money doing it.

Research shows that because a prevented hospitalization leaves overhead uncovered, the loss of reimbursement can actually mitigate a hospital’s incentive to reduce readmissions — the payment system fighting the clinical goal.
Shared savings frequently fail to fully offset the fee-for-service revenue lost from reduced utilization, so a hospital can generate system savings and still come out behind if too little of its revenue is value-based.
Care is migrating as well as shrinking — inpatient knee replacements fell 21.2% year over year to outpatient settings — even amid strong overall revenue (20 straight months of growth, outpatient up 8.0%, margins reaching 6% in late 2024).
Hospitals manage the straddle by working toward a tipping point: the share of value-based revenue at which cutting unnecessary volume finally rewards more than it costs.
Transitional bridges — new billing codes for care coordination, remote monitoring, and chronic-care management, plus sequencing from upside-only to two-sided risk — tie the canoes together during the crossing.

######## hospital-finance | shared-savings-risk-capitation | Shared Savings, Risk Corridors, and Capitation
Shared Savings, Risk Corridors, and Capitation: The Risk Continuum
A Spectrum, Not a Switch
The previous lesson described the painful straddle between fee-for-service and value-based care. This lesson maps the destination side of that straddle in detail, because "value-based payment" is not one thing — it is a continuum of arrangements that transfer progressively more financial risk from the payer to the provider. At one end, a provider can earn a bonus for good performance while bearing no real downside. At the other, a provider receives a fixed payment to cover all of a population’s care and bears the full financial consequence if costs run high. Understanding where a contract sits on this continuum is the single most important thing to know about it.
The reason the continuum matters so much is that risk and reward move together. Arrangements with little downside risk are safe but offer modest upside; arrangements with full risk offer the largest rewards but can bankrupt a provider that miscalculates. Hospitals and physician groups generally move along this continuum over time — starting cautiously and taking on more risk as they build the capabilities to manage it. This lesson walks the spectrum from the gentlest to the most aggressive forms of risk-bearing.
Key Concept: Value-based payment is a continuum of risk transfer: from upside-only shared savings (bonus, no penalty), to two-sided risk (share savings and losses), to risk corridors (capped sharing), to capitation (a fixed payment covering all care, full provider risk). More risk means more potential reward — and more potential loss.
Capitation is paid "per member per month" — a fixed amount per attributed patient regardless of services used (American College of Physicians)
The Capitation Unit
PMPM
Capitation represents one of the highest degrees of risk transfer a provider can take on, short of starting its own insurance plan (industry sources)
Capitation’s Risk Level
Full risk
Upside-Only: The Gentle On-Ramp
The first step onto the risk continuum is upside risk, also called one-sided risk or shared savings. The provider is measured against a predetermined financial benchmark — typically the expected total cost of care for its attributed population. If the provider keeps actual costs below that target while meeting quality standards, it shares in the savings, earning a portion of the difference. Crucially, if costs exceed the target, the provider is not penalized: there is upside but no downside.
This asymmetry makes upside-only the natural starting point. It lets a provider learn to manage cost and quality, build the necessary data and care-coordination infrastructure, and earn rewards — all without risking a loss. The Medicare Shared Savings Program’s entry-level tracks work this way. The trade-off is that the rewards are modest precisely because the risk is low; payers do not pay large bonuses to providers who share none of the downside. Upside-only is a training ground, not a permanent home.
Indeed, the entire system is designed to push providers off the on-ramp over time. Because organizations typically grow into downside risk after starting upside-only — either pulled by larger financial incentives or pushed by contract mandates and program rules — two-sided arrangements are described as the more mature or advanced form of risk sharing. The gentle on-ramp exists to get providers ready for the road ahead.
Two-Sided Risk and Risk Corridors
The next step is two-sided risk, where the provider shares both savings and losses. If total cost of care comes in under the benchmark, the provider shares the savings as before; but if costs exceed the benchmark, the provider must share the loss — facing reimbursement cuts or owing money back to the payer. This is a fundamentally different proposition: the provider now has real money at stake in both directions, which sharpens the incentive to control costs but also exposes it to genuine financial danger.
To make two-sided risk survivable, contracts use risk corridors. A risk corridor caps the shared savings or losses using "risk bands": as actual results deviate further from the benchmark, the provider moves into bands where it shares a smaller percentage of the gains or losses. The effect is to limit how much a provider can win or lose in any period, protecting both sides from catastrophic swings. Risk corridors are the shock absorbers that let providers take on downside risk without betting the entire organization on a single bad year.
Upside-Only (One-Sided)
Share savings if costs beat the benchmark
No penalty if costs exceed the benchmark
Lower reward, minimal danger
The entry-level on-ramp to value
Builds capabilities with limited exposure
Two-Sided Risk
Share savings AND losses against the benchmark
Owe money back if costs exceed the target
Higher reward, real financial danger
Considered mature/advanced risk sharing
Often cushioned by risk corridors (risk bands)
One-Sided vs. Two-Sided Risk
Capitation: Taking on the Full Risk
At the far end of the continuum sits capitation — the most complete transfer of financial risk to the provider. Under capitation, a provider receives a fixed payment per attributed patient, paid per member per month (PMPM), to cover a defined scope of care regardless of how many services that patient actually uses. The PMPM amount represents the expected cost of providing those services. If the provider’s actual costs for its patient panel come in below the capitation budget, it keeps the difference as surplus; if costs exceed the budget, the provider absorbs the loss.
Capitation comes in degrees of breadth. Primary care capitation pays a fixed PMPM for routine primary care and care coordination — a relatively contained risk. Specialty capitation pays specialists a fixed amount for a defined service area like oncology or behavioral health. Global capitation is the most sweeping: a provider or group takes full financial responsibility for all of a population’s care — hospital, specialist, and ancillary services alike. Global capitation makes the provider function almost like an insurer, which is why it represents one of the highest degrees of risk transfer short of starting an insurance plan.
Earn a share of savings; no penalty for overspending. The training ground.
Upside-only shared savings
Share both savings and losses, usually cushioned by risk corridors.
Two-sided risk
Fixed PMPM for a defined scope, such as primary care or a specialty.
Partial / professional capitation
A fixed PMPM covering all of a population’s care — the provider bears full risk, like an insurer.
Global capitation
The Risk Continuum, From Lowest to Highest
Because capitation transfers so much risk, it requires sophisticated protective machinery. Risk adjustment is essential: PMPM rates must be adjusted upward for sicker patients, or providers would be paid too little to care for high-need populations (and would be tempted to avoid them). Risk pools — a portion of the capitation withheld and paid out only if costs stay controlled — align incentives within physician groups. And stop-loss or reinsurance protects the provider against catastrophic individual cases, capping the loss any single very-sick patient can impose. Without these mechanisms, capitation would be a reckless bet rather than a managed risk.
Choosing Where to Stand on the Continuum
The central strategic question for any provider is not whether to take risk, but how much, how fast, and with what protections. Moving up the continuum increases both the potential reward and the required capability. Upside-only demands basic cost and quality reporting. Two-sided risk demands genuine ability to manage total cost of care. Capitation demands actuarial sophistication, robust data, deep care-management infrastructure, and enough scale to spread risk across a population — capabilities a small or unprepared provider simply will not have.
The risk continuum is like levels of investing. Upside-only shared savings is a savings account with a bonus — safe, modest returns, no chance of loss. Two-sided risk is a diversified portfolio with stop-loss orders — real gains and losses, but bounded. Capitation is running your own fund where you keep all the profit but cover all the losses. You move to higher-risk levels only as your knowledge, reserves, and tools grow — and you use protections (risk corridors, reinsurance) the same way an investor uses hedges.
The value-based risk continuum
The mismatch between risk and capability is where providers get hurt. A group that jumps to capitation without the infrastructure to manage utilization, or without adequate risk adjustment for a sick population, can be financially destroyed by costs it cannot control. Conversely, a sophisticated, well-capitalized system that stays in upside-only leaves substantial reward on the table and signals it is not serious about value. Matching the level of risk to the organization’s real capabilities — and building those capabilities deliberately before advancing — is the essence of value-based financial strategy.
This continuum connects directly to the models covered in the value-based-care course: accountable care organizations typically operate in the shared-savings-to-two-sided-risk range, while Medicare Advantage and advanced primary care models push toward capitation. The same logic governs all of them. As payers and federal policy increasingly favor downside risk and full accountability, providers across the country are being pushed steadily rightward along this continuum. Knowing exactly what each arrangement transfers — and what capabilities and protections each demands — is what separates organizations that thrive under value-based payment from those that merely survive it.
Value-based payment is a continuum of increasing risk transfer from payer to provider: upside-only shared savings, two-sided risk, risk corridors, and capitation — with reward and danger rising together.
Upside-only (one-sided) risk lets providers share savings if they beat a cost benchmark with no penalty for overspending; it is the low-reward training ground for building value-based capabilities.
Two-sided risk requires providers to share both savings and losses, exposing them to real financial danger and marking the more mature, advanced stage of risk sharing.
Risk corridors cap shared savings and losses using risk bands, acting as shock absorbers that make two-sided risk survivable by limiting how much a provider can win or lose.
Capitation pays a fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) amount to cover a defined scope of care regardless of utilization; it ranges from primary care to specialty to global capitation, the broadest and riskiest.
Global capitation transfers full financial risk for all of a population’s care, making the provider function almost like an insurer — one of the highest degrees of risk transfer possible.
Capitation requires protective machinery: risk adjustment (higher PMPM for sicker patients), risk pools (withheld payments tied to performance), and stop-loss/reinsurance against catastrophic cases.
The strategic key is matching the level of risk to the organization’s real capabilities and building those capabilities before advancing; ACOs sit in the shared-savings-to-two-sided range while Medicare Advantage and advanced primary care push toward capitation.

######## hospital-finance | population-health-business-case | Building the Business Case for Population Health Investment
Building the Business Case for Population Health Investment
The Investment That Only Pays Off If the Incentives Are Right
Everyone agrees that keeping people healthy is better than treating them after they get sick. Helping a patient find stable housing, reliable food, or transportation to appointments can prevent expensive emergencies down the line. So why don’t hospitals pour money into population health and the social determinants that drive it? The answer is the hardest problem in this entire course: under the wrong payment incentives, investing in keeping people healthy is financially irrational, and even under the right ones, proving the return is genuinely difficult.
A population health investment is any spending aimed at improving the health of a defined group and reducing their need for costly care — care management for high-risk patients, chronic-disease programs, community health workers, food-as-medicine initiatives, housing support. The "business case" for such investment asks a deceptively simple question: will this spending pay for itself by reducing future health care costs? Building that case requires confronting two stubborn obstacles — who captures the savings, and when — that determine whether population health is a smart investment or a charitable cost.
Key Concept: The business case for population health rests on whether upstream investments (care management, SDOH interventions) reduce future high-cost care by more than they cost. Two obstacles dominate: the "wrong pocket problem" (whoever pays may not capture the savings) and long, uncertain timeframes for returns.
A systematic review of 52 studies found a median return of 14.3 to 1 on public health interventions — yet such spending is often cut, because the payer rarely captures the return (Masters et al., J Epidemiol Community Health, 2017)
Median ROI, Public Health Interventions
14.3:1
Revenue opportunities for population health ROI can be 7 to 10 times greater in "keeping patients inside the system" than in accountable-payment shared-savings buckets (Healthcare Innovation)
Where the ROI Is Larger
7–10x
The Promise: Why the Business Case Can Work
The logic of the population health business case is straightforward and, in the right conditions, compelling. A large share of health care spending is concentrated in a small number of high-need patients, and much of their cost comes from preventable crises — an uncontrolled diabetic landing in the ICU, a heart-failure patient readmitted because no one followed up after discharge, a homeless patient cycling through the emergency department. Investments that address the underlying drivers can reduce the use of high-cost services and yield savings for the health care organization.
The evidence increasingly supports this for targeted interventions. Research suggests that investments in social determinants of health can be cost-effective and even cost-saving: helping people find safe housing or healthy food reduces use of high-cost care. This is why hospital CEOs and CFOs are seeing a rising number of investment requests for social-determinant solutions — the shift to value-based care is evolving from treating disease toward community-based engagement that keeps people well in the first place. When a provider is paid to keep a population healthy, every prevented crisis becomes a financial gain.
That last clause is the entire ballgame. The business case for population health works only when the organization making the investment is financially rewarded for the resulting health improvement. Under capitation or strong shared-savings contracts, reduced utilization flows back to the provider as savings — so prevention pays. Under fee-for-service, the same prevention destroys revenue. The business case is not a fixed fact about population health; it is contingent on the payment model, which is why this lesson lives in the value-based-finance module.
The Wrong Pocket Problem
The single most important barrier to population health investment has a memorable name: the wrong pocket problem. It describes the mismatch between who pays for an intervention and who reaps the savings. A hospital might fund a housing program that dramatically reduces emergency visits — but if those savings accrue to Medicaid or a commercial insurer rather than the hospital, the hospital has spent money to enrich someone else’s budget. The investment is socially worthwhile and financially irrational for the party making it. The money comes out of one pocket and the savings land in another.
This misalignment paralyzes investment even when the overall return is positive. Studies have documented declines in public health spending despite positive societal returns, precisely because no single stakeholder captures enough of the benefit to justify the cost. The crux of the wrong pocket problem is shortages of political will and of evidence estimating stakeholder-specific returns over policy-relevant timelines — that is, evidence showing not just that an intervention saves money overall, but that it saves money for the specific entity being asked to pay.
An intervention can save the health care system money in aggregate and still be a bad investment for the hospital that funds it, if the savings flow to a different payer. Building a real business case means showing the return to the specific organization holding the checkbook — not just to "the system."
A Positive Societal ROI Is Not Enough
The wrong pocket problem also explains why payment model and ROI are inseparable. Analysts note that revenue opportunities to capture population-health ROI can be 7 to 10 times greater in the "keeping patients inside the system" bucket than in the "accountable payment" bucket — meaning where and how an organization gets paid dramatically changes whether a given investment pencils out. The same care-management program is a winner or a loser depending entirely on which pocket the savings land in.
The Timeframe and Measurement Problem
Even when the savings land in the right pocket, two more obstacles complicate the business case: time and proof. Many population health benefits materialize years or even decades after the investment — childhood obesity prevention, smoking cessation, early chronic-disease management. These long horizons clash with annual budgets, executive tenures, and the patience of boards and investors. An intervention that pays back over ten years is a hard sell when the CFO must show results this fiscal year, and the patient who benefits may have switched insurers long before the savings appear.
Measurement compounds the difficulty. The literature on the return from population health and SDOH investments is genuinely scarce and inconsistent: differences in study populations and methods make it hard to quantify and generalize results, and the lack of conclusive evidence that addressing social needs reliably reduces cost creates a real dilemma for decision-makers. Published evaluations of population health programs report results ranging from net losses to substantial savings per member — a spread that underscores how much success depends on design, population, and execution. Averages hide enormous variation.
Two health systems launch nearly identical community health worker programs targeting high-risk patients.

System A holds capitated and strong shared-savings contracts for these patients, carefully targets the highest-cost individuals, and tracks results over multiple years. Its program reduces avoidable admissions, and because System A bears the risk, the savings return to it — a strong positive ROI. System B runs the same program but is still largely fee-for-service for these patients, targets a broader and lower-risk group, and measures over a single year. Its prevented admissions cut its own revenue, the savings (such as they are) flow to insurers, and the short window misses the longer-term benefits. Same intervention, opposite business case — driven by payment model, targeting, and timeframe.
Why the Same Program Succeeds or Fails
Building a Business Case That Actually Holds
Given these obstacles, how do leaders build a population health business case that survives scrutiny? Several principles emerge from the evidence. First, align the investment with the payment model: pursue population health most aggressively for the populations where the organization holds risk (capitation, shared savings) and therefore captures the savings. Second, target precisely: focus interventions on the high-cost, high-need patients where the potential to reduce avoidable utilization — and thus the ROI — is greatest, rather than spreading resources thinly across a low-risk population.
Third, estimate stakeholder-specific returns over realistic timelines, using tools like the Commonwealth Fund’s ROI calculator and evidence guides to project what the savings will be and to whom they will accrue. Fourth, address the wrong pocket problem structurally — through shared-savings arrangements, value-based contracts, or cross-sector partnerships that let multiple stakeholders share both the investment and the return, so no single party bears the full cost while others capture the benefit.
The population health business case is like a landlord deciding whether to install better insulation. If the landlord pays the heating bill, the savings flow back to them and the investment is obvious. But if the tenant pays the utilities, the landlord spends the money and the tenant pockets the savings — the wrong pocket problem. The fix is to align who pays with who benefits: raise the rent, share the savings, or sign a lease that splits both. Hospitals do the same through risk contracts and partnerships.
The wrong pocket problem in population health
The honest conclusion is that population health is one of the most promising and most treacherous investments in health care. The promise is real: targeted, well-measured interventions for the right populations under the right payment models can both improve health and save money. The treachery is equally real: under misaligned incentives, long timeframes, and weak measurement, the same investment can be a money-loser that good intentions cannot rescue. This is the capstone of value-based finance — it shows that the financial wisdom of doing the right thing for patients depends entirely on building a payment system that rewards it. The business case for population health is, ultimately, the business case for value-based care itself.
A population health investment (care management, SDOH interventions, community health workers) aims to reduce future high-cost care; the business case asks whether it pays for itself through avoided spending.
The business case works only when the organization making the investment is financially rewarded for the health improvement — under capitation or shared savings prevention pays, but under fee-for-service it destroys revenue.
The "wrong pocket problem" is the central barrier: whoever funds an intervention may not capture the savings, making a socially worthwhile investment financially irrational for the party paying for it.
A positive societal ROI is not enough; the business case must show the return to the specific organization holding the checkbook, since savings can flow to a different payer.
Returns are often delayed for years or decades, clashing with annual budgets and executive tenures, and patients may switch insurers before the savings appear.
Measurement is hard and evidence is inconsistent — published program evaluations range from net losses to substantial savings per member, reflecting a wide range of success and failure.
A durable business case aligns the investment with the payment model, targets high-cost/high-need patients, estimates stakeholder-specific returns over realistic timelines, and uses shared savings or partnerships to fix the wrong pocket problem.
Population health is both promising and treacherous: the same intervention can save money or lose it depending on incentives, targeting, and timeframe — making its business case ultimately the business case for value-based care itself.

######## hospital-finance | board-financial-oversight | Board Financial Oversight and Fiduciary Duty
Board Financial Oversight and Fiduciary Duty
Who Is Actually Responsible When a Hospital’s Finances Fail?
When a hospital makes a disastrous financial decision — overbuilds, mismanages its debt, or quietly slides toward insolvency — the question of accountability eventually lands in one place: the board of directors. Hospital executives run the institution day to day, but the board holds ultimate responsibility for its financial health and its faithfulness to its mission. Understanding board financial oversight is understanding the last line of defense in hospital finance, and the legal duties that make board service a serious obligation rather than an honorary title.
This responsibility is rooted in the concept of fiduciary duty — the legal obligation to act in the best interest of the organization and the community it serves. For the governing board of a nonprofit hospital, the fundamental fiduciary duty is to ensure the organization’s fidelity to its core mission, and all board members are liable and accountable for their actions. A board member who rubber-stamps management without genuine scrutiny is not fulfilling a ceremonial role poorly; they are breaching a legal duty.
For nonprofit hospitals especially, this oversight carries public weight. These organizations hold billions in tax-exempt assets and enjoy tax exemptions justified by their community benefit. The board is the body that holds the institution to that bargain — ensuring the hospital is financially sound enough to survive and mission-driven enough to deserve its privileged status. Board financial oversight sits at the intersection of finance, law, and public trust.
Key Concept: A hospital board holds ultimate fiduciary responsibility for the organization’s financial health and mission. Fiduciary duty — the legal obligation to act in the organization’s best interest — makes board members accountable and liable for their oversight, not merely advisory.
The Three Fiduciary Duties
Fiduciary duty is traditionally broken into three components, and every board financial decision can be tested against them. The duty of care requires board members to exercise reasonable care and diligence — to stay informed and understand the financial reports, budgets, strategic initiatives, and risks that materially affect the organization, and to make decisions thoughtfully rather than carelessly. A director who never reads the financials or asks a probing question has failed the duty of care regardless of good intentions.
The duty of loyalty requires board members to put the organization’s interests ahead of their own — avoiding conflicts of interest and never using their position for personal gain. This is why hospitals require conflict-of-interest policies and disclosures: a board member who steers a contract to their own company, even if the deal seems fair, violates the duty of loyalty. The duty of obedience requires the board to ensure the organization stays faithful to its mission and complies with the law, including the obligations that underpin its tax-exempt status.
What Each Duty Requires
Duty of Care: stay informed, read the financials, decide diligently
Duty of Loyalty: put the organization first, avoid conflicts of interest
Duty of Obedience: uphold the mission and comply with the law
What Violates Each Duty
Care: rubber-stamping management without scrutiny
Loyalty: self-dealing or undisclosed conflicts
Obedience: straying from mission or breaching legal/tax obligations
The Three Fiduciary Duties in Practice
A board member who means well but never reviews actual financial statements, or who approves a deal benefiting a relative without disclosure, has breached their fiduciary duty. These duties are legal standards measured by conduct and diligence — not by sincerity.
Good Intentions Do Not Satisfy Fiduciary Duty
The Board’s Core Financial Responsibilities
Fiduciary duty translates into a concrete set of financial responsibilities. A hospital board has six core financial duties: to specify financial objectives, to review and align management’s financial plan with those objectives, to enhance the organization’s creditworthiness, to ensure capital is effectively allocated, to monitor financial performance, and to verify the financial statements. Notice how these map onto earlier lessons — creditworthiness ties to the debt-financing and bond-rating material, and capital allocation to the capital-planning material. The board is the body that governs all of it.
The most important ongoing duty is monitoring financial performance — and here the duty of care has a sharp, practical edge. Genuine oversight requires reviewing actual financial statements, not summaries or verbal updates: the treasurer’s report should always include the current balance sheet and income statement so the board can see the institution’s true position. A board that accepts a reassuring slide saying "finances are fine" has not exercised oversight; one that reviews the statements, tracks the ratios from Module 1, and questions variances has.
Set the targets — margin, liquidity, growth — the organization should achieve.
Specify financial objectives
Review the financial plan and ensure it serves the stated objectives.
Align management’s plan
Steward the balance sheet and ensure scarce capital goes to the right investments.
Enhance creditworthiness & allocate capital
Review actual financial statements regularly and confirm their accuracy.
Monitor performance & verify statements
The Board’s Six Core Financial Responsibilities
The Tools of Oversight: Committees, Audits, and Form 990
Boards cannot exercise oversight on instinct; they rely on structures and documents. The most important structure is the audit committee — and best practice, drawn from the principles of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act, holds that if a tax-exempt hospital lacks a separate audit committee, it should establish one composed of members completely independent from management who receive no consulting or advisory fees. The audit committee oversees independent external audits, internal controls, and risk, providing the board an objective check on management’s financial reporting. Other Sarbanes-Oxley-inspired practices include auditor independence (periodic rotation), whistleblower protection, and document-retention policies.
The central oversight document for a nonprofit hospital is the IRS Form 990, the annual information return that publicly discloses the organization’s finances, governance, and compensation. Board review of the Form 990 before filing has long been a best practice — and the IRS itself has concluded that nonprofits with a board review process are more likely to be in compliance with tax laws. For hospitals specifically, Schedule H reports the Section 501(r) policies covered earlier: community health needs assessments, financial assistance, emergency care, and billing and collection practices. The 990 is where the board’s stewardship of the tax-exempt bargain becomes public and auditable.
Modern boards increasingly rely on dashboards and reporting tools that present real-time financial and compliance data, letting them track the key ratios and metrics continuously rather than quarterly. But tools do not replace judgment. The IRS scrutiny of nonprofit hospitals’ tax-exempt status has intensified, and a board that cannot demonstrate active, documented oversight of both financial performance and community-benefit obligations exposes the institution to real regulatory and reputational risk.
Why Governance Determines Destiny
It is tempting to treat board governance as a formality far removed from the real work of running a hospital. The evidence says otherwise: board configuration and oversight practices are associated with hospital financial performance. One study of hospital boards found that structural features such as meeting frequency and term limits were associated with financial performance — though not always in the intuitive direction: boards meeting fewer than six times a year posted higher margins than those meeting more than twelve times. What matters is the quality of oversight, not the number of meetings. Governance is not separate from finance; it is the mechanism that steers it.
A hospital board is like the flight crew’s oversight of an aircraft. Management flies the plane day to day, but the board is responsible for ensuring the instruments are accurate, the fuel reserves are adequate, the route is sound, and the airline’s rules and the law are followed. A board that simply trusts the pilot and never checks the gauges is not being polite — it is abdicating the very responsibility that justifies its existence, and everyone on board bears the consequences.
The board’s financial oversight role
The duties also create a structural tension the board must manage: the same body responsible for financial soundness is responsible for fidelity to a charitable mission, and these can pull against each other. A board fixated only on margins may neglect community benefit and the duty of obedience; a board fixated only on mission may let the institution slide toward insolvency, failing the duty of care. Good board financial oversight holds both — keeping the hospital financially viable precisely so it can fulfill its mission, recognizing that an insolvent hospital serves no one.
This is why board financial oversight is the right capstone for the governance side of hospital finance. Every concept in this course — margins and ratios, payer mix, cost accounting, capital and debt, value-based payment — ultimately rolls up to a board that must understand it well enough to govern it. The board does not need to be expert in every detail, but it must be diligent enough to ask the right questions, independent enough to get honest answers, and loyal enough to act on them in the organization’s and community’s interest. When hospital finance fails, it is most often because that oversight failed first.

######## hospital-finance | health-system-integration | Systemness: Financial Integration Across Health Systems
Systemness: Financial Integration Across Health Systems
From Standalone Hospitals to Sprawling Systems
The independent community hospital, once the norm in American health care, is now the exception. Nearly 70% of U.S. hospitals are affiliated with a health system, and the trend toward consolidation continues. Standalone hospitals have merged into regional and national systems, hospitals have acquired physician practices and outpatient centers, and the result is a landscape dominated by large, integrated organizations. This lesson examines the financial logic behind that transformation — the pursuit of "systemness" — and the uncomfortable gap between what consolidation promises and what the evidence shows it delivers.
"Systemness" refers to the financial and operational benefits a health system aims to capture by integrating its parts into a coordinated whole rather than a collection of separate facilities. The theory is appealing: a unified system can achieve economies of scale, negotiate better with payers and suppliers, access capital more cheaply, pool data, standardize care, and shift services to lower-cost settings. These are real potential advantages, and they explain why consolidation has been one of the most powerful forces reshaping hospital finance.
But the gap between theory and reality is where this lesson earns its keep. A large and consistent body of evidence shows that consolidation reliably raises prices while rarely lowering costs or improving quality. Understanding both the genuine financial benefits of integration and its well-documented harms is essential to thinking clearly about one of the central trends in American health care.
Key Concept: "Systemness" is the set of financial and operational benefits — economies of scale, payer leverage, capital access, pooled data, standardized care — that health systems seek through integration. The evidence shows consolidation reliably raises prices but rarely lowers costs or improves quality.
69% of U.S. hospitals are now part of a larger health system, up from 56% in 2010 (KFF)
Hospitals in a System
~70%
One or two systems controlled the entire inpatient market in 47% of metropolitan areas in 2024; in 83% they controlled over 75% (KFF)
Markets Dominated by 1–2 Systems
47% of metros
Two Directions of Integration
Integration happens along two axes, and the distinction matters financially. Horizontal integration occurs when one hospital or system merges with or acquires another hospital — combining like with like to gain size and market share within the same level of care. Vertical integration occurs when a system acquires other parts of the care chain, most notably physician practices and outpatient centers — combining different stages of care delivery under one owner. A system pursuing systemness typically does both: growing horizontally to dominate markets and vertically to control the patient’s full care journey.
The stated rationales are genuine business logic. Consolidation can provide economies of scale (spreading fixed administrative, IT, and overhead costs across more facilities), access to capital (a large system borrows more cheaply, as the debt-financing lesson showed), pooled data (enabling population health and analytics), and bargaining leverage against market-dominant payers. Proponents also cite the ability to move care to lower-cost outpatient settings, standardize quality, and rescue financially struggling rural hospitals and physician practices that cannot survive alone.
Horizontal Integration
Hospital merges with or acquires another hospital
Combines the same level of care
Increases size and local market share
Can raise prices 6%–65% in concentrated markets
Vertical Integration
System acquires physician practices or outpatient centers
Combines different stages of the care chain
Controls more of the patient’s care journey
Physician-practice acquisition raises prices ~14% on average
Horizontal vs. Vertical Integration
The Evidence: Higher Prices, Not Lower Costs
Here the data delivers an inconvenient verdict. Despite economies-of-scale rhetoric, mergers and acquisitions of U.S. hospitals rarely improve quality or lower costs and prices — and they frequently raise them. Horizontal hospital-to-hospital mergers in concentrated markets can raise hospital prices anywhere from 6% to 65%. One review found hospital charges increased with integration 93% of the time, in 13 of 14 studies measuring price changes. The promised savings, when they exist at all, rarely reach patients or payers.
Vertical integration shows the same pattern. When hospitals acquire physician practices, prices for those physicians’ services rise about 14% on average — and patients sometimes find prices doubled or more simply because their practice was purchased by a hospital and can now bill at hospital rates. Cross-market mergers (combining hospitals in different geographic markets) raised prices by almost 13% over six years, with even larger increases when the acquired hospital had a bigger market share. The mechanism is straightforward: market power. A system that dominates a market can demand higher rates from insurers, who pass the cost to employers and patients.
The most common justification for consolidation — economies of scale lowering costs — is largely not borne out. Improved health care value cannot be achieved by hospital mergers and acquisitions alone; the dominant measurable effect is higher prices from increased market power, not lower costs passed on to patients.
Economies of Scale Are Often a Rationale, Not a Result
The macroeconomic consequences are sobering. Higher provider prices from consolidation raised insurance premiums and out-of-pocket costs, which come out of workers’ paychecks — contributing to an estimated reduction in U.S. worker wages of nearly $1 trillion from 2012 to 2022. Consolidation is not a victimless reshuffling of corporate boxes; it transfers real money from workers and patients to dominant systems through higher prices.
The Regulatory Response
Because the price evidence is so consistent, antitrust regulators have intensified their scrutiny of health care consolidation. The Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and Department of Justice have ramped up enforcement, and in 2023 jointly released modernized merger guidelines that expanded the analytical tools for evaluating health care transactions, with particular attention to already-concentrated hospital and physician-group markets. Regulators have grown skeptical of the "efficiency" justifications systems offer for mergers, given how rarely those efficiencies materialize as lower prices.
This scrutiny has teeth. The FTC has blocked or deterred multiple hospital mergers, and in June 2024, Novant Health in North Carolina canceled its planned acquisition of two hospitals after the FTC argued the deal would create near-monopoly conditions. These actions signal a regulatory environment far less willing to accept consolidation on faith. For health systems, this means that the path to systemness through acquisition now runs through a much more demanding antitrust gauntlet — and that the financial case for a merger must increasingly account for the risk of regulatory rejection.
Consider a system that already operates the largest hospital in a metro area and seeks to acquire its main competitor. The stated rationale is economies of scale and integrated care. But the practical effect — as the FTC argued in blocking such deals — is that the combined system would control most of the market’s inpatient capacity, giving it the leverage to demand higher rates from every insurer in the region.

This is the heart of the consolidation paradox: the same market dominance that delivers the financial "benefit" of payer leverage is precisely what harms patients and employers through higher prices. Systemness and market power are often two names for the same thing — which is why regulators increasingly treat the efficiency story with skepticism.
When Market Dominance Becomes the Strategy
Thinking Clearly About Systemness
How should a student of hospital finance hold these competing realities? The honest synthesis is that integration has genuine potential benefits and a documented record of disappointing on them. The economies of scale, capital access, and data pooling are real and can, in principle, support better and more efficient care — especially the legitimate rescue of failing rural hospitals and the shift of care to lower-cost settings. But the dominant, measurable effect of consolidation as actually practiced has been higher prices driven by market power, not lower costs or better quality.
Systemness is like merging several neighborhood hardware stores into a single chain. In theory, the chain buys in bulk, shares a warehouse, and passes savings to customers. In practice, once it is the only hardware store in town, the incentive to pass along savings evaporates — it can simply charge more because shoppers have nowhere else to go. The efficiencies may be real, but without competition, they tend to enrich the chain rather than the customer.
The promise vs. reality of health system consolidation
This tension also connects to value-based care in a revealing way. Consolidation’s defenders increasingly justify it as necessary infrastructure for value-based, population-health-oriented care — the scale and pooled data needed to manage populations and bear risk. There is something to this: bearing capitation risk does require scale and capabilities. But the evidence that integration alone improves value is lacking, which means systemness is at best a potential enabler of value, not a guarantee of it. A system can consolidate, raise prices, and never deliver the value it promised.
For the board and the finance leader, the lesson is to separate the rhetoric of systemness from its measurable results. A merger may genuinely strengthen an organization’s balance sheet and capabilities — or it may simply buy market power that raises prices while doing little for patients. Distinguishing the two requires exactly the analytical discipline this course has built: looking past the strategic narrative to the actual financial and quality evidence. Systemness is neither salvation nor villainy; it is a powerful financial strategy whose benefits accrue unevenly, and whose price effects make it one of the most scrutinized and consequential forces in American health care.

######## hospital-finance | financial-sustainability | Financial Sustainability in a Changing Landscape
Financial Sustainability in a Changing Landscape
The Question Every Other Lesson Has Been Building Toward
Every concept in this course — payer mix and margins, cost accounting, capital and debt, value-based payment, governance — ultimately serves a single question: can this hospital survive? Financial sustainability is the capacity of a hospital to remain financially viable over the long term while continuing to fulfill its mission. It is not a single metric but a condition: enough margin to reinvest, enough liquidity to weather shocks, enough access to capital to modernize, and a business model durable enough to withstand a relentlessly changing landscape. This capstone lesson examines the forces threatening that sustainability today and the strategies hospitals are using to defend it.
The central threat is deceptively simple and increasingly severe: expenses are growing faster than revenue. In 2025, hospital expenses increased by 7.5% — over twice the rate of growth in hospital prices over the same period. When the cost of providing care rises faster than the payment for it, margins compress, and for many hospitals, health systems, and medical groups, margin pressure in 2026 is intense, with the median hospital operating margin slipping below zero early in the year. The thin margins documented throughout this course are now being squeezed harder than ever.
This is not a temporary post-pandemic hangover; it is a structural challenge driven by labor and drug costs, an aging population shifting payer mix toward government programs, and looming federal funding cuts. Understanding financial sustainability means understanding both why the pressure is mounting and what separates the hospitals that will adapt from those that will close.
Key Concept: Financial sustainability is a hospital’s capacity to stay viable long-term while fulfilling its mission — requiring adequate margin, liquidity, and capital access. The defining threat today is expense growth outpacing revenue growth, compressing already-thin margins.
Total hospital expenses grew 7.5% in 2025 — more than twice the rate of growth in hospital prices (AHA, Costs of Caring, March 2026)
Hospital Expense Growth, 2025
