Message Structure: Segments, Fields, and the Pipe-Delimited Format
HL7 v2 messages are plain text, structured hierarchically using delimiter characters rather than XML tags or JSON keys. The vertical bar (pipe, "|") separates fields within a segment. The caret ("^") separates components within a field. The tilde ("~") separates repetitions of a field. And the ampersand ("&") separates sub-components. This means a raw HL7 v2 message looks, to the uninitiated, like line noise — but to integration engineers, each position carries precise clinical meaning. Every message begins with an MSH (Message Header) segment, which encodes the sending application, receiving application, message type, timestamp, and a unique message control ID. If any segment is the "shipping label" of the HL7 envelope, it is MSH.
After MSH, a patient-level message will typically contain a PID (Patient Identification) segment carrying demographics: medical record number, name, date of birth, sex, address, and contact information. The PID segment is the foundation for patient matching across disparate systems — a notoriously difficult problem given that the same patient may have different identifiers in the EHR, the lab system, and the insurance system. For clinical orders and results, the OBR (Observation Request) segment describes what was ordered — the test, the ordering provider, the specimen collection time — while one or more OBX (Observation Result) segments carry the actual result values, reference ranges, and abnormal flags. A single lab panel can generate dozens of OBX segments, one per analyte.
A realistic HL7 v2 lab result message (ORU^R01) might look like this: "MSH|^~\&|LAB_SYS|MAIN_HOSPITAL|EHR|MAIN_HOSPITAL|20240315143022||ORU^R01|MSG00123|P|2.5" on the first line, followed by "PID|1||MRN123456^^^MAIN_HOSPITAL||JOHNSON^SARAH^M||19820714|F" identifying the patient, then "OBR|1|ORD987654|LAB987654|85025^COMPLETE BLOOD COUNT^CPT" describing the CBC order, and finally a series of OBX lines such as "OBX|1|NM|718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN||13.8|g/dL|12.0-16.0|N|||F" carrying the hemoglobin result with value, units, reference range, and a normal flag. Parsing that string correctly requires knowing not just the delimiters but the HL7 data type and table definitions for every field position. This is why integration engines and parser libraries exist.
OBX|1|NM|718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN||13.8|g/dL|12.0-16.0|N|||F

Field 1 (Set ID): 1 — sequence number within the message
Field 2 (Value Type): NM — numeric
Field 3 (Observation Identifier): 718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN — LOINC code, name, coding system
Field 5 (Observation Value): 13.8 — the result
Field 6 (Units): g/dL
Field 7 (Reference Range): 12.0–16.0
Field 8 (Abnormal Flag): N — normal
Field 11 (Observation Result Status): F — final result
Anatomy of an OBX Segment
Common Message Types and Clinical Workflows
The ADT (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) family of messages is the heartbeat of hospital operations. When a patient arrives and is admitted, the registration system fires an ADT^A01 message to every downstream system — the pharmacy, the dietary system, the billing engine, the clinical documentation platform — so that each knows a new patient encounter has begun. When that patient moves from the emergency department to the ICU, an ADT^A02 transfer message propagates the location change. When they go home, ADT^A03 closes the encounter. And whenever patient demographics are corrected — a misspelled name, an updated insurance ID — ADT^A08 broadcasts the update. These four event types (A01, A02, A03, A08) alone account for the majority of ADT message volume in most health systems, and their reliable delivery is a prerequisite for accurate care coordination, billing, and quality reporting.
The ORM (Order Message) and ORU (Observation Result Unsolicited) pair forms the backbone of the diagnostic cycle. When a clinician places a lab or radiology order, the EHR sends an ORM^O01 to the laboratory or radiology information system. The receiving system acknowledges with an ACK (acknowledgment) message, then begins processing. When results are available, the lab system returns an ORU^R01 carrying OBX segments for each result. This bidirectional ORM-to-ORU loop happens millions of times per day across U.S. hospitals. For scheduling, SIU (Scheduling Information Unsolicited) messages — ranging from SIU^S12 (notification of new appointment) to SIU^S15 (notification of appointment cancellation) — synchronize scheduling modules across EHR, radiology, and referral management platforms. MDM (Medical Document Management) messages, particularly MDM^T02, carry transcribed clinical notes, operative reports, and discharge summaries from dictation and transcription platforms back into the EHR.
Understanding these message types is essential for anyone troubleshooting an integration failure or designing a new interface. When a provider complains that lab results are not appearing in the EHR, the problem is almost certainly in the ORU pipeline — perhaps a malformed OBX segment, an unrecognized LOINC code in OBX-3, or a mismatch in the patient identifier that prevents the result from attaching to the correct encounter. When the pharmacy does not know a patient has been admitted, the ADT^A01 message likely failed delivery or was silently dropped due to a message profile mismatch. Tracing the HL7 message type immediately narrows the diagnostic search space from the entire hospital IT ecosystem to a specific interface and segment.
Clinician selects a lab test in the EHR; the system generates an ORM^O01 message containing the order details in OBR and patient details in PID.
Provider Places Order
The integration engine routes the ORM via MLLP over TCP to the Laboratory Information System (LIS). The LIS sends back an ACK to confirm receipt.
Order Transmitted to Lab
The lab collects the specimen, runs the analyzer, and records results. The LIS generates an ORU^R01 with one OBX segment per result value.
Specimen Collected and Analyzed
The LIS transmits the ORU^R01 back through the integration engine to the EHR. The EHR parses the message and attaches results to the patient encounter.
Result Delivered to EHR
The EHR alerts the ordering provider that results are available, completing the diagnostic loop.
Provider Notified
The Order-Result Cycle in HL7 v2
The HL7 v2 Interoperability Problem: Standards That Do Not Standardize
HL7 v2's greatest strength — flexibility — is also its deepest flaw. The standard defines message structures but does not enforce vocabulary, implementation choices, or local customizations. Two systems that both claim compliance with HL7 v2.3 can be entirely incompatible in practice. One laboratory might encode hemoglobin results using a local code "HGB" in OBX-3, while another uses the LOINC code "718-7^HEMOGLOBIN^LN". Both are technically valid under HL7 v2.3. The receiving EHR, however, may only be configured to recognize LOINC codes — meaning the first lab's results will be received but silently fail to map, leaving clinicians staring at an empty result field while the data sits orphaned in an integration engine queue. This kind of silent failure is more dangerous than an outright error.
The Z-segment mechanism exemplifies this tension between flexibility and interoperability. Every HL7 v2 segment beginning with the letter "Z" is a locally defined, proprietary extension. Vendors use Z-segments to transmit data that either does not fit in standard segments or that they prefer to keep in custom structures — patient consent flags, scheduling metadata, insurance authorization codes. A ZIN segment from one vendor and a ZIN segment from a different vendor may share a name but carry completely different fields. Receiving systems that encounter an unknown Z-segment are typically configured to ignore it silently. This means critical data encoded in Z-segments by the sending system may simply vanish at the receiving end unless both parties have explicitly agreed on the custom structure, documented it, and implemented it — which requires ongoing bilateral coordination that rarely scales across a health system with hundreds of interfaces.
The practical consequence of HL7 v2's implementation flexibility is a phenomenon called "interface engine proliferation." Because each connection between two systems requires custom translation logic to reconcile differences in field usage, code sets, and Z-segments, health systems have accumulated integration engines — Mirth Connect, Rhapsody, InterSystems HealthShare, Cloverleaf — running thousands of individual channel configurations. A large academic medical center may operate a very large number of active HL7 interfaces, each one a small bespoke software artifact. This creates a massive, hidden infrastructure burden: every upgrade to an EHR or lab system can break dozens of interfaces, each of which must be individually tested and repaired. The interfaces collectively represent years of engineering effort and institutional knowledge that is rarely documented adequately.
HL7 v2 interfaces frequently accept and acknowledge messages (sending back an ACK) that they then fail to process correctly due to code mapping errors or unrecognized Z-segments. This means clinical data — lab results, medication orders — can appear to have been delivered successfully while actually being lost or misfiled. Integration monitoring tools that check beyond ACK status are essential for detecting these silent failures.
The Silent Failure Risk
Imagine if the United States had a national standard for electrical outlets that specified the shape of the plug but not the voltage, frequency, or current rating — and allowed any manufacturer to add extra pins labeled with whatever letters they chose. Every device would technically use the "standard" outlet, but you would need a custom adapter for every device-outlet combination. That is HL7 v2 interoperability in practice.
HL7 v2 defines message structure (the plug shape) but leaves vocabulary, coding systems, and local extensions (the voltage and custom pins) to each implementer — creating the illusion of standardization while preserving the reality of point-to-point incompatibility.
HL7 v2 and FHIR Coexistence: The Long Transition
HL7 FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), published in 2014 and now at Release 4 and beyond, was designed to address almost every limitation of HL7 v2: it uses RESTful APIs and JSON/XML, enforces structure through defined resource types, mandates standard terminologies, and is natively web-compatible. The question is not whether FHIR is technically superior to HL7 v2 — it clearly is. The question is how to get from here to there without disrupting the billions of clinical transactions that depend on HL7 v2 every day. The answer, increasingly, is that they will coexist for decades. HL7 International has explicitly recognized this reality by publishing the official HL7 Version 2 to FHIR Implementation Guide, a project maintained by the Orders and Observations working group that provides standardized mappings from HL7 v2 messages, segments, and data types to their FHIR R4 equivalents.
The transport layer for HL7 v2 — MLLP, the Minimal Lower Layer Protocol — is another dimension of the legacy that will persist. MLLP wraps HL7 v2 messages in a simple envelope using start-of-block (ASCII 0x0B) and end-of-block (ASCII 0x1C) characters, then transmits the wrapped message over a persistent TCP connection. MLLP has no inherent security or encryption; it relies on TLS or IPsec at the network layer for protection of PHI in transit. IANA registers port 2575 for HL7, though in practice each interface listens on whatever port the two parties agree — and it requires a persistent, stateful TCP connection between sender and receiver. Every major integration engine — Mirth Connect, Rhapsody, InterSystems, Cloverleaf — maintains MLLP listener and sender components as core capabilities. As long as legacy systems speak only MLLP, the integration engine's job is to receive MLLP HL7 v2, transform it to FHIR, and deliver it to modern API endpoints — acting as a universal translator at the boundary between eras.
The v2-to-FHIR mapping project (available at build.fhir.org/ig/HL7/v2-to-fhir) defines, for example, how the fields of an HL7 v2 PID segment map to FHIR Patient resource attributes: PID-3 (Patient Identifier List) maps to Patient.identifier, PID-5 (Patient Name) maps to Patient.name, PID-7 (Date of Birth) maps to Patient.birthDate, and so on. Similarly, an ADT^A01 message maps to a FHIR Bundle containing a MessageHeader, Patient, Encounter, and related resources. These mappings allow integration engines to serve as automated translators — converting the legacy pipe-delimited messages arriving from a 20-year-old laboratory system into standards-conformant FHIR resources that can be consumed by a modern clinical decision support platform or a patient-facing app operating under 21st Century Cures Act API mandates. The coexistence of v2 and FHIR is not a failure of modernization; it is the realistic, pragmatic path forward for an industry where patient safety cannot tolerate a big-bang replacement of working infrastructure.

HL7 v2 vs. FHIR: Key Differences
The HL7 v2-to-FHIR Implementation Guide (published by HL7 International, Orders and Observations WG) is the authoritative bridge document for organizations managing the transition. Integration engines use these mappings to auto-translate incoming HL7 v2 traffic into FHIR resources, enabling modern applications to consume legacy data without requiring source system upgrades.
HL7 Version 2 was created in 1987–1988 to solve the N-squared interface problem in hospitals, and remains the dominant messaging standard in U.S. hospitals.
HL7 International reports that 95% of U.S. healthcare organizations use HL7 v2 and more than 35 countries have implemented it.
HL7 v2 messages are pipe-delimited plain text; the MSH segment is the mandatory header, PID carries patient identity, OBR carries order details, and OBX carries individual result values.
ADT messages (A01 admit, A02 transfer, A03 discharge, A08 update) are the heartbeat of hospital operations; ORU carries results; ORM carries orders; SIU carries scheduling events; MDM carries clinical documents.
HL7 v2's fatal flaw is implementation flexibility without enforcement: two v2.3-compliant systems can be incompatible due to different code sets, field usage, and proprietary Z-segments.
Z-segments (any segment beginning with "Z") are local custom extensions; receiving systems typically ignore unknown Z-segments, creating silent data loss risks.
MLLP (Minimal Lower Layer Protocol) is the standard transport for HL7 v2 over TCP — it wraps messages in start/end block characters and has no built-in security.
HL7 International has published an official v2-to-FHIR Implementation Guide; integration engines serve as translators between the HL7 v2 legacy world and modern FHIR APIs, enabling coexistence rather than replacement.
The positive ACK confirms the message was received at the transport layer, but it does not guarantee the EHR successfully parsed and filed the data. A mismatch between the laboratory's local observation code in OBX-3 and the EHR's expected coding system (e.g., LOINC) is the most common cause of this "ghost delivery" failure pattern — the message arrives, is acknowledged, and is then silently discarded or queued as unmapped. This is one of the most dangerous failure modes in HL7 v2 integration because clinical staff receive no alert and may believe results are simply pending.
The MLLP connection timed out before the ACK was transmitted.
A code mapping failure — the OBX observation identifier uses a local code the EHR does not recognize — caused the result to be received but not filed.
The ADT^A03 discharge message closed the encounter before the result arrived.
The PID segment was missing, so the entire message was rejected at the MLLP layer.

FHIR Fundamentals: The Modern Standard for Healthcare Data Exchange
Why FHIR Exists: The Problem It Solves
For most of the past four decades, healthcare data exchange ran on a standard called HL7 version 2, first released in 1987. HL7 v2 is a pipe-delimited text format — essentially a structured text file where each field is separated by a vertical bar character. Hospitals still send tens of millions of these messages every day for lab results, admission notifications, and discharge summaries. The problem is that HL7 v2 was never truly standardized: each hospital, lab, and payer customized the format to their own needs. The result was that two organizations could each claim HL7 v2 compliance yet be completely unable to exchange data without expensive custom interface engines sitting between them.
HL7 attempted to solve this chaos with version 3 and its companion standard, the Clinical Document Architecture (CDA). Released in 2005, CDA introduced XML-based documents like the Continuity of Care Document (CCD) and brought more rigorous modeling using a formal Reference Information Model (RIM). On paper, CDA was a major step forward. In practice, it proved so complex to implement that adoption required months of training, and the resulting documents were sprawling XML files sometimes hundreds of kilobytes long for a single patient encounter. Ambiguous specifications meant different vendors interpreted the standard differently, recreating the same fragmentation problem at a higher level of sophistication.
The breakthrough came from an unexpected direction. In 2011, Grahame Grieve — an Australian health informaticist running a small consulting firm called Health Intersections — put forward a proposal called "Resources for Healthcare." He argued that instead of modeling the entire healthcare universe in a single monolithic schema, the industry should define discrete, self-contained data objects — resources — that could be exchanged individually over the web using the same RESTful HTTP conventions already powering every modern web application. HL7 adopted the proposal, renamed the project Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), and Grieve went on to lead its development as HL7's FHIR Product Director. FHIR's foundational insight was simple and radical: make healthcare data exchange feel like using the internet, not like implementing a mainframe EDI system.
HL7 v2 and CDA are like sending a fax — the technology works, but every machine has its own quirks, and you need a human on both ends to interpret the smudged output. FHIR is like sending a JSON API response — any developer with a browser and twenty lines of code can read it immediately.
FHIR replaces proprietary healthcare message formats with the same web-native conventions that power modern software, dramatically lowering the barrier to interoperability.
The original pipe-delimited standard that still carries the majority of clinical messages today

Core Concepts: Resources, RESTful APIs, and Profiles
The fundamental unit of FHIR is the resource. A resource is a discrete, self-contained piece of healthcare information: a Patient, a Condition, a Medication, an Observation, an Encounter. Each resource has a defined structure — a set of typed fields, cardinality constraints, and a standard identifier — and can be serialized as either JSON or XML. FHIR R4 defines 145 resource types spanning clinical data, administrative data, financial records, and the specification infrastructure itself. Because each resource is independently addressable via a URL, any developer who can make an HTTP GET request can retrieve a patient's medication list without needing to parse thousands of lines of XML or understand a complex proprietary schema.
FHIR uses standard RESTful HTTP verbs to operate on resources. GET retrieves a resource or a collection of resources. POST creates a new resource. PUT updates an existing resource by replacing it in full. PATCH applies a partial update. DELETE removes a resource. This means that a FHIR server is, at its core, a web API — and developers already experienced building or consuming REST APIs can begin working with FHIR data without a steep learning curve. The specification also defines a search interaction with a rich query syntax, allowing applications to retrieve, for example, all Observations for a given patient with a specific LOINC code within a date range — expressed as a URL query string any web developer would recognize.
Because a generic resource like Observation must serve everything from a blood pressure reading to a pregnancy test result, FHIR introduces the concept of profiles to constrain and extend base resources for specific use cases. A profile is a StructureDefinition that narrows the allowable values in certain fields, makes optional elements required, and adds extensions for data elements not present in the base resource. Collections of profiles, terminology bindings, and example instances are packaged into Implementation Guides (IGs). The US Core Implementation Guide, developed by HL7 and referenced by U.S. federal regulation, defines the minimum data set that certified EHR systems must expose — ensuring that a patient's medications, allergies, and problem list are available in a predictable, consistent format regardless of the underlying vendor.

A minimal Patient resource looks like: { "resourceType": "Patient", "id": "12345", "name": [{ "family": "Smith", "given": ["Jane"] }], "birthDate": "1975-04-12", "gender": "female" }. That entire record — parseable by any JSON library in any language — is retrieved with a single HTTP GET to https://server.example.com/fhir/Patient/12345.
A FHIR Patient Resource in JSON
FHIR R4 vs R4B vs R5: Understanding the Version Landscape
FHIR R4, published on January 2, 2019, was a landmark release for one specific reason: for the first time, core components of the FHIR specification — the RESTful API framework, the XML and JSON serialization formats, and a set of foundational data types — passed HL7's normative ballot process. "Normative" in HL7 terminology means the specification has been formally reviewed, balloted, and approved as a stable standard that will not undergo breaking changes without a full new normative ballot cycle. This stability was what regulators and health systems needed to mandate FHIR in law: you cannot require vendors to implement a standard that might break next year. R4 became the regulatory baseline for U.S. federal interoperability rules and remains so today.
FHIR R4B (version 4.3.0) was published on May 28, 2022. Rather than a full new release, R4B was a limited, targeted update designed to bring selected new clinical features — particularly around subscriptions, citations, and evidence-based medicine resources — to maturity without breaking R4 compatibility. R4B maintained full backward compatibility with R4 for the vast majority of resources, meaning an R4 server could largely interoperate with an R4B client. For most implementers, especially those building systems to meet U.S. regulatory requirements, R4B represented a refinement rather than a migration target.
FHIR R5 was published on March 26, 2023. R5 expanded the normative core, refined the subscription framework, improved support for clinical reasoning and evidence-based medicine, and introduced a number of new resource types and cross-version analysis tools. However, because U.S. regulation explicitly cites FHIR R4 as the required standard, and because certification bodies and major EHR vendors have invested years building R4 implementations, R4 remains the de facto deployment standard for regulated healthcare in the United States. R5 adoption will grow over time — particularly as new Implementation Guides are written against it — but implementers in 2025 still encounter R4 as the universal baseline in production systems.
Draft Standard for Trial Use — the first public release, used for early pilots. No normative components.

FHIR Version Timeline at a Glance
FHIR in U.S. Regulation: Federal Mandates Driving Adoption
The single most consequential event in FHIR's adoption history was the publication of two companion federal rules on May 1, 2020. The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule — formally titled "21st Century Cures Act: Interoperability, Information Blocking, and the ONC Health IT Certification Program" — required certified EHR developers to implement a new standardized API criterion (§ 170.315(g)(10)) based specifically on HL7 FHIR Release 4. EHR developers were originally given 24 months from publication to update their technology; ONC's November 2020 interim final rule moved the deadline to December 31, 2022. This rule also codified information blocking prohibitions — making it illegal for EHR vendors, health systems, and health information networks to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information.
On the same day, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services published the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F). This rule required Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid programs, CHIP programs, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the federal marketplace to implement FHIR-based Patient Access APIs — giving patients the right to request their claims data and clinical information through any third-party app of their choosing. Payers were required to make this API available by July 1, 2021. Together, these two rules created an unprecedented regulatory pull: the entire U.S. healthcare ecosystem — hospitals, clinics, payers, and health IT vendors — faced federal mandates to deploy FHIR R4 APIs within a defined timeline.
These rules operate alongside the U.S. Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI), ONC's standardized set of data elements that certified health IT must be capable of exchanging. USCDI defines the "what" — the clinical data classes and elements — while FHIR and the US Core Implementation Guide define the "how": the technical format and API by which that data is made accessible. TEFCA, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement, extends this further by establishing a national framework for health information network interoperability through designated Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs). The FHIR Roadmap for TEFCA, published by the Sequoia Project in December 2023, laid out a phased four-stage plan for FHIR exchange under TEFCA, targeting full production availability of QHIN-facilitated FHIR exchange (Stage 2) in 2024 and pilots of QHIN-to-QHIN FHIR exchange (Stage 3) in 2025.
The ONC Cures Act Final Rule prohibits EHR vendors, health systems, and health information networks from taking any action that interferes with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information. Violations can result in civil monetary penalties. Withholding data from patients or restricting API access without a defined exception is a federal violation, not merely a best-practice failure.

SMART on FHIR and Real-World Adoption
A FHIR API alone tells you what data is available and how to retrieve it. SMART on FHIR answers a different question: how should a third-party application authenticate, identify which patient context it's operating in, and receive the scoped access token it needs to retrieve only the data it's authorized to see? SMART — which stands for Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies — originated in 2010 as a project at Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital, funded by a four-year, $15 million grant from the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology. The project's goal was radical: write a medical application once and run it, unmodified, across different EHR systems. In the second half of 2013, the SMART team updated their framework to use FHIR as the underlying data model, and SMART on FHIR was publicly demonstrated at HIMSS in February 2014.
SMART on FHIR works by layering OAuth 2.0 authorization flows on top of FHIR APIs. When a clinician opens a SMART app from within their EHR, the EHR launches the app with a launch context — communicating which patient is currently in view and which practitioner is logged in. The app exchanges this context for an access token scoped to specific FHIR resources and operations (for example, patient/Observation.read or patient/MedicationRequest.read). The app then uses this token to make authenticated FHIR API calls. The entire flow uses industry-standard OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect protocols, meaning healthcare apps can leverage the same security infrastructure as consumer and enterprise software. SMART on FHIR 2.0 added backend services authorization for server-to-server use cases — enabling population health analytics, quality reporting, and payer data exchange without a human in the loop.
The major EHR vendors have fully embraced FHIR R4 and SMART on FHIR, in large part because federal regulation left them no choice — but adoption has also created genuine market opportunity. Epic operates fhir.epic.com, a developer portal for building against its FHIR APIs, and the Epic Showroom (successor to App Orchard) lists third-party applications, many of them SMART on FHIR apps. Oracle Health's Ignite APIs — the FHIR platform for the former Cerner EHR — operate entirely on R4 and support SMART on FHIR launches from within the clinical workflow. A single SMART on FHIR application can, in principle, be registered with Epic, Oracle Health, and other EHRs separately, but the core application code — the JavaScript, Python, or mobile app logic — remains identical across platforms. This write-once, run-anywhere vision, first articulated in 2010, is now a practical reality across the majority of U.S. hospital beds.
SMART on FHIR real-world examples include: patient-facing apps that pull medication lists and vaccination records directly from hospital EHRs into a personal health record; clinical decision support tools that launch inside the EHR workflow and query live patient data to generate recommendations; payer-facing apps that retrieve prior authorization data and claims history; and research cohort tools that use backend SMART services to query populations across multiple institutions without requiring a human login session.

FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) was created in 2011 by Grahame Grieve to replace the complexity of HL7 v2 and CDA with a web-native, resource-oriented approach to health data exchange.
FHIR R4, published January 2, 2019, was the first normative release — meaning core components (REST API, JSON/XML formats, foundational data types) are stable and will not break without a new ballot cycle.
FHIR R4 defines 145 discrete resource types, each independently addressable over HTTP using standard REST verbs: GET, POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE.
Profiles and Implementation Guides constrain generic FHIR resources for specific use cases. The US Core IG defines the minimum clinical data set all certified U.S. EHRs must expose.
The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (May 2020) and the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Rule (CMS-9115-F) together mandated FHIR R4 APIs across EHR vendors and payers, with hard compliance deadlines.
SMART on FHIR — originating at Harvard and Boston Children's Hospital in 2010 — provides the OAuth 2.0 authorization layer that enables third-party applications to securely launch within EHR workflows and retrieve scoped patient data.
FHIR R4B (May 2022) and R5 (March 2023) have been published, but R4 remains the U.S. regulatory baseline; implementers will encounter R4 in virtually every production healthcare environment.
Major EHR vendors including Epic and Oracle Health (Cerner) have deployed FHIR R4 + SMART on FHIR developer platforms, with third-party applications now operating in clinical workflows.
FHIR R4, published January 2, 2019, was the first release in which core components — specifically the RESTful API framework, XML and JSON serialization formats, and foundational data types — passed HL7's normative ballot process. Previous versions (DSTU1, DSTU2, STU3) were all Draft Standard for Trial Use or Standard for Trial Use, meaning they could change without a full normative ballot cycle. This normative stability was a prerequisite for regulators to mandate FHIR in federal law.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-cda-ccda | CDA & C-CDA: Clinical Documents in Motion
CDA and C-CDA: The Clinical Document Architecture Standard
What Is the Clinical Document Architecture?
The Clinical Document Architecture (CDA) is an HL7 document markup standard that uses XML to define the structure, encoding, and semantics of clinical documents for the purpose of exchange. HL7 CDA Release 1 was approved as an ANSI standard in November 2000, and the far more widely adopted Release 2 achieved ANSI approval in May 2005 and later became an ISO standard in 2009. CDA Release 2 remains the foundation of nearly every structured clinical document exchanged in the United States today — from hospital discharge summaries sent to primary care physicians, to the care summaries that flow between EHR systems at care transitions.
A CDA document is divided into two logical regions: a header and a body. The header is the administrative and provenance layer — it identifies the patient, the author, the organization that created the document, the type of encounter, and the legal custodian. The body carries the clinical content itself. Inside the body, content is organized into nested sections, and each section must contain a narrative block — a chunk of human-readable text that any browser can render without special software. This design principle is fundamental to CDA's philosophy: a CDA document must always be renderable by a human, even if the machine-processable entries inside it cannot be decoded.
Below the narrative block sits an optional entries layer. Entries encode the same clinical facts in machine-readable form using coded vocabularies — SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, and ICD. A receiving system that cannot interpret the entries can safely ignore them and render only the narrative. A system that can parse them gains structured, computable data. This dual-layer design — human-readable narrative plus machine-processable entries — was innovative for its time and is what separates CDA documents from simple PDF attachments or plain-text discharge summaries. It is the architectural decision that made CDA durable enough to underpin two decades of US health information exchange policy.
Think of a CDA document like a legal contract with attached exhibits. The contract body (the narrative block) is written in plain English so any lawyer or judge can read it. The exhibits (the structured entries) contain the same information in a precise, machine-indexable format that automated systems can search and process. You can act on the contract using only the narrative — but the exhibits make automation possible.
CDA dual-layer architecture: human-readable narrative block plus optional machine-processable entries

C-CDA: The Consolidated Implementation Guide
The base CDA standard defines the document framework but deliberately leaves the clinical content largely unconstrained. This flexibility created a proliferation of competing, incompatible CDA implementation guides across US states, health systems, and specialty societies. By the early 2010s, a physician receiving a CDA document might find that allergies were coded in one section in one system, a completely different section in another, and not coded at all in a third. The Consolidated CDA — C-CDA — was HL7's answer to this fragmentation. The S&I Framework, coordinated by the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC), drove the consolidation of previously separate CDA implementation guides — from the HL7 Health Story project, IHE, HITSP C32, and the original CCD — into a single, nationally harmonized specification.
C-CDA defines a specific set of document types, each with required sections, required coded entries, and vocabulary bindings. The core document types include: the Continuity of Care Document (CCD), which aggregates a patient's full longitudinal health record for transfer between providers; the Discharge Summary, limited to information generated at the point of hospital release; the Progress Note, used for ongoing encounter documentation in inpatient or outpatient settings; the History and Physical (H&P); the Consultation Note; the Operative Note; the Procedure Note; the Diagnostic Imaging Report; the Referral Note; the Transfer Summary; and the Care Plan. Each document type is governed by a template that specifies which sections are required, which are optional, and which data elements inside each section must be present in both narrative and coded form.
C-CDA 2.1, published in 2015, has been the regulatory cornerstone of US interoperability requirements for nearly a decade and has seen only errata updates since its publication. C-CDA 3.0 merged the 2.1 guide with the C-CDA Companion Guide, added enhancement requests, and incorporated USCDI V4 alignment. The HL7 community then moved quickly: C-CDA 3.0 (May 2024, USCDI v4), 4.0 (June 2025, USCDI v5), and 5.0 (June 2026, USCDI v6) — all Standards for Trial Use — with 5.0 the current version. On the regulatory side, ONC's adoption of the C-CDA R2.1 Companion Guide, Release 2 expired on January 1, 2026; certification now references Companion Guide Release 4.1, aligned with USCDI v3.

CDA vs. C-CDA: What Each Standard Provides
CDA in Meaningful Use and CEHRT
The C-CDA standard did not become ubiquitous through organic market adoption. It was mandated. Meaningful Use Stage 2, finalized by CMS and ONC in 2012, required eligible professionals and eligible hospitals to provide a summary of care record for more than 50% of transitions of care and referrals — and to transmit more than 10% electronically — using certified technology that produced those records as C-CDA documents. The specific regulatory hook was 45 CFR 170.314(b)(2), which required EHR technology to create, display, and transmit C-CDA documents as a precondition of certification. ONC's CEHRT (Certified EHR Technology) program embedded C-CDA compliance at the product level — no certification meant no Meaningful Use incentive payments.
The 2015 Edition certification criteria, published in the Federal Register in October 2015, extended and refined the C-CDA requirements. Under 45 CFR 170.315(b)(1), "Transitions of Care," certified health IT had to both create and receive C-CDA documents. Receive was the harder requirement — it forced vendors to parse and incorporate incoming C-CDA data into their systems, not merely generate outbound documents. This bidirectional mandate pushed every major EHR vendor to invest in C-CDA production and consumption, creating the foundation for today's national clinical document exchange infrastructure through networks like CommonWell, Carequality, and the eHealth Exchange.
The role of ONC in C-CDA adoption cannot be overstated. ONC coordinated the original consolidation effort through the S&I Framework, funded testing infrastructure at the Standards Implementation and Testing Environment (SITE), and published Companion Guides to clarify ambiguous requirements in the base specification. ONC also funded the C-CDA Scorecard — a free online tool at site.healthit.gov that allows providers and vendors to submit a C-CDA document and receive an automated quality score highlighting deviations from best practices. The interplay between regulatory mandate and publicly funded tooling is what transformed C-CDA from a technical specification into infrastructure.

The C-CDA Regulatory Pathway: From Standard to Mandate
The Transition to FHIR: C-CDA vs. FHIR Documents
HL7 FHIR has emerged as the preferred API framework for modern health data exchange, and it is reasonable to ask: does FHIR make C-CDA obsolete? The honest answer is nuanced. FHIR and C-CDA were designed for different primary use cases. C-CDA excels at producing a complete, human-readable clinical document — a discharge summary or care summary that can be rendered in a browser, signed by a physician, and attached to a patient record. FHIR excels at granular, API-driven retrieval of specific clinical resources: a patient's current medications, a single lab result, or a list of active problems. These are complementary, not competing, capabilities.
The FHIR community recognized this complementarity and created two bridges. The first is the C-CDA on FHIR Implementation Guide (version 2.0.0, published June 2026 as a Standard for Trial Use, based on FHIR R4). This guide defines FHIR profiles on the Composition resource that map directly to C-CDA document types — CCD, Discharge Summary, Progress Note, and others. The second bridge is a wrapping approach: a C-CDA document can be referenced via a FHIR DocumentReference resource, allowing FHIR-native systems to discover and retrieve C-CDA documents without requiring full conversion. Both strategies support incremental migration rather than a hard cutover.
C-CDA will not disappear quickly. EHR installations across the country generate and consume C-CDA documents daily, and the regulatory infrastructure — CEHRT certification, Carequality, eHealth Exchange — remains organized around C-CDA payloads. Replacing it requires not just updating software but rewriting certification criteria, retesting vendors, renegotiating network participation agreements, and retraining implementation teams. Realistically, C-CDA will coexist with FHIR for at least a decade. The trajectory is clear — FHIR is the direction of travel — but the journey is long, and C-CDA remains the workhorse of clinical document exchange in the United States today.

C-CDA vs. FHIR Documents: Strengths and Trade-offs
FHIR APIs are the future direction for health data exchange, but C-CDA remains a current, active regulatory requirement for CEHRT certification and health information network participation. Implementers who abandon C-CDA competency prematurely risk compliance gaps. Build both capabilities — they solve different problems.
Common Misconception: "FHIR Replaces C-CDA Now"
Real-World C-CDA Implementation: Quality, Validation, and Common Pitfalls
Despite two decades of standardization effort, production C-CDA documents frequently suffer from quality problems that impair interoperability. Research has documented that real-world system-generated C-CDA documents regularly contain data represented inconsistently or incompletely. Common failure patterns include: missing coded entries despite a narrative section being present; misuse of null flavors (the XML mechanism for representing unknown or unavailable data) to mask absent data rather than convey its true status; section templates applied to incorrect content types; date and time precision errors; and vocabulary codes that are valid in isolation but semantically incorrect in context. One study (D'Amore et al., AMIA 2018) found that automated tools identified 13 times more issues than schematron validation alone — meaning that passing basic schema validation is a floor, not a ceiling.
The primary validation stack for C-CDA has three layers. First, XML schema validation confirms that the document is well-formed and matches the CDA XML schema. Second, schematron validation applies the business rule constraints defined in the C-CDA implementation guide — for example, that a CCD must contain a Problem section, or that every Medication Activity entry must include a route code. Third, the ONC SITE C-CDA Scorecard goes beyond schema and schematron to assess best practices: are LOINC codes used for lab results instead of local codes? Are date-times recorded with appropriate precision? Are section templates applied correctly? The Scorecard generates a quantitative grade and a detailed issue report that implementers can act on.
In addition to the free SITE tooling, EHR vendors seeking CEHRT certification must submit to testing through ONC-Authorized Testing Laboratories (ATLs). ONC-ATLs such as Drummond Group and SLI Compliance test C-CDA creation and reception as part of the 45 CFR 170.315(b)(1) Transitions of Care criterion. A mature C-CDA implementation practice includes automated validation in the document generation pipeline — not just during certification testing — so that quality problems are caught before documents reach receiving systems.
When a patient is discharged from an acute care hospital, the hospital EHR must generate a C-CDA Discharge Summary or Continuity of Care Document. This document must contain — in both narrative and coded form — the discharge diagnosis (ICD-10-CM coded), the reconciled medication list (RxNorm coded), allergy list (SNOMED CT coded), pending follow-up instructions, and any referrals. The document is transmitted via Direct Secure Messaging or a network like Carequality to the receiving primary care provider's EHR. The receiving system must parse the C-CDA, reconcile the medication list against the patient's existing record, and flag any discrepancies for the physician to review. If the sending system used local codes instead of RxNorm, the receiving system cannot perform automated reconciliation — the document arrives but the computable value is lost.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-cures-act | The 21st Century Cures Act: A Landmark in Health IT Law
The 21st Century Cures Act and Interoperability: What the Law Actually Requires
On December 13, 2016, President Obama signed the 21st Century Cures Act into law. The legislation was one of the most sweeping health information technology reforms in the United States since the HITECH Act of 2009, and its interoperability provisions — concentrated in Title IV — set off a regulatory cascade that would reshape how hospitals, insurers, app developers, and patients exchange electronic health information for years to come.
Yet the law itself was only the opening act. The actual requirements that providers and health IT vendors had to meet came primarily through two landmark final rules published simultaneously on May 1, 2020: the ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (85 FR 25642) and the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F). Together these rules translated congressional intent into specific, enforceable mandates around APIs, data standards, and a new federal prohibition called information blocking. Understanding what each layer of this legal framework actually requires — and what it does not — is essential for anyone working at the intersection of health policy, technology, or clinical care.
This lesson walks through the five pillars of the interoperability framework created by the Cures Act: the legislative architecture of Title IV, the information blocking prohibition and its exceptions, the FHIR API mandates and certification requirements, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) that aims to create a network of networks, and finally the real-world impact measured since enforcement began — including the significant gaps that remain.
Title IV: The Legislative Architecture
The 21st Century Cures Act is a sprawling omnibus law covering topics ranging from cancer research to mental health to drug approvals. Title IV ("Delivery," Sections 4001–4012) holds its health information technology provisions, alongside a few Medicare items such as telehealth. Four of its sections — 4001 through 4004 — together define the statutory framework for interoperability and information blocking. Section 4001 directed HHS to set a strategy for reducing the regulatory and administrative burden that EHR use places on clinicians. Section 4002 updated the certification program for electronic health records, requiring that certified technology not block information sharing. Section 4003 directed ONC to develop a Trusted Exchange Framework for nationwide interoperability. And Section 4004 — the most consequential from a compliance standpoint — formally prohibited information blocking and established penalties for violations.
What makes Title IV unusual in federal health IT law is the breadth of entities it covers. Prior federal health IT legislation primarily targeted providers participating in federal programs and the EHR vendors serving them. Title IV extended new legal obligations to health information exchanges (HIEs), health information networks (HINs), and health IT developers far beyond the narrow scope of EHR certification. The law also created a definition of interoperability that set a new standard: health IT should enable the secure exchange and use of health information without special effort on the part of the user. That phrase — without special effort — became a touchstone in subsequent regulatory debates.
ONC used its Cures Act rulemaking to adopt the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI), a standardized set of health data elements that must be supported by certified systems. USCDI Version 1, which became the baseline for the Cures Act final rules, defined 16 data classes including patient demographics, clinical notes, laboratory results, medications, vital signs, and provenance information. Subsequent versions have expanded these requirements, with USCDI v2 adding social determinants of health data elements, v3 becoming the certification baseline under HTI-1, and v4 incorporating additional clinical data.

The Information Blocking Prohibition: Section 4004 in Detail
Section 4004 of the Cures Act created an entirely new category of federal health care violation: information blocking. The statute defines information blocking as a practice that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI), and that the actor knows — or should know — is likely to have that effect. Unlike HIPAA, which regulates what information must be protected, the information blocking prohibition regulates practices that unnecessarily restrict what information can flow.
The law identifies three categories of regulated actors: health IT developers of certified health IT; health information exchanges and health information networks (HIEs/HINs); and health care providers. The knowledge standard differs by actor type. For health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, the standard is whether they know or should know that a practice is likely to interfere with EHI access. For providers, it is a slightly higher bar — the provider must actually know that the practice is unreasonable. The definition of EHI itself was phased in: initially limited to data elements in USCDI v1, and then expanded by October 2022 to encompass the full scope of a patient's designated record set as defined under HIPAA.
ONC's 2020 final rule established eight regulatory exceptions that, when met, mean a practice does not constitute information blocking. These are: (1) Preventing Harm — blocking is permitted when it substantially reduces a genuine risk of harm to a patient or third party; (2) Privacy — compliance with state or federal privacy laws or patient-requested restrictions; (3) Security — protecting against threats to the confidentiality, integrity, or availability of EHI, but only when applied consistently and non-discriminatorily; (4) Infeasibility — technically or organizationally impossible to fulfill a specific request; (5) Health IT Performance — system maintenance or upgrades requiring temporary unavailability; (6) Content and Manner — responding in an alternative manner when a request is unreasonable in its scope; (7) Fees — charging fees based on objective, verifiable criteria that are applied uniformly and reasonably related to costs; and (8) Licensing — licensing interoperability elements on reasonable and non-discriminatory terms. HTI-1 (December 2023) later added a TEFCA Manner exception and narrowed Content and Manner to Manner, and a December 2024 rule added a Protecting Care Access exception; ASTP's HTI-5 proposed rule (December 2025) would eliminate the TEFCA Manner exception. From April 5, 2021 through July 31, 2026, ONC's Report Information Blocking Portal logged 2,450 claims of possible information blocking; patients are the largest group of claimants, and health care providers are the most frequently named actors.

No federal prohibition on EHI access interference
EHR contracts routinely included data-blocking clauses
Patients had no federal right to machine-readable health data
No penalty framework for vendor lock-in practices
After Cures Act (post-2020 rules)

OIG can impose CMPs up to $1M per violation for IT developers/HIEs

Information Blocking: Before vs. After Cures Act
OIG's final information blocking penalty rule took effect September 1, 2023, meaning conduct before that date is not subject to CMPs. As of mid-2025, OIG has not publicly disclosed completed enforcement actions under the rule, but has indicated it is actively prioritizing cases involving patient harm, large financial loss, or long duration of blocking.
Enforcement is active but developing
FHIR APIs and CEHRT Requirements: The Technical Mandate
The ONC Cures Act Final Rule's most technically consequential provision was the creation of a new certification criterion for standardized APIs using HL7 FHIR Release 4 (FHIR R4). This criterion — codified at 45 CFR 170.315(g)(10) — requires that certified EHR technology (CEHRT) support application programming interfaces that allow both individual patients and authorized third-party apps to access health data programmatically, without special effort, and at no cost to the patient. The standard chosen was not arbitrary: FHIR R4 had emerged from a multi-year HL7 standards development process and had already seen significant industry adoption before it became mandatory.
The (g)(10) criterion covers two use cases. The first is single-patient services: a read-only API that allows patients to authorize third-party applications — including smartphone health apps — to retrieve their records from their provider's EHR. The second is population services through FHIR Bulk Data Access: data export capabilities that allow authorized entities to retrieve records for multiple patients simultaneously. SMART on FHIR — the SMART App Launch implementation guide, which (g)(10) requires — provides the authorization and authentication layer that allows apps to plug into EHRs much as apps plug into a smartphone operating system.
The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Rule (CMS-9115-F) extended parallel FHIR API requirements to payers — specifically Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care organizations, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plans in the Federally Facilitated Marketplace. These payers were required to implement a FHIR R4-based Patient Access API making claims, encounter data, and clinical data (conforming to USCDI v1) available to members. CMS also required payers to implement a Provider Directory API, enabling providers to verify network information programmatically. Data had to be available from January 1, 2016 forward for all current enrollees. A subsequent CMS rule — CMS-0057-F, the Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule finalized in January 2024 — added prior authorization exchange via FHIR APIs, with compliance deadlines extending to 2026–2027.

Compliance Milestones: ONC Cures Update Timeline
Think of FHIR R4 as the USB-C standard for health data. Before FHIR mandates, every EHR vendor used a proprietary connector — a health app had to build a custom integration for Epic, another for Cerner, another for Athena. FHIR R4 creates one universal port. Once a vendor certifies to the standard, any authorized app can plug in without custom development.
FHIR R4 as universal interoperability standard for health data APIs
TEFCA: Building the Network of Networks
Section 4003(b) of the Cures Act gave ONC a specific mandate: publish a Trusted Exchange Framework — a common set of principles that all health information networks should follow — and a Common Agreement that health information networks could sign to participate in nationwide, query-based exchange. The resulting initiative, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA), took several years to develop through public comment and stakeholder engagement. ONC published TEFCA's foundational documents in January 2022, and in December 2023 reached the pivotal milestone of designating the first Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) — the organizations that anchor TEFCA's exchange infrastructure.
TEFCA operates through a three-tier governance structure. At the top is ONC, which sets policy. Below ONC is the Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE) — currently the Sequoia Project — which manages the Common Agreement, handles QHIN applications, and oversees technical standards through the QHIN Technical Framework (QTF). At the operational level are the QHINs themselves: large health information networks that sign the Common Agreement and agree to exchange data with one another under shared rules for patient identity matching, authentication, and performance. By February 2024, seven organizations had been designated as QHINs: eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, Health Gorilla, KONZA, MedAllies, CommonWell Health Alliance, and Kno2. eClinicalWorks (January 2025), Surescripts (April 2025), Netsmart (August 2025), and Oracle Health Information Network (November 2025) brought the total to eleven.
The transformative promise of TEFCA is query-based exchange at national scale. Before TEFCA, a clinician at a hospital in Vermont wanting to access records from a hospital in Texas faced a patchwork of bilateral agreements, network memberships, and technical barriers. TEFCA creates a single on-ramp: join any QHIN, and you can query any other QHIN's participants under the shared rules of the Common Agreement. TEFCA defines six exchange purposes: Treatment, Payment, Health Care Operations, Public Health, Government Benefits Determination, and Individual Access Services (IAS) — the last being a critical pathway for patients to access their own data. In August 2024, Carequality — one of the largest existing interoperability frameworks in the country — announced alignment with TEFCA, signaling a broad industry convergence around this infrastructure.
A patient is admitted to a Vermont hospital after a car accident. The treating physician needs medication history from the patient's primary care practice in Florida. Under TEFCA: (1) The hospital's EHR, connected to TEFCA through a QHIN, sends a Treatment-purpose query to the TEFCA network. (2) The TEFCA infrastructure routes the query to any QHIN whose participants include the Florida practice. (3) The QHIN serving the Florida practice returns the patient's medication list, problem list, and allergy information, typically as a standardized C-CDA document. (4) The Vermont EHR displays the results — no phone calls, no fax, no bilateral agreement required. The entire exchange occurs under the legal and technical governance of the Common Agreement.
How TEFCA Exchange Works in Practice
Real-World Impact and What Remains Unfinished
Since the information blocking prohibition took effect in April 2021 and the FHIR API certification deadlines began hitting in late 2022, measurable change has occurred in the health IT landscape. Patient access to health data through third-party apps has expanded dramatically. ONC reported in August 2022 that only about 5% of certified health IT developers had updated to the certified API technology, yet those developers supported roughly 66% of inpatient and 77% of ambulatory users, because the dominant vendors adopted the criterion early. Payers subject to CMS-9115-F have stood up Patient Access APIs, giving millions of Medicaid and marketplace enrollees machine-readable access to their claims and clinical data for the first time.
Despite this progress, significant gaps persist. First, provider directory accuracy remains a chronic problem. CMS required payers to publish Provider Directory APIs, but the underlying data in those directories — which provider is in network, what their practice address is, what specialties they offer — is notoriously inaccurate. CMS's own reviews of Medicare Advantage online directories found that 45–52% of listed provider locations had at least one inaccuracy (2016–2018 review rounds), undermining the value of the API mandate. Second, consent portability is largely unsolved. TEFCA's Common Agreement governs what QHINs can share with one another, but patient consent preferences expressed in one system — say, a request not to share behavioral health records — are not reliably honored when records travel across TEFCA or between EHR systems. Third, data quality and completeness vary widely. A FHIR API can return a medication list that is months out of date, or clinical notes that were never coded into structured data. The Cures Act mandated access to data, not the accuracy or completeness of that data.
Ongoing rulemaking is attempting to address some of these gaps. ONC's Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability (HTI-1) final rule, published in December 2023, added a TEFCA Manner exception to the information blocking rules and made USCDI v3 the certification baseline. A subsequent HTI-2 rulemaking proposed additional standards and strengthened API transparency requirements. HHS also finalized provider disincentives for information blocking in June 2024 — a separate track from OIG enforcement — under which CMS can, for example, zero out a clinician's MIPS Promoting Interoperability score, withhold part of a hospital's market-basket update, or bar a provider from the Medicare Shared Savings Program for at least a year. The cumulative effect of these rules, if fully implemented, would represent the most comprehensive federal interoperability infrastructure the United States has ever had. Whether it will deliver seamless, patient-centered health data exchange in practice remains an open question.
A common misconception is that FHIR API mandates override HIPAA privacy rules. They do not. HIPAA governs what information covered entities must protect; the Cures Act governs practices that unreasonably block access. When a patient authorizes a third-party app to receive their records through a FHIR API, the provider is permitted to share those records despite HIPAA — but HIPAA still applies to how the receiving app handles that data if it is a covered entity or business associate. The two frameworks intersect but do not cancel each other.
HIPAA still governs privacy — FHIR does not override it

The 21st Century Cures Act was signed December 13, 2016; its core interoperability and information blocking rules were published May 1, 2020, in two simultaneous final rules from ONC (85 FR 25642) and CMS (CMS-9115-F).
Title IV, Section 4004 prohibits information blocking — practices that knowingly and unreasonably impede EHI access — by three actor types: health IT developers, HIEs/HINs, and health care providers.
ONC's 2020 rule established eight exceptions to the information blocking prohibition (preventing harm, privacy, security, infeasibility, health IT performance, content and manner, fees, licensing), and later rules added TEFCA Manner and Protecting Care Access; meeting an exception means a practice is not information blocking.
Both ONC and CMS mandated HL7 FHIR Release 4 as the required API standard: ONC for certified EHRs, CMS for Medicaid, CHIP, and marketplace payer Patient Access APIs.
TEFCA — directed by Section 4003 — is a voluntary nationwide framework connecting Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) under a Common Agreement; seven QHINs were designated by February 2024 and eleven by November 2025, enabling query-based exchange at national scale.
OIG's civil monetary penalty rule took effect September 1, 2023, allowing fines up to $1 million per information blocking violation for non-provider actors; provider disincentives are a separate HHS track.
Significant gaps remain: provider directory inaccuracy, lack of cross-system consent portability, and variable data quality undermine the promise of FHIR-enabled access even where APIs are technically compliant.
Ongoing rulemakings — including HTI-1 (Dec 2023), the CMS Prior Authorization Rule (Jan 2024), and the June 2024 provider disincentives rule — are layering additional requirements on top of the original 2020 rules.
The Cures Act's information blocking prohibition applies to three categories of actors: health IT developers of certified health IT, health information exchanges and networks, and health care providers. Individual patients are the intended beneficiaries of the law, not regulated actors subject to its prohibitions. Patients exercising their right to access their own records — including through third-party apps authorized via FHIR APIs — are explicitly protected by, not constrained by, the information blocking framework.

Information Blocking: The Law, the Exceptions, and the Enforcement
What Is Information Blocking?
In 2016 Congress passed the 21st Century Cures Act with a deceptively simple goal: make health data flow freely. Section 4004 of that law created a legal prohibition against "information blocking" — defined in regulation at 45 CFR 171.103 as any practice by an "actor" that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI), unless required by law or covered by one of the enumerated regulatory exceptions. The definition is intentionally broad. Congress wanted to capture the full spectrum of behaviors — technical, contractual, and cultural — that had historically kept data siloed inside individual systems.
Three categories of entities qualify as "actors" under the rule: (1) health IT developers of certified health IT, (2) health information exchanges and health information networks (HIEs/HINs), and (3) healthcare providers. The law applies a slightly different knowledge standard to each group. For health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, information blocking occurs when the actor knows, or should know, that a practice is likely to interfere with EHI access. For healthcare providers, the standard is higher — the provider must actually know that the practice is unreasonable and likely to interfere. This asymmetry reflects Congress's view that technology vendors are more sophisticated market actors who should be held to a more demanding standard.
The scope of electronic health information covered by the rule has expanded since the regulation first took effect. From April 5, 2021 through October 5, 2022, EHI was limited to the data classes and elements defined in the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) Version 1 — a relatively narrow set of clinical data including demographics, vital signs, laboratory results, and medications. Starting October 6, 2022, the definition expanded dramatically to encompass all information in a patient's HIPAA Designated Record Set (DRS) — every medical record, billing record, and other documentation used to make decisions about a patient, including images, wave files, and any other form of ePHI. This full-EHI expansion dramatically broadened the universe of data that actors must make available on request.
Information blocking provisions became applicable to all actors (penalties came later)

Think of information blocking like a toll bridge that was built with public funds but operated by a private company that then charges prohibitive tolls, only lets certain cars cross, and keeps the roadway in disrepair to discourage use. The 21st Century Cures Act is the law that says: the bridge must be open, the tolls must be reasonable, and the road must actually be drivable.
Information blocking uses technical, contractual, or operational barriers to prevent the free flow of patient health data that patients and clinicians have a legal right to access.
The Eight Exceptions
The prohibition on information blocking is not absolute. ONC's 2020 rule finalized eight regulatory exceptions — codified at 45 CFR Part 171, Subparts B and C — that describe the circumstances under which an actor's practice of limiting EHI access does NOT constitute information blocking. Later rules added a TEFCA Manner exception (HTI-1, December 2023; Subpart D), renamed Content and Manner to Manner, and added a Protecting Care Access exception (December 2024); ASTP's HTI-5 proposed rule (December 2025) would eliminate TEFCA Manner. The original eight are divided into two categories: five exceptions describing reasons an actor might not fulfill a request for EHI, and three exceptions describing procedures actors may use when they do fulfill such requests. Critically, meeting an exception is voluntary — an actor is never required to invoke one. And satisfying an exception requires meeting all of the conditions specified in the regulation; partial compliance does not shield an actor from liability.
The five "not fulfilling" exceptions are: (1) the Preventing Harm Exception, which allows actors to limit EHI access when there is a reasonable belief that doing so would prevent substantial harm to a patient or another person; (2) the Privacy Exception, which covers situations where applicable state or federal privacy law prohibits the disclosure — this exception has multiple sub-conditions tied to specific HIPAA and state law scenarios; (3) the Security Exception, which permits practices directly related to safeguarding the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of EHI, tailored to specific security risks and implemented consistently and non-discriminatorily; (4) the Infeasibility Exception, which acknowledges that there are genuine technical, operational, or legal constraints that can make it infeasible to fulfill a particular request; and (5) the Health IT Performance Exception, which permits health IT systems to be taken offline or have performance temporarily degraded for maintenance, upgrades, and other routine operational activities.
The three "fulfilling requests" exceptions govern the manner in which actors respond to legitimate EHI requests: (6) the Content and Manner Exception allows actors to negotiate and maintain reasonable terms for the access, exchange, and use of EHI — but importantly, this exception requires that the actor first attempt to reach agreement using content and manner that meets the requestor's needs; (7) the Fees Exception permits actors to charge fees for providing EHI access, but those fees must be based on objective and verifiable cost-based criteria uniformly applied to all similarly situated requestors — a $50,000 fee for a connection that costs $500 to maintain would fall well outside this exception; and (8) the Licensing Exception allows health IT developers to require licensees to obtain licenses for interoperability elements, so long as the licensing terms are non-discriminatory and commercially reasonable.

Exception vs. Violation: Common Scenarios
Penalties and Enforcement
The enforcement architecture for information blocking is divided between two HHS agencies with distinct authorities over distinct actor categories. The HHS Office of Inspector General (OIG) holds primary enforcement authority over health IT developers, HIEs, and HINs. OIG finalized its civil monetary penalty (CMP) rule on June 27, 2023, with enforcement becoming effective September 1, 2023. Under this rule, OIG may impose penalties of up to $1 million per violation against covered health IT actors. OIG will consider the nature and extent of the practice, the harm or potential harm caused, the duration of the conduct, the actor's history of compliance, and whether financial loss to federal health care programs resulted.
Healthcare providers face a different enforcement mechanism — "disincentives" administered through existing Medicare payment programs rather than standalone fines. On June 24, 2024, HHS finalized the provider disincentives rule (published in the Federal Register at 89 FR 54662 on July 1, 2024, effective July 31, 2024). Under this rule, eligible hospitals found to have committed information blocking lose the ability to earn three-quarters of their annual market basket increase under the Inpatient Prospective Payment System (IPPS). Critical Access Hospitals see their Medicare reimbursement drop from 101% of reasonable costs to 100%. Individual clinicians in the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) face estimated median losses of $686, while the median group practice of six clinicians could lose about $4,116 (HHS estimates). Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) and ACO participants may be barred from the Medicare Shared Savings Program for at least one year — potentially worth millions in forgone shared savings payments.
The complaint and referral process runs through ONC (now rebranded as ASTP — the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy). Any person or entity may submit a complaint through the ONC Information Blocking Complaint Portal. By February 2026 nearly 1,600 complaints had been submitted; by July 31, 2026, ONC had logged 2,450 claims of possible information blocking, about 76 percent filed by patients or by third parties on their behalf and about 79 percent naming a healthcare provider as the potential actor. ONC reviews complaints and shares those with potential violations with OIG, which investigates all three actor types; when OIG finds that a healthcare provider committed information blocking, it refers the provider to CMS for the applicable Medicare disincentive. Enforcement escalated significantly in September 2025 when HHS Secretary Kennedy directed agency resources toward active information blocking enforcement — marking the most aggressive federal posture since the law took effect.
