OIG has confirmed it will exercise enforcement discretion and generally not pursue conduct that occurred before July 31, 2024 for healthcare providers. However, health IT developers and HIEs have been subject to enforcement since September 1, 2023. Conduct that is ongoing — even if it began before these dates — remains actionable.
No Retroactive Enforcement for Providers
Common Scenarios: What Counts as Information Blocking
ONC has published extensive sub-regulatory guidance illustrating the types of practices that are likely — or unlikely — to constitute information blocking. One of the clearest categories involves unreasonable fees. The Fees Exception permits cost-based charges, but ONC guidance makes clear that fees must be objectively verifiable, uniformly applied, and proportionate to the actual cost of providing access. Charging a third-party app developer or competing health system dramatically inflated fees — while offering no-cost or nominal-cost connections to affiliated or non-competing partners — is a paradigmatic information blocking violation. The disparate treatment itself is the red flag, independent of the absolute dollar amount.
Requiring proprietary data formats when standardized FHIR APIs are available is another common scenario. The 21st Century Cures Act requires certified health IT to offer a standardized API "without special effort" for any individual patient or population of patients. An actor that makes data technically available only through a legacy HL7 v2 feed, a proprietary export format, or a cumbersome portal download — while refusing to enable the certified FHIR API — may be engaging in information blocking even if the data is theoretically accessible. Similarly, conditioning access on proprietary software licenses, requiring patients or clinicians to use specific applications, or building technical obstacles into the API workflow (such as excessive authentication steps applied only to competitors' apps) can all constitute information blocking.
Refusing to connect with competing health systems or vendor-neutral platforms is one of the most commercially significant patterns ONC has identified. A hospital system that shares discharge summaries, referral records, and care plans freely within its own affiliated network — but systematically delays, degrades, or refuses data exchange with providers at competing health systems — is likely engaging in information blocking, even if each individual refusal has a stated operational justification. ONC has specifically flagged "excessive delays" as a concern: a weeks-long processing time for a records request that could be fulfilled in minutes through existing technology is not a technical limitation; it is a practice that discourages access and may constitute information blocking absent a valid exception.
A regional HIE offers FHIR API connections to health system members at no charge. When a digital health startup applies for a connection to access de-identified population data for a public health analytics project, the HIE quotes $50,000 in upfront fees plus $10,000 per month in maintenance — terms offered to no other connection partner. The startup files a complaint with ONC. The HIE cannot satisfy the Fees Exception because the fees are not based on objective, verifiable, uniformly applied cost criteria. OIG would likely find this to be information blocking.
Scenario: The $50,000 API Connection Fee
A large EHR vendor's app marketplace approves hundreds of third-party applications. When a competing EHR vendor submits an app designed to help patients migrate their records to the new platform, the app is denied approval. The reason given is vague "security concerns" — but no security review was conducted and similar apps from non-competing developers were approved without review. This is a textbook Licensing Exception failure: the terms are discriminatory based on competitive status, not objective security criteria.
Scenario: Blocking a Competitor's App
Real Enforcement Cases and Industry Impact
As of early 2026, no entity has been publicly named as the subject of a completed enforcement action with a final penalty imposed — a reality that reflects both the complexity of information blocking investigations and the deliberate sequencing of the federal enforcement ramp-up. The enforcement machinery has been built in visible stages. OIG finalized its CMP rule in June 2023. Provider disincentives were finalized in June 2024. HHS Secretary Kennedy issued a high-profile enforcement directive in September 2025. In February 2026, ASTP/ONC announced it was issuing notices of investigation of potential nonconformity to certain certified health IT developers. The industry has been operating in an enforcement environment that was fully assembled only within the prior eighteen months.
The industry response to the information blocking framework has been substantial even in the absence of completed enforcement cases. Epic, the largest EHR vendor by U.S. market share, ran its App Orchard marketplace (since replaced by Epic Showroom) and has supported SMART on FHIR app authorization across its installed base. Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) upgraded its APIs to HL7 FHIR R4, the standard mandated by the ONC certification program. In a 2023 five-site test of the Bulk FHIR API (Jones et al., a medRxiv preprint from the SMART Cumulus Network), the Oracle Cerner platform exported 5 to 16 million resources at over 8,000 resources per minute, while three Epic sites exported at 1,555 to 2,500 resources per minute. These numbers reflect genuine technical investment in interoperability infrastructure — investment directly incentivized by the information blocking framework and the threat of CMP liability.
The population-level impact on data liquidity has been meaningful. The requirement that all certified health IT support standardized FHIR APIs has created the technical substrate for a new generation of interoperability use cases — from payer-to-provider data exchange under the CMS Interoperability Rule to patient-directed data aggregation through apps like Apple Health and CommonHealth. The ONC complaint portal data offers a revealing window into where friction remains: the fact that about 79 percent of claims name healthcare providers, not health IT developers, suggests that the cultural and organizational barriers to data sharing — not just the technical ones — remain the primary obstacle. Hospitals and clinician practices that have long treated patient data as an institutional asset are now being told, by federal law, that the patient's right to that data supersedes institutional convenience.
Industry Watch: In September 2025, the HHS-OIG and ASTP jointly issued an Enforcement Alert — a formal agency communication signaling that investigations are underway and that completed enforcement actions will be made public. Compliance officers at health IT companies and health systems should treat this alert as a direct warning that the years-long ramp-up period is ending.

Public Final Penalties (as of early 2026)
Information blocking is defined at 45 CFR 171.103 as any practice by a health IT developer, HIE/HIN, or healthcare provider that is likely to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of EHI — unless required by law or covered by a regulatory exception.
Three actor categories are covered: health IT developers of certified health IT, health information exchanges and networks, and healthcare providers. Each faces a distinct knowledge standard under the law.
EHI expanded dramatically on October 6, 2022 — from USCDI Version 1 data elements to the full HIPAA Designated Record Set, covering essentially all patient medical and billing information held in any format.
ONC's 2020 rule finalized eight exceptions to information blocking (later rules added TEFCA Manner and Protecting Care Access), divided into five "not fulfilling" exceptions (Preventing Harm, Privacy, Security, Infeasibility, Health IT Performance) and three "fulfilling" exceptions (Content and Manner, Fees, Licensing). All conditions of an exception must be met for it to apply.
OIG can impose civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation against health IT developers and HIEs — effective September 1, 2023. Healthcare providers face Medicare payment disincentives under the June 2024 final rule, including loss of market basket increases and potential exclusion from the Medicare Shared Savings Program.
ONC had logged 2,450 claims of possible information blocking by July 31, 2026 — about 76 percent from patients or their representatives and 79 percent naming healthcare providers — revealing that cultural resistance to data sharing remains the dominant barrier.
As of early 2026, no completed enforcement actions with public penalty determinations have been announced, but investigations are active. ASTP/ONC began issuing notices of investigation of potential nonconformity to health IT developers in February 2026, and HHS Secretary Kennedy declared enforcement a department priority in September 2025.
The information blocking framework has already driven significant industry investment in FHIR APIs and interoperability infrastructure, with major EHR vendors like Epic and Oracle Health (Cerner) building out standardized API capabilities directly in response to the certification and enforcement requirements.
Charging dramatically different fees to competing versus non-competing developers fails the Fees Exception, which requires that fees be based on objective, verifiable, and uniformly applied cost criteria. Offering favorable terms to non-competitors while imposing punitive fees on competitors is a textbook discriminatory practice that ONC guidance explicitly identifies as likely information blocking. The other three options fall within recognized exceptions: the Security Exception covers ransomware incidents, the Privacy Exception covers state mental health privacy laws, and the Health IT Performance Exception covers scheduled maintenance.
A hospital temporarily blocks API access during an active ransomware incident and restores it within 48 hours after the threat is contained.
An EHR vendor charges one competing health app developer $50,000 for an API connection while offering the same connection to non-competing developers at no charge.
A provider declines to share a patient's psychiatric notes because applicable state mental health privacy law prohibits disclosure without specific written consent.
A health IT developer takes its system offline for four hours on a Sunday morning for a scheduled database maintenance upgrade.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-cehrt | Certified EHR Technology: What CEHRT Means in Practice
CEHRT: Certified EHR Technology and What Certification Actually Means
What CEHRT Is and Why It Exists
Certified EHR Technology — universally shortened to CEHRT — is the federally defined standard that an electronic health record system must meet before it can be used to satisfy the requirements of Medicare and Medicaid quality and incentive programs. The term sounds bureaucratic, but the concept is straightforward: the federal government will not pay clinicians or hospitals for demonstrating "meaningful use" of a health IT system unless that system has been independently tested and found to meet a published set of technical criteria. CEHRT is the stamp that says the system passed.
The legal foundation for the entire certification machinery is the Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health Act — the HITECH Act — which was signed into law on February 17, 2009, as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act. HITECH authorized the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) to establish a certification program and directed the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) to tie billions of dollars in EHR incentive payments to the use of certified technology. Without HITECH, there would be no certification program; without the certification program, there would be no agreed-upon baseline for what an EHR must do.
ONC published its first set of certification criteria in the 2011 Edition Final Rule, establishing the inaugural CEHRT definition to support Meaningful Use Stage 1. The program has gone through multiple editions since — 2014 Edition, 2015 Edition, and the landmark 2015 Edition Cures Update — each ratcheting up the technical bar as the healthcare system's expectations for data sharing and interoperability evolved. ONC's HTI-1 rule (2024) then retired year-named editions; the criteria are now simply the ONC Certification Criteria for Health IT. Today, CEHRT is not merely an eligibility checkbox for incentive payments; it also underpins the 21st Century Cures Act's information-blocking prohibitions and the Promoting Interoperability performance category inside CMS quality payment programs.

The 2015 Edition Cures Update Requirements
The single most consequential regulatory update to the certification program arrived on May 1, 2020, when ONC published the "21st Century Cures Act: Interoperability, Information Blocking, and the ONC Health IT Certification Program" Final Rule in the Federal Register (85 FR 25642). This rule — commonly called the Cures Act Final Rule — substantially upgraded the 2015 Edition certification criteria and created what is now known as the 2015 Edition Cures Update. Developers of certified health IT were required to meet the new API standards and provide them to customers by December 31, 2022 (the original May 2, 2022 deadline was extended by a COVID-19 interim final rule).
The headline technical requirement introduced by the Cures Update is a standardized API for both single-patient and population-level data services, built on HL7 FHIR Release 4 (FHIR R4). Specifically, certified products must implement the FHIR US Core Implementation Guide, the FHIR Bulk Data Access Implementation Guide for population-level queries, and the HL7 SMART Application Launch Framework Implementation Guide so that third-party applications can authenticate and retrieve data securely. These three implementation guides together form the technical spine of modern app-based interoperability in U.S. healthcare.
Alongside the API requirement, the Cures Update mandated support for the United States Core Data for Interoperability Version 1 (USCDI v1) as the minimum data set. USCDI v1 defines 52 individual data elements organized into 16 data classes — covering allergies and intolerances, assessment and plan of treatment, care team members, clinical notes, goals, health concerns, immunizations, laboratory, medications, patient demographics, problems, procedures, provenance, smoking status, unique device identifiers for implantable devices, and vital signs. Any CEHRT system must be able to expose all of these data classes through its FHIR API. The Cures Update also required an Electronic Health Information (EHI) export function, allowing patients or their authorized representatives to download a complete export of their entire record — not just the USCDI subset.
Before the Cures Update, a hospital could use a 2015 Edition-certified EHR that supported only proprietary or HL7 v2 interfaces for data exchange. After the update, that same hospital's vendor was required to ship a FHIR R4-based patient-facing API, a bulk data export endpoint for population analytics, and an EHI export tool — all tested against specific implementation guides. This meant that a patient could, for the first time, connect a smartphone app directly to their hospital's EHR using the same open standards their bank uses for account aggregation.

ONC-ATLs and the Certification Testing Process
Before any product can appear on the Certified Health IT Product List (CHPL) at chpl.healthit.gov, it must be tested by an ONC-Authorized Testing Laboratory (ONC-ATL) and then certified by an ONC-Authorized Certification Body (ONC-ACB). These are separate but often overlapping roles. In 2022, when Leidos was added, there were four ONC-ATLs: Drummond Group, ICSA Labs, SLI Compliance — a division of Gaming Laboratories International — and Leidos. ONC's current list (June 2026) shows two: Drummond Group and SLI Compliance.
Testing at an ONC-ATL is methodical and criterion-by-criterion. The lab works through each applicable certification criterion in 45 CFR § 170.315, running the vendor's software against standardized test procedures and test data to verify conformance. For the FHIR API criterion, this includes executing specific API queries, validating FHIR resource structures, testing SMART App Launch sequences, and verifying that the bulk data export endpoint returns well-formed FHIR bundles. Passing the lab tests earns a "test report," which the vendor then submits to an ONC-ACB — such as Drummond Group or SLI Compliance, which hold dual ATL and ACB status — for final certification and listing on the CHPL.
Certification is not a one-time event. ONC-ACBs conduct ongoing surveillance — both reactive, triggered by complaints or anomalies, and random-sample surveillance — to verify that certified modules continue to function as certified in real-world deployments. If an ONC-ACB finds a non-conformity, the developer must correct it within a defined remediation period. At the program level, ONC itself can initiate Direct Review under 45 CFR § 170.580 if it has reasonable belief that a developer has violated a Condition or Maintenance of Certification. Severe or uncorrected violations can result in suspension or termination — decertification — of one or more modules, with the status publicly visible on the CHPL so that providers can see when a product they rely on is under corrective action.
The vendor identifies which certification criteria (45 CFR § 170.315) apply to their product and designs or upgrades functionality to meet each one.
Design to Criteria
An authorized testing lab — currently Drummond Group or SLI Compliance — executes standardized test procedures and issues a test report.
ONC-ATL Testing
An authorized certification body reviews the test report, confirms documentation, and issues a Certificate of Compliance for each criterion passed.
ONC-ACB Certification
The ONC-ACB publishes the certified product to chpl.healthit.gov, making the certification details, criteria met, and CHPL ID number publicly searchable.
CHPL Publication
The ONC-ACB monitors the product through random and reactive surveillance; ONC may conduct Direct Review; corrective actions or decertifications are updated on CHPL in real time.
Ongoing Surveillance
The Path from Code to CHPL Listing
Providers and administrators should always verify a vendor's certification status directly on chpl.healthit.gov before relying on marketing materials. A product can have some criteria certified and others not; the CHPL shows exactly which criteria each module meets — and whether any are under surveillance action.
CHPL Is Your Source of Truth
CEHRT in CMS Quality Programs
The most direct way most clinicians encounter CEHRT requirements is through the Promoting Interoperability (PI) performance category inside the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS). MIPS is CMS's consolidated quality reporting framework under MACRA, and the PI category carries a weight of 25 percent of a clinician's total MIPS final score. To report PI, a clinician must attest to using CEHRT and must provide their EHR's CMS EHR Certification ID (CEHRT ID) — a unique identifier visible on the CHPL — as part of their submission.
The 2024 PI performance category is organized around four objectives: Electronic Prescribing, Health Information Exchange, Provider to Patient Exchange, and Public Health and Clinical Data Exchange. Each objective contains required and optional measures. The Electronic Prescribing objective includes the e-Prescribing measure and the Query of Prescription Drug Monitoring Program (PDMP) measure. The Health Information Exchange objective includes measures for sending and receiving care summaries. The Provider to Patient Exchange objective focuses on enabling patients to access their data via API-enabled apps. Under Public Health and Clinical Data Exchange, Immunization Registry Reporting and Electronic Case Reporting are required; Public Health Registry Reporting, Clinical Data Registry Reporting, and Syndromic Surveillance Reporting are optional bonus measures worth up to 5 additional points.
Clinicians must also provide four required attestations as part of their PI submission: an attestation that they have not taken actions to limit or restrict the compatibility or interoperability of their CEHRT; an ONC Direct Review attestation; a Security Risk Analysis measure confirmation; and a Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience (SAFER) Guides attestation. The maximum attainable PI score is 105 points — the extra 5 come from optional bonus measures — but the score is capped at 100 for final MIPS weighting purposes. Advanced APM participants are generally excluded from MIPS reporting requirements but often must still use CEHRT to qualify for the Advanced APM bonus.
Think of the CEHRT ID on a PI attestation like the VIN number on a car title. The car still has to pass a safety inspection (ONC-ATL testing), be registered (CHPL listing), and have its registration current (ongoing surveillance). Without a valid VIN matching current registration, you cannot legally operate the vehicle in programs that require one — just as a clinician cannot claim PI credit without a valid, active CEHRT ID.
CEHRT ID in MIPS PI reporting works like a vehicle VIN: it uniquely identifies the certified product and proves the regulatory requirements are met.

What Certification Does NOT Guarantee
CEHRT certification is a necessary condition for participating in federal quality programs — but it is emphatically not a sufficient condition for real-world interoperability or safe, usable software. This distinction matters enormously in practice. Certification testing occurs in a controlled lab environment with standardized synthetic data, scripted workflows, and idealized network conditions. A vendor's software might pass every criterion in the lab and still behave very differently when deployed in a busy emergency department with legacy infrastructure, thousands of active patient records, and staff under time pressure.
Usability researchers point to the same gap: certification testing does not reproduce how clinicians actually use an EHR, and vendor-reported usability results rest on scripted test cases rather than real clinical scenarios. The testing environment lacks variables such as task interruptions, increased noise levels, concurrent alerts, and other stressors that characterize real clinical settings. Poorly designed screen layouts, redundant workflow sequences, and alert fatigue are documented consequences — all of which survived the certification process untouched.
ONC acknowledged this gap and, through the Cures Act Final Rule, created a Real World Testing requirement. Health IT developers certified under the program must annually submit Real World Testing plans describing how they will demonstrate interoperability and functionality in actual production environments — not just in the lab. However, a 2025 study in JAMIA Open (Handley et al.) reviewed the transitions-of-care Real World Testing results of the 10 developers with the largest market share and found that none presented results in a meaningful way with appropriate context, suggesting that Real World Testing as currently implemented falls short of providing genuine transparency. ONC and the authorized certification bodies have been called on to more closely inspect report quality and impose clearer metric requirements.
A CHPL listing tells you a product met the federal technical bar on the day it was tested. It does not tell you whether the product is easy to use, whether it will interoperate with your specific trading partners, or whether it will perform reliably at scale. Procurement decisions should include real-world reference checks, usability testing with actual clinical staff, and review of the vendor's Real World Testing results on CHPL.

What Certification Confirms vs. What It Does Not
CEHRT stands for Certified EHR Technology — the federal designation required to participate in Medicare and Medicaid quality and incentive programs.
The ONC Health IT Certification Program was created by the HITECH Act of 2009 and has evolved through multiple editions, culminating in the 2015 Edition Cures Update.
The 2015 Edition Cures Update (May 2020) mandated FHIR R4 APIs, USCDI v1 (52 data elements, 16 classes), SMART App Launch, Bulk Data export, and an EHI export function.
Products are tested by ONC-ATLs (currently Drummond Group and SLI Compliance) and listed on the CHPL at chpl.healthit.gov — always verify certification status there directly.
Ongoing ONC-ACB surveillance and ONC Direct Review can result in decertification; CHPL shows real-time corrective action status.
The Promoting Interoperability category in MIPS carries a 25% weight; clinicians must submit a valid CEHRT ID, report PI measures across four objectives, and provide four required attestations.
Certification is a technical floor — it does not guarantee real-world interoperability, clinical usability, or production reliability; Real World Testing requirements exist but remain inconsistently implemented.
When evaluating an EHR, use the CHPL to verify criteria, check surveillance history, and review the vendor's Real World Testing results alongside direct reference checks.
The 2015 Edition Cures Update, finalized in the ONC's May 2020 Cures Act Final Rule, introduced the mandatory FHIR Release 4 standardized API requirement — including SMART App Launch and Bulk Data support — as a new criterion. HL7 v2 messaging and audit logging were required in earlier certification editions, and electronic prescribing of controlled substances is governed by DEA rules rather than by a Cures Update certification criterion.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-patient-access | Patient Access Rights: HIPAA, Cures Act & Third-Party Apps
Patient Access to Health Data: Rights, APIs, and the Road to True Portability
Your health data tells a story that spans decades — every diagnosis, every medication, every lab value, every surgery. Yet for most of American healthcare history, patients have been passive observers of that story, unable to read it, let alone share it. Physicians held records in file cabinets. Hospitals locked data inside proprietary systems. Insurers sat on years of claims that patients never saw. The 21st century brought electronic health records, but digitizing a locked file cabinet does not make information free.
That reality is now changing — not because the industry chose transparency voluntarily, but because federal law now mandates it. A converging set of regulations — the 21st Century Cures Act, the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), and the ONC Cures Act Final Rule — have created enforceable patient rights to electronic health data. APIs are the pipes. FHIR is the language. SMART on FHIR is the security handshake. Together, they are building the infrastructure for true health data portability. This lesson examines the legal foundations of those rights, the technical systems built to fulfill them, the real-world barriers that still limit access, and the road ahead.

The Original Foundation: HIPAA's Right of Access
Long before FHIR or APIs existed, patients already had a federal right to their health information. The HIPAA Privacy Rule, codified at 45 CFR §164.524, grants every patient the right to inspect and obtain a copy of their protected health information (PHI) maintained in a designated record set. This right covers medical records, billing records, and any other records used to make decisions about the individual.
The mechanics are straightforward on paper. A patient submits a written request to a covered entity — a hospital, physician practice, insurer, or their business associates — and the covered entity must act on that request within 30 calendar days of receipt. A single 30-day extension is permitted if the entity notifies the patient in writing of the reason for delay and provides a date by which it will complete the action. Covered entities may charge a reasonable, cost-based fee — but that fee can only cover labor for copying, supplies, and postage. They cannot charge for retrieving or reviewing the records, a distinction the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) at HHS has repeatedly emphasized in enforcement actions. When a patient uses a patient portal's View, Download, and Transmit functionality, no fee may be charged at all.
Despite this longstanding right, compliance was historically poor. Providers routinely imposed excessive fees, demanded notarized requests, required patients to appear in person, or simply failed to respond within the legally required window. OCR launched a Right of Access Initiative in 2019, specifically targeting providers who delayed, denied, or overcharged patients for their records. The initiative has resulted in dozens of settlements and civil monetary penalties. In December 2024, OCR finalized a $200,000 civil monetary penalty against OHSU — its 53rd Right of Access enforcement action — and in January 2025 it announced a $60,000 settlement with South Broward Hospital District (Memorial Healthcare System). These enforcement actions signal that HHS treats patient access as a genuine legal obligation — not a courtesy.
Under HIPAA 45 CFR §164.524, patients have the right to direct their PHI to a third party of their choosing — including a health app, a caregiver, or another provider. Covered entities cannot refuse on the grounds that they do not trust the receiving app or question the patient's reason for sharing.
HIPAA's Right of Access applies to 'designated record sets' — not necessarily every record a clinician ever created. Psychotherapy notes, certain quality assurance records, and information compiled for legal proceedings may be excluded. The 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking rules extend further, covering all electronic health information (EHI) — a broader category than HIPAA's designated record set.
21st Century Cures Act: The Information Blocking Prohibition
The 21st Century Cures Act, signed into law in December 2016, took the concept of patient access and reframed it as a prohibition framework. Rather than simply granting rights to patients, it made it illegal for 'actors' in the healthcare ecosystem — health IT developers, health information networks, and healthcare providers — to engage in practices that interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI). This prohibition, codified in the ONC Cures Act Final Rule at 45 CFR Part 171, took effect April 5, 2021.
The statute defines information blocking broadly: any practice that a provider knows — or that a health IT developer or health information network knows or should know — is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage access, exchange, or use of EHI — unless the practice falls within a defined exception. ONC's 2020 rule codified eight exceptions — among them preventing harm, privacy, security, and infeasibility — and later rules added TEFCA Manner and Protecting Care Access; practices required by law fall outside the definition itself. A practice that misses every exception is not automatically information blocking: whether it meets the definition is decided case by case. The scope of EHI covered by the prohibition expanded in October 2022 from a subset of structured data to nearly all information in a patient's designated record set — including clinical notes, imaging reports, and behavioral health records.
Enforcement unfolded in stages. HHS-OIG began enforcing against health IT developers and health information exchanges and networks for conduct on or after September 1, 2023, with civil monetary penalties of up to $1,000,000 per violation. Disincentives for healthcare providers became effective July 31, 2024 — making the prohibition fully operational across all actor types. Providers found to have committed information blocking may lose meaningful EHR user status (for hospitals, three-quarters of the annual market-basket increase), receive a zero score in the MIPS Promoting Interoperability performance category, or be excluded from the Medicare Shared Savings Program for at least one year. HHS's September 2025 announcement of a crackdown on health data blocking, with a joint OIG–ASTP enforcement alert, signals continued and intensifying enforcement.
A regional hospital system charges patients $1 per page plus a $25 administrative fee to retrieve records requested for care coordination with another provider. Under HIPAA, the $25 fee is impermissible — it covers retrieval, not copying. Under the Cures Act information blocking rules, any policy that systematically discourages patients from exercising their access rights, without a valid exception, could constitute information blocking — even if the fee would survive HIPAA scrutiny. The two frameworks overlap but are not identical; compliance with one does not guarantee compliance with the other.
CMS-9115-F: The Patient Access API Mandate for Payers
While the 21st Century Cures Act and the ONC Cures Act Final Rule primarily regulate providers and health IT developers, CMS took parallel action on the payer side with the Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F), finalized in May 2020. This rule targets a data trove that patients had almost never been able to access: their insurance claims and clinical data held by Medicare Advantage plans, Medicaid managed care organizations, CHIP plans, and Qualified Health Plan (QHP) issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges.
CMS-9115-F requires affected payers to implement a Patient Access API — a FHIR R4-based interface that patients can use to retrieve their own data. The API must expose adjudicated claims and encounter data, clinical data (including laboratory results), and — for Medicare Advantage drug plans — formulary information; CMS-0057-F later added prior authorization information starting in 2027. Critically, the rule requires that payers make data available going back to January 1, 2016 — giving patients a multi-year view of their own insurance history, not just recent claims. CMS enforced compliance beginning July 1, 2021 after exercising enforcement discretion through the first half of that year.
The Patient Access API uses SMART on FHIR for authorization. When a patient wants to connect a third-party app to their insurance data, the app redirects the patient to the payer's authorization server. The patient logs in with their insurer credentials and grants the app specific permissions using OAuth 2.0 scopes. The payer's server then issues a time-limited access token — the patient's credentials are never shared with the third-party app. The app presents this token to the FHIR API and retrieves the patient's data. The patient can revoke access at any time through the payer's portal. This architecture brings health insurance data access into alignment with how consumers already authorize apps to access their bank accounts or email.
Subsequent rulemakings have layered additional requirements on top of CMS-9115-F. The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F) added requirements for Prior Authorization APIs, mandating that payers expose prior authorization decisions and timelines via FHIR and publicly report prior authorization metrics beginning in 2026. Each new mandate extends the scope of payer data that patients can access programmatically, steadily dismantling the information asymmetry that has defined the payer-patient relationship for decades.

Blue Button 2.0, Apple Health Records, and the Patient App Ecosystem
CMS's own implementation of the Patient Access API concept predates CMS-9115-F. Blue Button 2.0 — launched as a production API in 2018 — gives Medicare beneficiaries the ability to authorize third-party apps to access their Medicare Part A (hospital), Part B (outpatient), and Part D (prescription drug) claims and encounter data. At launch the API offered FHIR-formatted claims data for 53 million Medicare beneficiaries — one of the largest repositories of longitudinal health claims data in the world. Beneficiaries authorize apps through Medicare.gov, retaining full control over which applications can access their information and for how long.
Blue Button 2.0 demonstrated both the promise and the persistent challenge of patient-facing health data APIs. On the promise side, the program proved that a FHIR API could operate at Medicare's scale — hundreds of millions of claims records served to authorized apps on demand. It attracted dozens of registered production applications spanning personal health management, care coordination, research platforms, and benefits navigation services. On the challenge side, actual beneficiary uptake remained modest: despite the size of the eligible population, the fraction of Medicare beneficiaries who connected an app to Blue Button 2.0 was small. Access rights and technical capability do not automatically translate into patient engagement.
Apple Health Records represents perhaps the most visible consumer-facing implementation of FHIR-based patient access. Launched with 12 hospital partners in 2018, the feature uses the FHIR R4 standard and the SMART on FHIR authorization framework to pull clinical records directly into the iPhone Health app. Apple now reports more than 500 supporting institutions in the U.S. ONC data from 2024 found that 70% of U.S. hospitals enabled patient access via FHIR-configured apps — up from 57% in 2021 — and ONC's 2024 survey data showed 57% of individuals using an app to access their records, compared to 38% in 2020. The program demonstrates that patients will adopt health data apps when the user experience is genuinely frictionless.
The SMART on FHIR standard, developed originally at Boston Children's Hospital and HL7, provides the authorization layer that makes the app ecosystem interoperable. SMART App Launch version 2.2.0 layers OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect on top of FHIR, providing a standardized way for apps to request specific scopes of patient data, confirm patient identity via OpenID Connect claims, and receive time-limited access tokens. This framework is now required by the ONC Cures Act Final Rule for certified health IT — meaning any EHR vendor seeking ONC certification must support it. The result is a genuine ecosystem: any SMART-compatible patient app can, in principle, connect to any certified EHR, without custom integration work.
Think of SMART on FHIR like the 'Sign in with Google' button that thousands of apps use. You never give the third-party app your Google password — Google's servers verify your identity and issue a limited permission token. SMART on FHIR does the same thing for health data: your EHR or payer verifies who you are and hands the app a time-limited key to specific parts of your record — nothing more, nothing less. The result is consent-based, scoped, revocable access that puts the patient in control.
The Gap Between Rights and Reality: Persistent Barriers
Despite a robust legal framework and steadily improving technical infrastructure, patient access to health data remains far from universal in practice. ASTP's analysis of 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS) data found that 77% of individuals nationally were offered online access to their health information, and 65% were both offered access and used it — leaving a sizable group who were offered access but never logged in.
The barriers are both structural and sociodemographic. On the structural side, patients with care scattered across multiple health systems face fragmentation: a portal from each provider, each requiring separate login credentials, each showing only that system's data. Patients who have seen five specialists in three health systems may need five portals to assemble a complete picture of their care. CommonWell Health Alliance and Carequality — the two major nationwide health information exchange frameworks, with CommonWell now a designated TEFCA QHIN and Carequality aligning its framework with TEFCA — enable provider-to-provider data sharing across organizations. But patient-initiated cross-provider exchange, where a patient directs their records from one system to another without involving a clinician, remains technically complex and poorly supported in most consumer-facing applications.
On the sociodemographic side, ONC data consistently documents disparities in portal access and use by race, ethnicity, income, education, and geography. Patients with lower health literacy may struggle to interpret clinical notes and lab values even when they can access them. Non-English speakers face language barriers in portal interfaces designed primarily for English-language users. Rural patients may lack reliable broadband for app-based access. Lower-resourced hospitals — small, rural, and Critical Access facilities — lag significantly behind large academic medical centers in deploying FHIR-enabled app APIs, meaning patients at those facilities may not yet have the same technical access as patients at well-resourced systems.
There is also the question of what patients can do once they have their data. A FHIR bundle of clinical data is rich and machine-readable, but it was not designed for lay audiences. Allergy codes, procedure codes, SNOMED-coded diagnoses, and LOINC-coded lab values are meaningful to clinicians and software systems — but a patient staring at a raw FHIR JSON file is not meaningfully informed. The real frontier of patient access is not just getting data out of systems — it is translating that data into actionable insight for the person it belongs to.
In 2024, 70% of U.S. hospitals enabled patient access via FHIR app APIs — up from 57% in 2021. Progress is real, but 30% of hospitals still do not, and small (66%), rural (66%), and Critical Access (64%) hospitals lag behind.
The Road to True Portability: What Comes Next
The regulatory infrastructure built between 2016 and 2024 has established that patients have enforceable rights to their electronic health information. The technical infrastructure — FHIR R4, SMART on FHIR, Patient Access APIs, Blue Button 2.0, TEFCA — has created standardized pipes through which that data can flow. What the ecosystem now needs is the final layer: applications, data intermediaries, and user experiences that make portable health data genuinely useful to patients in the moments that matter.
TEFCA, the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement finalized by ONC in January 2022 and operationalized through Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) beginning in 2023, is building the nationwide backbone for patient-directed exchange at scale. CommonWell and Carequality have both committed to TEFCA connectivity, potentially unifying the major nationwide exchange frameworks under a single governance structure. Under TEFCA's Individual Access Services, patients will be able to direct the movement of their records from any TEFCA-connected organization to any other — regardless of which EHR or payer system those organizations use.
The longer-term vision — a single, patient-controlled longitudinal health record — aggregates data from every provider, payer, pharmacy, lab, and device the patient has ever interacted with. Several companies are building toward this model, pulling FHIR data from multiple sources simultaneously using SMART on FHIR and assembling it into a unified timeline. As AI-powered interpretation layers mature, patients may eventually receive not just a copy of their records, but a personalized, plain-language explanation of what those records mean — closing the loop between access and understanding.
Two risks deserve attention as patient access expands. First, privacy: when patients share data with apps via SMART on FHIR, those apps are not necessarily covered entities under HIPAA — they may be regulated only by the FTC, which applies a weaker standard. A patient who shares their Medicare claims with a wellness app may have significantly less protection than they realize. Second, equity: if the apps and platforms that make portable data useful are designed for the already-connected and already-literate patient, the information blocking prohibition will have succeeded technically while failing the patients who most need to benefit from it. True portability is not just a legal right — it is an equity imperative.
Patients should not have to fight for their own health information. Data blocking is a patient safety issue — when records do not follow the patient, care suffers.
HIPAA's Right of Access (45 CFR §164.524) gives patients the right to their records within 30 days; fees can only cover copying costs — not retrieval, search, or review.
The 21st Century Cures Act prohibits information blocking by providers, health IT developers, and health information networks under 45 CFR Part 171; full enforcement across all actor types has been active since July 2024.

As of 2024, 77% of individuals were offered online access and 65% were offered and used it — legal access rights and technical availability do not automatically produce patient engagement.
CommonWell, Carequality, and TEFCA are building nationwide exchange infrastructure; patient-directed exchange across system boundaries remains the hardest problem to solve at scale.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-smart-fhir | SMART on FHIR: Authorization for Healthcare Apps
SMART on FHIR: The App Launch Framework That Opens the EHR
The Problem SMART Solves: Vendor Lock-In and the Closed EHR
Before SMART on FHIR, integrating a third-party application with an EHR was an expensive, bespoke engineering project. Every major EHR vendor — Epic, Cerner, Allscripts — had its own proprietary API, its own authentication scheme, and its own data model. A clinical decision support tool built for Epic needed to be almost entirely rewritten to run in Cerner, and then rewritten again for Meditech. The result was that innovation happened slowly, mostly inside large vendors, while smaller companies with genuinely useful ideas could not afford the integration tax required to reach clinicians at scale.
The conceptual breakthrough came in 2010 when researchers at Harvard Medical School and Boston Children's Hospital launched a project called Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies — SMART. Led by Kenneth Mandl and Isaac Kohane, with physician-informaticist Josh Mandel as lead architect, the project's explicit goal was to create an "app store for healthcare": a standard platform layer so that a developer could write an application once and run it, unmodified, on any EHR that supported the standard. Early SMART used its own clinical data models (now called SMART Classic). In the second half of 2013, the team updated the platform to use the emerging HL7 FHIR standard for data exchange, giving birth to SMART on FHIR. The new platform debuted publicly at the HIMSS conference in February 2014, with prototype demonstrations from several commercial EHR vendors and app developers.
The fundamental promise of SMART on FHIR is separation of concerns. The EHR remains responsible for storing and managing clinical data. The SMART framework provides a standardized mechanism for a third-party application to request access to that data, receive permission from the user, and launch inside the clinical workflow — all without the EHR vendor having to build the feature themselves. For the first time, the EHR could become an extensible platform rather than a monolithic silo.

How SMART on FHIR Works: OAuth 2.0 Meets the Clinical Workflow
At its core, SMART on FHIR is a profile on top of two well-established internet standards: OAuth 2.0 for authorization and HL7 FHIR for clinical data. OAuth 2.0 is the same protocol that powers "Sign in with Google" and "Connect with Facebook" across the web — a battle-tested framework for letting a user grant a third-party application limited access to their data without sharing their password. SMART on FHIR adapts this framework specifically for the healthcare context, adding the concept of clinical launch context (which patient is currently on the screen?), healthcare-specific scopes, and EHR-embedded app launching.
Imagine the EHR is a secured apartment building. OAuth 2.0 is the intercom system. When a SMART app wants in, it rings the intercom (authorization request). The resident — the clinician or patient — decides whether to buzz the app in (grant consent). The building then issues a temporary keycard (access token) that only opens the specific doors the resident approved. The app never learns the master key.
SMART on FHIR uses OAuth 2.0 to grant apps time-limited, scoped access to EHR data — never the master credentials.
SMART defines two primary launch patterns. In the EHR Launch flow, the EHR initiates the sequence: a clinician clicks an app icon inside the EHR interface, and the EHR passes a launch token and the FHIR server base URL to the app. The app uses these to request an authorization code, which it exchanges for an access token along with the current patient context (patient ID, encounter ID, practitioner ID). The app then uses the access token to call FHIR APIs and retrieve the data it needs — all without the clinician needing to log in again or manually identify the patient. In the Standalone Launch flow, the app starts independently (e.g., from a mobile phone or patient portal) and prompts the user to select a patient or log in directly. Both flows use the same underlying OAuth 2.0 authorization code exchange mechanism.
Clinician clicks the SMART app icon. The EHR redirects the browser to the app's launch URL, passing a launch parameter and the FHIR server base URL as query parameters.
EHR Initiates Launch
The app fetches the FHIR server's .well-known/smart-configuration document to discover the authorization and token endpoints — eliminating hardcoded URLs.
App Discovers Authorization Endpoint
The app redirects the user to the EHR's authorization server, requesting specific scopes (e.g., patient/*.read, launch/patient) and including a PKCE code challenge for security.
Authorization Request
The EHR presents a consent screen. The clinician (or patient) approves the requested permissions. The authorization server redirects back to the app with a short-lived authorization code.
User Grants Consent
The app sends the authorization code to the token endpoint and receives an access token, a refresh token, and the patient context (patient ID, encounter ID) in the response body.
Token Exchange
The app uses the access token as a Bearer token in HTTP Authorization headers to call FHIR R4 endpoints — e.g., GET /Patient/{id}/MedicationRequest — and retrieves structured clinical data.
FHIR API Calls
EHR Launch Authorization Flow
SMART scopes are the permission language of the framework. They follow the pattern context/ResourceType.action. The context is patient (data limited to the in-context patient), user (data the logged-in user can see), or system (machine-to-machine, no user in the loop). The ResourceType is any FHIR resource name such as Observation, MedicationRequest, or Condition. The action is read (r), search (s), or write (c, u, d). So patient/Observation.rs means "read and search Observations for the current patient." Scopes give EHR administrators fine-grained control over what any given app is permitted to access, and users can review exactly what permissions they are granting before approving.
The SMART App Gallery and Real-World Clinical Use Cases
SMART Health IT maintains a publicly accessible App Gallery at apps.smarthealthit.org where developers can list applications built on the SMART standard. The gallery is organized by audience (clinicians, patients, researchers) and serves as a discovery mechanism for healthcare organizations evaluating third-party tools. Dozens of clinical applications are listed, spanning cardiovascular risk, pain management, oncology, mental health, and population analytics — demonstrating that the platform has moved well beyond proof-of-concept into active clinical use at institutions including Boston Children's Hospital and Duke Medicine.
Several production SMART apps illustrate the breadth of what the platform enables. The ASCVD Risk Calculator, embedded in EHRs at multiple institutions, pulls a patient's lab results, demographics, and medication list via FHIR and computes a 10-year cardiovascular risk score in real time — without the clinician copying any data. The Pain Management Summary dashboard aggregates opioid prescription history, pain assessments, and PDMP data into a single view, supporting safer prescribing decisions. COSRI (Clinical Opioid Summary with Rx Integration) connects directly to state Prescription Drug Monitoring Programs via SMART. Each of these apps runs inside the EHR workflow, launched with a single click, and presents information in the context of the patient already on screen.
CDS Hooks is the complementary standard that extends SMART's reach into proactive clinical decision support. Where SMART apps are user-launched, CDS Hooks allows external services to automatically fire decision support suggestions at defined moments in the clinical workflow — when a medication is ordered, when a patient's chart is opened, or when a diagnosis code is entered. CDS Hooks is now published by HL7 as part of the broader FHIR-based interoperability ecosystem, and the two standards are designed to work together: a CDS Hook suggestion can launch a SMART app for deeper investigation or action. Together they represent a complete architecture for embedded clinical intelligence.

SMART Backend Services: Machine-to-Machine Authorization
Not every FHIR integration involves a human sitting at a keyboard. Population health analytics platforms, payer data pipelines, automated quality reporting systems, and Bulk FHIR export jobs all need to authenticate against a FHIR server without a user present. The SMART Backend Services specification, published by HL7 International as part of the SMART App Launch Implementation Guide, defines exactly how to handle this scenario. It uses the OAuth 2.0 Client Credentials grant flow, adapted for healthcare, with JSON Web Token (JWT) assertions for client authentication.
The SMART Backend Services flow works as follows. The client system is pre-registered with the FHIR authorization server and is assigned a set of pre-authorized scopes — for example, system/Patient.rs and system/Observation.rs, which grant read and search access to those resources for all patients the client has been authorized to access. At runtime, the client generates a short-lived, one-time-use authentication JWT signed with its private key. It posts this JWT to the authorization server's token endpoint using a standard OAuth 2.0 client credentials request. The server validates the JWT signature against the client's registered public key, confirms the pre-authorized scopes, and issues an access token. The client then uses this token to call FHIR APIs — including the $export operation for Bulk FHIR — without any human interaction. The specification requires TLS 1.2 or higher for all exchanges.
SMART Backend Services is the authorization backbone for the Bulk FHIR ecosystem. When a hospital system needs to export a million patient records to a population health vendor for annual quality reporting, or when a payer needs to automatically retrieve claims-linked clinical data, Backend Services provides the secure, auditable, machine-to-machine credential exchange that makes it possible. Unlike the EHR Launch flow, there is no consent screen — the data access has been negotiated and pre-authorized at the system administration level, with appropriate Business Associate Agreements in place. This makes Backend Services powerful but also requires careful governance: the scopes granted to a backend client should follow the principle of least privilege, requesting only the resource types and actions the pipeline genuinely needs.
SMART Backend Services does not involve a real-time consent screen. Access is granted based on prior administrative agreements between the client system and the FHIR server. Organizations deploying backend clients must ensure appropriate data use agreements, audit logging, and scope minimization policies are in place before go-live.
Backend Services Requires Pre-Authorization
Regulatory Mandate: How SMART on FHIR Became Required Law
SMART on FHIR moved from an academic research project to a federal legal requirement through the 21st Century Cures Act and the ONC's Health IT Certification Program. The original 2015 Edition rules introduced patient-facing API criteria without mandating FHIR. The 2015 Edition Cures Update — implementing the Cures Act final rule — went significantly further, requiring a FHIR R4 API secured with the SMART App Launch Implementation Guide Release 1.0.0. ONC approved SMART v2.0.0 as a voluntary upgrade in 2022, and its HTI-1 rule made v2.0.0 the required version by December 31, 2025. Any EHR seeking ONC certification must now support SMART on FHIR compliant application access, including verifying SMART authorization flows, refresh tokens, and token revocation as part of the certification testing process.
The three largest EHR vendors have built developer ecosystems around SMART on FHIR. Epic's App Orchard (now called the Epic Showroom) is a vetted marketplace where third-party developers list SMART-compatible applications. Developers register their apps, receive sandbox credentials, and go through a validation process before their apps can be deployed at Epic customer sites. Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) operates the Code Console developer portal, where developers register SMART applications, configure redirect URIs, and access Cerner Millennium sandbox environments. Validated integrations can be listed on the Oracle Healthcare Marketplace. These marketplaces collectively represent hundreds of commercially available SMART applications across clinical decision support, patient engagement, revenue cycle, and population health.
The SMART brand has also extended beyond EHR integration into patient-held credentials through SMART Health Cards. Developed in response to COVID-19 by the Vaccination Credential Initiative — a coalition that included Epic, Cerner, Microsoft, Salesforce, and dozens of health systems — SMART Health Cards use a combination of W3C Verifiable Credentials and HL7 FHIR to encode vaccination records as cryptographically signed QR codes. By January 2022, approximately 80% of Americans who had received a COVID-19 vaccine had access to a SMART Health Card through state health departments, healthcare systems, pharmacies, and employer portals. The same technical framework is now being extended to other health documents including lab results, insurance cards, and referral authorizations — demonstrating that the SMART ecosystem has grown far beyond its original EHR launch use case.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-cms-patient-access-api | CMS Interoperability Rule: Patient Access & Provider Directory APIs
CMS Patient Access API: Giving Members Control of Their Health Data
The Policy Origin: CMS-9115-F and the Interoperability Mandate
On May 1, 2020, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services published the landmark Interoperability and Patient Access final rule, formally known as CMS-9115-F. The rule arrived amid a pandemic, yet it represented years of policymaking work aimed at dismantling one of the most persistent barriers in American healthcare: the inability of patients to easily obtain and move their own health data. For decades, insurance claims, encounter records, and clinical results sat locked inside payer systems, accessible only through cumbersome request processes. CMS-9115-F changed the legal landscape fundamentally by requiring regulated payers to open standardized, secure digital doors directly to patients and the applications patients choose.
The rule applies to a broad set of federally regulated payers: Medicare Advantage (MA) organizations, Medicaid Fee-for-Service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, Children's Health Insurance Program (CHIP) Fee-for-Service programs, CHIP managed care entities, and issuers of Qualified Health Plans (QHPs) on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges. This scope is intentional — together these programs cover well over 100 million Americans, and establishing a uniform standard across them creates the critical mass needed to make patient-facing data exchange a market reality rather than a pilot curiosity. Notably, large commercial plans sold outside the exchanges were not directly captured, a gap that some states have moved to close through their own legislation.
The technical standard chosen by CMS was HL7 FHIR Release 4.0.1, the then-current version of the Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources specification. FHIR R4 provides a REST-based API architecture with well-defined resource types, enabling developers to build consumer applications without requiring bespoke integrations for each payer. CMS recognized implementation complexity created by the COVID-19 pandemic and exercised enforcement discretion through July 1, 2021, at which point active enforcement of the Patient Access API and Provider Directory API requirements began in earnest. Missing either deadline was not a technicality — CMS signaled it would use existing program oversight authorities, including corrective action plans and, for Medicare Advantage, contract termination.

What the Patient Access API Must Expose
The Patient Access API is not a single data dump — it is a structured set of FHIR resource endpoints that collectively give a member a longitudinal view of what their insurance plan knows about them. CMS-9115-F identified three primary categories of data that must be available: claims and encounter information (including cost data such as provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing), clinical data including laboratory results when maintained by the payer, and formulary and coverage data. The CARIN Alliance for Blue Button Implementation Guide (CARIN IG) was explicitly endorsed by CMS as the recommended specification for the claims and encounter data layer, defining profiles for the Patient, Coverage, and ExplanationOfBenefit FHIR resources that form the foundation of every compliant implementation.
The clinical data requirement is where many payer implementations have stumbled. CMS requires that payers expose data classes and elements aligned with the U.S. Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) standard, as reflected in the US Core FHIR Implementation Guide. This means exposing resources such as MedicationRequest, Condition, Procedure, and CareTeam — data elements that can logically be derived from claims even when payers do not hold provider-sourced clinical records. CMS-0057-F (the 2024 successor rule) escalated the bar by requiring conformance with USCDI v3, a step up from the USCDI v1 that most CMS-9115-F implementations targeted. Because payers primarily hold administrative data, the clinical data tier remains the most challenging compliance frontier.
Access to this data is member-authorized and flows through the OAuth 2.0 SMART App Launch protocol, which allows a member to grant a third-party application permission to retrieve their records directly from the payer's FHIR server. The application receives a token scoped to that member's data, and the payer must return the applicable FHIR resources without filtering or degrading the data. CMS explicitly prohibits payers from using the app registration process as a competitive gatekeeping mechanism — registration must be open to any legitimate developer, and delays or denials without documented security justification constitute compliance violations.
Tier 1 — Claims & Encounter (Broadly Implemented)
Adjudicated claims via ExplanationOfBenefit FHIR resource
Coverage information (plan, subscriber, deductible)
Provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing amounts
Prior authorization data profiled in ExplanationOfBenefit
Tier 2 — Clinical & Formulary (Lower Adoption)

Laboratory results when held by the payer
Formulary data (drug coverage, tiers, cost-sharing)
Care team and care plan information
Patient Access API: Data Tiers
Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange: From CMS-9115-F to CMS-0057-F
One of the most ambitious provisions of the original CMS-9115-F was the requirement that payers exchange data with each other when a member transitions between plans. The vision: when you switch from one insurance plan to another, your new insurer automatically receives up to five years of your claims, encounter, and clinical history from your prior insurer — reducing redundant testing, filling dangerous care gaps, and enabling your new care team to understand your complete medical story from day one. However, implementation challenges proved severe. On December 8, 2021, CMS announced enforcement discretion on the payer-to-payer provisions of CMS-9115-F, acknowledging that the member-mediated authentication model outlined in the original rule was not well-suited for business-to-business data transfers.
The 2024 CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F), published January 17, 2024, resolved these tensions with a redesigned Payer-to-Payer API framework. Under CMS-0057-F, payers are no longer required to use patient-mediated SMART App Launch authentication for payer-to-payer exchanges — CMS recognized that "protocols requiring user level credentials managed by the payer are generally not appropriate for business-to-business data exchanges." Instead, the new model requires that when a member enrolls in a new plan, the receiving payer must collect the member's opt-in consent and information about former or concurrent plans, then — within one week of receiving both — request the required data from identified prior payers. The full Payer-to-Payer API compliance deadline under CMS-0057-F is January 1, 2027.
The technical vehicle for payer-to-payer exchange is the Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange (PDex) Implementation Guide, which CMS recommends as the specification for this API. PDex defines how payers package FHIR resources — including claims, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history — into standardized bundles that receiving payers can ingest. A critical feature of PDex is its provenance framework, which preserves the chain of custody for clinical information as it moves across payer boundaries. The data scope is substantial: up to five years of adjudicated claims and encounters (excluding provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing), data classes aligned with USCDI, and prior authorization information excluding drug authorizations. Plain-language educational resources explaining the Payer-to-Payer API to members must also be provided, underscoring that member trust and informed consent are foundational to the design.
Imagine every time you moved to a new city, your entire medical file automatically transferred to your new doctor's office before your first appointment — without you having to carry a folder of records or repeat your history from scratch.
The Payer-to-Payer API aims to create the same seamless longitudinal data continuity when members change insurance plans, ensuring new payers and providers start with a complete picture instead of a blank slate.

The Provider Directory API: Making Network Data Trustworthy
Alongside the Patient Access API, CMS-9115-F required covered payers to implement a publicly accessible, FHIR R4-based Provider Directory API. The purpose is straightforward but long-elusive: give consumers, providers, and app developers reliable, machine-readable information about which clinicians and facilities participate in a given insurance network. The implementation guide endorsed by CMS for this purpose is the Da Vinci PDEX Plan-Net IG, currently at version 1.2.0 (published February 25, 2025). Plan-Net defines FHIR profiles for the key entities in a provider network: Practitioner, PractitionerRole, Organization, OrganizationAffiliation, HealthcareService, InsurancePlan, Endpoint, and Location. Together these resources allow a third-party application to answer questions like "Which cardiologists in Burlington, Vermont accept my Blue Cross plan?"
Provider directory accuracy has been a chronic industry problem, and the No Surprises Act — which took effect January 1, 2022 — added regulatory teeth by creating a 90-day attestation cycle. Health plans must verify all provider details at least once every 90 days, including physician name, specialty, address, phone number, and network participation status. Inaccurate directories create concrete patient harm: a member who selects an in-network provider based on a stale directory and then receives an unexpected out-of-network bill has experienced both a financial injury and a failure of the information infrastructure that was supposed to protect them.
Despite mandatory requirements, the state of provider directory FHIR APIs as of 2024 remains uneven. Many payers have struggled to maintain accurate Practitioner-to-Plan relationships. The core challenge is organizational: provider directory data is collected through credentialing, contracting, and roster processes that often exist in siloed systems. Surfacing this data through a coherent FHIR API requires not only technical integration work but also operational governance to ensure that roster updates flow promptly into the API. CMS-0057-F introduced a Provider Access API — distinct from the public-facing Provider Directory API — that allows providers to query payer data about their own patients, with a separate compliance deadline of January 1, 2027.
A "ghost network" occurs when a provider appears in an insurance directory but is no longer accepting new patients, has left the network, or has moved locations. CMS's own reviews of Medicare Advantage online directories found that 45–52 percent of listed provider locations had at least one inaccuracy (2016–2018). The Provider Directory API requirement creates a machine-readable surface for auditing — but the data quality it reflects is only as good as the operational processes feeding it.
Ghost Networks: A Persistent Patient Safety Problem
A developer querying a compliant Plan-Net endpoint can retrieve a PractitionerRole resource that bundles the practitioner's NPI, specialty taxonomy code, the specific InsurancePlan network they participate in, their office address as a Location resource, accepted patient telephones, and the network's HealthcareService offerings — all in a single structured FHIR response. This is the machine-readable equivalent of the printed directory booklet, updated continuously rather than annually.

Adoption, Enforcement, and the Gaps That Remain
More than four years after the July 2021 enforcement date, the Patient Access API landscape reflects the messy reality of federal mandates meeting real-world implementation complexity. Flexpa's November 2024 report, covering more than 488 payer endpoints across 28 vendors, found that many payers had yet to implement a Patient Access API; Flexpa itself had facilitated about 120,000 successful member connections across 216 health plans — modest against the more than 100 million people the rule covers. The contrast with established health information networks is stark: Carequality reports moving approximately 940 million clinical documents per month through provider-initiated queries, while patient-mediated FHIR pulls via the Patient Access API are orders of magnitude smaller.
CMS enforcement has been measured rather than aggressive. The agency uses existing program oversight mechanisms — annual survey instruments for Medicare Advantage, the QHP certification process for Marketplace plans, and state-level oversight for Medicaid and CHIP — rather than a centralized enforcement unit issuing fines. Enforcement actions can escalate from corrective action plans to public reporting of violations and ultimately to contract termination for Medicare Advantage organizations, but documented cases of termination specifically for Patient Access API non-compliance remain rare. CMS did, however, signal a new accountability lever: starting January 1, 2026, impacted payers must annually report Patient Access API usage metrics to CMS (first report due March 31, 2026), creating a transparency mechanism that will enable comparative assessment of engagement across plans.
Perhaps the most consequential unresolved gap is the privacy protection asymmetry for data that leaves the payer system. When a member authorizes a third-party app to receive their health data through the Patient Access API, that data exits the HIPAA regulatory perimeter. Most third-party health apps are not covered entities and are not bound by HIPAA — they are instead subject to the Federal Trade Commission Act, which prohibits unfair or deceptive practices, and to the FTC's Health Breach Notification Rule — but no federal law imposes HIPAA-style limits on how such a company may use or monetize health data it has disclosed in its privacy policy. This creates a scenario where a member's complete insurance claims history — a detailed proxy for their medical conditions, prescriptions, and provider relationships — could lawfully be sold to data brokers or used for targeted advertising, with the only safeguard being whatever terms the app's privacy policy contains. The ONC and FTC have flagged this gap repeatedly, but as of mid-2025 no federal legislation has closed it comprehensively.
The state-level response has begun to fill some voids. California's SB 1419 (enacted 2022; compliance extended to January 1, 2025) and Tennessee's SB 2012 (signed May 2024; APIs due July 1, 2024) extended Patient Access API-style requirements to commercial plans sold outside the federally facilitated exchanges — populations not covered by CMS-9115-F. These state actions are early indicators that interoperability mandates may eventually reach all lines of business, not just government-program-adjacent markets. Meanwhile, the January 2027 deadline under CMS-0057-F for the full suite of new APIs — Payer-to-Payer, Provider Access, and Prior Authorization — represents the next major wave of compliance pressure that will test whether payers can scale from partial Patient Access API conformance to a comprehensive interoperability architecture.

What This Means for Vermont's Health Ecosystem
Vermont's health system occupies a distinctive position in the national interoperability landscape. The state operates a unified Health Information Exchange (Vermont HIE/VHIE) and has long pursued All-Payer Model ambitions that require rich data flows between payers, providers, and the state itself. In Vermont, the CMS-9115-F and CMS-0057-F requirements reach Medicare Advantage plans and the state Medicaid program, overlaying existing state data-sharing expectations. They do not reach qualified health plans sold on Vermont Health Connect: CMS-9115-F covers QHP issuers only on the federally facilitated exchanges, and Vermont runs its own state-based marketplace.
The practical implication for Vermont consumers is significant but still largely unrealized. A Vermont resident enrolled in Medicaid or a Medicare Advantage plan today has the legal right to connect any SMART-on-FHIR application to their payer's Patient Access API and retrieve their complete claims history, formulary information, and available clinical data. Yet awareness of this right is minimal, and the ecosystem of trustworthy, Vermont-specific health management apps built on these APIs is nascent. Closing the gap between legal entitlement and consumer benefit requires not just API compliance but also member education, app vetting frameworks, and policy clarity on downstream data use protections that Vermont could model through state-level privacy legislation.
For healthcare organizations and technologists building on Vermont's health platform, the Patient Access API represents an underutilized data source. Aggregating member-authorized payer data alongside provider-sourced clinical data from the VHIE creates the longitudinal health record that care coordination programs need but have historically lacked. Population health analytics, care gap identification, and medication reconciliation all improve meaningfully when claims data — the most complete record of what services a member actually received — is available alongside clinical documentation. The CMS-0057-F Payer-to-Payer API will further amplify this by ensuring that members who transition between Vermont plans or arrive in Vermont from out of state bring their prior history with them automatically.
The Patient Access API is not an IT project. It is a patient rights framework built on top of an IT standard. The goal is not API uptime — it is a Vermont where every resident can walk into any healthcare encounter with their complete insurance and clinical history in hand.
