######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-payer-to-payer | Payer-to-Payer Exchange: Following the Patient
Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange: Continuity of Coverage in a Mobile Population
Americans move between jobs, between states, and between life stages. When they do, their health coverage often moves with them or, more precisely, it disappears and reappears in a different form. A factory worker switches from employer-sponsored coverage to a Marketplace plan after a layoff. A retiree transitions from commercial insurance to Medicare Advantage. A young adult ages off a parent's plan and enrolls in a state Medicaid program. Each of these transitions is not just an administrative event. It is a potential rupture in the continuity of care. The new payer inherits a member but not a record. The patient's diagnosis history, prior authorization approvals, chronic medication regimen, and recent specialist consultations exist somewhere on a server operated by the previous plan but are invisible to the clinicians and care managers now responsible for that person's health.
This invisibility has real consequences. A care manager at the new plan who does not know about a patient's recent hospitalization cannot schedule appropriate follow-up. A prior authorization reviewer who cannot see a previously approved six-month course of specialty medication may deny continuation, creating an abrupt gap in treatment. A disease management program that does not know a member has diabetes cannot enroll them in population health outreach. Every one of these failures costs money in duplicated diagnostic tests, avoidable hospitalizations, and adverse drug events, and most importantly it costs health. The problem is structural: the health insurance system has historically treated membership data as proprietary, not portable.
Payer-to-payer data exchange is the regulatory and technical effort to fix this structural failure. The concept is straightforward: when a member changes health plans, the new payer should be able to request and receive relevant clinical and administrative data from the previous payer, so that care continues without interruption. The execution has proved far more complex. This lesson traces the regulatory journey from CMS-9115-F's original 2022 mandate through its supersession by CMS-0057-F's January 2027 deadline, explains the technical architecture built on HL7's Da Vinci PDex Implementation Guide, and examines the real-world challenges of member identity matching, consent management, and data operationalization that stand between the regulatory vision and clinical impact.
The Coverage Gap Problem: Who Actually Switches Plans and Why It Matters
The scale of health plan switching in the United States is large enough to constitute a persistent public health challenge in its own right. The problem is most acute in Medicaid, where administrative-driven disenrollment and re-enrollment, a phenomenon researchers call churning, affects millions of people each year. Before the COVID-19 public health emergency froze Medicaid eligibility redeterminations, studies found that among full-benefit Medicaid beneficiaries enrolled at any point in a given year, roughly 10% experienced a gap in coverage of less than one year. Approximately 4% were disenrolled and re-enrolled within three months, and nearly 7% within six months. Many of these are not people who became ineligible for coverage. They are people who lost coverage due to paperwork failures, outdated addresses, or administrative processing errors, and then regained it shortly after.
The Medicaid unwinding that followed the end of pandemic-era continuous enrollment protections in April 2023 provided a stark illustration of this dynamic at extreme scale. States resumed eligibility redeterminations after a pause of more than three years, and over the following two years, more than 25 million people were disenrolled from Medicaid. Studies found that 69% of disenrollments were procedural rather than eligibility-based, meaning the vast majority of people who lost coverage were likely still eligible. Many re-enrolled within weeks or months, but each gap represented a period during which the re-enrolling member was invisible to their plan. Any care coordination, disease management, or prior authorization history accumulated during years of prior enrollment was gone from the new plan's view.
In Medicare Advantage, KFF found that about one in ten enrollees (11% of those in MA drug plans in 2013) voluntarily switched to another plan for the following year. In the Affordable Care Act Marketplace, switching rates are substantially higher: 43% of enrollees switched plans between 2015 and 2016, driven by premium volatility, insurer exits, and annual re-evaluation of cost-sharing structures. Each of these transitions creates a potential data gap. And unlike Medicaid churning where the member may return to the same plan, Marketplace switching typically involves entirely different payers who have no established data-sharing relationship.

The root problem: when a member moves from one health plan to another, the new plan has their enrollment demographics but none of their clinical history. Diagnoses, prior authorizations, chronic condition status, and care plans must be rebuilt from scratch at cost to both the member's health and the system's efficiency.
The Regulatory Journey: From CMS-9115-F to CMS-0057-F
The regulatory effort to mandate payer-to-payer data exchange begins with the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule, published May 1, 2020 and commonly cited as CMS-9115-F. This landmark rule required Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plans on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges to implement not only a Patient Access API for members but also a payer-to-payer data exchange process. Specifically, payers were required to, upon member request, send clinical and administrative data to another payer when the member changed plans. The original compliance deadline for the payer-to-payer provisions was January 1, 2022.
That deadline proved aspirational. On December 8, 2021, weeks before the deadline, CMS announced that it would exercise enforcement discretion and not take action to enforce the payer-to-payer provisions of CMS-9115-F. The agency's rationale was candid: the FHIR-based technical standards needed for payer-to-payer exchange had not yet matured to the point where standardized, reliable exchange was feasible at scale. CMS wanted to avoid a situation where payers exchanged data in inconsistent, non-standard formats that would undermine interoperability rather than advance it. The agency committed to addressing the challenges through future rulemaking and delivered on that commitment through CMS-0057-F.
The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule, known as CMS-0057-F, was released on January 17, 2024 and represents the definitive federal framework for payer-to-payer data exchange. The rule establishes that the same categories of impacted payers must implement and maintain a FHIR R4-based Payer-to-Payer API. The compliance deadline is January 1, 2027. The rule explicitly recommends the Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange PDex Implementation Guide as the technical standard for this API, building on the HL7 infrastructure that payers were already deploying for the Patient Access API.
The scope of data that must be exchanged under CMS-0057-F is substantial and specific. Payers must make available adjudicated claims and encounter data excluding provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing details, data classes and elements from the content standards adopted by ONC under USCDI, and prior authorization information excluding drugs. Critically, the rule requires payers to exchange data with a date of service within five years of the exchange request, and for data originating before January 1, 2016, the requirement is limited to data with a service date on or after that date. This means a newly enrolled member can trigger a request for up to five years of claims, clinical data, and prior authorization history from their previous plan.

CMS-9115-F vs. CMS-0057-F: Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange
How Payer-to-Payer Exchange Works: The PDex Technical Architecture
The technical foundation for payer-to-payer exchange is the Da Vinci Payer Data Exchange Implementation Guide, version 2.2.0, developed by the Da Vinci Project, a collaboration of HL7 and health industry members including payers, providers, and health IT vendors. The PDex IG defines how FHIR R4 resources should be packaged, queried, and exchanged specifically for payer use cases. It establishes the data model covering which FHIR profiles apply to claims, diagnoses, medications, and prior authorizations in a payer context, the access pattern using FHIR RESTful APIs with SMART on FHIR authorization, and the identity-matching operation called $member-match that allows a requesting payer to establish that the member they are asking about is the same person the previous payer has records for.
The $member-match operation is the linchpin of the entire exchange. When a member enrolls with a new payer and consents to data exchange, the new payer does not have the previous plan's internal member ID. What it has is the member's enrollment demographics: name, date of birth, gender, and potentially a subscriber ID from the previous plan if the member can provide it. The $member-match operation allows the new payer acting as the requesting payer to send these demographics to the previous payer's FHIR endpoint and receive back a confirmed patient identifier, specifically a FHIR UMB Unique Member Business identifier, that can then be used to query clinical and administrative data. The operation uses mTLS mutual Transport Layer Security for the connection and OAuth 2.0 dynamic client registration for authorization, ensuring that only verified, credentialed payers can initiate data requests.
The PDex IG supports two exchange patterns: single-member exchange and bulk exchange. Single-member exchange handles individual member data requests, the primary use case when a specific member enrolls and requests their history. Bulk exchange, added as draft guidance in PDex STU 2.1 to meet CMS-0057-F, allows a new payer to perform member matching and data requests for large populations simultaneously, for example at the end of an open enrollment period when thousands of new members join at once. Bulk exchange uses the FHIR Asynchronous Request Pattern with an HTTP POST kick-off that returns a 202 Accepted response with a Content-Location status endpoint, followed by polling until a completion manifest referencing NDJSON output files is available. This mirrors the bulk data export pattern already used for provider access and analytics.
Think of payer-to-payer exchange like porting your phone number when you switch carriers. When you leave one carrier, you do not lose your number. You authorize the transfer, your new carrier sends a request to your old carrier using a standardized protocol, and your number follows you. Payer-to-payer exchange works the same way: when you switch health plans, you give consent, your new payer sends a $member-match request to your old payer using FHIR APIs, and your five years of claims history and clinical records follow you to your new plan instead of disappearing when you sign up.
Payer-to-payer FHIR exchange as phone number porting for health records
A member enrolls with a new health plan and provides consent for their previous plan to share data. CMS-0057-F requires payers to obtain and honor member consent; the new payer must initiate the data request within one week of enrollment.
Member Enrolls and Consents
The new payer acting as requesting payer establishes a mutual TLS connection to the previous payer's FHIR endpoint, verifying both parties' identity cryptographically before any data flows.
Establish Secure Connection
Using the secure connection, the requesting payer performs OAuth 2.0 Dynamic Client Registration to acquire client credentials from the previous payer's authorization server.
OAuth 2.0 Client Registration
The requesting payer calls the $member-match operation on the previous payer's FHIR endpoint, submitting the member's enrollment demographics. The previous payer returns a confirmed FHIR patient identifier if a match is found.
Run the Member Match Operation
Using the matched patient identifier and an OAuth 2.0 access token, the requesting payer queries the previous payer's FHIR API for up to five years of adjudicated claims, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history.
Query Clinical and Administrative Data
The requesting payer receives FHIR resources including ExplanationOfBenefit, Condition, MedicationRequest, and Coverage resources, ingests them into its systems, and makes them available to care managers, prior authorization reviewers, and disease management programs.

The Payer-to-Payer Data Exchange Workflow
The previous payer must respond to data requests within one business day under CMS-0057-F. This tight turnaround is designed to ensure that clinical continuity information is available to the new plan before the first care interaction, not weeks later when the member may have already faced a prior authorization denial or a duplicated diagnostic workup.
What Data Must Flow: Claims, Clinical Records, and Prior Authorizations
The data scope defined by CMS-0057-F for payer-to-payer exchange is deliberately broad. The goal is not merely to transmit a summary. It is to give the new plan enough context to meaningfully continue care. The three primary categories of required data are adjudicated claims and encounter data, USCDI-standard clinical information, and prior authorization history. Each category serves a distinct clinical and administrative purpose, and together they constitute something close to a portable health record from the payer's perspective.
Adjudicated claims and encounter data forms the backbone of the exchange. In FHIR terms, claims are represented primarily through the ExplanationOfBenefit resource, which encodes the provider who rendered care, the date of service, the diagnosis and procedure codes, the amount billed, and the amount paid. Five years of this data gives the receiving plan a longitudinal picture of a member's care utilization: how many times they have been hospitalized, what specialists they regularly see, what chronic conditions drive most of their claims, and what their total cost of care looks like. This information is invaluable for risk stratification, care gap identification, and accurate actuarial modeling. CMS-0057-F explicitly excludes provider remittances and enrollee cost-sharing information from the required exchange, focusing the mandate on clinically relevant data rather than financial settlement details.
The USCDI clinical data requirement builds on the United States Core Data for Interoperability standard, which ONC updates annually to define the minimum clinical data set that health IT systems must be able to exchange. In the payer context, USCDI data includes patient demographics, active problems and diagnoses, medications, allergies, immunizations, laboratory results, vital signs, and clinical notes where the payer holds them. Not every payer holds rich clinical data, as some hold only claims. But where clinical data exists, for example from value-based care arrangements that include clinical data feeds from provider networks, it must be included in the exchange. This requirement ensures that exchange is not limited to administrative claims codes but includes the richer clinical context that claims alone cannot convey.
Prior authorization history may be the most operationally critical component of the exchange. A member with a complex condition such as metastatic cancer, multiple sclerosis, or severe rheumatoid arthritis may have an active prior authorization for a specialty medication or an ongoing approval for a home health service. If the new plan does not know about this authorization, its clinical reviewers may treat the member as a new case, requiring them to re-submit clinical documentation, go through a fresh review process, and potentially experience a gap in treatment during the review period. CMS-0057-F requires the previous payer to include prior authorization data in the exchange package, including the service authorized, the authorization number, the dates, and the clinical rationale. For members with active authorizations, this single requirement may be the highest-value element in the entire exchange.

A 52-year-old woman with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis switches from a Medicaid managed care plan to a Marketplace plan during open enrollment. Her previous plan had an active prior authorization for natalizumab, a high-cost specialty infusion administered monthly. Without payer-to-payer exchange, her new plan's prior authorization team would receive a fresh PA request from her neurologist with no context and might require a step therapy protocol starting with lower-cost alternatives, even though she has already demonstrated failure on multiple prior agents. With payer-to-payer exchange, the new plan receives the prior authorization history including the clinical rationale, the active approval status, and the treatment duration. The care manager can onboard her into the specialty pharmacy program on day one, avoiding a treatment gap that could trigger a relapse.
Real-World Scenario: Prior Authorization Continuity for a Complex Patient
The Hard Problems: Identity Matching, Consent, and Data Operationalization
If payer-to-payer data exchange were purely a regulatory and technical standards problem, the January 2027 deadline would be straightforward to meet. The real difficulty lies in three operational challenges that no regulation or implementation guide can fully solve: member identity matching, consent management, and post-ingestion data operationalization. These challenges sit at the intersection of incomplete data, legal complexity, and organizational capability, and industry experience with early implementations suggests they are where most exchange attempts break down in practice.
Member identity matching is the foundational challenge. The $member-match operation in the PDex IG provides a standardized protocol for matching demographics, but it cannot compensate for demographic data quality problems that are endemic to the health insurance industry. Names are recorded inconsistently, with William at one plan and Bill at another. Dates of birth contain transcription errors. Women who have changed their name after marriage may appear under different names at different plans. Addresses are outdated. Social Security Numbers, which would provide a reliable matching key, are not universally collected for privacy reasons and are not included in the FHIR $member-match operation's standard input. The United States has no national patient identifier, a persistent gap in the country's health IT infrastructure, meaning that matching must rely on probabilistic algorithms applied to imperfect demographic data. A match that fails produces no data transfer. A false match could result in the wrong patient's records being disclosed.
Consent management presents its own complexity. CMS-0057-F requires member opt-in consent before a payer can initiate a data request to a previous plan. This sounds straightforward but raises several operational questions. How does the new plan verify that the consent it has obtained is legally sufficient to authorize the previous plan to disclose data? Will one covered entity accept a consent record gathered by another covered entity as sufficient authorization for disclosure under HIPAA? The PDex IG includes consent resource handling within the $member-match workflow, but payers must implement internal processes for capturing, storing, and transmitting consent documentation in a way that both the requesting plan and the disclosing plan trust. For members who have behavioral health or substance use disorder treatment history, categories of data that carry heightened legal protections under 42 CFR Part 2, consent requirements are even more stringent, and the current PDex framework does not yet have a fully standardized solution for segmenting these sensitive records from a bulk exchange.
Post-ingestion operationalization may be the least-discussed but most consequential challenge. A payer can successfully receive a FHIR bundle of ExplanationOfBenefit resources from a previous plan and still fail to use them effectively. This happens when the internal systems receiving the data lack the workflow integration to surface prior authorization history to reviewers at the moment of decision, or when member identity confidence scores from the matching process are not propagated through the data pipeline, leaving care managers uncertain whether they are looking at the right patient's records. A 2026 Black Book Research report concluded that payer-to-payer interoperability most often fails in the post-ingestion layer where member identity confidence, provenance clarity, completeness signaling, workflow routing, and exception handling remain too immature to translate received data into clinical action. Receiving the data and using the data are not the same thing.
CMS-0057-F establishes a compliance deadline for implementing and maintaining the Payer-to-Payer FHIR API, meaning the technical capability must be in place and functional. But regulatory compliance does not guarantee clinical impact. A payer can pass an API audit and still fail to route prior authorization history to reviewers in time to prevent a treatment gap, or fail to surface a member's chronic condition profile to care managers during onboarding. The measure of true success in payer-to-payer exchange is not whether the API endpoint responds. It is whether the data received improves outcomes for the member who switched plans.
The January 2027 Deadline Is a Floor, Not a Ceiling

Payer-to-Payer Exchange: Technical Compliance vs. Clinical Impact
The Road to 2027 and Beyond: Adoption Landscape and Future Trajectory
With the January 2027 deadline approaching, the health insurance industry faces a substantial implementation sprint. Unlike the Patient Access API where payers had years of experience building FHIR infrastructure and SMART on FHIR authorization before the compliance date arrived, the Payer-to-Payer API introduces genuinely new complexity: payer-to-payer trust frameworks, mTLS endpoint management, bulk member matching, and the operational workflows described above. Early industry assessments suggest that while most large national payers have PDex development programs underway, regional plans and smaller Medicaid managed care organizations face significant resource and technical capability gaps.
The Sequoia Project — the nonprofit that serves as TEFCA's Recognized Coordinating Entity — convenes an Interoperability Matters workgroup on payer-to-payer implementation. A shared trust framework such as TEFCA could give payers pre-built trust agreements, endpoint directories, and identity assurance that bilateral agreements cannot efficiently provide. That would address one of the most persistent operational barriers to payer-to-payer exchange: the need for each requesting payer to negotiate individual trust agreements with each potential responding payer, creating an exponential scaling problem in a market with hundreds of health plans.
The longer-term regulatory trajectory points toward increasingly granular and comprehensive data exchange. CMS-0057-F is not the final word on payer-to-payer exchange. It is the framework on which subsequent requirements will be built. Likely areas for future rulemaking include real-time exchange rather than the one-week initiation window currently permitted, expanded data scope to include more structured clinical data as payers acquire it through value-based arrangements, and integration with national patient identity initiatives. The Da Vinci Project continues to evolve the PDex IG, with STU 2.1 (2025) adding draft bulk exchange guidance and STU 2.2 published in August 2026, and future versions expected to address behavioral health data segmentation and enhanced provenance requirements.
For members, the potential impact is substantial but conditional on execution quality. A Medicaid member who churns and loses coverage for three months due to a paperwork failure before re-enrolling should, under a fully implemented payer-to-payer exchange regime, have their chronic condition history, active care plans, and prior authorization approvals available to the re-enrolling plan within days rather than requiring months of manual record reconstruction. A Medicare Advantage enrollee who switches plans during open enrollment should not have to re-document their medical history to a new care manager. An ACA Marketplace member who changes plans because their previous insurer exits the market should not lose their oncologist's prior authorization for chemotherapy continuation. These are the outcomes that the regulatory framework is designed to produce, and they will only materialize if payers invest not just in API compliance, but in the operational infrastructure that turns received data into clinical action.
Payer-to-payer exchange is the missing link in health data continuity. The Patient Access API gave members the right to retrieve their own data. Provider access APIs gave clinicians direct access to payer data. Payer-to-payer exchange closes the loop by ensuring that when a member changes plans, their history follows them automatically without requiring the member to personally gather and transport their own records between insurers.
CMS-9115-F (2020) originally required payer-to-payer data exchange by January 1, 2022, but CMS exercised enforcement discretion in December 2021 because FHIR standards had not yet matured sufficiently for reliable standardized exchange at scale.
CMS-0057-F (January 2024) supersedes the earlier framework with a definitive mandate: impacted payers must implement a FHIR R4 Payer-to-Payer API by January 1, 2027, exchanging up to 5 years of claims, USCDI clinical data, and prior authorization history.
The technical backbone is the Da Vinci PDex Implementation Guide (current release 2.2.0, August 2026), which defines the $member-match operation for identity resolution, mTLS and OAuth 2.0 for security, and both single-member and bulk asynchronous exchange patterns.
The $member-match operation resolves the identity problem: the requesting payer submits enrollment demographics and the previous payer returns a confirmed FHIR patient identifier that unlocks the clinical data query, without relying on a national patient identifier that the U.S. does not yet have.
The previous payer must respond to data requests within one business day, and the new payer must initiate the request within one week of member consent and enrollment, ensuring clinically relevant data arrives before the first care interaction.
Three operational challenges dominate real-world implementation: member identity matching failures from demographic data quality problems, consent management complexity especially for sensitive behavioral health records under 42 CFR Part 2, and post-ingestion operationalization failures where received data never reaches clinical workflows.
More than 25 million Medicaid disenrollments occurred during the 2023-2025 unwinding with 69% attributable to administrative rather than eligibility reasons, illustrating the massive scale of the coverage continuity problem that payer-to-payer exchange is designed to address.
Regulatory compliance with the January 2027 API mandate is necessary but not sufficient: the measure of success is whether prior authorization history, chronic condition profiles, and care plans are surfaced to the right people at the right moment to prevent treatment gaps for members who switch plans.
CMS-0057-F sets the compliance deadline at January 1, 2027 for the Payer-to-Payer FHIR API. Impacted payers must make available adjudicated claims and encounter data, USCDI clinical information, and prior authorization history with a date of service within five years of the exchange request and no earlier than January 1, 2016. The rule builds on the foundation of CMS-9115-F, which originally required payer-to-payer exchange by January 1, 2022 but was never enforced after CMS exercised enforcement discretion in December 2021.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-bulk-fhir | Bulk FHIR: Population-Level Data Export
Bulk FHIR: Exporting Population-Level Data at Scale
Why Individual-Record APIs Are Not Enough
Standard FHIR REST APIs are brilliant for the single-patient interaction: a clinician clicks into a chart, the app fires a GET /Patient/{id}/$everything, and within seconds the full record arrives. That model works perfectly at the bedside. It falls apart, however, the moment you need data on thousands or millions of patients simultaneously. A payer managing a Medicare Advantage panel of 500,000 members cannot issue half a million sequential HTTP requests to compute a single quality measure. Network latency alone would make the job take days, and the server on the other end would almost certainly throttle or block the traffic long before completion.
Population health analytics, value-based care reporting, actuarial modeling, public health surveillance, and clinical research all share a common requirement: access to cohort-level data in bulk. Quality measure programs such as HEDIS require health plans to assemble longitudinal records spanning years of encounters, lab results, prescriptions, and diagnoses for every enrolled member. Doing that record-by-record through a patient-facing API is not just slow — it is architecturally wrong. The data pipeline breaks down at scale.
Payer-to-payer data exchange introduces a second pressure point. When a member switches insurance plans, the incoming payer must receive the full claims and clinical history for that member from the prior payer. Under CMS rules finalized in 2024, impacted payers must support this exchange via FHIR APIs and must provide data going back five years. Doing that for thousands of concurrent member transitions demands a purpose-built bulk mechanism, not patient-by-patient REST calls. Bulk FHIR was designed precisely for these scenarios, enabling server-side export jobs that run asynchronously and deliver data as downloadable files.
Individual FHIR REST
One request per patient per resource type
Optimized for real-time, interactive workflows
Hundreds of thousands of round trips for large populations
Server throttling and rate limits hit quickly
Impractical for quality reporting or research at scale
Bulk FHIR Export
Single kick-off request covers an entire group or system
Asynchronous: server builds files in the background
Data delivered as NDJSON files, one per resource type
Designed for pipelines, warehouses, and analytics platforms
Supports population health, payer exchange, and research
Individual FHIR API vs. Bulk FHIR
The Bulk FHIR Specification: How It Works
The governing standard is the HL7 FHIR Bulk Data Access Implementation Guide, a Standard for Trial Use currently at version 3.0.0 (STU 3, December 2025), published by HL7 International and available at hl7.org/fhir/uv/bulkdata/. The specification builds on top of FHIR R4 and defines three export endpoints that correspond to different scopes of data. The Group/$export endpoint exports all FHIR resources for members of a named Group resource — the most common use case for payer populations and clinical cohorts. The Patient/$export endpoint exports resources for all patients on the server. The System/$export endpoint (sometimes written /$export) exports every resource in the system regardless of patient linkage, useful for operational data migrations.
The protocol follows an asynchronous kick-off pattern. The client sends a GET or POST request to the chosen export endpoint with the HTTP header Prefer: respond-async. The server immediately returns an HTTP 202 Accepted response — it does not start streaming data yet. Crucially, the 202 response includes a Content-Location header whose value is a polling URL. The client then polls that URL at regular intervals (using exponential back-off as recommended by the specification) until the server returns a 200 OK response with a JSON manifest listing the completed output files. Each output file contains resources of exactly one FHIR type — for example, all Patient resources in one file, all Condition resources in another.
The output format is NDJSON — Newline Delimited JSON — with the MIME type application/fhir+ndjson. NDJSON serializes each FHIR resource as a single line of compact JSON with no internal whitespace, separated from the next resource by a newline character. This design enables streaming parsers to process files line by line without loading the entire document into memory, making it practical to handle files that contain millions of resources. Analytics platforms, data warehouses, and research data pipelines can ingest NDJSON files directly into columnar storage engines such as Apache Parquet or BigQuery without additional transformation overhead.
Client sends GET [base]/Group/{id}/$export with header Prefer: respond-async and optional parameters like _type (resource types to include) and _since (date filter). Server responds 202 Accepted with Content-Location header pointing to a status URL.
Kick-Off Request
Client polls the Content-Location URL. Server returns 202 (still in progress) with optional X-Progress header, or 200 OK (complete) with JSON manifest of output files. Client should use exponential back-off; server may include Retry-After hints.
Status Polling
The 200 OK body is a JSON object with fields: transactionTime, request (original URL), requiresAccessToken (boolean), output (array of file descriptors), and error (array of error file descriptors for any resources that failed to export).
Manifest Inspection
Client downloads each NDJSON file listed in the output array using bearer token authentication if requiresAccessToken is true. Files are organized by resource type; large resource sets may be split across multiple numbered files.
File Download
After successfully retrieving all files, client sends DELETE to the status URL to signal the server that files can be cleaned up, freeing server storage.
Delete Request
The Bulk FHIR Async Export Workflow
Think of bulk FHIR like ordering a freight shipment rather than buying items one by one at a store counter. You place a single order (kick-off request), the warehouse assembles your pallet in the background (server builds NDJSON files), you check the tracking number periodically (status polling), and then you pick up the whole shipment at once (file download). Walking into the store and buying 500,000 items individually would be absurd — yet that is exactly what individual FHIR REST calls require at population scale.
Bulk FHIR async export is to population data what freight shipping is to retail: designed for volume, not individual transactions.

Regulatory Drivers: CMS and ONC Requirements
Bulk FHIR moved from a promising technical idea to a federal mandate through two landmark rules. The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule, published in May 2020, required certified health IT developers to support the HL7 FHIR Bulk Data Access IG (v1.0.0, STU 1) as part of their certification criteria. Specifically, the rule mandated support for the Group/$export operation, enabling population-level data extraction from electronic health records. The compliance deadline for certified EHR systems was December 31, 2022, meaning that since January 2023, any CEHRT-certified system must support bulk export of USCDI data elements for defined patient groups.
On the payer side, CMS issued the Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F) in 2020, requiring Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP agencies, and QHP issuers to implement FHIR-based Patient Access APIs. The subsequent CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), published February 2024, extended these requirements and introduced mandatory Payer-to-Payer Bulk Data Exchange. Under CMS-0057-F, impacted payers must implement a FHIR-based payer-to-payer API that uses Bulk FHIR to transfer clinical data, claims and encounter data, and prior authorization records for members transitioning between plans. Payers must exchange data covering the prior five years of a member's history. The enforcement deadline for this requirement is January 1, 2027.
The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) adds a third layer of momentum. ONC's FHIR Roadmap for TEFCA Exchange version 2 (January 2024) charts three phases toward full FHIR adoption across Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs): facilitated FHIR exchange through QHINs (targeted for early 2024), QHIN-to-QHIN FHIR exchange, and end-to-end FHIR exchange. While TEFCA does not yet mandate bulk FHIR specifically, its FHIR roadmap creates the network infrastructure through which bulk transfers between organizations will eventually flow. TEFCA-connected QHINs are expected to support bulk exchange as the framework matures toward end-to-end FHIR exchange.
CMS-0057-F set the compliance date for payer-to-payer API requirements at January 1, 2027. Payers subject to CMS-0057-F — including Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid managed care plans, and QHP issuers — must have compliant Bulk FHIR APIs operational by that date. CMS enforces compliance through each program's existing oversight tools, from corrective action plans to Medicare Advantage sanctions.
CMS-0057-F Deadline: January 1, 2027
Under the ONC Cures Act Final Rule, certified health IT must support: (1) the HL7 FHIR Bulk Data Access IG including mandatory Group/$export; (2) SMART Backend Services authorization for system-to-system access; (3) export of all USCDI v1 data elements — 52 elements expressed through US Core profiles — for defined patient groups. These requirements apply to any system seeking ONC certification, covering the vast majority of hospitals and large ambulatory practices in the United States.
What ONC Requires in Certified EHRs
Real-World Use Cases: From Quality Measures to Research
The most prominent active initiative involving Bulk FHIR in 2024 and 2025 is the NCQA Bulk FHIR Quality Coalition. The National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) — the organization that administers HEDIS, the industry-standard quality measurement program — launched the coalition to perform end-to-end testing of regulated FHIR data using digital HEDIS measurement as the real-world test case. Representatives from CMS and the Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy (ASTP, formerly ONC) participate as observers. The coalition brings together cohorts of health plans, Data Aggregator Validation (DAV)-certified data partners, and technology vendors to build FHIR data pipelines from clinical and claims data, then test those pipelines against HEDIS-specific FHIR Implementation Guides.
HEDIS electronic measures represent a paradigm shift in quality reporting. NCQA has converted the lengthy HEDIS Volume 2 measure specifications into Clinical Quality Language (CQL), enabling automated, consistent computation directly against FHIR data rather than relying on manual chart abstraction, fax-based data collection, or proprietary extracts. A Bulk FHIR pipeline for HEDIS measurement works as follows: a health plan kicks off a Group/$export against a network provider's FHIR server for its enrolled members, receives NDJSON files containing claims (via CARIN Blue Button FHIR IG) and clinical data (via US Core FHIR IG), and runs CQL measure logic against the combined dataset. NCQA aims to transition HEDIS reporting to fully digital measures by 2030, and Bulk FHIR is the foundational data transport layer for that transition.
Research platforms represent a third major use case. Academic medical centers and research networks use Bulk FHIR to build longitudinal patient datasets for clinical trials, retrospective cohort studies, and machine learning model training. The combination of Group/$export with _type filtering (limiting exports to specific resource types) and _since date parameters enables incremental data updates — a research platform can pull only the new encounters and lab results since its last extract, keeping a population dataset current without re-downloading the entire history. This incremental export pattern dramatically reduces server load and network transfer volumes while maintaining dataset freshness.
When a Medicare Advantage member switches plans on January 1, the incoming payer must request five years of historical data from the prior payer. Under CMS-0057-F, the prior payer's Payer-to-Payer Bulk API must return: US Core clinical data (conditions, medications, allergies, procedures), claims and encounter data with financial fields excluded, and active and pending prior authorization records. The data is exported as NDJSON via Group/$export for the cohort of transitioning members, transferred securely, and ingested into the incoming payer's care management systems — enabling continuity of care without gaps in clinical context.

Implementation Challenges and Security Considerations
Authentication for Bulk FHIR is handled by the SMART Backend Services Authorization specification, defined within the SMART App Launch IG (currently v2.2.0) and referenced by the Bulk Data Access IG. Unlike user-facing SMART on FHIR apps, bulk clients operate without a human in the loop — there is no browser redirect or login screen. Instead, the client registers its public key (as a JSON Web Key Set, or JWKS) with the authorization server, then uses an asymmetric key pair to sign a JWT assertion. The authorization server validates the JWT against the registered public key and issues a short-lived OAuth 2.0 bearer token. This token is then presented with each bulk export request. The entire flow requires TLS 1.2 or higher for all connections.
Large file handling presents engineering challenges that developers frequently underestimate. A bulk export for a payer with millions of members can produce tens of thousands of NDJSON files totaling hundreds of gigabytes or more. Servers must implement file expiration policies (the Bulk Data IG notes files may be deleted after retrieval), and clients must download files promptly — implementations commonly expire export files after 24 to 72 hours. On the client side, NDJSON files must be streamed and processed line by line rather than loaded entirely into memory. Parallelizing downloads across multiple files, using S3-compatible object storage as a landing zone, and employing streaming ETL pipelines are standard patterns for production bulk FHIR consumers.
Privacy risks at population scale are qualitatively different from single-patient access. A bulk export grants access to the records of thousands or millions of individuals simultaneously, meaning a misconfigured authorization scope or a compromised client credential exposes an entire population's data in a single breach. When bulk FHIR data is used for research without patient authorization or an IRB waiver, it must be de-identified: HIPAA Safe Harbor removes all 18 specified identifiers, or a qualified expert must determine that the re-identification risk is very small. Rate limiting is equally important — servers enforce HTTP 429 Too Many Requests responses when clients exceed agreed traffic levels, and production systems must implement tenant-specific rate limits to prevent any single bulk consumer from degrading service for others. Security best practices recommend regular audits of registered backend service credentials and rotation of asymmetric key pairs on a defined schedule.
Unlike single-patient APIs where a misconfigured scope exposes one record, a bulk FHIR scope error exposes an entire population simultaneously. Organizations must implement least-privilege scoping (e.g., system/Patient.read rather than system/*.read), audit all registered backend service credentials regularly, and monitor export job logs for anomalous access patterns. SMART Backend Services credentials should be treated with the same security controls as privileged database accounts.

SMART Backend Services vs. Patient-Facing SMART
Standard FHIR REST APIs require one request per patient — impractical for populations of thousands or millions. Bulk FHIR solves this with a single async kick-off that exports entire cohorts as downloadable NDJSON files.
The HL7 Bulk Data Access Implementation Guide (current release 3.0.0, STU 3) defines three export endpoints: Group/$export for defined cohorts, Patient/$export for all patients, and System/$export for all server resources.
The async kick-off pattern returns 202 Accepted immediately. Clients poll a status URL until they receive a 200 OK with a JSON manifest listing NDJSON output files ready for download.
NDJSON (application/fhir+ndjson) encodes one FHIR resource per line, enabling streaming parsers to process files without loading them entirely into memory — critical for files containing millions of resources.
The ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule mandated that certified EHRs support Bulk FHIR (Group/$export) for USCDI data elements by December 31, 2022. CMS-0057-F requires payer-to-payer Bulk FHIR data exchange by January 1, 2027.
NCQA's Bulk FHIR Quality Coalition is actively using bulk exports as the data pipeline for digital HEDIS measurement, targeting full digital quality reporting by 2030.
SMART Backend Services authorization — using asymmetric JWT key pairs and OAuth 2.0 client credentials flow — provides the system-to-system authentication layer required for Bulk FHIR, with no human user in the loop.
Privacy and security risks are amplified at population scale: a single misconfigured bulk credential can expose millions of records. Least-privilege scoping, credential rotation, and rate limiting are non-negotiable safeguards.
The Bulk Data Access IG specifies that a successful kick-off request receives an HTTP 202 Accepted response, confirming the export job has been queued but not yet completed. The response also includes a Content-Location header with the URL the client must poll to check progress — 200 OK only arrives when the export files are fully ready for download.
200 OK — the data is returned synchronously in the response body
202 Accepted — the job is queued and a Content-Location polling URL is provided
302 Found — the client is redirected to the output file location
204 No Content — the server acknowledges the request without further detail

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-hie-models | HIE Models: Centralized, Federated & Hybrid
HIE Architecture Models: Centralized, Federated, and Hybrid Approaches to Health Information Exchange
What Is Health Information Exchange?
Health information exchange (HIE) is the electronic mobilization of health care information across organizations within a region, community, or hospital system. The Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) defines HIE as the "electronic movement of health-related information among organizations according to nationally recognized standards." The purpose of HIE is simple but profound: when a patient is seen by any provider in a connected network, the relevant clinical history — diagnoses, medications, lab results, imaging, and care plans — should be available at the point of care, regardless of where it was originally created. Without HIE, clinicians too often make decisions without complete information, leading to duplicated tests, drug interactions, and preventable errors.
ONC recognizes three distinct forms of health information exchange. Directed exchange is the secure, point-to-point transmission of patient data from one known provider to another — the digital equivalent of a referral packet or discharge summary, transmitted via encrypted Direct Messaging rather than fax. Query-based exchange allows providers to search for and retrieve patient records from other providers on demand, which is especially valuable for unplanned or emergency care when the patient cannot provide a complete history. Consumer-mediated exchange gives patients themselves the ability to aggregate, control, and share their health information — for example, through a personal health record or a patient-facing app connected to their providers via FHIR APIs. Each mode addresses a different coordination scenario, and mature HIE ecosystems support all three simultaneously.
The scope of HIE in the United States is substantial. California alone has 15 HIEs, Texas has 12, and states like New York, New Jersey, and Pennsylvania each operate 8, reflecting a largely decentralized, market-driven pattern of exchange organization. Nationally, health information exchanges serve approximately 92 percent of the U.S. population, though coverage does not always translate to meaningful clinical use. HIE is foundational to population health management — enabling public health surveillance, care gap identification, and chronic disease registries — and to value-based care contracts that require providers to demonstrate coordinated, outcome-driven care. The shift from fee-for-service payment to value-based models has made HIE not merely convenient but economically essential for providers and payers alike.

Centralized HIE Architecture
In a centralized HIE architecture, participating organizations transmit copies of clinical documents to a shared, centrally managed repository — a Clinical Data Repository (CDR) — maintained by the HIE authority. Queries against this store are resolved locally within the repository, which means response times are fast and predictable. The HIE operator maintains a Master Patient Index (MPI) — a comprehensive registry that links every patient's demographic record across all contributing organizations to a single enterprise identifier. When a clinician queries the network, the MPI resolves the patient identity and the CDR returns the consolidated record. This architecture is particularly well-suited to regional networks where participants agree to cede data custody in exchange for a richer, continuously updated longitudinal record.
Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL), Vermont's designated statewide HIE, illustrates the real-world evolution of a centralized approach. Founded in 2005 as a public-private collaboration between the Vermont Association of Hospitals and Health Systems and state government, VITL has operated a central data infrastructure for Vermont's small but clinically complex population. Its strategic plan anticipates a hybrid data model blending a federated approach with a centralized repository for population health analytics. As of 2025, VITL is implementing a new, FHIR-native data repository as part of the state's broader vision for a Unified Health Data Space — a modern evolution that retains centralized analytical power while embracing open standards. Vermont's model demonstrates how small states can leverage centralization to build clinically rich, analytics-ready data assets that a purely federated network would struggle to assemble.
The governance complexity of centralized models is real and often underestimated. When patient data lives in a repository operated by a third-party HIE, critical questions arise: Who owns the data? Who can access it for secondary purposes such as research or quality reporting? What liability does the HIE bear if there is a breach? Centralized repositories also present a single point of failure — a successful cyberattack or catastrophic infrastructure failure could simultaneously disrupt access to records across every participating organization. These risks demand robust security controls, redundant infrastructure, and explicit legal agreements (often called data use and reciprocal support agreements, or DURSA) that define data rights, breach notification obligations, and permitted uses. Governance boards typically include representatives from member hospitals, payers, and patient advocates to balance competing interests over the shared repository.

Centralized vs. Federated: Core Trade-offs
Federated HIE Architecture
The federated model inverts the custody logic of centralization: clinical data remains within each participating organization's own systems, and the HIE provides only the connective tissue needed to locate and retrieve it on demand. The key infrastructure component is a Record Locator Service (RLS), sometimes called a patient index, which maintains a directory of where patient records exist — not the records themselves. When a clinician initiates a query, the RLS identifies which member organizations hold data for that patient, routes the query to those endpoints, and assembles the results into a coherent response. Because no copy of clinical content is stored centrally, participating organizations retain physical and legal control of their own data, making this model politically attractive in competitive markets where hospitals are reluctant to share data with a central authority that their rivals can also access.
CommonWell Health Alliance exemplifies the federated approach at national scale. Founded in 2013 by leading health IT vendors, CommonWell operates a vendor-neutral network in which data remains within the provider health IT systems where it was collected. CommonWell's core services include patient enrollment and identity management, record location (creating a virtual table of contents of where information about a patient exists across the network), and a query-and-retrieve capability that allows caregivers to pull needed data across trusted network members. The network covers more than 261 million unique individuals and has facilitated the exchange of more than 11 billion health care records since its founding. In February 2024, CommonWell was officially designated as a Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN) under TEFCA, validating its federated architecture as a backbone for the emerging national interoperability framework.
Federated architectures face two structural challenges that centralized designs avoid. First, query latency: because each query must be routed to multiple source systems, resolved, and assembled, response times depend on the slowest participating endpoint. A clinician in an emergency department waiting for records from three different health systems may find that one is temporarily offline, returning an incomplete picture. Second, data currency: federated queries retrieve records as they exist at the moment of the query, but there is no mechanism to proactively notify a care team when a patient's condition changes at another organization. This "pull only" model misses the event-driven use cases — such as an alert when a patient is admitted to an ED — that are increasingly important for care coordination and population health management. Emerging FHIR subscription mechanisms, discussed in Section 5, are beginning to address this gap within federated architectures.
A federated HIE works like a library catalog system: the catalog (the Record Locator Service) tells you which branch holds the book you need, but the book itself stays on the shelf at that branch until you request it. A centralized HIE is more like a single main library that collects copies of every book from every branch — faster to retrieve, but requiring trust that the main library will safeguard and return what was deposited.
Federated vs. Centralized HIE data custody
Hybrid Architecture and the Network-of-Networks Era
Most real-world HIEs today do not fit neatly into either the centralized or federated category. Instead, they combine elements of both: a central directory or MPI for identity resolution, a centralized repository for high-value analytical data sets (e.g., ADT alerts, lab results, and medication histories), and federated query for detailed clinical documents held at source systems. This hybrid approach attempts to capture the query speed and analytical richness of centralization without requiring every participating organization to surrender custody of its entire record set. Vermont's VITL, for instance, explicitly describes its architecture as a hybrid blending centralized repository capabilities with federated exchange for certain data types. As FHIR APIs proliferate, the boundary between centralized and federated is increasingly blurred: an organization can expose FHIR endpoints that make its data queryable in near-real-time while also contributing certain data sets to a shared analytical environment.
At the national level, the United States has embraced a network-of-networks model through two complementary frameworks: Carequality and TEFCA. Carequality, a 501(c)(3) nonprofit and the nation's most widely adopted interoperability framework, provides a common package of legal terms, policy requirements, technical specifications, and governance processes that any health information network can adopt. Once two networks both subscribe to Carequality's rules, they can exchange data without negotiating separate bilateral agreements — the framework acts as a mutual recognition treaty for clinical data. As of 2024, Carequality enables the flow of more than 1.2 billion clinical documents every month. The eHealth Exchange — originally launched as the federal Nationwide Health Information Network (NHIN) and rebranded in 2012 — is one of Carequality's largest members, facilitating secure exchange of records for more than 300 million patients and processing roughly 25 billion data exchanges annually. Its network reaches all 50 states, 75 percent of U.S. hospitals, and four federal agencies including the Department of Defense, Veterans Affairs, CMS, and the Social Security Administration.
TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — represents ONC's most ambitious attempt to establish a nationwide, government-backed exchange floor. Under TEFCA, networks apply to become Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs), entities that agree to meet a common set of technical and policy requirements and to exchange data with every other QHIN without additional negotiation. The first QHINs were designated in December 2023. By late 2025, eleven networks had achieved QHIN status: eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, Health Gorilla, Konza, MedAllies, Kno2, CommonWell Health Alliance, eClinicalWorks (designated January 2025), Oracle Health Information Network (designated November 2025), Surescripts, and Netsmart. The QHIN model is explicitly federated at the network level — no single QHIN stores all the data — but each QHIN may itself be centralized, federated, or hybrid internally. FHIR-based exchange within TEFCA was piloted in 2025, and beginning January 1, 2026, QHINs must adopt HL7 FAST security procedures for all FHIR transactions.
The requesting organization submits a query to its QHIN, identifying the patient by demographic data or a known identifier.

Sustainability, Governance, and the FHIR Transformation
Financial sustainability has been the Achilles' heel of health information exchange since the earliest community HIE experiments of the 1990s. Research consistently shows that only about 46 percent of operational HIEs can cover their operating costs with revenue from participants; among HIEs still in the planning stage, that figure drops to 36 percent. The core economic problem is a misalignment between who bears the cost of enabling exchange and who captures the benefit. A hospital that invests in HIE connectivity incurs real infrastructure and staffing costs, but many of the savings — avoided duplicate imaging, reduced readmissions, better-coordinated post-acute care — accrue to payers and to the health system as a whole rather than to the investing provider. Assessment fees have historically been the largest single revenue source for HIEs, followed by membership or subscription fees and state or federal grants. Continued dependence on grant funding, however, is widely recognized as a marker of poor long-term sustainability potential.
Governance structures shape both HIE sustainability and the quality of the data they produce. The dominant model is the private nonprofit, governed by a board representing member organizations — hospitals, physician groups, payers, and sometimes consumer advocates. Some scholars and policymakers have argued for treating HIE infrastructure as a public utility — regulated, mandated, and funded through a combination of government appropriations and assessed fees, much like the electrical grid or the public water system. Vermont's VITL approaches this model: it was created by legislative action, receives state funding, and operates as a designated statewide HIE with explicit public responsibilities. The public-utility framing aligns incentives better than a purely voluntary market model, but it requires sustained political will and a state government willing to backstop the HIE's operating costs through economic downturns and leadership transitions.
FHIR — HL7's Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources standard — is fundamentally reshaping HIE architecture. Mandated as the baseline requirement under the 21st Century Cures Act and ONC's interoperability regulations, FHIR R4 exposes clinical data via RESTful APIs that any application can query using standard web technologies. This democratizes access to health data, allowing new entrants — patient-facing apps, analytics platforms, care coordination tools — to participate in HIE without traditional integration engines or point-to-point interfaces. More significantly, FHIR R5 introduced topic-based subscriptions that enable event-driven exchange: rather than pulling records on demand, a care team can subscribe to receive a notification the moment a patient is admitted to another facility, discharged, or has a critical lab result. This event-driven capability bridges the most important gap in federated architectures and points toward a future where HIE is less about routing documents and more about delivering timely, actionable signals to the right person at the right moment. The 2025 State of FHIR survey by HL7 International and Firely, with respondents from 57 countries, found that 71 percent reported FHIR already in use for at least a few use cases in their country, and that FHIR is mandated or recommended in 73 percent of countries with health data regulation.
HIEs that rely primarily on grant funding rather than participant-generated revenue are at elevated risk of closure when grant cycles end. When evaluating an HIE's long-term viability, look for diversified revenue (membership fees, transaction fees, analytics services) and evidence that participating organizations view the HIE as operationally essential rather than optionally convenient.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-vermont-vitl | Vermont's HIE: VITL and the Vermont Health Information Network
Vermont's Health Information Exchange: VITL and the All-Payer Claims Database
Vermont is a small state — fewer than 650,000 residents spread across rugged, rural terrain. Yet Vermont has built one of the most mature statewide health information exchange ecosystems in the United States, connecting nearly every hospital, most health centers, and hundreds of independent practices into a single, governed data network. At the center of that network sits Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL), a nonprofit designated by state law to operate the Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE). Alongside it, the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB) administers VHCURES — Vermont's All-Payer Claims Database — providing a complementary financial lens on how care is delivered and paid for across the state. Together, VITL and VHCURES form the twin pillars of Vermont's interoperability architecture, demonstrating both the promise and the hard-won lessons of state-led health IT.
This lesson traces Vermont's journey: the legislative mandate that created VITL, the clinical and administrative services the VHIE provides, the population-level power of claims data, the integrations that tie it all together through the Blueprint for Health, and the challenges that remain — from rural connectivity gaps to questions of long-term funding sustainability.
VITL: A Legislative Mandate for Statewide Connectivity
VITL was founded in 2005 as a private, nonprofit organization charged with advancing health care delivery and reform in Vermont through the aggregation and exchange of health information. Vermont's legislature subsequently codified VITL's role through Act 107 of 2006, formally designating it as the exclusive operator of the statewide health information exchange network. This legislative backstop was critical: unlike many states where HIE efforts fragmented into competing regional networks, Vermont's approach created a single, authoritative exchange from the start.
Under Vermont statute (18 V.S.A. Chapter 219), VITL is required to be named in the state's Health Information Technology Plan as the operator of the statewide HIE network. The statute also mandates that privacy standards applied on the network be no less stringent than those required under HIPAA. This statutory foundation gave VITL both legitimacy and accountability — participating organizations knew they were connecting to a legally recognized, regulated infrastructure rather than a voluntary pilot project.
Key framing: VITL's mission is to securely aggregate, standardize, and share the data needed to improve the effectiveness of healthcare for Vermonters. Its vision is to be a leader in collaboratively delivering actionable data that leads to better health.
For its first decade, VITL focused primarily on building connectivity — signing up hospitals, health centers, and physician practices, and standing up the core technical infrastructure. The Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB), established by Act 48 of 2011, was later given oversight authority over VITL's budget and strategic plan, ensuring that VITL's priorities remained aligned with Vermont's broader health care reform goals. However, as of July 1, 2025 — through Act 62 of 2025 — responsibility for the Health IT Plan and VITL oversight was formally moved away from the GMCB as Vermont reorganized its health system governance.

What the Vermont Health Information Exchange Actually Does
The Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE) is a secure, statewide data network that enables health care providers, ACOs, and other approved users to electronically exchange and access medical records. Far from a passive data warehouse, the VHIE delivers a suite of active services that change how care is coordinated across Vermont.
VITLAccess: The Clinical Portal
VITLAccess is VITL's web-based clinical portal — the primary interface through which authorized clinicians and care coordinators access patient data. Rebuilt in spring 2022 with a significantly improved user interface, VITLAccess provides a longitudinal, consolidated health record drawing from all contributing organizations. A clinician seeing a patient in a rural emergency department at 2 a.m. can pull up that patient's medication list, allergy history, recent lab results, imaging reports, and care plans — all from a single screen, even if the data originated from a hospital on the other side of the state.
The 2022 redesign added several critical capabilities: immunization data drawn from the Vermont Immunization Registry and hospital systems, improved patient-matching algorithms to reduce duplicate records and ensure comprehensive record assembly, and the ability to print or download multiple results or documents simultaneously. These improvements reflected lessons from clinician feedback about the original portal and represent the iterative, user-centered design approach VITL has pursued.
Core Data Services
Beyond the portal itself, the VHIE supports several distinct data service categories. Clinical document exchange allows participating organizations to push and pull structured clinical documents such as Continuity of Care Documents (CCDs) generated at the point of care. Medication history aggregation draws from pharmacies connected to the network, giving prescribers visibility into what a patient has actually filled — not just what was prescribed in their own system. Lab results delivery routes results from connected laboratories back to ordering providers. And care alerts notify care coordinators when patients experience significant clinical events such as emergency department visits or hospitalizations, enabling timely follow-up.
A patient with diabetes managed by a primary care practice in Rutland is admitted to a hospital in Burlington following a hypoglycemic episode. The VHIE immediately gives the Burlington ED clinicians access to the patient's full medication list — including insulin dosing — their most recent HbA1c, and the care plan from their endocrinologist. When the patient is discharged, a care alert flows back to the Rutland practice, triggering a follow-up call within 48 hours. No fax machine, no phone tag — just connected systems.
Example
VITL has also progressively expanded the scope of data flowing through the VHIE. Under Beth Anderson's leadership as CEO (2019-2025), the exchange broadened participation to include pharmacies, clinical laboratories, behavioral health providers, and ambulance services. This expansion was not merely additive — it addressed longstanding gaps where patients' behavioral health and substance use treatment records were invisible to the acute care system, creating dangerous information asymmetries at critical moments.

VHCURES: Vermont's All-Payer Claims Database
Where the VHIE captures the clinical story of a patient's care, VHCURES — Vermont's Health Care Uniform Reporting and Evaluation System — captures the financial story. VHCURES is Vermont's All-Payer Claims Database (APCD), maintained and managed by the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB). It is one of the most comprehensive claims datasets in the country, and it plays a central role in Vermont's ability to understand, evaluate, and regulate its health care system.
VHCURES receives medical and pharmacy claims data from three payer categories: commercial health insurers (including third-party administrators and pharmacy benefit managers), Vermont Medicaid, and Medicare. Any insurer serving 200 or more Vermont resident members is required to submit data to VHCURES. The database contains eligibility information — whether a patient is covered — as well as the full claims record of services delivered and payments made.

VHCURES is a powerful analytical tool precisely because it crosses payer boundaries. A researcher studying opioid prescribing patterns, a policymaker evaluating hospital pricing, or a health plan benchmarking its network performance can all draw on VHCURES to understand Vermont's health care system in ways that no single payer's data could support. The GMCB uses VHCURES as a core input for its hospital budget review process, its analysis of health care spending growth, and its assessment of the All-Payer ACO Model's impact on Vermont's cost trajectory.
Data from VHCURES is released in two formats: a Public Use File, which is de-identified and available for broad research use, and a Limited Use Dataset, which contains more granular information and is available to qualified researchers under data use agreements with privacy protections. The GMCB's APCD Snapshot tool provides publicly accessible metadata about what is in VHCURES — which health plans are contributing, the highest-volume procedures in the state, and how the dataset has evolved over time — giving policymakers and the public a window into the data without requiring full data access.
Critical distinction: VHCURES (claims data) and the VHIE (clinical data) are complementary but separate systems. Claims data tells you what was billed and paid. Clinical data tells you what actually happened at the point of care. Vermont is one of a handful of states actively working to link these two data streams to build a more complete picture of health and care delivery.
The Blueprint for Health: Where VITL Data Drives Reform
Vermont's Blueprint for Health is a statewide quality improvement program that has, since its expansion in the late 2000s, worked to transform primary care delivery across the state. It is one of the most long-running and closely studied multi-payer primary care reform efforts in the United States. And it could not function at scale without VITL.
Practices participating in the Blueprint for Health are required to sign agreements with VITL and connect their EHR systems to the VHIE. This connectivity serves two core purposes: care coordination at the individual patient level (through VITLAccess), and population-level outcomes measurement through the state's clinical data registry. The registry aggregates clinical data from participating practices and makes it available for quality reporting — allowing the state to track metrics like diabetes control rates, blood pressure management, and preventive care delivery across its entire primary care network.
VITL also shares data with other key reform initiatives. OneCare Vermont — the state's All-Payer ACO until the model ended and OneCare wound down at the end of 2025 — used VHIE data to support care management for its attributed population. The Vermont Department of Health connects to VITL for public health reporting, including immunization registries, disease surveillance, and population health monitoring. This web of data-sharing agreements, each governed by formal legal agreements and privacy protections, is what transforms a simple health information exchange into a reform infrastructure.
Think of Vermont's health data ecosystem as a utility grid: VITL is the transmission network that moves power (data) from generators (EHRs, pharmacies, labs) to consumers (clinicians, care coordinators, public health agencies). VHCURES is the billing meter that tracks how much power was consumed and what it cost. The Blueprint for Health is the efficiency program that uses both the transmission data and the billing data to reduce waste and improve outcomes. None of these pieces works as well without the others.
