Persistent Challenges: Rural Connectivity, Small Practices, and Sustainability
Vermont's health information exchange achievements are real and significant, but so are the headwinds VITL and its partners face. Three challenges stand out as particularly structural: rural broadband limitations, the burden on small practices, and long-term funding sustainability.
Rural Broadband: Infrastructure Before Interoperability
Vermont is one of the most rural states in the country — approximately 93% of its land area is classified as rural, and thousands of residents live in areas with no reliable broadband access. Vermont's own 2021 telecommunications planning documents identified 51,000 homes and businesses as unserved or underserved, with limited private-market incentive to extend service to those locations. For health IT, this is a foundational barrier: an EHR cannot connect to the VHIE if the practice does not have reliable internet. Telehealth cannot substitute for in-person care if patients cannot maintain a stable video connection.
Vermont has pursued state and federal funding to address this gap. However, in 2025, federal cancellation of Vermont's $5.3 million Digital Equity Grant — funding intended to support broadband expansion and digital literacy — underscored the fragility of relying on federal dollars for infrastructure that is foundational to the state's health reform strategy.
Small rural practices — often a single physician or a small group — face the steepest interoperability challenges. They may lack the IT staff to manage an EHR, the bandwidth to use the VHIE reliably, or the financial resources to absorb interface build costs. Vermont's HIE is comprehensive in coverage, but coverage statistics must be read with an eye toward which practices are connected versus which remain on the margins.
Watch Out
Funding Sustainability
VITL's funding has historically depended on a combination of state appropriations, federal grants, and fees from participating organizations. Research into VITL's early development identified funding sustainability as a persistent challenge: stakeholders recognized the need for a sustainable business model but had not yet resolved it, with interviewees concluding that some form of ongoing public-private partnership would be the only viable long-term approach. That tension has not fully resolved. Federal health IT funding has fluctuated, and the political environment around health IT investment continues to shift.
TEFCA and National Connectivity: Protective Trade-offs
As TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — has grown into a national interoperability framework, with over 9,200 organizations signed up across 10 Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) as of early 2026, Vermont has moved carefully. Vermont enacted shield laws protecting reproductive health data and gender-affirming care data, and state officials have noted that participating in national data-sharing at the TEFCA level makes it difficult to guarantee those protections will be honored when data crosses state lines. Vermont is actively exploring what TEFCA participation might look like while maintaining its protective legal framework — a real tension between connectivity and privacy that other states with similar laws will increasingly face.
With Randy Farmer — previously chief operating officer of the Delaware Health Information Network — in place as president and CEO since December 2025, following Beth Anderson's departure in July 2025, VITL stands at a pivotal inflection point between its foundational work connecting Vermont's providers and the next phase of contributing to national interoperability.
Lessons for the Broader Interoperability Field
Vermont's approach offers several lessons that have influenced thinking about HIE design nationally. First, legislative designation matters. By naming VITL as the exclusive statewide network operator in statute, Vermont avoided the fragmentation that plagued many states that allowed multiple competing HIEs to develop in parallel. A single, authoritative, governed network is structurally more efficient for building participation than a competitive marketplace where providers must choose which network to join.
Second, the combination of clinical data (VHIE) and claims data (VHCURES) under coordinated state oversight creates analytical power that neither dataset alone provides. Vermont policymakers can examine not just what care was delivered but whether that care aligned with clinical guidelines, whether it was delivered efficiently, and whether it produced outcomes that justify its cost. This dual-lens approach is increasingly recognized as the gold standard for health system evaluation.
Third, embedding HIE participation as a requirement — rather than an option — for participating in reform programs like the Blueprint for Health creates a natural on-ramp that ties financial incentives to connectivity. Practices that want the enhanced payments that come with Blueprint participation must connect to VITL. This approach produced broad participation in a small, rural state that might otherwise have struggled to achieve critical mass.
Vermont is a proof point that a small state with the right legislative framework, a nonprofit operator with a clear mandate, and persistent integration with reform programs can build health information exchange infrastructure that serves nearly an entire state's population.
At the same time, Vermont's experience underscores the limits of what an HIE alone can accomplish. Data flows through VITL only because organizations have connected — and connecting requires broadband, EHR systems, staff capacity, and funding. The hardest-to-reach patients and providers are also the hardest to connect to the network. Vermont's next chapter in interoperability will likely depend as much on solving broadband access and small-practice IT support as it does on any technical advances in data standards or exchange protocols.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-query-vs-event | Query-Based vs. Event-Driven Exchange
Query vs. Event-Based Exchange: Choosing the Right Interoperability Pattern
The Two Fundamental Patterns of Health Data Exchange
Every interoperability transaction in U.S. healthcare ultimately reduces to one of two architectural patterns: a system asks for data it needs right now (query-based, or pull), or a system automatically sends data when something clinically significant happens (event-based, or push). These are not competing standards — they are complementary strategies, each built for a different workflow need. Understanding when to reach for each pattern is one of the most important practical skills in health IT.
Query-based exchange assumes that the receiver knows they need data and knows roughly when to ask for it. A primary care physician opening a patient chart before an annual wellness visit might query a health information network to retrieve recent specialist notes, lab results, or medication lists from other institutions. The request is deliberate, human-initiated, and tied to a moment of care. The network responds with whatever it can locate, and the clinician reviews the results. This model works well for planned encounters and scheduled workflows.
Event-based exchange, by contrast, assumes that something has already happened — a patient was admitted to the emergency department, a lab value crossed a critical threshold, a prescription was filled — and that the receiving party needs to know about it immediately, without waiting to be asked. The originating system pushes a notification or full message to one or more recipients who have subscribed to that type of event. The receiver does not need to poll or remember to check; the information arrives in their workflow automatically. This model is essential for care transitions, population health monitoring, and time-sensitive clinical alerts.
Think of query-based exchange like a library: you walk in when you need a book and search the catalog yourself. Event-based exchange is like a subscription service: the moment the next issue is published, it lands in your mailbox — you never had to ask.
Library vs. subscription service as a metaphor for pull vs. push data exchange
Query-Based (Pull)
Receiver initiates the request
Triggered by a scheduled or ad-hoc care need
Well-suited for pre-visit chart prep
Latency acceptable — seconds to minutes
Receiver must know a record may exist elsewhere
Examples: FHIR RESTful GET, XCA document query
Event-Based (Push)
Sender initiates the message without a request
Triggered by a clinical event (admit, discharge, lab)
Well-suited for care transitions and alerts
Latency must be near-real-time — seconds
Receiver does not need to know to look for data
Examples: HL7 v2 ADT, FHIR Subscription, Direct
Query-Based vs. Event-Based Exchange at a Glance
Query-Based Exchange: FHIR, CommonWell, and Carequality
Query-based exchange is the backbone of the two largest U.S. health information networks: CommonWell Health Alliance and Carequality. Both networks enable participating providers to locate and retrieve patient records from other members, regardless of which EHR vendor they use. CommonWell leverages IHE standards — including PIX for patient identity matching, XCA for cross-community document retrieval, and XDS.b for document registration — as well as modern FHIR-based interfaces such as the IHE MHD profile. Carequality overlays governance and legal reciprocity on top of the same technical substrate, enabling providers on CommonWell to exchange with providers on other frameworks such as Epic's CareEverywhere and eHealth Exchange.
The FHIR RESTful model has transformed query-based exchange by making individual clinical data elements — not just documents — retrievable on demand. A FHIR R4 server exposes standardized endpoints such as GET /Patient, GET /Condition, GET /MedicationRequest, and GET /Observation. A requesting system authenticates via SMART on FHIR, presents a patient identifier, and the server returns a JSON bundle containing only the data elements requested. This granularity is a significant upgrade from CDA-based document exchange, where a 200-page continuity of care document might be returned when all a clinician needed was the current medication list.
CommonWell has been investing in transitioning its network toward discrete FHIR resource exchange. Its Record Locator Service (RLS) enables a querying system to discover where a given patient's records reside across member organizations, then retrieve specific FHIR resources such as labs, medications, and allergies — in addition to traditional documents. This combination of a centralized patient identity index and distributed FHIR data retrieval is the emerging architecture for national-scale query-based exchange.
The querying system submits patient demographics to a Master Patient Index or Record Locator Service to find matching identifiers at other organizations. CommonWell uses IHE PIX; TEFCA-aligned networks use the TEFCA Common Agreement patient matching requirements.
Patient Identity Resolution
The network returns the FHIR endpoint URLs of organizations that hold records for the identified patient. The querying system now knows where to look.
Endpoint Discovery
The querying system authenticates to each remote server, typically via SMART on FHIR OAuth 2.0, presenting patient context and purpose-of-use.
Authorization
The querying system sends one or more RESTful GET requests — for example, GET /Condition?patient=<id>&category=problem-list-item — to retrieve targeted clinical data. The server responds with a FHIR Bundle.
FHIR GET Request
The returned resources are surfaced in the clinician's EHR, reconciled with the local record, and incorporated into the care plan.
Clinical Review
How a FHIR Query-Based Exchange Works
TEFCA, which went live in December 2023 and had seven designated Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) by February 2024, is built primarily around query-based document exchange. By mid-2025 participants could also run FHIR-based queries through TEFCA-trusted FHIR APIs, with QHIN-to-QHIN FHIR exchange the roadmap's next phase of network evolution from document retrieval toward discrete resource query.
Event-Based Exchange: HL7 v2 ADT, FHIR Subscriptions, and Direct
Event-based exchange has been part of health IT since the earliest days of HL7. HL7 version 2 (v2), first released in 1988 and still running on the majority of hospital interfaces worldwide, is fundamentally an event-driven messaging standard. When something happens in a clinical system — a patient is registered, transferred, or discharged — the system generates a v2 message and pushes it to every downstream system that needs to know. The most common v2 message type for this purpose is the ADT (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) message. ADT A01 signals an admission; ADT A02 signals an intra-facility transfer; ADT A03 signals a discharge. These three message types, along with ADT A04 (registration) and ADT A08 (patient information update), handle the vast majority of care transition notifications in U.S. hospitals today.
The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (85 FR 25510), finalized in May 2020 and effective April 30, 2021, codified event-based exchange as a federal Condition of Participation. Under 42 CFR 482.24(d), Medicare and Medicaid participating hospitals, psychiatric hospitals, and critical access hospitals (CAHs) that use an EHR must send electronic patient event notifications upon admission, discharge, and transfer to the patient's established primary care practitioner, the patient's established care team, and post-acute care providers with whom the patient has an established relationship. The rule permits hospitals to transmit notifications using HL7 v2 ADT messages, C-CDA summary care records, or FHIR-based APIs, giving flexibility while mandating the workflow.
CMS required hospitals to send ADT event notifications by April 30, 2021. This mandate made event-based exchange a federal compliance requirement for every Medicare- and Medicaid-participating inpatient facility in the country — not just a best practice.
On the modern FHIR side, the R4 Subscription resource introduced a mechanism for clients to register interest in data changes on a FHIR server. However, the original R4 Subscription model — based on criteria strings evaluated against the server's data set — proved difficult to implement consistently across vendors. The FHIR community responded with a significant redesign in R5, introducing SubscriptionTopic resources that define specific event types (such as "patient admitted" or "lab result critical") as canonical, versioned artifacts. Because FHIR R4 remains the dominant version in production systems, HL7 published the Subscriptions R5 Backport Implementation Guide (version 1.2.0-ballot) to extend topic-based subscription semantics to R4 and R4B servers through extensions and profiles, without requiring a full upgrade.
The HL7 Da Vinci Project's Unsolicited Notifications Implementation Guide (version 1.1.0, published April 2025) builds directly on the R5 backport to define a standardized FHIR messaging framework for Admit, Discharge, and Transfer notifications. The Da Vinci Alerts IG specifies FHIR MessageBundle structures for each event type, defines required profiles such as the ADT Notification Condition and ADT Notification Coverage, and describes the roles of Sender, Intermediary (such as an HIE), and Recipient. An intermediary can receive a notification from a hospital and forward it to multiple downstream recipients — PCPs, care managers, post-acute facilities — using a single standardized pipeline.
A 72-year-old Medicare patient with congestive heart failure presents to an emergency department not affiliated with her primary care practice. The hospital's EHR fires an HL7 v2 ADT A04 (registration) message to its HIE interface engine within seconds of registration. The HIE translates the message to a FHIR MessageBundle conformant with the Da Vinci Alerts IG and routes it to the patient's PCP practice via the practice's care management platform. The care manager sees the alert within three minutes of the patient's arrival, reaches out to the ER care team to share the patient's active medication list and recent echocardiogram, and schedules a transitional care management visit before the patient is discharged. The PCP practice bills a TCM code 99496 — a reimbursable workflow that would not have been triggered without the real-time notification.

Direct Messaging: Secure Push for Care Coordination
Direct Secure Messaging — often called simply "Direct" — is a push-based interoperability standard built on S/MIME-encrypted email over SMTP, governed by the DirectTrust network of accredited Health Information Service Providers (HISPs). Every certified EHR in the United States must support Direct as a condition of ONC certification. Unlike HL7 ADT, which sends structured event messages to known endpoints registered in an interface engine, Direct allows any credentialed provider to push a C-CDA summary document to any other credentialed provider using a Direct address that looks like a standard email address (provider@hospital.directaddress.net).
Direct is most commonly used for care transition summaries — the transition of care (ToC) and referral documents sent when a patient moves from a hospital to a skilled nursing facility, from a specialist back to a primary care physician, or from one care setting to another. Meaningful Use Stage 2 required providers to electronically transmit a C-CDA summary of care for more than 10% of transitions and referrals, and Direct became the most common way to do it.
Direct has real limitations: it carries documents, not discrete data elements, and support for its delivery-confirmation messages (MDNs) is uneven across HISPs. Nevertheless, Direct remains widely deployed and relevant, particularly for referral workflows, transition of care summaries, and secure communication between clinicians at different organizations. In many markets, a single patient discharge triggers both a Direct C-CDA push to the receiving facility's Direct address and an HL7 ADT push to the PCP's care management platform — both event-based mechanisms, but serving different receivers and different purposes.
Direct Messaging is frequently confused with FHIR-based exchange. Direct is an encrypted email protocol that carries C-CDA XML documents. FHIR is a RESTful API standard for structured data resources. They address different problems: Direct delivers a complete clinical summary to a known recipient; FHIR APIs expose queryable, structured data to authorized applications. Modern interoperability strategies often deploy both.
Common Misconception: Direct Is Not FHIR
Choosing the Right Pattern: A Decision Framework
Selecting between query-based and event-based exchange is not an either/or decision — most mature interoperability architectures deploy both. The choice of which pattern to use for a given workflow depends on four key variables: the urgency of the information, whether a care event has already occurred, whether the receiver knows to look for data, and the technical capabilities of both the sending and receiving systems.
When urgency is high and a care transition has just occurred — an admission, a discharge, a transfer, a critical lab result — event-based push is almost always the right answer. Waiting for a clinician to manually query for a record that may not yet be associated with the patient in a network index introduces exactly the delay that causes preventable readmissions and medication errors. The receiver needs to know something happened before they know to ask.
When the receiver is initiating a scheduled care encounter and wants to assemble the most complete picture of a patient's history before the visit — annual wellness, specialist consultation, post-acute admission assessment — query-based exchange is more appropriate. The clinician can pull records from multiple institutions, reconcile them against the local record, and use the consolidated view to inform care planning. FHIR RESTful queries through networks like CommonWell/Carequality or TEFCA are well-suited to this use case.
A growing class of workflows benefits from combining both patterns. Payers and care management organizations, for example, may subscribe to ADT event notifications to learn when a member is admitted to any facility in the network. Upon receiving that event, they automatically trigger a FHIR query against the admitting hospital to retrieve the patient's current problem list, active medications, and recent labs — enabling a care manager to contact the patient within hours of admission with a complete clinical picture. This event-triggered query pattern is increasingly common in value-based care programs and is explicitly supported by the Da Vinci Project's broader suite of implementation guides.
Reach for Event-Based (Push) When…
A care transition just occurred (admit, discharge, transfer)
Time to notification is measured in minutes, not hours
The receiver doesn't know to look for the data
You need to trigger a downstream workflow automatically
Regulatory compliance (CMS ADT CoP) is required
Monitoring a patient population for status changes
Reach for Query-Based (Pull) When…
A scheduled care encounter is upcoming
The clinician needs a complete longitudinal record
Latency of seconds to minutes is acceptable
The receiver knows the patient may have records elsewhere
Pre-visit chart prep or care plan reconciliation
A specific data element (e.g., last A1C) is needed on demand
When to Use Each Pattern
TEFCA and the Evolving Landscape
TEFCA's Common Agreement governs both query-based document exchange and message-based (push) exchange across QHINs. The initial TEFCA launch in 2024 focused on query-based document retrieval — enabling providers to locate and retrieve C-CDA documents across all participating QHINs through a single governance framework. FHIR-based query through TEFCA-trusted FHIR APIs became available by mid-2025; QHIN-to-QHIN FHIR exchange, enabling discrete resource queries at national scale, is the next phase of ONC's FHIR roadmap for TEFCA. As TEFCA matures, both query and event-based exchange are expected to be available as first-class exchange modalities within the national network.
An accountable care organization (ACO) managing 15,000 Medicare beneficiaries subscribes to ADT feeds from every hospital within a 50-mile radius. When an attributed patient is admitted, the ACO's care management platform receives an ADT A01 notification within minutes. The platform automatically fires a series of FHIR GET requests — Condition, MedicationRequest, AllergyIntolerance, Observation (recent labs) — against the hospital's FHIR R4 endpoint. The care manager reviewing the case sees a consolidated view of the admission diagnosis, current medications, and active conditions in a single screen, without any manual chart pulling. The ACO's analytics layer simultaneously flags whether the admission was potentially avoidable, feeding quality improvement workflows.
Event-Triggered Query in Value-Based Care
Implementation Considerations and Common Pitfalls
Organizations implementing event-based exchange must solve three technical problems that do not arise in query-based workflows: endpoint management, duplicate notification handling, and patient matching at speed. In a query model, the querying system controls the request and has time to resolve patient identity before retrieving data. In an event-based model, notifications arrive asynchronously and may reference patients using identifiers unfamiliar to the receiving system. A robust ADT notification receiver must be able to match incoming notifications to local patients in near-real time, handle duplicate ADTs for the same event (common in production environments), and route notifications to the correct care team member without manual intervention.
On the sending side, hospitals deploying ADT notifications under the CMS Conditions of Participation must maintain accurate, current lists of the patients' established care providers and their electronic endpoints. A notification sent to an outdated Direct address or decommissioned HL7 endpoint meets the letter of the rule but fails to achieve its clinical purpose. Several intermediaries — HIEs, notification networks such as Bamboo Health (formerly PatientPing) and CarePort (part of WellSky), and interface-engine vendors such as Rhapsody — provide ADT notification routing services that maintain endpoint directories and handle delivery confirmation on behalf of hospitals.
FHIR Subscription implementations face their own challenges. The original R4 Subscription model required servers to evaluate arbitrary criteria strings — essentially running live queries — for every data change across the entire resource set, creating significant performance burdens. The topic-based model in R5 and the backport IG shifts this burden from runtime query evaluation to compile-time topic definition: a SubscriptionTopic is a canonical resource that defines exactly which events trigger notifications, reducing server overhead and enabling vendors to optimize notification pipelines. Implementers adopting the Da Vinci Alerts IG should verify that their FHIR server vendor supports the R5 backport SubscriptionTopic extensions before committing to this pattern.
Event-based exchange, if poorly scoped, can overwhelm care teams with notifications. ADT alerts for every patient encounter — regardless of attribution, care relationship, or clinical urgency — rapidly become noise that clinicians learn to ignore. Effective implementations filter notifications by panel membership, risk score, or care program enrollment, and route alerts to the appropriate team member rather than broadcasting to everyone.
Alert Fatigue Is a Real Risk
Query-based exchange (pull) is initiated by the receiver and best suited for planned encounters, pre-visit chart prep, and longitudinal record assembly; FHIR RESTful APIs and networks like CommonWell/Carequality are the primary mechanisms.
Event-based exchange (push) is initiated by the sender when a clinical event occurs and is essential for care transitions, real-time alerts, and population health monitoring — the receiver does not need to know to ask.
HL7 v2 ADT messages remain the dominant event-based mechanism in U.S. hospitals; ADT A01, A02, A03, and A04 cover the vast majority of care transition notifications.
The CMS Interoperability Final Rule (effective April 30, 2021) mandated that Medicare/Medicaid hospitals send electronic ADT notifications to PCPs and post-acute providers upon admission, discharge, and transfer.
FHIR Subscriptions, and specifically the Da Vinci Unsolicited Notifications IG (v1.1.0), provide a modern, standardized FHIR messaging framework for ADT-type events that integrates with the R5 Subscriptions Backport IG.
Direct Secure Messaging is a widely deployed push mechanism for care transition summary documents (C-CDA) but carries documents — not discrete FHIR resources — and is complementary to, not a replacement for, ADT notifications.
Event-triggered query — subscribing to ADT events and then automatically firing FHIR GET requests for discrete data — is the emerging pattern for value-based care and ACO care management workflows.
Alert fatigue is a real implementation risk; effective event-based exchange requires filtering by panel membership, risk stratification, and intelligent routing to prevent notification overload.
Event-based ADT notification is the correct answer because the practice needs to be informed of the admission event in real time — without having to proactively query or wait until discharge. Query-based exchange requires the practice to know when and where to ask; Direct messaging occurs at discharge, too late for proactive transitional care management outreach. The ADT push model is exactly what the CMS ADT Conditions of Participation was designed to mandate and support.
Query-based FHIR exchange, where the practice queries hospital FHIR servers each morning for new admissions from the prior 24 hours.
Event-based ADT notification, where the hospital pushes an admission notification to the practice's care management platform in real time upon patient registration.
Direct Secure Messaging, where the hospital sends a C-CDA care summary document to the practice's Direct address at the time of discharge.
TEFCA query-based document exchange, where the practice retrieves continuity of care documents from all regional hospitals weekly.
A primary care practice wants to be notified within minutes whenever one of their attributed patients is admitted to any hospital in the region, so they can proactively reach out and schedule a transitional care management visit. Which interoperability pattern is best suited for this workflow?

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-consent-models | Consent Models: Opt-In, Opt-Out & Granular Consent
Consent Models in Health Information Exchange: Opt-In, Opt-Out, and Everything In Between
The Consent Baseline: What HIPAA Allows Without Patient Authorization
Before examining consent models in health information exchange (HIE), it is essential to understand what the law already permits without any patient signature. The HIPAA Privacy Rule, codified at 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164, establishes a baseline under which covered entities — hospitals, physicians, health plans, and their business associates — may use and disclose protected health information (PHI) without obtaining patient consent or authorization for three overarching categories: Treatment, Payment, and Health Care Operations, collectively known as TPO. These exceptions are not loopholes; they are deliberate design choices reflecting Congress's intent to allow the healthcare system to function efficiently while still protecting sensitive data from non-clinical misuse.
Under the Treatment exception, a primary care physician can share a patient's medication history with a referring cardiologist without asking the patient to sign anything first. Under the Payment exception, a hospital can send a patient's diagnosis codes and procedure records to a payer for claim adjudication. Under Health Care Operations, a hospital quality team can review records to evaluate outcomes without triggering authorization requirements. The minimum-necessary standard still applies to Payment and Operations disclosures — meaning only the PHI reasonably necessary to accomplish the purpose should be shared — but Treatment disclosures carry no such restriction, recognizing that a treating clinician may need the full clinical picture.
This federal floor does not stop states from enacting stronger protections. Many states have enacted "super-HIPAA" statutes that require explicit written consent even for some TPO disclosures, particularly for mental health records, HIV/AIDS status, genetic information, and reproductive health data. Vermont, for instance, imposes strict confidentiality requirements on HIV-related records beyond what HIPAA mandates. Other states layer extra protections onto mental health records. These state variations create a patchwork that HIE operators must navigate carefully: a network spanning multiple states must honor the most restrictive applicable law, which often means building consent workflows even when HIPAA alone would not require them.
Treatment, Payment, and Health Care Operations — all permissible without patient authorization under HIPAA
TPO Categories

Key principle: HIPAA is a floor, not a ceiling. States may — and frequently do — require stronger patient protections. HIE networks operating across state lines must determine which jurisdiction's law governs each disclosure and build their consent architecture accordingly.
Opt-In vs. Opt-Out: Definitions, Trade-offs, and State Variation
The central policy question for any HIE is whether patient data flows into the network by default — with patients able to withdraw — or only after patients affirmatively agree to participate. These two approaches, opt-out and opt-in respectively, represent fundamentally different theories of patient autonomy and administrative practicality. In an opt-out model, patients are enrolled automatically and must actively contact the HIE or their provider to restrict sharing. In an opt-in model, the patient must affirmatively sign a consent form before any records are accessible through the network. Each model carries meaningful trade-offs for data completeness, care coordination, and administrative burden.
Research published in the American Journal of Managed Care found that hospitals located in states with opt-in consent policies were 7.8 percentage points more likely than hospitals in opt-out states to report regulatory barriers to health information exchange. This gap illustrates the operational weight of opt-in consent: providers must manage consent tracking for every patient, consent forms expire, patients move, and the administrative cost compounds across millions of encounters. By contrast, opt-out models produce more complete network data because the default is inclusion. The trade-off is that patients who never read the enrollment notice may not realize their records are being shared, raising autonomy concerns — particularly among historically marginalized communities with legitimate reasons to distrust data sharing.
State policies vary considerably. New York uses a consent-to-access model through its Statewide Health Information Network (SHIN-NY) in which patients must sign a consent form for each provider who wishes to access their records — giving patients granular control but creating administrative complexity. California does not have a statewide statutory mandate, but most California HIE organizations have implemented opt-out mechanisms that allow data sharing by default while honoring patient withdrawal requests. Texas legislation frames HIE participation as "voluntary," placing it outside a strict opt-in or opt-out classification. Beyond binary models, some HIEs have moved toward granular consent, where patients can say yes to sharing their diabetes records but no to sharing their mental health records — a more patient-centered approach that requires significantly more sophisticated technical infrastructure.
Opt-In (Explicit Consent)
Patient must actively agree before records flow into HIE

Incomplete network data if enrollment rates are low
Higher administrative burden: consent tracking, renewal, revocation

Opt-In vs. Opt-Out: Core Trade-offs
Some HIEs now offer patients a tiered consent menu rather than a single on/off switch. A patient might permit their primary care records and lab results to be shared broadly, while restricting mental health visit notes to only their psychiatrist, and blocking substance use disorder records entirely from the HIE. This granular model reflects the sensitive categories that federal and state laws single out — genetics, mental health, substance use, communicable disease, and sexual/reproductive health — and more closely matches individual patient preferences.
Granular Consent in Practice
42 CFR Part 2: The Special Rule for Substance Use Disorder Records
No federal regulation creates more friction in health information exchange than 42 CFR Part 2, the Confidentiality of Substance Use Disorder Patient Records rule. Originally enacted in the 1970s to encourage people with addiction to seek treatment without fear that their records could be used against them in criminal proceedings or by employers, Part 2 has historically imposed requirements far stricter than HIPAA's TPO framework. Under the pre-2024 regime, substance use disorder (SUD) treatment records could not be disclosed — even to other treating physicians — without a patient-signed consent form that named the specific recipient, the specific purpose, and had an expiration date. A patient treated at an opioid treatment program could not have those records routinely shared with their cardiologist without a valid consent — only a bona fide medical emergency allowed disclosure without one.
On February 8, 2024, the Department of Health and Human Services announced a Final Rule modifying 42 CFR Part 2 (published in the Federal Register on February 16, 2024), implementing changes Congress required in the 2020 CARES Act. The rule took effect on April 16, 2024, with a compliance deadline of February 16, 2026. The 2024 Final Rule makes four landmark changes. First, it allows a single patient consent to cover all future uses and disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations — eliminating the need to name every specific recipient. Second, it aligns Part 2 breach notification requirements with HIPAA's Breach Notification Rule. Third, it grants Part 2 patients new rights to request an accounting of disclosures and to request restrictions on certain disclosures, mirroring rights already available under HIPAA. Fourth, it replaces Part 2's criminal-only penalties with HIPAA-aligned civil and criminal enforcement authority, administered by HHS Office for Civil Rights.
Despite these improvements, the consent segmentation challenge for HIEs remains significant. Even under the 2024 rule, Part 2 records require consent before they can flow through an HIE — the single-consent mechanism helps, but HIE platforms must be able to identify which records originated from a Part 2 program and apply the appropriate controls. Historically, many HIE vendors simply blocked all exchange of SUD records to avoid compliance exposure, meaning a patient's treatment for opioid use disorder was invisible to the emergency department treating that same patient for an overdose. Implementing Part 2-compliant segmentation requires labeling records at the source, propagating those labels through the exchange infrastructure, and enforcing access rules at the point of query — a technically demanding sequence that most legacy HIE platforms were not built to support.
A common compliance mistake is assuming that a HIPAA-compliant HIE automatically handles 42 CFR Part 2 records correctly. It does not. Until a provider's HIE platform explicitly implements Part 2 consent tracking and record segmentation, the safest default is to exclude SUD records from HIE exchange entirely — which means care gaps. The 2024 Final Rule alignment helps, but technical implementation remains the bottleneck.

FHIR Consent Resource and Digital Consent Management
The emergence of HL7 FHIR as the dominant interoperability standard has introduced a structured, computable mechanism for expressing consent: the FHIR Consent resource. Available since FHIR Release 3 and substantially refined in R4 and R5, the Consent resource can encode a wide range of privacy policies in machine-readable form. The resource's core structure begins with a base decision — either permit or deny — and then layers in provisions that represent exceptions to that decision. Each provision can be scoped by data category, purpose of use, actor (the individual or organization authorized to access), date range, and security label. Nested sub-provisions allow for arbitrarily complex policy trees: a patient could grant broad access to a care team but exclude a specific data category or specific provider role.
The HL7 Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) Implementation Guide, published by the HL7 Security Working Group, extends this capability by defining how security labels should be applied to individual FHIR resources based on their sensitivity classification. The DS4P IG specifies the sec-label-basis extension, which records which policy or regulation drove the label assignment — allowing a system to know, for instance, that a MedicationRequest resource carries a Part 2 label because it originated from a certified opioid treatment program. The sec-label-related-artifact extension can then point to the specific consent directive that authorizes a disclosure, creating an auditable chain from consent to data release. Packages for both R4 and R4B are available, and the SAMHSA-sponsored Consent2Share (C2S) open-source platform, built on the earlier DS4P specifications, demonstrated feasibility.
The technical challenges of enforcing granular consent at scale in production FHIR APIs are considerable. First, consent must be checked at query time — not just at ingestion — meaning every FHIR API call must be evaluated against the patient's current consent record before any data is returned. Second, consent records themselves can change: a patient revokes consent, updates a provision, or grants new access. The HIE's query engine must either maintain a consent cache that is updated in near real-time or query the authoritative consent store synchronously, adding latency. Third, many clinical workflows generate bulk queries — document queries, summary patient records, care gap analyses — and applying row-level consent filtering to millions of records requires purpose-built data access control infrastructure that most EHR vendors have not yet standardized. The FHIR Consent resource provides the grammar; building a scalable enforcement engine is the engineering work the industry is still completing.
Think of the FHIR Consent resource as a sophisticated key-ring management system. Each consent provision is like a copy of a key that grants access to a specific room (data category) in a building (the patient record). The base decision sets whether the default is "all doors locked" (deny) or "all doors open" (permit), and each provision adds or removes specific keys. The DS4P security labels are like the room labels on each door. The enforcement engine is the security guard who checks every key against every door at every entry point — in real time, at scale.
FHIR Consent provisions map data access rules in a machine-readable hierarchy, but enforcement requires an active policy decision point at every API query.

The Path to Standardization: TEFCA, ONC, and Consent Interoperability
The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA), administered by ONC and operated through the Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE), represents the federal government's most ambitious attempt to create a national, interoperable HIE fabric. TEFCA's architecture is built around Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) — large-scale networks that interconnect regional HIEs, provider networks, payers, and public health agencies under a single governance framework and set of technical standards. As of 2024, Common Agreement Version 2.0 was published in the Federal Register on May 1, 2024, with updated standard operating procedures released in August 2024 to support new exchange purposes including public health and benefit determination.
TEFCA's consent approach rests on the concept of Exchange Purposes (XPs). Every data request transmitted through TEFCA must identify the lawful purpose for which it is made — Treatment, Payment, Health Care Operations, Public Health, Benefits Determination, or Individual Access Services. For Individual Access Services, entities must obtain express consent from the individual before providing access. For other exchange purposes, TEFCA relies on the applicable federal and state laws that already govern those disclosures — meaning HIPAA's TPO framework applies to Treatment, Payment, and Operations queries, while state law may layer additional requirements. TEFCA does not yet impose a unified national consent standard, and state-level variation remains a significant interoperability barrier within the network of networks. A QHIN receiving a Treatment query from a provider in a state with opt-in HIE consent requirements must still honor those requirements even if the data originates in an opt-out state.
ONC's Data Segmentation for Privacy (DS4P) initiative, launched as a pilot program in October 2011, laid the conceptual and technical groundwork for what is now the HL7 DS4P Implementation Guide. The initiative demonstrated that metadata tags could be used to label sensitive data categories and enforce selective sharing across organizational boundaries. SAMHSA's Consent2Share platform — an open-source consent management and data segmentation tool — was built on DS4P specifications and designed to integrate with existing EHR and HIE systems. For production-grade consent management, organizations including CommonWell Health Alliance, Carequality, and regional HIEs have been developing or procuring consent management platforms capable of storing, evaluating, and enforcing patient consent decisions at the speed required for real-time clinical exchange. The convergence of TEFCA governance, FHIR R4 APIs, and DS4P security labels is creating the technical foundation for a national consent interoperability layer — but full standardization across all fifty states remains a multi-year effort.
TEFCA Common Agreement Version 2.0 was published May 1, 2024, with updated SOPs released August 2024. Every TEFCA query must declare an Exchange Purpose; Individual Access Services require express patient consent. State law still governs consent requirements for Treatment, Payment, and Operations queries within QHIN networks.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-ehr-market | The EHR Market: Epic, Oracle/Cerner & the Concentration Problem
The EHR Market: Vendors, Market Share, and What Dominance Means for Interoperability
The EHR Market Today: Concentration and Scale
The U.S. electronic health records market is large, concentrated, and growing. Grand View Research estimated the U.S. EHR market at approximately $12.87 billion in 2024, with projections for sustained growth as adoption deepens and cloud-based platforms replace older on-premise installations. That dollar figure, however, obscures the most important structural fact: a small number of vendors command the overwhelming majority of the market, especially in the hospital sector where the highest-acuity and highest-cost care is delivered.
According to KLAS Research's 2024 acute care market analysis, four vendors — Epic, Oracle Health (formerly Cerner), MEDITECH, and TruBridge — together account for roughly 87% of acute care hospital EHR installations in the United States. Epic alone holds 42.3% of all acute care hospitals by count, but when the metric shifts from hospital count to hospital beds — a proxy for the volume of care actually delivered — Epic's share jumps to 54.9%. This distinction between counting hospitals and counting beds matters enormously: large academic medical centers and health systems serve exponentially more patients than small critical-access hospitals, so the vendor that dominates large institutions controls the data environment for a disproportionate share of American patients.
The ambulatory market — outpatient physician offices and clinics — tells a different story. Here the field is more fragmented, with eClinicalWorks capturing roughly 12–14% of the ambulatory market, Epic near 10–20% depending on methodology, and athenahealth around 7%. The ambulatory segment is far more price-sensitive than the inpatient segment, which explains why cloud-native vendors with subscription pricing models have found durable footholds even as Epic expands into large health system ambulatory practices. The U.S. ambulatory EHR market alone was estimated at $5.49 billion in 2024.

Epic's Dominance: A Private Company Running Half of America's Hospital Records
Epic Systems Corporation is headquartered in Verona, Wisconsin — a deliberate choice by its founder and CEO, Judy Faulkner, who started the company in a Madison, Wisconsin basement in 1979 with a $70,000 investment from friends and family. Faulkner has kept Epic entirely private, never taking venture capital or private equity money, and has stated publicly that Epic will never go public. This unusual corporate structure — a multi-billion-dollar private company with no outside investors — gives Epic extraordinary freedom to prioritize long-term strategic moves over quarterly earnings. By 2024, Epic reported $5.7 billion in annual revenue and held the medical records of more than 325 million people.
The scale of Epic's reach becomes concrete through MyChart, its patient-facing portal. As of early 2024, Epic reported 185 million active MyChart users — a number that rivals the active user base of many major consumer apps. When a patient logs into MyChart at a hospital in Boston, a clinic in rural Iowa, or a health system in California, they are interacting with the same underlying platform. This patient-portal ubiquity is both a convenience and a strategic lock-in mechanism: patients who are enrolled in MyChart have a strong implicit incentive to seek care within the Epic ecosystem, because their records, messaging threads, and appointment history are all resident there.
Epic's dominance at large academic medical centers is not accidental. The company historically pursued a strategy of landing flagship institutions — the University of Pennsylvania, Johns Hopkins, Kaiser Permanente, Cleveland Clinic — understanding that smaller community hospitals and physician practices would follow the referral patterns of the dominant regional health system. KLAS confirmed that in 2024, Epic added a net 176 acute care multispecialty hospitals, its largest-ever annual net gain, and won nearly 70% of all hospitals impacted by EHR decisions that year regardless of size. The competitive flywheel is self-reinforcing: more Epic installations mean more Epic-to-Epic data exchange, which is dramatically smoother than cross-vendor exchange, giving clinical staff at Epic sites a perceived interoperability advantage that further pressures non-Epic competitors.
Think of Epic's network effect like an operating system that everyone in an office already runs: sharing files is frictionless within the system, but the moment you need to exchange data with someone on a different platform, compatibility issues multiply. The more people adopt the dominant platform, the more the others face pressure to convert.
Epic's Care Everywhere network makes data exchange nearly seamless between Epic sites, creating a powerful network effect that disadvantages hospitals still on competing EHRs.
When a patient cared for at a Mayo Clinic facility (Epic) is transferred to a Mass General Brigham hospital (also Epic), clinicians can pull that patient's full longitudinal record — allergies, medications, prior diagnoses, imaging reports — almost instantly via Epic's Care Everywhere framework. Performing the same query across a vendor boundary, say from an Epic site to an Oracle Health site, requires the hospitals to rely on external interoperability frameworks like Carequality, introducing additional query steps, potential data mapping inconsistencies, and latency. The technical gap is narrowing with FHIR APIs, but the lived experience for clinicians remains meaningfully different.
Care Everywhere: Epic-to-Epic Seamlessness
Oracle Health (Formerly Cerner) and the Troubled VA Contract
Cerner was Epic's primary rival for decades, particularly at mid-size community hospitals and large integrated delivery networks. That competitive landscape shifted in June 2022, when Oracle Corporation completed its acquisition of Cerner for $28.3 billion, rebranding the company as Oracle Health. Oracle's ambition was to layer its cloud infrastructure and database technology underneath Cerner's clinical software, creating a unified platform that could compete with Epic at scale. The reality of the post-acquisition integration has proven considerably messier. According to KLAS 2024 data, Oracle Health saw a net loss of 74 acute care hospitals during the year, with its market share declining from 23.4% to 22.9% — a continuation of a multi-year erosion.
The most high-profile test of Oracle Health's capabilities is the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs EHR modernization contract. The VA signed a deal with Cerner in May 2018, originally valued at $10 billion, to replace its legacy VistA system with the Cerner Millennium platform — later branded MHS GENESIS after the Department of Defense adopted the same system for its military health system. The DoD implementation has been comparatively successful: MHS GENESIS is now live at roughly 3,890 garrison facilities with over 197,200 end-users serving more than 9.5 million beneficiaries across the United States, Europe, and the Asia-Pacific. The VA implementation, however, has faced repeated delays, safety incidents, and congressional scrutiny, with lawmakers at various points demanding the contract be restructured or cancelled.
The VA contract's estimated lifetime cost has ballooned — some estimates project it could exceed $50 billion over 28 years — and as of recent reporting, the VA had spent roughly $5 billion to implement the system at only six of its 171 medical centers. The VA renegotiated the contract with Oracle Health to introduce stronger performance metrics and larger monetary penalties for non-compliance. The saga illustrates how even the best-resourced government healthcare agencies can struggle when a dominant EHR transition encounters the full complexity of a legacy clinical environment. For the broader interoperability agenda, the VA case demonstrates that vendor selection is only the starting point — implementation fidelity, change management, and sustained governance are equally determinative of whether new systems deliver value.
The Oracle Health VA contract is a live case study in the risks of large-scale EHR transitions. As of 2024–2025, the VA had spent approximately $5 billion implementing the system at only 6 of 171 medical centers, with costs projected to eventually exceed $50 billion over the full contract lifetime. Patient safety concerns, clinician dissatisfaction, and congressional pressure have accompanied the rollout. Policymakers and health systems alike cite this project as evidence that technical interoperability alone cannot compensate for poor implementation planning and insufficient workflow integration.
VA EHR Modernization: A Cautionary Tale
The Ambulatory and Community Health Market: A More Competitive Landscape
The outpatient physician office market operates under different economic logic than the hospital sector. A 10-physician internal medicine practice does not have a multi-million-dollar IT budget, a dedicated implementation team, or the negotiating leverage of a large health system. This price sensitivity has made the ambulatory market fertile ground for cloud-native, subscription-priced vendors. eClinicalWorks — a privately held company based in Westborough, Massachusetts — has built a substantial ambulatory presence serving roughly 12–14% of the U.S. ambulatory EHR market. The company's success is built on aggressive pricing, a broad feature set, and deep penetration into independent physician practices and specialty clinics.
athenahealth, now owned by Veritas Capital and Bain Capital after a 2019 buyout from Optum/UnitedHealth, holds approximately 7% of the ambulatory EHR market and distinguishes itself through a network-based model that provides revenue cycle management alongside clinical documentation. NextGen Healthcare and Modernizing Medicine serve specific specialty niches — NextGen has historically been strong in large specialty practices, while Modernizing Medicine's EMA platform dominates in dermatology, ophthalmology, and orthopedics. The ambulatory market's fragmentation means interoperability is harder to achieve: a patient's records may be split across a hospital Epic instance, a primary care eClinicalWorks installation, and a specialty Modernizing Medicine environment, with no single platform holding the complete picture.
Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) — the safety-net clinics that serve uninsured and low-income communities — face even sharper cost constraints and have developed a distinct ecosystem. OCHIN, a nonprofit health IT cooperative, has emerged as a critical infrastructure provider for FQHCs, enabling them to access the Epic platform through a shared instance model that dramatically reduces per-site cost. In 2024 alone, 33 rural and community health organizations implemented OCHIN's Epic model, with OCHIN Epic now supporting more than 1,900 care delivery sites in 37 states and reaching over 7 million patients. eClinicalWorks also serves a significant FQHC population, and multiple FQHCs selected its AI-enhanced EHR solutions in 2024. The FQHC market underscores a recurring theme: the economics of EHR adoption are inseparable from the economics of care delivery, and vendor decisions made at the market's lowest-margin margin have outsized consequences for health equity.

Inpatient vs. Ambulatory EHR Market Dynamics
Market Concentration and What It Means for Interoperability
The relationship between market concentration and interoperability is complex and contested. On one hand, a highly concentrated market dominated by a single vendor creates a de facto network: if most hospitals run the same platform, data can flow readily within that platform's native exchange mechanisms. Epic's Care Everywhere framework exemplifies this — Epic sites can query one another for patient records with minimal friction, and the 185 million MyChart users represent an enormous longitudinal dataset that is navigable within the Epic ecosystem. From a pure data-flow perspective, a world where everyone ran the same EHR would minimize many interoperability challenges at the point of care.
The problem is what happens at the boundaries. The 22.9% of hospitals on Oracle Health, the 14.8% on MEDITECH, the vast ambulatory market on eClinicalWorks and athenahealth, and the millions of patients receiving care at FQHCs on mixed platforms — all of these are outside Epic's native exchange universe. When care flows across that boundary, the friction increases. This is where federal interoperability policy becomes essential. The 21st Century Cures Act's information blocking provisions, finalized by ONC, prohibit EHR vendors from practices that unreasonably restrict access to, exchange of, or use of electronic health information. The FHIR R4 standard has reached near-universal EHR vendor adoption — 92% of EHR vendors support it, 90% of health systems have FHIR-enabled APIs, and 81% of hospitals have enabled patient access APIs — creating a common technical language that theoretically enables cross-vendor exchange regardless of underlying platform.
TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement — represents the most ambitious federal attempt to operationalize nationwide interoperability atop this FHIR foundation. TEFCA designates Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) as the connecting hubs, and organizations that participate in TEFCA agree to share data under a common governance framework. Crucially, a final rule issued in December 2024 established a "TEFCA Manner Exception" — providing that limiting exchange to TEFCA channels will not constitute information blocking when both parties are TEFCA participants and other conditions are met. This regulatory move is designed to steer the entire ecosystem toward TEFCA participation by giving vendors a safe harbor for TEFCA-based exchange while maintaining anti-blocking obligations elsewhere. Whether TEFCA can override the gravitational pull of dominant vendor networks remains the central open question for health data policy in the coming decade.
Required ONC to establish information blocking prohibitions and certified EHR technology standards, laying the statutory foundation for data access rights.
21st Century Cures Act (2016)
Operationalized information blocking prohibitions; required FHIR R4 APIs for certified EHRs; mandated patient access to their data via open APIs.
ONC Interoperability Final Rule (2020)
Updated USCDI (U.S. Core Data for Interoperability) to Version 3, requiring EHRs to support a broader standardized data set and tightened information blocking enforcement.
HTI-1 Final Rule (2024)
Established the TEFCA Manner Exception — participating organizations can limit exchange to TEFCA channels without triggering information blocking liability, channeling the market toward unified nationwide exchange.
HTI-2 / TEFCA Final Rule (December 2024)
Third-party developers now build apps on top of EHR FHIR APIs, creating a competitive application layer that reduces the lock-in power of any single EHR vendor's proprietary features.
Open APIs and Market Response
How the Federal Interoperability Regulatory Stack Works
The open API mandate is changing competitive dynamics in ways the market has not fully absorbed. When any developer can build on top of Epic, Oracle Health, or athenahealth using standardized FHIR APIs, the EHR vendor loses some of its ability to lock customers into proprietary workflows. Patients and providers can increasingly choose best-of-breed applications — scheduling tools, remote monitoring platforms, AI-assisted documentation — that connect to any certified EHR via API. This "unbundling" of EHR functionality is one of the most significant structural shifts in the market.
The U.S. acute care EHR market is highly concentrated: Epic holds 42.3% of hospitals by count and 54.9% by bed share (KLAS 2024), giving it effective control over the data environment for more than half of U.S. inpatient care.
Oracle Health (formerly Cerner, acquired by Oracle in June 2022) holds 22.9% of acute care hospitals but lost 74 net hospital customers in 2024; its flagship VA modernization contract has been plagued by delays and ballooning costs.
The ambulatory EHR market is more fragmented, with eClinicalWorks (~12–14%), Epic (~10–20%), and athenahealth (~7%) leading a field of specialized vendors — and FQHCs relying on cooperative models like OCHIN to access enterprise-class systems affordably.
Epic's Care Everywhere framework creates near-seamless data exchange between Epic sites, generating a powerful network effect that disadvantages non-Epic hospitals and increases friction at cross-vendor boundaries.
Federal interoperability policy — particularly the 21st Century Cures Act, ONC's information blocking rules, and the TEFCA framework finalized in December 2024 — is designed to counteract the lock-in power of dominant vendors by mandating open FHIR APIs and anti-blocking compliance.
FHIR R4 has reached near-universal adoption among certified EHR vendors (92%), but technical standards alone do not eliminate the operational and governance challenges of cross-vendor data exchange in a concentrated market.
The VA EHR modernization contract illustrates that vendor dominance and platform standardization do not automatically produce better outcomes — implementation quality, change management, and sustained governance are equally decisive.
The emergence of open APIs and the TEFCA marketplace is beginning to unbundle EHR functionality, allowing third-party applications to compete on top of any certified EHR platform and gradually reducing the competitive advantage of proprietary vendor ecosystems.
Epic's share of acute care hospitals by count was 42.3% in 2024, but when the metric shifts to hospital beds — a better proxy for actual care volume — Epic's share rises to 54.9%. This distinction matters because large academic medical centers and health systems have far more beds and serve far more patients than small critical-access hospitals, so bed share better reflects Epic's effective control over the patient data environment in the United States.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-interface-engines | Interface Engines: The Plumbing of Health IT
Interface Engines and Integration Platforms: The Plumbing of Healthcare Interoperability
Every time a patient is admitted to a hospital, an invisible machine swings into motion. The registration clerk's keystrokes in the admissions system must instantly reach the lab, the pharmacy, the radiology scheduling software, the billing engine, and the nursing floor's electronic whiteboard — all of which may be built by different vendors, running different software versions, and speaking subtly different dialects of the same messaging standard. The device that makes this happen is the interface engine, sometimes called an integration engine. It is among the least glamorous and most mission-critical pieces of infrastructure in healthcare IT.
Interface engines sit at the heart of hospital interoperability, acting as simultaneous translators, traffic directors, and circuit breakers for the flood of clinical data generated every second in a modern health system. Understanding how they work, who the major vendors are, and where the technology is heading is essential for anyone involved in health IT strategy, clinical informatics, or digital health product development.
What Interface Engines Do: The Translator and Router Function
At their core, interface engines perform three functions: they receive a message from a source system, transform it into the format the destination system expects, and route it to the right place at the right time. In a hospital without an interface engine, every system that needs to talk to every other system requires its own custom, hand-coded connection — what the industry calls a point-to-point interface. With ten systems, that means potentially 90 individual connections. Add a twentieth system and the number explodes to 380. This combinatorial nightmare is why the hub-and-spoke architecture that interface engines enable was such a transformative idea: each system connects once to the central engine, and the engine handles the rest.
The dominant message format flowing through these engines is HL7 version 2 (HL7 v2), a standard developed in the late 1980s that never quite standardized in practice. Each EHR vendor implements HL7 v2 slightly differently — different segment orderings, custom Z-segments carrying proprietary data, and varying interpretations of optional fields. An ADT (Admit-Discharge-Transfer) A01 message from Epic looks meaningfully different from one produced by Cerner or MEDITECH, even though all three claim compliance with the same specification. The interface engine's transformation layer — typically expressed as mapping logic written in a proprietary scripting language or JavaScript — handles these differences, reshaping the incoming message into exactly what the downstream system needs.
These messages travel between systems and engines using MLLP — the Minimal Lower Layer Protocol. MLLP is a lightweight TCP/IP wrapping protocol that solves a fundamental problem: TCP/IP delivers a continuous stream of bytes with no natural message boundaries. MLLP wraps each HL7 message in a start-block character (ASCII 0x0B) and an end-block character (ASCII 0x1C followed by a carriage return), allowing the receiving application to know precisely where one message ends and the next begins. Despite being technically simple, MLLP remains the backbone of clinical messaging in 2025 — it is reliable, low-overhead, and baked into decades of installed software that no one is eager to touch.
An interface engine is like an international airport hub. Passengers (messages) arrive from dozens of origin cities (source systems), speaking different languages and holding tickets in different formats. The hub translates their documents, routes them to the correct departure gate, and ensures they make their connecting flight — even when the rules change seasonally and new airlines keep arriving.

The Major Platforms: Rhapsody, Mirth Connect, Cloverleaf, and InterSystems
The commercial interface engine market is dominated by a handful of platforms that have each been battle-tested across thousands of hospital deployments. Rhapsody, now a standalone company after spinning out of Orion Health, is the most recognized name in the space. It has earned the Best in KLAS Integration Engine award for fifteen consecutive years as of 2024, a track record that reflects both its technical depth and its support quality. Rhapsody supports all major healthcare message standards — HL7 v2, HL7 v3, FHIR, DICOM, X12 — and is used by more than 1,900 healthcare teams across 31 countries. A 2024 Forrester Consulting Total Economic Impact study, commissioned by Rhapsody, found a 193% three-year return on investment for the health technology teams it interviewed.
Infor Cloverleaf, which has been in the healthcare integration market for over 20 years, occupies a similar enterprise tier. Its strengths lie in its mature HL7 v2 processing capabilities and its long track record in large academic medical centers and integrated delivery networks. InterSystems Health Connect (part of the HealthShare family) takes a different architectural approach, embedding the integration engine within a broader data platform built on the InterSystems IRIS data platform. One documented large health system deployment runs 1,000 interfaces, processes 104 million messages per weekday, and connects 136 systems — all through a single InterSystems installation built in under a year.
Mirth Connect, historically the go-to open-source option, powered roughly one-third of all public Health Information Exchanges in the U.S. and was deployed in over 40 countries. Owned and maintained by NextGen Healthcare, it offered a free community edition alongside a commercial support tier. However, with the release of version 4.6, NextGen has transitioned Mirth Connect from its dual open-source/commercial licensing model to a single proprietary license — meaning the source code for new versions is no longer publicly available. This shift prompted the community to fork the codebase into a project called Open Integration Engine, which aims to preserve the open-source option for organizations that built workflows around the free tier. The Mirth transition is a cautionary tale about the risks of building critical infrastructure on vendor-controlled open-source projects.

InterSystems reports that a large health system built its enterprise integration platform on HealthShare Health Connect in under a year; it now supports 1,000 interfaces and 136 connected systems and processes 104 million messages on a typical weekday. A separate InterSystems case study describes an Epic-based integrated delivery network whose message volume rose 330%, to 73 million messages a day, after its Epic go-live — the kind of growth that makes queue monitoring and volume alerting essential.
Real-World Scale: InterSystems at a Large Health System
Modern iPaaS and API Management: The Cloud Era of Integration
Traditional interface engines were designed for an era of on-premises data centers, persistent TCP connections, and relatively stable message volumes. The shift to cloud computing, mobile applications, and consumer-facing health platforms has created demand for a different kind of integration tool: the Integration Platform as a Service, or iPaaS. These cloud-native platforms are built around RESTful APIs, event-driven architectures, and elastic scalability — properties that legacy MLLP-based engines were never designed to deliver. Federal FHIR API mandates and the expansion of telehealth have accelerated their adoption in healthcare.
MuleSoft, now part of Salesforce, is among the most widely deployed iPaaS platforms in healthcare. Its API-led connectivity model organizes integrations into three layers: System APIs that expose raw data from source systems (like an EHR), Process APIs that orchestrate business logic across multiple systems, and Experience APIs that deliver tailored data to specific consumers like mobile apps or patient portals. MuleSoft's healthcare accelerator includes pre-built assets for converting HL7 v2 messages, C-CDA documents, and X12 transactions into FHIR R4 resources, then ingesting them into data stores like AWS HealthLake. This FHIR facade pattern — where an API layer presents a modern FHIR interface over a legacy backend — is one of the most common architectural patterns in current healthcare integration projects.
Cloud providers have also entered the integration space with native healthcare services. AWS HealthLake provides a FHIR R4-compliant data store with built-in natural language processing for unstructured clinical data. Azure Health Data Services combines a FHIR server, DICOM service, and analytics capabilities into a single managed platform. Google Cloud's Healthcare API supports FHIR, HL7 v2, and DICOM natively. These services are not interface engines in the traditional sense — they do not perform the complex message transformation and routing that Rhapsody or Cloverleaf handle — but they serve as the destination and normalization layer that modern integration architectures route data toward. The practical result is a hybrid architecture: legacy interface engines handling v2 traffic on the hospital side, feeding cloud-native FHIR platforms that serve the analytics and application layers.

Building and Managing Interfaces: The Full Lifecycle
Building a new interface is rarely as simple as connecting two systems and pressing go. The lifecycle of a single interface — from initial requirements gathering to production monitoring — takes weeks for a straightforward feed and can stretch to months for complex multi-system integrations involving custom segment mapping, error handling logic, and compliance with specific data governance rules. A full enterprise implementation involving dozens of interfaces takes longer still. Every custom interface carries build and maintenance labor, which is why large health systems with hundreds of interfaces carry substantial annual integration budgets.
Interface management does not end at go-live. Every time a source system undergoes a version upgrade — a new EHR release, a lab analyzer software update, a billing system migration — every interface connected to that system must be reviewed, potentially retested, and possibly rewritten. This change management burden is one of the most underestimated costs in healthcare IT. A large hospital system might execute dozens of EHR upgrades and vendor changes per year, each touching multiple interfaces. Interface inventory management — maintaining an accurate, up-to-date catalog of every active interface including its business owner, message types, volume baseline, and dependencies — is considered a best practice but is poorly implemented at many organizations.
Modern interface engines provide monitoring dashboards that track message queue depth, throughput rates, error rates, and acknowledgment latency in real time. A sudden drop in message volume on an ADT feed can indicate that the sending system has crashed or lost network connectivity — catching this through monitoring is far preferable to discovering it when a nurse notices the patient board has stopped updating. Sophisticated engines support dead-letter queues, where messages that cannot be processed are held for human review rather than silently dropped, and reprocessing capabilities that allow a backlog of held messages to be replayed once an issue is resolved. These operational features are often the deciding factor when health systems choose between competing platforms.
Define the business need, identify source and destination systems, document required data elements, message types (ADT, ORU, SIU, etc.), and trigger events. Agree on error handling and acknowledgment behavior.
Requirements & Design
Write transformation logic in the engine's scripting environment. Map source segments and fields to destination equivalents, handle Z-segments and custom fields, and implement any filtering or enrichment rules.
Mapping & Build
Test with synthetic and de-identified real messages. Validate that edge cases (empty fields, unusual character sets, high-volume bursts) are handled correctly. Coordinate with both source and destination system teams.
Unit & Integration Testing
Enable the interface in production with close monitoring for the first 48–72 hours. Watch queue depths, acknowledgment rates, and error logs. Keep rollback procedures ready if unexpected issues emerge.
Go-Live & Hypercare
Set up automated alerting on volume anomalies and error thresholds. Maintain the interface inventory record. Re-test and potentially remap when either connected system undergoes a version upgrade.
Ongoing Monitoring & Change Management
The Interface Lifecycle: From Requirements to Monitoring
Many health systems inherit hundreds of undocumented interfaces built over decades by staff who have since left. When a source system is decommissioned or upgraded, discovering what depends on it becomes an emergency archaeology project. Maintaining a living interface inventory — including business owners, downstream dependencies, and message volume baselines — is not glamorous work, but it dramatically reduces the cost and risk of every future system change.
The Hidden Cost of Interface Debt
The Transition to FHIR: Will Interface Engines Disappear?
FHIR has generated enormous enthusiasm in the interoperability world, and for good reason: it replaces the opaque, pipe-delimited structure of HL7 v2 with clean JSON resources accessible via standard RESTful APIs. ONC and CMS rules now require certified EHRs and payers to expose FHIR US Core APIs, and the UK's NHS, Australia's My Health Record, and health systems in dozens of other countries are embedding FHIR into national interoperability strategies.
Despite this momentum, HL7 v2 is not going away on any near-term horizon. HL7 International reports that 95% of U.S. healthcare organizations use HL7 v2. The reason is embedded infrastructure: laboratory instruments, medical devices, legacy pharmacy systems, and decades-old departmental applications speak HL7 v2 natively and will not be replaced simply because a superior standard exists. Replacing every HL7 v2 feed in a large health system would require years of parallel operation, enormous capital investment, and careful change management — resources most health systems are not in a position to commit simultaneously.
The realistic ten-year outlook is a hybrid architecture in which interface engines play a transformed but persistent role. Rather than disappearing, they evolve into v2-to-FHIR translation layers: receiving legacy HL7 v2 messages from clinical systems, converting them to FHIR R4 resources, and handing them off to cloud-based FHIR servers for storage and downstream consumption. Major vendors are already investing in exactly this capability — Rhapsody, InterSystems, and Cloverleaf all support FHIR natively alongside v2. The interface engine of 2030 will look less like a message broker and more like a universal translator standing between a legacy clinical world and a modern API ecosystem. The organizations that navigate this transition most successfully will be those that treat integration as a strategic competency rather than a back-office function.
FHIR is not replacing interface engines — it is giving them a new job. The engine of the future translates HL7 v2 messages from legacy systems into FHIR resources for cloud platforms, serving as the essential bridge between the clinical world that exists and the interoperability world we are building toward.
