######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-ehr-burden | EHR Burden: Documentation, Inbox & the Pajama Time Problem
EHR Burden and Clinician Burnout: How Poor Interoperability Hurts Clinicians
The Burden Problem: Physicians Spend More Time on EHRs Than on Patients
When the electronic health record was introduced into American medicine, it arrived with a promise: replace error-prone paper charts with a searchable, shareable digital record that would improve care quality and save time. Decades later, the promise has been only partially kept. The digital record exists — but the time savings never arrived. Instead, a mountain of peer-reviewed evidence now documents one of the most consequential unintended consequences in modern medicine: physicians routinely spend more hours each day interacting with their EHR than they spend in face-to-face contact with patients. This is not hyperbole — it is a measurable, replicated finding that is reshaping how health systems think about clinician well-being and workforce sustainability.
A landmark time-motion study by Sinsky and colleagues, published in the Annals of Internal Medicine, found that for every hour physicians spent in direct clinical face time with patients, they spent nearly two additional hours on EHR and desk work. Subsequent research has only deepened this picture. A 2024 study of 141 academic primary care physicians, published in the Annals of Family Medicine, found that their EHR time per 8 hours of scheduled appointments kept rising after the pandemic — up 28.4 minutes (7.8%) between 2019–20 and 2022–23, driven by order entry (+58.9%) and the inbox (+24.4%). Overall, physicians today report spending roughly 13 hours per week on indirect patient care tasks such as order entry, documentation, and referral management, within a 57.8-hour reported workweek. That math leaves precious little time for the human encounter that drew most physicians to medicine in the first place.
What is perhaps most striking is what happens after clinic hours. Researchers coined the term "pajama time" to describe the hours physicians spend in the EHR at home, after their clinical day has technically ended. A study in the Annals of Family Medicine found that primary care physicians spent approximately 86 minutes — nearly an hour and a half — on the EHR after clinic hours every day. Among upper-year family medicine residents, nearly one-third report spending three or more additional hours per day on after-hours EHR work. This chronic overflow of documentation into personal time has been directly linked to burnout, reduced professional satisfaction, and lower examination performance. The AMA's 2024 national burnout survey of nearly 18,000 physicians across 43 states found that 43.2 percent of physicians reported at least one burnout symptom — and ineffective EHR systems ranked among the most consistently cited sources of occupational stress.

Imagine hiring a carpenter whose tools are so cumbersome that they spend two hours filing paperwork for every hour they actually build. The carpenter is technically productive — paperwork is real work — but the building is going up slower, and the carpenter is exhausted. That is the situation facing American physicians with today's EHR systems: real documentation is necessary, but the cognitive and time burden has grown so large that it crowds out the core work of patient care.
EHR documentation burden displacing clinical time
Root Causes: Poor Design, Alert Fatigue, and Fragmented Data
Understanding why EHRs consume so much physician time requires looking beneath the surface of the software itself. Most commercial EHR systems were not designed with usability as the primary objective — they were designed to fulfill billing and compliance requirements, and the clinical workflow was often an afterthought. As a result, physicians routinely navigate dozens of screens, click through cascading dropdown menus, and manually enter data that could theoretically be auto-populated if systems communicated with one another. Poor interoperability is at the heart of this problem: when a patient arrives from another health system, their prior lab results, imaging reports, and medication lists frequently do not follow them. The physician or their staff must manually re-enter that information, dramatically extending visit preparation time and increasing the risk of transcription errors.
One of the most pervasive and dangerous documentation behaviors to emerge from EHR design failures is copy-forward documentation — the practice of copying a prior note into the current encounter and editing only minimally. A 2022 analysis of over 100 million EHR notes found that 50.1 percent of all text in clinical notes was duplicated from prior documentation on the same patient. As many as 90 percent of clinicians admit to using copy-and-paste functions in the EHR. While this behavior saves time in the short run, it systematically degrades note quality: outdated medication lists persist, resolved problems remain active, and contradictory information accumulates across encounters. Patient safety researchers at the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality have documented that copy-forward errors contribute directly to diagnostic mistakes and adverse events, including hospitalizations that might have been prevented had the clinical record been accurate.
Alert fatigue is another root cause that compounds the burden of fragmented data. Clinical decision support (CDS) systems embedded in EHRs are designed to catch dangerous drug interactions, flag abnormal values, and remind clinicians of overdue preventive care. In theory, these alerts save lives. In practice, the volume has become overwhelming: some physicians and nurses report receiving between 100 and 200 CDS alerts per day. At Brigham and Women's Hospital — one of the most prestigious academic medical centers in the country — physicians override approximately 98 percent of medication order alerts. Research published in JMIR Medical Informatics found that in one medication-related CDS system, only 7.3 percent of generated alerts were clinically appropriate. When physicians learn that the vast majority of alerts are irrelevant, they begin dismissing them reflexively — a conditioned response that creates exactly the kind of cognitive blind spot the alerts were designed to prevent. The result is a system that adds burden without proportional benefit, eroding trust in the very tools meant to support clinical judgment.
Billing-First EHR Design
Optimized for code capture and compliance documentation
Complex multi-screen workflows for each order
Copy-forward encouraged by poor note templates
Alert thresholds set broadly to minimize liability
Limited FHIR integration — manual data re-entry required
Clinician-First EHR Design
Streamlined workflows matching clinical thought process
Smart defaults and auto-population from prior visits
Structured templates that discourage copy-forward
Alert logic refined to clinically actionable thresholds
FHIR APIs pre-populate data from external health systems
EHR System Design: Billing-First vs. Clinician-First
When physicians override 98% of EHR alerts — as documented at Brigham and Women's Hospital — the few clinically critical warnings become invisible in the noise. Alert fatigue is not just a workflow inefficiency; it is a direct mechanism for medication errors and missed diagnoses.
Alert Fatigue Is a Patient Safety Issue
The Prior Authorization Crisis: When Interoperability Gaps Meet Insurance Bureaucracy
No single administrative burden in American medicine has generated more physician frustration — or caused more direct patient harm — than prior authorization. Prior authorization is the process by which insurers require physicians to obtain approval before prescribing certain medications, ordering specific imaging studies, or proceeding with recommended procedures. In principle, it is a cost-management tool. In practice, it has become a bureaucratic labyrinth that consumes an extraordinary share of physician and staff time. The AMA's 2024 nationwide survey of 1,000 practicing physicians found that practices complete an average of 39 prior authorization requests per physician per week, consuming approximately 13 hours of physician and staff time — roughly one and a half business days — every single week. Two in five physician practices employ staff dedicated exclusively to prior authorization tasks.
The connection to EHR interoperability is direct and underappreciated. Prior authorization processes are slow largely because clinical data does not flow automatically between provider EHR systems and insurer systems. Physicians must manually extract clinical information from the EHR, re-enter it into insurer portals or fax it via paper forms, and then wait — sometimes for days — for a decision. If interoperable APIs existed to transmit structured clinical data directly, the information exchange could happen in minutes rather than days. The status quo is expensive in human terms: 89 percent of physicians in the AMA's 2024 survey (fielded December 2024) reported that prior authorization somewhat or significantly contributes to physician burnout. That near-universal figure makes prior authorization one of the most universally agreed-upon sources of professional dissatisfaction in medicine today.
The patient consequences are equally alarming. According to the AMA's 2023 survey (fielded December 2023), 94 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization delays patients' access to care. Seventy-eight percent of physicians reported that prior authorization often or sometimes results in patients abandoning a recommended course of treatment entirely — unable or unwilling to wait for approval, they simply go without care. Most seriously, nearly one in four physicians (24 percent) reported that prior authorization has led to a serious adverse event for a patient in their care, including hospitalization, permanent impairment, or death. Of those reporting adverse events, 19 percent cited delays leading to hospitalization, 13 percent identified life-threatening events, and 7 percent reported disability, birth defects, or patient death as downstream consequences of authorization delays. In the AMA's 2024 survey, the share reporting a serious adverse event rose to 29 percent.

A primary care physician prescribes a biologic medication for a patient with severe rheumatoid arthritis. The insurer requires prior authorization. The physician's staff submits a paper form. Nine days pass. The insurer requests additional clinical documentation. The staff re-submits. Five more days pass. The patient, unable to manage pain and unable to take time off work for repeated calls to the insurer, abandons the prescription and returns to lower-efficacy over-the-counter options. Three months later, the patient presents to the emergency department with advanced joint damage. The total cost of the ED visit and specialist follow-up exceeds the annual cost of the biologic — and the patient has suffered irreversible harm. This scenario plays out thousands of times each day across the United States.
The Cascading Harm of a Delayed Authorization
What Regulation Is Doing About EHR Burden
Federal policymakers have recognized for years that EHR burden and poor interoperability are not merely nuisances — they are structural failures of the health information technology ecosystem that cause measurable patient harm. The legislative response began in earnest with the 21st Century Cures Act of 2016, which included sweeping provisions designed to promote the free flow of electronic health information and prohibit "information blocking" — practices by EHR vendors, health systems, or health information networks that impede access to or exchange of patient data. Penalties for information blocking violations can reach up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers and health information networks. Enforcement against healthcare providers became effective July 1, 2024, marking a turning point in the federal government's willingness to hold the ecosystem accountable.
On the interoperability infrastructure side, the Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) has advanced the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA), a nationwide framework designed to enable any HIPAA-covered entity to connect to a single network and exchange data with any provider connected to any participating Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN). The ONC's HTI-1 Final Rule, which took effect March 11, 2024, further implements the EHR Reporting Program from the Cures Act, requiring transparent reporting on certified health IT metrics. Together, these initiatives aim to shift the EHR ecosystem from fragmentation toward genuine clinical interoperability — a shift that, if successful, would directly reduce the manual data re-entry burden that consumes so much physician time.
The most targeted federal intervention on prior authorization specifically is the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule, known as CMS-0057-F. Finalized in early 2024, the rule requires impacted payers — including Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and qualified health plan issuers on federal exchanges — to implement FHIR-based Prior Authorization APIs, establish turnaround time limits of 72 hours for expedited requests and 7 calendar days for standard requests, and provide specific reasons for denial decisions. The operational provisions took effect January 1, 2026, with full API requirements due January 1, 2027. The rule also requires payers to implement a Provider Access API, enabling in-network providers to retrieve patient claims and encounter data directly — a foundational step toward the kind of data pre-population that could eliminate much of today's manual re-entry burden.
Prohibits information blocking; mandates open APIs for patient data access; establishes ONC health IT certification requirements.
21st Century Cures Act (2016)
Defines eight narrow exceptions to the information blocking prohibition; applies to EHR developers, health information networks, and providers.
ONC Information Blocking Rule (2021)
Implements EHR Reporting Program; expands information blocking enforcement; advances USCDI data standards for interoperability.

Mandates FHIR-based Prior Auth APIs; requires 72-hr expedited / 7-day standard decision turnaround; operational compliance began January 1, 2026.

Key Federal Interventions Targeting EHR Burden and Interoperability
The U.S. Surgeon General and the AMA have both issued formal calls for systemic action on EHR burden. In 2022, Surgeon General Vivek Murthy's advisory on health worker burnout explicitly identified EHR and administrative burden as a primary structural driver of the crisis, and called on health systems, payers, and technology vendors to redesign workflows that prioritize clinician well-being alongside patient safety.
Interventions That Actually Work: From Ambient AI to FHIR Pre-Population
Amid the grim statistics on EHR burden, a set of interventions has emerged with genuine evidence of efficacy. The most discussed — and arguably the most promising — is ambient artificial intelligence documentation, often called the "ambient AI scribe." These systems use natural language processing to listen to physician-patient conversations and automatically generate structured clinical notes inside the EHR, dramatically reducing the manual typing and clicking that consumes so much of a physician's cognitive bandwidth. A quality improvement study of 263 physicians and advanced practice practitioners across six health care systems — published in JAMA Network Open — found that after 30 days of using an ambient AI scribe, burnout rates dropped significantly from 51.9 percent to 38.8 percent. The odds of burnout fell by 74 percent. Eighty-four percent of physicians reported a positive effect on patient communication, and 82 percent said their overall work satisfaction improved.
Health systems deploying ambient AI at scale are reporting similarly encouraging results. Between October 2023 and December 2024, 7,260 Permanente physicians used ambient AI tools across more than 2.5 million patient encounters, saving an estimated 15,791 hours of documentation time — equivalent to approximately 1,800 eight-hour workdays. Platforms such as Nuance DAX Copilot (integrated with Epic and other major EHRs), Abridge, and Suki are now deployed across hundreds of health systems. Studies consistently report reductions in after-hours charting, decreased cognitive load, and improved patient-physician eye contact and conversation quality. A 2026 real-world prospective observational time-motion study published in JMIR Medical Informatics documented significant time savings per clinical encounter using ambient AI tools in outpatient settings. Fifty-six percent of patients reported that ambient AI scribes had a positive impact on the quality of their visit, suggesting that the benefits extend beyond the clinician experience to the patient relationship itself.
Beyond ambient AI, several other high-impact interventions have evidence behind them. FHIR-enabled data pre-population — where a patient's prior labs, medications, and diagnoses flow automatically into the new encounter note from external health systems — directly attacks the manual re-entry burden that fragmented interoperability creates. Team-based inbox management, in which clinical staff handle prescription refill requests, routine test result communications, and referral coordination, can reduce physician inbox volume by 30 to 40 percent in well-designed implementations. Human medical scribes remain effective where ambient AI is not yet deployed: studies show they reduce physician documentation time by approximately 10 minutes per patient encounter and are associated with reduced after-hours EHR time. ONC's SAFER (Safety Assurance Factors for EHR Resilience) guides provide health systems with a structured self-assessment framework for identifying and mitigating EHR-related patient safety risks — including alert fatigue, poor workflow design, and inadequate usability testing — before they cause harm.

Documentation Burden: Status Quo vs. Optimized Workflow
Mass General Brigham — the Boston-based academic health system — conducted a formal evaluation of ambient AI documentation technology across its clinical enterprise. The program demonstrated reductions in physician burnout, improved patient interaction quality, and meaningful decreases in time spent on post-visit documentation. Physicians reported being able to make eye contact with patients during conversations rather than focusing on a screen, and many described rediscovering aspects of the clinical encounter they had lost to years of EHR demands. Mass General Brigham's public reporting on this program has become a reference point for health systems evaluating ambient AI investments nationally.

The EHR Business Case: Total Cost of Ownership & 5-Year ROI
Choosing and adopting an EHR is one of the largest capital and operational decisions a health system makes — and the business case is notoriously hard to build. The benefits are diffuse and delayed; the costs are concentrated and immediate. This module breaks the decision into the numbers that actually drive it: total cost of ownership, the go-live productivity dip, and the multi-year return.
Why the EHR business case is hard
Unlike a piece of revenue-generating equipment, an EHR's return shows up indirectly — through better coding capture, fewer duplicate orders, reduced transcription, and downstream quality incentives — and it shows up over years, not quarters. Meanwhile the costs hit all at once: licensing, implementation, hardware or cloud subscription, training, and a temporary drop in clinical throughput during go-live. A credible business case has to make those diffuse benefits explicit and time-phased.
The cost components
Total cost of ownership has four parts. (1) Implementation — configuration, data migration, interface build, and vendor professional services, typically the largest one-time line. (2) Licensing or subscription — per-provider annual cost, higher for on-premise capex-heavy models, recurring for cloud/SaaS. (3) Training — scaled to headcount and to how long the rollout runs. (4) The go-live productivity loss — see below. Hosting model (cloud, on-premise, or hybrid) shifts the balance between upfront capex and recurring opex.
In 2017 the University of Vermont Medical Center asked the Green Mountain Care Board for a certificate of need to replace the EHR and related IT systems at four UVM Health Network hospitals — UVM Medical Center, Central Vermont Medical Center, Porter Medical Center and Champlain Valley Physicians Hospital — with a single Epic platform. Because Vermont subjects hospital capital spending above $3 million to CON review, the whole cost model went on the public record.
The applicant estimated a total cost of ownership of about $151.7 million over six years: $109.3 million of capital (including a 9.9% contingency) and $42.4 million of net operating expense. The operating figure is already net of two offsets — $12.4 million for legacy systems Epic would retire and $31.0 million in staffing offsets — which is how a business case shows avoided cost explicitly instead of leaving it implicit.
The comparison the applicant drew was not Epic versus zero: it estimated that updating, maintaining and replacing the existing legacy systems could cost up to $200 million over the same six years. The Board's own consultant, Deloitte, stress-tested the plan with a contingency twice as large as budgeted, volume growth beyond management projections and savings that were not fully realized, and concluded the network could absorb the project while keeping an A credit rating.
Vermont Case Study
The Board approved the project on January 5, 2018 (Docket GMCB-001-17con) with conditions including six-month implementation reports carrying detailed financial information. Wave 1 went live at UVM Medical Center on November 9, 2019. A 2020 amendment adding Alice Hyde and Elizabethtown raised the combined project cost to $171.5 million ($174.6 million with capitalized interest); the Board found that folding them into Wave 3 avoided about $9.5 million (33%) against a roughly $30 million standalone implementation.

Read the table for its proportions, not its total. The Epic software line is about one-seventh of capital. People — outside consultants, Epic's own implementation services and UVMHN's internal team — account for about 65% of it ($64.9 million of $99.4 million). The Board called the roughly 10% contingency "standard and customary for Epic implementation projects of similar size and scope." A business case that starts from the vendor's licence quote and adds a margin is therefore starting from the smallest of its big numbers.
The go-live productivity dip
During the weeks around go-live, clinicians see fewer patients while they learn the system. A common planning assumption is a peak dip of around 25% in the first weeks, recovering to baseline over the rollout window. That lost clinical revenue is a real cost of adoption — often underestimated — and it scales with both the number of providers and the length of the go-live.
Plus $85,500 of maintenance in the first year. 26 primary care practices in the Baylor HealthTexas network. Source: Fleming et al., Health Affairs 2011

What practice-level evidence shows about implementation cost and the dip
The ~25% peak-dip figure is a planning convention, not a measured constant. The Baylor data support its shape — a fall followed by recovery to or near baseline within about a year — but not a specific depth. They also add something the dip alone hides: expenses did not fall back. Staffing and practice expenses were still higher 12 months after go-live, so "recovery" meant productivity came back, not that the cost base returned to where it was.
In 2022 the Department of Veterans Affairs asked the Institute for Defense Analyses (IDA) for an independent life-cycle cost estimate of its EHR Modernization program. IDA put it at $49.8 billion in constant FY2022 dollars — $32.7 billion over 13 years of implementation plus $17.1 billion over 15 years of sustainment — against VA's 2019 program-office estimate of $16.1 billion. About 75 percent of the gap came from cost elements VA's estimate did not include: sustainment, and productivity loss during rollout, which IDA costed as the supplemental staffing and extra community care needed to cover disrupted facilities, plus the revenue lost to the disruption. IDA called deployment productivity loss "a cost element with substantial risk." At any scale the lesson is the same: a business case that prices the licence and the consultants but not the go-live disruption is not conservative — it is incomplete. (The EHR Market Landscape module covers the VA–Oracle Health contract itself.)
The cost line most business cases leave out
Modeling five-year ROI and break-even
A defensible model phases the benefit stream: little to no benefit in year one (while the organization is still climbing the learning curve), ramping to a steady state — frequently modeled as a few percent of clinical revenue — by year two or three. Subtract annual cost from annual benefit, accumulate, and find the year the cumulative net turns positive. That break-even year, not the sticker price, is the number executives should anchor on.
Modeled — Wang et al., Am J Med 2003
Method: cost-benefit model of an ambulatory EMR in primary care, from the health system's perspective (Partners HealthCare data plus published literature)
Five-year result: estimated net benefit of $86,400 per primary care provider
What drove it: savings on drug spending, better use of radiology tests, better charge capture and fewer billing errors
Spread: most sensitive to the share of capitated patients; the five-way sensitivity range ran from a $2,300 net cost to a $330,900 net benefit
Surveyed — Adler-Milstein et al., Health Affairs 2013
Method: survey data from 49 community practices in the Massachusetts eHealth Collaborative pilot, projected to five-year ROI
Five-year result: the average physician would lose $43,743
What drove it: practices that came out ahead used the EHR to raise revenue — more patients per day, fewer rejected claims, more accurate coding
Spread: only 27% reached positive ROI; the $44,000 meaningful-use incentive would have pushed just 14% more over the line, and almost half never captured paper savings because they kept paper records
Modeled vs. surveyed five-year EHR returns: two landmark studies
The gap between the two studies is the gap between a benefit that is available and a benefit that is captured. Wang's model assumes the organization does the things that produce savings; the Massachusetts practices often did not. The EMR/EHR Lab's 4% steady-state benefit is that same kind of capture assumption — treat it as the number you will have to defend, not as a given.
Worked example: the Lab's default scenario
Open the Adoption & Cost mode with its defaults — Epic selected, 50 provider FTEs, a 12-month go-live window and $550,000 of clinical revenue per provider. The model produces implementation of $1.55 million (50 × $31,000), training of $120,000, annual licence and support of $490,000 (50 × $9,800), and a go-live productivity loss of about $3.44 million: a 25% peak dip recovering linearly averages 12.5% of the year's $27.5 million clinical revenue. Year-one cost is $5.6 million, and the productivity loss alone is 61% of it.

EMR/EHR Lab defaults — Epic, 50 providers, 12-month go-live, $550K revenue/provider
On these assumptions the investment does not break even within five years, and the Lab says so. The reason is structural: at steady state the benefit ($1.1 million a year) exceeds licence cost by only $610,000, so recovering a $5.05 million year-one deficit takes more than eight years. Now pull the levers. Cutting the go-live window to 6 months halves the productivity loss to about $1.72 million, yet Epic still ends Year 5 $828,750 short. Switch to athenahealth with the same 6-month window and the model breaks even in Year 5; at 3 months it breaks even in Year 4. These vendor figures are illustrative anchors, not quotes — the point is that the go-live plan moves break-even as much as the vendor's price does.
Include implementation services, internal and external staffing, hardware and network, training and third-party software. In UVM Health Network's filing, Epic software was about 14% of pre-contingency capital; staffing and implementation services were about 65%.
Price the full TCO, not the licence
The Board found UVMHN's ~9.9% contingency standard for Epic projects of that size. IDA reported a $46–54 billion 20th–80th percentile range around its VA point estimate rather than a single number.
Carry an explicit contingency and a range
Model the productivity dip, backfill staffing and lost revenue. It was among the elements missing from VA's 2019 estimate, and it is the largest single year-one cost in the Lab's default scenario.
Cost the go-live disruption as a line item
Retired legacy systems and staffing changes belong in the model as negative costs — UVMHN booked $12.4 million and $31.0 million — but only if the old systems are actually switched off. Nearly half of the Massachusetts practices kept paper and never realized paper savings.
Count only the offsets you will actually realize
Revenue-side gains — visit throughput, fewer rejected claims, more accurate coding — separated positive-ROI practices from negative ones. Give each benefit stream an owner and a metric.
Name the behaviors that produce each benefit
Benchmark against the do-nothing alternative (UVMHN's estimate of up to $200 million to keep its legacy systems) and run downside cases on contingency, volume and savings shortfall, as the Board's consultant did.
Compare against standing still, then stress-test
Building a defensible EHR business case
What to take away
The EHR decision is a financial model, not just a feature comparison. Vendor choice and hosting model change the cost profile; the go-live plan changes the productivity loss; and the benefit assumptions determine whether — and when — the investment pays back. Build the model explicitly, stress-test the assumptions, and revisit the hosting and timeline levers before signing.
Software licences are a minority of EHR cost: in UVM Health Network's public CON filing, Epic software was about 14% of $99.4 million in pre-contingency capital, while implementation services and staffing were about 65%.
Go-live productivity loss is a real, budgetable cost. IDA's independent VA estimate included it, with sustainment; VA's 2019 estimate did not — and those added elements explained about 75% of the gap between $16.1 billion and $49.8 billion.
At practice level, productivity and net income dipped and recovered to or near baseline in about 12 months, but practice expenses stayed about 6% higher (Fleming et al., 2014).
ROI depends on capture, not installation: a modeled $86,400 five-year net benefit per provider (Wang et al., 2003) sits beside an average $43,743 five-year loss and only 27% positive-ROI practices in Massachusetts (Adler-Milstein et al., 2013).
In the EMR/EHR Lab's default scenario the go-live timeline moves break-even as much as vendor price does — test it as a lever, not a given.
Key Takeaways
IDA's estimate added about $25.9 billion of elements beyond the scope of VA's estimate — sustainment over 15 years and productivity loss during rollout (supplemental staffing, extra community care and lost revenue) — and IDA said these account for about 75% of the difference. Both figures were stated in constant FY2022 dollars, and IDA explicitly excluded the cost of, and savings from, legacy EHR systems.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-snomed-loinc-rxnorm | Clinical Terminology: SNOMED CT, LOINC & RxNorm
SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm: The Vocabularies That Make Clinical Data Computable
Every day, billions of clinical observations, diagnoses, prescriptions, and lab results move between hospitals, pharmacies, payers, and public health agencies. But data moving between systems is not the same as data being understood by those systems. A lab result labeled 'Glucose' in one EHR might arrive at a receiving system as a free-text string with no machine-readable meaning. A diagnosis coded 'Type 2 DM' in one notation may be opaque to a clinical decision support engine expecting a different code. Without a shared vocabulary — a universal clinical language — every data exchange risks producing noise instead of knowledge.
Three terminologies sit at the heart of clinical data interoperability in the United States: SNOMED CT for clinical concepts (diseases, findings, procedures), LOINC for observations and measurements (lab tests, vital signs, assessments), and RxNorm for medications and drugs. Together, these standards form the computable foundation that allows software to reason about patient data rather than merely store it. Federal regulators — ONC (now ASTP/ONC) and CMS — mandate their use in certified EHR systems and FHIR-based APIs, making fluency in these vocabularies non-negotiable for any healthcare interoperability professional.
Think of SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm as three different dictionaries in a single clinical language. SNOMED CT is the medical encyclopedia — it defines what conditions, procedures, and findings are. LOINC is the measurement handbook — it defines what was tested or observed and how. RxNorm is the pharmacy formulary — it defines what was prescribed and in what form. A complete clinical picture requires all three.
SNOMED CT: The Clinical Concept Backbone
SNOMED CT (Systematized Nomenclature of Medicine — Clinical Terms) is the world's most comprehensive multilingual clinical healthcare terminology. Governed by SNOMED International, a nonprofit standards development organization founded in 2007, SNOMED CT is licensed in more than 40 countries and serves as the preferred vocabulary for encoding clinical findings, diagnoses, symptoms, procedures, body structures, organisms, and substances within electronic health records.

The January 2020 International Edition already surpassed 350,000 active concepts, and the terminology continues to grow with each biannual release. In the US, NLM distributes the US Edition of SNOMED CT — which extends the International Edition with US-specific content — through the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) Terminology Services. Users must accept the UMLS Metathesaurus License Agreement and hold a UMLS account; for US-based healthcare organizations, access is free of charge as part of a national arrangement managed through the NLM.
Structure: More Than a Code List
Unlike ICD-10-CM — which is a flat classification system built primarily for billing and epidemiology — SNOMED CT is a poly-hierarchical, description logic-based terminology. Each concept has a unique numeric identifier (ConceptID), one or more human-readable descriptions (Fully Specified Name, Preferred Term, synonyms), and a set of relationships to other concepts that define its meaning formally. A concept like 'Type 2 diabetes mellitus' carries relationships expressing that it is a subtype of diabetes mellitus and that its finding site is the endocrine pancreas — information that a classification code alone cannot convey.
The two systems are complementary, not competing. The NLM publishes and maintains an official SNOMED CT-to-ICD-10-CM map that enables semi-automated billing code generation from SNOMED CT-encoded clinical data. This means a clinician can document in SNOMED CT for clinical precision, and the EHR can automatically suggest the correct ICD-10-CM billing code — reducing administrative burden while preserving clinical fidelity.
USCDI and ONC Mandate: The ONC HTI-1 Final Rule requires certified health IT to use SNOMED CT US Edition for clinical conditions and problems. USCDI v3 — mandatory for certified EHRs by January 2026 — specifies SNOMED CT as the required terminology for the Problems data class. The March and September US Edition releases ensure providers have access to the latest concepts for compliance.
LOINC: Naming What Was Tested or Observed
LOINC (Logical Observation Identifiers Names and Codes) provides the universal standard for identifying medical laboratory observations, clinical measurements, and health assessments. Developed and maintained by the Regenstrief Institute — a health informatics research organization at Indiana University — LOINC was created in 1994 and has grown into one of the most widely adopted health data standards in the world. As of 2023, LOINC contains approximately 101,632 terms covering everything from a routine serum albumin level to a zygomatic arch X-ray report, with thousands of new concepts added in each semiannual release.

Defining Axes
What LOINC Names
LOINC's primary focus is answering the question: 'What was measured or observed, and how?' Every LOINC code represents a unique combination of up to six defining attributes — the component (analyte), the property being measured (e.g., mass concentration), the time aspect (point in time vs. 24-hour collection), the system (specimen type — serum, urine, blood), the scale of measurement (quantitative, ordinal, narrative), and optionally the method used. This six-part axis structure means that a serum sodium measured on a point-in-time specimen with a quantitative result gets a different LOINC code than a 24-hour urine sodium — even though both measure 'sodium.'
LOINC 2951-2: Sodium [Moles/volume] in Serum or Plasma. This code specifies: Component = Sodium; Property = Substance Concentration (SCnc); Time = Point; System = Serum/Plasma; Scale = Quantitative. A receiving laboratory information system can parse this code and know exactly what to render, what units to expect, and how to alert on abnormal values — without any free-text parsing.
LOINC's reach extends well beyond the clinical laboratory. Survey instruments and functional assessments — including the PHQ-9 depression screen, the GAD-7 anxiety scale, and dozens of social determinants of health (SDOH) screenings — are encoded in LOINC. Vital signs such as blood pressure, heart rate, body weight, and oxygen saturation have standardized LOINC codes used in FHIR Observation resources. Document types (discharge summaries, progress notes, operative reports) also carry LOINC codes, enabling document-level indexing and retrieval across health systems.
LOINC is the mandated standard for laboratory tests in USCDI v3 and for the Observations data class in US Core FHIR profiles. Certified FHIR APIs under the 21st Century Cures Act regulations must follow US Core, whose laboratory result profile binds the test code to LOINC.
LOINC and the Lab Ecosystem
The Regenstrief Institute collaborates extensively with the FDA, CDC, and the Association of Public Health Laboratories (APHL) to create LOINC codes for emerging needs. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the Regenstrief team began coordinating with CDC, public health and reference labs, and test manufacturers in January 2020 and published dedicated SARS-CoV-2 test codes as pre-release terms, ahead of the normal release cycle. This agility illustrates why LOINC is indispensable for public health response: without standardized observation codes, surveillance data from thousands of labs would have been irreconcilable.
RxNorm: Making Drug Data Interoperable
RxNorm is the National Library of Medicine's standardized nomenclature for clinical drugs. First introduced as a full monthly release in 2005, RxNorm celebrated its 20th anniversary in 2025. Its core purpose is deceptively simple but enormously powerful: assign a single normalized name and unique identifier (called an RxCUI — RxNorm Concept Unique Identifier) to each distinct combination of active ingredient, strength, and dose form, regardless of which manufacturer made it or what brand name it carries.

The Problem RxNorm Solves
Drug naming in the United States is a labyrinth. A single active ingredient may appear under dozens of brand names across hundreds of National Drug Code (NDC) entries — each representing a specific manufacturer, package size, and labeler. Metformin hydrochloride 500 mg oral tablet, for instance, might have hundreds of distinct NDC codes from different generic manufacturers. Without normalization, a clinical decision support rule written against one NDC would miss all the others. A pharmacist's allergy alert system would fail to recognize a therapeutic duplicate if the incoming order used a different brand name than the one in its database.
RxNorm resolves this fragmentation by mapping all NDC codes for equivalent drug products to a single RxCUI representing the normalized clinical drug concept. The December 2025 RxNorm full release contains 14,592 base ingredients, 17,544 clinical drug entries, and 9,721 branded drug entries. NLM normalizes NDCs to the 11-digit HIPAA format without dashes, ensuring consistent identification. RxNorm also models relationships between concepts: an ingredient links to all its dose forms, which link to all their strengths, which link to all NDC packages — creating a navigable drug knowledge graph.
A patient is prescribed 'Metformin HCl 500 mg oral tablet' (RxCUI: 861007). This single RxCUI represents the normalized concept regardless of whether the dispensed product is from Teva, Mylan, or any other manufacturer. An EHR sending a FHIR MedicationRequest with this RxCUI allows any receiving system — a pharmacy, a care management platform, a payer — to unambiguously identify what was prescribed without needing to know the specific NDC.
NDC codes are NOT suitable for clinical interoperability on their own. They encode manufacturer, package size, and labeler — not the clinical drug concept. A clinical decision support rule built on NDC codes must be updated every time a manufacturer changes packaging or enters the market. RxNorm abstracts above this variability to support durable, maintainable clinical logic.
RxNorm is designated as the required standard for medication information in USCDI, and the HTI-1 Final Rule mandates the July 2022 RxNorm Full Monthly Release (or later) as the minimum standard for certified health IT systems as of December 31, 2025. FHIR MedicationRequest, MedicationDispense, and MedicationAdministration resources in US Core all require RxNorm codes for medication representation.
How SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm Work Together
In a modern EHR or FHIR-based health information exchange, these three terminologies operate as complementary layers of a unified clinical data model. SNOMED CT encodes the clinical context — the patient's conditions, findings, and procedures. LOINC encodes the observations that inform that context — the lab test that confirmed a diagnosis, the vital sign that prompted an intervention. RxNorm encodes the therapeutic response — the medication prescribed as a result. Together, they make a complete clinical record computable.
A patient presents with fatigue and polyuria. The clinician's EHR problem list captures suspected diabetes using SNOMED CT concept 73211009 (Diabetes mellitus).
The clinician orders a fasting plasma glucose and HbA1c. The orders carry LOINC codes 1558-6 (Fasting glucose in serum/plasma) and 4548-4 (Hemoglobin A1c/Hemoglobin.total in Blood).
Results return from the laboratory with LOINC-coded observation codes and UCUM-coded units, enabling automated interpretation and alert generation.
Diagnosis confirmed: the problem list is updated to 'Type 2 diabetes mellitus' (SNOMED CT 44054006). The ICD-10-CM map automatically suggests E11.9 for billing.
Metformin 500 mg oral tablet is prescribed. The MedicationRequest carries RxCUI 861007 alongside the NDC for the specific dispensed package.
The complete, coded record — conditions in SNOMED CT, labs in LOINC, medications in RxNorm — flows to the payer, care manager, and public health registry without loss of meaning.
Value Sets: Curating Subsets for Specific Purposes
Raw terminologies contain hundreds of thousands of concepts, but most clinical applications need only relevant subsets. A quality measure for diabetes management needs only the SNOMED CT codes for type 2 diabetes mellitus — not all 350,000 concepts. A FHIR-based allergy list needs only the RxNorm codes for common allergens. These curated subsets are called value sets, and the Value Set Authority Center (VSAC) — maintained by the NLM — is the authoritative repository for value sets used in US clinical quality measures and regulatory requirements.
VSAC serves as the official source for value sets used in CMS electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs) and digital quality measures (dQMs). Each value set consists of carefully selected codes drawn from SNOMED CT, LOINC, RxNorm, ICD-10-CM, and other standard vocabularies, with explicit versioning tied to specific terminology releases. As CMS transitions its eCQMs to FHIR-based dQMs, VSAC — which already serves value sets through a FHIR terminology API — becomes an even more critical infrastructure component, linking regulatory requirements directly to computable clinical terminology.
VSAC Integration: Any certified EHR or quality reporting system participating in CMS quality programs must implement value sets from VSAC. These value sets reference specific versions of SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm — meaning a terminology update in one vocabulary can cascade into required value set updates across the entire quality measurement ecosystem.
Cross-Terminology Mapping
The SNOMED CT-to-ICD-10-CM map is the most widely used cross-terminology map in US healthcare, enabling automated generation of billing codes from clinical documentation. Similarly, the SNOMED CT-to-LOINC collaboration — formalized as the SNOMED-LOINC ontology — defines formal relationships between SNOMED CT clinical concepts and LOINC observation codes, enabling richer semantic queries. For example, the SNOMED CT concept for 'Measurement of serum creatinine' can be formally linked to LOINC 2160-0 (Creatinine [Mass/volume] in Serum or Plasma), allowing a FHIR server to answer queries that span both terminologies seamlessly.
Real-World Impact: When Vocabularies Fail — and When They Succeed
The stakes of clinical terminology interoperability are not abstract. When terminologies are absent, inconsistent, or incorrectly mapped, the consequences range from administrative inefficiency to direct patient harm. For a sense of scale, the West Health Institute estimated in 2013 that making medical devices interoperable with each other and with EHRs could save more than $30 billion a year — through less redundant testing, less manual data entry, fewer adverse events, and shorter stays.
Terminology Failures in Practice
Consider a patient with a documented penicillin allergy in one hospital's EHR system. When that patient transfers to a different hospital or visits an urgent care clinic, their record arrives as a PDF or a raw HL7 v2 message with a free-text allergy field reading 'PCN allergy.' The receiving EHR's clinical decision support engine, which checks for SNOMED CT-coded allergy concepts, does not recognize 'PCN allergy' as a coded entry. The alert does not fire. Without the proper SNOMED CT allergy concept code (e.g., 91936005 — Allergy to penicillin), the safety net disappears at the exact moment the patient crosses organizational boundaries.
Medication errors are another critical failure mode. A clinician attempting to prescribe 3.125 mg of carvedilol (a common heart failure dose) may find the EHR's medication picker lists only 6.25 mg tablets — because the EHR was not mapped to the correct RxNorm concepts for the 3.125 mg strength (RxCUI 686924). The clinician must manually override, creating both cognitive burden and documentation ambiguity. When RxNorm normalization is incomplete or out of date, these gaps propagate across e-prescribing, pharmacy dispensing, and medication reconciliation workflows.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, the rapid creation of LOINC codes for SARS-CoV-2 tests (e.g., LOINC 94500-6 for the SARS-CoV-2 RNA PCR test) enabled the CDC to aggregate standardized lab results from thousands of testing sites across the country within a unified surveillance framework. HHS's June 2020 CARES Act laboratory reporting guidance then required LOINC-coded results, so every testing site reported the same test the same way — a real-world demonstration of what standardized terminology makes possible at scale.
ONC and CMS Enforcement
Federal regulations have progressively tightened terminology requirements to address these failure modes. The 21st Century Cures Act established information blocking prohibitions and required ONC-certified health IT to support USCDI data elements with required terminologies. The HTI-1 Final Rule (effective February 2024) mandates specific minimum releases of SNOMED CT, LOINC, and RxNorm in certified systems and made USCDI v3, exposed through US Core 6.1.0 FHIR APIs, the certification baseline from January 1, 2026 — with labs coded in LOINC, medications in RxNorm, and conditions in SNOMED CT. Developers, HIEs, and HINs that commit information blocking face civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation, imposed by the HHS Office of Inspector General.
The goal is not just data exchange — it is data understanding. A lab result that cannot be interpreted by the receiving system is not interoperability; it is just file transfer.
The convergence of regulatory pressure, FHIR adoption, and value-based care incentives is accelerating the transition from free-text and proprietary coding to standardized, computable vocabularies. Health systems that invest in clean SNOMED CT problem lists, LOINC-coded lab results, and RxNorm-normalized medication records today are building the data foundation for AI-driven clinical decision support, population health analytics, and seamless patient data portability that will define the next decade of healthcare.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-uscdi | USCDI: The Minimum Dataset for Interoperability
USCDI: The United States Core Data for Interoperability Standard
What Is USCDI?
The United States Core Data for Interoperability — universally abbreviated as USCDI — is a standardized set of health data classes and constituent data elements that ONC (the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology) has designated as the minimum dataset required for nationwide, interoperable health information exchange. Think of USCDI as the federal government's official answer to a fundamental question: when any two health IT systems in the United States share patient data, which fields must both sides be capable of sending and receiving?
USCDI was first published in July 2020 as part of the ONC 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule. Before USCDI existed, its predecessor — the Common Clinical Data Set (CCDS) — served a similar purpose, but lacked the structured versioning and annual update cycle that USCDI introduced. USCDI is not a FHIR implementation guide, a claims format, or a coding system. It sits one level above all of those: it defines *what* data must be interoperable, leaving the technical *how* to implementation guides like HL7 FHIR US Core.
USCDI defines the minimum dataset for interoperability — it tells the healthcare ecosystem which data elements every certified health IT system must be able to exchange, regardless of vendor or care setting.
The standard is managed entirely by ONC, an agency within the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS). ONC maintains USCDI through an open, publicly participatory process: any stakeholder — a hospital, a health IT developer, a patient advocacy group, or an individual clinician — can submit new data element proposals via the ONC New Data Element and Class (ONDEC) Submission System. Submissions go through a maturity-level review. Elements that reach Level 2 maturity by October of a given year are eligible for inclusion in the following year's draft USCDI, which is published in January. After public comment and review by the Health IT Advisory Committee (HITAC), the final version is published each July.
Year USCDI v1 was first published

USCDI Version History: From v1 to v6
ONC has published new USCDI versions every year since 2020, each one expanding the required dataset to reflect evolving clinical practice, public health priorities, and equity goals. Understanding the version history helps explain why compliance timelines vary across programs and why EHR vendors may support different versions simultaneously.
Version 1 — July 2020
USCDI v1 was the first published version and became the regulatory baseline for Certified EHR Technology (CEHRT) under the 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule. It encompassed 52 data elements across 16 data classes. Key additions over the predecessor CCDS included Clinical Notes, Provenance, Pediatric Vital Signs, and patient Address. USCDI v1 set the floor for what any ONC-certified EHR must be capable of exchanging.
Version 2 — July 2021
USCDI v2 added three new data classes and 22 new data elements, with an explicit focus on advancing health equity. The most significant additions were Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity (SOGI) data elements — long requested by LGBTQ+ health advocates, and later removed or revised in USCDI v3.1 (June 2025) under Executive Order 14168 — and Social Determinants of Health (SDOH) data elements that allow clinicians to document housing instability, food insecurity, and transportation barriers.
Version 3 — July 2022 (Now the Regulatory Baseline)
USCDI v3 is the most consequential version to date from a regulatory standpoint. The HTI-1 Final Rule, effective February 2024, adopted USCDI v3 as the new baseline standard for certified health IT. Importantly, ONC mandated that all health IT modules certified to criteria referencing USCDI must upgrade to v3 by January 1, 2026 — a hard compliance deadline that is reshaping EHR upgrade cycles across the industry. USCDI v3 expanded to 19 data classes and 94 data elements.
The 19 data classes in USCDI v3 cover: Allergies and Intolerances, Assessment and Plan of Treatment, Care Team Members, Clinical Notes, Clinical Tests, Diagnostic Imaging, Encounter Information, Goals, Health Insurance Information (new in v3), Health Status/Assessments (new in v3, absorbing Health Concerns), Immunizations, Laboratory, Medications, Patient Demographics/Information, Problems, Procedures, Provenance, Unique Device Identifier(s) for a Patient's Implantable Device(s), and Vital Signs. New equity-focused data elements include Disability Status, Mental/Cognitive Status, Functional Status, and Pregnancy Status.
USCDI v3 is the current mandatory baseline. All ONC-certified EHRs must support v3 by January 1, 2026 under the HTI-1 Final Rule.
Versions 4, 5, and 6 — Continued Annual Expansion
USCDI v4 added 20 data elements and one new data class to v3, including Alcohol Use, Substance Use, Physical Activity Assessments, Treatment Intervention preferences, Care Experience Preferences, and Medication Adherence data elements. USCDI v5, published July 2024, added 16 new data elements and two new data classes. USCDI v6 was published July 2025 with 6 additional data elements. Draft USCDI v7, released January 2026 for public comment, proposes 30 new data elements — the largest single-version expansion in the standard's history.
USCDI and the ONC Certification Program
USCDI does not exist in a vacuum — its power comes from its direct linkage to the ONC Health IT Certification Program. To participate in federal programs like the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS), the Medicare and Medicaid Promoting Interoperability programs, and several value-based care models, providers must use Certified EHR Technology (CEHRT). Certification, in turn, requires EHR products to demonstrate they can exchange the specific data classes and elements defined in the current regulatory baseline version of USCDI.
This creates a powerful compliance chain: federal payment programs require CEHRT → CEHRT certification requires USCDI support → USCDI defines which data elements must be interoperable. The result is that every major EHR vendor selling to hospitals, physician groups, or ambulatory clinics that accept Medicare or Medicaid must build USCDI compliance into their core product.
A regional hospital system using Epic or Oracle Health must make sure it is running its vendor's release certified to USCDI v3 — able to send and receive all 94 data elements, including the new Health Insurance Information class and the equity-focused Disability Status element. Certification belongs to the vendor's product, but the hospital carries the risk: without CEHRT that meets the updated criteria it cannot satisfy the Promoting Interoperability requirements, exposing it to Medicare payment reductions.
Real-World Application
The 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (2020) was the original legislative trigger that made USCDI certification mandatory. The subsequent HTI-1 Final Rule (effective February 8, 2024) updated the regulatory baseline from USCDI v1 to USCDI v3 and introduced the January 1, 2026 transition deadline. Notably, after January 1, 2026, ONC will no longer allow new certifications to reference USCDI v1 — v3 becomes the only valid baseline. This is not a soft guideline but a hard regulatory requirement.

USCDI+: Domain-Specific Extensions Beyond the Core
USCDI defines the national minimum dataset — but minimum is often not enough for specialized programs. ONC created USCDI+ (pronounced 'USCDI plus') to address exactly this gap. USCDI+ is an extension mechanism that allows federal agencies and programs to define domain-specific datasets that go beyond the core USCDI standard without fragmenting the broader interoperability ecosystem.
Under the USCDI+ framework, a program identifies additional data elements it needs beyond USCDI — elements that are too specialized or too nascent to be appropriate for the universal baseline but that the program's participants must be able to exchange. These elements are documented, published, and harmonized using the same structured USCDI methodology, creating a consistent, machine-readable specification for developers.
USCDI+ is not a replacement for USCDI — it is a structured extension layer. Every USCDI+ dataset builds on top of the core USCDI standard. Programs using USCDI+ still require full USCDI compliance as the foundation.
The most developed USCDI+ domain is USCDI+ Quality, built by ONC with CMS, CDC, and HRSA to support digital quality measurement. USCDI+ Quality establishes a harmonized baseline of data elements needed for a wide range of quality measurement use cases — including CMS electronic clinical quality measures (eCQMs), CMS's Data Element Library, AHRQ Common Formats, and NCQA HEDIS measures. By creating a consistent USCDI+ Quality data element list, ONC and CMS aim to reduce the fragmentation that currently exists when different quality programs require the same underlying clinical data but specify it in incompatible ways.
CDC has also engaged with the USCDI+ framework for public health reporting extensions. The model reflects a broader philosophy: rather than allow each federal program to independently define and require its own proprietary dataset — which would force EHR vendors to build dozens of separate integrations — USCDI+ creates a managed, centrally coordinated extension layer where new program needs are documented and harmonized against each other and against the core standard.

How USCDI Maps to the US Core FHIR Implementation Guide
USCDI tells you *what* data must be interoperable. The US Core FHIR Implementation Guide (IG) — published by HL7 and maintained in close coordination with ONC — tells you *how* to represent and exchange that data using FHIR resources and profiles. Understanding the relationship between these two standards is essential for any health IT developer building interoperability solutions.
The US Core IG defines FHIR profiles — constrained versions of base FHIR resources — that implement each USCDI data class and element with Must Support constraints, terminology bindings, and search parameters. For example, the USCDI Allergies and Intolerances data class maps to the US Core AllergyIntolerance profile; the USCDI Clinical Notes data class maps to the US Core DocumentReference and DiagnosticReport profiles; the USCDI Patient Demographics class maps to the US Core Patient profile.
Each new version of US Core is designed to align with a corresponding version of USCDI. US Core v6 aligns with USCDI v3; US Core v7 and later versions align with subsequent USCDI releases. However, the mapping is not always one-to-one. A single USCDI data class may map to multiple FHIR profiles, and many US Core profile elements have no direct USCDI counterpart — because US Core's scope is broader than certification. US Core also includes elements needed to make FHIR technically functional that USCDI does not explicitly require.
USCDI data class names and FHIR resource names often differ. 'Health Status/Assessments' in USCDI does not map cleanly to a single FHIR resource — it spans Observation, Condition, and other resources depending on the specific data element. Always consult the US Core USCDI mapping table when implementing FHIR APIs for USCDI compliance.
FHIR Naming vs. USCDI Naming
For ONC certification, EHRs must demonstrate they support the FHIR-based APIs specified in the certification criteria — which reference US Core profiles as the implementation specification for USCDI-required data. In practice, this means demonstrating that a FHIR server can return Patient, AllergyIntolerance, Condition, MedicationRequest, DiagnosticReport, Observation, DocumentReference, and other US Core-profiled resources for the data elements required by the certified USCDI version.
USCDI and FHIR US Core are complementary initiatives, with USCDI defining high-level data requirements and FHIR US Core providing detailed FHIR-based profiles for meeting those requirements. Mapping between them is necessary for achieving interoperability and consistency in healthcare data exchange.
Real-World Implementation Challenges
Despite USCDI's clear regulatory mandate and structured versioning process, real-world implementation remains far from uniform. Multiple categories of challenges have emerged as the standard has expanded from 52 data elements in v1 to 94 in v3 — and continues to grow with each annual release.
Data Class Ambiguity
One of the most persistent criticisms of USCDI — raised prominently by the Electronic Health Record Association (EHRA) — is the ambiguity in data class definitions. When a data class definition is broad or imprecise, EHR vendors may implement it in materially different ways while both claiming compliance. This ambiguity creates friction at exactly the point where standardization is supposed to reduce it: when two certified systems try to exchange the 'same' data element and find it encoded differently.
Legacy Systems and Upgrade Costs
Many hospitals — particularly critical access hospitals, rural facilities, psychiatric hospitals, and safety-net providers — run older EHR infrastructure that was certified to USCDI v1 or earlier CCDS standards. Upgrading to USCDI v3 compliance is not a configuration change; it often requires significant software development, data migration, and staff retraining. ONC data from 2015 showed 96% of non-federal acute care hospitals using certified EHR technology, while only 15% of psychiatric hospitals had adopted even a basic EHR — a gap rooted in their exclusion from the Meaningful Use incentive payments.
Coded vs. Unstructured Data
USCDI compliance assumes data exists in structured, coded form. But in clinical practice, a substantial portion of medically significant information lives in unstructured clinical notes, scanned documents, and free-text fields. Oncology is a stark example: many pathology results remain uncoded in EHRs because clinicians manually transcribe pathology reports without applying standardized terminologies like SNOMED CT or LOINC. An EHR may be technically certified to send the Laboratory data class, but if the underlying data is unstructured, the API call returns incomplete or absent records.
Version Lag Between Certification and Clinical Reality
Because USCDI is updated annually but regulatory baselines are set through formal rulemaking — USCDI v3, published in July 2022, was not adopted until the HTI-1 rule of January 2024 — there is always a gap between the most current USCDI version and the version required for certification. As of 2026, the regulatory baseline is USCDI v3 (published 2022), while ONC has already published v5 and v6 and is drafting v7. Programs that want to use elements from v4 or v5 for quality measurement must rely on USCDI+ or non-regulatory mechanisms — adding complexity for developers who must support multiple versions simultaneously.
A care coordination vendor building a post-discharge follow-up platform wants to capture Medication Adherence data — an element added in USCDI v4. If the EHRs they integrate with are only certified to USCDI v3, they have no standardized way to request that data element via the FHIR API. They must either negotiate custom extensions with each EHR vendor, use an HL7 FHIR Questionnaire workaround, or wait until the regulatory baseline advances to v4 — which may be years away.

Key Takeaways
USCDI is ONC's standardized minimum dataset for interoperability — it defines which health data classes and elements every certified EHR must be capable of exchanging.
The standard launched in July 2020 (v1) and is updated annually, with draft versions published each January and final versions each July.
USCDI v3 (19 data classes, 94 elements) is the current regulatory baseline, mandated for all ONC-certified EHRs by January 1, 2026 under the HTI-1 Final Rule.
USCDI+ is an extension mechanism for sector-specific data needs, used for CDC public health reporting, CMS quality measurement, cancer, behavioral health, and maternal health.
USCDI and FHIR US Core are complementary: USCDI defines what data must be exchangeable; US Core defines how to represent it in FHIR.
Implementation challenges include version lag (v1 vs v3 gaps), inconsistent mapping to FHIR resources, and the shift from free text to coded data elements.
Key Takeaways
The HTI-1 (Health Data, Technology, and Interoperability) Final Rule, effective February 8, 2024, adopted USCDI v3 as the new certification baseline and set January 1, 2026 as the hard deadline for all certified health IT to transition from USCDI v1 to v3. The original 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule established USCDI v1 as the initial baseline in 2020.

Da Vinci and Gravity: FHIR Implementation Guides Solving Real Payer and SDOH Problems
What Are FHIR Implementation Guides?
FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) is often called "the language of modern healthcare data," but a language alone is not enough. Two systems can both speak FHIR and still be unable to exchange data usefully if they use different resource structures, terminology codes, or workflow expectations. This is where Implementation Guides — IGs — come in. An IG is a formal, published specification that narrows the broad flexibility of FHIR into precise, agreed-upon rules for a specific use case. It defines which resources must be supported, which data fields are required versus optional, which code systems to use, and how the API calls should flow between systems.
HL7 International publishes FHIR IGs through a rigorous multi-stage process. A project team drafts the IG, submits it for community ballot as a "Standard for Trial Use" (STU), receives and reconciles hundreds of public comments from implementers, vendors, and regulators, and then publishes a revised version that reflects real-world feedback. Only after sustained, demonstrated implementation does a specification mature toward Normative status. This process ensures that IGs are not just theoretical documents — they are living standards shaped by the engineers, clinicians, and payers who actually build and operate systems against them.
Two HL7 FHIR Accelerator programs have produced the most influential IGs in the payer-provider space: the Da Vinci Project and the Gravity Project. An Accelerator is a structured program inside HL7 that brings together industry stakeholders to build and test IGs faster than the traditional standards process alone allows. Each Accelerator has a specific domain focus, a governing structure, and a commitment to testing in real pilots before declaring work complete.
Think of FHIR as the English language and an Implementation Guide as a legal contract written in English. Both parties understand the words, but the contract specifies exactly which terms mean what, what must be delivered by when, and what happens when something goes wrong. Without the contract, two fluent English speakers can still talk past each other.
FHIR is flexible by design; IGs add the constraints that make interoperability precise and reliable.
The Da Vinci Project was founded in 2019 as an HL7 FHIR Accelerator with a specific mandate: accelerate FHIR adoption in value-based care by solving the most painful payer-provider data exchange problems. The project started with twenty-two founding member organizations and has grown to more than sixty industry-leading payers, providers, and health IT vendors. Its work is organized into use cases — discrete problem statements — each of which produces its own Implementation Guide and reference implementation. CMS's prior authorization interoperability mandates, finalized in the 2024 CMS-0057-F rule, cite Da Vinci IGs directly as the required technical standards.
The Gravity Project has a different origin and a different focus. It was initiated in November 2018 by the Social Interventions Research and Evaluation Network (SIREN) at the University of California, San Francisco, in collaboration with EMI Advisors LLC of Bethesda, Maryland. With initial funding from the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, SIREN launched Gravity in 2019 as a national collaborative effort to develop structured data standards for social determinants of health (SDOH). Where Da Vinci attacks billing and authorization friction, Gravity attacks a different gap: the absence of standardized, machine-readable codes for the social conditions — food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers — that drive as much as 80 percent of health outcomes but are almost never documented in a form that clinical systems can act on.

Key Da Vinci IGs: PDex, PAS, CRD, and DTR
Da Vinci has published more than a dozen Implementation Guides. Four have become the centerpiece of federal interoperability mandates and real-world payer-provider integrations: the Payer Data Exchange IG (PDex), the Prior Authorization Support IG (PAS), the Coverage Requirements Discovery IG (CRD), and the Documentation Templates and Rules IG (DTR). Together these four IGs address the most administratively burdensome touchpoints in the American healthcare system: sharing a patient's longitudinal record when they switch payers, submitting and adjudicating prior authorization requests in near real-time, and ensuring that providers surface payer coverage rules inside their own EHR workflow before ordering a service.
The Payer Data Exchange IG (PDex), currently at version 2.1.0 (STU2.1) with version 2.2.0 in continuous development, defines the FHIR API surface that enables two critical data flows. First, payer-to-payer exchange: when a patient changes health plans, the new payer can call the old payer's PDex API to retrieve the patient's complete clinical history as FHIR resources conforming to US Core profiles. Second, payer-to-provider exchange: providers can call a payer's PDex endpoint to retrieve administrative and claims-derived clinical data about a patient, eliminating fax-based information requests. PDex has been updated to align with both US Core 6.1.0 and 7.0.0, enabling compliance with both CMS-0057-F and the ONC HTI-1 rule simultaneously.
The Prior Authorization Support IG (PAS), at version 2.1.0, defines a FHIR-based API workflow that replaces traditional X12 278 prior authorization transactions. Under PAS, a provider's EHR submits a FHIR Claim resource — bundled with all required supporting documentation — to the payer's PAS endpoint. The payer's system evaluates the request, potentially in real-time using clinical decision support, and returns a ClaimResponse resource. The entire round-trip can happen in seconds for straightforward cases, compared to the 72-hour or multi-day waits that characterize traditional PA processes. CMS-0057-F identifies PAS IG version STU 2.0.1 as the normative standard for the Prior Authorization API that covered payers must implement by January 1, 2027.
When a clinician opens an order in their EHR, CRD fires a FHIR hook to the payer. The payer returns coverage requirements — whether PA is needed, which documentation templates apply — directly inside the EHR workflow, before the order is placed.
CRD: Discover Coverage Rules at the Point of Care
If CRD signals that documentation is required, DTR launches a SMART-on-FHIR app within the EHR. The app pre-populates documentation templates with data already in the record, prompting the clinician only for missing information. This dramatically reduces manual data entry.
DTR: Complete Documentation Inside the EHR
Once documentation is complete, the EHR assembles a FHIR Bundle and submits it to the payer's PAS endpoint. The payer evaluates the request and returns a real-time response — approved, pended, or denied — with the explanation included in the structured FHIR response.
PAS: Submit the Prior Auth Request as FHIR
The entire workflow — from order placement to authorization decision — happens inside structured, auditable FHIR API calls. No faxes, no phone queues, no manual re-keying of data that already exists in the EHR.
Close the Loop: Eliminate the Fax
How the Da Vinci CRD + DTR + PAS Workflow Flows
Coverage Requirements Discovery (CRD), currently at version 2.1.0, is the upstream trigger in the Da Vinci burden-reduction workflow. It leverages CDS Hooks — a standard for embedding clinical decision support into EHR workflows — to allow payers to inject coverage information at the exact moment a clinician is making a treatment decision. CRD answers the question "Does this patient's plan require prior authorization for this service?" before the order is finalized, not after. This timing is critical: it is far more efficient to surface a coverage requirement during the ordering workflow than to discover a PA is needed only after a claim is denied.
Documentation Templates and Rules (DTR), at version 2.1.0, is the companion to CRD. Where CRD identifies what is required, DTR provides the mechanism for gathering it. DTR uses SMART on FHIR to launch a payer-curated questionnaire application inside the provider's EHR. Using CQL (Clinical Quality Language) logic, the app queries the patient's FHIR records to pre-populate answers wherever the data already exists, surfacing only the truly missing information to the clinician. CMS has established its own Document Requirements Lookup Service (DRLS) — which combines CRD and DTR functionality — specifically for Medicare Fee-for-Service programs, validating the architecture at the federal level.
