Da Vinci in Regulation: How CMS-0057-F Codified These IGs into Law
The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule — formally CMS-0057-F — was published in January 2024 and represents the most consequential federal interoperability mandate since the 2020 CMS and ONC interoperability rules. The rule applies to Medicare Advantage organizations, state Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service programs, Medicaid managed care plans, CHIP managed care entities, and Qualified Health Plan issuers on the Federally Facilitated Exchanges. Collectively, these plans cover the majority of Americans with government-sponsored or exchange-based coverage.
CMS-0057-F establishes a two-phase compliance timeline. The first phase took effect January 1, 2026: covered payers must now respond to standard prior authorization requests within 7 calendar days and to expedited requests within 72 hours; they must include specific, structured reasons for any denial; and they must begin publicly reporting prior authorization metrics, with the first annual reports due March 31, 2026 covering calendar year 2025 data. These provisions are not FHIR-specific — they are operational requirements that any payer must meet regardless of their technology approach. However, they create enormous pressure for automation, because manual PA processes cannot reliably meet 72-hour response windows at scale.
The second phase — and the one that directly references Da Vinci IGs — takes effect January 1, 2027. By that date, covered payers must have four FHIR-based APIs live and in production: a Patient Access API (based on PDex), a Provider Access API (also based on PDex), a Payer-to-Payer API (PDex again), and a Prior Authorization API based on Da Vinci PAS IG version STU 2.0.1. This is a landmark moment in U.S. healthcare standards history: for the first time, a specific named private-sector Implementation Guide — developed by a multi-stakeholder coalition, not a government body — is cited by name in a federal rule as a required technical standard. The Da Vinci Project's architecture has, in effect, become federal infrastructure.
CMS-0057-F requires covered payers to implement the Da Vinci PAS IG (STU 2.0.1) as the technical standard for their Prior Authorization API by January 1, 2027 — making Da Vinci specifications enforceable federal requirements for Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and exchange plans.
The compliance landscape is challenging. Survey data from WEDI (Workgroup for Electronic Data Interchange) from late 2025 found that many payers were still in early stages of implementation for the Prior Authorization API specifically, with readiness varying widely across plan types and sizes. Smaller plans and state Medicaid agencies face particularly steep technical lift, as they may lack the internal engineering capacity to build FHIR API infrastructure from scratch. This has driven a cottage industry of FHIR platform vendors offering turnkey compliance solutions built on top of the Da Vinci specifications.
The regulation also reflects a broader policy strategy: rather than CMS building and mandating its own proprietary technology, the agency is leveraging privately developed, community-consensus standards that have already been tested in real implementations. This approach reduces the risk of government-mandated technology failures and creates a market-driven path to adoption — payers who implement Da Vinci IGs well will have a competitive compliance advantage, which accelerates the overall ecosystem. In mid-2025, more than fifty major health insurers voluntarily committed to targeting at least 80 percent real-time electronic prior authorization approval rates by 2027, reflecting the industry's recognition that FHIR-based PA is not just a regulatory requirement but a genuine operational efficiency driver.
Regence BlueCross BlueShield and MultiCare Connected Care became early proof that Da Vinci's architecture works at production scale. They launched what was described as the nation's first scalable FHIR-based prior authorization system using Da Vinci specifications. The results were dramatic: 94 percent of prior authorization inquiries received an immediate response — meaning the request was either approved or determined to require no PA at all — within seconds of submission. Clinicians at MultiCare could make requests directly from within their EHR, and the authorization decision flowed back into the same workflow without phone calls or faxes. At HIMSS23, MultiCare's Anna Taylor and Regence's Heidi Kriz presented this outcome as a benchmark for what standards-based prior authorization can achieve in practice.
Regence and MultiCare: The Nation's First Scalable FHIR Prior Authorization System
The Gravity Project: Putting Social Determinants of Health into FHIR
Social determinants of health — the conditions in which people are born, live, learn, work, and age — are estimated to drive 80 percent or more of health outcomes, yet they have historically been invisible to clinical information systems. A clinician might know that a patient's diabetes is poorly controlled, but unless food insecurity is documented in a structured, coded field, the health system has no way to connect that clinical problem to its social cause, refer the patient to a food pantry, or measure whether that referral reduced hospitalizations. The Gravity Project exists specifically to close that gap.
Gravity's approach is rigorous and consensus-driven. For each SDOH domain, a multi-stakeholder work group assembles the evidence base for how that condition should be defined, screened for, and documented. The group then works with SNOMED CT International, Regenstrief Institute (which stewards LOINC), and the ICD-10 Coordination and Maintenance Committee to create or curate the actual codes that represent each concept. This is painstaking work — getting a new concept into SNOMED CT or LOINC can take 12 to 18 months — but it ensures that Gravity's value sets are grounded in internationally recognized, maintained terminology systems rather than local codes that fragment data across organizations.
The Gravity SDOH Clinical Care Implementation Guide, currently at version 2.3.0 (STU 2.3, generated May 2025 and based on FHIR R4), defines FHIR profiles, value sets, and workflows for the full SDOH care cycle: screening a patient for social needs, documenting findings as FHIR Observations and Conditions, creating FHIR ServiceRequests for community referrals, and tracking the status of those referrals through FHIR Tasks. Version 3.0.0 is currently in ballot as of early 2026, with expanded domain coverage and improved alignment with the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI).
Including food insecurity, housing instability, transportation, education, employment, and more

Terminology Bodies Partnering with Gravity
The SDOH domains covered by the Gravity IG span far beyond the two most commonly discussed. Food insecurity and housing instability were the first domains completed — the Gravity Project completed its initial food insecurity and housing data identification work before expanding. The current IG includes value sets and profiles for transportation insecurity, utility insecurity (inability to pay for heat, electricity, or water), educational attainment barriers, employment and financial strain, social isolation, intimate partner violence, and digital access barriers, among others. Each domain has a corresponding set of screening questions (mapped to LOINC panel codes), condition codes (mapped to SNOMED CT and ICD-10), and intervention codes for referrals.
State health systems and Medicaid programs are now formally recognizing Gravity standards. Washington State's 2025 FHIR Infrastructure Roadmap named the Gravity SDOH Clinical Care IG as a core interoperability standard for community and clinical data exchange. New York sought to leverage Gravity standards for exchange of SDOH screenings between clinical systems and community-based organizations like Unite Us and FindHelp, ensuring that FHIR-compliant screenings could be ingested by social care platforms in real-time. Colorado's vendor contracts for its statewide social care platform explicitly require Gravity-aligned terminology and FHIR-based exchange. These state-level mandates are creating the network effects that transform a voluntary standard into a de facto requirement.
A patient comes in for a diabetes follow-up. The nurse administers the LOINC-coded AHC HRSN screening panel (LOINC panel code 96777-8) inside the EHR. The patient screens positive for food insecurity. The EHR creates a FHIR Observation with LOINC code 88122-7 ("Within the past 12 months, we worried whether our food would run out before we got money to buy more") and a FHIR Condition with SNOMED CT code 733423003 ("Food insecurity"). The care coordinator creates a FHIR ServiceRequest for a food pantry referral, which is transmitted via Task to the community-based organization's FHIR endpoint. When the referral is fulfilled, the CBO updates the Task status, and the EHR receives a structured confirmation — all without a fax machine or a phone call.
How Gravity Codes Flow Through a Real Care Encounter
Implementation Reality: Adoption, Challenges, and What Comes Next
Real-world adoption of both Da Vinci and Gravity IGs is accelerating but uneven. On the Da Vinci side, the Regence-MultiCare prior authorization pilot is no longer an outlier — it is a benchmark. The Da Vinci Trebuchet pilot program organizes multi-organization cohorts to test specific IGs in production environments, with 2026 cohorts already forming. CMS's regulatory deadline of January 1, 2027 for FHIR-based PA APIs is creating real urgency across the industry. Roughly 65 percent of EHR transactions on Epic systems achieved electronic prior authorization by 2025, with ePA transaction volumes nearly doubling from 2023 to early 2025.
The barriers to full PAS IG adoption are real and multi-layered. Technical complexity is one factor — implementing a compliant FHIR Claim submission endpoint that correctly handles all PAS workflow states (pended, approved, denied, modified) requires significant engineering investment. Organizational alignment is another: the PAS workflow requires both the EHR vendor and the payer platform to implement complementary sides of the same API, which means bilateral negotiations that take time. Smaller regional health plans and safety-net providers face resource constraints that make in-house implementation difficult. And despite a January 2027 deadline, WEDI's 2025 surveys found that a meaningful share of covered entities had not yet begun implementation work for the Prior Authorization API specifically.
ONC has provided an important tool to support PAS adoption: the Da Vinci Prior Authorization Support Test Kit, launched on Inferno (the federal FHIR testing platform). This test kit allows implementers to validate their PAS implementations against the IG's conformance requirements before going live, reducing the risk of interoperability failures in production. The existence of an authoritative, publicly available test kit is a meaningful maturity signal — it means the IG has progressed from specification to executable, testable infrastructure.
CMS-0057-F's January 1, 2027 API implementation deadline applies to Medicare Advantage, Medicaid managed care, CHIP managed care, and exchange plans. Plans that fail to meet requirements face potential compliance action. The prior authorization operational requirements (72-hour expedited, 7-day standard response) already took effect January 1, 2026. Organizations that have not begun their Da Vinci PAS implementation should treat this as an urgent priority, not a future concern.
The 2027 Deadline Is Not a Soft Target
On the Gravity side, the implementation picture is more heterogeneous. Major EHR platforms including Epic have built SDOH screening and documentation modules that align with Gravity value sets, making it easier for health systems to capture structured SDOH data. But the harder problem — closing the referral loop with community-based organizations — remains a work in progress. CBOs typically lack the technical capacity to build FHIR endpoints, so interoperability between clinical systems and the social care sector depends on intermediary platforms like Unite Us, FindHelp, and Aunt Bertha that can translate between FHIR and the APIs those organizations actually use. States like New York and Colorado are addressing this through explicit vendor contract requirements, creating the contractual obligation that drives technical investment.
Looking ahead, both projects have substantial roadmaps. Da Vinci is expanding into clinical data exchange between providers and payers for value-based care performance measurement, and is developing IGs for attachments — the structured clinical documents that support claims adjudication. Gravity is developing version 3.0 of its SDOH Clinical Care IG with expanded domain coverage and is pursuing deeper integration with the United States Core Data for Interoperability (USCDI) — the federally required minimum dataset for EHR certification. As SDOH data elements enter USCDI and EHR certification criteria, Gravity's approach shifts from voluntary best practice to the floor that every certified EHR must support. That normative shift, once complete, will make structured social needs documentation as routine as recording a blood pressure.

HIPAA Security Rule: Protecting Health Data in Motion and at Rest
HIPAA Security Rule: What It Is and Who It Covers
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) established foundational privacy and security protections for health information. While the broader statute passed in 1996, the Security Rule that specifically governs electronic protected health information (ePHI) was published as a final rule in February 2003, took effect that April, and required compliance by April 21, 2005 — giving the industry two years to build compliance programs before enforcement began. For over two decades, this single regulatory framework has governed how hospitals, insurers, clinics, and their vendors protect the most sensitive data Americans share with anyone: their medical records.
The Security Rule applies exclusively to ePHI — health information that is created, received, maintained, or transmitted in electronic form and that can be used to identify an individual. This is a critical distinction: paper records and purely verbal communications fall under the Privacy Rule, not the Security Rule. Every piece of digitally stored patient data, from an EHR record to a lab result sent by secure message, is ePHI and therefore subject to the Security Rule's three categories of safeguards: administrative, physical, and technical. Understanding which data qualifies as ePHI is the first step in building a defensible compliance posture, because scope errors — assuming a system is out of scope when it is not — are among the most common gaps auditors and regulators find.
Two categories of organizations must comply with the Security Rule: covered entities and business associates. Covered entities are health plans, healthcare clearinghouses, and healthcare providers who transmit health information electronically. Business associates are any vendors or contractors that create, receive, maintain, or transmit ePHI on a covered entity's behalf — from cloud storage providers to billing companies to telehealth platforms. The HITECH Act of 2009 extended direct Security Rule liability to business associates, meaning regulators can sanction a vendor directly, not merely through the covered entity that hired them. Business associate agreements (BAAs) — contracts specifying how ePHI may be used and protected — are the contractual mechanism that operationalizes this shared responsibility.

Required vs. Addressable Specifications (2003 Rule)
A persistent misconception is that "addressable" means "optional." Under the 2003 rule, an addressable specification still requires implementation unless the organization formally documents why it is not reasonable and appropriate and adopts an equivalent alternative. Regulators have sanctioned organizations that treated addressable as a free pass. The proposed 2025 update eliminates this distinction entirely, making all specifications required — discussed in Section 4.
Any system that touches ePHI — even indirectly, such as a log aggregation tool that ingests audit trails from an EHR — may be considered in-scope for the Security Rule. Conduct a thorough data flow mapping exercise to identify every system that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits ePHI before scoping your compliance program.
Scope Creep Is a Compliance Risk
Administrative Safeguards: The Compliance Foundation That Most Organizations Get Wrong
Administrative safeguards are the policies, procedures, and training programs that govern how an organization manages the security of ePHI. They are the largest category in the Security Rule and, by OCR's own enforcement data, the most consistently deficient. Among all administrative requirements, the security risk analysis stands out as the single most commonly cited deficiency in OCR enforcement actions year after year. A 2016–2017 OCR compliance audit found that only 14 percent of covered entities were substantially fulfilling their regulatory responsibilities for risk analysis — meaning roughly 86 percent had meaningful gaps at the time of audit. That figure has improved since but risk analysis failures remain the dominant enforcement trigger.
What does a compliant risk analysis actually require? The Security Rule mandates an accurate and thorough assessment of the potential risks and vulnerabilities to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all ePHI the organization creates, receives, maintains, or transmits. OCR has been explicit that a risk analysis must cover all ePHI across all systems — not just the primary EHR. Organizations that base their risk analysis on a template form, or that scope it only to one system without mapping all data flows, are producing a non-compliant document. Following a risk analysis, the organization must implement a risk management plan that reduces identified risks to a reasonable and appropriate level — and that plan must be reviewed and updated on a regular basis, not filed and forgotten.
Other administrative safeguards include designation of a security official responsible for developing and implementing security policies, a workforce security program that grants access only to employees who need it, an information access management process, security awareness training for all workforce members (including phishing simulations and periodic refreshers), security incident procedures, and a contingency plan covering data backup, disaster recovery, and emergency mode operations. Each of these must be documented in written policies. In October 2024, OCR launched a dedicated "Risk Analysis Initiative" and by April 2025 had announced eight enforcement actions — all citing failure to conduct an adequate risk analysis as a foundational violation that enabled or worsened subsequent breaches.

After a March 2023 ransomware attack on Elgon Information Systems — a Massachusetts business associate providing EMR and billing services, with about 31,000 people affected — OCR found the company had failed to conduct an accurate and thorough risk analysis of the risks and vulnerabilities to ePHI. The case settled in January 2025 for $80,000 plus a corrective action plan, the second action under OCR's Risk Analysis Initiative. The penalty illustrates that even smaller business associates face direct financial consequences for administrative safeguard failures — OCR does not reserve enforcement solely for large health systems.
Elgon Information Systems: $80,000 for Skipping Risk Analysis
Physical Safeguards: Protecting the Hardware That Holds Health Data
Physical safeguards govern the physical access to facilities, workstations, and devices that store or process ePHI. The Security Rule organizes physical safeguards into four standards: facility access controls, workstation use, workstation security, and device and media controls. While technical controls like encryption and firewalls receive more attention, physical safeguards address an equally important attack surface — the reality that an attacker who can walk into a server room, pick up an unencrypted laptop, or photograph a monitor displaying patient records has bypassed every technical control in place. Physical breaches also include less dramatic but highly common failures such as leaving a workstation unlocked, disposing of a hard drive without secure erasure, or allowing unauthorized visitors into restricted areas.
Facility access controls require covered entities to implement policies that limit physical access to electronic information systems and the facilities where they are housed to authorized personnel. Implementation specifications under this standard include contingency operations (ensuring authorized personnel can access facilities during an emergency), a facility security plan, access establishment and modification procedures, and validation procedures for personnel requesting access. Workstation use and security standards require that every workstation handling ePHI has a documented policy describing its expected use and physical surroundings, and that physical safeguards restrict access to authorized users — including locked screen policies, privacy screens in public-facing areas, and physical positioning of monitors away from foot traffic in reception areas.
Device and media controls address the movement of hardware and electronic media containing ePHI. Required specifications include disposal procedures (ensuring ePHI is destroyed before a device is retired), and media re-use policies (ensuring ePHI is cleared before a device is reassigned). Addressable specifications include accountability (tracking the movement of devices and media) and data backup and storage before movement. The rise of bring-your-own-device (BYOD) policies has significantly complicated physical safeguard compliance: HIPAA does not distinguish between corporate-owned and personal devices — if a personal smartphone stores or transmits ePHI, it falls within the Security Rule's scope and must be subject to the same device controls, including the ability to remotely wipe ePHI if the device is lost or the employee departs. Mobile Device Management (MDM) platforms have become a near-mandatory operational tool for organizations with any BYOD exposure.
Organizations that allow employees to access ePHI on personal devices without a formal BYOD policy and MDM enrollment face compounding risks: no remote wipe capability, no audit trail, no configuration enforcement. When a device is lost or stolen, the inability to confirm whether ePHI was present — let alone protected — may trigger breach notification obligations.
BYOD Without MDM Is a High-Risk Configuration

Physical Safeguard Controls: Facility vs. Device Focus
In February 2024, OCR announced a $4.75 million settlement with Montefiore Medical Center after an employee stole and sold patient data affecting 12,517 individuals over a six-month period. The investigation found that Montefiore had failed to implement adequate access controls and workforce monitoring that would have detected or prevented the insider theft. This case demonstrates that physical and administrative safeguards are intertwined: workforce access controls, audit logging, and anomaly detection working together are what catch insider threats.
Montefiore Medical Center: $4.75M for Insider Theft Enabled by Access Control Gaps
Technical Safeguards and the 2025 Security Rule Overhaul
Technical safeguards are the technology controls and related policies that protect ePHI and control access to it. The Security Rule identifies four technical safeguard standards: access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, and transmission security. Access controls require covered entities to implement technical policies that allow only authorized persons to access ePHI — implemented through required specifications for unique user identification (every user gets their own login, no shared credentials) and emergency access procedures, plus addressable specifications for automatic logoff and encryption and decryption. Audit controls require hardware, software, and procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in systems that contain or use ePHI — the logs that let you answer "who accessed this patient's record and when?" after an incident.
Transmission security — the requirement that covered entities guard against unauthorized access to ePHI being transmitted over electronic communications networks — is where the 2003 rule's age shows most clearly. Encryption of data in transit was listed as an addressable specification in 2003, meaning organizations could technically document a rationale for not encrypting. In practice, the industry has converged on Transport Layer Security (TLS) as the baseline for any network transmission of ePHI, and OCR has made clear through enforcement guidance that failure to encrypt transmissions is difficult to justify as reasonable and appropriate. Encryption of data at rest — stored on servers, databases, and portable devices — was also addressable under the 2003 rule and has similarly become a de facto requirement through enforcement pressure even before the proposed 2025 update.
On January 6, 2025, HHS published a Notice of Proposed Rulemaking (NPRM) representing the most significant overhaul of the HIPAA Security Rule since its original publication — the first substantive update in over two decades. The proposed rule makes five structural changes that healthcare organizations must prepare for: First, the required/addressable distinction is eliminated — every implementation specification becomes mandatory, with only narrowly defined exceptions. Second, encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit is explicitly required, not merely addressable. Third, multi-factor authentication (MFA) is required, not optional. Fourth, regulated entities must conduct biannual vulnerability scans and annual penetration testing. Fifth, network segmentation to isolate systems that contain ePHI from other networks is required. The comment period closed March 7, 2025. HHS has not finalized the rule: the 2026 Unified Agenda lists it as a long-term action with final action projected for July 2027. As proposed, organizations would have 240 days after final publication to comply.
Think of the 2003 Security Rule as a building code that said walls "should generally" be fireproof — individual builders could document why drywall was sufficient for their situation. The 2025 proposed rule tears out that flexibility and says: every wall must meet the same fire-rating standard, period. The discretion that once allowed cost-based trade-offs is replaced by specific, measurable, auditable technical requirements.

Preparing for the Proposed Security Rule Changes
Breach Statistics, Enforcement, and the Change Healthcare Wake-Up Call
The scale of healthcare data breaches has grown dramatically since OCR began publishing its breach portal in 2009. From October 2009 through April 2026, OCR received reports of 7,670 healthcare data breaches affecting 500 or more individuals, collectively exposing the protected health information of more than 1 billion individuals — more than 2.9 times the U.S. population, reflecting the reality that many individuals have been breached multiple times. In 2023, OCR logged 732 large breaches affecting an average of 154,609 individuals each. The single largest breach that year — HCA Healthcare — affected 11.27 million individuals. Hacking and IT incidents accounted for 81% of 2023 breaches and 96% of breached records, with ransomware emerging as the dominant attack vector. OCR reported that large breaches involving ransomware increased 264% between 2018 and 2023.
In 2024, the Change Healthcare ransomware attack rewrote the scale of what a single healthcare data breach could look like. On February 21, 2024, ALPHV/BlackCat ransomware operators gained access to Change Healthcare — a subsidiary of UnitedHealth Group and the largest healthcare payment processing network in the United States. The attack disrupted the ability of pharmacies to process prescription claims and of providers to submit bills for weeks. UnitedHealth Group put the count at about 190 million in January 2025, and the HHS breach portal raised it to 192.7 million in July 2025 — making it the largest healthcare data breach in U.S. history by a wide margin. The stolen data included health insurance information, medical records, billing data, and in many cases Social Security numbers. The company estimated the financial cost at $2.45 billion for the nine months ending September 30, 2024, and that figure continued to rise.
Total 2024 breach numbers reflected the Change Healthcare effect: large breaches occurring in the year fell to 663 (from 732 in 2023), yet the total number of individuals affected reached 242.9 million — the vast majority attributable to a single incident. Hacking and IT incidents accounted for 99.45% of all breached records in 2024. OCR's enforcement activity ran in parallel: the agency imposed 22 financial penalties in calendar year 2024, collecting $9.94 million in settlements. The Risk Analysis Initiative that launched in October 2024 added eight enforcement actions by April 2025. The message from regulators is unambiguous: the cybersecurity crisis in healthcare has made HIPAA Security Rule compliance an urgent operational priority, not a check-the-box exercise.

Through 2024, OCR closed a run of ransomware investigations — Heritage Valley Health System ($950,000), Plastic Surgery Associates of South Dakota ($500,000), Cascade Eye and Skin Centers ($250,000), and Providence Medical Institute ($240,000 civil money penalty) — repeatedly citing failures to conduct adequate risk analyses and to implement appropriate security controls. Settlements came with corrective action plans requiring the controls that had been absent before the attacks. OCR's consistent message: ransomware is often preventable, and when it is not, the inadequate security program that allowed it represents independent HIPAA violations.
OCR's 2024 Run of Ransomware Enforcement Actions
The Change Healthcare breach is a systemic risk illustration, not just a company failure. A single vendor providing payment processing for hundreds of thousands of providers meant that one successful ransomware attack disrupted care delivery nationally. It is the strongest argument yet for aggressive third-party risk management and the elimination of single points of failure in healthcare infrastructure.
The HIPAA Security Rule, published February 2003 with compliance required by April 21, 2005, governs electronically protected health information (ePHI) — not paper records — for both covered entities and their business associates.
Three safeguard categories structure compliance: administrative (policies and training), physical (facility and device controls), and technical (access, audit, integrity, and transmission controls).
Risk analysis is the most commonly cited Security Rule deficiency — a 2016–17 OCR audit found only 14% of covered entities substantially meeting the requirement, and OCR's Risk Analysis Initiative (launched October 2024) generated eight enforcement actions by April 2025.
Physical safeguards are often underestimated: BYOD devices that handle ePHI are in scope regardless of ownership, and unencrypted portable devices remain a persistent breach cause.
The 2025 NPRM — the first major Security Rule update in over two decades — eliminates the required/addressable distinction, mandates encryption at rest and in transit, requires MFA, and adds biannual vulnerability scanning and annual penetration testing.
In 2024, hacking/IT incidents accounted for 99.45% of all breached records, with the Change Healthcare ransomware attack alone affecting about 192.7 million people.
OCR collected $9.94 million in HIPAA settlements in 2024 across 22 enforcement actions, signaling sustained regulatory pressure despite the administration change.
Organizations should begin preparing for the final Security Rule now (final action projected for July 2027) — audit all addressable specifications, verify encryption coverage, and establish formal vulnerability management programs before the 240-day compliance clock starts.
The 2025 NPRM's most consequential structural change is eliminating the longstanding required/addressable distinction that allowed organizations to document why encryption was not "reasonable and appropriate" for their situation. Under the proposed rule, encryption of ePHI at rest and in transit becomes an explicit requirement with no cost-based exception — meaning organizations that previously documented away their encryption obligation will need to implement it regardless of their rationale.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-deidentification | De-identification: Safe Harbor vs. Expert Determination
De-identification and Synthetic Data: Protecting Privacy While Enabling Research
Why De-identification Matters
Every time a patient visits a clinic, fills a prescription, or receives a laboratory result, that encounter generates data — and that data contains some of the most sensitive details a person can share about themselves. The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) defines Protected Health Information, or PHI, as any individually identifiable health information that is created, received, maintained, or transmitted by a covered entity or its business associates. The scope is deliberately broad: PHI covers information in any format, whether electronic, paper, or spoken, if it relates to a person's physical or mental health, the provision of care, or payment for that care.
The tension in modern healthcare data is acute. On one side, patients have a legitimate expectation that the intimate details of their medical histories will not flow freely through the world. On the other side, researchers, public-health officials, health systems, and software developers need large, representative datasets to answer important questions — how does a new treatment perform across different demographic groups? What risk factors predict hospital readmission? How can an EHR be tested without exposing real records? De-identification is the legal and technical bridge that allows health data to move across this tension without dissolving the privacy protection that patients deserve.
The regulatory stakes have also increased sharply. The 21st Century Cures Act and the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Rule have accelerated data sharing mandates across payers, providers, and health information networks. As more data flows through APIs and exchanges, the volume of PHI potentially exposed to secondary use has grown exponentially. Getting de-identification right is no longer a compliance checkbox — it is a foundational requirement for operating responsibly in a connected health system.

HIPAA's Two De-identification Methods
HIPAA's Privacy Rule, codified at 45 CFR § 164.514(b), provides two legally recognized pathways for de-identifying health information. Once either pathway is satisfied, the resulting data is no longer considered PHI and is no longer subject to HIPAA's use and disclosure restrictions. Choosing the right pathway depends on the resources available, the level of statistical rigor required, and the downstream use of the data.
The first and most commonly used method is Safe Harbor. Under Safe Harbor, a covered entity must remove all 18 categories of direct identifiers specified in the regulation: (1) names; (2) geographic subdivisions smaller than a state, including street address, city, county, precinct, and ZIP codes, with a narrow exception for three-digit ZIP codes serving populations greater than 20,000; (3) all date elements other than year that are directly related to an individual, plus ages over 89 which must be aggregated into a single "90+" category; (4) telephone numbers; (5) fax numbers; (6) email addresses; (7) Social Security numbers; (8) medical record numbers; (9) health plan beneficiary numbers; (10) account numbers; (11) certificate and license numbers; (12) vehicle identifiers and serial numbers including license plates; (13) device identifiers and serial numbers; (14) web URLs; (15) IP addresses; (16) biometric identifiers including fingerprints and voice prints; (17) full-face photographs and comparable images; and (18) any other unique identifying number, characteristic, or code. The entity must also have no actual knowledge that the remaining information could identify an individual. Safe Harbor is rules-based and requires no special statistical expertise, making it widely accessible.
The second method is Expert Determination. Here, a qualified statistician or other expert applies generally accepted principles of statistical and scientific methods to analyze the data and concludes that the risk of identifying any individual is very small. The regulation does not define "very small" numerically, leaving this to professional judgment. The expert must document their methods and findings so that the covered entity can justify the conclusion if challenged. Expert Determination is more flexible than Safe Harbor — it can retain ZIP codes or date elements that Safe Harbor would require removing — but it demands rigor, resources, and defensible documentation. Most large academic medical centers and research consortia rely on Expert Determination when they need richer geographic or temporal granularity in their datasets.
Safe Harbor

No statistical expertise required
Clear, auditable checklist
May over-strip useful data (e.g., all ZIP codes)
Best for routine data releases and smaller organizations
Expert Determination

Best for large research datasets needing analytical depth
Safe Harbor vs. Expert Determination
Re-identification Risks: The Limits of De-identification
De-identification is a risk-reduction strategy, not a guarantee of permanent anonymity. This distinction matters enormously, and a series of landmark empirical studies has demonstrated just how porous the anonymity of seemingly de-identified data can be when an adversary has access to even modest amounts of auxiliary information.
The most cited demonstration came from computer scientist Latanya Sweeney in 1997. The state of Massachusetts had released medical encounter data for approximately 135,000 state employees with obvious identifiers — names, addresses, and Social Security numbers — removed. Sweeney obtained the publicly available Cambridge, Massachusetts voter registration list, which contained name, address, date of birth, sex, and ZIP code for each voter. By linking the two datasets on the combination of five-digit ZIP code, date of birth, and sex, she was able to uniquely identify the medical records of then-Governor William Weld — demonstrating that the combination of these three "non-identifying" fields was sufficient to pinpoint an individual. Her subsequent analysis of the 1990 U.S. Census showed that 87 percent of the American population could be uniquely identified by ZIP code, date of birth, and sex alone. This trio of fields, none of which appears on HIPAA's Safe Harbor list except for detailed dates, illustrates the concept of quasi-identifiers: attributes that are individually innocuous but collectively identifying.
A decade later, in 2008, Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin published "Robust De-anonymization of Large Sparse Datasets," applying their methodology to the Netflix Prize dataset — a collection of 100 million movie ratings submitted by approximately 500,000 anonymous subscribers that Netflix released for a machine-learning competition. Narayanan and Shmatikov showed that by knowing just a few of a subscriber's movie ratings and approximate dates, an adversary could cross-reference the Netflix data with publicly available Internet Movie Database (IMDb) reviews to uniquely identify that subscriber's record with high confidence. The attack worked even when the adversary had imprecise or partial knowledge, and it succeeded even when some ratings were deliberately perturbed as a privacy defense. The Netflix study crystallized a broader principle: sparse, high-dimensional data is extraordinarily difficult to anonymize because each data point narrows down the set of plausible individuals so rapidly.
Imagine you are given a jigsaw puzzle with most pieces removed, but you can still recognize the full picture. De-identified data is like a puzzle with the corner pieces removed — it looks incomplete, but someone with a second puzzle box (auxiliary data) can fill in just enough to reconstruct the original image.
Re-identification works by combining a de-identified dataset with auxiliary external data — each additional piece narrows the field of candidates until a single individual is identified.
DNA sequences present a categorical re-identification risk that goes beyond quasi-identifiers. Even a partial genome can be matched against public genealogical databases (such as GEDmatch) to identify an individual or their relatives. The HIPAA Safe Harbor rule requires removing "biometric identifiers" but does not explicitly enumerate genomic sequences, creating an interpretive gap. Any organization sharing genomic data should treat it as permanently identifiable regardless of accompanying metadata removal.
Genomic Data Cannot Be Truly De-identified
k-anonymity, introduced by Sweeney in 1998, is a formal privacy model that requires every record in a dataset to be indistinguishable from at least k-1 other records with respect to all quasi-identifier fields. A dataset with k=5 guarantees that any re-identification attempt narrows the adversary's target to a pool of at least five people. Higher k values offer stronger protection but reduce analytical utility because they require more generalization (e.g., replacing exact age with an age range). Extensions such as l-diversity and t-closeness address additional attack vectors where k-anonymity alone is insufficient, such as when all records in a k-anonymous group share a sensitive attribute value.
The k-Anonymity Framework
Synthetic Data: A Different Privacy Approach
Where de-identification tries to protect real patients by removing or generalizing information that could identify them, synthetic data takes an entirely different approach: it generates entirely fictional records that statistically resemble a real population without corresponding to any actual individual. If no real person's data is present in the dataset, there is no real person to re-identify. This philosophical shift — from "hide the individual" to "replace the individual" — makes synthetic data an increasingly attractive option for certain use cases.
There are two broad families of synthetic data generation. Statistical synthesis methods model the marginal and joint distributions of variables in a real dataset and then draw new records from those distributions. These approaches, which include techniques such as multiple imputation and Gaussian copulas, can preserve complex correlations between variables such as the relationship between age, diagnosis codes, and medication lists. Generative model approaches use machine learning — particularly generative adversarial networks (GANs) and variational autoencoders — to learn the underlying structure of a dataset and generate new samples that are statistically realistic but do not directly copy any training record. Generative models are more powerful but also more difficult to validate and more susceptible to memorization attacks, in which the model effectively reproduces a real training record.
The most widely used open-source synthetic patient generator in health IT is Synthea, developed by MITRE Corporation. Synthea simulates the entire medical history of synthetic patients from birth to death using probabilistic disease models, clinical guidelines, and demographic data drawn from public sources. It generates output in standard formats including HL7 FHIR and C-CDA, and MITRE has made one million synthetic patient records freely available for download. Synthea has been adopted across health IT development, FHIR API testing, clinical decision support validation, machine learning model training, and healthcare education — any context where a realistic but risk-free patient dataset is needed. Because Synthea records are built from models rather than real encounters, they carry no HIPAA obligations and require no IRB approval for use.
Developers building EHR interfaces, FHIR APIs, or patient portals can use synthetic data to populate test environments with realistic records, avoiding the legal and ethical burden of using real PHI in non-production systems.
Software Development and Testing
Training predictive models requires large, labeled datasets. Synthetic data can augment real training sets or provide baseline data where real data is scarce — particularly valuable for rare diseases or underrepresented populations.
AI and Machine Learning Model Training
Medical and nursing students, health informatics trainees, and clinical staff can practice with realistic patient scenarios without exposing real patient information, supporting competency development in a safe environment.
Healthcare Education and Simulation
Researchers can release a synthetic version of their study dataset alongside a publication, enabling reproducibility and peer verification without disclosing the underlying real patient records.
Privacy-Preserving Research Publication
Key Use Cases for Synthetic Health Data
Synthetic data, however realistic, reflects the model used to generate it — not ground truth. Statistical associations that were not captured in the generation model will be absent from the synthetic dataset. Rare events and edge cases are often underrepresented. For regulatory submissions, clinical trial analysis, or population health surveillance that requires legally defensible results from real-world evidence, synthetic data is a supplement, not a replacement, for appropriately governed access to real patient records.
Synthetic Data Is Not a Perfect Substitute for Real Data
Governance Framework: When to Use What
Selecting the right privacy-preserving approach requires matching technical options to regulatory context, research purpose, and organizational risk tolerance. HIPAA provides a tiered framework for research data use that maps roughly to increasing levels of identifiability — and increasing governance requirements.
Fully de-identified data, produced by either the Safe Harbor or Expert Determination method, falls outside HIPAA entirely. Organizations can share, publish, or sell de-identified data without patient authorization, data use agreements, or IRB oversight under HIPAA (though state law and institutional policy may impose additional requirements). This is why de-identification is so valuable for large-scale data sharing initiatives: once data crosses the de-identification threshold, the regulatory friction drops substantially. However, as the re-identification literature demonstrates, fully de-identified data still carries residual risk — particularly when the data is rich in quasi-identifiers or when it will be merged with other datasets.
Between identified data and fully de-identified data sits the Limited Data Set, defined at 45 CFR § 164.514(e). A Limited Data Set retains certain geographic and date elements — city, state, ZIP code, and dates of admission, discharge, service, birth, and death — that Safe Harbor would require removing. Because a Limited Data Set still contains PHI, it must be protected: any disclosure requires a Data Use Agreement (DUA) executed between the covered entity and the recipient. The DUA must specify permitted uses and disclosures (limited to research, public health, and health care operations), identify who may access the data, require the recipient to implement appropriate safeguards, prohibit re-identification, and obligate reporting of any unauthorized use or disclosure. Limited Data Sets are a practical middle ground for research that needs geographic precision or temporal patterns but does not require full patient-level identification.
For research that requires identified data — full medical record numbers, individual diagnoses, and linked longitudinal records — covered entities must obtain patient authorization or qualify for a waiver of authorization approved by an IRB or Privacy Board under 45 CFR § 164.512(i). The IRB evaluates whether the research could practicably be conducted without the waiver, whether it poses minimal risk, and whether it includes adequate privacy safeguards. In practice, large health systems and academic medical centers maintain dedicated data governance committees that evaluate data requests, classify the appropriate tier, and require data use agreements or IRB documentation before any data leaves the institution.
An emerging alternative to any form of data sharing is federated learning — a machine-learning paradigm in which model training occurs locally at each data-holding institution, and only model updates (gradients or parameters) are shared across sites rather than the underlying patient data itself. PCORnet, the national patient-centered clinical research network, runs distributed queries so that patient data stays at each participating site, while the NIH's National COVID Cohort Collaborative (N3C) took the enclave route — pooling limited data sets into a single secure environment where approved analysts work without downloading records. These architectures fundamentally reframe the privacy problem: instead of asking "how do we safely share data?", they ask "how do we bring computation to the data?"

Data Sharing Tiers Under HIPAA
Governance Rule of Thumb: Match the data tier to the analytical need. If ZIP code precision is not required for the research question, use Safe Harbor de-identification and eliminate the DUA burden. If it is required, use a Limited Data Set with a DUA. Reserve identified data access for questions that genuinely cannot be answered with less.

######## interoperability-data-exchange | interop-data-governance | Data Governance for HIEs: Policies, Participation & Trust
Health Data Governance: Who Owns the Data, Who Controls It, and Who Is Responsible
Who Owns Health Data? The Legal Reality
One of the most persistent misconceptions in American health care is that patients "own" their medical records. The intuition is understandable — the information is about the patient, generated in service of the patient, and feels intensely personal. Yet federal law does not grant patients ownership of the documents or data in their medical record. What HIPAA actually confers is a right of access — the right to inspect and obtain copies of protected health information held in a covered entity's "designated record set." The covered entity — the hospital, physician practice, or health plan — retains custody and legal control of the originals. This distinction between access rights and ownership rights has profound consequences for every downstream governance question about who can use, sell, or delete health data.
State law adds another layer of complexity. Medical records statutes vary considerably across jurisdictions. Some states grant patients a stronger right to compel disclosure, set shorter response deadlines, or cap the fees providers may charge for copies. A handful of states have begun experimenting with broader patient rights language, but none has fully codified patient ownership in the property-law sense. Meanwhile, EHR vendor contracts routinely include clauses that assert the vendor's right to de-identify and aggregate data from the platform for product improvement, benchmarking, or sale — rights that providers often unknowingly sign away during procurement negotiations. The practical result is a three-way tension among the patient's access interests, the covered entity's custody rights, and the technology vendor's contractual data claims.
The HIPAA Privacy Rule's right of access has been actively enforced. HHS Office for Civil Rights ran a dedicated Right of Access Initiative beginning in 2019, resolving dozens of cases against covered entities that delayed, denied, or overcharged patients seeking their own records. Penalties ranged from thousands to hundreds of thousands of dollars. The message was clear: while patients may not "own" their data in a legal sense, covered entities are obligated to make it swiftly and affordably available. The confusion between access and ownership persists because in practical terms the distinction rarely matters to a patient who simply wants their lab results — but it matters enormously to anyone designing governance policy, setting data licensing terms, or building a secondary-use research program.
HIPAA gives patients the right to obtain copies of their health records, but the covered entity retains legal custody. Patients cannot unilaterally delete their records from a provider's system or prevent a provider from retaining the data for legally required periods.

Data Stewardship Roles and Frameworks
Governance frameworks clarify accountability by separating three related but distinct roles: the data owner, the data steward, and the data custodian. These roles, codified in the DAMA International Data Management Body of Knowledge (DAMA-DMBOK), now in its second edition with a third edition under active community development begun in 2025, provide a globally recognized vocabulary for assigning responsibility without conflating technical capability with policy authority. In healthcare, where the stakes of data misuse include regulatory penalties, patient harm, and reputational damage, clearly delineated roles are not administrative overhead — they are a patient safety mechanism.
The data owner is typically a senior executive or department head who bears ultimate accountability for a specific data asset — for example, the Chief Medical Officer who owns the clinical data domain, or the CFO who owns the revenue cycle dataset. The data owner defines the strategic policy: who may access the data, under what conditions, for what purposes, and with what retention schedule. The data steward is the operational role, often filled by a health information manager or clinical informaticist, who translates those policies into day-to-day practice — reviewing data quality exceptions, resolving identity-matching disputes, and serving as the business contact when a downstream team needs access. The data custodian is the technical role, typically an IT professional responsible for the infrastructure that stores, moves, and secures the data — managing encryption, backup schedules, access logs, and disaster recovery. None of these three roles is interchangeable; collapsing them into one person or one title is a governance anti-pattern that healthcare organizations frequently pay for during audits or breaches.
The American Health Information Management Association (AHIMA) published its Information Governance Principles for Healthcare (IGPHC) framework, organizing health information governance around eight principles: accountability, transparency, integrity, protection, compliance, availability, retention, and disposition. These principles apply not just to the EHR but to every information asset in the enterprise — claims data, scheduling systems, research databases, and even the informal data shadows created in spreadsheets and email attachments. AHIMA's emphasis on organization-wide scope was deliberate: data governance failures often occur precisely in the "shadow IT" spaces that formal governance programs ignore.
Data Steward
Implements governance policies day-to-day
Resolves data quality and identity disputes
Acts as business liaison for data access requests
Monitors metadata and data dictionary entries
Data Custodian
Manages storage infrastructure and security controls
Enforces technical access controls and audit logs
Handles backup, recovery, and encryption
Ensures systems meet compliance requirements
Data Stewardship Role Comparison
Think of health data governance like property management: the data owner is the property owner who sets the rules for the building; the data steward is the building manager who enforces those rules daily and handles tenant requests; the data custodian is the maintenance crew that keeps the pipes, locks, and electrical systems running safely.
Data governance role hierarchy in healthcare organizations
Organizational Data Governance Programs
Translating governance frameworks into organizational reality requires structures that span clinical, operational, and technical domains. Most mature health systems establish a Data Governance Council — a cross-functional body with representation from clinical informatics, health information management, IT security, compliance, finance, and increasingly, patient experience teams. The council's charter defines its decision rights: which decisions require council approval (data sharing agreements, secondary-use policies), which can be delegated to domain stewards (data dictionary updates, access request approvals), and which are escalated to the executive team (breach response, vendor data-rights disputes). Without a formal charter, governance councils tend to become advisory bodies with no enforcement power — capable of producing policies that nobody follows.
Two foundational capabilities underpin any serious governance program: the data dictionary and master data management (MDM). A data dictionary is a centralized catalog that defines every data element in the enterprise — its name, definition, permitted values, source system, owner, and data classification. Without a data dictionary, different departments routinely use the same term to mean different things ("admission date" in the EHR versus "admission date" in the financial system are often calculated differently), generating inconsistencies that corrupt analytics and reports. Master data management addresses the complementary problem of patient identity integrity — ensuring that John H. Smith born 3/4/1962 in the EHR is correctly recognized as the same person as John Harold Smith born 3/4/1962 in the claims system. Poor patient matching generates duplicate records, which can lead to clinicians treating the wrong patient's history.
Patient identity integrity is not merely an operational inconvenience — it is a clinical safety issue. Duplicate or overlaid medical records put the wrong history in front of clinicians, and ECRI has named patient misidentification among its top ten patient safety threats. Health systems with mature governance programs invest in probabilistic matching algorithms, regular duplicate detection runs, and clear escalation paths when a potential overlay is discovered. Governance programs also extend to the contract review process: before a new technology vendor is onboarded, governance policies should require a review of data-rights clauses to ensure the organization is not inadvertently granting the vendor rights to patient data that exceed the minimum necessary standard or conflict with the organization's own data use agreements.
Define the council's scope, decision rights, membership, meeting cadence, and escalation paths. Specify which decisions require quorum versus which can be delegated to domain stewards.
Draft the Charter
Identify executive-level owners for each major data domain: clinical, revenue cycle, supply chain, HR. Owners bear accountability for policy compliance within their domain.
Appoint Domain Data Owners
Produce a current-state map of all data systems, feeds, and repositories. Classify each by sensitivity, regulatory obligation, and business criticality.

Stand up a centralized catalog with standardized definitions for all high-priority data elements. Begin with the elements that appear in enterprise dashboards and regulatory submissions.

Codify policies for internal data access, research use, secondary analytics, and external sharing. Link policies to specific regulatory obligations (HIPAA, state law, federal research rules).

Deploy audit logging for sensitive data access, schedule periodic reviews of user entitlements, and establish a clear process for investigating policy violations.

Standing Up a Health System Data Governance Council
TEFCA and National Governance Infrastructure
Individual health system governance programs, however mature, cannot solve the governance problem at the national scale. Health data routinely crosses organizational and state boundaries as patients seek care from multiple providers, insurers process claims, and public health agencies monitor disease trends. The Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) is the federal government's framework for governing nationwide health information exchange. Authorized under the 21st Century Cures Act, TEFCA establishes a set of common policies, technical requirements, and legal obligations that all participants in the network must follow as a condition of participation. The Common Agreement, now at Version 2.1 (published November 2024, updated January 17, 2025), is the legally binding document that governs relationships among the Recognized Coordinating Entity, Qualified Health Information Networks, and their downstream participants.
The Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE) role is the linchpin of TEFCA's governance structure. ONC selected The Sequoia Project, a non-profit public-private collaborative, as the RCE in 2019 following a competitive process. In August 2023, ONC renewed The Sequoia Project's contract for a further five years, confirming its ongoing role in developing, implementing, and maintaining the Common Agreement and the QHIN Technical Framework. The Sequoia Project works with ONC's Assistant Secretary for Technology Policy (ASTP) to update governance documents, onboard new QHINs, and operate the RCE Directory Service that allows QHINs to locate and route messages to other participants in the network. This governance structure — a federal agency setting overall policy while a private non-profit manages operational implementation — is intentionally designed to balance government accountability with the flexibility of private-sector execution.
Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs) are the operational nodes of the TEFCA network. They must meet rigorous technical and governance standards, complete a formal onboarding and designation process overseen by the RCE, and sign the Common Agreement before they can exchange data under TEFCA. As of late 2025, eleven QHINs had been designated, including CommonWell Health Alliance, eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, Health Gorilla, KONZA, Kno2, MedAllies, eClinicalWorks (designated January 2025), Surescripts Health Information Network (designated April 2025), and Oracle Health (designated November 2025). TEFCA exchange is constrained to lawful purposes defined in the Common Agreement — treatment, payment, health care operations, public health, government benefits determination, and individual access services. Using the network for marketing, selling data, or other non-enumerated purposes is a material violation of the Common Agreement.
Every TEFCA query must be tagged with one of the defined Exchange Purposes. A clinician looking up a patient's medication history uses XP: Treatment. A health plan verifying a claim uses XP: Payment. A state health department tracking influenza cases uses XP: Public Health. This tagging requirement is not bureaucratic overhead — it is the governance mechanism that limits data use to the purpose for which the exchange was authorized, and it creates an audit trail that the RCE and ONC can use to detect misuse.
TEFCA's Exchange Purpose (XP) Framework

Patient Data Rights: Access, Correction, and Portability
The patient data rights landscape has expanded significantly since the original HIPAA Privacy Rule took effect in 2003. The ONC's 21st Century Cures Act Final Rule (effective April 2021, with full scope expanded October 2022) codified the information blocking prohibition, making it unlawful for healthcare providers, health IT developers, and health information networks to interfere with the access, exchange, or use of electronic health information except under specific enumerated exceptions. As of October 6, 2022, the information that must not be blocked encompasses all electronic protected health information in the designated record set — not just a limited subset of structured data. Enforcement includes civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation for health IT developers and networks, with CMS-administered disincentives for providers (effective July 31, 2024) such as reduced payment adjustments under the Merit-based Incentive Payment System.
State legislatures have moved to fill gaps that federal law leaves unaddressed, particularly for consumer health data held by non-HIPAA entities — fitness apps, period trackers, direct-to-consumer genetic testing companies, and wellness platforms. Washington State's My Health MY Data Act (HB 1155), signed by Governor Jay Inslee on April 27, 2023, was the first U.S. law to specifically regulate consumer health data outside HIPAA's scope. The Act requires regulated entities to obtain consumer consent before collecting or sharing consumer health data, prohibits geofencing around healthcare facilities, grants consumers the right to delete their health data, and — critically — includes a private right of action allowing individuals to sue for violations. Geofencing prohibitions took effect July 23, 2023; full compliance obligations for large entities began March 31, 2024.
The Federal Trade Commission has pursued parallel authority over non-HIPAA health data through the Health Breach Notification Rule (HBNR). In April 2024, the FTC finalized significant amendments to the HBNR (effective July 29, 2024) that expanded the rule's scope to clearly cover health apps and connected devices, even those that do not interact with a HIPAA-covered entity. The revised rule defines "breach of security" to include unauthorized disclosures — not just hacking events — and requires covered entities to notify the FTC simultaneously with individual notifications for breaches affecting 500 or more people, within 60 days of discovering the breach. Taken together with Washington's My Health MY Data Act and similar state laws under development in other jurisdictions, the regulatory landscape for consumer health data is rapidly converging toward a HIPAA-like accountability regime for previously unregulated actors.
Apps and platforms that collect health data but do not qualify as HIPAA covered entities or business associates are no longer in a regulatory vacuum. The FTC HBNR amendments and state laws like Washington's My Health MY Data Act impose real obligations and enforcement risk. Organizations in this space should conduct a data mapping exercise and review their consent, sharing, and breach notification practices against both federal and applicable state requirements.

HIPAA grants patients a right of access to their health records — not legal ownership. The covered entity retains custody and control of the original record.
EHR vendor contracts frequently include broad data rights clauses that organizations should scrutinize before signing; data rights granted to vendors can conflict with patient privacy interests.
The DAMA-DMBOK (currently v2, with v3 in development) defines the three core governance roles — data owner (accountability), data steward (operations), and data custodian (technical infrastructure) — while AHIMA's IGPHC sets eight enterprise-wide governance principles.
Effective organizational governance requires a formal Data Governance Council with a written charter, domain-level data owners, a maintained data dictionary, and enforceable access policies.
TEFCA's Common Agreement (v2.1, January 2025) and the Sequoia Project as RCE form the national governance backbone for health data exchange, constraining exchange to enumerated lawful purposes.
As of late 2025, eleven QHINs have been designated under TEFCA, with exchange required to be tagged by Exchange Purpose — a governance mechanism that limits use and creates an audit trail.
Patient data rights are expanding beyond HIPAA through the ONC information blocking rule, Washington's My Health MY Data Act (2023), and the FTC Health Breach Notification Rule amendments (effective July 2024).
Poor patient identity matching is not just an operational problem — duplicate or overlaid records are a recognized patient safety hazard that data governance programs must address through MDM and probabilistic matching.
HIPAA's Right of Access gives patients the ability to inspect and obtain copies of their PHI in the designated record set, but does not transfer ownership of the records from the covered entity to the patient. The covered entity retains custody and legal control of the originals, and patients cannot compel deletion under HIPAA alone — though newer state laws like Washington's My Health MY Data Act add deletion rights for some categories of data.

######## health-equity-sdoh | health-equity-definitions | Health Equity: Definitions, Evidence & the US Context
Health Equity: Definitions, Evidence & the US Context
What Health Equity Actually Means
Health equity means that everyone has a fair and just opportunity to be as healthy as possible. The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation, whose definition is among the most widely cited in the field, frames it this way: achieving health equity requires removing obstacles to health such as poverty, discrimination, and their consequences — including powerlessness and lack of access to good jobs, quality education, safe housing, and environments free of toxins.
The critical word is "opportunity." Health equity is not a promise that everyone will end up equally healthy — people make different choices and face different circumstances. It is a commitment that the conditions required for health are not rationed by race, income, ZIP code, disability, or language. When a Black mother is three times more likely to die in childbirth than a white mother with the same education and insurance, that is not a difference in opportunity that society can shrug at — it is a signal that the system is distributing health unjustly.
Health equity is frequently confused with three other ideas it is related to but distinct from. It is not the same as equality (giving everyone the identical thing). It is not the same as diversity (representation of different groups). And it is not the same as inclusion or belonging (whether people feel welcome). Equity is specifically about outcomes and the upstream conditions that produce them.
Equity is about fair opportunity, not identical treatment or guaranteed identical outcomes. The test is whether the conditions for health are distributed justly — not whether everyone receives the same resources.
Equity vs. Equality: Why the Distinction Matters
Equality means giving everyone the same thing. Equity means giving people what they need, which differs based on their starting circumstances. The popular illustration is three people of different heights trying to watch a game over a fence: equality gives each person one identical box, which still leaves the shortest person unable to see. Equity gives the shortest person two boxes and the tallest none, so all three can see over the fence.
In health care, "equal" treatment can actively perpetuate disparities. Mailing every patient the same colorectal cancer screening reminder is equal. But if a population has lower literacy, no reliable transportation, or limited English proficiency, the identical mailer reaches them far less effectively — and the screening gap widens. An equity approach allocates extra outreach, language-concordant scheduling, or transportation support precisely to the groups facing the steepest barriers.
This is why equity is sometimes politically harder than equality: it requires deliberately giving more to some groups in order to close a gap. That is not favoritism — it is the only way to produce fair outcomes when starting points are unequal. The fence does not move; the boxes do.
Equality hands every runner identical shoes at the starting line. Equity notices that some runners are starting a hundred meters back — and the race is only fair once that gap is addressed, not once the shoes are matched.
The difference between equal treatment and just outcomes
Disparity vs. Inequity: A Distinction With Moral Weight
Not every difference between groups is an injustice. A disparity is any measurable difference in a health outcome between populations. An inequity is a disparity that is unjust and avoidable — the product of systemic disadvantage rather than biology or genuinely free choice. The 75-and-older population has more heart disease than 25-year-olds; that is a disparity, but not an inequity, because it reflects aging rather than unfairness.
The framing carries moral weight. Calling a gap an "inequity" rather than a "disparity" asserts that it is wrong and that someone bears responsibility to act. The evidence increasingly supports that framing for racial and socioeconomic health gaps: most are not explained by genetic or biological differences but by differences in social and structural conditions — income, housing, neighborhood, exposure to discrimination, and access to care.
This distinction matters operationally because it determines whether a finding triggers action. A health system that reports "our diabetes control rate varies by race" has named a disparity. A health system that says "this gap is avoidable and we are accountable for closing it" has named an inequity — and committed to doing something about it.
Historically, racial health gaps were often attributed to innate biological difference, which justified inaction. Modern evidence shows the overwhelming majority of racial disparities trace to social and structural causes, not genetics. Race is a social category, not a biological one — treating a disparity as "just how that population is" is both scientifically wrong and a barrier to acting on it.
Do not treat all disparities as biological
The Scale of US Health Disparities
The disparities in American health are not subtle. They span years of life and the most basic outcomes — whether a mother survives childbirth, whether an infant reaches its first birthday. They persist across the entire socioeconomic ladder, not only at the very bottom. And by international standards they are extreme: the United States tolerates internal health gaps that most peer nations do not.
Consider the racial gap in life expectancy. In 2023, life expectancy was approximately 74.0 years for Black Americans versus 78.4 years for white Americans — a gap of about 4.4 years, even after the pandemic-era gap narrowed somewhat. Maternal mortality is starker still: in 2023, Black women died at 50.3 deaths per 100,000 live births compared with 14.5 for white women, roughly 3.5 times higher — and that ratio widened from 2022 to 2023 rather than improving.
Geography compounds race. A 2017 JAMA Internal Medicine study found that in 2014 the gap in life expectancy between the highest- and lowest-performing US counties was 20.1 years — a span comparable to the difference between a wealthy nation and a developing one, inside the same country. Related work by Raj Chetty and colleagues found the richest 1% of American men live roughly 15 years longer than the poorest 1%.

The Evidence That Disparities Are Not Inevitable
A natural objection is that some of these gaps simply reflect poverty or personal behavior, and are therefore beyond the reach of policy. The landmark Whitehall studies of British civil servants, led by Sir Michael Marmot beginning in 1967, demolished the simplest version of that argument.
The Whitehall researchers followed thousands of civil servants — none of them poor, all employed in stable government jobs — across employment grades. They found a steep, continuous "social gradient" in mortality: the lower the employment grade, the higher the death rate from a wide range of diseases. Crucially, the gradient appeared at every rung, not just at the bottom. Senior administrators outlived middle managers, who outlived clerks, who outlived messengers. And it held even after controlling for smoking and other lifestyle factors.
The Whitehall finding reframed the entire field. Health disadvantage is not only about absolute material deprivation; it tracks relative social position, control over one's work and life, and chronic stress along the whole ladder. If health were determined by biology or simple poverty, a smooth gradient among salaried civil servants would not exist. Because the gradient is produced by social conditions, it can be changed by social policy — which is precisely the claim health equity rests on.
Sir Michael Marmot's research team enrolled British civil servants and tracked their health over decades. The first study began in 1967; Whitehall II launched in 1985 with over 10,000 participants.
The defining result: a continuous inverse relationship between job grade and mortality. The largest single contributor to the coronary heart disease gradient was low control at work — a psychosocial factor, not a clinical one. The studies established that health follows social hierarchy, and therefore that reducing inequality is a health intervention.
The Whitehall Studies (UK, 1967-present)
