Two Paths to a Biased Algorithm
Evaluating Clinical Algorithms for Bias
The practical response is not to abandon algorithms — many improve care — but to subject them to disciplined equity evaluation before and after deployment. That starts with asking the right questions of any tool a health system is considering. What data was it trained on, and does that data reflect historical inequities? Was its performance validated separately across racial, ethnic, and socioeconomic groups? What proxy variables does it use, and are those proxies distributed unevenly across populations?
Two further questions matter just as much. Who is the tool designed to help, and who might it systematically disadvantage if its assumptions are wrong? And is there an ongoing monitoring protocol after deployment — because a model can drift, and a population can change, in ways that introduce bias over time. An algorithm that was fair at launch is not guaranteed to stay fair.
These questions are increasingly being formalized into governance. The point is to treat algorithmic equity the way the field now treats clinical safety: as something that must be actively engineered, tested across the people it will affect, and continuously monitored — not assumed. The Optum and eGFR cases show how much harm a single unexamined design choice can do; disciplined evaluation is how the field stops repeating that mistake.

######## health-equity-sdoh | pulse-oximetry-racial-bias | Pulse Oximetry & Hidden Bias in Medical Devices
Pulse Oximetry & Hidden Bias in Medical Devices
A Bias Built Into the Hardware
The previous lesson examined bias in software algorithms. But disparity can be built into physical medical devices too — into the hardware on the wall and the clip on a patient's finger. The pulse oximeter, one of the most ubiquitous devices in all of medicine, is the clearest and most consequential example. It is on nearly every hospital finger, in clinics, ambulances, and millions of homes — and it works less accurately on patients with darker skin.
A pulse oximeter estimates blood oxygen saturation (SpO2) by shining light through tissue and measuring how much is absorbed. The problem is that skin pigmentation also absorbs light. In patients with darker skin, this can cause the device to overestimate the true oxygen level — to read a reassuring number when the patient is actually dangerously hypoxic. The reading looks fine; the patient is not.
This is not a minor calibration quirk. Oxygen saturation is a core vital sign that drives decisions about hospital admission, oxygen therapy, ICU transfer, and eligibility for treatments. A systematically falsely-high reading in darker-skinned patients means their hypoxia can go unrecognized and untreated — a bias with direct, life-or-death clinical consequences, hiding in a device almost no one thinks to question.
Pulse oximeters estimate oxygen saturation using light, and skin pigmentation interferes with that measurement — causing the device to overestimate true oxygen levels in patients with darker skin.
The Landmark Evidence: Sjoding et al., 2020
Although clinicians had noted the discrepancy for years, the study that crystallized the issue was published in the New England Journal of Medicine in December 2020 by Michael Sjoding and colleagues at the University of Michigan. They compared pulse oximeter readings (SpO2) against the gold-standard arterial blood gas measurement (SaO2) in two large patient cohorts, looking specifically for "occult hypoxemia."
Occult hypoxemia is the dangerous scenario this bias produces: a true arterial oxygen saturation below 88% — clinically low — despite a pulse oximeter reading in the reassuring 92-96% range. In other words, the patient is hypoxic but the device says they are fine. The researchers measured how often this hidden hypoxia occurred in Black versus white patients.
The finding was striking. In the multicenter cohort, occult hypoxemia occurred in 17.0% of Black patients but only 6.2% of white patients — Black patients had nearly three times the rate of dangerously low oxygen that the pulse oximeter failed to detect. The mechanism was attributed to greater melanin causing falsely elevated SpO2 readings. The timing made it urgent: the study landed during the COVID-19 pandemic, when oxygen saturation was the central triage variable for a disease that was already killing Black Americans at disproportionate rates.
Nearly 3x higher in Black patients, per Sjoding et al., NEJM 2020
Occult hypoxemia, Black vs white patients

The Clinical Consequences
A falsely reassuring oxygen reading is not a statistical curiosity — it changes what happens to a patient. If a pulse oximeter tells a triage nurse that a patient's saturation is 93% when it is truly 85%, that patient may be sent home instead of admitted, denied supplemental oxygen, not escalated to the ICU, or judged ineligible for a therapy that requires documented hypoxia. The device's error becomes the clinician's error, made in good faith on bad data.
During COVID-19, this dynamic was especially dangerous. Oxygen saturation was the key marker used to decide who needed hospitalization and oxygen, and many treatment protocols and even drug eligibility were keyed to specific SpO2 thresholds. Subsequent research found that pulse oximeter inaccuracy was associated with delayed recognition of eligibility for COVID treatment in patients with darker skin — meaning the device bias plausibly contributed to the pandemic's already severe racial mortality gap.
The case is a sobering illustration of how a single biased tool, used billions of times, can produce harm at population scale without anyone intending it. No clinician using the oximeter was being prejudiced; they were trusting a calibrated medical device. The bias lived in the device's development, not in the people using it — which is exactly why the response has to focus on the device and the system, not just on individual clinical judgment.
In February 2021, shortly after the NEJM study, the FDA issued a safety communication cautioning that pulse oximeters have limitations and that readings should not be the sole basis for assessing a patient's condition — explicitly noting that skin pigmentation can affect accuracy.
Because COVID-19 triage, oxygen therapy, and some treatment eligibility were keyed to SpO2 thresholds, falsely high readings in darker-skinned patients risked delaying admission and treatment. Given that COVID-19 mortality was already significantly higher in Black patients, unreliable oximetry likely contributed to the gap.
Pulse Oximetry During COVID-19
Why the Bias Existed: Device Development and Testing
How does a bias like this get built into a device used worldwide? The answer lies in how pulse oximeters were developed and validated. Historically, the calibration studies used to bring oximeters to market enrolled very few participants with darker skin — sometimes as few as a handful — so the devices were effectively tuned and validated on predominantly light-skinned populations. A device that is accurate on the people it was tested on can be systematically off for people it was not.
This mirrors the broader pattern of inequity in medical research: when the populations used to develop and test a technology do not reflect the populations that will use it, the technology can carry hidden disparities. It is the device-hardware version of the algorithmic problems in the previous lesson — bias entering through unrepresentative development data rather than malicious design.
Crucially, the fix is not a "race correction" applied to readings — applying a race-based adjustment would repeat the eGFR mistake of baking a crude racial assumption into a clinical number. The real solution is better devices, validated across the full range of skin tones, plus clinical awareness of the limitation. Skin pigmentation, measured directly (for example with the Monk Skin Tone scale), is the relevant physical variable — not race as a social category.
It is tempting to "correct" oximeter readings by race, but that would repeat the eGFR error of embedding a crude racial assumption into a clinical number. The correct response is devices validated across the full range of skin tones, direct measurement of skin pigmentation in testing, and clinician awareness — confirming with arterial blood gas when hypoxia is suspected despite a reassuring reading.
The fix is better devices, not a race-based correction
The Response: Regulation and Practice
The pulse oximetry case has driven both regulatory action and changes in clinical practice. On the regulatory side, the FDA convened its advisory committee on the issue and, in early 2025, issued draft guidance to improve the accuracy of pulse oximeters across skin tones. The draft recommends dramatically larger and more diverse validation studies — on the order of 150 participants representing a broad range of skin pigmentation, up from prior recommendations as low as around 10 — and measuring skin tone directly rather than by self-reported race.
On the clinical side, the practical guidance is awareness and confirmation. Clinicians should know that a pulse oximeter reading may overestimate true oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin, treat borderline readings in those patients with appropriate suspicion, and confirm with arterial blood gas analysis when the clinical picture suggests hypoxia despite a reassuring SpO2. The device remains valuable — it is not to be discarded — but it must be used with knowledge of its limitation.
More broadly, the case has become a touchstone for the field of equity in medical devices and technology. It demonstrates that the principles developed for algorithmic bias — representative validation, subgroup testing, ongoing monitoring, and resisting crude race-based corrections — apply just as much to hardware. Any tool that produces a clinical number, whether software or device, deserves to be asked whether it performs equally well for everyone it will be used on.

Treat borderline readings in darker-skinned patients with appropriate caution.
Heightened suspicion
Use arterial blood gas analysis when hypoxia is suspected despite a reassuring SpO2.
Confirm when in doubt
Support devices validated across the full range of skin tones (FDA 2025 draft guidance: ~150 diverse participants).
Better validation
Use direct skin-tone measurement (e.g., Monk Skin Tone scale) rather than a race-based correction.
Measure pigmentation, not race
Responding to Pulse Oximeter Bias
Pulse oximeters estimate oxygen using light, and skin pigmentation interferes — causing the device to overestimate true oxygen saturation in patients with darker skin.
Sjoding et al. (NEJM 2020) found occult hypoxemia in 17.0% of Black vs 6.2% of white patients — nearly three times more missed dangerous hypoxia.
A falsely reassuring reading can delay admission, oxygen therapy, ICU transfer, and treatment eligibility — turning a device error into a clinical one.
During COVID-19, when SpO2 drove triage and treatment thresholds, this bias likely contributed to the already severe racial mortality gap.
The bias arose because oximeters were historically validated on mostly light-skinned participants — unrepresentative development data, not malicious design.
The fix is better devices validated across all skin tones, not a race-based correction (which would repeat the eGFR mistake); pigmentation is the real variable.
FDA issued draft guidance (early 2025) for larger, more diverse validation studies, and clinicians should confirm suspected hypoxia with arterial blood gas.
Occult hypoxemia is dangerously low true oxygen (arterial saturation <88%) that the pulse oximeter misses, showing a reassuring 92-96% reading instead. Sjoding et al. found it in 17.0% of Black patients versus 6.2% of white patients — nearly three times more often — because greater skin pigmentation causes the device to overestimate oxygen saturation. This means hypoxia in darker-skinned patients can go undetected and untreated.
Pulse oximeters underestimated oxygen in Black patients, causing unnecessary oxygen therapy
Occult hypoxemia (true arterial saturation <88% despite a 92-96% oximeter reading) occurred nearly three times as often in Black patients — 17.0% vs 6.2%
There was no measurable difference in accuracy once disease severity was controlled
The device was equally inaccurate for all patients, so race was not a factor

######## health-equity-sdoh | cms-equity-strategy | CMS Health Equity Strategy: From Aspiration to Requirement
CMS Health Equity Strategy: From Aspiration to Requirement
Why CMS Matters More Than Any Other Player
Health equity stops being optional when the largest payer in the country attaches money to it. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) administers Medicare and Medicaid, covering well over 150 million Americans and accounting for a huge share of all US health spending. When CMS decides equity is a priority — through data requirements, program rules, or payment incentives — health systems and plans across the country respond, because their revenue depends on CMS's rules.
This gives CMS unique leverage to move equity from aspiration to requirement. A hospital may ignore a foundation's recommendation about REaL data, but it cannot ignore a Medicare condition of participation. A Medicare Advantage plan may treat equity as a values statement until its Star Rating — and the billions in bonus payments tied to that rating — depends on outcomes for disadvantaged enrollees. Payment is the mechanism that converts good intentions into operational change.
This lesson traces how CMS has used that leverage: through its overarching Framework for Health Equity, through quality-measurement and reporting requirements, and through payment incentives like the Star Ratings system. It also covers an essential and current caveat — that the strength of these requirements rises and falls with federal policy, and that several CMS equity provisions were scaled back in 2026.
CMS covers over 150 million Americans, so when it ties equity to program rules and payment, the whole system responds. Payment is what turns equity from an aspiration into an operational requirement — but it is also subject to shifting federal policy.
The CMS Framework for Health Equity 2022-2032
CMS articulated its strategy in the CMS Framework for Health Equity 2022-2032, a ten-year plan published by the CMS Office of Minority Health. The Framework is not itself a regulation; it is the organizing strategy that guides how equity is built into CMS's many programs over the decade. It is structured around five priorities that map closely to the themes of this entire course.
The five priorities are: (1) expand the collection, reporting, and analysis of standardized data; (2) assess the causes of disparities within CMS programs and address inequities in policy and operations; (3) build the capacity of health care organizations and the workforce to reduce disparities; (4) advance language access, health literacy, and culturally tailored services; and (5) increase access to health care services for people living with disabilities.
Notice how directly these track the earlier lessons. Priority 1 is the REaL-data foundation. Priority 2 is the data-to-action pipeline. Priority 4 is the language-access and CLAS material in the next lesson. Priority 5 extends the equity lens to disability, a population often left out of race-focused equity work. The Framework is essentially CMS committing to operationalize, across its programs, the same logic this course teaches.
Improve collection, reporting, and analysis of demographic and social-risk data across CMS programs.
Expand standardized data
Identify the causes of disparities within CMS programs and fix inequities in policy and operations.
Assess and address disparities
Strengthen the ability of health care organizations and the workforce to reduce disparities.
Build organizational capacity
Promote language access, health literacy, and culturally tailored services.
Advance language and literacy
Increase access to care for individuals living with disabilities.
Expand access for disability
The Five Priorities of the CMS Framework for Health Equity (2022-2032)
From Framework to Teeth: Data and Payment
A framework only matters if it is wired into requirements and money. CMS has done this through two main channels: quality measurement and payment incentives. On measurement, CMS has pushed stratification of quality measures by social risk and demographics — the operational expression of "you cannot improve what you cannot see." Stratified measurement turns the aggregate trap from a concept into something programs are expected to confront.
The most powerful lever, though, is payment, and the clearest example is the Medicare Advantage and Part D Star Ratings system. Star Ratings score plans on dozens of quality measures, and the ratings drive enormous bonus payments — billions of dollars annually flow to high-rated plans. Because the money is so large, anything CMS builds into Star Ratings commands the immediate attention of every Medicare Advantage plan in the country.
CMS designed a specific equity mechanism for Star Ratings: a Health Equity Index (later renamed the "Excellent Health Outcomes for All," or EHO4all, reward). It was built to reward plans that achieve good outcomes specifically for enrollees with social risk factors — those who are dually eligible for Medicare and Medicaid, receive the Part D low-income subsidy, or qualified for Medicare due to disability. The reward, ranging up to 0.4 added to a plan's star rating, was structured so that a plan could only earn it by performing well for its most disadvantaged members — directly tying bonus dollars to equity.
CMS developed a Health Equity Index reward — later renamed Excellent Health Outcomes for All (EHO4all) — to replace the legacy "reward factor" in Medicare Advantage and Part D Star Ratings. It targets enrollees with social risk factors: dual-eligible, low-income-subsidy, and disabled members.
The design adds a bonus (0 to 0.4) to a plan's raw star rating based on how large its disadvantaged population is and how well the plan scores for those members on a subset of measures. The point was structural: make billions in Star Ratings bonuses depend, in part, on closing outcome gaps for the most disadvantaged enrollees.
The Health Equity Index / EHO4all Reward in Star Ratings
A Crucial Caveat: Equity Requirements Are Reversible
It would be a mistake to present CMS's equity strategy as a settled, one-directional march. These requirements are creatures of federal policy, and federal policy changes with administrations. The most important current example: in its Contract Year 2027 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule — finalized in 2026 — CMS reversed course on several equity provisions.
CMS finalized that it would not implement the Health Equity Index / EHO4all reward for the 2027 Star Ratings, instead continuing the historical reward factor that rewards consistently high performance across all enrollees. CMS also removed specific Medicare Advantage health-equity requirements, including the requirement that utilization-management committees include a health-equity expert, conduct annual health-equity analyses, and publicly post those analyses. In other words, a set of equity mechanisms that had been built and announced were rolled back before taking full effect.
The lesson here is not cynicism but realism. The structural insight — that payment and data requirements are the levers that move equity — remains true. But which specific requirements are in force at any given moment depends on current rulemaking. Anyone doing this work needs to track CMS rules in real time rather than assuming a framework announced in one year is fully operational in the next. The durable equity work in an organization should not depend solely on whether a particular federal incentive happens to be active.
CMS equity provisions can be reversed by rulemaking. The Health Equity Index / EHO4all reward was developed for the 2027 Star Ratings but then finalized as NOT implemented in the CY2027 final rule (2026), and several MA health-equity requirements were removed. Always confirm the current rule before relying on a specific CMS equity incentive — frameworks announced one year may be scaled back the next.
Verify which CMS equity requirements are currently in force
What This Means for Organizations
For health systems and plans, CMS's strategy carries a clear practical message regardless of the year-to-year fluctuations. The foundational capabilities CMS has pushed — high-quality demographic and social-risk data, stratified quality measurement, language access, and disability access — are valuable on their own terms and align with everything the evidence in this course supports. Organizations that build these capabilities are well-positioned whether or not a specific federal incentive is active.
It also means organizations should not outsource their equity commitment entirely to CMS incentives. An equity strategy that exists only because a Star Ratings bonus rewards it will evaporate the moment that bonus does — as the 2026 reversal illustrates. The durable approach is to treat equity as core to quality and mission, using CMS incentives as accelerants when they are available rather than as the sole reason for acting.
Finally, CMS's framework is a useful map even when its specific requirements shift. The five priorities — data, disparity assessment, organizational capacity, language and literacy, and disability access — describe a comprehensive equity program that any organization can adopt on its own initiative. The Framework tells you what a serious equity strategy looks like; whether CMS is currently paying for each piece is a separate, and changeable, question.

######## health-equity-sdoh | clas-standards-language-access | CLAS Standards & Language Access: Legal Requirements & Best Practices
CLAS Standards & Language Access: Legal Requirements & Best Practices
Communication Is a Safety Issue
A patient who cannot understand their diagnosis, their medication instructions, or the questions a clinician is asking is a patient at risk. Limited English proficiency (LEP) and unaddressed cultural differences are not soft "experience" concerns — they are direct threats to safety, quality, and equity. A mis-taken medication dose, a missed warning sign, an uninformed consent: these are the predictable results of a communication breakdown between a patient and a system that does not speak their language.
The United States is profoundly multilingual. Tens of millions of people speak a language other than English at home, and a large share have limited English proficiency. For these patients, language access is the difference between care that works and care that fails — and the evidence shows that LEP patients receive worse care, experience more adverse events, and have poorer outcomes when language services are inadequate.
This lesson covers the two pillars of addressing this: the National CLAS Standards, which define what culturally and linguistically appropriate care looks like, and the federal civil-rights laws that make language access a legal requirement rather than a courtesy. Together they move language and cultural access from optional to obligatory.
Language and cultural barriers are patient-safety issues, not just experience issues. Inadequate language access leads to worse care, more adverse events, and poorer outcomes for patients with limited English proficiency.
The National CLAS Standards
The framework for culturally and linguistically appropriate care is the National CLAS Standards — Culturally and Linguistically Appropriate Services in Health and Health Care — developed by the HHS Office of Minority Health. First released in 2001 and enhanced in 2013, the standards consist of one Principal Standard and 14 supporting standards, for 15 in total.
The Principal Standard sets the overarching expectation: "Provide effective, equitable, understandable, and respectful quality care and services that are responsive to diverse cultural health beliefs and practices, preferred languages, health literacy, and other communication needs." The 14 remaining standards are organized into three themes: governance, leadership, and workforce; communication and language assistance; and engagement, continuous improvement, and accountability.
The structure is deliberate and worth absorbing. CLAS is not just "hire some interpreters." It treats cultural and linguistic competence as an organizational property that must be built into leadership and workforce, delivered through concrete communication services, and sustained through measurement and accountability — the same three-legged structure (capacity, service, accountability) that good equity work shares everywhere. The CLAS Standards are foundational guidance, not law in themselves, but they define the standard of practice that the legal requirements then enforce.
Provide effective, equitable, understandable, and respectful care responsive to cultural beliefs, preferred languages, health literacy, and communication needs.
Principal Standard
Build cultural and linguistic competence into leadership, policy, and a diverse, trained workforce.
Governance, leadership & workforce
Offer language assistance, qualified interpreters, and translated materials to those who need them, at no cost.
Communication & language assistance
Collect data, engage communities, conduct assessments, and hold the organization accountable for CLAS.
Engagement, improvement & accountability
The Three Themes of the National CLAS Standards
The Legal Mandate: Title VI and Section 1557
Language access in health care is not optional for most providers — it is a civil-rights requirement. The foundation is Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination on the basis of race, color, or national origin by any program receiving federal financial assistance. Courts and federal agencies have long interpreted national-origin discrimination to include failing to provide meaningful access to people with limited English proficiency. Because nearly every health care provider receives federal funds through Medicare or Medicaid, Title VI reaches most of the health system.
Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act builds directly on Title VI and sharpens the language-access requirements. It mandates that covered health programs and activities provide free, accurate, and timely language assistance to patients (and their companions) with LEP. The Section 1557 final rule adds concrete definitions of what counts as a "qualified" interpreter, translator, and bilingual staff member, and requires covered entities to post notices informing patients that free language assistance is available.
A few specific rules carry real operational weight. Being bilingual is not the same as being a qualified interpreter — interpreters must be competent in interpreting and familiar with relevant medical vocabulary. Language services must be free to the patient. And the use of minor children to interpret is prohibited, except as a temporary emergency measure when there is an imminent threat and no qualified interpreter is available. Relying on a patient's child to relay a cancer diagnosis is both unsafe and, as a routine practice, unlawful.
Section 1557 of the ACA extends Title VI's national-origin protections with specific language-access duties for covered health programs. Its final rule requires free, accurate, and timely language assistance for LEP patients and companions, and defines who qualifies as an interpreter or translator — clarifying that being bilingual alone is not sufficient.
It also requires covered entities to provide notices of the availability of free language assistance, and it prohibits using minor children to interpret except in a genuine emergency with no qualified interpreter available. These are enforceable requirements, not best-practice suggestions.
Section 1557 Language-Access Requirements
What Good Language Access Looks Like in Practice
Meeting these standards operationally means building a real language-access infrastructure rather than improvising at the bedside. The core components are professional interpreter services — in person, by phone, or by video remote interpreting — available across the languages a health system's patient population actually speaks, and reliably accessible at the point of care rather than after a long delay.
It also means avoiding the common shortcuts that compromise safety. Using family members, especially children, as interpreters introduces errors, breaches confidentiality, and places inappropriate burdens on relatives. "Getting by" with a clinician's rusty second language risks serious miscommunication. Ad hoc bilingual staff pulled from other duties may lack medical interpreting competence. Each of these shortcuts is exactly what qualified interpreter requirements are meant to prevent.
Beyond interpreting, full language access includes translated written materials — discharge instructions, consent forms, medication labels, and patient-education materials in the patient's preferred written language — and attention to health literacy, since plain, understandable communication matters even when language is shared. And it connects back to REaL data from earlier in the course: a system can only deliver language-concordant care if it has actually recorded each patient's preferred spoken and written language. Language access begins with knowing who needs it.
Relying on family members to interpret is a widespread shortcut that compromises accuracy and confidentiality. Using minor children to interpret is specifically prohibited under Section 1557 except as a temporary emergency measure when there is an imminent threat and no qualified interpreter is available. Routine use of a patient's child to interpret is both unsafe and unlawful.
Do not use family members — especially children — as interpreters
From Compliance to Equity
It is possible to treat language access purely as a compliance obligation — do the minimum to satisfy Title VI and Section 1557 and avoid a civil-rights complaint. But the organizations that do this well understand it as an equity and quality strategy. Language-concordant care measurably improves comprehension, adherence, satisfaction, and outcomes; it is one of the more direct and proven ways to reduce disparities for a large and identifiable population.
This connects language access to the broader CMS and equity strategy from the previous lesson — recall that advancing language access, health literacy, and culturally tailored services is one of the five priorities in the CMS Framework for Health Equity. Language access sits at the intersection of legal requirement, quality improvement, and equity, which is part of why it is one of the most actionable pieces of equity work an organization can undertake.
The throughline of this lesson is that culturally and linguistically appropriate care is simultaneously the right thing, the safe thing, the legally required thing, and the high-quality thing. The CLAS Standards describe the destination; Title VI and Section 1557 make the journey mandatory; and professional language services, translated materials, and good REaL data are the vehicle. For LEP and culturally diverse patients, getting this right is often the single most concrete equity improvement a system can make.

######## health-equity-sdoh | community-health-workers | Community Health Workers: Evidence, Roles & Sustainability
Community Health Workers: Evidence, Roles & Sustainability
Who Community Health Workers Are
Much of the equity work in this course points to the same need: someone who can bridge the gap between a health system and the daily lives of the patients it struggles to reach. Community health workers (CHWs) are that bridge. The American Public Health Association defines them as frontline public health workers who are trusted members of, or have an unusually close understanding of, the community they serve. That trust and shared experience is their defining asset.
A CHW is typically from the same community as the patients they work with — sharing language, culture, neighborhood, and often lived experience of the same challenges. They go by many names: promotores, community health representatives, patient navigators, peer support specialists, outreach workers. What unites them is a role grounded in relationship rather than clinical authority. They are not mini-doctors; they are connectors, educators, advocates, and navigators.
This positioning lets CHWs do what credentialed clinicians often cannot. They can meet patients in their homes and neighborhoods, understand the practical barriers behind a missed appointment or an unfilled prescription, and help solve them — and they can earn trust from communities that have good historical reasons to distrust the medical system. For exactly the populations that experience the worst disparities, a trusted person from their own community is sometimes the most effective intervention available.
Community health workers are trusted frontline workers from the communities they serve. Their power comes from shared language, culture, and lived experience — they connect, educate, advocate, and navigate rather than provide clinical care.
What CHWs Actually Do
The CHW role is broad by design, shaped around whatever stands between a patient and good health. In practice, the work clusters into a few core functions. They provide health education and coaching — explaining a diagnosis, demonstrating how to use a glucometer, reinforcing a care plan in plain, culturally familiar language. They provide navigation — helping patients schedule appointments, understand insurance, find a specialist, or apply for benefits.
They also do the social-needs work that ties this whole course together. A CHW is often the person who screens for and acts on social determinants — connecting a patient to a food bank, a housing navigator, transportation, or utility assistance, and following up to make sure the connection actually happened. In the language of earlier lessons, CHWs are frequently the human infrastructure that turns a positive SDOH screen into a closed-loop referral.
And they provide something harder to categorize: advocacy and relationship. CHWs accompany patients to appointments, advocate for them within a confusing system, and offer consistent human support to people who are often isolated. This relational continuity is part of why CHW interventions work — they address not just discrete tasks but the trust and engagement that make everything else possible. The model is most powerful when CHWs are integrated into the care team, not bolted on as an afterthought.
Explain diagnoses and care plans in plain, culturally familiar terms; coach on self-management.
Health education and coaching
Help patients schedule care, understand coverage, find specialists, and apply for benefits.
Navigation
Screen for SDOH and connect patients to food, housing, transportation, and utility resources — with follow-up.
Social-needs connection
Accompany and advocate for patients within the system and provide consistent, trusted human support.
Advocacy and support
Core Community Health Worker Functions
The Evidence: Outcomes and Return on Investment
CHW programs are sometimes dismissed as feel-good initiatives without rigorous evidence. That dismissal is outdated. The strongest body of evidence comes from the IMPaCT program developed at the University of Pennsylvania's Penn Center for Community Health Workers, which has been tested in multiple randomized controlled trials — a far higher evidentiary bar than most social interventions clear.
Across three randomized controlled trials, IMPaCT improved chronic disease control, mental health, and quality of care while reducing total hospital days substantially and improving patient satisfaction with primary care. These are not soft outcomes — they are the hard clinical and utilization measures health systems care about, demonstrated in the gold-standard study design.
The economic evidence is equally important for sustainability. A widely cited Health Affairs analysis found that every dollar invested in the IMPaCT model returned about $2.47 to an average Medicaid payer within the same year — meaning the program more than paid for itself. This was the first economic analysis of a health-system-based CHW intervention for adults built on randomized-trial data. The combination of improved outcomes and positive ROI is what moves CHWs from a nice idea to a financially defensible investment.

The Sustainability Challenge
Despite strong evidence, CHW programs have historically struggled to survive — not because they do not work, but because of how they are funded. For years, CHW programs were financed largely through time-limited grants. A grant funds a program for two or three years; the program demonstrates good results; the grant ends; the program disappears. This boom-and-bust cycle has repeatedly destroyed effective CHW programs and wasted the trust they built in communities.
The core problem is the absence of a stable, recurring payment mechanism. Unlike a physician visit, a CHW's work did not traditionally generate a billable, reimbursable service, so it had no natural place in health care's revenue streams. Sustainable CHW programs need an ongoing funding source tied to the value they produce — which, given the ROI evidence, is economically justified but operationally hard to wire into payment systems.
The most promising path is Medicaid financing. In a 2013 rule (effective January 2014), CMS allowed state Medicaid programs to reimburse for preventive services delivered by non-licensed providers, including CHWs, when recommended by a licensed practitioner. Since then, more than half of state Medicaid programs have implemented some form of CHW coverage and payment policy. This shift — from grant-dependent to Medicaid-reimbursable — is the single most important development for putting CHW programs on durable footing, though adequate payment rates remain a real concern.
The IMPaCT model, developed at the University of Pennsylvania, is the most rigorously evaluated CHW program in the US, tested in three randomized controlled trials and serving more than 12,000 patients in the Philadelphia region.
Its trials showed improved chronic-disease control, mental health, and care quality with reduced hospital days, and a Health Affairs economic analysis found a $2.47 return per $1 invested for Medicaid. IMPaCT is widely used as a blueprint precisely because it pairs strong outcomes with a documented business case — the combination needed to make CHW programs sustainable.
Penn Center for Community Health Workers (IMPaCT)
Building CHW Programs That Last
Translating the evidence into durable programs requires attention to design as well as financing. The trials make clear that CHW effectiveness depends on doing the model well: hiring genuinely from the community, training adequately, integrating CHWs into the care team with clear roles, giving them manageable caseloads, and supporting them with supervision. A CHW program that hires the wrong people, isolates them from the team, or overloads them will not reproduce the trial results.
Sustainability also has a workforce dimension. CHWs deserve professional respect, fair pay, and career pathways — and increasingly a voice in the policies that govern their own field. The APHA has emphasized CHW self-determination, including the principle that CHWs themselves should have a substantial role in decisions about CHW definition, training, and standards. Certification requirements vary by state; some require state-level certification through an approved program, while others do not, and the field continues to work toward consistent standards without over-professionalizing away the community-rootedness that makes CHWs effective.
The bottom line is that CHWs are one of the best-evidenced, most directly equity-relevant interventions available — a workforce explicitly designed to reach the populations that experience the worst disparities. The remaining challenge is not proving they work but financing and structuring them so they endure. The shift toward Medicaid reimbursement, combined with disciplined program design, is what can finally break the grant-funded boom-and-bust cycle and let effective programs persist.
The classic failure mode is funding a CHW program entirely through a time-limited grant: it works, the grant ends, and the program — and the community trust it built — disappears. Durable programs need recurring funding, increasingly through Medicaid reimbursement (enabled by the 2013/2014 CMS rule). Plan for sustainable financing from the start, not as an afterthought when the grant runs out.
Grant funding alone is a trap for CHW programs

CHWs educate and coach, navigate the system, connect patients to social-needs resources, and provide advocacy and trusted support — often the human infrastructure for closed-loop referrals.

######## health-equity-sdoh | cross-sector-partnerships | Cross-Sector Partnerships: Health Systems & Community Organizations
Cross-Sector Partnerships: Health Systems & Community Organizations
No Health System Can Do This Alone
The recurring lesson of this entire course is that most of what produces health happens outside the health care system — in housing, food, neighborhoods, education, and social conditions. That fact has an unavoidable implication: a health system, no matter how well-run, cannot fix those upstream conditions by itself. Hospitals do not build housing, run food banks, operate transit systems, or fund early childhood education. The organizations that do those things live in other sectors entirely.
This is why cross-sector partnership is not an optional add-on to equity work but a structural necessity. Closing disparities requires health systems to work with community-based organizations, social-service agencies, public health departments, housing authorities, schools, and local government — each of which controls levers the health system does not. The hard part is that these sectors have different funding streams, cultures, timelines, and data systems, which makes genuine collaboration difficult.
This lesson covers how that collaboration is structured: the models that connect health care to community resources, the financing and legal mechanisms that fund cross-sector work, and the named programs that show what works and what is hard. The goal is to move from the abstract idea that "we should partner" to a concrete understanding of how partnerships are actually built and sustained.
Most health is produced outside health care, so health systems cannot close disparities alone. Cross-sector partnership with community, social-service, public-health, and government organizations is a structural necessity, not an add-on.
The Accountable Health Communities Model
The most ambitious federal test of cross-sector partnership was the CMS Accountable Health Communities (AHC) Model, which ran from 2017 to 2023. Its theory was simple and directly tied to the SDOH evidence in this course: systematically screen Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries for health-related social needs — housing, food, transportation, utilities, and interpersonal safety — and connect those with needs to community resources, then measure whether doing so reduced cost and utilization.
The model was built around "bridge organizations" — 32 diverse entities, including community-based organizations, hospitals, health systems, payers, and health information exchanges, that coordinated screening and referral across sectors in their communities. In its assistance track, some beneficiaries were randomly offered navigation services to help them actually connect with resources, allowing a rigorous evaluation. Over its life, AHC organizations screened more than one million beneficiaries — a genuinely large-scale test.
The results were instructive and mixed. In the assistance track, the evaluation found lower total expenditures for beneficiaries offered navigation and fewer Medicaid inpatient admissions and unplanned readmissions; CMS’s final evaluation credited the model with more than $200 million in net savings, almost 80% of it among Medicaid-only beneficiaries. These were meaningful but modest effects, and a central lesson was that screening and referral alone are not enough if the community resources people are referred to do not have the capacity to meet the need. AHC demonstrated both the promise and the limits of the screen-and-refer approach.
AHC was CMS's flagship cross-sector demonstration: screen Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries for five core social needs and connect them to community resources through 32 "bridge organizations." It screened over 1.1 million beneficiaries.
In the randomized assistance track, beneficiaries who received navigation showed lower total expenditures and fewer unplanned readmissions — more than $200 million in net savings overall, per CMS’s final evaluation. A key lesson: referral only works if community resources have the capacity to meet the identified needs, so investing in community capacity matters as much as screening.
CMS Accountable Health Communities Model (2017-2023)
Connecting the Sectors: Referral Networks and Infrastructure
For cross-sector partnership to function day to day, health care and community organizations need a shared way to connect patients to services and track what happens. This is the same closed-loop referral infrastructure introduced in the SDOH screening lesson — platforms like Unite Us and findhelp that link clinical settings with community-based organizations, route electronic referrals, and report back whether the patient was actually served.
These platforms matter for partnership because they create the connective tissue that makes collaboration operational rather than aspirational. Without shared infrastructure, a "partnership" is often just a list of phone numbers and a hope that patients follow through. With it, a clinic and a food bank can function as parts of a single coordinated network, with visibility into whether referrals close. The infrastructure does not replace relationships, but it makes the relationships scalable.
Crucially, this infrastructure also begins to address the capacity problem that AHC surfaced. By tracking referral outcomes across a network, it makes visible where community resources are overwhelmed or missing — which is the information needed to direct investment toward building community capacity rather than just generating more unfulfilled referrals. Partnership infrastructure, used well, is both an operational tool and a planning instrument.
Identify health-related social needs in clinical settings using validated tools.
Screen for social needs
Route electronic referrals to community organizations via platforms like Unite Us or findhelp.
Refer through shared infrastructure
Help patients connect, and confirm back to the care team whether the need was met.
Navigate and close the loop
Use referral data to see where community resources are overwhelmed or missing.
Track network capacity
Direct funding to strengthen the community organizations the network depends on.
Invest in community capacity
How Cross-Sector Partnerships Operate
Financing Cross-Sector Work: Community Benefit
Partnerships need money, and one of the most significant funding levers is the community benefit obligation that nonprofit hospitals carry. Most US hospitals are tax-exempt 501(c)(3) organizations, and in exchange for that exemption they are required to provide community benefit. The Affordable Care Act sharpened these requirements considerably, turning a vague expectation into specific, enforceable obligations.
Under Section 9007 of the ACA (codified as Internal Revenue Code Section 501(r)), every tax-exempt hospital must conduct a Community Health Needs Assessment (CHNA) at least once every three years, with input from people representing the broad interests of the community, including public health expertise — and must adopt an implementation strategy describing how it will address the priority needs identified. Hospitals report their community benefit spending and compliance on IRS Form 990, Schedule H. The requirements have teeth: a hospital that fails to conduct its triennial CHNA can face a $50,000 excise tax.
For equity work, the CHNA process is a major opportunity. It legally requires hospitals to systematically assess community needs in partnership with community voices, and to commit to addressing them — which is essentially a mandate for cross-sector engagement. Health systems that treat the CHNA as a genuine planning process, rather than a compliance checkbox, can use it to direct community benefit dollars toward the social conditions and community partners that actually move equity. It is one of the clearest places where law, financing, and cross-sector partnership converge.

What Makes Partnerships Succeed
Cross-sector partnerships are easy to announce and hard to sustain. The evidence and experience point to a few factors that separate durable, effective partnerships from press-release collaborations. The first is genuine shared power and trust, especially with community-based organizations. Health systems are large and well-resourced; community organizations are often small and close to the community. Partnerships fail when the health system treats community partners as subcontractors rather than equals — and when it extracts data and effort without sharing resources and decision-making.
The second is sustainable financing for the community side. The AHC lesson — that referrals fail when community capacity is lacking — generalizes: a health system that refers patients to an underfunded food bank or housing agency without investing in that organization's capacity is setting the partnership up to fail. Effective partnerships move money, not just referrals, toward the community organizations doing the upstream work, whether through community benefit dollars, contracts, or shared-savings arrangements.
The third is shared data and aligned goals. Partners need compatible ways to share information (within privacy rules), common definitions of success, and the patience to work across the very different timelines and cultures of health care, social services, and government. None of this is easy, which is exactly why cross-sector partnership is genuinely hard work rather than a slogan. But because the upstream conditions that drive disparities live outside health care, this hard work is unavoidable for any organization serious about equity.
A common failure mode is the health system extracting data and referrals from community-based organizations while controlling all the resources and decisions. Durable partnerships require shared power, shared data, and shared money — investing in the capacity of community partners rather than offloading work onto under-resourced organizations and expecting them to absorb it.
Do not treat community partners as subcontractors

######## health-equity-sdoh | organizational-equity-transformation | Organizational Equity Transformation: From Policy to Culture
Organizational Equity Transformation: From Policy to Culture
Pulling the Course Together
This course has moved from awareness to action — from defining health equity, through the social determinants and disparity data, to algorithmic bias, CMS requirements, language access, community health workers, and cross-sector partnership. Each of those is a piece. This final lesson is about the whole: how an organization actually becomes equitable, weaving these pieces into its strategy, structure, and culture rather than treating them as a scattered collection of initiatives.
The central failure mode is the equity initiative that exists in isolation — a committee here, a dashboard there, a screening pilot somewhere else — none of it connected to how the organization sets strategy, allocates resources, or evaluates leaders. Such efforts produce activity without transformation. They are visible enough to claim credit and disconnected enough to change nothing fundamental, and they tend to evaporate when budgets tighten or attention shifts.
Genuine organizational equity transformation is different. It treats equity as a core dimension of quality and mission, embeds it in governance and accountability, builds the infrastructure to act on it, and sustains it as a cultural commitment rather than a campaign. This lesson covers the frameworks and requirements that describe what that transformation looks like — and why culture, not policy alone, is what ultimately determines whether it sticks.
Scattered equity initiatives produce activity without transformation. Real change comes from embedding equity into strategy, governance, infrastructure, and culture — treating it as core to quality and mission, not a side campaign.
The IHI Framework for Organizational Equity
The most influential roadmap for organizational transformation is the Institute for Healthcare Improvement's 2016 white paper, "Achieving Health Equity: A Guide for Health Care Organizations." It lays out a framework of five interdependent components, and its core argument is that meaningful progress requires work across all five — not cherry-picking the comfortable ones.
The five components are: make health equity a strategic priority (embed it in the organization's mission, strategy, and goals at the highest level); develop structure and processes to support health equity work (governance, dedicated leadership, and infrastructure); deploy specific strategies to address the multiple determinants of health on which the organization can have direct impact; decrease institutional racism within the organization; and develop partnerships with community organizations to improve health and equity in the community.
Two of these components are the ones organizations most often skip, and they are the ones that distinguish transformation from theater. Making equity a genuine strategic priority — with board and C-suite ownership, not a side office — is what gives the work resources and durability. And explicitly addressing institutional racism within the organization, rather than only treating disparities as external phenomena, requires examining the organization's own policies, practices, and culture. Avoiding these two is how organizations stay busy without changing.
Embed health equity in mission, strategy, and goals — owned by the board and C-suite, not a side office.
Make equity a strategic priority
Establish governance, dedicated leadership, and the infrastructure to do equity work.
Build structure and processes
Deploy concrete strategies on the social determinants the organization can directly affect.
Address the determinants of health
Examine and change the organization's own policies, practices, and culture — not just external disparities.
Decrease institutional racism
Build genuine partnerships with community organizations to improve health and equity.
Partner with the community
The IHI Five Components of Achieving Health Equity
When Equity Becomes a Requirement: The Joint Commission
Organizational equity is no longer purely voluntary for accredited hospitals. The Joint Commission — the body that accredits most US hospitals — issued new Leadership standards on health equity effective January 1, 2023, and then elevated health equity to a National Patient Safety Goal effective July 1, 2023. That elevation is significant: a National Patient Safety Goal places health equity alongside core safety priorities, signaling that inequitable care is a safety failure.
The standard (LD.04.03.08) was deliberately placed in the Leadership chapter, with the Joint Commission explaining that "success demands leadership" and that achieving equity requires commitment from the C-suite and the board. Its elements of performance are concrete and map almost exactly onto this course: designate an individual to lead equity work, assess patients' health-related social needs, analyze quality and safety data to identify disparities, develop an action plan to address them, act when the organization falls short of its goals, and inform stakeholders about progress.
Read as a checklist, those requirements are a compact summary of organizational equity: leadership ownership, SDOH screening, stratified data analysis, a data-to-action plan, accountability for results, and transparency. The Joint Commission essentially codified the operational core of this course into accreditation. As with CMS, the strength and persistence of such requirements depends on the accreditor's ongoing priorities — but the elevation to a National Patient Safety Goal marked a real shift from equity as aspiration to equity as a measured standard of practice.
Effective January 1, 2023, the Joint Commission introduced a Leadership standard requiring accredited hospitals to treat health care disparities as a quality and safety priority; effective July 1, 2023, it elevated this to a National Patient Safety Goal.
Its elements of performance require designating an equity leader, assessing patients' health-related social needs, analyzing data to identify disparities, creating and acting on an improvement action plan, and informing stakeholders of progress — placing equity in the Leadership chapter because, in the Joint Commission's words, "success demands leadership."
The Joint Commission Health Care Equity Standard (LD.04.03.08)
Governance, Accountability, and Infrastructure
Both the IHI framework and the Joint Commission standard converge on the same insight from the data-to-action lesson: equity work succeeds or fails on governance and accountability. The organizations that transform have senior, named ownership of equity — often a chief health equity officer or equivalent reporting at the executive level — and board-level attention, not a junior coordinator buried in an org chart. Leadership ownership is what converts equity from a values statement into a resourced priority.
Accountability is the mechanism, and it echoes the strongest finding of this course: tying leadership performance and compensation to measurable equity outcomes is what most distinguishes organizations that make progress. A board that reviews stratified equity metrics with the same seriousness as financial metrics, and a C-suite whose evaluations include equity targets, will produce sustained attention. Without that, equity competes against everything that is actually measured and rewarded — and loses.
Infrastructure makes the accountability real. That means the REaL data systems to measure disparities, the disparity dashboards to make them visible, the screening and referral workflows to act on social needs, and the staff capacity — including community health workers — to do the relational work. The pieces from earlier lessons are not separate projects; they are the infrastructure that an equity-committed organization assembles into a coherent capability. Transformation is, in large part, the work of connecting them.
Equity Theater
Scattered, disconnected initiatives
A committee or junior coordinator with no power

Equity Transformation
Equity embedded in strategy and governance

Equity Theater vs. Equity Transformation
From Policy to Culture
The final and hardest step is cultural. Policies, standards, and dashboards are necessary, but an organization can have all of them and still deliver inequitable care if equity is not woven into how people actually think and behave day to day. Culture is what determines whether a clinician pauses at a borderline pulse-oximeter reading in a darker-skinned patient, whether a registration clerk asks the REaL data question well, whether a team treats a disparity on the dashboard as a real problem or a number to explain away.
Cultural transformation is slower and less tidy than policy change, and it cannot be mandated into existence. It is built through sustained leadership messaging, through training that connects to real clinical situations, through hiring and promotion that value equity competence, and through repeatedly demonstrating that the organization acts on disparities rather than merely measuring them. It is reinforced every time leadership funds an equity intervention over a competing priority, and undermined every time equity is the first thing cut under pressure.
The throughline of this entire course has been the move from awareness to action — and organizational transformation is where that move is completed. An organization that has internalized equity does not need a campaign to remember it; it shows up in strategy, governance, infrastructure, daily practice, and the assumptions people no longer have to be reminded of. That is the destination: not a set of programs, but an organization for which equitable care is simply how it does its work. Getting there is difficult, ongoing, and — given the disparities documented throughout this course — among the most important work in health care.
Equity that lives only in policy can be revoked with a memo. Equity that lives in culture is how an organization behaves when no one is checking.
Scattered equity initiatives produce activity without transformation; real change embeds equity in strategy, governance, infrastructure, and culture.

######## revenue-cycle-management | what-is-rcm | What is Revenue Cycle Management?
What is Revenue Cycle Management?
The Money Side of Care
Every time a patient receives care, two things happen in parallel. There is the clinical story — the diagnosis, the treatment, the outcome. And there is a financial story — someone has to be billed, an insurer has to be charged, and the provider has to actually get paid for the work. Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the discipline that governs that second story.
Formally, the revenue cycle is comprised of all the administrative and clinical functions that contribute to the capture, management, and collection of patient service revenue. In plainer terms: it is everything a healthcare organization does to get paid for the care it delivers — from the moment a patient schedules an appointment to the moment the final dollar is collected.
This matters enormously because, in American health care, getting paid is genuinely hard. Care is delivered first and billed later; payment flows through a maze of insurers each with their own rules; and a single error anywhere in the chain can mean the provider is never paid at all. RCM exists to manage that complexity so that providers stay financially viable and can keep their doors open.
Revenue cycle management (RCM) is the set of administrative and clinical functions that capture, manage, and collect the revenue a provider earns for patient care — everything involved in getting paid, from scheduling to final collection.
Why RCM Is Such a Big Deal
The scale of the money and effort involved is staggering. Administrative costs — much of which is billing- and insurance-related work — are estimated at roughly 15 to 25 percent of total U.S. national health expenditures (Chernew and Mintz, JAMA, 2021). The largest single category of healthcare "waste," about $266 billion a year, comes from administrative complexity.
That complexity translates into real money lost when RCM fails. A Change Healthcare analysis found that about $262 billion in hospital claims were initially denied in 2016, and in 2024 payers initially denied about 11.8 percent of the dollars billed on hospital claims (Kodiak Solutions) — roughly one in eight dollars, even though most were eventually paid after rework. Each denied claim costs somewhere between $25 and $181 just to rework.
Unsurprisingly, RCM has become a massive industry in its own right. The U.S. revenue cycle management market is measured in the tens of billions of dollars and growing at double-digit rates, as providers invest heavily in people, software, and outsourced services to capture revenue they would otherwise lose. RCM is not back-office trivia — it is central to whether a hospital or practice survives.

The Three Phases of the Revenue Cycle
The revenue cycle is conventionally divided into three phases, and this front-to-back structure is the map for the entire course. The first is the front-end: everything that happens before and at the point of care — scheduling, registration, insurance verification, prior authorization, and financial counseling.
The second is the mid-cycle, where clinical care meets the financial process. This is where the care delivered during the visit gets translated into billable form: clinical documentation, medical coding (ICD-10, CPT, HCPCS), and charge capture. The mid-cycle is the bridge — what happens here directly determines how much the provider can bill and how cleanly.
The third is the back-end: everything after the bill is created — claim submission, payment posting, denial management, appeals, accounts receivable follow-up, and patient collections. A useful way to remember it: the front-end sets up the claim, the mid-cycle builds the claim, and the back-end collects on the claim.
Scheduling, registration, insurance verification, prior authorization, financial counseling.
Front-End (pre-service)
Clinical documentation, medical coding, and charge capture — translating care into a bill.
Mid-Cycle (point of care)
Claim submission, payment posting, denials, appeals, AR follow-up, and patient collections.
Back-End (post-service)
The Three Phases of the Revenue Cycle
Where Clinical Meets Financial
One of the most important ideas in RCM is that it is not purely a financial function — it is deeply clinical. The mid-cycle makes this explicit: what a clinician documents during a visit directly affects how much the organization gets paid and how quickly. A service that was delivered but not documented, or documented but not coded, simply does not get billed.
This clinical-financial link runs throughout the cycle. A registration clerk who mistypes an insurance ID, a physician who under-documents a complex visit, a coder who selects the wrong code — each is a clinical-adjacent action with direct financial consequences downstream. RCM is therefore a team sport spanning the entire organization, not the job of a billing department alone.
This is also why RCM is increasingly understood as a quality-and-finance discipline together. Accurate documentation and coding are simultaneously about getting paid correctly and about reflecting the care actually delivered. The same data that drives a clean claim also feeds quality measurement, which connects RCM to the broader work of running a health system well.
Think of RCM like a relay race. The front-end runner gets the baton cleanly off the line (correct patient and insurance info). The mid-cycle runner carries it through the hard middle stretch (documentation and coding). The back-end runner sprints to the finish (claims and collections). Drop the baton at any handoff and the whole team loses the race — no matter how fast the other runners are.
How the phases of the revenue cycle depend on each other
Who Does RCM and How It Is Measured
RCM is performed by a wide cast: schedulers and registrars, financial counselors, medical coders, billing specialists, denial and appeals analysts, and accounts-receivable teams, all supported by software and often by outsourced vendors. Many organizations now blend in-house staff with specialized RCM companies and technology platforms.
Because RCM determines whether a provider gets paid, it is measured rigorously. The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) maintains a set of standardized revenue-cycle metrics known as MAP Keys, which establish industry benchmarks for revenue cycle excellence across hospitals, physician groups, and other provider types. Later lessons in this course dive into these key performance indicators in detail.
The goal of all this measurement and effort is simple to state and hard to achieve: get paid the right amount, for the right care, as quickly as possible, with as little waste and rework as possible. Every lesson that follows is, at bottom, about improving one piece of that goal — and this course walks the full cycle from scheduling to collections.
The Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) is the leading professional body for healthcare finance, and its MAP Keys are the industry-standard set of revenue-cycle KPIs.
MAP Keys let an organization benchmark metrics like clean-claim rate, days in accounts receivable, and denial rate against national peers — turning RCM performance from a guess into a measurable, comparable discipline.

######## revenue-cycle-management | ten-steps-revenue-cycle | The 10 Steps of the Revenue Cycle
The 10 Steps of the Revenue Cycle
The Cycle, Step by Step
The previous lesson described the revenue cycle in three broad phases — front-end, mid-cycle, and back-end. This lesson zooms in to the individual steps that make up those phases, giving you the end-to-end map of how a single patient encounter becomes collected revenue.
A note on numbering: different sources count the revenue cycle in anywhere from 7 to 13 steps, depending on how finely they slice the work. The exact count is not sacred — what matters is understanding the sequence and how each step depends on the one before it. This lesson uses a clean 10-step framework that captures the essential flow.
The single most important principle to carry through all ten steps is that they are a chain. Each step hands off to the next, and an error early in the chain (a wrong insurance ID at registration) silently propagates downstream and often surfaces only as a denied claim weeks later. Getting the early steps right is far cheaper than fixing the late ones.
The revenue cycle is a sequential chain from scheduling to collection. Sources count 7-13 steps; what matters is the flow and the dependencies — early errors propagate downstream and become expensive denials.
Steps 1-3: Getting the Patient in the Door (Front-End)
Step 1 is scheduling and pre-registration. Before the visit, the practice captures the patient's demographic and insurance information — ideally in real time while the patient is still on the phone — so problems can be caught early. Step 2 is registration, where that information is confirmed and completed at check-in.
Step 3 is eligibility verification and prior authorization. The provider confirms with the insurer that the patient's coverage is active and that the planned service is covered, and obtains prior authorization for services that require the payer's advance approval. This step is the front line of denial prevention: services delivered to an ineligible patient or without required authorization are frequently never paid.
These first three steps are deceptively important. They generate no clinical care and feel like paperwork, but they determine whether the eventual claim has any chance of being paid. The industry rule of thumb is that the cheapest denial to fix is the one prevented here, before the patient is ever seen.
Capture demographic and insurance information, ideally in real time.
1. Scheduling & Pre-registration
Confirm and complete patient and insurance information at check-in.
2. Registration
Verify active coverage and obtain required payer pre-approvals.
3. Eligibility & Prior Authorization
Front-End Steps
Steps 4-6: Turning Care Into a Bill (Mid-Cycle)
Step 4 is clinical documentation: the provider records what was assessed and done during the visit. This is the raw material for everything financial that follows — if it is not documented, it cannot be coded or billed. Step 5 is medical coding, where certified coders translate the documented diagnoses and services into standardized codes (ICD-10 for diagnoses, CPT and HCPCS for procedures and services).
Step 6 is charge capture: the coded services are recorded as charges in the billing system, ensuring the provider bills for everything that was actually performed. Missed charge capture is pure lost revenue — care delivered but never billed — while incorrect charges drive denials.
This mid-cycle trio is where clinical care literally becomes money. It is also where accuracy is hardest and most consequential: the codes and charges generated here are exactly what the payer scrutinizes. Good documentation, accurate coding, and complete charge capture together determine both whether the claim is paid and whether it is paid the correct amount.
Record what was assessed and done — the basis for all billing.
4. Clinical Documentation
Translate documentation into ICD-10, CPT, and HCPCS codes.
5. Medical Coding
Record coded services as charges so all care performed is billed.
6. Charge Capture
Mid-Cycle Steps
Steps 7-10: Getting Paid (Back-End)
Step 7 is claim submission. The charges are assembled into a claim, "scrubbed" (checked for errors before it goes out), and submitted to the payer — usually through a clearinghouse. A claim that arrives clean gets paid much faster than one that arrives with errors.
Step 8 is payment posting and remittance. When the payer adjudicates the claim, it sends back a remittance (an electronic remittance advice, or the patient-facing explanation of benefits) showing what it paid, adjusted, or denied; the provider posts those payments to the patient's account. Step 9 is denial management and appeals: analyzing why claims were denied, correcting and resubmitting them, and appealing when the denial is wrong.
Step 10 is accounts receivable follow-up and patient collections: chasing unpaid balances still sitting with insurers (third-party follow-up) and billing patients for whatever portion they owe. The cycle "closes" only when the full balance is collected or written off. Then, with the next encounter, it begins again — which is why it is called a cycle, not a line.
Scrub and submit the claim, typically via a clearinghouse.
7. Claim Submission
Post payer remittances (ERA/EOB) to patient accounts.
8. Payment Posting
Analyze, correct, resubmit, and appeal denied claims.
9. Denial Management & Appeals
Pursue unpaid insurer balances and bill patients for their share.
10. AR Follow-Up & Patient Collections
Back-End Steps
Why the Chain Matters
The power of viewing RCM as a 10-step chain is that it reveals where revenue actually leaks. A denial at step 9 is almost never really a step-9 problem — it usually traces back to a missed verification at step 3, weak documentation at step 4, or a coding error at step 5. The back-end is where problems become visible, but the front-end and mid-cycle are where they are created.
This is why high-performing organizations push effort "upstream." Preventing a denial at registration costs a fraction of reworking it after the fact, and a clean claim avoids the entire expensive cycle of denial, appeal, and follow-up. The whole discipline of RCM is largely about catching errors as early in the chain as possible.
Each remaining lesson in this course examines one or more of these steps in depth — verification, prior authorization, coding, clean claims, denials, appeals, payment posting, AR, collections, and the technology that ties them together. Keep this 10-step map in mind as the backbone; everything else hangs off it.
Denials surface at the back of the cycle but are typically created at the front — a wrong insurance ID, a missing authorization, a documentation gap, or a coding error. Fixing problems upstream is far cheaper than reworking them downstream, which is why RCM pushes effort toward the front of the chain.
A Back-End Denial Is Usually a Front-End Failure

Back-end steps (7-10): claim submission, payment posting, denial management and appeals, and AR follow-up plus patient collections.

######## revenue-cycle-management | rcm-kpis | Key Performance Indicators in RCM
Key Performance Indicators in RCM
How You Know the Revenue Cycle Is Healthy
A revenue cycle has many moving parts and a lot of money flowing through it, which means you cannot manage it by intuition. You need numbers — key performance indicators (KPIs) — that tell you, objectively, whether claims are going out clean, whether cash is coming in fast, and whether revenue is leaking. KPIs are the dashboard of the revenue cycle.
The challenge is that everyone calculates metrics slightly differently, which makes benchmarking against peers meaningless. To solve this, the Healthcare Financial Management Association (HFMA) created the MAP Keys — a standardized set of revenue-cycle KPIs with consistent, objective calculations. There are about 29 MAP Keys organized into five groups: Patient Access, Pre-Billing, Claims, Account Resolution, and Financial Management.
Standardization is what makes a KPI trustworthy. When a "denial rate" or "days in AR" is computed the same way everywhere, an organization can compare itself to national benchmarks and know whether it is leading or lagging. This lesson covers the handful of KPIs that matter most and the benchmarks that define good performance.
RCM KPIs are standardized metrics that reveal revenue-cycle health. HFMA's MAP Keys (~29 KPIs across five groups) provide consistent calculations so organizations can benchmark against national peers rather than guess.
Speed: Days in Accounts Receivable
The most watched RCM metric is "Days in Accounts Receivable" (Days in AR) — the average number of days it takes to collect payment after a service is delivered. It is a measure of speed: lower is better, because money owed but not yet collected is money the organization cannot use.
The widely cited benchmark is 30 to 40 days, with the MGMA benchmark at under 40 days and leading organizations achieving under 30. A companion metric, "AR over 90 days," tracks the share of receivables that have aged past 90 days; the benchmark is to keep this under 10 percent, because older receivables are progressively harder to collect.
Days in AR is powerful because it integrates the health of the whole cycle into one number. If claims are denied, delayed, or poorly followed up, the money sits in AR longer and the metric rises. A creeping Days in AR is often the first sign that something upstream is broken.
MGMA <40; leaders under 30 (industry benchmarks)
Days in AR Benchmark
30-40 days
Share of receivables aged past 90 days (industry)
AR Over 90 Days
<10%
Higher tolerance for patient balances (industry)
Self-Pay AR >90 Days
<30%
Faster collection frees up cash
Direction = Better
Lower
Cleanliness: Clean Claim Rate and First-Pass Resolution
Two closely related KPIs measure how often claims are done right the first time. The clean claim rate is the percentage of claims submitted without errors that are accepted by the payer on first submission. The benchmark is 95 percent or higher, with high performers aiming for around 98 percent.
The first-pass resolution rate (sometimes called first-pass yield) measures the percentage of claims that are paid without any resubmission or appeal — "claims paid right the first time." The industry standard here is also 95 percent or higher. The two metrics are related but distinct: a claim can pass the clearinghouse clean yet still be denied by the payer, so first-pass resolution is the stricter, more outcome-focused measure.
These cleanliness metrics matter enormously because rework is expensive. Every claim that is rejected or denied must be corrected and resubmitted, costing staff time and delaying cash. A high clean claim rate directly shortens Days in AR — the cleaner the claim, the faster the payment — which is why these are among the most actionable KPIs in the cycle.
