% of claims paid without resubmission or appeal

Yield: Denial Rate and Net Collection Rate
Two KPIs measure how much of what is owed actually gets collected. The denial rate is the percentage of claims denied by payers. The optimal benchmark is under 5 percent, with the best performers near 2 percent; an industry average tends to run between 5 and 10 percent. A rising denial rate is a direct hit to revenue and a signal of upstream problems.
The net collection rate (NCR) measures the percentage of collectible revenue an organization actually captures — that is, of the money it was contractually entitled to (after legitimate contractual adjustments), how much did it collect. Strong performers exceed 95 percent. A net collection rate well below 95 percent means real, earned money is being lost to write-offs, missed follow-up, and unworked denials.
Net collection rate is especially important because it strips out the contractual discounts that make "gross" numbers misleading. It answers the bottom-line question: of the dollars we should have collected, how many did we actually get? That is the truest measure of whether the revenue cycle is doing its job.
Best ~2%; industry average ~5-10% (industry benchmarks)

Efficiency and Using KPIs Well
A final essential KPI is cost to collect — total revenue-cycle expenses divided by total collections. It answers how much it costs the organization to collect each dollar. A lower cost to collect means a more efficient revenue cycle, and it is the metric that keeps efficiency honest: you can improve collections by throwing endless staff at the problem, but cost to collect reveals whether that effort is worth it.
No single KPI tells the whole story, and they interact. A practice can post a high net collection rate while its Days in AR balloons (it collects everything, but slowly), or a low denial rate while leaving easy money uncollected. The discipline is to watch a balanced set — speed (Days in AR), cleanliness (clean claim / first-pass), yield (denial rate / net collection), and efficiency (cost to collect) — together.
Used well, these KPIs turn the revenue cycle into a managed system: trends are tracked over time, benchmarked against HFMA MAP Keys and specialty norms, and used to target improvement where the numbers say it is needed. Every later lesson in this course ultimately moves one of these KPIs — fewer denials, cleaner claims, faster AR, higher net collections. They are the scoreboard for everything that follows.
A single KPI can mislead — high net collection with ballooning Days in AR, or a low denial rate while easy revenue goes uncollected. Track speed, cleanliness, yield, and efficiency together, and compare them to standardized benchmarks (HFMA MAP Keys) rather than judging any one metric alone.
Watch KPIs as a Balanced Set, Not in Isolation

######## revenue-cycle-management | pre-registration-insurance-verification | Pre-Registration and Insurance Verification
Pre-Registration and Insurance Verification
The Front Door of the Revenue Cycle
The revenue cycle begins before any care is delivered, at scheduling and registration. This is the front door, and what happens here quietly determines the fate of the eventual claim. Two activities dominate: pre-registration, which captures the patient's demographic and insurance information, and insurance verification, which confirms that coverage actually exists for the planned service.
Pre-registration ideally happens before the visit — often while the patient is still on the phone scheduling — so that any problem (an inactive plan, a wrong ID, a missing authorization) can be caught and fixed while there is still time. Registration then confirms and completes that information when the patient arrives.
These steps feel like clerical busywork, but they are among the highest-leverage activities in the entire cycle. A clean front door means clean claims downstream; a sloppy one guarantees denials weeks later, when they are far more expensive to fix.
Pre-registration captures patient demographic and insurance information before the visit; insurance verification confirms active coverage for the planned service. Together they are the front door that determines whether the eventual claim can be paid.
Why the Front-End Matters So Much
The data is blunt: about 44 percent of claim denials stem from front-end problems, and registration and eligibility issues alone account for about 24 percent (Change Healthcare Denials Index). The very first step of the cycle is also its single largest source of preventable revenue loss.
Most of these denials are entirely preventable. Many of them come down to human input errors — a mistyped member ID, a misspelled name, a wrong date of birth. Eligibility systems match patient data against the payer's enrollment records exactly, so even a small mismatch causes an automatic rejection. The care was fine; the data entry was not.
This is why the front-end deserves disproportionate attention. A denial prevented at registration costs almost nothing; the same denial caught after submission must be researched, corrected, resubmitted, and followed up — at an estimated cost of roughly $25 per claim for physician practices (MGMA) and about $118 for hospitals (Change Healthcare), plus weeks of delay. The economics overwhelmingly favor getting it right at the front door.
Share of denials caused by front-end problems (Change Healthcare Denials Index)
Denials From Front-End Issues

Share of denials from registration and eligibility (Change Healthcare Denials Index)

How Verification Works: The 270/271 Transaction
Insurance verification is largely automated through a standardized electronic exchange. The provider sends the payer an electronic eligibility inquiry — a HIPAA "270" transaction — and the payer returns an electronic response, the "271" transaction. This 270/271 pair is the technical backbone of eligibility verification.
Done in real time, the round trip typically returns a response within about 10 to 30 seconds — fast enough to verify a patient during check-in. The 271 response is rich: it can confirm whether coverage is active and its effective dates, list benefit details by service type, report copay, coinsurance, deductible, and out-of-pocket maximum status, flag whether prior authorization is required, and confirm network participation.
That last set of details is what makes verification so valuable — it not only confirms the patient is covered but surfaces exactly what they will owe and whether extra steps (like prior authorization) are needed before the service. This is the same standardized-data, EDI machinery that runs throughout RCM, applied to the very first step.
An electronic eligibility/benefit inquiry to the payer.
Provider sends a 270 inquiry
Typically within 10-30 seconds in real time.
Payer returns a 271 response
Active status, dates, copay/coinsurance/deductible, out-of-pocket, prior-auth flags, network status.
Response details coverage
Fix mismatches, collect estimated patient responsibility, trigger prior authorization if flagged.
Front-end acts on it
The Eligibility Verification Exchange
Coordination of Benefits
A particular verification challenge is coordination of benefits (COB): determining the correct order of payment when a patient has more than one insurance plan. If a patient has both a primary and a secondary payer, claims must go to the primary first, and only the remaining balance to the secondary.
Getting COB wrong is a common denial cause: a claim sent to the secondary payer first, or to a plan that is actually secondary, will be rejected with instructions to bill the correct primary. The eligibility exchange helps here, since the 270/271 supports coordination-of-benefits information, but it still requires the front-end staff to ask the right questions and record which plan is primary.
COB is a good example of why verification is more than a yes/no coverage check. It is about establishing the complete, correct picture of who pays, in what order, and for what — so the claim goes to the right payer the first time. A patient with Medicare and a commercial plan, or two employed spouses each with coverage, needs this sorted before the claim ever goes out.
A patient is covered by their own employer plan and, as a dependent, by their spouse's plan. If the front-end staff bill the spouse's plan as primary when the patient's own plan should be primary, the claim is denied and must be rebilled in the correct order.
The care was appropriate and covered — the loss came entirely from getting the payment order wrong at verification, a classic preventable front-end denial.
A Coordination-of-Benefits Mistake
Building a Strong Front-End Process
Because the stakes are so high and the errors so preventable, organizations invest heavily in front-end discipline. The core practices are straightforward: verify eligibility before every visit (not just at the first), confirm and re-confirm demographic data against a photo ID, and run real-time 270/271 checks so problems surface while they can still be fixed.
Automation is increasingly central. Real-time and batch eligibility tools can verify entire schedules of upcoming patients automatically, flagging inactive coverage, term dates, and authorization requirements before anyone arrives. This shifts the front-end from reactive (fix the denial later) to proactive (prevent it now), which is exactly where the economics point.
The mindset to instill is that the front-end is where money is saved, not spent. Every minute invested verifying coverage and cleaning up patient data at intake prevents a multiplied cost downstream. The next lessons — prior authorization and financial counseling — build directly on this foundation, completing the front-end's job of setting up a claim that can actually be paid.
Coverage changes — patients switch jobs, plans terminate, benefits reset annually. Verifying eligibility only at the first encounter and assuming it holds is a frequent cause of denials. Re-verify before each visit, ideally with an automated real-time check against the schedule.
Verify Every Visit, Not Just the First
Pre-registration captures patient demographic and insurance data before the visit; insurance verification confirms active coverage for the planned service.
The front-end is the largest source of preventable revenue loss: front-end issues cause about 44% of denials, and registration/eligibility alone about 24%.
Many denials stem from human input errors like mistyped member IDs — eligibility systems require an exact match to payer records.
Verification runs on the HIPAA 270 (inquiry) and 271 (response) EDI transactions, with real-time responses typically in 10-30 seconds.
The 271 response reports active status, dates, copay/coinsurance/deductible, out-of-pocket status, prior-auth requirements, and network participation.
Coordination of benefits (COB) determines payment order when a patient has multiple plans; billing the wrong plan first is a common preventable denial.
Strong front-ends verify before every visit, confirm demographics against ID, and automate real-time eligibility checks to prevent denials rather than rework them.
The 270/271 pair is the standardized EDI exchange for eligibility verification: the provider sends a 270 inquiry asking about a patient's coverage, and the payer returns a 271 response — typically within 10-30 seconds in real time — reporting active status, dates, copay/coinsurance/deductible, prior-authorization requirements, and network participation.

######## revenue-cycle-management | prior-authorization | Prior Authorization: Process and Pitfalls
Prior Authorization: Process and Pitfalls
Getting Permission Before You Treat
Prior authorization (often "prior auth" or "PA") is a requirement that a provider obtain approval from the patient's insurer before delivering certain services, medications, or procedures — or the insurer will not pay for them. It is, in blunt terms, a cost-control tool: the payer wants to vet that the planned care is necessary and covered before it is on the hook for the bill.
For the revenue cycle, prior authorization is a front-end gatekeeper. A service that requires authorization but is delivered without it is very likely to be denied — and "no authorization" denials are particularly painful because the care has already been provided and the cost incurred. The money is simply lost.
Prior authorization sits at the uncomfortable intersection of finance and clinical care. It is a billing requirement, but it directly affects whether and when patients get treatment. That tension is why it is one of the most contentious topics in all of health care, and why it deserves a lesson of its own.
Prior authorization requires a provider to get the insurer's approval before delivering certain services or drugs. Without it, the claim is typically denied — and because the care has already been delivered, that revenue is usually lost.
The Process
The basic workflow is: identify that a planned service requires authorization, gather the clinical documentation justifying medical necessity, submit the request to the payer, wait for a determination, and only then proceed (or appeal a denial). Identifying which services need authorization is itself a challenge, because requirements vary by payer and plan and change frequently.
Once submitted, the request is reviewed against the payer's medical-necessity criteria. The payer may approve, deny, or request more information. Approvals often come with limits — a specific number of visits, a defined timeframe, or a particular site of care — that the provider must then track and not exceed.
The technical standard for the prior-authorization transaction under HIPAA is the X12 278. Increasingly, though, the industry is moving toward FHIR-based electronic prior authorization (ePA) APIs that integrate directly with the EHR, aiming to replace fax-and-phone workflows with automated, real-time exchange.
Determine whether the planned service or drug needs authorization for this payer/plan.
Identify the requirement
Assemble the clinical evidence of medical necessity.
Gather documentation
Send to the payer (HIPAA X12 278, or increasingly a FHIR ePA API).
Submit the request
Record approval limits, or appeal a denial, before proceeding.
Track the determination
The Prior Authorization Workflow
The Enormous Burden
Prior authorization is widely regarded as one of the heaviest administrative burdens in health care, and the data is stark. According to the American Medical Association's 2024 prior authorization survey, physicians and their staff spend an average of 13 hours per week completing prior authorization requests, processing an average of 39 requests per physician per week.
The clinical consequences are serious. In the AMA survey, 93 percent of physicians reported that prior authorization delays access to necessary care, 89 percent said it increases physician burnout, and 82 percent said it can sometimes lead patients to abandon treatment altogether. Forty percent of physicians have staff working exclusively on prior authorizations.
For the revenue cycle, this burden cuts two ways. It is a major operational cost — staff time, dedicated personnel, software — and a major risk, because every required authorization that is missed, delayed, or done wrong becomes a denial. Prior authorization is simultaneously expensive to do and expensive to get wrong.

Common Pitfalls
Several recurring mistakes turn prior authorization into lost revenue. The first is failing to identify that a service required authorization at all — easy to do given how requirements vary and change. The service is delivered, the claim goes out, and it is denied for "no authorization on file," with the care already rendered.
The second is exceeding the authorization's limits — delivering more visits than approved, at the wrong site of care, or after the authorization's timeframe expired. The third is poor documentation of medical necessity, leading the payer to deny the request even when the care is appropriate. The fourth is letting authorizations expire before the service is performed, especially for scheduled procedures that get rescheduled.
The throughline is that prior authorization is unforgiving of process gaps. Because it must happen before the service, there is often no way to fix a missed authorization after the fact — unlike a coding error, you cannot simply resubmit. This is why organizations build dedicated authorization workflows, track expirations, and verify requirements as part of front-end verification (the previous lesson).
Unlike a coding error you can correct and resubmit, a prior authorization usually must be obtained BEFORE the service. Deliver care that required authorization without it, and the resulting denial is frequently unappealable — the revenue is simply lost. Identifying PA requirements at scheduling is essential.
A Missed Authorization Often Cannot Be Fixed
Reform and the Move to Automation
Because the burden is so widely recognized, prior authorization is a major target of reform. The most significant federal action is the CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule (CMS-0057-F), which imposes new requirements on many payers (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA marketplace plans).
The rule requires impacted payers to send prior authorization decisions within 72 hours for expedited (urgent) requests and seven calendar days for standard requests — which in some cases cuts current timeframes in half — and to provide specific reasons for denials. It also requires payers to build FHIR-based Prior Authorization APIs to automate the exchange, with operational provisions generally phasing in from 2026 and API requirements by 2027.
The direction of travel is clear: from fax-and-phone toward electronic, EHR-integrated, real-time prior authorization, with regulatory pressure for faster, more transparent decisions. For the revenue cycle, this promises to reduce both the labor cost and the denial risk over time — but for now, prior authorization remains a heavy, high-stakes front-end task that every RCM operation must manage carefully.
CMS-0057-F requires impacted payers (Medicare Advantage, Medicaid/CHIP, ACA marketplace) to return prior authorization decisions within 72 hours for urgent and seven days for standard requests, give specific denial reasons, and build FHIR-based Prior Authorization APIs.
Operational provisions generally begin in 2026 with API requirements by 2027 — a concrete federal push to make prior authorization faster, more transparent, and electronic.

######## revenue-cycle-management | patient-financial-counseling | Patient Financial Counseling and Estimates
Patient Financial Counseling and Estimates
The Patient Became a Major Payer
For most of the history of health insurance, the patient owed relatively little out of pocket — a small copay, perhaps. That has changed dramatically. The rise of high-deductible health plans means patients now shoulder a large and growing share of the bill, often thousands of dollars before insurance pays anything. The patient has become, in effect, one of the provider's major payers.
This shift created a new front-end discipline: patient financial counseling. Its job is to help patients understand what they will owe, set up how they will pay, and ideally collect some of it up front — before the patient leaves and the balance becomes much harder to collect. It is the front-end's answer to the reality that patient balances are now a serious revenue stream and a serious collection risk.
Financial counseling also serves the patient. Surprise medical bills are a leading cause of financial distress and medical debt. Clear, upfront estimates and conversations about payment options and assistance are both good revenue-cycle practice and good patient care — one of the places where the financial and ethical interests genuinely align.
Patient financial counseling helps patients understand their out-of-pocket responsibility, arrange payment, and pay up front where possible — a front-end discipline that grew as high-deductible plans made patients a major payer.
Calculating What the Patient Owes
A good estimate starts with the eligibility data from verification (the earlier lesson). To calculate a patient's estimated out-of-pocket responsibility, the provider combines the negotiated price for the service with the patient's specific benefit details: copay, coinsurance percentage, how much of the deductible remains, and progress toward the out-of-pocket maximum.
This is genuinely hard to get right. The provider may not know in real time exactly how much of a patient's deductible has already been spent elsewhere, and some charges (pathology, anesthesia, an affiliated physician's services) come from separate billers the hospital does not control. Facility fees and unforeseen charges from complications or longer stays add further uncertainty.
Because of this, an estimate is exactly that — an estimate, not a guarantee. Patients should be told clearly that the final bill may differ. Managing that expectation honestly is part of good counseling; an estimate presented as a promise sets up a dispute later when the real bill arrives.
Use the contracted rate for the planned service, not the gross charge.
Get the negotiated price
Factor in copay, coinsurance, remaining deductible, and out-of-pocket maximum.
Apply benefit details
Note charges from pathology, anesthesia, or affiliated physicians billed separately.
Account for separate billers
Make clear the final bill may differ; set honest expectations.
Communicate it as an estimate
Building a Patient Cost Estimate
The Legal Framework: Price Transparency
Two federal rules now require much of this estimation rather than leaving it optional. The Hospital Price Transparency rule, effective January 1, 2021, requires every U.S. hospital to post its standard charges online in two ways: a comprehensive machine-readable file covering all items and services, and a consumer-friendly display of at least 300 "shoppable" services (or a compliant price-estimator tool).
The machine-readable file must include gross charges, the discounted cash price, payer-specific negotiated charges, and the de-identified minimum and maximum negotiated charges. The intent is to let patients shop and compare prices — though in practice the data has been criticized as inconsistent and hard for ordinary patients to use.
For the revenue cycle, price transparency is both a compliance obligation and an opportunity. Organizations that build accurate, usable estimator tools satisfy the rule and simultaneously give their financial counselors the data to produce reliable estimates — turning a regulatory burden into a collections advantage.
Note the distinction: price transparency applies broadly to hospital charges, while the No Surprises Act's Good Faith Estimate (next section) targets the uninsured and self-pay specifically. Both push in the same direction — patients should know costs before care.
The No Surprises Act and Good Faith Estimates
The No Surprises Act, effective January 1, 2022, added specific protections — including the Good Faith Estimate (GFE) requirement for uninsured and self-pay patients. When such a patient schedules a service (or asks), the provider must give a good faith estimate of the expected charges within defined timeframes (generally one to three business days depending on how far out the service is scheduled).
The GFE has real teeth. If the final billed charges exceed the estimate by $400 or more, the patient can use a Patient-Provider Dispute Resolution (PPDR) process — within 120 days of the bill — to challenge the charge. Crucially, while a dispute is underway, the provider may not move the bill to collections, threaten collections, or must pause collections if already started.
For the revenue cycle, this raises the stakes on estimate accuracy for self-pay patients: a lowball estimate is not just bad service, it creates a legal dispute right and a collections freeze. Done well, though, the GFE process can actually support collections — a clear, accurate estimate given upfront makes patients more willing to pay at or near the time of service.
Under the No Surprises Act, if an uninsured/self-pay patient's final charges exceed their Good Faith Estimate by $400 or more, they can invoke dispute resolution within 120 days — and the provider must not pursue collections while the dispute is pending. Accurate self-pay estimates are both a service and a compliance necessity.
A Good Faith Estimate Off by $400+ Triggers Dispute Rights
Point-of-Service Collections and Compassion
The payoff of good estimation is point-of-service (POS) collections — collecting the patient's expected responsibility at or before the time of care. POS collection is a tracked RCM metric because money collected upfront dramatically improves cash flow and reduces bad debt: once a patient leaves with a balance, the odds of collecting fall sharply, and a large share of patient balances ultimately go unpaid.
But POS collections must be balanced with compassion and compliance. Counseling should surface options for patients who cannot pay in full: payment plans, sliding-scale discounts, and — critically — screening for charity care and financial assistance, which nonprofit hospitals are obligated to offer. Aggressively demanding payment from a patient who qualifies for charity care is both unethical and, increasingly, legally risky.
The mature view is that financial counseling sits exactly where revenue and patient welfare meet. Done poorly, it produces surprise bills, disputes, and medical debt. Done well, it gives patients clarity and options while improving collections — converting the front-end's financial conversation from an adversarial one into a transparent, manageable part of care. This completes the front-end; the next module turns to the mid-cycle, where care becomes a coded bill.
When a provider gives a patient a clear, accurate out-of-pocket estimate before a procedure, the patient can plan — and is far more likely to pay at or near the time of service.
This is why estimation and POS collections go together: the same data that satisfies price-transparency and Good Faith Estimate rules also gives financial counselors the basis to collect upfront, improving cash flow and reducing the bad debt that piles up once a patient leaves with an unpaid balance.
Estimates That Drive Point-of-Service Collections

######## revenue-cycle-management | icd10-cpt-hcpcs | ICD-10, CPT, and HCPCS Coding Fundamentals
ICD-10, CPT, and HCPCS Coding Fundamentals
The Language That Turns Care Into a Bill
A claim is not written in English — it is written in codes. To bill for care, the clinical encounter must be translated into standardized codes that payers recognize, and getting those codes right is the heart of the mid-cycle. Medical coding is the language that converts what happened in the exam room into something an insurer can adjudicate and pay.
There are three primary code sets, and the easiest way to keep them straight is by the question each answers. ICD-10 codes answer "why" — the diagnosis or reason for care. CPT codes answer "what" — the procedure or service performed. HCPCS Level II codes answer "what else" — the supplies, drugs, equipment, and services CPT does not cover.
Every claim weaves these together: a diagnosis (why) that justifies a procedure (what), plus any supplies or drugs (what else). Understanding these three code sets — who maintains them, what they cover, and how they connect — is foundational to everything downstream in billing.
Three code sets carry a claim: ICD-10 (the diagnosis — "why"), CPT (the procedure or service — "what"), and HCPCS Level II (supplies, drugs, and equipment — "what else"). Together they translate an encounter into a billable claim.
ICD-10: The Diagnosis Codes
ICD stands for the International Classification of Diseases, developed by the World Health Organization as the global standard for reporting diagnoses. The U.S. uses a clinical modification called ICD-10-CM for diagnoses — the codes physicians use to report why a patient was seen, submitted on claims to explain why care was provided.
ICD-10-CM in the U.S. is maintained by the CDC's National Center for Health Statistics (NCHS). There is also a separate, distinct code set — ICD-10-PCS — used specifically for inpatient hospital procedures; its codes are seven characters, with each character an "axis" specifying details of the procedure. Do not confuse the two: ICD-10-CM is diagnoses (everywhere), ICD-10-PCS is inpatient procedures (hospitals).
The single most important role of ICD-10 codes in billing is establishing medical necessity. Payers want proof that a procedure was justified by the patient's condition, and the diagnosis code is how that justification is communicated. A procedure that is not supported by an appropriate diagnosis will be denied as not medically necessary, no matter how well it was performed.
ICD-10-CM (diagnoses)
Reports the "why" — diagnoses and symptoms
Used in all care settings
Maintained by CDC/NCHS
Establishes medical necessity
ICD-10-PCS (procedures)
Reports inpatient hospital procedures
7-character codes, each an axis of classification
Used by hospitals for inpatient stays
Separate from CPT, which covers most other procedures
ICD-10-CM vs. ICD-10-PCS
CPT: The Procedure and Service Codes
CPT stands for Current Procedural Terminology. CPT codes describe the services that providers and facilities deliver — surgeries, office visits, consultations, diagnostic tests. Where ICD-10 codes describe the "why," CPT codes describe the "what." CPT is maintained and copyrighted by the American Medical Association (AMA), whose CPT Editorial Panel decides additions, deletions, and revisions.
CPT codes are five characters, mostly numeric and always beginning with a number. A heavily used category is Evaluation and Management (E/M) codes, which describe office and hospital visits. For example, CPT 99204 is a Level 4 evaluation-and-management visit for a new patient, requiring moderate medical decision-making or 45 minutes of total time.
CPT coding is where much of a claim's dollar value is set, because the procedure code largely determines reimbursement. It is also where some of the most consequential errors and compliance risks live — selecting a higher-level code than the documentation supports ("upcoding") or a lower one ("downcoding") — topics the documentation-compliance lesson takes up next.
A practical note: CPT codes are often paired with two-digit "modifiers" that add detail (e.g., that a procedure was bilateral, or distinct from another service the same day). Modifiers are small but mighty — a missing or wrong modifier is a frequent denial cause.
HCPCS Level II: Everything Else
HCPCS (the Healthcare Common Procedure Coding System) has two levels. Level I is essentially CPT. Level II — what people usually mean by "HCPCS codes" — covers the products, supplies, and services that CPT does not: certain drugs and biologicals, ambulance services, and durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (collectively "DMEPOS").
HCPCS Level II codes are maintained by CMS and have a distinctive format: a single letter followed by four digits — which is how you tell them apart from numeric CPT codes at a glance. A well-known subset is the "J-codes," which identify drugs administered other than by mouth, such as injectable and infused medications.
HCPCS Level II matters because a lot of real cost lives in supplies and drugs. An infusion clinic, a DME supplier, or an ambulance service depends on accurate HCPCS coding to be paid for the products it provides. Omitting or miscoding these is direct lost revenue, the same way a missed CPT charge is.

The Three Code Sets at a Glance
How the Codes Work Together
The codes are not independent — they must link coherently on a claim. The diagnosis (ICD-10) must support the procedure (CPT) it is paired with, demonstrating medical necessity. The supplies and drugs (HCPCS Level II) must be consistent with the procedure and diagnosis. A claim is essentially an argument: "this diagnosis justified this procedure, which used these supplies."
When the links break, the claim is denied. A procedure code with an unrelated diagnosis triggers a medical-necessity denial. A drug J-code without a supporting diagnosis or procedure looks unjustified. This is why coding is a skilled profession: certified coders read the clinical documentation and select codes that are not just individually correct but coherent together and fully supported by the record.
Finally, the bedrock rule of coding is that the code must reflect what was actually documented and done — no more, no less. Coding what was not documented is fraud; failing to code what was documented is lost revenue. That balance, and the documentation that underpins it, is the subject of the next lesson. For now, the key is that these three code sets are the alphabet of the entire claim — master them and the rest of billing becomes legible.
Individually correct codes are not enough. The diagnosis (ICD-10) must justify the procedure (CPT), and supplies/drugs (HCPCS) must fit both. A procedure unsupported by an appropriate diagnosis is denied as "not medically necessary" — coding is about coherent, documented linkage, not isolated code accuracy.
Codes Must Link, Not Just Exist
Medical coding translates a clinical encounter into standardized codes payers can adjudicate; three code sets dominate.
ICD-10-CM codes report the diagnosis ("why"), are maintained by the CDC/NCHS, and establish medical necessity for procedures.
ICD-10-PCS is a separate 7-character code set for inpatient hospital procedures — distinct from ICD-10-CM diagnoses and from CPT.
CPT codes describe the procedure or service ("what"), are maintained by the AMA, are five characters starting with a number, and include E/M codes like 99204.
HCPCS Level II codes cover supplies, drugs, and DMEPOS ("what else"), are maintained by CMS, and use a letter-plus-four-digits format (e.g., J-codes for injectable drugs).
CPT codes often carry two-digit modifiers that add detail; a missing or wrong modifier is a common denial cause.
The codes must link coherently — the diagnosis must justify the procedure — and must reflect exactly what was documented and done, no more and no less.
CPT codes describe what was done and largely drive reimbursement; ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes describe why and establish medical necessity. Payers require that a procedure be justified by an appropriate diagnosis — a CPT code not supported by a relevant ICD-10 code is denied as not medically necessary. Supplies and drugs are captured by HCPCS Level II codes.
It sets the dollar amount the procedure will be reimbursed
It establishes medical necessity — justifying why the procedure was performed
It identifies the supplies and drugs used
It replaces the need for a CPT code

######## revenue-cycle-management | charge-capture | Charge Capture: From Service to Bill
Charge Capture: From Service to Bill
Billing for What You Actually Did
A service can be delivered flawlessly, documented thoroughly, and coded correctly — and still never get billed. The step that prevents that catastrophe is charge capture: the process of recording every billable service, procedure, supply, and medication a patient received so it ends up on the claim. If charge capture fails, the work was done for free.
Charge capture is the bridge between the clinical event and the financial claim. After the diagnosis and procedure are coded, charge capture ensures those coded services — plus the supplies and drugs used — are formally recorded as charges in the billing system. It answers a deceptively simple question: did we actually bill for everything we did?
The answer, distressingly often, is no. Missed charges are one of the most common and most invisible forms of revenue loss, because nothing alerts you to a charge that was never entered. Unlike a denial, which is at least visible, a missed charge simply never appears — silent, lost revenue.
Charge capture is the process of recording every billable service, procedure, supply, and medication so it reaches the claim. A service that is not captured is never billed — silent, invisible lost revenue.
The Chargemaster: The Master Price List
Charge capture rests on the chargemaster, also called the Charge Description Master (CDM). The chargemaster is the organization's master database of every billable item and service, mapping each one to its code, price, department, and applicable modifiers. It is, quite literally, the backbone of the revenue cycle — every charge that gets captured is pulled from it.
Because the chargemaster defines what can be charged and at what price, errors in it propagate everywhere. An outdated code, a missing item, or an incorrect price in the CDM produces wrong or rejected charges across thousands of claims. Maintaining the chargemaster — keeping codes current, prices accurate, and items complete — is an ongoing revenue-integrity discipline of its own.
Charge entry is the specific administrative step where finalized codes and their fees from the chargemaster are entered into the billing system, creating the line items that form the claim. In some settings this is automated from the EHR; in others it is manual. Either way, charge entry is where the chargemaster's data becomes an actual charge on a patient's account.
The clinician performs and records the care.
Service delivered & documented
Certified coders assign ICD-10, CPT, and HCPCS codes.
Coded

Charge entry from the chargemaster

Charge reconciliation
From Service to Charge
How Charges Get Lost
Missed and inaccurate charges arise in several recurring ways. A procedure may be documented but never billed. Ancillary services (a lab, an imaging study) may become disconnected from the encounter. Supplies and implants may be used but never linked from the usage log to the claim. Charges on the hospital (facility) claim may contradict those on the professional (physician) claim.
A particular problem is the "late charge" — a charge that arrives after the claim has already been submitted. Late charges either get dropped entirely (lost revenue) or force a costly claim correction. High-volume, supply-heavy, and ancillary-dependent departments (the OR, the ED, infusion, cath lab) are the classic hotspots where charges slip through.
The defense is charge reconciliation: systematically comparing what was documented against what was charged, ideally on a daily basis, to catch missing charges before the claim goes out. Daily reconciliation is a recognized best practice precisely because charge capture is a major, ongoing source of revenue leakage that must be actively hunted, not assumed.
Unlike a denial, a charge that was never entered triggers no alert — it simply never appears. This makes missed charges one of the most insidious revenue leaks. Daily charge reconciliation against documentation is the main defense, especially in supply-heavy areas like the OR, ED, and infusion.
A Missed Charge Is Invisible
The Scale of the Leak
The financial stakes of charge capture are larger than they first appear. The Healthcare Financial Management Association reports that up to 1 percent of a health system's net charges are lost to charge-capture leakage, and broader estimates put annual losses in the range of 1 to 3 percent of net revenue.
One percent may sound small until you apply it to a large organization's revenue — for a health system, it can mean millions of dollars vanishing every year, invisibly, into uncaptured charges. Because the loss is silent and recurring, it often goes unnoticed for years, which is exactly what makes it so damaging.
Conversely, fixing charge capture is one of the highest-ROI activities in the revenue cycle. Organizations that implement robust charge-capture systems commonly recover a meaningful share of previously lost revenue in the first year — money that was always earned but never collected. The point is not to bill more than was done; it is to bill for all of what was done.

Capturing Charges Well
Strong charge capture combines process and technology. On the process side: daily charge reconciliation, regular charge-capture audits, a well-maintained chargemaster, and clear accountability for charge entry in every department. On the technology side: EHR-integrated charge capture that records charges at the point of care, and automated tools that flag missing, duplicate, or inconsistent charges.
Automation is increasingly powerful here. Modern revenue-cycle software uses algorithms and machine learning to detect likely missed charges, and natural language processing can read clinical documentation to surface billable services that were documented but never coded or charged — directly attacking the "documented but not billed" leak.
But charge capture must always stay tethered to documentation and compliance. Capturing a charge for something that was not documented or not done is not revenue recovery — it is fraud. The goal is integrity: bill for everything actually performed and documented, and nothing else. That integrity link between documentation and charges is exactly the territory of the next lesson, on documentation requirements and compliance.
The OR is a classic charge-capture hotspot: a single surgery involves the procedure, anesthesia, implants, instruments, and consumable supplies, each a potential charge that must be linked back to the encounter.
When supplies and implants used in the case are not captured from the usage log onto the claim, the organization loses real money on high-cost items — which is why supply-heavy departments get the most intensive charge reconciliation and audit attention.
Charge Capture in the Operating Room

######## revenue-cycle-management | documentation-compliance | Documentation Requirements and Compliance
Documentation Requirements and Compliance
If It Wasn't Documented, It Wasn't Done
The previous two lessons covered coding and charge capture — but both rest on something more fundamental: documentation. The codes and charges on a claim are only as good as the clinical record that supports them. This gives rise to the oldest maxim in health information: "if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done."
To a payer, the documentation IS the care. Brilliant physicians have been denied reimbursement not because they provided bad care, but because they could not prove what they did. The clinical record is the evidence, and a service that is performed but not adequately documented cannot be billed — or, if billed, cannot survive an audit.
Documentation therefore sits at the center of the mid-cycle, and it is simultaneously a revenue issue and a compliance issue. Get it right and the claim is defensible and fully paid. Get it wrong and you face denials, lost revenue, and — at the extreme — allegations of fraud. This lesson covers both sides: documenting to get paid, and documenting to stay compliant.
To payers, the documentation is the care. The principle "if it wasn't documented, it wasn't done" means a claim is only defensible to the extent the clinical record supports its codes and charges.
Medical Necessity: The Cornerstone
The central thing documentation must establish is medical necessity — proof that the service was reasonable and necessary for the patient's condition. Medical necessity is the cornerstone of reimbursement: payers will not pay for a service unless the record clearly shows it was justified by the diagnosis and clinical picture.
This is where documentation, coding, and payment lock together. The ICD-10 diagnosis code (from the coding lesson) signals medical necessity, but the diagnosis code is only valid if the underlying documentation actually supports it. A payer auditing a claim reads the clinical notes, treatment plan, and results to confirm the service genuinely matched the documented need.
When documentation fails to establish medical necessity, the claim is denied — even for care that was entirely appropriate. This is one of the most common and frustrating denial types, because the problem is not the care or even the coding, but the written justification. Strong documentation closes that gap by telling a clear, patient-specific story of why each service was needed.
A practical shift reinforces this: the 2021 Evaluation and Management (E/M) guidelines for office visits moved away from counting history and exam "bullets" toward basing the visit level on medical decision-making or total time. Documentation now must convey the complexity of clinical thinking, not just check boxes.
Clinical Documentation Integrity
The discipline of ensuring documentation is accurate, complete, and supports the codes is called Clinical Documentation Integrity (CDI) — sometimes Clinical Documentation Improvement. CDI specialists review records, often concurrently with care, to confirm that the documentation accurately reflects the patient's condition and the services provided, and that it supports the codes billed.
A core CDI tool is the query: when documentation is ambiguous, incomplete, or conflicting, a CDI specialist or coder formally asks the provider to clarify — without leading them toward a particular answer. Query practices are carefully governed (organizations decide what clinical indicators justify a query and whether queries become part of the legal record) precisely because a leading or improper query can itself create a compliance problem.
CDI is both offense and defense. On offense, it captures the full, accurate complexity of care so the organization is paid correctly (not under-paid for under-documented complexity). On defense, it ensures that if a payer audits later, the documentation stands behind every code — letting the organization demonstrate its accuracy and its commitment to compliance.
Documentation is ambiguous, incomplete, or conflicting relative to the clinical indicators.
Identify a gap
Formally request clarification without leading to a specific answer.
Query the provider
The provider amends or confirms the documentation in the record.
Provider clarifies
Coders assign codes supported by the now-complete documentation.
Code to the record
The CDI Query Process
Upcoding, Downcoding, and Fraud
Documentation defines the boundary between correct billing and fraud, and two errors sit on either side of it. Upcoding is submitting a code for a higher level of service or complexity than was actually performed and documented. Downcoding is the reverse — billing a lower level than was provided and documented, leaving money on the table.
Upcoding is the dangerous one. Consistently billing a higher level of service than the documentation supports is a classic sign of fraud or abuse, depending on whether it is intentional. Related schemes include "unbundling" (billing separately for services that should be billed together) — also a compliance violation.
The legal teeth come from the False Claims Act (FCA), which imposes liability for submitting false or fraudulent claims to federal programs like Medicare and Medicaid. The FCA holds the provider accountable for the final submission, and the Department of Justice and Office of Inspector General (OIG) actively pursue billing fraud. Penalties are severe, which is why documentation-to-code integrity is not optional — it is a legal obligation.
Billing a higher level of service than the documentation supports — consistently — is a classic fraud/abuse pattern under the False Claims Act, which holds the provider liable for the claim submitted. Downcoding loses revenue; upcoding risks legal liability. The safe path is always: code exactly what is documented.
Upcoding Is Fraud When the Record Doesn't Support It
Building a Compliance Program
Because the stakes span both revenue and legal liability, organizations build formal compliance programs around documentation and coding. The hallmark practices include enforced documentation standards (favoring patient-specific narratives over generic templates), regular internal audits, and — critically — "pre-bill" audits that catch patterns of over- or under-billing before claims ever reach the payer.
These programs are shaped by external authorities: CMS rules, OIG compliance guidance, Joint Commission standards, and payer-specific requirements all define what good documentation and coding compliance look like. The OIG has long published guidance on the elements of an effective compliance program, and recent enforcement has increasingly targeted "technology-enabled" failures — for example, copy-paste and templated notes that inflate documentation without reflecting real care.
The unifying principle is integrity: code and bill exactly what was documented and done — never more (which is fraud), never less (which is lost revenue). Good documentation simultaneously maximizes legitimate reimbursement and protects the organization legally. With the claim now coded, charged, and documented defensibly, it is ready to be assembled and submitted — which is where the next module, on clean claims and submission, begins.
A compliance program might run pre-bill audits that sample claims before submission, comparing the documentation against the codes to catch upcoding, unbundling, or unsupported services before they go out the door.
This proactive approach reflects OIG compliance guidance: it is far better to catch and fix a pattern internally than to have the DOJ or OIG discover it later under the False Claims Act, where the provider bears liability for every claim submitted.
Pre-Bill Audits and the OIG

######## revenue-cycle-management | clean-claims | Clean Claims: What They Are and Why They Matter
Clean Claims: What They Are and Why They Matter
The Goal of the Whole Front End
Everything in the front-end and mid-cycle — verification, authorization, documentation, coding, charge capture — has been building toward one thing: a clean claim. A clean claim is a claim that is complete and accurate, with no errors, so that the payer accepts and pays it on the first submission without rejection or denial.
The clean claim is the payoff for all the upstream discipline. When a claim arrives clean, it gets paid fast and the encounter is essentially done. When it arrives dirty — missing a field, carrying a wrong code, failing an edit — it bounces back, and the organization enters the expensive cycle of correction, resubmission, and follow-up that defines the back end.
Because of this, the clean claim rate is one of the most important RCM metrics, benchmarked at 95 percent or higher (with top performers near 98 percent). Every percentage point of clean claim rate translates directly into faster cash, lower rework cost, and shorter days in accounts receivable.
A clean claim is complete and accurate with no errors, so the payer accepts and pays it on first submission. It is the payoff of all upstream work, and the clean claim rate (benchmark 95%+) directly drives cash speed and cost.
The Two Claim Forms
A claim is a structured document, and there are two primary formats depending on who is billing. Professional claims — from individual providers like physicians and suppliers — use the CMS-1500 form (the paper version), whose electronic equivalent is the 837P. Institutional claims — from facilities like hospitals and skilled-nursing facilities — use the UB-04 form (also called the CMS-1450), whose electronic equivalent is the 837I.
The forms differ in structure. The CMS-1500 uses 33 numbered fields; the UB-04 uses 81 alphanumeric "form locators." The big conceptual difference is that the UB-04/837I organizes charges around revenue codes — categorizing services by department or type — whereas the CMS-1500/837P bills line-by-line by procedure. A hospital stay and a physician's office visit are billed on fundamentally different documents.
In modern practice, almost all claims are submitted electronically as 837 transactions rather than on paper, because the electronic versions are faster, scalable, and preferred (often required) by payers. Knowing which form applies — professional vs. institutional — is foundational, because the wrong form, or the wrong fields for that form, produces an immediate rejection.

Professional vs. Institutional Claims
What Makes a Claim Clean
A clean claim requires that all the required fields are completed accurately — and which fields are required depends on the payer (Medicare, Medicaid, or commercial) and the form. On a CMS-1500, critical fields include the patient's insurance ID, diagnosis codes (ICD-10), dates and place of service, CPT/HCPCS codes with modifiers, charges, and the rendering and billing provider NPIs and tax ID.
The claim must also be internally coherent — the same linkage from the coding lesson. The diagnosis must support the procedure; the codes must be valid and current; the modifiers must be correct; the provider identifiers (NPI and taxonomy) must match the payer's records. A claim can have every box filled and still be "dirty" if the contents do not hang together correctly.
Cleanliness is unforgiving of small things. A mistyped insurance ID, an invalid date format, an improper taxonomy code in the billing-provider field, or a missing referring-provider entry can each trigger a rejection. This is why the front-end verification and accurate coding covered earlier matter so much: they are what populate these fields correctly in the first place.

Elements of a Clean Claim
Claim Scrubbing
The mechanism that catches errors before a claim goes out is claim scrubbing: a thorough automated (and sometimes manual) review of the claim against thousands of edits and rules to flag inconsistencies, missing fields, and likely denials. Scrubbing is the last line of defense, sitting between the billing system and the payer.
Scrubbers check the obvious (missing or invalid fields, wrong formats) and the subtle (code combinations that violate payer or national edit rules, diagnosis-procedure mismatches, modifier problems). The principle is simple and powerful: it is vastly cheaper to catch an error in scrubbing — before submission — than to have the payer catch it as a denial weeks later.
Professional bodies like the AAPC and AMA emphasize scrubbing precisely because it reduces denials and improves submission efficiency. A good scrubbing process is one of the highest-leverage investments in the cycle: it converts would-be denials into clean claims at the point of lowest cost, directly raising the clean claim rate.
A claim is built with a valid procedure code but an outdated diagnosis code that the payer no longer accepts. Submitted as-is, it would be rejected and bounce back days later.
The claim scrubber flags the invalid code before submission, the biller corrects it, and the claim goes out clean — turning a future denial into a first-pass payment at a fraction of the cost of reworking it after the fact.
A Scrubber Catching a Rejection
Rejections vs. Denials, and Why Clean Pays
A useful distinction: a rejected claim never made it into the payer's system — it failed a format or front-line edit (at the clearinghouse or payer intake) and can usually be corrected and resubmitted quickly. A denied claim was accepted and adjudicated but the payer decided not to pay it. Clean-claim discipline aims to prevent both, but rejections are the cheaper, earlier failure to fix.
The economics overwhelmingly reward cleanliness. A clean claim is paid in one pass; a dirty claim triggers research, correction, resubmission, and follow-up — at roughly $25 per claim for practices and about $118 for hospitals — plus the delay of additional weeks in AR. A high clean claim rate is therefore not a vanity metric; it is one of the most direct levers on both cost and cash speed in the entire revenue cycle.
The throughline of this lesson is that "clean" is the goal everything upstream serves and everything downstream depends on. The front-end gathers correct information, the mid-cycle codes and documents it accurately, scrubbing verifies it, and only then does the claim go out. Get the claim clean and the back end is short and cheap; let it go out dirty and the back end becomes the expensive, multi-step ordeal that the rest of this course's modules address.
A rejection means the claim failed a format/edit check and never entered the payer's system — usually a quick fix and resubmit. A denial means the claim was processed but the payer declined to pay. Both are prevented by clean claims, but they are worked differently — don't treat a rejection like a denial or vice versa.
Rejection and Denial Are Not the Same Thing
A clean claim is complete and accurate with no errors, so the payer pays it on first submission; it is the payoff of all upstream front-end and mid-cycle work.
The clean claim rate (benchmark 95%+, top performers ~98%) directly drives faster cash, lower rework cost, and shorter days in AR.

######## revenue-cycle-management | clearinghouses-edi | Clearinghouses and EDI Transactions
Clearinghouses and EDI Transactions
The Post Office of Health Care Billing
Once a clean claim is built, it has to get to the payer — and there are thousands of payers, each with its own systems, formats, and rules. A provider does not connect directly to every one of them. Instead, claims flow through an intermediary called a clearinghouse, which acts as the central post office of healthcare billing.
A clearinghouse receives claims from providers, checks and reformats them to meet each payer's specific requirements, and routes them to the correct payer — then carries the payer's responses back. It is a hub-and-spoke model: providers connect to a clearinghouse, the clearinghouse connects to the payers, and the clearinghouse translates between them.
This intermediary role is enormously valuable. Without clearinghouses, every provider would need a custom connection to every payer. With them, a provider maintains one connection and reaches the whole payer universe — while gaining an extra layer of error-checking along the way.
A clearinghouse is the intermediary that receives provider claims, applies payer-specific edits, and routes them to the correct payer (and carries responses back). It lets providers reach thousands of payers through one connection.
What a Clearinghouse Actually Does
A clearinghouse does more than forward claims. Its core value-add is applying payer-specific edits — checking each claim against the unique rules of the destination payer before sending it. This is a second, payer-aware layer of claim scrubbing on top of the provider's own, catching errors that would otherwise become rejections or denials.
The typical flow: the provider submits a batch of claims to the clearinghouse; the clearinghouse validates and scrubs them, returning any that fail for correction; it then formats the passing claims to each payer's specification and transmits them. When payers respond — with acknowledgments, status updates, or remittances — those come back through the clearinghouse to the provider.
This upfront validation is why clearinghouses are described as preventing avoidable denials: they catch problems at the lowest-cost point, before the payer ever sees the claim. They also consolidate reporting, giving the provider a single view of claim status across all payers rather than separate logins for each.
A batch of claims (837 transactions) goes to the clearinghouse.
Provider submits claims
Applies payer-specific edits; returns failures for correction.
Clearinghouse scrubs & validates
Formats each claim to the payer's specification and transmits it.
Routes to payers
Acknowledgments, status (277), and remittances (835) return to the provider.
Carries responses back
How a Claim Flows Through a Clearinghouse
EDI: The Standardized Language
All this exchange runs on EDI — Electronic Data Interchange — the standardized electronic format for transmitting healthcare administrative transactions between providers, payers, and clearinghouses. HIPAA mandated these standards in the early 2000s and adopted the ANSI X12 standard (the same family used in industries like banking and logistics) as the format.
Each type of administrative transaction has a numbered X12 standard. You have already met several in this course: the 270/271 eligibility inquiry and response, and the 278 prior-authorization transaction. The submission and payment transactions complete the set.
Knowing the key transaction numbers is part of the working vocabulary of RCM, because people refer to them constantly ("we got the 835," "check the 277"). The numbers are not arbitrary trivia — each names a specific, standardized step in the electronic conversation between provider and payer.
Health Care Claim

Key HIPAA X12 EDI Transactions
The Two Big Ones: 837 and 835
Two transactions form the heart of the billing exchange. The 837 is the claim itself — it carries the patient, subscriber, provider, diagnosis, procedure, and charge details the payer needs to adjudicate (in its 837P professional, 837I institutional, and 837D dental variants). When you "submit a claim" electronically, you are sending an 837.
The 835 is the answer: the electronic remittance advice (ERA). It communicates how the payer adjudicated the claim — what was paid, what was adjusted, and what was denied — using standardized codes for the reasons and amounts on each service line. The 835 is what enables automated payment posting and reconciliation, the subject of a later lesson.
Together, 837 out and 835 back form the core loop: the provider sends the claim, the payer sends the remittance. The 276/277 status transactions let the provider check on a claim in between, and the 270/271 and 278 handle the pre-service checks. The whole cycle, electronically, is a structured conversation in these numbered transactions.
A subtle but important point: the 835 (electronic) is not the same as the patient-facing Explanation of Benefits (EOB). They convey related information, but the 835 is the machine-readable remittance used for auto-posting — a distinction the payment-posting lesson revisits.
Critical Infrastructure: The Change Healthcare Lesson
Clearinghouses are so central that their failure can paralyze the system — a fact made vivid in early 2024. On February 21, 2024, Change Healthcare, the largest medical claims clearinghouse in the United States, was hit by a ransomware cyberattack. Change Healthcare processes about 15 billion health care transactions a year and touches roughly one in three U.S. patient records, so the attack effectively shut down the claims-clearing process for a huge share of the industry.
The fallout was severe and immediate. Tens of thousands of physicians, hospitals, and pharmacies could not submit claims or get paid; cash flow froze; some pharmacies could not confirm insurance or fill prescriptions. Providers reverted to manual workarounds, and the disruption stretched on for weeks. The parent company, UnitedHealth, reportedly paid about $22 million in ransom.
The episode was a stark lesson in concentration risk: the clearinghouse layer is critical infrastructure, and over-reliance on a single dominant vendor created a systemic single point of failure. For RCM, the takeaways are practical — understand your clearinghouse dependency, and recognize that the smooth, invisible flow of EDI transactions is something the entire payment system quietly depends on. With claims now routed and adjudicated, the next lessons turn to what the payer actually owes (payer contracts) and what happens when claims come back denied.
In February 2024, a ransomware attack on Change Healthcare — the largest U.S. clearinghouse, processing about 15 billion transactions a year — halted claims processing for much of the country for weeks.
Providers could not submit claims or receive payments, cash flow froze, and the sector scrambled to reroute through other clearinghouses or manual processes. It demonstrated that clearinghouses are critical infrastructure and that concentration in one vendor is a systemic risk.

######## revenue-cycle-management | payer-contracts | Payer Contracts and Fee Schedules
Payer Contracts and Fee Schedules
The Price Is Not What You Charge
A fundamental and surprising truth of healthcare billing: the amount a provider charges has almost nothing to do with what it actually gets paid. The real price is set in advance, in a contract between the provider and each payer. That contract — and the fee schedule attached to it — determines how much the provider will collect for every service, no matter what its chargemaster lists.
This is why a hospital can "charge" $5,000 for a procedure and collect $1,200: the $5,000 is the gross charge, but the payer contract says the allowed amount is $1,200, and that is all the provider can collect. The gap is not a discount the provider chose to give at the register — it was negotiated into the contract long before the patient ever arrived.
Understanding payer contracts is therefore essential to understanding the back end of the revenue cycle. Every payment that comes in must be checked against what the contract said it should be — and the difference between charges, allowed amounts, and actual payments is where much of RCM's analytical work lives.
A payer contract and its fee schedule set the "allowed amount" — the maximum a provider will be paid for each service — in advance. The provider's gross charge is largely irrelevant; the contracted rate governs what is actually collected.
The Allowed Amount and Contractual Adjustment
The central number in a payer contract is the allowed amount — also called the maximum allowable or contracted rate — the maximum a payer will reimburse for a specific service under the negotiated agreement. It is set when the contract is signed and is typically tied to a fee schedule: a negotiated dollar amount per CPT code, or a percentage of Medicare's rates.
The difference between what the provider billed and the allowed amount is the contractual adjustment — the portion of the bill the provider agrees to write off in exchange for being in the payer's network. The formula is simple: Contractual Adjustment = Billed Charges − Allowed Amount. This write-off is not a loss to chase; it is a contractual obligation the provider agreed to.
This is a crucial distinction for the back end. A contractual adjustment is a legitimate, expected write-off and should never be pursued as if it were unpaid revenue. The money to actually collect is the allowed amount, split between what the payer pays and what the patient owes (copay, coinsurance, deductible). Confusing a contractual adjustment with an underpayment is a classic RCM error.
The gross amount from the chargemaster (e.g., $5,000).
Billed charge
The contracted rate the payer recognizes (e.g., $1,200).
Allowed amount
Billed minus allowed — a legitimate write-off (e.g., $3,800).
Contractual adjustment
The allowed amount, split between payer payment and patient responsibility.
Collectible
From Charge to Collectible
In-Network vs. Out-of-Network
Whether a contract exists at all is the in-network/out-of-network distinction. When a provider is in-network, there is a signed contract that fixes the allowed amount for each covered code, and the provider agrees to accept that allowed amount as payment in full for a covered service — billing the patient only their cost-sharing.
When a provider is out-of-network, there is no contract setting a negotiated fee. The plan still determines an allowed amount, often using a "usual, customary, and reasonable" (UCR) methodology or a percentage of a public fee schedule, but the dynamics are entirely different — typically higher patient cost-sharing and, historically, the risk of balance billing (now constrained for many situations by the No Surprises Act).
For the revenue cycle, network status changes the entire payment picture. In-network claims pay predictably per the contract; out-of-network claims are less predictable and shift more cost to the patient. Knowing a patient's network status — established back at eligibility verification — is essential to setting correct expectations and posting payments accurately.
In-Network
Signed contract fixes the allowed amount
Provider accepts allowed amount as payment in full
Predictable, contracted reimbursement
Patient owes only contracted cost-sharing
Out-of-Network
No contract setting a negotiated rate
Plan sets an allowed amount (often UCR)
Less predictable reimbursement
Higher patient cost-sharing; balance-billing risk
In-Network vs. Out-of-Network
Reimbursement Methodologies
Contracts do not all pay the same way. A fee schedule that pays a set amount per CPT code is the classic fee-for-service approach, but several other reimbursement methodologies appear in payer contracts, especially for facilities.
Common methodologies include: DRG-based payment (a fixed amount per diagnosis-related group for an inpatient stay, regardless of the individual services); per diem (a fixed amount per day of stay); case rates (a single bundled price for an episode, like a global surgical fee); and capitation (a fixed per-member-per-month amount regardless of services used). A single contract often blends several — a percentage-of-Medicare fee schedule for outpatient, DRGs for inpatient, carve-outs for specific services.
These methodologies matter because each pays differently and must be modeled differently to know what to expect. A DRG payment is not validated the same way as a fee-schedule line item, and a per-diem stay's expected payment depends on length of stay. The contract's methodology determines how the provider calculates "expected reimbursement" for each claim — the benchmark against which actual payment is checked.

Managing Contracts and Catching Underpayments
Because the contract defines expected payment, comparing actual payments to contract terms is how providers catch underpayments — instances where the payer paid less than the contract requires. Without modeling the contract, an underpayment is invisible: the payment looks "paid," and the shortfall is silently lost, much like a missed charge.
Modern payer-contract-management systems extract the structured terms (fee schedules, DRG rates, lesser-of provisions, stop-loss, escalators, timely filing limits) and automatically compare expected reimbursement to actual payment on every claim, flagging underpayments for recovery. Providers routinely find recoverable underpayments this way — real money that contract management surfaces.
Contracts also carry critical operational terms beyond price. Timely filing limits cap how long a provider has to submit a claim (Medicare requires filing within 12 months of the date of service; Medicaid and commercial limits vary) — miss the deadline and the claim is denied with no recourse. Prompt-payment clauses set how fast the payer must pay; dispute-resolution terms define how to challenge payment problems. Mastering these terms is what lets the back-end of the revenue cycle hold payers accountable to what they actually agreed to pay.
A contractual adjustment (billed minus allowed) is a legitimate, agreed write-off and should not be chased. An underpayment is when the payer pays less than the contract's allowed amount — that IS recoverable. Telling them apart requires modeling the contract; otherwise real underpayments hide inside "paid" claims.
Don't Confuse a Contractual Adjustment With an Underpayment

The contractual adjustment (Billed Charges − Allowed Amount) is a legitimate write-off the provider agreed to for being in-network, not unpaid revenue to chase.
The collectible amount is the allowed amount, split between payer payment and patient cost-sharing (copay, coinsurance, deductible).
In-network means a signed contract fixes the allowed amount accepted as payment in full; out-of-network has no contract, often using UCR with higher patient cost-sharing.
Reimbursement methodologies vary: fee-for-service, DRG (inpatient), per diem, case rate, and capitation — each must be modeled differently to set expected payment.

The $3,800 (billed $5,000 minus allowed $1,200) is the contractual adjustment — the portion the provider agreed to write off in exchange for being in-network. It is legitimate and should not be pursued. The collectible is the $1,200 allowed amount, here split into the payer's $1,000 payment and the patient's $200 coinsurance. ######## revenue-cycle-management | why-claims-denied | Why Claims Are Denied: Root Cause Categories
Why Claims Are Denied: Root Cause Categories
The Inevitable Reality of Denials
No matter how clean the front-end and mid-cycle, some claims will come back denied. Denial management is the back-end discipline of dealing with that reality, and it begins with a deceptively simple question: why was this claim denied? Understanding the root-cause categories of denials is the foundation for both fixing individual claims and preventing the next batch.
The scale makes this urgent. Payers initially denied about 11.8 percent of hospital claims in 2024 (Kodiak Solutions), and an earlier Change Healthcare analysis estimated that roughly $262 billion in hospital claims — about 9 percent of charges — were initially denied in 2016. Denials are not an edge case — they are a constant, massive drain that every organization must actively manage.
The single most important fact about denials, though, is hopeful: Change Healthcare’s 2020 Denials Index found that 86 percent of denials are potentially avoidable. The vast majority of denials trace to fixable, upstream causes — which means understanding the categories is the first step to driving the denial rate down.
Denials are a constant: initial denial rates hit ~11.8% in 2024. But about 86% of denials are potentially avoidable, so understanding root-cause categories is the key to both fixing claims and preventing future denials.
Soft Denials vs. Hard Denials
A foundational distinction shapes how a denial is handled: soft versus hard. A soft denial is temporary — it can often be reversed by submitting additional information or correcting and resubmitting the claim. The money is recoverable if the team acts. A duplicate claim or a missing-information denial is typically soft.
A hard denial is final — it generally results in lost revenue and cannot simply be corrected and resubmitted (though some can still be appealed). A denial for a service that was genuinely not covered, or one where the timely filing deadline has irrevocably passed, is typically hard. Hard denials are the ones that become write-offs.
This distinction drives triage. Soft denials should be worked quickly, because they are recoverable with effort; hard denials require judgment about whether an appeal is worth pursuing or whether to write off. Knowing which is which prevents teams from wasting effort on unrecoverable claims while letting recoverable ones age past the point of recovery.
Soft Denial
Temporary and reversible
Fixable with corrected info / resubmission
Money still recoverable if worked
e.g., duplicate, missing information
Hard Denial
Final, generally lost revenue
Cannot simply be corrected and resubmitted
Often becomes a write-off (some appealable)
e.g., non-covered service, missed timely filing
Soft vs. Hard Denials
The Major Root-Cause Categories
Denials cluster into a recognizable set of root causes, and learning them is essential because each maps to a different prevention strategy upstream. Missing or inaccurate information (wrong demographics, missing fields) and prior authorization problems consistently rank as the top causes in industry surveys, followed closely by eligibility/coverage issues.
The other major categories: medical necessity (the documentation did not justify the service — research has found this among the top denial reasons); coding errors (mismatched diagnosis and procedure, wrong modifiers, invalid codes); timely filing violations (the claim was submitted past the payer's deadline); duplicate claims (the same service billed twice); and coordination-of-benefits problems (billed the wrong payer first).
Notice that nearly every category traces back to an earlier lesson in this course: missing info and eligibility to the front-end; prior auth to its own lesson; medical necessity to documentation; coding errors to coding; timely filing to payer contracts. This is the practical proof of the "back-end denial is a front-end failure" principle — the denial categories are essentially a catalog of where upstream processes broke.
Wrong demographics, incomplete fields — a leading cause.

No prior authorization, or coverage inactive/not verified.
Authorization & eligibility

Medical necessity & coding

Timely filing, duplicates, COB
Major Denial Root-Cause Categories
Reading the Denial: CARC and RARC Codes
Payers do not deny claims with a written paragraph — they use standardized codes. The primary one is the Claim Adjustment Reason Code (CARC), which states the reason for an adjustment or denial. CARCs appear on the remittance, telling the provider exactly why the claim was not paid in full. X12 maintains several hundred CARCs.
Alongside CARCs are Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARCs), which provide supplementary explanation and instructions. The rule of thumb: the CARC tells you what happened to your claim, and the RARC adds context or next steps. RARCs are not always present — they appear when extra explanation is needed.
A handful of CARCs account for the majority of denials, so learning the common ones is high-leverage. Examples include CO-16 (claim lacks information), CO-18 (duplicate claim), CO-50 (deemed not medically necessary), CO-97 (service included/not separately covered), and CO-22 (coordination of benefits needed). The "CO" prefix indicates a contractual obligation (provider write-off), while a "PR" prefix indicates patient responsibility — the prefix itself tells you who owes the balance.

From Categorizing to Preventing
Categorizing denials is not bookkeeping — it is the engine of prevention. Because roughly 86 percent of denials are potentially avoidable, the path to a lower denial rate runs through systematically tracking which categories and CARCs are driving an organization's denials, then fixing the upstream process responsible.
This is classic root-cause analysis applied to revenue. If "no prior authorization" denials spike, the fix is in the front-end authorization workflow, not the appeals team. If "missing information" denials dominate, the fix is registration data quality. If "medical necessity" denials rise, the fix is documentation. The CARC distribution is essentially a diagnostic readout of where the revenue cycle is leaking.
This is why reducing denials became a top priority for so many organizations — and why denial root-cause analysis sits at the center of the back-end. Understanding why claims are denied is the prerequisite for the next two lessons: building a workflow to work denials efficiently, and appealing the ones that were wrong. But the ultimate goal is always to drive the denial rate down by preventing the categories at their source.
Fixing an individual denied claim recovers one payment; fixing the root-cause category prevents hundreds of future denials. Because about 86% of denials are potentially avoidable, tracking CARC patterns to find and fix the upstream process is far higher-leverage than working denials one at a time.
Work the Category, Not Just the Claim
