######## revenue-cycle-management | denial-management-workflow | Building an Effective Denial Management Workflow
Building an Effective Denial Management Workflow
Knowing Why Isn't Enough
The previous lesson explained why claims are denied. But understanding root causes does nothing for revenue unless an organization actually works the denials it receives — and, just as importantly, learns from them to prevent the next ones. That requires a structured denial management workflow: a repeatable system for handling denials, not a pile of rejected claims someone gets to eventually.
The stakes of not having one are alarming. According to MGMA research, more than half of denied claims are never reworked at all — not appealed, not resubmitted, just abandoned. That is earned revenue, already worked for and delivered, simply written off because no one got to it in time or at all. A weak denial workflow is one of the largest silent revenue losses in health care.
A denial workflow turns that around. Put bluntly: if you are not tracking denials by type, payer, date received, and appeal outcome, you do not have a denial management workflow — you have a hope-and-resubmit strategy. This lesson lays out what a real workflow looks like.
A denial management workflow is a repeatable system to work and learn from denials. Without one, more than half of denied claims can go unreworked — earned revenue abandoned simply because no one got to it.
The IMMP Framework
A useful structure for the workflow is the IMMP framework — Identify, Manage, Monitor, and Prevent. It captures the full lifecycle: catch the denial, work it, track the outcome, and feed the lessons back upstream to stop it recurring. The framework's power is that it links the tactical (working today's denials) to the strategic (reducing tomorrow's).
Identify means promptly catching every denial as remittances come in and categorizing each by root cause — administrative errors (missing info, authorization), clinical denials (medical necessity, coding), and technical rejections (electronic submission problems). Manage means routing each denial to the right person to correct, resubmit, or appeal it. Monitor means tracking outcomes — what was recovered, what was lost, which payers and reasons dominate.
Prevent is the part that actually shrinks the denial rate. It uses the patterns from Monitor to fix the upstream process responsible — registration training, authorization workflow redesign, coding education. Without Prevent, a team is on a treadmill, working the same denials forever; with it, the denial volume itself falls over time.
Promptly catch every denial and categorize it by root cause.

The IMMP Denial Workflow
Prioritization: You Can't Work Them All at Once
Denials arrive faster than any team can work them instantly, so prioritization is the difference between recovering revenue and watching it expire. A good worklist sorts every denied claim by three factors: dollar value, days until the timely filing window closes, and the specific denial reason and its historical reversal rate.
The rules that fall out are practical. High-dollar claims generally get worked first, because the recovery is largest. But claims approaching their timely filing deadline get worked immediately regardless of dollar amount — because once that window closes, the claim becomes a hard denial with no recourse. And claims with a high historical reversal rate are prioritized over those payers rarely overturn, so effort goes where it actually pays off.
This is triage. Just as an emergency department does not treat patients first-come-first-served, a denial team should not work denials in the order they arrived. The timely-filing clock is the unforgiving constraint — a high-value claim worked a day after its filing deadline is worth nothing, while the same claim worked the day before is fully recoverable.
High-dollar denials usually get worked first — but a claim nearing its timely filing deadline must be worked immediately regardless of amount. Once that window closes (e.g., 90 days for some commercial plans), the denial becomes hard and unrecoverable. Let a deadline lapse and the revenue is simply gone.
The Timely-Filing Clock Overrides Dollar Value
Root-Cause Analysis and Tracking
The Monitor and Prevent steps depend on disciplined tracking. High-performing organizations track denials by type, payer, origin point in the revenue cycle, date received, and appeal disposition. This data is what turns anecdote ("we get a lot of authorization denials") into actionable insight ("Payer X denied 40% of imaging claims for missing authorization in Q2").
With that data, root-cause analysis pinpoints where in the cycle the problem originated, enabling targeted correction. If denials cluster at registration, the fix is registration training and verification. If they cluster in authorization, the fix is the authorization workflow. If in coding, the fix is coder education or documentation. The CARC distribution (from the previous lesson) is the diagnostic readout that drives this.
This tracking also feeds the KPIs from earlier in the course — denial rate, clean claim rate, days in AR — closing the loop between denial management and overall revenue-cycle performance. A denial workflow without tracking can recover individual claims but can never reduce the denial rate, because it has no way to know what to fix.
A denial team's tracking shows that one commercial payer accounts for a disproportionate share of "no authorization" denials on advanced imaging. Root-cause analysis traces it to schedulers not checking that payer's specific authorization requirements.
The fix is upstream — a targeted update to the scheduling/verification workflow for that payer. Months later, that denial category has fallen sharply. That is the Prevent step working: the data identified the leak, and fixing the process stopped it at the source.
Turning Tracking Into Prevention
Automation, Speed, and the Payoff
Denial volume has grown faster than staffing, which is why automation is increasingly central. AI and automation now handle much of the classification and triage that most denials require, rank claims by urgency and collectability, draft payer-specific appeals, and learn over time which approaches work for which payers. This makes it economical to work smaller-dollar denials that would otherwise be abandoned.
Speed is a recurring theme. Strong teams work denials quickly, because every day a denial sits unworked is a day closer to a filing deadline and a day longer in AR. A workflow that moves denials quickly — automated triage, clear ownership, fast resubmission — directly protects revenue that a slow process would lose.
The payoff of a strong denial workflow is large and measurable: structured workflows combined with automation can shorten accounts-receivable days while recovering revenue that would otherwise vanish. The discipline is straightforward to state — catch every denial, prioritize by deadline and value, work them fast, track everything, and fix the root causes — and it converts the denial problem from a silent leak into a managed, shrinking cost. The next lesson covers what to do when working a denial means formally fighting it: the appeals process.

######## revenue-cycle-management | appeals-process | Appeals Process and Payer Relations
Appeals Process and Payer Relations
When You Disagree With the Denial
Not every denial is correct. Payers deny claims that should have been paid — for incomplete information they could have requested, for "medical necessity" the documentation actually supported, or simply in error. When a provider believes a denial is wrong, the remedy is the appeal: a formal request that the payer reconsider its decision.
Appeals are the back-end's tool for fighting denials, distinct from simply correcting and resubmitting. You resubmit when the claim had a fixable error; you appeal when you believe the claim was correct and the denial was not. Appeals are more formal, more documentation-heavy, and governed by strict deadlines and levels.
The most striking fact about appeals is how underused they are relative to how often they work. In Medicare Advantage, only 11.5 percent of denied Medicare Advantage prior authorization requests were appealed in 2024 — yet 80.7 percent of those appeals overturned the denial (KFF). That gap represents enormous recoverable revenue left on the table simply because providers do not pursue it.
An appeal is a formal request that a payer reconsider a denial believed to be wrong. Strikingly, only ~11.5% of denied Medicare Advantage prior authorization requests were appealed in 2024 — yet ~81% of those appeals succeeded, meaning huge recoverable revenue goes unpursued.
The Levels of Appeal
Appeals proceed through escalating levels, and you generally must exhaust each internal level before moving to the next. A first-level appeal is the initial formal request asking the payer to reconsider, reviewed by insurance-company personnel. The payer typically has a defined window (often around 30 days) to respond.
If the first-level appeal is denied, a second-level appeal triggers another internal review — usually by a different medical reviewer who did not participate in the original decision — supported by additional evidence and stronger documentation. Only after exhausting internal appeals can a provider (or patient) usually request an external review by an Independent Review Organization (IRO), a neutral third party whose decision the payer must honor.
Each level raises the bar and the independence of the reviewer. The internal levels give the payer a chance to correct itself; the external review removes the decision from the payer entirely. This escalation structure exists for commercial and ACA-plan appeals, and a parallel (more elaborate) structure governs Medicare.
Formal request for reconsideration, reviewed by payer personnel.
First-level (internal)
Another internal review by a different reviewer, with stronger evidence.
Second-level (internal)
A neutral independent review organization decides; the payer must comply.
External review (IRO)
Medicare extends through ALJ, Appeals Council, and federal court.
(Medicare adds further levels)
Escalating Levels of Appeal
The Medicare Five-Level Process
Medicare has its own, formally defined five-level appeals process that is worth knowing because Medicare is so large. Level 1 is Redetermination by a Medicare Administrative Contractor (MAC); Level 2 is Reconsideration by a Qualified Independent Contractor (QIC); Level 3 is a hearing before an Administrative Law Judge (ALJ); Level 4 is review by the Medicare Appeals Council; and Level 5 is judicial review in federal district court.
Each level has strict deadlines. A redetermination must be requested within 120 days of the initial determination; a reconsideration within 180 days of the redetermination notice, with the QIC having 60 days to decide. Miss a deadline and the appeal right is generally forfeited — the same unforgiving clock that governs timely filing governs appeals.
In practice, most disputes are decided at the first two levels. This means a well-prepared first- or second-level appeal is where most recoverable revenue is actually won — the higher levels are rare and reserved for the hardest cases.

The Five Levels of Medicare Appeal
Winning an Appeal: Documentation and the Peer-to-Peer
Appeals are won on evidence. The core of any appeal is a clear, specific appeal letter that states exactly why the claim should be paid, paired with as much supporting documentation as possible — the medical records, physician statements, and clinical evidence that establish the case. A missing physician statement or an incomplete record can sink an otherwise valid appeal.
For clinical denials (especially medical necessity), a powerful tool is the peer-to-peer review: the treating physician speaks directly with a physician reviewer at the payer to argue the clinical case. It is requested by the provider and, for some denials, must be completed quickly. A peer-to-peer can overturn a denial before a formal written appeal is even needed, because it lets two clinicians resolve a clinical disagreement directly.
The recurring theme is that appeals reward preparation and specificity. A generic "please reconsider" letter rarely works; an appeal that cites the specific policy, attaches the exact documentation that rebuts the denial reason, and addresses the CARC code head-on is what succeeds. This is also why good documentation (the earlier lesson) pays off twice — once in preventing the denial, and again in winning the appeal if one happens.
A payer denies an inpatient admission as "not medically necessary." Rather than file a written appeal immediately, the hospital requests a peer-to-peer review, and the admitting physician speaks directly with the payer's physician reviewer to explain the clinical picture that justified admission.
The reviewer, hearing the clinical reasoning directly, overturns the denial — resolving it faster than a formal multi-level appeal and recovering the full payment.
A Peer-to-Peer Reversing a Denial
Payer Relations and the Bigger Picture
Appeals are one front in a broader, ongoing relationship between providers and payers. Beyond individual appeals, strong payer relations involve tracking each payer's denial and reversal patterns, escalating systemic problems (a payer denying a whole category of valid claims), and using contract terms — prompt-payment clauses, dispute-resolution provisions — to hold payers accountable.
The data from appeals feeds back into this relationship. If a particular payer consistently denies valid claims that are then overturned on appeal, that pattern is leverage — in contract renegotiation, in regulatory complaints, and in operational pushback. Appeals are not just claim-by-claim recovery; in aggregate they are evidence about payer behavior.
The practical bottom line connects back to the opening fact: because most appeals succeed but few are filed, building real appeal capacity — clear ownership, deadline tracking, strong documentation, and routine use of peer-to-peer — is one of the highest-return investments in the back end. An organization that appeals diligently recovers revenue its peers abandon. With denials worked and appealed, the cycle turns to posting the payments that do come in — the subject of the next module.
Most appeals succeed, yet only a small fraction of denied claims are ever appealed (~11.5% of Medicare Advantage prior authorization denials in 2024). Failing to appeal valid denials abandons revenue that would very likely be recovered. Track appeal deadlines, build strong documentation, and use peer-to-peer reviews — diligent appealing recovers what competitors write off.
Don't Leave Winnable Appeals Unfiled

######## revenue-cycle-management | era-eob-reconciliation | ERA/EOB Reconciliation and Payment Posting
ERA/EOB Reconciliation and Payment Posting
Recording the Money That Comes In
When a payer adjudicates a claim and sends payment, the work is not over — the provider must record what happened. Payment posting is the act of recording each payment (or denial) into the practice management system, applying it to the correct patient account and the specific charges. It is the back-end step where the abstract "claim submitted" becomes a concrete "payment received and recorded."
Payment posting sounds clerical, but it is where the truth about a claim is finally established: how much the payer actually paid, what it adjusted off, what it denied, and what the patient now owes. Done accurately, it gives a true picture of revenue and surfaces problems; done sloppily, it distorts everything downstream — patient balances, AR, and the KPIs that depend on accurate posting.
To post payments, the provider needs to read the payer's explanation of what it did with the claim. That explanation comes in two forms — the ERA and the EOB — and understanding the difference between them is the starting point.
Payment posting records each payer/patient payment or denial into the system, applied to the right account and charges. It is where the true outcome of a claim — paid, adjusted, denied, patient-owed — is finally established.
ERA vs. EOB
The payer communicates how it processed a claim through a remittance. There are two formats. The Electronic Remittance Advice (ERA) is the machine-readable electronic version — it follows the HIPAA X12 835 standard (so "ERA" and "835" are used interchangeably) and can be imported automatically into the billing system. The Explanation of Benefits (EOB) is the human-readable version (paper or PDF) that requires manual entry or OCR to post.
There is also an audience difference worth noting. The ERA/835 is sent to the provider's billing team for posting. The EOB, in the sense most patients know it, is the document sent to the patient explaining how their insurance was applied and what they owe. Both convey related information about the same claim, but they serve different users.
Whichever form it takes, the remittance carries the same essential content: the payment amount, the contractual adjustments, the Claim Adjustment Reason Codes (CARCs) and Remittance Advice Remark Codes (RARCs) explaining any reductions or denials, and the patient's responsibility. The remittance is, in effect, the payer's itemized answer to the claim — and the source document for posting.

ERA (835) vs. EOB
Auto-Posting and the Electronic Payment Cycle
The great advantage of the ERA is auto-posting. Because the 835 is structured and machine-readable, it can post payments, adjustments, and denials to patient accounts automatically — drastically reducing the staff time and keying errors of manual posting from paper EOBs. Most practices auto-post routine payments and reserve manual posting for exceptions and payers that do not support ERA.
The ERA pairs naturally with EFT — Electronic Funds Transfer — the electronic payment that delivers the money directly to the provider's bank account (instead of a paper check). Together they create a fully electronic payment cycle: the money arrives via EFT and the posting detail arrives via ERA, ideally at the same time, enabling complete automated reconciliation.
This electronic cycle is the modern ideal: a claim goes out as an 837, the payer pays via EFT and explains via 835, and the 835 auto-posts. The whole loop runs with minimal manual touch. The transactions from the clearinghouse lesson (837 out, 835 back) are exactly the machinery that makes this possible — payment posting is where the 835 finally does its job.
The provider sends the claim electronically.
Claim submitted (837)
Money is deposited directly to the provider's bank account.
Payer pays (EFT)
A machine-readable remittance details payment, adjustments, denials.
Payer explains (ERA/835)

Auto-post & reconcile
The Electronic Payment Cycle
Reconciliation: Making Sure It All Matches
Posting and reconciliation are related but distinct. Posting records the payment; reconciliation is the broader quality-control step that verifies everything matches afterward. The most fundamental reconciliation is deposit matching — confirming, ideally daily, that the money actually deposited in the bank (the EFT or checks) matches the remittances posted in the system.
Deposit matching catches a whole class of problems: a remittance posted but the money never arrived, money deposited but not posted, or amounts that do not tie out. Until the posted payments reconcile to the bank deposits, the organization cannot trust its own revenue numbers. This is the financial-integrity backbone of the back end — the point where the books are proven to reflect reality.
Reconciliation also includes payment variance analysis: checking that what was paid matches what the payer contract said should be paid. This is exactly the underpayment detection from the payer-contracts lesson, and payment posting is where it operationally happens — as each payment posts, it can be compared to the expected reimbursement, and any shortfall flagged for recovery.
Posting records a payment; reconciliation proves it is correct. Skipping reconciliation — especially daily deposit matching of posted remittances against actual bank deposits — means the organization's revenue figures may not reflect reality, with money posted-but-not-received or received-but-not-posted going undetected.
Posting Is Not Reconciliation
Why Accurate Posting Matters
Payment posting is deceptively high-stakes because everything downstream depends on it being right. A key metric is the posting accuracy rate — the percentage of audited postings with no errors in patient, claim, amount, or adjustment. Wrong posting distorts patient balances (billing patients the wrong amount), corrupts AR (making accounts look paid or unpaid incorrectly), and breaks the KPIs that drive management decisions.
Accurate posting is also the trigger point for back-end follow-up. As payments post, the system should automatically route exceptions: underpayments flagged for recovery, denials sent to the denial workflow, and remaining patient balances queued for patient billing. Posting is not just record-keeping — it is the dispatcher that hands each claim's outcome to the right next process.
In short, payment posting closes the loop on the payer side of each claim: it records the truth, reconciles it against the bank and the contract, and dispatches the leftovers (denials, underpayments, patient balances) to be worked. Once the payer has paid and posted, what remains is the unpaid balance — which leads directly into the next two lessons on accounts receivable management and patient collections.

######## revenue-cycle-management | ar-management | AR Management: Aging Buckets and Follow-Up
AR Management: Aging Buckets and Follow-Up
The Money Still Owed
After claims are submitted, paid, and posted, there is always a residual: money that has been billed but not yet collected. That outstanding balance — owed by payers and patients — is accounts receivable (AR). Managing AR is the back-end discipline of systematically chasing that unpaid money until it is collected or appropriately written off.
AR management matters because billed revenue is not collected revenue. A claim can be perfectly submitted and still sit unpaid for weeks because the payer is slow, the claim got stuck, or no one followed up. AR is where revenue goes to wait — and where, without active management, it quietly ages, becomes harder to collect, and eventually dies as bad debt.
The core insight driving all of AR management is that money gets harder to collect the older it gets. Young accounts are highly collectible, but once an account passes 90 days, the probability of ever collecting it falls sharply. Time is the enemy, which is why AR is organized entirely around age.
Accounts receivable (AR) is billed-but-uncollected revenue owed by payers and patients. The central truth of AR management: money gets harder to collect the older it gets — collectibility is high for young accounts but falls sharply past 90 days.
Days in AR: The Headline Number
The single most important AR metric is Days in Accounts Receivable — the average number of days it takes to collect after billing. The calculation is straightforward: Total Accounts Receivable divided by Average Daily Charges (total charges over a period divided by the number of days in that period). The result is "how many days of billing is currently sitting uncollected."
Lower is better. A widely used industry rule of thumb is to keep Days in AR under 40, with leading organizations under 30. A rising Days in AR is one of the earliest warning signs that something is wrong upstream — claims are being denied, delayed, or not followed up — because all of that backs up into uncollected receivables.
Days in AR is powerful precisely because it is a summary number that reflects the health of the whole cycle. You cannot fix it directly; you fix it by fixing the things that feed it — cleaner claims, faster denial work, diligent follow-up. It is the thermometer, not the disease.
Industry rule of thumb; leaders under 30

Aging Buckets: Organizing AR by Time
Because age determines collectibility, AR is organized into "aging buckets" — groupings of receivables by how long they have been outstanding. The standard buckets are 0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-120, and 120+ days, each showing the dollar amount sitting in it. The AR aging report is the back-end's primary worklist and dashboard.
The aging report instantly reveals the shape of the problem. A healthy AR profile is weighted toward the youngest buckets, with little money in 90+ days. When dollars pile up in the older buckets, it signals that claims are getting stuck and not being worked — and that revenue is sliding toward the point of no return. High performers keep less than about 15 percent of total AR in the 90+ day bucket.
Aging buckets also separate the two kinds of AR: insurance (payer) AR and patient AR. They behave differently — patient balances are generally harder and slower to collect, so a higher tolerance for older self-pay AR is normal. Reading the aging report means looking not just at totals but at where the money sits, who owes it, and which buckets are growing.

Standard AR Aging Buckets
The Follow-Up Process
AR follow-up is the systematic work of tracking unpaid claims and balances, contacting payers or patients to resolve them, correcting errors, resubmitting claims, and filing appeals when needed. It is the active, hands-on chasing that turns aged receivables back into cash — and it is organized around the aging buckets.
Effective follow-up assigns staff to specific buckets — someone focused on accounts approaching 60 days, another on the 90-plus accounts — and prioritizes the worklist by both age and dollar value. The principle mirrors denial prioritization: work the highest-value and most time-sensitive accounts first, and document every payer call and response so the follow-up has a trail.
Cadence matters. Most organizations review AR reports at least weekly for operational follow-up, because catching a stuck claim at 35 days and resolving it is vastly better than discovering it at 95 days when it is half-uncollectible. The discipline is to keep accounts moving down toward resolution before they age into the low-collectibility buckets — proactive follow-up rather than reactive cleanup.
Group AR into buckets by age; separate payer and patient AR.
Generate the aging report
Work highest-value and most time-sensitive (near-deadline, near-90-day) accounts first.
Prioritize the worklist
Contact payer/patient, correct errors, resubmit, or appeal; document everything.
Resolve the account
Review at least weekly, moving accounts toward resolution before they age out.
Re-age and repeat
The AR Follow-Up Loop
Why Speed Wins
The throughline of AR management is that speed wins, because of the collectibility curve. An account worked in the 31-60 bucket is highly collectible; the same account left to reach 120+ days may be worth a fraction of its face value, even though nothing about the underlying claim changed. The decline is not about the claim's validity — it is purely about elapsed time.
This is why the youngest buckets deserve attention too, not just the old ones. Preventing a claim from aging is cheaper and more effective than rescuing it after it has aged. Strong AR management is therefore front-loaded: catch and resolve issues early, keep the aging report weighted young, and reserve heroic recovery efforts for the genuinely hard cases.
Eventually, some AR is uncollectible and must be written off — but that decision should be deliberate, based on real recovery probability, not the accidental result of neglect. Well-managed AR keeps Days in AR low, the 90+ bucket small, and write-offs intentional. What remains after payer AR is worked is the patient's portion — which is its own distinct challenge, and the subject of the final lesson in this module: patient collections.
Collectibility falls with age regardless of whether the claim is correct — high for young accounts, dropping sharply past 90 days. Letting accounts drift into older buckets destroys recoverable revenue. Work AR proactively and weekly to keep it young; do not wait until accounts are nearly uncollectible.
Aged AR Loses Value Even If the Claim Is Valid
Accounts receivable (AR) is billed-but-uncollected revenue owed by payers and patients; managing it means systematically chasing that money until collected or deliberately written off.
The central truth: collectibility declines with age — high for young accounts, falling sharply once accounts pass 90 days.
Days in AR (Total AR ÷ Average Daily Charges) is the headline metric; the benchmark is under 40 (leaders under 30), and a rising figure signals upstream problems.
AR is organized into aging buckets (0-30, 31-60, 61-90, 91-120, 120+) shown on the AR aging report — the back-end's primary worklist.
A healthy AR profile is weighted toward young buckets; high performers keep less than ~15% of AR in the 90+ day bucket, and separate payer AR from (slower) patient AR.
AR follow-up assigns staff to buckets, prioritizes by age and dollar value, documents every contact, and is reviewed at least weekly.
Speed wins because of the collectibility curve — work accounts before they age out, keep the aging report young, and make write-offs deliberate rather than accidental.

Aging buckets organize AR by time so teams can work accounts before they slide into low-collectibility ranges. ######## revenue-cycle-management | patient-collections | Patient Collections and Bad Debt
Patient Collections and Bad Debt
The Hardest Money to Collect
After the payer has paid its share, a balance often remains that the patient owes — the deductible, coinsurance, copay, or the full amount for uninsured care. Collecting that patient portion is the final step of the revenue cycle, and it is the hardest. Patient balances are slower, more expensive, and less likely to be collected than payer balances.
This challenge has grown with the rise of high-deductible plans, which shifted thousands of dollars of responsibility onto patients (the theme from the financial-counseling lesson). The result is a national medical-debt problem: medical debt has climbed, and roughly 15 million Americans carry medical collections on their credit reports, per a 2024 CFPB report.
Patient collections sits at the uncomfortable intersection of revenue and human hardship. The same balance is simultaneously money the provider needs to stay viable and a potential source of financial distress for a patient. Handling it well requires both effective collection practice and genuine compassion and compliance — a balance this lesson works to strike.
Patient collections — recovering the portion the patient owes after insurance — is the final and hardest step of the revenue cycle. Patient balances are slower, costlier, and less collectible than payer balances, especially as high-deductible plans grow.
Best Practices for Patient Collections
The most effective patient collections happen early, not late. The single biggest lever is to collect at or before the point of service (the POS collections from the counseling lesson), because the odds of collecting fall sharply once the patient leaves. Clear upfront estimates and financial conversations prevent the surprise bills that drive non-payment.
When a balance does remain, proven practices include: clear, timely, easy-to-understand statements; multiple convenient payment channels (online, mobile, autopay); and flexible options like payment plans or negotiated settlements that recover the debt while preserving the patient relationship. Engaging patients early and often about their responsibility prevents misunderstandings and overdue balances.
Increasingly, organizations use "propensity-to-pay" models — machine-learning models that estimate a patient's likelihood and ability to pay — to focus collection effort where it will actually work and to tailor the approach (payment plan vs. financial assistance vs. standard billing). This makes collections both more efficient and more humane, directing assistance to those who need it and gentle reminders to those who can simply pay.
Estimate upfront and collect at or before the point of service.
Collect early
Send timely, understandable statements through convenient channels.
Communicate clearly
Provide payment plans and negotiated options to recover debt while keeping goodwill.
Offer flexibility
Use data to direct effort and route patients to assistance vs. standard billing.
Segment with propensity-to-pay
Patient Collections Best Practices
Bad Debt vs. Charity Care
When a patient balance is not collected, it is written off — but how it is classified matters enormously, both financially and ethically. There are two categories. Bad debt is care for which the provider expected payment but ultimately did not receive it — typically from patients who could pay but did not, or who were ineligible for assistance. Charity care is care for which the provider did not expect payment, provided to patients who are uninsured or experiencing poverty.
The distinction is not just accounting semantics. Charity care reflects a deliberate decision not to pursue payment from someone who cannot afford it; bad debt reflects a failure (or refusal) to collect from someone who could. Crucially, hospitals generally are not supposed to pursue collections for bills that qualify for financial assistance or charity care — so a balance that should be charity care must not be treated as bad debt and chased.
Getting this classification right is both a compliance obligation and a matter of integrity. Misclassifying charity-care-eligible patients as bad debt and sending them to collections harms vulnerable people and can violate the rules described in the next section. The screening that distinguishes the two — checking whether a patient qualifies for assistance — is therefore a required step, not an optional courtesy.
Bad Debt
Payment was expected but not received
Often from patients who could pay but did not
May be pursued through collections
A collection failure or refusal
Charity Care
Payment was not expected
For uninsured / low-income patients
Should NOT be pursued through collections

Bad Debt vs. Charity Care
Section 501(r): Rules for Nonprofit Hospitals
Nonprofit hospitals — the majority of U.S. hospitals — operate under specific federal rules in Section 501(r) of the tax code, added by the Affordable Care Act, that constrain how they handle patient collections. These rules exist to ensure that tax-exempt hospitals genuinely serve their communities, including those who cannot pay.
Section 501(r)(4) requires a hospital to establish a written Financial Assistance Policy (FAP) covering emergency and medically necessary care. Section 501(r)(6) requires the hospital to make reasonable efforts to determine whether a patient is eligible for assistance under that FAP before engaging in "extraordinary collection actions" (ECAs) — aggressive steps like selling the debt, suing, or reporting it to credit bureaus.
The practical effect is a required sequence: before a nonprofit hospital can pursue aggressive collection against a patient, it must first screen the patient for financial assistance. This bakes the bad-debt-versus-charity-care distinction into law for nonprofits — you cannot treat a balance as bad debt to be aggressively collected until you have confirmed the patient does not qualify for charity care.
Under Section 501(r), nonprofit hospitals must make reasonable efforts to determine whether a patient qualifies for financial assistance BEFORE taking "extraordinary collection actions" (suing, selling the debt, credit reporting). Pursuing aggressive collection without that screening violates the rule — and may target someone who actually qualified for charity care.
Screen for Assistance Before Aggressive Collection
The Shifting Rules on Medical Debt
The regulatory environment around patient collections is in flux, and practitioners must track it. A high-profile example: in January 2025, the federal Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) finalized a rule to remove most medical bills from consumer credit reports. However, in July 2025 a federal court vacated that rule, finding it exceeded the Bureau's authority under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. The federal ban, in other words, did not ultimately take effect.
Meanwhile, a number of states (such as California, New York, and Connecticut) have enacted their own laws restricting or prohibiting medical debt from being reported to credit bureaus, though the interaction between these state laws and federal law has itself become contested. The net result is a patchwork that varies by state and continues to change.
For the revenue cycle, the lesson is that patient collections is not just an operational discipline but a compliance-sensitive, ethically charged, and evolving area. The durable best practices — collect early, communicate clearly, offer flexibility, screen for assistance, and classify write-offs honestly — hold regardless of which way specific regulations swing. Patient collections is where the entire revenue cycle ends, and doing it well means collecting what is genuinely owed while protecting patients who cannot pay. With this, the seven-step cycle is complete; the final module turns to the technology and analytics that run across all of it.

######## revenue-cycle-management | rcm-software-ehr | RCM Software and EHR Integration
RCM Software and EHR Integration
The Systems That Run the Cycle
Every step covered so far — verification, coding, charge capture, claims, posting, AR, collections — runs on software. Modern revenue cycle management is impossible to do at scale by hand, so this module turns to the technology that powers it. The starting point is understanding the core systems and, critically, how they connect to the electronic health record (EHR).
Two systems sit at the center. The EHR is the clinical system of record — where care is documented, orders are placed, and the data that drives coding and charges originates. The practice management system (PMS) — or its hospital equivalent, the patient accounting system — handles the financial side: scheduling, registration, billing, claims, payments, and AR. RCM software is the family of tools that manages the revenue functions, whether built into these systems or layered on top.
The single most important fact about this technology is the relationship between the clinical and financial systems. Because what is documented clinically determines what can be billed financially, the EHR and the billing system must share data cleanly. How well they integrate largely determines how well the whole revenue cycle works.
RCM runs on software: the EHR (clinical system of record) and the practice management / patient accounting system (financial side). Because clinical documentation drives billing, how well these systems integrate largely determines revenue-cycle performance.
Why EHR Integration Matters
When the EHR and billing systems are integrated, patient and clinical data flows continuously from documentation into billing without re-keying. A registration entered once populates the claim; a documented and coded service flows into charge capture automatically; a posted payment updates the patient's account everywhere at once. Integration eliminates the silos that traditionally separated clinical and financial workflows.
The payoff is concrete: less manual data entry, fewer transcription errors, more accurate CPT and charge capture, and faster claims. Recall that administrative complexity wastes an estimated $266 billion a year (Shrank et al., JAMA 2019) — a category that includes the billing and coding friction of disconnected systems and manual re-entry. Integration attacks that waste directly by letting data move once and be used everywhere.
Technically, this integration is built on the interoperability standards from elsewhere in the HTR curriculum — HL7 and FHIR APIs, plus direct database connections — to create the continuous data flow between clinical documentation and billing. The same standards that move data between organizations also move it between the clinical and financial systems within one organization.
Patient and insurance data entered at registration populates downstream systems.
Register once
Clinical documentation in the EHR flows into coding and charge capture.
Document & code
Charges generate claims without manual re-entry.
Bill automatically
Payments and balances update the patient account across the platform.
Post & update
How Integrated Data Flows
The Big Platforms
In the hospital and large-health-system world, two integrated platforms dominate. Epic's revenue cycle module (Resolute, alongside its registration and scheduling tools) ties billing and coding workflows directly to the patient record, offering automated claim generation, coding assistance, denial management, and revenue reporting inside the same system clinicians use.
Oracle Health (formerly Cerner) offers comparable integrated revenue-cycle capabilities (its newer platform branded RevElate), spanning registration through claim submission and reimbursement, with the goal of improving coding accuracy, reducing denials, and improving revenue capture by keeping clinical and financial functions on one system.
For smaller practices, integrated EHR-plus-practice-management products from many vendors serve the same role on a smaller scale. The common thread is that these are enterprise systems designed so registration, clinical documentation, coding, billing, and AR all live in one connected platform — the "single system of record" model.
It is worth knowing these names because the platform an organization runs shapes its entire RCM operation — its workflows, its reporting, its integration burden, and even which third-party tools it can bolt on.
Integrated vs. Best-of-Breed
A fundamental strategic choice underlies all RCM technology: the integrated (enterprise) approach versus the best-of-breed approach. An integrated system is a single-vendor platform handling clinical and financial functions together. A best-of-breed strategy selects the leading specialized product for each function — a top EHR, a top RCM tool, a top denial-analytics platform — and integrates them.
Each has clear trade-offs. Integrated systems offer seamless internal data flow, one vendor for support and updates, and minimal integration points — everything is designed to work together. But they typically offer less depth in any single function than a specialized standalone product. Best-of-breed offers superior depth in each area but introduces the significant challenge of interoperability: the specialized systems must be connected with robust HL7/FHIR interfaces, or the benefits dissolve into data silos.
The right choice depends on the organization. A large system with complex payer contracts and high claim volume may need the denial-analytics depth that a dedicated RCM platform provides, accepting the integration work. A smaller practice may be far better served by one integrated system that "does most of this" and connects cleanly to a few outside tools, avoiding the integration burden entirely.
Integrated (Enterprise)

Best-of-Breed
Leading specialized product per function
Superior depth (e.g., denial analytics)

Integrated vs. Best-of-Breed
Choosing and Living With RCM Technology
The practical reality is that most organizations land somewhere on a spectrum between fully integrated and fully best-of-breed — typically a core integrated platform supplemented by a few specialized tools where the platform falls short (often denial management, contract management, or patient-payment tools). The integration question becomes "how do I get a system that does most of this, then connects cleanly to the few outside tools I really need?"
Whatever the architecture, the success criterion is the same: clean, continuous data flow from registration through collection, with minimal manual re-entry and minimal silos. A beautiful denial-analytics tool that does not receive timely, accurate data from the EHR is useless; a perfectly integrated platform with weak denial logic still loses revenue. Technology serves the cycle, not the other way around.
This sets up the rest of the module. With the core systems and their integration understood, the next lessons examine the more advanced technology layered on top: predictive analytics and AI that mine this integrated data to prevent denials and predict payment, and the dashboards that turn all of it into the KPIs and benchmarks that manage the revenue cycle.
A best-of-breed tool with cutting-edge features is worthless if it cannot get clean, timely data from the EHR — and a slick integrated platform with weak denial logic still loses revenue. When evaluating RCM technology, the quality of data flow between clinical and financial systems matters more than any single feature list.

######## revenue-cycle-management | predictive-analytics-rcm | Predictive Analytics and AI in Revenue Cycle
Predictive Analytics and AI in Revenue Cycle
From Reacting to Predicting
Most of the revenue cycle as described so far is reactive: a claim is denied, then someone works it; a balance ages, then someone chases it. The promise of predictive analytics and artificial intelligence is to flip that — to predict which claims will be denied before they go out, which patients will struggle to pay, and where revenue will leak, so the organization can act before the problem happens.
This shift is possible because the integrated systems from the previous lesson generate enormous volumes of data — millions of past claims, payer responses, denial codes, and payment outcomes. Machine learning models mine that history to find patterns invisible to humans, turning the revenue cycle's data exhaust into forward-looking predictions.
AI in RCM is moving fast from experiment to mainstream, but unevenly. Surveys show a large majority of organizations adopting or piloting AI, yet far fewer running it at scale or seeing clear ROI yet. This lesson covers the major use cases, the real results, and the important caveats — because this is a domain with as much hype as substance.
Predictive analytics and AI shift the revenue cycle from reactive to proactive — predicting denials, payment likelihood, and revenue leaks before they happen by mining the huge data sets that integrated RCM systems generate.
Predicting and Preventing Denials
The flagship use case is denial prediction. Machine-learning models analyze millions of historical claims, payer responses, and denial codes to flag claims likely to be denied before submission — so the team can fix them while it is still cheap (the clean-claims principle, now powered by prediction).
Vendors report meaningful results — fewer denials, fewer registration-caused denials when AI checks eligibility and coverage gaps, and higher clean claim rates — but most published figures come from the vendors themselves rather than independent evaluations, so treat any specific percentage with caution.
This is the highest-value application because it attacks denials at their cheapest point — prevention — rather than the expensive back-end work of appeals and rework. By predicting which claims a specific payer is likely to deny and why, AI lets the organization fix the issue or gather supporting documentation up front, raising first-pass resolution.
Across multiple revenue-cycle functions (HFMA survey, Feb 2026, n=95)

Autonomous Coding and Generative AI
A second major use case is autonomous (or AI-assisted) medical coding. Natural-language and generative AI read clinical documentation and suggest or assign codes automatically, attacking the slow, expensive, error-prone coding step. Reported results include large coding-cost reductions, lower "discharged not final billed" (DNFB) backlogs, and improved charge capture.
Generative AI is also being applied to the document-heavy steps: reading unstructured notes, auto-coding them, and drafting prior-authorization requests and appeal letters in seconds. The denial-management and appeals lessons noted this: AI now drafts payer-specific appeals and triages denials at scale.
But autonomous coding carries a serious caveat. AI can introduce coding errors, fraud risk, and upcoding — exactly the compliance dangers from the documentation lesson. And the provider, not the software vendor, remains liable under the False Claims Act for every code it submits. The emerging model is "AI-plus-human": AI does the heavy lifting, a certified coder reviews and attests. AI does not erase the compliance obligations; it amplifies the need for them.
Autonomous coding can speed work but also introduce errors, upcoding, and fraud risk under the False Claims Act. The provider remains liable for the claim submitted. The safe model is AI-assisted with certified-coder review, never fully unattended.
AI Coding Amplifies Compliance Risk
Propensity-to-Pay and Patient-Side AI
On the patient side, propensity-to-pay models (introduced in the collections lesson) use AI to combine internal and external financial and socioeconomic data into a prediction of how likely a patient is to pay their balance. This lets financial teams direct collection effort where it will work — and, just as importantly, route patients who are unlikely to be able to pay toward charity care and assistance instead of fruitless collection.
The reported ROI can be striking — one vendor, Experian Health, says clients using its propensity-to-pay tool saw a 10-to-1 return in 2024 — though such figures come from the vendors themselves, not independent evaluations. Done well, propensity-to-pay is both more efficient (effort goes where it pays off) and more humane (assistance goes to those who need it).
The caution mirrors the equity concerns from elsewhere in the HTR curriculum: a model that predicts payment using socioeconomic data must be designed and governed carefully, lest it encode bias or treat vulnerable patients unfairly. The technology that routes someone to charity care is good; technology that quietly deprioritizes care or harasses those least able to pay is not. Governance matters here as much as accuracy.
A health system applies a propensity-to-pay model to its outstanding patient balances. Accounts scored as high-likelihood-to-pay get standard reminders; accounts scored low get proactively routed to financial counseling and charity-care screening rather than aggressive collection.
The result is higher recovery from those who can pay and appropriate assistance for those who cannot — when governed well, more efficient AND more compassionate than a one-size-fits-all collections push.
Propensity-to-Pay Targeting
The Reality: Hype, Adoption, and the AI Arms Race
The honest picture is mixed. Adoption is broad but shallow: in a February 2026 HFMA survey, 27 percent of organizations reported deploying AI at scale across multiple functions and 53 percent were running pilots in select areas, leaving about a fifth with neither. In an earlier HFMA poll (May 2025), 63 percent used AI or automation in the revenue cycle, but only 15 percent of those had achieved positive ROI. The market is moving beyond experimentation, yet denial rates remain stubbornly high.
A defining dynamic is the "AI arms race" between payers and providers. Payers are aggressively adopting AI too — for claims review, utilization management, and prior authorization — which can mean more denials generated faster. Providers increasingly need AI simply to keep up: to submit clean, contract-compliant claims and to fight AI-driven denials. There is real concern that automated payer review can "supercharge" flawed denials, raising fairness and oversight questions.
The mature view is that AI is a powerful tool, not a panacea. It works best on a foundation of clean, well-integrated data (the previous lesson) and sound human governance — and analysts warn that without better payer-provider data standards and transparency, even sophisticated tools fall short. The throughline of this whole course holds: technology serves the cycle. AI can predict, draft, and triage at scale, but the fundamentals — accurate data, sound process, human judgment, and compliance — are what make it deliver. The final lesson brings it together with the dashboards and benchmarking that measure whether any of it is actually working.
For anyone entering the field, the practical posture is enthusiasm tempered by realism: learn the AI use cases and adopt them where they demonstrably help, but treat vendor claims skeptically, demand measured ROI, and never let automation override the compliance and patient-care obligations that the rest of this course has emphasized.
Predictive analytics and AI shift the revenue cycle from reactive to proactive, mining the large data sets integrated RCM systems produce to predict denials, payment likelihood, and revenue leaks.
The flagship use case is denial prediction: models flag likely denials before submission so they can be fixed while it is still cheap (most published results are vendor-reported).
Autonomous/AI-assisted coding and generative AI speed coding, prior-auth requests, and appeal drafting, but introduce error, upcoding, and fraud risk.
The safe model is AI-assisted coding with certified-coder review, since the provider remains liable.
Propensity-to-pay models target collection effort and route unlikely-to-pay patients to assistance, with strong vendor-reported ROI — but require careful governance to avoid bias.

######## revenue-cycle-management | performance-dashboards | Performance Dashboards and Benchmarking
Performance Dashboards and Benchmarking
Bringing the Whole Cycle Into View
This is the capstone of the course, and it brings everything together. You have now walked the full revenue cycle — from scheduling and verification, through coding and claims, to denials, payments, AR, and collections, all running on integrated technology. The performance dashboard is where all of that becomes visible at once: a single management view of how the entire cycle is performing.
A revenue cycle dashboard is a curated, visual display of the KPIs that reveal the health of the cycle. It is how leaders see, at a glance, whether claims are going out clean, cash is coming in fast, denials are under control, and revenue is being collected — and where to intervene when something slips. Without it, an organization is flying blind on its most important financial process.
The dashboard is also the natural close of the course because it consumes everything that came before. Every step has a metric; the dashboard assembles those metrics into a coherent picture and compares them against benchmarks. It turns the revenue cycle from a series of disconnected tasks into a managed, measured system.
A revenue cycle dashboard is a curated visual display of the KPIs that reveal the health of the whole cycle — letting leaders see at a glance whether claims are clean, cash is fast, and denials are controlled, and where to intervene.
The KPIs on the Dashboard
A dashboard is only as good as the metrics on it, and this course has already introduced the essential ones. The core revenue-cycle KPIs span four dimensions: speed (Days in AR), cleanliness (clean claim rate, first-pass resolution rate), yield (denial rate, net collection rate), and efficiency (cost to collect). A complete dashboard tracks a balanced set across all four.
Beyond those headline numbers, a good dashboard drills into the cycle's stages: point-of-service collection rate (front-end), discharged-not-final-billed days (mid-cycle), denial rate by payer and reason, AR aging distribution, and patient-collection performance. Each maps to a stage and a lesson in this course, so the dashboard is essentially the whole cycle rendered as numbers.
The discipline, as in any measurement, is to track a balanced set rather than fixate on one figure. A dashboard showing a great net collection rate but ballooning Days in AR, or a low denial rate while easy revenue goes uncollected, reveals problems a single metric would hide. The dashboard's power is showing the metrics together so their interactions are visible.
Days in Accounts Receivable; AR aging distribution.

Clean claim rate; first-pass resolution rate.

Benchmarking With HFMA MAP Keys
A number means little without something to compare it to. Is a 38-day AR good? Only relative to a benchmark. This is where the HFMA MAP Keys return — the industry-standard set of about 29 revenue-cycle KPIs, organized into five groups: Patient Access, Pre-Billing, Claims, Account Resolution, and Financial Management.
The MAP Keys' value is standardization and comparability. Because they are calculated the same way across organizations, they give every stakeholder a common baseline for evaluating performance and let an organization benchmark itself against national peers. They answer concrete questions: are we collecting what we should at the point of service? How long are claims sitting unbilled after discharge (the PB-1 "DNFB days" key)? How does our cost to collect compare to peers?
The five MAP Key groups map neatly onto this course's structure — Patient Access (the front-end module), Pre-Billing (coding and charge capture), Claims (submission), Account Resolution (denials, AR, collections), and Financial Management (overall health). A dashboard built on MAP Keys is, in effect, this entire course turned into a benchmarked scorecard.

Designing a Dashboard That Drives Action
A dashboard only helps if it drives action, and that depends on design. The most important shift is from periodic to real-time. Monthly reports are too slow for today's fast-moving challenges — by the time a monthly report shows a denial spike, weeks of claims have already been affected and some have aged toward filing deadlines. Front-line teams and executives alike need immediate feedback loops to adjust in the moment.
Good dashboards are interactive with drill-down: an executive sees the organization-level Days in AR, then drills into the payer, department, or denial reason driving it. They surface trends before they become problems — a slowly rising denial rate flagged early is fixable; discovered late, it is lost revenue. And they present data so different stakeholders see the level relevant to them, from the C-suite to the biller working a worklist.
Crucially, dashboards should show metrics over time, not just a single current number, so teams can tell a real trend from normal fluctuation — the same signal-versus-noise discipline that good measurement always requires. A dashboard that reduces the revenue cycle to a wall of static numbers, with no trend and no benchmark, cannot tell anyone whether things are getting better or worse.
By the time a monthly report reveals a denial spike or AR creep, weeks of revenue are already affected and some claims have aged toward filing deadlines. Effective revenue-cycle dashboards are real-time, trended, and benchmarked — surfacing problems early enough to act, not just documenting them after the fact.
Monthly Reporting Is Too Slow
The Whole Cycle as a Managed System
The dashboard is the management layer that turns the entire revenue cycle into a measured, improvable system. It closes the loop that this whole course has traced: the front-end gathers correct data, the mid-cycle codes and documents it, the back-end collects, technology runs it all, and the dashboard measures whether every piece is working — feeding insight back to fix what is not.
This is also where the course's recurring theme — that back-end problems are usually front-end failures — becomes actionable. A good dashboard does not just show that denials are high; benchmarked and drilled down, it shows that a particular payer's authorization denials are driving the spike, pointing straight to the front-end fix. The metrics, traced to their source, turn symptoms into diagnoses.
In the end, the goal of the entire revenue cycle is the one stated in the first lesson: get paid the right amount, for the right care, as quickly as possible, with as little waste as possible. The dashboard is how an organization knows whether it is achieving that — and where to focus next. Master the cycle's steps, measure them with standardized KPIs, benchmark against peers, and manage from a real-time dashboard, and the revenue cycle becomes not a source of leakage and frustration but a well-run engine that keeps the organization financially healthy enough to keep caring for patients.
A revenue cycle dashboard shows Days in AR climbing past 50 and the denial rate ticking up. Drilling down, the spike traces to one payer's "no authorization" denials on imaging — benchmarked against peers, clearly an outlier.
The fix is upstream in the front-end authorization workflow for that payer. Weeks later, the dashboard shows the denial rate and Days in AR back to benchmark. That is the dashboard working: turning a high-level symptom into a specific, benchmarked diagnosis and confirming the fix.

######## health-equity-analytics | hea-measurement-foundations | From Awareness to Measurement: Why Health Equity Needs Analytics
From Awareness to Measurement: Why Health Equity Needs Analytics
Naming a Gap Is Not Measuring It
A companion course on this platform, "Health Equity & SDOH: From Awareness to Action," covers what a disparity is, why the United States has more of them than peer nations, and why they are treated as unjust rather than inevitable. This course starts one step further down the pipeline. Assume a system has already accepted that a disparity is a problem worth solving. The next question is entirely different in kind: how do you measure it reliably enough to act on, and honestly enough to know later whether the action actually worked?
That turns out to be a genuinely hard analytic problem, not a simple counting exercise. Every disparity measurement requires a numerator, a denominator, a reference group to compare against, a sample large enough to trust, and a choice among several defensible ways to summarize the resulting gap. Different defensible choices, applied to the exact same underlying reality, produce different-looking pictures of it. This course is about making those choices well and disclosing them honestly — the discipline the book calls the Equity Imperative, translated into method.
Health equity analytics is the set of methods for turning a suspected disparity into a defensible, actionable number — and for being explicit about every judgment call embedded in that number.

The Five-Dimension Framework This Course Teaches
This platform's own Health Equity Studio computes a composite it calls HEROI — Health Equity Return on Investment — as a weighted average across five dimensions: Access Equity (25%), Quality Equity (25%), Outcome Equity (25%), SDOH Burden (15%), and Trust & Engagement (10%). Those five weights are not arbitrary; they come from the book's own definition of the metric (Chapter 10, section 10.13.1) and they map directly onto the five lessons in this course.
Lesson 2 covers the decomposition arithmetic underneath Access, Quality, and Outcome equity — rate differences, rate ratios, and summary indices. Lesson 3 covers how quality gets stratified in practice through HEDIS and NCQA reporting. Lesson 4 covers how SDOH Burden actually gets scored, from individual screening tools to area-level composite indices. Lesson 5 covers the weighting logic itself — how five separate 0–100 scores become one number — using HEROI as a fully worked, hands-on example. Lesson 6 closes the loop from score to organizational action.
This platform's Health Equity Studio implements the exact five-dimension framework this course teaches, live, in the Research Lab. Open /research-lab/population-equity?tab=equity and select the "HEROI Composite Score" tab.

The Measurement Build-Out — and Where It Has Stalled
The infrastructure for this kind of measurement has expanded rapidly since 2022. NCQA began requiring race and ethnicity stratification for HEDIS measures in Measurement Year 2022, starting with 5 measures; that grew to 22 measures by Measurement Year 2024, part of what NCQA describes as folding health equity into all of its offerings rather than treating it as a side program. Separately, the CMS Office of Minority Health published a ten-year Framework for Health Equity 2022–2032, organized around five priorities, the first of which is expanding the collection, reporting, and analysis of standardized demographic data — the raw material every method in this course depends on.
But measurement infrastructure and payment incentive are not the same system, and they are not currently moving at the same speed. CMS's Contract Year 2027 Medicare Advantage and Part D final rule did not implement the Health Equity Index reward for Star Ratings that CMS had finalized in 2023 — a reward that would have specifically incentivized closing gaps for disadvantaged enrollees. Instead, CMS continued the historical Reward Factor, which rewards consistently high performance across all enrollees rather than the narrowing of gaps between them. NCQA's own stratification requirement kept expanding in the same period. A careful analyst reads both facts together: the ability to see a disparity is not the same as an entity being financially rewarded for closing it.
Watch for this pattern across every lesson in this course: measurement infrastructure (the ability to see a gap) tends to move ahead of incentive infrastructure (a financial or regulatory reason to close it). A well-built analytic tool can tell you precisely how large a disparity is without anyone being obligated to act on the number.

A home inspector does not issue one overall "condition score" for a house. They check the roof, the foundation, the wiring, and the plumbing separately, because a house can be sound in three of those and failing in the fourth — and averaging the four into one number would hide exactly the failure a buyer needs to know about.
Why health equity analytics scores five separate dimensions (Access, Quality, Outcome, SDOH Burden, Trust) instead of one blended equity number
Why Data Completeness Breaks Naive Measurement
Every method in this course depends on demographic and social-risk data actually existing for the population being measured — and that data is frequently incomplete in ways that are easy to miss. Race and ethnicity fields go unanswered at enrollment. Social risk factors go undocumented in a clinical encounter even when a patient discloses them verbally, because documenting them requires an extra coding step a busy clinician may skip.
The scale of that gap is measurable in its own right. ICD-10-CM has carried a dedicated block of diagnosis codes for social determinants — Z55 through Z65, covering housing instability, food insecurity, transportation barriers, and similar factors — for years, and the Gravity Project has partnered with the American Medical Association to build standardized crosswalks from common screening tools directly to those codes. Despite that infrastructure, an analysis of the 2016–2017 National Inpatient Sample (Truong et al., Medical Care, 2020) found that only about 1.9% of inpatient hospital admissions carried an SDOH Z-code. A scoring system built on top of that data does not see zero social risk where a code is absent — it sees an absence of documentation, and it will systematically understate the true burden unless it corrects for that gap.
Under-measurement
Real disparities go undetected because demographic/SDOH data is incomplete
A composite score looks better than the underlying reality because bad news never gets coded
Resources get allocated as if the problem does not exist
Over-interpretation
A rate built from a handful of patients is treated as a stable, real disparity
Small-cell noise gets reported as an actionable finding
An analyst chases a "gap" that disappears with the next quarter's data

######## health-equity-analytics | hea-disparity-decomposition | Disparity Decomposition: From Raw Gaps to Actionable Signals
Disparity Decomposition: From Raw Gaps to Actionable Signals
Two Honest Ways to Describe the Same Gap
Suppose Group A has an adverse-outcome rate of 20% and Group B has a rate of 10%. The rate difference — the absolute disparity — is 10 percentage points. The rate ratio — the relative disparity — is 2.0: Group A's rate is twice Group B's. Both descriptions are simultaneously true of the identical underlying data, and each is more informative in a different context.
The rate difference answers "how many more people in Group A are affected, in absolute terms?" The rate ratio answers "how much more likely is Group A to be affected, relative to Group B?" A disparity that looks modest on one scale can look large on the other: a rate difference of 2 percentage points sounds small, but if the reference rate is only 1%, that same gap is a 3x rate ratio. AHRQ's National Healthcare Quality and Disparities Report — the federally mandated annual disparities report — uses both scales at once: it counts a gap as a disparity only when the absolute difference between a priority population and its reference group is statistically significant and the relative difference is at least 10%.
Absolute disparity (rate difference) and relative disparity (rate ratio) are both legitimate summaries of the same underlying gap. Reporting only the smaller-looking one is a framing choice, not a neutral default.
10 percentage points
2.0x
Group A 20% vs. Group B 10%
2 percentage points
3.0x
Group A 3% vs. Group B 1%

Worked Example: Two Ways to Report the Same Gap
Notice the second and third rows: an identical 10-point rate difference (row 1 and row 3) produces very different rate ratios (2.0x vs. 1.2x) depending on the baseline rate, and a small 2-point difference (row 2) can still be a 3x ratio when the baseline is low. This is why AHRQ's NHQDR tests the relative difference alongside the absolute one — the relative scale surfaces gaps that a raw percentage-point comparison can hide.
Summarizing Disparity Across Many Subgroups
A single rate ratio compares exactly two groups. Real populations usually split into many subgroups at once — several racial and ethnic categories, multiple income bands, several education levels — and tracking a dozen separate two-group ratios over time gets unwieldy fast. Jeffrey Pearcy and Kenneth Keppel addressed this directly in a 2002 Public Health Reports paper written to help track progress toward the original Healthy People 2010 disparity-elimination goal.
Their proposed Index of Disparity (ID) is a modified coefficient of variation computed across all subgroup rates relative to a chosen reference rate, expressed as a single percentage that can be tracked over time. Applying it, they found that gender disparity in cardiovascular disease deaths declined between 1989 and 1998, while racial and ethnic disparity in the same outcome stayed essentially unchanged over the same period — a single index number carrying two very different underlying trends, disaggregated by which grouping variable you choose.

The Reference-Group Problem
Every disparity ratio needs something to compare against, and that choice of reference group is not neutral. AHRQ's NHQDR methods documentation states its choice explicitly — the largest subgroup or the subgroup that typically receives the best care (for example non-Hispanic White, high income, private insurance) — and the choice matters: comparing every subgroup to the population's single best-performing group makes every gap look as large as possible, since the comparison point is the ceiling. Comparing every subgroup to the overall population average makes gaps look smaller, because the average already has the lower-performing groups folded into it.
Neither choice is wrong on its own terms. A best-group reference is more useful for setting an aspirational target — it shows exactly how far the furthest-behind group is from what is demonstrably achievable elsewhere in the same population. A population-average reference is more useful for tracking whether the population as a whole is converging over time. The failure mode is switching between them across years or across measures without disclosing the switch, which can make progress — or the absence of it — look different than it actually is.
Best-performing group as reference
Larger, more visible gaps
Best for setting an aspirational target
Can look alarmist without context
Population average as reference
Smaller-looking gaps
Best for tracking population-wide trend
Can understate the worst-off group's true gap
Reference-Group Choice Changes What You See
Small Numbers Break Naive Stratification
Stratifying a rate by subgroup necessarily shrinks each subgroup's sample size relative to the whole population. A rate computed from 20 patients can jump from 5% to 15% with just two additional events (1 of 20 to 3 of 20) — noise, not a real change in underlying risk. AHRQ and NCQA both apply minimum-cell-size suppression rules before publishing a stratified rate, withholding or flagging any cell too small to be statistically reliable rather than publishing an unstable number as if it were solid.
A disparity dashboard built without a minimum-N suppression rule will manufacture false disparities out of pure statistical noise in its smallest subgroups — this is a design requirement, not an optional refinement.
Case Study: The Mapping Medicare Disparities Tool
CMS's Office of Minority Health launched the MMD Tool in March 2016 to increase understanding of disparities among Medicare beneficiaries — and in doing so it makes the reference-group and small-numbers problems this lesson describes solvable for public users without requiring each analyst to make those calls independently. It offers two views: a Population View, identifying disparities between subgroups (race/ethnicity, sex, age, dual-eligibility status) in outcomes, utilization, and spending; and a Hospital View for facility-level comparisons.
The tool tracks up to 60 chronic and potentially disabling conditions plus end-stage renal disease and disability status, along with Medicare spending, hospital and emergency-department utilization, preventable hospitalizations, readmissions, and mortality — and it applies its own pre-set suppression rules and reference-group conventions consistently across all of that, so a researcher or advocate downloading its tables inherits a defensible, disclosed set of methods choices rather than having to invent one from scratch.
CMS Mapping Medicare Disparities (MMD) Tool
The rate difference (absolute disparity) and the rate ratio (relative disparity) describe the same gap differently — both are legitimate, and reporting only one is a framing choice.
Pearcy and Keppel's 2002 Index of Disparity summarizes a gap across many subgroups at once into a single trackable percentage, developed to monitor progress toward Healthy People 2010's disparity-elimination goal.
Choosing a best-performing-group reference makes disparities look larger; choosing a population-average reference makes them look smaller — both are defensible, but the choice must be disclosed and held constant to track real change.
Small subgroup sample sizes produce statistically unstable rates; AHRQ and NCQA apply minimum-cell-size suppression rules specifically to prevent noise from being reported as a real disparity.
CMS's Mapping Medicare Disparities Tool (2016) is a working example of solving these problems once, centrally, rather than leaving every downstream analyst to remake the same methods decisions inconsistently.
These decomposition methods are the arithmetic underneath the Access, Quality, and Outcome dimensions of this platform's HEROI composite, covered in Lesson 5.
Comparing every group to the ceiling (the best-performing group) produces larger visible gaps than comparing to a population average, because the average already blends in the lower-performing groups — which is why AHRQ's NHQDR methods documentation states its reference groups explicitly.

######## health-equity-analytics | hea-stratified-quality-measurement | Stratified Quality Measurement: HEDIS, NCQA, and the Star Ratings Fight
Stratified Quality Measurement: HEDIS, NCQA, and the Star Ratings Fight
What "Stratified" Means, Operationally
A standard HEDIS measure reports a single plan-wide number — for example, the share of eligible members who received a colorectal cancer screening. A stratified version of that same measure reports it separately by race, ethnicity, and, for some measures, language: the screening rate for Black members, for Hispanic members, for Asian members, for White members, side by side. Nothing about the clinical definition of the measure changes. What changes is that a plan can no longer average away a gap between subgroups inside one clean headline number.
NCQA began requiring this for HEDIS measures in Measurement Year 2022, starting with 5 measures. By Measurement Year 2024, that had grown to 22 measures, and NCQA continued proposing further additions and revisions for Measurement Year 2025 — part of a stated strategy of building health equity into all of its measurement offerings rather than running it as a separate initiative alongside standard HEDIS.
NCQA

Direct vs. Indirect Race and Ethnicity Data
Stratification only works if a plan actually has race and ethnicity data on its members, and much of that data is missing at the individual level. NCQA's reporting requirement addresses this directly: for every stratified value, plans must disclose whether it came from direct data (the member self-reported it, typically at enrollment or during a clinical encounter) or indirect data (an alternate source, most commonly geocoding a member's address against Census tract demographics, used to infer a probable value when no self-report exists).
Direct data is more accurate for any given individual — the member stated it — but is frequently incomplete, since many members never answer a demographic question at all. Indirect data can fill most or all of the population-level gap but introduces real risk of individual misclassification, especially in racially and ethnically mixed neighborhoods where geocoding a single address to a single inferred race is a much blunter instrument than an actual self-report. The disclosure requirement exists precisely so a reader of a stratified result can tell how much of the underlying data is a self-report versus an inference, rather than being handed one clean-looking number that hides the difference.
Direct (self-reported)
High individual accuracy — the member stated it
Often incomplete — many members never respond
NCQA's preferred source when available
Indirect (geocoded/imputed)
