######## transformation-leadership | tl-managing-resistance-global-budgets | Managing Organizational Resistance in a Fixed-Revenue-Envelope Transition
Managing Organizational Resistance in a Fixed-Revenue-Envelope Transition
Why This Reform Type Is Different
A payment reform that adds a bonus on top of existing fee-for-service revenue asks an organization to do something extra for more money — a relatively easy sell. A global budget or a mandatory bundle asks an organization to accept that growing volume no longer grows revenue at all. That is a zero-sum reframing of every department's underlying incentive to do more, and it is why fixed-revenue reforms produce a resistance pattern that milder value-based arrangements typically do not: the threat to an individual department, service line, or physician group's existing model is not hypothetical or marginal. It is structural and immediate.
Resistance under this specific reform type tends to follow a small number of predictable patterns rather than a diffuse, unstructured objection to change in general. Naming those patterns in advance — rather than discovering them in the first year's performance data — is the difference between managing resistance proactively and reacting to it after it has already produced a measurable result.
Pattern One: Gaming the Boundary
CMS's Comprehensive Care for Joint Replacement model made a 90-day bundled payment mandatory for lower-extremity joint replacement in a defined set of metropolitan statistical areas, launching in April 2016. It is one of the most directly documented examples in Medicare policy of how organizations respond, in practice, to a hard payment boundary imposed on them rather than one they chose.
Research on hospital behavior under CJR found that in the metropolitan areas where participation was mandatory, hospitals tended to treat healthier patients on average than in areas without the mandate, and were more likely to perform knee replacements in the inpatient setting — which the bundle covered — even when the same procedure performed outpatient, which the bundle did not cover, would have been the less costly option. Roughly 77% of CJR participant hospitals earned reconciliation payments in one or both of the model's first two performance years. When CMS made participation voluntary in half the areas and let outpatient knee replacements be billed outside the bundle in the model's third year, hospitals responded to the new boundary: the highest-spending hospitals dropped out where they could, and hospitals still in the mandatory bundle kept healthier knee patients in the covered inpatient setting rather than shifting them outpatient. A 2021 JAMA Internal Medicine study found savings fell from about $976 per episode in year two to $331 in year four — no longer statistically significant — with patient and site-of-care selection explaining three-quarters of the decline.
CMS's Mandatory CJR Bundle
The CJR pattern is not evidence of bad faith. It is evidence that organizations respond rationally to whatever boundary a payment reform draws. A fixed-revenue or fixed-bundle boundary will be optimized around unless the reform's design anticipates that response — which is why monitoring for boundary-shifting behavior has to be built into a transformation from its first year, not added after the data has already revealed a problem.
Pattern Two: Autonomy Anxiety
The second predictable pattern is resistance driven not by the financial mechanics of the reform but by the perceived loss of institutional independence — a hospital board or leadership team's anxiety about ceding operational control to an outside regulator, even when the regulator has no intention of dictating day-to-day decisions.
Maryland's own governance design, discussed in the previous lesson, treated this directly: "protecting hospital autonomy" was named explicitly, alongside close communication and calibrated budgets, as one of the specific themes leaders identified as necessary to manage the shift to global budgets. The lesson generalizes: a regulator or state agency that can credibly demonstrate it is not seeking to control operational decisions beyond the budget itself will face measurably less resistance than one whose intentions on that point remain ambiguous to the organizations being regulated.
Pattern Three: The Missing Coalition Seat
The third pattern connects directly back to Kotter's Step 2. Clinical staff who have no real seat in the guiding coalition — who experience the reform as something decided about them rather than with them — will disengage from implementation even when they have no legal ability to block the mandate itself. Disengagement is quieter than open opposition and correspondingly harder to detect: a clinician who simply does not change documentation habits, does not refer into a new care-management program, or does not flag early warning signs of a process breaking down produces exactly the kind of silent underperformance that shows up in outcome data a year later with no obvious single cause.
Transformation that clinical leaders oppose will fail regardless of administrative mandate, because clinical decision-making authority in a hospital sits with medical staff governance, not the administrative org chart that issued the mandate.
A Mandate Cannot Substitute for Coalition Membership
A Resistance-Management Playbook
The three patterns above point toward a common structural response: name the zero-sum trade-off explicitly rather than letting departments discover it on their own, build a data-informed reallocation process instead of an opaque top-down cut, create a visible pipeline of genuine early wins, monitor for boundary-shifting behavior from the reform's first year rather than its third, and formalize clinical leadership's coalition seat rather than treating clinical input as optional consultation.

A fixed-revenue-envelope reform reframes every department's incentive to grow volume into a zero-sum trade-off, producing more resistance than a bonus-on-top value-based arrangement.

######## transformation-leadership | tl-sustaining-change-benefits-realization | Sustaining the Change: Benefits Realization and Avoiding Reform Fatigue
Sustaining the Change: Benefits Realization and Avoiding Reform Fatigue
The Step With No Finish Line
Kotter's eighth step — institute the change in culture and systems — is the step this course has now flagged twice as the one most transformation efforts skip, and it is worth being precise about why. Steps 1 through 7 each have a visible event attached: a public presentation that creates urgency, a coalition's first meeting, a launch, an early win, a period of visible acceleration. Institutionalization has no equivalent event to point to. It is the absence of an event — the new behavior simply continuing to be normal long after the program that created it has stopped being anyone's actively managed project.
That absence of a natural finish line is precisely why sustainment has to be planned and budgeted for deliberately, rather than assumed to happen automatically once a transformation has launched successfully. The Project Management Institute's Benefits Realization Management Framework (2016) gives this planning a formal structure.
PMI's Three-Part Discipline
Benefits realization management is the process of planning, tracking, realizing, and sustaining the strategic benefits a project, program, or portfolio is meant to produce. PMI's framework organizes it into three core elements: identify the benefits a program is meant to produce, execute the changes needed to produce them, and sustain those benefits after the program has formally concluded.
The third element — sustain — is the one most transformation plans never explicitly budget for. Most plans identify a target benefit clearly and execute a defined set of changes to reach it. Far fewer plans assign a named owner, a review cadence, and a monitoring mechanism to the period after the program has officially closed — which is exactly when a hard-won gain is most vulnerable to quietly reversing.
Maryland General Assembly — the HSCRC's founding statute
Maryland's rate-setting authority created

Case Study in Durability: Maryland's Five-Decade Run
Maryland's hospital rate-setting authority has operated continuously since a 1971 state statute — more than five decades, spanning multiple governors, legislatures, and federal administrations. The model has not been static across that period. It has been repeatedly revised: extended to private payers in 1974, to Medicare and Medicaid in 1977, converted to global budgets for all acute-care hospitals in 2014, and extended again into a Total Cost of Care model covering non-hospital spending in 2019. Each of those revisions was a course correction by the commission, CMS, and the hospitals — the model has never been a single design left to run unchanged.
The relevant lesson from Maryland is not that its original 1971 or 2014 design was perfect and therefore never needed to change. It is the opposite: the model survived and expanded specifically because it had a standing structure — the HSCRC as a permanent independent commission, with an ongoing relationship to CMS — that could keep making course corrections indefinitely, long after the original 1971 or 2014 launch events were no longer news. Durability came from a standing governance structure built to keep adjusting, not from getting the design right once and leaving it alone.
Maryland as the Institutionalization Benchmark
Case Study in Sustainment Infrastructure: CPC+'s Learning Collaboratives
CMS's Comprehensive Primary Care Plus model, a national advanced primary care medical home model that launched in 2017 across 14 regions and expanded to 18 by 2018, built its sustainment mechanism directly into the program's design rather than treating it as a follow-up activity after launch.
CPC+ included a standing national and regional learning system — in-person and web-based learning communities, national webinars, an annual national stakeholder meeting, cross-region collaboration, and individualized on-site coaching — organized around five core primary-care functions: access and continuity, care management, comprehensiveness and coordination, patient and caregiver engagement, and planned care and population health. The infrastructure did not end when a practice completed its initial transformation; it continued operating for the life of the model precisely so that gains made in year one did not depend on a single training event holding permanently.
CPC+'s Learning System
Case Study in Collapse: What Happens Without Sustainment Infrastructure
The NHS's National Programme for IT, examined in Lesson 3 for its governance-structure failure, offers a second, distinct lesson here about sustainment specifically. The UK's National Audit Office found not only that the programme itself failed, but that the lessons from its failure were not being captured or applied systematically — meaning the same structural risks remained live in the government's later digital transformation programmes. A program that has no mechanism for sustaining even its own institutional learning is unlikely to have a mechanism for sustaining the operational benefits it was originally built to produce.
Sustained (Maryland, CPC+)
A standing governance body empowered to keep making course corrections indefinitely
A learning/coaching infrastructure that continues after initial go-live
A named review cadence that outlives the original launch team
Collapsed (NPfIT)

Institutional learning not systematically transferred to later programs
What Sustains a Transformation vs. What Lets It Collapse
Building a Sustainment Plan
A transformation's launch team should not be the same body responsible for its indefinite maintenance — the skills, incentives, and attention span required are different. A concrete sustainment plan names a benefit owner for each targeted gain, sets a review cadence that continues well past go-live, keeps the risk register open rather than closing the file at launch, and budgets ongoing resources for the kind of learning-collaborative-style support CPC+ built in, rather than treating training as a one-time event.
Assign a specific, named individual responsible for each targeted benefit continuing to hold — not the launch project manager by default.

A Sustainment Plan
If the dashboard does not exist, the transformation is not being managed. If it exists but the milestones are consistently incomplete, the transformation is not on track — and either way, the legislature, board, or executive sponsor needs to know before the gap becomes irreversible.
Kotter's Step 8, institutionalization, has no natural finish-line event, which is exactly why it is the step most healthcare transformations leave incomplete.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-intro-what-is-hie | What Is Health Information Exchange?
What Is Health Information Exchange?
Start Here: The Simple Idea
Before any of the laws, standards, or acronyms, health information exchange rests on one simple, human idea: your health information should be able to follow you. When you go from your primary care doctor to a specialist, to the emergency room, to the pharmacy, the people caring for you should be able to see the relevant parts of your story — your medications, allergies, recent tests, and diagnoses — without you having to remember and repeat everything yourself.
Health Information Exchange — almost always shortened to HIE — is the electronic sharing of health-related information between authorized organizations. The federal Office of the National Coordinator for Health IT (ONC) defines it as the electronic exchange of health care information across organizations within a region, community, or hospital system. That is the whole concept. Everything else in this course is detail layered on top of it.
Note that "HIE" is used two ways, and both are fine. It can mean the activity — exchanging information — or the organization that makes the exchanging possible (as in "the state HIE"). Context tells you which one someone means.
Health Information Exchange (HIE) is the electronic sharing of a patient's health information between authorized organizations, so that critical information can follow the patient across the places they receive care.
The Problem HIE Solves: A Fragmented System
To understand why HIE exists, picture the problem it was built to fix. American health care is delivered by a vast, disconnected patchwork of independent hospitals, clinics, labs, pharmacies, and specialists. Historically, each kept its own records in its own system, and those systems did not talk to each other.
The result was fragmentation: your records sat in silos scattered across every place you had ever been seen. A specialist might not know what your primary care doctor prescribed; an emergency room might have no idea about your allergies; the same blood test might be ordered three times because no one could see it had already been done. Care was being delivered with an incomplete picture.
This fragmentation persisted partly because providers compete with one another and partly because their software came from different vendors that were not designed to interoperate. HIE is the deliberate effort to bridge those silos so that information can move with the patient even when the organizations do not share a common owner or a common software system.
Imagine moving to a new city and discovering that your bank, your old landlord, and your employer all keep your records on paper in locked filing cabinets that only they can open — and none of them will mail copies to anyone. Every time you need to prove something, you start from scratch. HIE is like giving all the trustworthy parties a secure, shared way to look up exactly the records they need, when they need them.
Why a fragmented health system needs information exchange
The Three Ways Information Is Exchanged
Not all exchange looks the same. The ONC describes three basic forms of HIE, and almost everything you will encounter fits into one of them. Learning these three is the single most useful mental model for the whole field.
The first is directed exchange (sometimes called "push"). One provider securely sends specific information directly to another — for example, a primary care doctor sending a referral and recent labs to a specialist, or a hospital sending a discharge summary to a patient's regular physician. It is point-to-point, like secure email between care providers.
The second is query-based exchange (sometimes called "pull"). Here a provider searches for and requests information about a patient from other organizations — for example, an emergency room looking up a newly arrived, unconscious patient's medication and allergy history from wherever that data lives. The third is consumer-mediated exchange, where patients themselves access, manage, and direct the sharing of their own health information.
A provider securely sends information directly to another provider — referrals, lab results, discharge summaries.
Directed (push)
A provider searches for and requests a patient's information from other organizations — e.g., an ER pulling medication history.
Query-based (pull)
Patients access and control the sharing of their own health information between their providers.
Consumer-mediated
The Three Forms of HIE
Why It Matters: The Benefits
HIE is not technology for its own sake — it changes care in concrete ways. With a fuller picture of a patient, providers can avoid ordering tests that were already done elsewhere. Among physicians who use HIE, about 8 in 10 report that it reduces duplicate test ordering, and studies have linked HIE use to fewer repeat CT scans, ultrasounds, and chest X-rays.
Safety improves too. Access to a patient's medication history, allergies, and potential drug interactions helps providers avoid dangerous prescribing errors and adverse drug events. And in emergencies — where a patient may be unable to speak for themselves — the ability to pull critical history quickly can directly improve the speed and accuracy of care.
The most consistently reported benefits, though, are about coordination. Surveyed physicians most often cite improved care quality (around 84 percent) and better care coordination (around 83 percent) as the payoffs of HIE. When information follows the patient across providers and settings, the whole care team can work from the same page.

How We Got Here, and What HIE Looks Like Today
For decades, exchange barely happened because most records were on paper and the few electronic systems were islands. The turning point was the HITECH Act of 2009, which authorized billions of dollars to drive the adoption and "meaningful use" of electronic health records — and explicitly pushed providers toward exchanging information across organizational boundaries, not just digitizing their own files.
Once records were electronic, networks emerged to connect them. Today HIE happens through regional and statewide HIE organizations and through large national networks. For example, the eHealth Exchange provides connectivity for dozens of regional and state HIEs and a large majority of U.S. hospitals, while organizations like CRISP operate shared HIE services across several states. More recently, a federal framework called TEFCA is knitting these networks together through certified "Qualified Health Information Networks" (QHINs) so they can exchange with one another nationwide.
You do not need to memorize those names yet — later lessons cover the laws, standards, and architecture in depth. The goal of this first lesson is simply to leave you with the core picture: HIE exists to let trustworthy information follow the patient across a fragmented system, it happens in three basic ways, and it makes care safer and better coordinated. Everything that follows builds on that foundation.
The eHealth Exchange is one of the largest health information networks in the country, providing connectivity for roughly 60 regional and state HIEs and a large share of U.S. hospitals, and it was among the first networks designated as a Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN) under the federal TEFCA framework.
CRISP operates as a nonprofit data utility supporting statewide and district HIEs across several states. These are real, working examples of the organizations that make day-to-day exchange possible.
eHealth Exchange and CRISP

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-hipaa-fundamentals | HIPAA Fundamentals
HIPAA Fundamentals
What Is HIPAA and Who Does It Cover?
The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act of 1996 (HIPAA) is the foundational federal law governing the privacy and security of health information in the United States. Enacted by Congress and signed into law on August 21, 1996, HIPAA established national standards that apply to specific categories of organizations — not to every business that handles health data.
HIPAA applies to three categories of "covered entities": health plans (insurers, HMOs, Medicare, Medicaid), health care clearinghouses (organizations that process health data between nonstandard and standard formats), and health care providers who transmit health information electronically in connection with HIPAA-covered transactions. The regulatory definitions are codified at 45 CFR § 160.103.
A covered entity is any health plan, health care clearinghouse, or health care provider that transmits protected health information electronically. Only covered entities — and their business associates — are directly subject to HIPAA requirements.
HIPAA does not apply to all organizations that handle health data. An employer holding employee wellness program data, a fitness app tracking your steps, or a friend sharing health information is generally NOT a covered entity and is not bound by HIPAA. This is a frequent source of public confusion.
Common Misconception
Protected Health Information: What HIPAA Actually Protects
HIPAA protects "Protected Health Information" (PHI) — any individually identifiable health information created, received, maintained, or transmitted by a covered entity. PHI encompasses information in any format: paper records, electronic records (ePHI), and oral communications.
The law identifies 18 specific categories of identifiers that, when linked to health information, make that information PHI. These include names, geographic data smaller than a state, all date elements directly related to an individual (except year alone), phone numbers, fax numbers, email addresses, Social Security numbers, medical record numbers, account numbers, certificate/license numbers, URLs, IP addresses, biometric identifiers (fingerprints, voiceprints), full-face photographs, and any other unique identifying number or code.
The 18 HIPAA identifiers define PHI. Health information with ALL 18 identifiers removed is considered "de-identified" under the Safe Harbor method and is no longer subject to HIPAA Privacy Rule protections.
Think of PHI like a sealed envelope: the health data inside is the letter, and the 18 identifiers are the name and address written on the outside. Covered entities can share the letter contents in certain ways, but must protect the sealed envelope — the combination of identity and health information.
Protected Health Information (PHI)
The Privacy Rule: Patient Rights and Permissible Disclosures
The HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164) establishes the standards for when covered entities may use or disclose PHI, and what rights patients hold over their own health information. The Privacy Rule was finalized in 2002 and has been updated several times since.
The Privacy Rule permits — without patient authorization — uses and disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations (collectively "TPO"). Beyond TPO, covered entities may disclose PHI for specific public interest purposes: public health reporting, research with proper oversight, law enforcement, and national security. All other disclosures generally require written patient authorization.
Patients may request and receive a copy of their PHI from covered entities. Covered entities must respond within 30 days.
Right to Access
Patients may request corrections to inaccurate or incomplete PHI in their designated record set.
Right to Amend
Patients must receive a written notice explaining how their PHI will be used and disclosed.
Notice of Privacy Practices
Patients may request that covered entities limit certain uses or disclosures of their PHI.
Right to Restrict
Patients may request that covered entities communicate with them through alternative means or at alternative locations.
Confidential Communications
Patients may request a log of certain disclosures the covered entity has made of their PHI.
Accounting of Disclosures
Patients may file a complaint with HHS Office for Civil Rights (OCR) without fear of retaliation.
Right to Complain
Seven Core Patient Rights Under HIPAA
OCR has taken enforcement action specifically around patient access rights. In 2020 and 2021, OCR launched a series of Right of Access Initiative enforcement actions against providers who failed to timely provide patients with copies of their medical records. These cases resulted in settlements ranging from $3,500 to $200,000, signaling that patient access violations — not just large data breaches — carry real enforcement risk.
HHS Office for Civil Rights — Patient Access Enforcement
The Security Rule: Protecting Electronic PHI
The HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR §§ 164.302–318) applies specifically to electronic protected health information (ePHI). It requires covered entities and business associates to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI.
The Security Rule uses a "required vs. addressable" structure: required specifications must be implemented; addressable specifications must either be implemented or the entity must document why an equivalent alternative measure was used. This flexibility allows organizations of different sizes and complexity to tailor their security programs.
Administrative & Physical Safeguards
Administrative: Risk analysis and risk management programs (required)
Administrative: Workforce training and access management policies
Administrative: Security incident procedures
Physical: Facility access controls (locks, cameras, badge systems)
Physical: Workstation use policies (screen locks, clean desk)
Physical: Device and media controls (disposal, re-use procedures)
Technical Safeguards
Access controls: Unique user IDs, automatic logoff, encryption/decryption
Audit controls: Hardware and software activity logs for ePHI access
Integrity controls: Mechanisms to authenticate that ePHI has not been altered
Transmission security: Encryption of ePHI in transit (e.g., TLS)
Authentication: Verify that persons seeking access are who they claim to be
All technical safeguards must be documented in policies and procedures
Three Categories of HIPAA Security Safeguards
Business Associates and the BAA Requirement
A "business associate" is any person or organization that performs functions or activities on behalf of a covered entity that involve the use or disclosure of PHI. Common examples include cloud storage vendors, billing companies, EHR software vendors, and legal firms handling patient records.
HIPAA requires covered entities to enter into a written Business Associate Agreement (BAA) with each business associate before sharing PHI. The BAA must specify permitted uses, require the business associate to safeguard PHI, require reporting of breaches and security incidents, and set terms for termination. Under the 2013 Omnibus Rule, business associates became directly liable for HIPAA Security Rule compliance — not just contractually obligated.
A covered entity that shares PHI with a vendor without a signed BAA is already in violation of HIPAA — even if no breach has occurred. The BAA must be in place before PHI is shared.
HITECH Act and Breach Notification
The Health Information Technology for Economic and Clinical Health (HITECH) Act, enacted as part of the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act of 2009, significantly strengthened HIPAA. HITECH expanded HIPAA reach to business associates, increased civil monetary penalties, and created the Breach Notification Rule.
Under the Breach Notification Rule, covered entities must notify affected individuals without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovering a breach of unsecured PHI. If a breach affects 500 or more individuals, the covered entity must also notify HHS and prominent media outlets in the affected region.
HITECH increased HIPAA civil monetary penalties from a maximum of $100 per violation to up to $50,000 per violation, with annual caps up to $1.9 million per violation category (inflation-adjusted). Source: HHS OCR.

HIPAA applies to three categories of covered entities — health plans, health care clearinghouses, and electronic health care providers — and their business associates.
Protected Health Information (PHI) is any health information linked to one or more of 18 specific identifiers; removing all 18 identifiers renders data de-identified under the Safe Harbor method.
The Privacy Rule establishes seven core patient rights, including the right to access and amend health records, and permits disclosures for treatment, payment, and health care operations without patient authorization.
The Security Rule requires administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic PHI (ePHI), using a required/addressable distinction to allow flexible implementation.
Business Associate Agreements (BAAs) must be signed before PHI is shared with any vendor or contractor; since the 2013 Omnibus Rule, business associates are directly liable for HIPAA Security Rule compliance.
The HITECH Act (2009) expanded HIPAA enforcement by raising penalties to up to $50,000 per violation and establishing the 60-day Breach Notification Rule for unsecured PHI breaches.
A hospital that submits Medicare claims electronically is a covered entity — it is a health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with a HIPAA-covered transaction. Fitness apps, employer wellness programs, and non-health-care insurers generally are not covered entities and are not directly bound by HIPAA.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-21st-century-cures | 21st Century Cures Act
The 21st Century Cures Act
What Is the 21st Century Cures Act?
The 21st Century Cures Act — officially H.R. 34 — is one of the most consequential pieces of health legislation enacted in the United States in the past decade. President Barack Obama signed it into law on December 13, 2016, capping a multi-year, bipartisan effort to modernize the country's biomedical research enterprise, overhaul the federal mental health system, and drag the healthcare information technology sector into a genuinely interoperable future. The law passed by overwhelming margins — 392 to 26 in the House on November 30, 2016, and 94 to 5 in the Senate on December 7, 2016 — a rarity in an era of polarized legislating that underscores how broadly supported its core goals were across party lines.
At its core, the Act is best understood as three distinct but interlocking policy packages bundled into a single statute. The first package dramatically accelerates biomedical research by creating a dedicated NIH Innovation Account funded at $4.976 billion over ten years, with sub-appropriations targeting cancer, the brain, and precision medicine. The second package reforms the nation's fractured mental health delivery system by incorporating the long-stalled Helping Families in Mental Health Crisis Act and committing $1 billion in opioid crisis grants to states. The third package — and arguably the most operationally far-reaching — mandates true electronic health information interoperability, prohibits "information blocking," and requires federally certified EHR systems to offer open, standards-based APIs that patients can use to access their own records at no cost.
The total authorized funding across all three packages reaches $6.3 billion, making the Cures Act not just a policy milestone but a substantial investment in infrastructure. Critics at the time noted that authorization does not guarantee appropriation — Congress still had to fund the accounts annually — but supporters argued that the ring-fenced NIH Innovation Account structure created a more durable funding mechanism than ordinary discretionary spending, insulating flagship research programs from year-to-year budget battles.
The 21st Century Cures Act (H.R. 34, 2016) is a tripartite law that (1) funds landmark biomedical research through a dedicated NIH Innovation Account, (2) restructures federal mental health and substance use programs, and (3) mandates open, interoperable health IT through binding prohibitions on information blocking and requirements for FHIR-based patient access APIs.

Research Funding: Cancer, Brain, and Precision Medicine
The centerpiece of the Cures Act's research agenda is the NIH Innovation Account, a dedicated fund that sits outside the normal appropriations process and is designed to provide predictable, multi-year financing for three flagship initiatives. This structural choice was deliberate. Biomedical research programs that require sustained investment — building tissue banks, running decade-long longitudinal cohorts, funding research consortia — have historically been vulnerable to the unpredictability of annual appropriations. The Innovation Account attempts to solve that problem by giving Congress a framework to pre-commit funding over a ten-year window, even if the actual dollar transfers still require annual appropriation action.
The three flagship initiatives funded through the NIH Innovation Account each represent a different dimension of the federal research agenda. The Cancer Moonshot, later formally renamed the "Beau Biden Cancer Moonshot" in honor of Vice President Biden's son who died of brain cancer in 2015, received $1.8 billion to accelerate cancer prevention, detection, treatment, and data sharing. The BRAIN (Brain Research through Advancing Innovative Neurotechnologies) Initiative received $1.5 billion to map neural circuitry at unprecedented resolution and develop new tools for treating neurological and psychiatric conditions. The Precision Medicine Initiative — which later became the All of Us Research Program — also received $1.5 billion to build a national cohort of one million or more participants whose genomic, environmental, and lifestyle data would inform individually tailored treatments.
Beyond the three research flagships, the Act also invested $1 billion in opioid grants to states — a recognition that the opioid crisis ravaging communities across the country required not just more research but immediate, on-the-ground infrastructure to expand treatment access and improve prescription drug monitoring. The FDA provisions of the Act further accelerated the pipeline from research bench to patient bedside through new approval pathways for breakthrough devices and a framework for using real-world evidence from electronic health records and claims databases in post-market studies. Taken together, the research title of the Cures Act represents the most ambitious single legislative investment in biomedical science since the National Cancer Act of 1971.
The Cancer Moonshot was named for Beau Biden, son of then-Vice President Joe Biden, who died of glioblastoma multiforme at age 46 in May 2015. Vice President Biden personally championed the initiative and led the White House Cancer Moonshot Task Force before the Cures Act codified and funded it.

Under ordinary appropriations, NIH funding for a specific initiative must be re-requested and re-approved every fiscal year, creating uncertainty that can disrupt multi-year research programs. The NIH Innovation Account works differently: the Cures Act established the account in statute and authorized specific annual transfer amounts for each year from FY2017 through FY2026. This means Congress pre-committed to a funding trajectory in the authorizing legislation itself, rather than leaving each year's level entirely to the appropriations process. While actual transfers still require appropriations action, the statutory schedule creates a strong expectation — and a political baseline — that provides more stability for grantees, university research programs, and NIH program officers than traditional year-by-year discretionary spending would allow.
NIH Innovation Account: How the 10-Year Model Works
Mental Health and the Opioid Crisis
The mental health title of the Cures Act represented the culmination of years of work by Representative Tim Murphy (R-PA), a clinical psychologist who had spent much of his congressional tenure fighting for what he called "evidence-based mental health care." His Helping Families in Mental Health Crisis Act, introduced in multiple sessions of Congress, was incorporated nearly wholesale into the Cures Act after years of stalling. The legislation's core insight was that the federal mental health bureaucracy had become fragmented, underfunded, and disconnected from the evidence base — funding peer support and awareness programs while failing to adequately support the clinical treatment and hospital-based care that severe psychiatric illness actually requires.
The most structurally significant change in the mental health title was the creation of a new Assistant Secretary for Mental Health and Substance Use within the Department of Health and Human Services — a position that elevated mental health policy to the same bureaucratic level as other major health domains. The legislation also reorganized the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA), tightened requirements around evidence-based practices, and expanded the ability of states to use Assisted Outpatient Treatment (AOT) — court-ordered community-based care for individuals with severe mental illness who have a history of treatment non-adherence. Privacy rule clarifications in the Act also made it easier for providers to share mental health information with family members in crisis situations.
The $1 billion in opioid state grants represented one of the federal government's most direct financial interventions in the opioid crisis up to that point. The grants were authorized over two fiscal years and structured to flow through a formula-based allocation process that weighted states' burden of opioid overdose deaths and the capacity of their existing treatment infrastructure. States were required to submit plans demonstrating how funds would be used for evidence-based interventions — including medication-assisted treatment (MAT) expansion, prescription drug monitoring program (PDMP) improvements, and naloxone distribution — rather than general public awareness campaigns.
HHS distributes grant funds to states using a formula weighted by opioid overdose death rates and treatment capacity gaps — states with the highest burden receive proportionally more.
Formula Allocation
Each state must submit a plan to SAMHSA detailing how it will use the funds for evidence-based interventions, ensuring dollars are tied to measurable outcomes rather than open-ended programming.
State Plan Submission
A significant share of funds is directed toward upgrading prescription drug monitoring programs — the state databases that track controlled substance prescriptions — to improve cross-state data sharing and real-time prescriber access.
PDMP Improvements
States use funds to expand medication-assisted treatment (MAT) capacity, including buprenorphine and methadone access, and to reduce barriers for individuals seeking treatment in rural and underserved communities.
Treatment Access Expansion
Remaining funds support training for physicians, nurses, pharmacists, and peer recovery coaches to increase the number of providers equipped to treat opioid use disorder with evidence-based protocols.
Workforce Training
How the $1 Billion Opioid Grant Funds Flow to States
The $1 billion in opioid grants authorized by the Cures Act funds system infrastructure — PDMPs, workforce training, treatment capacity expansion — not direct payments for individual patient treatment services. Patients do not receive grants; states and local health agencies do. This distinction matters because it means the grants improve the system's ability to deliver care without replacing the insurance coverage and Medicaid financing that actually pays for individual treatment episodes.
Not Direct Treatment Funding
Information Blocking: The New Prohibition
Of all the provisions in the 21st Century Cures Act, the information blocking prohibition has proven to be the most disruptive to established business practices in the health IT industry. For years, critics argued that EHR vendors, hospitals, and health information exchanges were intentionally making it difficult — or prohibitively expensive — for patients and providers to access, exchange, or use electronic health information. The Act addressed this directly by making "information blocking" a federal offense subject to civil monetary penalties. The statutory definition is deliberately broad: any practice by a regulated actor that is likely to interfere with access, exchange, or use of electronic health information (EHI) — unless the practice falls within one of eight defined exceptions.
The Cures Act subjects three categories of actors to the information blocking rules. Health IT developers of certified health information technology (the EHR vendors themselves) are covered. Health information exchanges (HIEs) and health information networks (HINs) are covered. And healthcare providers — hospitals, physician practices, clinics — are covered. This tripartite scope was intentional: Congress recognized that information blocking could originate at any node in the health IT ecosystem, not just at the vendor level. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule, published May 1, 2020 in the Federal Register and effective June 30, 2020, fleshed out the specific regulatory definitions that give the statute operational meaning.
Enforcement of the information blocking rules began April 5, 2021 — the date when actors could first be formally reported to the Office of the Inspector General (OIG) of HHS for suspected violations. As of February 2026, OIG had received nearly 1,600 complaints, reflecting the breadth of perceived violations across the industry. Active enforcement actions began in September 2025. For health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, penalties can reach up to $1 million per violation — a figure large enough to create genuine compliance pressure even for the largest vendors. Healthcare providers face a different enforcement mechanism: disincentives established under a July 2024 final rule, which can affect Medicare reimbursement rates and meaningful use attestation.
Information blocking is defined as any practice by a covered actor (health IT developer, HIE/HIN, or healthcare provider) that is likely to interfere with, prevent, or materially discourage access, exchange, or use of electronic health information — unless the practice qualifies under one of the eight regulatory exceptions established by ONC.
Examples of Information Blocking
Charging excessive fees to access or export patient data that are not cost-based
Deploying non-standard or proprietary interfaces that prevent third-party apps from connecting
Including contract "gag clauses" that prevent customers from disclosing interoperability limitations
Delaying responses to API queries without technical justification
Conditioning data access on the purchase of additional vendor products or services
The 8 Regulatory Exceptions (Permitted Practices)
Privacy Exception — practices required to protect patient privacy under applicable law
Security Exception — practices necessary to protect the security of EHI
Preventing Harm Exception — practices needed to prevent endangerment of patients or others
Infeasibility Exception — practices technically or legally not feasible to perform
Health IT Performance Exception — routine system maintenance and downtime
Licensing Exception — reasonable and non-discriminatory licensing of IP
Content/Manner Exception — responding in a different form or manner than requested
Fees Exception — charging reasonable, cost-based fees for access or export
Information Blocking vs. Legitimate Restrictions
The Office of Inspector General (OIG) of HHS is authorized to impose civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per information blocking violation against health IT developers and HIEs/HINs. Healthcare providers face separate disincentives under a July 2024 HHS final rule, including reductions in Medicare reimbursement tied to meaningful use and promoting interoperability programs. OIG had received nearly 1,600 complaints as of February 2026, with active enforcement actions commencing in September 2025.
OIG Enforcement: Up to $1 Million Per Violation
Interoperability: FHIR APIs and Patient Access
The interoperability mandates in the Cures Act translate its broad policy goals into specific, enforceable technical requirements. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule — published May 1, 2020 and effective June 30, 2020 — requires that all ONC-certified health IT systems support FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources) Release 4.0.1 as the technical standard for patient-facing access APIs. FHIR R4 is a specification published by HL7 International that defines how healthcare data should be structured and exchanged using modern web standards — RESTful APIs, JSON, and OAuth 2.0 authentication. By mandating FHIR R4 specifically, ONC locked in a single, vendor-neutral standard that any compliant application can connect to, regardless of which EHR system a hospital uses.
The minimum data set that must be accessible through the FHIR API is defined by the United States Core Data for Interoperability version 1 (USCDI v1), which includes clinical notes, laboratory results, medications, allergies, immunizations, vital signs, demographics, and care team members. Patients have the right to access this data through any SMART on FHIR-compatible application of their choosing, at no cost, without the provider or EHR vendor being able to block or restrict that access. The Act also mandated the development of the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement (TEFCA) — a nationwide governance framework that establishes the legal, technical, and policy rules for how health information networks can share data across organizational and geographic boundaries.
The combined effect of the FHIR mandate, the information blocking prohibition, and TEFCA is to create — for the first time — a coherent federal framework for nationwide health data exchange. Before the Cures Act, the health IT landscape was a patchwork of proprietary interfaces, regional health information organizations with incompatible standards, and contractual barriers that prevented patients from exercising meaningful control over their own records. After the Act, any certified EHR system must publish a standards-based FHIR API, attest that it is not engaging in information blocking, and — as TEFCA networks mature — participate in a national exchange framework. The transformation is still in progress, but the legal architecture is now in place.
Requiring all certified EHRs to support FHIR Release 4.0.1 is like mandating the USB-C connector standard for all consumer electronics: once every device uses the same port, any compliant cable or accessory works with any device — no proprietary adapter needed. Before FHIR R4 was mandated, each EHR vendor had its own proprietary API (or no API at all), so a patient-facing app had to build a separate integration for each vendor. The standard port means the app only needs to be built once.
FHIR R4 Mandate as the USB-C Standard for Health Data
Develop and make publicly available a FHIR Release 4.0.1 compliant API that allows any authorized third-party application to request patient data using standard web protocols — at no cost to the patient or the application developer for access to USCDI data.
Publish a FHIR R4 API
Ensure the FHIR API surfaces at least the full USCDI v1 data set, including clinical notes, lab results, medications, allergies, immunizations, vital signs, problems, and demographics.
Support USCDI v1 Minimum Data Set
Submit attestation to ONC that the developer is not engaging in any information blocking practice and that the API is genuinely accessible to third-party developers without unreasonable conditions.
Attest to No Information Blocking
Conduct and publish results of real-world testing of the FHIR API with at least one third-party application to demonstrate that the API functions as documented under actual operating conditions.
Real-World Testing
As TEFCA governance matures, participate in or connect to a Qualified Health Information Network (QHIN) recognized under TEFCA to enable nationwide data exchange across organizational boundaries.
Join or Connect to a TEFCA-Recognized Network
What Certified EHR Developers Must Do Under the Cures Act
Epic Systems — the largest EHR vendor in the United States, used by about 42% of U.S. acute care hospitals at the end of 2024 (KLAS) — had launched its App Orchard developer marketplace in 2015, before the Cures Act was passed, and replaced it with Connection Hub and the Epic Showroom in 2022–2023. What the Cures Act changed was the floor: ONC's 2020 rule required certified EHRs to expose a standardized FHIR R4 API that third-party SMART on FHIR applications can connect to. Patients at Epic-using hospitals can authorize any SMART on FHIR app they choose to receive their health data via the standard API. Competitors like Oracle Health (Cerner) and Meditech built comparable API ecosystems. The result is that the Cures Act effectively forced the entire certified EHR market to open its data layer to patient-authorized third-party applications, creating the infrastructure for a generation of consumer health apps.
Epic and SMART on FHIR: What the Cures Act Changed
FDA Provisions and Real-World Evidence
The FDA title of the Cures Act addresses a set of long-standing criticisms of the regulatory pathway from medical innovation to patient access. The Act created or strengthened several mechanisms designed to accelerate the availability of breakthrough products while maintaining safety standards. The Breakthrough Device Designation program — building on the existing Breakthrough Therapy designation for drugs — allows novel medical devices that provide more effective treatment or diagnosis of life-threatening or irreversibly debilitating conditions to receive priority FDA review, with more frequent interaction between developers and FDA reviewers during the development process. The Act also expanded expanded access (compassionate use) pathways, making it easier for patients with serious conditions to access investigational products outside of clinical trials.
Perhaps the most forward-looking FDA provision in the Cures Act is the real-world evidence (RWE) framework. Traditional drug and device approval relies on randomized controlled trials — expensive, time-consuming, and often conducted on patient populations that do not reflect the diversity of real-world patients. The Cures Act directed FDA to develop a framework for using real-world data — including data from electronic health records, insurance claims databases, patient registries, and wearable devices — to support regulatory decisions, including post-approval studies and, in some cases, new indications for already-approved products. The Act also clarified the regulatory status of software as a medical device (SaMD), explicitly excluding certain low-risk wellness and administrative software from FDA oversight while preserving the agency's authority over clinical decision support tools that could cause patient harm if they malfunctioned.
Manufacturers of novel combination products and diagnostics
Accelerated access pathway for devices treating life-threatening conditions; priority review and frequent FDA interaction
Breakthrough Device
Drug and device manufacturers seeking label expansions or post-market confirmations
Post-approval and new-indication studies using EHR, claims, and registry data rather than traditional RCTs
Real-World Evidence
Digital health developers building apps, wellness tools, and EHR-embedded analytics
Excluded low-risk wellness and administrative software from FDA device regulation; preserved oversight of clinical decision support that poses patient risk
SaMD Clarification
The 21st Century Cures Act (H.R. 34) was signed December 13, 2016, with near-unanimous bipartisan support (392–26 House, 94–5 Senate), authorizing $6.3 billion across three policy pillars: research funding, mental health reform, and health IT interoperability.
The NIH Innovation Account ($4.976B over 10 years) funds three flagship research programs: the Cancer Moonshot ($1.8B), the BRAIN Initiative ($1.5B), and the Precision Medicine Initiative ($1.5B), with an additional $1B in opioid grants to states.
The Act incorporated the Helping Families in Mental Health Crisis Act (Rep. Tim Murphy), created the Assistant Secretary for Mental Health and Substance Use, and restructured SAMHSA around evidence-based practices.
Information blocking — any practice by a health IT developer, HIE/HIN, or provider that interferes with access to electronic health information — is now a federal offense with penalties up to $1 million per violation for developers and HIEs; providers face Medicare reimbursement disincentives.
Eight regulatory exceptions exist to the information blocking prohibition, covering privacy, security, harm prevention, infeasibility, IT performance, licensing, content/manner, and reasonable cost-based fees.
The ONC Cures Act Final Rule (effective June 30, 2020) mandates FHIR Release 4.0.1 as the standard for patient access APIs and USCDI v1 as the minimum data set — giving patients a legally enforceable right to their health data through any authorized app, at no cost.
FDA provisions established the Breakthrough Device Designation, expanded real-world evidence frameworks for regulatory decisions, and clarified that low-risk wellness software is excluded from FDA medical device oversight — shaping the entire digital health regulatory landscape.
The Office of Inspector General (OIG) of HHS — not ONC — is the enforcement authority for information blocking penalties against health IT developers and HIEs/HINs, with authority to impose civil monetary penalties of up to $1 million per violation. ONC administers the certification program and receives complaints, but it is OIG that investigates and adjudicates penalties. CMS administers the provider disincentive process established by the July 2024 final rule. The FTC has no information blocking enforcement authority under the Cures Act.

Vermont's Health IT Framework: VITL, Blueprint, and Act 167
Vermont as a National Health IT Laboratory
Vermont is one of the smallest states in the nation — with approximately 650,000 residents — but it has consistently punched above its weight in health system reform. Since the early 2000s, Vermont has built a comprehensive, legislatively-mandated health information infrastructure that integrates clinical data exchange, multi-payer payment reform, and population health management in ways that most larger states have only aspired to. Understanding Vermont's framework means understanding what coordinated, statewide health IT looks like when it is actually built.
Vermont's approach rests on three interlocking pillars: the Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE), operated by VITL under statutory designation; the Blueprint for Health, the state's multi-payer primary care transformation program; and a series of legislative acts — most recently Act 167 of 2022 — that have advanced the integration of claims data, clinical data, and social determinants information into a unified statewide health record infrastructure. Each pillar is codified in Vermont statute under Title 18, ensuring that the HIE and payment reform programs are not merely grant-funded pilots but durable state policy.
This lesson examines each pillar in depth: how VITL and the VHIE were established and how they operate; how the Blueprint for Health aligns financial incentives with care coordination; and what Act 167 of 2022 directed the state to do next — including the ambitious goal of merging Vermont's all-payer claims database with its statewide clinical HIE to create a single longitudinal health record for every Vermonter.
Vermont's health IT framework is codified in 18 V.S.A. Chapter 219, which requires a statewide Health Information Technology Plan, designates VITL as the exclusive operator of the Vermont Health Information Exchange, and mandates integration of the Blueprint for Health's IT components — making Vermont's HIE and payment reform programs matters of state law, not just policy preference.
Nonprofit designated by Vermont Legislature as exclusive statewide HIE operator

VITL and the Vermont Health Information Exchange
Vermont Information Technology Leaders (VITL) was founded in 2005 as a private nonprofit organization with support from the Vermont Association of Health and Hospital Systems, the Vermont Medical Society, and Fletcher Allen Health Care (now the University of Vermont Medical Center). Its founding mission was to help digitize Vermont's healthcare system and facilitate electronic exchange of patient information across the state. Vermont subsequently designated VITL in statute — under 18 V.S.A. § 9352 — as the exclusive operator of the Vermont Health Information Exchange (VHIE), making it the only entity authorized to operate a statewide HIE network in Vermont.
The VHIE connects Vermont's hospitals, primary and specialty care practices, Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs), home health agencies, nursing homes, commercial laboratories, and other healthcare organizations. Since 2005, VITL has collected, matched, and standardized patient data from these contributing organizations, building a longitudinal clinical data repository that spans care settings. VITL provides three primary services to the state: health information exchange (giving authorized providers access to a patient's records across organizations), quality reporting (aggregating data for population-level analysis), and analytics (supporting Vermont's Blueprint for Health and other initiatives).
Vermont's Health Information Technology Plan — required by 18 V.S.A. § 9351 — specifies what the VHIE must accomplish and how VITL must operate. Until Act 62 of 2025, DVHA submitted the Plan to the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB) each November 1 for approval; since July 1, 2025 the Board no longer approves it, and DVHA revises it annually with its HIE Steering Committee, with a comprehensive update every five years. It must include standards and protocols for patient education, patient privacy, physician best practices, electronic connectivity, and the delivery of cost-efficient care. The Plan also integrates the IT components of the Blueprint for Health, the Agency of Human Services' Enterprise Master Patient Index (EMPI), and all Medicaid management information systems — ensuring VITL's infrastructure is aligned with Vermont's broader health reform agenda. Act 62 also ended the GMCB's review of VITL's annual budget and of the HIE connectivity criteria.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Vermont's pre-existing VHIE infrastructure proved essential. VITL's statewide data exchange network enabled rapid aggregation of lab results, vaccination records, and hospital census data across Vermont's dispersed provider network — information that would have taken days to compile manually from individual facilities. The VHIE's existing connections to hospitals, labs, and primary care practices meant Vermont could operationalize statewide surveillance faster than states that lacked a functioning HIE. This real-world deployment illustrates the long-term value of investing in HIE infrastructure before a crisis demands it.
VITL's Role in Vermont's COVID-19 Response
A hospital, clinic, FQHC, or lab establishes a data feed to VITL's VHIE using HL7 v2 or FHIR standards; VITL's interface engine receives and standardizes the incoming data.
Provider Connects to VHIE
VITL's Enterprise Master Patient Index (EMPI) matches each incoming record to the correct patient across contributing organizations, creating a longitudinal identity link.
Patient Matching
When an authorized provider sees a patient, they can query the VHIE from within their EHR to retrieve records from other contributing organizations — lab results, hospital discharge summaries, medication lists.
Record Available for Query
VITL aggregates de-identified data for population health analysis, quality reporting for Blueprint practices, and state health surveillance.
Quality and Analytics
Vermont uses an opt-out consent model for the VHIE; patients are enrolled by default and must actively opt out if they do not wish their data shared through the exchange.

How the VHIE Works for a Vermont Provider
The Blueprint for Health: Multi-Payer Primary Care Reform
The Blueprint for Health is Vermont's state-led initiative for implementing sustainable health care delivery reform. First codified in Vermont statute in 2006 and significantly expanded in 2010 with Act 128, the Blueprint rests on a simple premise: if primary care practices are transformed into high-functioning, team-based medical homes, and if all payers share the cost of that transformation, the result will be better care, healthier populations, and lower total costs. The Blueprint is not a Medicaid-only or Medicare-only program — it is an all-payer reform that requires commercial insurers, Medicaid, and Medicare to participate together.
The Blueprint has four core components. The first is Patient-Centered Medical Homes (PCMHs) — primary care practices that have achieved National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) recognition for team-based care, care coordination, and population management. PCMHs receive a per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment from all payers, scaled to their NCQA score — higher scores earn higher payments, creating a financial incentive to continuously improve. The second is Community Health Teams (CHTs) — multi-disciplinary teams deployed regionally to support PCMHs. CHT staff include nurses, care coordinators, social workers, counselors, health educators, registered dietitians, nutrition specialists, health coaches, and community health workers. CHT capacity payments are approximately $350,000 per 20,000 patients, shared equally by Vermont's commercial and public payers.
In 2010, Vermont was selected to participate in the CMS Multi-Payer Advanced Primary Care Practice (MAPCP) Demonstration, through which Medicare formally joined the Blueprint as a paying partner alongside commercial insurers and Medicaid — one of the first instances in the US of Medicare participating in a state-led all-payer primary care transformation program. The Blueprint uses Vermont's all-payer claims database (VCHURES) and the Vermont Clinical Registry for data, analytics, and the Learning Health System component that enables practices to continuously evaluate and improve their performance.
Before Blueprint (Fragmented Primary Care)
Each payer contracts separately with each practice
No shared investment in care coordination or team-based care
PCPs paid FFS — rewarded for volume, not value
No community health teams to support complex patients
No shared population-level data across payers
Care transitions unsupported — patients fall through gaps
After Blueprint (Coordinated Multi-Payer Reform)
All payers (commercial + Medicaid + Medicare) aligned behind shared goals
PMPM payments support PCMH transformation at scale
Community Health Teams deployed regionally to support practices
VCHURES claims + VHIE clinical data enable population analytics
Learning Health System enables continuous quality improvement
Care coordinators proactively manage high-risk patients
Blueprint for Health — Before and After
Act 167 (2022): Toward One Health Record per Vermonter
Vermont Act 167 of 2022 (S.285), “An act relating to health care reform initiatives, data collection, and access to home- and community-based services,” represented a significant legislative step forward in Vermont's health IT agenda. Among its most consequential provisions was a directive to the HIE Steering Committee to work toward creating one health record per Vermonter — a longitudinal record that integrates health care claims data, clinical data, mental health and substance use disorder records, and social determinants of health data. Critically, the Act called for a data integration strategy to merge and consolidate Vermont's all-payer claims database (VHCURES) with the clinical data in the VHIE.
This merger — claims data plus clinical data plus SDOH data in a single longitudinal record — is the holy grail of health information management. Claims data tells you what services were billed and paid; clinical data tells you what actually happened clinically; SDOH data tells you what social and environmental factors shaped the patient's health. Each alone is powerful; combined, they create a complete picture of a patient's health journey across settings, payers, and social contexts. Vermont's Act 167 positioned the state to build this integrated view at a statewide level — a capability that most states lack the infrastructure to attempt.
Act 167 also addressed the Blueprint for Health's funding. The Director of Health Care Reform was required to recommend, by January 15, 2023, updated per-member-per-month payment amounts for insurers and Medicaid for Blueprint Community Health Teams and quality improvement facilitation. Additional provisions covered options for supporting Vermonters with moderate care needs, Green Mountain Care Board reporting requirements, Medicaid primary care reimbursement rates, and prior authorization reporting — reflecting the Act's comprehensive scope as a health care reform omnibus.
Act 167's vision — one longitudinal health record per Vermonter integrating claims, clinical, behavioral health, and SDOH data — represents the most ambitious health data integration goal in Vermont's history. It requires merging VHCURES (the all-payer claims database), the VHIE (clinical HIE), behavioral health records, and social needs data under a unified governance and consent framework.
Vermont's goal of integrating mental health and substance use disorder records into a unified health record must navigate 42 CFR Part 2 (federal SUD confidentiality rules) and Vermont's own behavioral health privacy statutes. Mental health and SUD records carry stricter protections than general medical records. Any data integration strategy for Act 167's unified health record must include a robust consent architecture that separately governs behavioral health data — with patient opt-in (not just opt-out) for this sensitive category.
Behavioral Health Data Requires Special Consent Governance
Vermont's Health IT Governance Evolution
Vermont's health IT governance has evolved through multiple legislative cycles. From 2011 through 2025, the Green Mountain Care Board (GMCB) held oversight authority for Vermont's statewide Health Information Technology Plan and VITL. The GMCB — an independent state agency — reviewed and approved Vermont's annual HIT Plan, ensuring that VITL's activities aligned with Vermont's broader health reform goals. This placed Vermont's HIE governance at the intersection of health care reform policy and health IT strategy in a way unique among US states.
Act 62 of 2025, effective July 1, 2025, restructured Vermont's health IT governance by removing VITL oversight and the HIT Plan from the Green Mountain Care Board's responsibilities. This change reflects Vermont's ongoing evolution in how it organizes health system reform functions — separating technical HIE governance from the broader health care cost and quality oversight mission of the GMCB. Vermont's health IT governance will continue to evolve as the state pursues the ambitious data integration goals set out in Act 167.
Vermont's experience offers national lessons about what statewide health IT requires to succeed. First, statutory designation matters: naming VITL the exclusive statewide HIE operator in law — rather than through a grant or contract — gave VITL the stability and authority to build long-term infrastructure. Second, multi-payer alignment is essential: the Blueprint's success depends on every payer participating, including Medicare — which requires federal CMS engagement through models like the MAPCP Demonstration. Third, data integration is generational work: merging claims, clinical, and SDOH data at statewide scale, as Act 167 envisions, requires years of governance, consent framework development, technical integration, and stakeholder trust-building. Vermont is further along this path than most states, but the work is not finished.
Vermont's health IT system is like a city's water infrastructure — invisible to most residents until it isn't working. The pipes (VITL's data connections), the treatment plant (the EMPI and data standardization), and the distribution system (the VHIE query and reporting platform) all had to be built before any water could flow. Act 167 is like adding a water recycling system — taking what already flows through the pipes and making it even more useful by integrating it with other sources. The infrastructure investment came first; the value follows from it.
Vermont's Statewide HIE as Shared Infrastructure

HL7 and FHIR: Healthcare Data Standards
Why Healthcare Needs Data Standards
Healthcare generates vast amounts of data — lab results, medication orders, diagnoses, vital signs, imaging reports — across thousands of incompatible software systems. Without common data standards, a lab result from one hospital cannot be reliably interpreted by a different hospital's EHR, and a patient's medication list cannot flow automatically from a physician's office to a pharmacy. Standards are the shared language that allows different healthcare systems to exchange, interpret, and act on information consistently.
Health Level Seven (HL7) International, founded in 1987 as an ANSI-accredited, not-for-profit standards organization, became the primary body responsible for healthcare data exchange standards in the United States and globally. The name "Health Level Seven" refers to Layer 7 — the application layer — of the Open Systems Interconnection (OSI) reference model. HL7's standards now underpin virtually every electronic clinical workflow, from patient admission to lab ordering to claims submission.
Two generations of HL7 standards dominate the landscape today: HL7 Version 2 (v2), the workhorse of hospital systems since the late 1980s, and FHIR (Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources), the modern API-based standard that is rapidly becoming the foundation for patient access, interoperability regulations, and digital health innovation. Understanding both — how they work, how they differ, and how they coexist — is essential for anyone working in health IT.
HL7 International is an ANSI-accredited, not-for-profit standards developing organization that provides a framework of international standards for the exchange, integration, sharing, and retrieval of electronic health information. It was founded in 1987 and its standards are now implemented in healthcare systems across 50+ countries.
ANSI-accredited standards body that created the foundational healthcare data exchange standards

HL7 Version 2: The Original Healthcare Messaging Standard
HL7's first specification (Version 1.0) appeared in October 1987 and Version 2.0 in September 1988; v2 became the dominant standard for real-time clinical data exchange in hospitals. It uses a pipe-delimited text message format where data elements are separated by the | character, sub-components by ^, repeating values by ~, and sub-sub-components by &. While this seems archaic by modern standards, it was revolutionary in 1987 — enabling the first automated exchange of admission, discharge, lab, and order data between disparate hospital systems.
HL7 v2 messages are organized into message types that correspond to clinical events. ADT messages (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) communicate patient movement and demographics — a new admission sends an ADT-A01, a discharge sends an ADT-A03. ORM messages carry orders from the ordering system to the fulfilling department (lab, pharmacy, radiology). ORU messages return results — an ORU-R01 carries lab results, vital signs, or radiology reports back to the ordering clinician. Every message contains segments — MSH (message header with sender, recipient, timestamp, and message type), PID (patient demographics), and type-specific segments like OBR (observation request) and OBX (observation result).
Despite being nearly 40 years old, HL7 v2 remains deeply embedded in healthcare IT. It is present in 95% of US healthcare organizations and installed in 35+ countries. Complex HL7 v2 integration projects can take months to implement because of the high degree of local customization — every hospital implements v2 slightly differently, with local Z-segments and non-standard field usage, creating integration complexity that FHIR was specifically designed to eliminate.
When a clinician orders a blood glucose test in a hospital EHR, an ORM^O01 message travels from the EHR to the laboratory information system (LIS). When the lab completes the analysis, the LIS sends an ORU^R01 message back to the EHR containing the patient ID, the test ordered (LOINC code in OBR), and the result value, units, and reference range (in OBX segments). This exchange — invisible to the clinician — happens in seconds and relies entirely on HL7 v2 message parsing. In a large academic medical center, thousands of these messages flow per hour, 24 hours a day.
HL7 v2 in Action: Lab Result Delivery
Despite being called a 'standard,' HL7 v2 is notorious for implementation variation. Two hospitals can both claim HL7 v2 compliance while implementing the same fields in incompatible ways. Z-segments (custom extensions) are common, field optionality is high, and there is no enforced terminology binding. This is why interface engines (Mirth Connect, Rhapsody) exist — to translate between the many dialects of v2 spoken by different systems.
v2 Is Not Truly Standardized
FHIR: The Modern Healthcare API Standard
Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR, pronounced "fire") is HL7 International's next-generation standard, designed from the ground up for the web era. Where HL7 v2 sends messages in response to clinical events, FHIR exposes data through RESTful APIs — the same technology that powers websites, mobile apps, and cloud services. A FHIR server makes clinical data available as discrete, addressable resources that any authorized application can retrieve using standard HTTP requests.
FHIR organizes clinical information into modular resource types — Patient, Observation, Encounter, Condition, MedicationRequest, DiagnosticReport, Immunization, AllergyIntolerance, and many more. Each resource has a defined structure and is accessible at a predictable URL. For example, to retrieve patient 123's blood pressure readings, a developer sends a standard HTTP GET request: GET /Observation?patient=123&code=55284-4 — and receives a JSON bundle of matching Observation resources. FHIR R4 (v4.0.1, released in 2019) is the current implementation baseline, mandated by both the ONC Cures Act Final Rule and the CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Rule.
FHIR's developer-friendly design dramatically reduces integration time. FHIR implementations of comparable scope are generally faster than HL7 v2 projects, because they rely on standard web tooling. Standard JSON libraries, HTTP clients, and FHIR reference implementations (HAPI FHIR in Java, Microsoft Azure Health Data Services, Google Cloud Healthcare API) provide off-the-shelf tooling. Epic reports that its USCDI v3 FHIR APIs alone have been called more than 8 billion times since their 2024 release — a scale that reflects both the standard's adoption and the explosive growth of patient-facing apps and third-party integrations built on top of it.
Think of HL7 v2 as the postal system — it delivers messages from one place to another, and has been doing so reliably for decades. FHIR is like the internet — instead of mailing documents, you query a live database using a URL, and get back structured data in real time that any app can use. Both carry health information; only one was designed for the world of smartphones and APIs.
HL7 v2 vs FHIR as Communication Paradigms

HL7 v2 vs FHIR
SMART on FHIR: Secure App Integration
SMART on FHIR (Substitutable Medical Applications, Reusable Technologies) is the standard framework for securely connecting third-party applications to EHR data via FHIR. It builds on OAuth 2.0 — the same authorization protocol used by Google, Facebook, and most major web platforms — and adds healthcare-specific scopes and launch context so that apps know which patient is being viewed and what data they are authorized to access.
SMART supports two launch modes. In an EHR Launch, the app is opened from within an active EHR session — the EHR passes the app a launch token containing the current patient ID, encounter ID, and FHIR server URL. The app uses this context to immediately display relevant patient data without requiring a separate login. In a Standalone Launch, the app opens independently (e.g., a patient-facing mobile app) and prompts the user to authenticate and select a patient context. SMART scopes control exactly what data the app can access — patient/Observation.read gives read-only access to a specific patient's observations, while user/MedicationRequest.write allows the app to create medication orders on behalf of a clinician.
SMART on FHIR has enabled the emergence of healthcare app ecosystems. Epic's App Orchard and Oracle Health's (formerly Cerner) App Market host thousands of third-party clinical apps — decision support tools, specialty workflows, patient engagement platforms, and analytics dashboards — all connecting to EHR data through SMART on FHIR without requiring custom point-to-point integrations. This shift from proprietary interfaces to open, standards-based app platforms is one of the most significant structural changes in health IT driven by FHIR adoption.
The clinician clicks a SMART app link within the EHR while viewing a patient record; the EHR generates a launch token tied to the current patient and encounter context.
Clinician Opens App
The app's launch URL receives the EHR's FHIR server URL (iss) and a launch handle; it uses these to discover the authorization endpoint.
App Receives Launch Context
The app redirects to the EHR's OAuth server, which authenticates the user (if not already logged in) and presents a consent screen showing what data the app is requesting.
OAuth 2.0 Authorization
The EHR returns an access token and the patient/encounter context (patient ID, encounter ID); the access token is scoped to the permissions the app requested.
Token Exchange
The app uses the access token to make FHIR API calls to retrieve patient data (e.g., GET /MedicationRequest?patient=123) and display the relevant clinical content.
