Regulatory Mandates and the Road Ahead
FHIR's rise from technical standard to regulatory requirement was driven by federal policy. The ONC Cures Act Final Rule, published May 1, 2020 and effective June 30, 2020, requires certified EHR developers to publish FHIR R4-based APIs at no cost to patients and authorized third parties. EHR developers must also attest that they will not engage in information blocking — refusing to share data through these APIs. Failure to comply exposes developers to penalties of up to $1 million per violation enforced by the HHS Office of Inspector General.
The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access Final Rule (CMS-9115-F) complements ONC's rule on the payer side. It requires CMS-regulated payers — Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, and ACA Marketplace plans — to implement a FHIR R4 Patient Access API covering claims, encounters, and a defined clinical data subset (USCDI v1). Payers must also implement a Provider Directory API and a Payer-to-Payer exchange mechanism. TEFCA's Common Agreement v2.0, released April 2024, added mandatory FHIR-based transaction support as a condition for QHINs, bringing FHIR into the national exchange infrastructure.
HL7 v2 and FHIR are not competitors — they are complementary. v2 remains the backbone of high-volume, real-time hospital transactions (admissions, lab orders, results) and will not be replaced overnight. FHIR is the standard for API-driven innovation: patient apps, payer-to-payer exchange, quality reporting, and clinical decision support. Most health systems today run both in parallel.
HL7 International, founded in 1987, is the ANSI-accredited body responsible for healthcare data exchange standards; the name refers to Layer 7 (application layer) of the OSI model.
HL7 v2, first released in 1988, uses pipe-delimited messages and is deployed in 95% of US healthcare organizations — but high local customization makes integration complex and time-consuming.
FHIR R4 (v4.0.1, released 2019) uses RESTful APIs, HTTP, and JSON to represent clinical data as modular resources (Patient, Observation, Encounter, etc.), enabling faster and more consistent integrations than v2.
SMART on FHIR provides a secure OAuth 2.0-based framework for launching third-party apps from within EHRs with patient and encounter context — enabling the healthcare app ecosystems on Epic, Cerner, and other platforms.
The ONC Cures Act Final Rule (2020) requires certified EHRs to expose FHIR R4 APIs at no cost; CMS-9115-F requires payers to implement FHIR R4 Patient Access APIs covering claims, encounters, and clinical data.
HL7 v2 and FHIR are complementary — v2 handles high-volume real-time hospital messaging; FHIR enables patient-facing apps, payer exchange, and API-driven interoperability innovation.
Epic's USCDI v3 FHIR APIs alone have been called more than 8 billion times since their 2024 release — a measure of how rapidly FHIR has moved from a regulatory requirement to the dominant infrastructure for health data exchange.
ADT (Admit, Discharge, Transfer) messages are the most common HL7 v2 message type, communicating patient movement events — a new admission generates an ADT-A01, a discharge generates an ADT-A03. ORU messages carry observation results (lab values, vitals), ORM carries orders, and MSH is a segment within every message that identifies the sender, recipient, and message type — not a message type itself.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-mpi-terminology | Master Patient Index & Terminology Services
Master Patient Index and Patient Matching
Why Patient Identity Matters
Every clinical decision depends on being confident that the data being viewed belongs to the right patient. When a physician reviews a medication list, orders a blood transfusion, or interprets a lab result, they must be certain the record in front of them is for the person sitting across from them. Patient identity — uniquely identifying each individual and correctly linking all their records — is the foundation on which every other health IT function depends.
The consequences of patient identity failures are severe. Duplicate patient records — two or more separate records created for the same patient — average about 10 percent of the records in a hospital’s MPI, according to AHIMA, and run far higher in some organizations. A 2018 Black Book survey found that duplicate records cost hospitals an average of $1,950 per patient per inpatient stay — and more than $800 per emergency visit — in repeated care. More critically, research cited by the UK’s Health Services Safety Investigations Body found that patient misidentification accounted for about 70 percent of adverse outcomes — wrong blood, unnecessary surgery, delayed diagnoses.
The most dangerous MPI error is an overlay — when two different patients’ records are merged into a single record. The result is a composite chart that contains data from two people: the first patient may receive a medication they are allergic to (because the allergy was in the second patient’s record), or receive a blood transfusion of the wrong type. Overlays are extremely difficult to detect and correct once they occur, because there is no obvious signal that something is wrong — the chart looks complete and internally consistent.
A Master Patient Index (MPI) is the enterprise system that uniquely identifies each patient and links all their records across clinical and administrative systems. Without a reliable MPI, a health system cannot safely exchange, aggregate, or analyze patient data.

What Is a Master Patient Index?
A Master Patient Index (MPI) is a centralized database that serves as the authoritative patient identifier repository for a healthcare organization. When a patient registers at a hospital, the MPI checks whether a record already exists for that person. If it does, the new encounter is linked to the existing record. If not, a new record — with a unique patient identifier (UPI), a non-changing alphanumeric key — is created. Every subsequent encounter, lab result, medication record, and clinical note is linked to that UPI, creating a longitudinal patient record across the organization’s systems.
An Enterprise Master Patient Index (EMPI) extends the concept across multiple organizations or facilities. Where an MPI serves a single institution, an EMPI identifies, links, and manages unique patient identities across disparate systems in a health system, an HIE, or a multi-state network. The EMPI is what makes it possible to say “this record from Hospital A and this record from Hospital B belong to the same person” — even when the two records were created with slightly different demographic information.
The MPI/EMPI does not store clinical data — it stores identity data. Its output is a set of record links and a master identifier that can be used to retrieve the correct clinical records from each contributing system. In an HIE, the EMPI is paired with a record-locator service (RLS): the EMPI finds that patient Jane Smith at Hospital A is the same as Jane J. Smith-Williams at Clinic B, and the RLS then queries both organizations for her clinical records and presents them to the requesting clinician.
A Master Patient Index is like the Social Security Administration’s database — not the agency that pays your benefits or issues your passport, but the authoritative system that assigns you a unique number, verifies your identity, and ensures that all records associated with you are correctly linked. In healthcare, the MPI plays the same role: not storing the medical records themselves, but ensuring all records point to the right person.
Master Patient Index as Identity Backbone
MPI (Single Organization)
Patient identity management within one hospital or clinic
Matches records across internal systems (EHR, LIS, pharmacy, billing)
Assigns a local unique patient identifier (MRN)
Covers one facility’s patient population
Managed by the facility’s HIM or IT department
Sufficient for standalone hospitals
EMPI (Enterprise / Multi-Org)
Patient identity management across multiple facilities or organizations
Matches records from different EHRs, HIEs, and clinical networks
Assigns an enterprise-wide unique patient identifier
Covers patients across a health system, region, or state
Requires cross-organizational governance and data sharing agreements
Essential for HIEs, health systems, and ACOs
MPI vs. EMPI
How Patient Matching Works
Patient matching — determining whether two records belong to the same individual — is the core function of the MPI. It sounds simple, but it is surprisingly difficult. Names are misspelled, abbreviated, or changed (marriage, divorce). Dates of birth are transposed. The same patient may have registered under a nickname at one facility and a legal name at another. Social Security numbers are frequently withheld or incorrectly entered. No single identifier reliably and uniquely identifies a patient across all settings in the US.
Two primary algorithmic approaches are used: deterministic matching and probabilistic matching. Deterministic matching requires an exact match on all specified fields — if the SSN, last name, and date of birth all match exactly, the records are linked; if any field differs, they are not. It is fast and highly precise but fails whenever data entry errors, name changes, or missing fields are present. Probabilistic matching assigns statistical weights to each data element based on how discriminating that element is; it calculates a composite match score and declares a match if the score exceeds a defined threshold. Probabilistic matching handles minor data variations — nickname vs. legal name, transposed birth year digits — but can produce false positives if thresholds are set too loosely.
Modern EMPIs use a hybrid approach: deterministic matching for high-confidence cases (exact SSN + exact DOB + exact last name), probabilistic matching for borderline cases, and referential matching for ambiguous records. Referential matching compares patient demographics against a large external reference database — such as credit bureau records or driver’s license data — to resolve identities with higher confidence. Vendors including Verato offer referential matching as a service integrated with hospital EMPIs. Name fuzzy-matching algorithms like Soundex and Jaro-Winkler are used to catch phonetic variants: “Smith” and “Smyth”, “Katherine” and “Catherine”, “Jose” and “José.”
A new patient registration or ADT message arrives; the EMPI standardizes name casing, address format, date format, and phone number to a canonical form before matching.
Receive & Standardize
The EMPI checks for exact matches on high-confidence identifier combinations (e.g., SSN + DOB + last name); exact matches are linked immediately with high confidence.
Deterministic Pass
Records that don’t clear the deterministic pass are scored probabilistically; each demographic field receives a weight; scores are summed; records above threshold are flagged as probable matches.
Probabilistic Scoring
Records near the threshold (potential matches requiring judgment) are routed to an HIM analyst or data steward for manual review and adjudication.
Human Review Queue
Confirmed matches are linked to the existing MPI record; non-matches result in a new unique patient identifier being assigned; the match decision is logged for audit.
Link or Create
How an EMPI Matches an Incoming Record
The National Patient Identifier Gap
Patient matching in the United States is harder than in almost any other developed country because the US has no national unique patient identifier (UPI). Since 1998, Congress has included a rider on the HHS appropriations bill prohibiting the agency from spending any funds to create or promote a national patient identifier, citing privacy concerns. Congressional report language has clarified that HHS may still work on patient-matching strategies, and the House voted to drop the ban in 2019 — but the rider has stayed in the final appropriations acts, and as of 2026 no national patient identifier exists.
The absence of a national UPI forces every health system and HIE to build its own patient matching infrastructure and to rely on probabilistic algorithms to resolve identities that a single authoritative identifier could resolve instantly. Countries with national health identifiers — the UK’s NHS Number, Canada’s provincial health card numbers, Australia’s Individual Healthcare Identifier — achieve dramatically higher patient matching accuracy at lower cost. Industry groups including AHIMA and HIMSS have long advocated for a US national patient identifier, arguing that the privacy risks of a known identifier are lower than the safety risks of persistent matching failures.
In the absence of a national identifier, the industry has moved toward voluntary frameworks. The Patient Matching Initiative — a collaboration between ONC, health systems, and vendors — has developed standardized matching attributes and best practices. TEFCA’s governance framework includes requirements for how QHINs must handle patient matching across the national exchange network.
When two different patients’ records are merged into one (an overlay), the combined record contains medications, allergies, diagnoses, and results from two people. Detecting an overlay requires noticing clinical inconsistencies — a blood type that doesn’t match, an allergy that conflicts with a current prescription — which may not happen until a harmful event has already occurred. Correcting an overlay requires manual HIM review to separate the records, which is time-consuming and may be incomplete. Prevention through strong matching rules and human review queues is far safer than remediation after the fact.
The Overlay Is Irreversible Without Careful Remediation
The US is the only major developed country without a national unique patient identifier. The result: every hospital, HIE, and health system must independently solve the same patient matching problem — spending billions collectively on a challenge that a single authoritative identifier would largely eliminate.
MPI in Health Information Exchange
Every health information exchange (HIE) requires a patient matching solution — typically an EMPI — to safely aggregate and exchange records across contributing organizations. When a clinician at Hospital A requests records for a patient who has also been seen at Clinic B and a nursing home, the HIE’s EMPI must first confirm that the “Jane Smith, DOB 1965-04-12” at Hospital A is the same person as “Jane J. Williams-Smith, DOB 04/12/1965” at Clinic B. Without that confirmation, the HIE cannot safely surface Clinic B’s records — the risk of displaying another patient’s data is too high.
The EMPI in an HIE works alongside a record-locator service (RLS). Once the EMPI has resolved that two records belong to the same patient, the RLS knows where that patient’s records are distributed across the network and can direct queries to the appropriate organizations. The clinical data itself may remain at each contributing organization (federated model) or be stored centrally (centralized model) — but the identity layer is always managed by the EMPI regardless of architectural choice.
CommonWell Health Alliance built a national patient identity and record-locator service connecting EHR systems from multiple vendors. When a provider in a CommonWell-enrolled Epic system needs records from a patient who was previously seen at a Cerner-connected facility, CommonWell’s EMPI resolves the patient identity across both systems and returns a record locator that allows the Epic clinician to retrieve the Cerner records. CommonWell uses a combination of deterministic and probabilistic matching, plus an enrollment process that gives patients and providers a mechanism to confirm or dispute matches. As of 2024, CommonWell connects thousands of sites across the US and illustrates how cross-vendor, cross-organization patient matching can be achieved at national scale.
CommonWell Health Alliance — Cross-Vendor Patient Matching
A Master Patient Index (MPI) uniquely identifies each patient within an organization and links all their records; an Enterprise Master Patient Index (EMPI) extends this across multiple organizations or facilities.
Duplicate patient records average about 10% of an MPI’s records (AHIMA) and add roughly $1,950 per inpatient stay in repeated care (Black Book, 2018), while misidentification underlies a large share of adverse outcomes.
An overlay — merging two different patients’ records into one — is the most dangerous MPI error; it can cause wrong-medication, wrong-blood-type, and wrong-treatment events that may not be detected until harm has occurred.
Patient matching uses three algorithmic approaches: deterministic (exact field match), probabilistic (weighted scoring for approximate matches), and referential (comparison against an external identity database); modern EMPIs combine all three.
The US has no national unique patient identifier — Congress has prohibited HHS from creating one since 1998 — forcing every health system and HIE to independently solve patient matching with probabilistic algorithms.
Every HIE requires an EMPI to safely match patient identities across contributing organizations; the EMPI works alongside a record-locator service (RLS) to direct queries to the correct organizations once identity is confirmed.
Common MPI errors include duplicates (multiple records for same patient), overlays (merged records from different patients), and false links (records incorrectly linked across patients) — all requiring active governance, human review queues, and ongoing data stewardship.
An overlay occurs when the MPI incorrectly merges records belonging to two different patients into a single chart. The resulting record contains medications, allergies, diagnoses, and test results from both individuals — creating a dangerous hybrid that can lead to wrong-medication or wrong-blood-type events. Unlike a duplicate (two records for the same patient), an overlay combines two different people’s data, making it the most dangerous class of MPI error.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-integration-architecture | Integration Engines & HIE Architecture
Healthcare Integration Architecture
The Integration Problem in Healthcare
A typical large academic medical center operates dozens of clinical and administrative systems — an EHR, a laboratory information system (LIS), a radiology information system (RIS), a picture archiving and communication system (PACS), a pharmacy system, a billing system, a patient portal, and more. Each was built by a different vendor, speaks a different data format, and was designed without knowledge of the others. Making them work together is the core challenge of healthcare integration architecture.
Poor integration has real clinical and financial consequences. A lab result that doesn't reach the ordering physician in time delays treatment. A medication list that doesn't follow a patient from hospital to pharmacy causes adverse drug events. A prior authorization status that can't be retrieved electronically triggers phone calls and fax loops that cost physicians' offices enormous time. Analysts estimate that a lack of interoperability costs the US healthcare system over $30 billion annually in avoidable inefficiencies — administrative overhead, unnecessary duplicate testing, and delayed clinical decisions.
Healthcare integration architecture is the discipline of designing the connections between these systems — choosing the right patterns, technologies, and standards to make data flow reliably, securely, and consistently. Three major architectural patterns have evolved over the past 40 years: point-to-point integration, hub-and-spoke (interface engine), and API-based architectures using modern standards like FHIR. Each represents a different trade-off between simplicity, scalability, and flexibility.
Healthcare integration architecture defines how disparate clinical and administrative systems exchange data — reliably, securely, and at scale. Getting it right is not just a technical problem; it is a patient safety and operational efficiency imperative.
Avoidable inefficiencies: admin overhead, duplicate testing, delayed decisions (industry estimates)

Point-to-Point: The Spaghetti Problem
The simplest integration approach is point-to-point: every system that needs to talk to another system gets a direct, custom connection. When a hospital has 5 systems, this is manageable — 10 connections. When a health system has 50 systems, point-to-point requires up to 1,225 custom connections. When systems are updated, every connection touching that system must be retested and potentially rebuilt. This exponential growth in complexity is called "spaghetti integration" — the architecture looks like a bowl of tangled noodles, and it becomes impossible to change anything without breaking something else.
Point-to-point integrations also create deep technical dependencies. If the lab system changes its patient ID format, every system connected to the lab — the EHR, the radiology system, the billing system — must update its interface simultaneously. Coordination across vendors at that scale is extremely difficult, and failed or mismatched updates cause data errors that can ripple into clinical decisions. The lack of a central routing or transformation layer means there is no single place to apply a fix or policy change.
Despite its problems, point-to-point integration remains common in healthcare — particularly among smaller organizations and for specific use cases where two systems have a single, stable connection that has worked for years. Legacy point-to-point interfaces are frequently the last to be migrated during enterprise integration modernization projects, because they are deeply embedded in workflows and the risk of touching a working interface is perceived as high.
With point-to-point integration, the number of interfaces grows as a function of the square of the number of systems: 5 systems = 10 interfaces; 10 systems = 45 interfaces; 50 systems = 1,225 interfaces. Every interface is a custom build, a maintenance liability, and a potential point of failure. This is why organizations that start with point-to-point inevitably hit a wall and are forced to adopt a hub-based or API-based architecture.
The n×(n-1)/2 Scaling Problem
Hub-and-Spoke: The Interface Engine Model
The hub-and-spoke model solves the scaling problem by introducing a central integration engine — the hub — that all systems (the spokes) connect to. Instead of each system needing to know how to communicate with every other system, each system only needs one connection to the hub. The hub handles all protocol translation, message transformation, routing logic, and delivery. A hospital with 50 systems needs only 50 connections in a hub-and-spoke model instead of 1,225. The hub is the single place where integration logic lives, where problems are diagnosed, and where changes are made.
Interface engines — the software that implements the hub — are specialized middleware platforms designed for healthcare data exchange. They ingest HL7 v2 messages (ADT, ORM, ORU), transform them between formats, apply routing rules (e.g., send all lab results for Cardiology patients to the Cardiology dashboard), and deliver them to destination systems. They also handle error management, message acknowledgment (ACK/NAK), retry logic, and audit logging — critical functions in a healthcare environment where a missed lab result can be a patient safety event.
The dominant interface engine platforms in the US market are Mirth Connect (now NextGen Connect), Rhapsody, Corepoint, Iguana (iNTERFACEWARE), and Cloverleaf (Infor). Mirth Connect was the most widely deployed open-source integration engine — but on March 19, 2025, NextGen Healthcare announced that Mirth Connect 4.6 would transition to a closed-source proprietary license. Version 4.5.2 is the last freely available open-source release. Two open-source forks emerged in response: BridgeLink (from Innovar Healthcare) and the community-governed Open Integration Engine. Rhapsody is consistently rated Best in KLAS for clinical data integration among large health systems.
Point-to-Point
Direct connection between every pair of systems
Scales as n×(n-1)/2 — exponential complexity
Each connection is custom-built and independently maintained
No central place to apply routing rules or fixes
Changes to one system break all connected interfaces
Common in small organizations or legacy environments
Hub-and-Spoke (Interface Engine)
All systems connect only to the central hub
Scales linearly — n connections for n systems
Centralized routing, transformation, and error management
Single place to apply business rules, policies, and fixes
Changes managed at the hub — spokes are shielded
Standard for mid-to-large health systems
Point-to-Point vs Hub-and-Spoke Integration
Modern API-Based and Event-Driven Architecture
The rise of FHIR has enabled a third architectural paradigm: API-based integration, where systems expose standardized endpoints rather than sending messages through a central engine. In a FHIR-native architecture, a lab system publishes Observation resources via a FHIR API; an EHR subscribes to those resources and displays them in the clinical workflow; a patient app pulls the same data via SMART on FHIR. No custom interface engine is required for simple read queries — the API is the interface.
For more complex workflows — particularly those requiring asynchronous processing, guaranteed delivery, and high throughput — modern healthcare architectures layer event-driven infrastructure on top of FHIR APIs. Message brokers like Apache Kafka and RabbitMQ decouple producers from consumers: a patient admission event is published to a Kafka topic and consumed by multiple downstream systems (care management, analytics, scheduling) independently. Cloud-native platforms — AWS HealthLake, Azure Health Data Services, Google Cloud Healthcare API — provide managed FHIR servers with built-in scalability, security, and compliance.
In practice, most health systems today operate hybrid architectures. HL7 v2 over TCP/IP (MLLP protocol) continues to handle high-volume real-time hospital transactions — ADT feeds, lab results, radiology orders — because these workflows are stable, well-tested, and running on existing infrastructure. FHIR APIs layer on top to enable patient-facing applications, payer data exchange, quality reporting, and third-party app integration via SMART on FHIR. The interface engine (Rhapsody, Mirth, etc.) bridges the two worlds, translating v2 messages into FHIR resources when needed.
ADT, ORM, ORU messages flow between hospital systems via interface engine over MLLP (Minimal Lower Layer Protocol) — reliable, real-time, and battle-tested
Legacy Transactions (HL7 v2 / MLLP)
Central engine (Rhapsody, Mirth/BridgeLink, Corepoint) receives, transforms, routes, and delivers messages; bridges v2 and FHIR worlds; handles error management and audit logging
Interface Engine / Integration Hub
Canonical FHIR data store (AWS HealthLake, Azure Health Data Services, HAPI FHIR) exposes standardized REST APIs; populated from interface engine transformations and directly from EHR FHIR APIs
FHIR Server
Decouples high-volume asynchronous events (admissions, discharges, result notifications) from downstream consumers; enables real-time population health, alerts, and analytics
Event Broker (Kafka / RabbitMQ)
Authenticates and authorizes third-party apps and patient portals via OAuth 2.0 / SMART; controls access to FHIR resources with fine-grained clinical scopes
API Gateway / SMART on FHIR
Modern Healthcare Integration Stack
Point-to-point integration is like every house in a neighborhood having a private telephone line to every other house — fine for 5 houses, impossible for 500. The interface engine is the telephone exchange — every house has one line to the central switch, which routes calls. FHIR APIs are the internet — instead of calling, you look up a website at a known address, and anyone with a browser and the right credentials can connect.
Healthcare Integration Architecture Evolution
Building a Reliable Integration: Key Principles
Regardless of the architecture pattern chosen, successful healthcare integration depends on a set of engineering principles that apply across approaches. The first is guaranteed message delivery: in healthcare, a message that is dropped — a lab result, a medication order, an ADT — can cause patient harm. Interface engines must implement acknowledgment (ACK/NAK) protocols, retry queues, and dead-letter handling so no message is silently lost.
The second principle is idempotency: the same message delivered twice should not create duplicate records in the destination system. Patient demographics sent twice should update, not create a second patient. Lab results retransmitted after a failure should not create duplicate result entries in the EHR. Designing integrations to handle duplicates gracefully requires either deduplication logic at the interface engine or at the receiving system — ideally both.
The third principle is observability: every message that enters and leaves the integration layer should be logged with enough metadata — sender, recipient, message type, patient ID, timestamp, status — to reconstruct what happened during a clinical incident. When a physician says "the lab result never arrived," the integration team needs to be able to trace the message's journey in minutes, not hours. Comprehensive audit logging is not optional in healthcare IT — it is a regulatory requirement under HIPAA and a patient safety imperative.
The three non-negotiable principles of healthcare integration engineering: (1) Guaranteed delivery — no message silently lost; (2) Idempotency — duplicate messages don't create duplicate records; (3) Observability — every message traceable from source to destination. Systems that violate any of these principles will eventually cause a patient safety event or a compliance failure.
CommonWell Health Alliance is a not-for-profit trade association of health IT companies that built a national patient identity and record-locator infrastructure on top of member EHR systems. Rather than centralizing clinical data, CommonWell uses a federated record-locator model: member organizations enroll patients and register their record locations; when a clinician requests a patient's records, CommonWell queries the network and returns document links from all participating sites. As of 2024, CommonWell's network connects thousands of sites across the US, enabling cross-organizational patient record access without requiring a central data repository. This real-world deployment illustrates how large-scale healthcare integration can be achieved through federated architecture and common governance standards rather than a single monolithic hub.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-ffs-vs-vbc | Fee-for-Service vs Value-Based Care
Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Care
Two Philosophies of Payment
For most of the twentieth century, fee-for-service was the unchallenged foundation of American healthcare finance. Hospitals billed for admissions, physicians billed for office visits, and laboratories billed for every test they ran. The logic was straightforward: you perform a service, you get paid for it. As healthcare grew in complexity and cost, however, that logic began to reveal a profound structural flaw. The United States now spends approximately 18 percent of its gross domestic product on healthcare — more than any other high-income nation — yet ranks well below peers on life expectancy, avoidable mortality, and access to primary care. The spending and the outcomes were moving in opposite directions, and the payment system was at least partly responsible.
The volume-to-value shift began in earnest with the Affordable Care Act of 2010, which created the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) and charged it with testing alternative payment models at scale. The underlying premise was that if you change what you pay for, you change what providers do. Instead of rewarding every procedure and encounter, value-based models reward providers for keeping patients healthy, reducing unnecessary hospitalizations, and coordinating care across settings. Changing the payment architecture, in other words, was seen as the most reliable lever for changing clinical behavior.
The stakes could not be higher. Medicare and Medicaid together cover more than 160 million Americans and account for the largest single share of national health expenditure. How CMS structures its payment models shapes what every hospital, physician practice, and post-acute facility does in practice. Understanding the difference between fee-for-service and value-based care — not just in theory but in operational detail — is essential for anyone working in health informatics, policy, or administration.
Fee-for-Service (FFS): A payment model in which providers receive a separate reimbursement for each individual service, procedure, or encounter they deliver. Payment rates are set prospectively (e.g., via Medicare's physician fee schedule or DRG-based inpatient rates) and are independent of whether the service improves the patient's health. The incentive is to deliver more services, not better outcomes.
Studies estimate that up to 30% of FFS healthcare spending may be attributable to unnecessary or low-value services

How Fee-for-Service Works — and Why It Creates Problems
In a fee-for-service system, every billable interaction has a code. Physicians use Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) codes to document what they did; hospitals use Diagnosis-Related Groups (DRGs) for inpatient stays and Ambulatory Payment Classifications (APCs) for outpatient services. Each code maps to a payment rate set by a prospective payment system. Medicare's physician fee schedule converts CPT codes into relative value units (RVUs) — composite measures of physician work, practice expense, and malpractice cost — then multiplies by a conversion factor to produce a dollar amount. More RVUs mean more revenue; no RVUs mean no revenue. Prevention, care coordination, and phone calls that keep patients out of the hospital generate few or no billable events under traditional FFS.
The perverse incentive chain that FFS creates is well documented. A cardiologist who orders an echocardiogram generates revenue; a primary care physician who spends forty minutes counseling a diabetic patient on lifestyle changes may barely cover overhead. Surgical specialties that perform high-RVU procedures are systematically better compensated than primary and preventive care, which contributes to specialist shortages in rural areas and underinvestment in chronic disease management. Studies suggest that up to 30 percent of FFS spending may be attributable to low-value or unnecessary services — imaging ordered out of habit, procedures performed on patients unlikely to benefit, hospitalizations that could have been avoided with better outpatient management.
Fragmentation is FFS's other structural legacy. Because each provider bills independently, specialists and primary care physicians have little financial incentive to communicate or coordinate. A patient with heart failure, diabetes, and chronic kidney disease may see five separate specialists who each optimize for their own domain without a unified treatment plan. Hospital readmissions — often preventable with proper discharge planning and follow-up — generate additional admissions revenue under FFS rather than creating a financial penalty. This architecture does not fail by accident; it produces exactly the behaviors the payment system rewards.
Fee-for-service is like paying a mechanic by the part they replace, not by whether the car runs — the incentive is to find more parts to replace, not to fix the root problem.
FFS payment incentivizes volume of services rather than patient outcomes, just as paying per repair part incentivizes more replacements rather than a well-functioning vehicle.
Under FFS, a provider who avoids an unnecessary hospitalization actually loses revenue. The system penalizes prevention and efficiency because neither generates a billable event. A well-coordinated care team that keeps a high-risk patient out of the emergency department is financially punished relative to one that admits the same patient for observation.

Fee-for-Service vs. Value-Based Care
The Value-Based Care Spectrum
Value-based care is not a single payment model — it is a spectrum ranging from modest quality bonuses layered on top of FFS to full capitation in which providers receive a fixed monthly payment per patient regardless of how many services they deliver. The common thread is that provider payment is linked, in some way, to quality metrics, outcome measures, or total cost of care benchmarks. The degree of financial risk the provider accepts varies dramatically across the spectrum, and that risk level largely determines how strongly the model changes provider behavior.
Pay-for-performance (P4P) sits at the low-risk end. Providers continue to receive FFS base payments but earn small bonuses — or face small penalties — based on performance on quality metrics such as HbA1c control rates, cancer screening adherence, or patient experience scores. Because the adjustments are typically small relative to total revenue, P4P alone has a limited effect on clinical practice. Shared savings models, like Medicare ACOs, occupy the middle of the spectrum: providers take responsibility for a defined population and share in any savings achieved versus a spending benchmark, with more advanced tracks adding downside risk. Full capitation — common in staff-model HMOs and some Medicaid managed care contracts — places the full utilization risk on the provider organization, creating the strongest incentive to invest in prevention and care management.
CMS has structured its Alternative Payment Model (APM) framework to encourage providers to move along the spectrum toward greater accountability. The Quality Payment Program designates certain two-sided risk models as Advanced APMs; clinicians who meet participation thresholds in Advanced APMs earned a 5 percent incentive bonus for payment years 2019 through 2024 (reduced to 3.5 percent for 2025 and 1.88 percent for 2026) and are exempt from the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) reporting requirements. By 2026, a record 82.8 percent of MSSP ACOs were in Advanced APM tracks — evidence that the financial incentives are working to push providers toward greater risk-sharing.
Small bonuses or penalties based on quality metrics; provider still paid FFS base rate; lowest risk transfer. Common examples include MIPS quality performance adjustments and commercial insurer quality withholds.
Pay-for-Performance (P4P)
Provider takes on a defined population; if total spending comes in below the benchmark, the ACO earns a share of savings. In upside-only tracks, providers face no penalty for spending above benchmark — moderate, one-sided risk.
Shared Savings (ACOs)
Provider earns a share of savings AND owes a share of losses versus benchmark. Stronger accountability than upside-only; qualifies as an Advanced APM under the Quality Payment Program, unlocking the APM incentive bonus.
Shared Risk / Two-Sided
A single payment covers all services related to a defined clinical episode — for example, a joint replacement plus 90 days of post-operative care. The provider keeps any amount spent below the target price and owes the difference if spending exceeds it.
Bundled / Episode Payments
Fixed per-member-per-month (PMPM) payment per patient regardless of services delivered. Provider bears full utilization risk and has the strongest incentive to invest in prevention, care management, and efficient resource use. Maximum accountability.
Full Capitation
The VBC Payment Model Spectrum
The Medicare Shared Savings Program: ACOs in Action
The Medicare Shared Savings Program (MSSP), launched in 2012 under the Affordable Care Act, is the largest value-based care program in the United States by beneficiary count. MSSP allows groups of physicians, hospitals, and other providers to form Accountable Care Organizations (ACOs) and accept accountability for the total cost and quality of care for an attributed population of Traditional Medicare beneficiaries. Attribution is largely based on primary care utilization: beneficiaries are assigned to the ACO whose primary care clinicians they see most frequently. The ACO is then measured against a benchmark — an estimate of what CMS would have spent on that population absent the ACO — and earns or owes a share of the difference.
The financial mechanics of MSSP are designed to balance risk and reward. ACOs in upside-only tracks (BASIC Level A/B) can earn up to 40–50 percent of savings above the minimum savings rate but owe nothing if they spend above benchmark. ACOs in two-sided tracks (BASIC Level E and ENHANCED) earn a higher savings share — up to 75 percent — but also owe a portion of losses. Benchmarks are updated annually and incorporate regional spending trends to prevent ACOs in low-cost markets from being penalized for historical efficiency. Quality performance gates apply: ACOs must meet minimum quality standards to receive shared savings, and quality scores affect the savings rate they earn.
Performance year 2024 produced the most compelling evidence yet that MSSP works at scale. With 476 ACOs caring for approximately 10.3 million Traditional Medicare beneficiaries, the program generated $4.1 billion in shared savings for participating ACOs and $2.5 billion in savings for Medicare — the highest figures since program inception in 2012. Seventy-five percent of ACOs earned performance payments, and only 16 ACOs owed shared losses totaling $20.0 million. The results suggest that the MSSP model, particularly as ACOs mature and move into two-sided risk, is delivering meaningful reductions in total cost of care while maintaining or improving quality.
In 2024, MSSP ACOs earned $4.1 billion in shared savings while Medicare saved $2.5 billion — the best results since the program launched in 2012.
476 ACOs cared for approximately 10.3 million Traditional Medicare beneficiaries. 75% of ACOs earned performance payments, while only 16 ACOs owed shared losses ($20.0 million total). CMS reported this as the highest shared savings earned and Medicare savings achieved since inception. The program is credited with driving care coordination improvements, chronic disease management, and reduced unnecessary hospitalizations.
(Source: CMS PY2024 SSP Financial & Quality Results Fact Sheet)

Hospital Value-Based Programs: VBP, HRRP, and HACRP
CMS applies value-based care logic to hospitals through three interlocking payment adjustment programs that together create significant financial stakes for quality performance. Unlike voluntary ACO participation, these hospital programs are mandatory for most Medicare-participating acute care hospitals. They operate by modifying the DRG-based inpatient prospective payment that hospitals would otherwise receive — rewarding strong performers and penalizing hospitals with poor quality metrics, high readmission rates, or elevated rates of hospital-acquired conditions.
The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP), launched in fiscal year 2013, has been particularly influential in reshaping hospital behavior around care transitions. By penalizing excess 30-day readmission rates for six specific conditions — acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, pneumonia, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, elective hip and knee replacement, and coronary artery bypass graft surgery — HRRP created a direct financial incentive to invest in discharge planning, medication reconciliation, post-acute follow-up, and community-based transitional care programs. Hospitals that previously regarded readmissions as additional revenue now face up to a 3 percent penalty on all Medicare inpatient discharges, not just those related to the penalized conditions.
The combined effect of these three programs is to create a multi-domain quality accountability framework for hospitals. VBP evaluates safety, clinical outcomes, efficiency (Medicare spending per beneficiary), and patient experience; HRRP focuses on post-discharge outcomes for high-risk conditions; HACRP targets patient safety events during the hospital stay itself. Together, they represent CMS's attempt to make hospital payment sensitive to the full arc of a patient's care — from admission through recovery — rather than rewarding the volume of services delivered during the inpatient episode alone.
CMS withholds 2% of Medicare payments from all participating hospitals and redistributes based on quality performance across four domains: safety, clinical outcomes, efficiency (Medicare spending per beneficiary), and patient experience (HCAHPS). Hospitals scoring above average receive more than the 2% withheld; hospitals scoring below average receive less, resulting in a net payment reduction.
Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP)
Launched FY 2013; penalizes hospitals with excess 30-day readmission rates for six conditions: AMI, CHF, pneumonia, COPD, hip/knee replacement, and CABG. The penalty — up to a 3% reduction on all Medicare inpatient discharges — applies hospital-wide, not just to readmission-related claims, creating a strong incentive to invest in care transition programs.
Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program (HRRP)
Bottom-quartile hospitals on hospital-acquired condition (HAC) measures receive a 1% payment reduction on all Medicare discharges. HAC measures include central line-associated bloodstream infections, catheter-associated urinary tract infections, surgical site infections, and patient safety indicators. Creates incentive to invest in infection control, falls prevention, and patient safety protocols.
Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program (HACRP)
CMS Hospital Quality Payment Programs
The term "value-based care" covers everything from tiny quality bonuses to full capitation. A small P4P adjustment does not meaningfully change provider incentives; only two-sided risk models where providers can owe money back reliably drive behavior change at scale. Policymakers and analysts should distinguish carefully between programs that modestly adjust FFS payments and those that fundamentally restructure financial accountability for total cost of care.
Not All VBC Is Created Equal
The Road Ahead: Challenges and Progress
Despite more than a decade of VBC expansion, significant barriers remain. Attribution methodology — determining which patients are accountable to which provider — remains contested and can produce misalignment between clinical relationships and financial accountability. Small and independent practices often lack the data infrastructure, care management staffing, and actuarial expertise needed to participate meaningfully in risk-bearing arrangements. Rural providers face population sizes too small to generate statistically stable quality or cost measurements. And the transition from FFS to VBC requires providers to invest upfront in care coordination infrastructure before the downstream savings materialize — a cash flow challenge that has slowed adoption among safety-net and critical access hospitals.
CMS's stated goal is to have all Medicare beneficiaries in an accountable care relationship by 2030, with a parallel goal of moving all Medicaid beneficiaries into value-based arrangements through state partnerships. In 2024, only 44.9% of US health care payments flowed through alternative payment models in HCP-LAN Categories 3 and 4 (28.5% with downside risk), and the pace of transition has been uneven across specialties and geographies. The record MSSP results in 2024 — and the milestone of 82.8 percent of MSSP ACOs in Advanced APM tracks by 2026 — suggest the trajectory is positive, but reaching the 2030 goal will require sustained policy commitment, technical assistance for smaller providers, and continued refinement of benchmark-setting methodologies to ensure that efficiency gains are genuinely rewarded rather than competed away in future benchmark resets.
"The fee-for-service system rewards doing more, not doing better. The transition to value-based care is fundamentally about realigning financial incentives with patient health."

Fee-for-service reimburses providers per service rendered, creating a structural incentive for volume over value — studies suggest up to 30% of FFS spending may be low-value or unnecessary.
Value-based care realigns financial incentives by tying provider payment to quality, outcomes, and total cost of care rather than the count of services delivered.
The VBC spectrum ranges from pay-for-performance (minimal risk transfer) through shared savings ACOs and bundled payments to full capitation (maximum provider risk).
The Medicare Shared Savings Program reached record performance in 2024: 476 ACOs, 10.3 million beneficiaries, $4.1 billion in ACO earned savings, and $2.5 billion in Medicare savings.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-high-low-value-care | High-Value vs Low-Value Care
High-Value and Low-Value Care
Defining Value in Healthcare
What does "value" mean in healthcare? The simplest formulation — popularized by Harvard's Michael Porter — is Value = Outcomes / Cost. High-value care delivers meaningful, evidence-based clinical benefit relative to its cost and risk to the patient. Low-value care is the inverse: interventions where cost or risk exceeds the likely benefit. But value is not just about money — it is about whether care actually improves or risks patient health.
The scale of low-value care in the United States is staggering. The Institute of Medicine's landmark 2012 report "Best Care at Lower Cost" estimated that approximately 30% of US health spending in 2009 — roughly $750 billion — was wasted. That waste included unnecessary services, excessive administrative costs, fraud, and inflated prices. More recent estimates place annual spending on low-value care at $100 billion to $700 billion depending on what is counted. Up to 40% of Medicare beneficiaries receive at least one low-value service per year.
The consequences are not just financial. Unnecessary services expose patients to real harm — radiation from imaging, surgical complications, drug side effects, healthcare-associated infections, and the cascade of follow-up tests triggered by false-positive results. A healthcare system that provides more care than is needed is not just wasteful; it is actively dangerous.
High-value care = meaningful clinical benefit relative to cost and risk. Low-value care = interventions where cost or harm exceeds likely benefit. The goal is not to spend less — it is to spend on care that works.

What Makes Care Low Value?
Low-value care is not always obvious. It ranges from blatantly wasteful services — antibiotics for viral infections, routine pre-operative testing before low-risk surgery — to subtler overuse driven by habit, anxiety, or financial incentive. JAMA research estimated that $12.8 to $28.6 billion could be saved annually by targeting the most common low-value services alone.
The IOM identified six categories of healthcare waste: unnecessary services (overuse beyond evidence), inefficiently delivered services (care that could be done better or cheaper), excess administrative complexity, inflated prices, missed prevention opportunities, and fraud and abuse. Unnecessary services — the clinical waste category — is the most directly actionable through clinical behavior change, but it is also the hardest to reduce because it requires changing the habits of individual providers.
A concrete example: more than 200,000 unnecessary back surgeries took place over a three-year period, costing Medicare more than $1.9 billion, according to the Lown Institute. The evidence shows that most patients with chronic low back pain do better with physical therapy and conservative management than with surgery — yet the financial incentive for surgery, combined with patient expectations, drives continued overuse. Imaging without clear clinical indication, routine urine cultures in asymptomatic patients, and repeat imaging for stable findings are other common offenders documented in Choosing Wisely recommendations.

Annual flu vaccination in eligible patients
Low-Value vs. High-Value Care Examples
The instinct to 'do something' is understandable in both clinicians and patients. But evidence consistently shows that in many situations, watchful waiting, lifestyle modification, or conservative management produces outcomes equivalent — or superior — to aggressive intervention, at far lower risk and cost. The most courageous clinical decision is sometimes to not order the test.
More Care Is Not Always Better Care
Choosing Wisely: A National De-Implementation Campaign
In 2012, the ABIM Foundation and Consumer Reports launched the Choosing Wisely campaign — the highest-profile national effort to reduce low-value care through clinical engagement rather than regulatory mandate. The campaign launched with nine specialty societies offering 45 recommendations about tests and treatments that clinicians and patients should question. By 2023, more than 80 specialty societies had joined, producing over 700 recommendations spanning imaging, laboratory testing, medications, and procedures. The campaign has since spread to more than 25 countries.
Each Choosing Wisely recommendation is generated by a specialty society based on evidence that a particular service is frequently ordered, has significant cost or risk, and is often not necessary given current clinical evidence. Examples include: don't order routine imaging for uncomplicated low back pain; don't prescribe antibiotics for non-specific upper respiratory infections; don't perform routine pre-operative tests for low-risk procedures. Importantly, the recommendations are framed as starting points for conversation — not prohibitions.
The evidence on Choosing Wisely's impact is mixed but instructive. Active interventions — clinical decision support alerts, audit and feedback, educational outreach, leadership engagement — reduced overuse in 65% of studies. Simply disseminating the recommendations without an active change strategy produced reductions in only 13% of studies. The lesson: awareness alone does not change behavior. Sustained de-implementation requires targeted strategies matched to the local barriers driving the overuse.
Antibiotic prescribing for acute respiratory infections is one of the most documented cases of low-value care. A CDC-led study (Fleming-Dutra et al., JAMA, 2016) estimated that at least 30% of US outpatient antibiotic prescriptions — and about half of those written for acute respiratory conditions — are unnecessary — contributing to antimicrobial resistance and patient harm from side effects. Choosing Wisely lists from the AAFP and other specialty societies recommend against prescribing antibiotics for viral pharyngitis, bronchitis, and sinusitis without bacterial confirmation. Active strategies tied to these recommendations — clinical decision support prompts, peer comparison, and audit and feedback — are what move prescribing; dissemination alone rarely does. (Sources: Fleming-Dutra et al., JAMA, 2016; ABIM Foundation / Choosing Wisely)
Choosing Wisely — Antibiotic Overprescription
Barriers to Reducing Low-Value Care
Knowing that a service is low-value does not automatically stop it from being ordered. Research on barriers to de-implementation consistently identifies a cluster of factors that make it difficult for clinicians — even those who understand the evidence — to stop providing unnecessary care.
Patient expectations and requests are the most commonly cited barrier: 85% of primary care physicians in a multinational survey identified patient expectations as a challenge, and 83% cited direct patient requests for tests or treatments. Clinicians also fear medical error (81%) — the anxiety that the one patient they do not image or test will be the one who has something serious. Time pressure (81%) and fear of under-diagnosis (79%) round out the top barriers. These are not irrational fears; they reflect the asymmetry of accountability in medicine, where doing too much is rarely penalized and doing too little can result in lawsuits.
System-level factors compound individual barriers. Fee-for-service payment rewards volume — ordering more generates more revenue, even when the additional care provides no benefit. Fragmented care means that multiple providers order overlapping tests without visibility into what has already been done. Electronic health records that make ordering easy but provide no feedback on cumulative cost or redundancy also contribute to overuse.
Embed evidence-based Choosing Wisely recommendations as soft stops or hard stops in the EHR order entry workflow; alert clinicians when ordering a potentially low-value service and prompt documentation of clinical justification.
Clinical Decision Support (CDS) Alerts
Regularly share individual and team-level data on low-value service rates compared to peers; social comparison ('you order imaging for back pain more than 80% of your colleagues') is a powerful behavioral lever.
Audit and Feedback
Engage patients in evidence-based conversations about the likely benefit and harm of a proposed service; patients who understand low pretest probability often choose watchful waiting over testing.
Shared Decision Making
Stop paying for services designated as low-value; CMS and commercial payers have begun excluding certain services from coverage when ordered outside of evidence-based indications.
Payment Reform
Require prior authorization for high-cost imaging, procedures, or medications with documented overuse; use peer-to-peer review for outlier prescribers.
Preauthorization and Peer Review
Strategies to Reduce Low-Value Care
High-Value Care in Practice
High-value care is not simply cheap care — it is care that delivers the right outcome for the right patient at the right time, with evidence supporting both the clinical benefit and the cost-effectiveness. Many of the highest-value interventions in medicine are also among the least expensive: blood pressure control, cholesterol management, colorectal cancer screening, smoking cessation, and vaccination. These interventions prevent enormous amounts of downstream disease, hospitalization, and premature death.
The CMS Million Hearts Cardiovascular Disease Risk Reduction Model demonstrated this principle at scale. The model paid providers to systematically measure patients' cardiovascular risk using a validated tool, and to intensify treatment for high- and medium-risk beneficiaries. The result was reduced first-time heart attacks and strokes — without increasing total care costs. The program exemplifies value-based care logic: invest in evidence-based prevention upstream to avoid expensive acute events downstream.
High-value care is like maintaining a car on schedule — oil changes, tire rotations, brake checks. It seems like spending money on something that isn't broken. But it prevents the catastrophic breakdown that costs ten times more and strands you on the highway. Low-value care is like buying expensive fuel additives based on a TV commercial — you spend real money for no proven benefit, and you might damage the engine.
High-Value vs. Low-Value Care Logic
The highest-value interventions in American medicine — controlling blood pressure, managing diabetes, screening for cancer, vaccinating against flu and pneumonia — are also among the most underprovided. The US simultaneously over-provides low-value services and under-provides high-value ones, producing the worst of both worlds: excess cost and avoidable harm.
High-value care delivers meaningful clinical benefit relative to its cost and risk; low-value care is care where cost or harm to the patient exceeds likely benefit.
The IOM estimated roughly $750 billion — about 30% of US health spending in 2009 — was waste, with unnecessary services being the most directly reducible category.
Up to 40% of Medicare beneficiaries receive at least one low-value service per year; annual low-value spending estimates range from $100 billion to $700 billion.
The Choosing Wisely campaign, launched by the ABIM Foundation in 2012, produced more than 700 specialty society recommendations on overused services; active interventions based on those recommendations reduced overuse 65% of the time.
The top barriers to de-implementing low-value care are patient expectations (85%), patient requests (83%), fear of medical error (81%), and time pressure (81%) — requiring both cultural and structural change, not just education.
Effective de-implementation strategies include clinical decision support alerts, audit and feedback, shared decision making, payment reform, and prior authorization — and work best in combination.
The US simultaneously over-provides low-value care and under-provides high-value preventive care — indicating that the solution is not simply spending less, but spending on what works.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-clinical-quality-measures | Clinical Quality Measures
Clinical Quality Measures in Healthcare
Why Quality Measurement Matters
Healthcare quality in the United States has long been characterized by profound variation. The Institute of Medicine's landmark 2001 report "Crossing the Quality Chasm" catalogued the gap between the care Americans receive and the care they should receive, organizing the challenge around six dimensions: care should be safe, effective, patient-centered, timely, efficient, and equitable. Two decades later those six aims remain the organizing principle behind virtually every major quality measurement program in the country — including those run by CMS, NCQA, and The Joint Commission. The persistent variability in clinical outcomes across hospitals, health plans, and geographic regions is both the problem quality measurement was designed to expose and the reason it continues to expand.
Measurement is the prerequisite for improvement. A health system cannot reliably close a gap it cannot see. Quality measures translate abstract aims — "be safer," "be more equitable" — into specific, reportable rates that clinicians, administrators, payers, and policymakers can act on. A 30-day readmission rate tells a hospital CEO that something is breaking down in care transitions. A low rate of A1C testing in diabetic patients tells a health plan that its network may not be providing guideline-concordant care. Without these concrete signals, improvement efforts are speculative rather than targeted. Quality measurement converts clinical ambition into operational data.
The stakes are no longer purely clinical — they are financial. Federal payment programs now link reimbursement directly to measured quality performance. The Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) adjusts Medicare payments to individual clinicians based partly on how well they score on quality measures. Hospital Value-Based Purchasing ties a portion of inpatient reimbursement to performance on clinical, safety, and patient experience measures. The Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program penalizes facilities with excess readmission rates. As the healthcare system shifts from volume to value, the ability to measure, report, and improve on quality measures has become a core business competency for every provider organization.
CMS defines quality measures as "tools that help measure or quantify healthcare processes, outcomes, patient perceptions, and organizational structure and/or systems that are associated with the ability to provide high-quality health care and/or that relate to one or more quality goals for health care — effective, safe, efficient, patient-centered, equitable, and timely care."

The Donabedian Framework: Structure, Process, Outcome
In 1966, Avedis Donabedian published "Evaluating the Quality of Medical Care" in the Milbank Memorial Fund Quarterly — now considered one of the most cited articles in public health history. Donabedian proposed that quality could be assessed through three interconnected lenses: the structure in which care is delivered, the processes of care that occur, and the outcomes that result. His framework gave healthcare a vocabulary for measurement that had previously been missing, and it remains the conceptual backbone of virtually every quality program in use today, more than fifty years after its publication.
Structure refers to the context in which care is delivered: the physical facilities, the equipment available, the qualifications and number of staff, how financing is organized, and whether the organization uses an electronic health record. Structure measures are often the easiest to collect but the least directly tied to patient outcomes. Process measures capture the transactions between patients and providers — whether a diabetic patient had their hemoglobin A1C tested, whether a patient with hypertension was prescribed an ACE inhibitor, whether a smoker received cessation counseling. Because they describe actions that clinicians take (or fail to take), process measures are highly actionable. Outcome measures capture the ultimate effects on health: 30-day readmission rates, in-hospital mortality, hospital-acquired infections, patient satisfaction scores.
Donabedian's framework implies a causal chain: better structure enables better processes, and better processes produce better outcomes. That logic underpins all modern quality improvement programs. But the chain has real limits. Structure does not guarantee good process — a well-equipped hospital can still deliver inconsistent care. Process does not guarantee good outcomes — sometimes the right care is delivered and the patient still deteriorates due to disease complexity. And outcomes are influenced by factors entirely outside the health system, including socioeconomic conditions and patient behavior. This is why high-quality measurement programs typically balance all three dimensions rather than relying on outcomes alone.
Think of structure as a kitchen, process as the recipe followed, and outcome as the dish that arrives — you need all three to understand why a meal was good or bad.
The Donabedian framework: structure + process + outcome each explain a different layer of quality.

Three Donabedian Measure Types
HEDIS: The Health Plan Quality Standard
The Healthcare Effectiveness Data and Information Set — universally known as HEDIS — is maintained by the National Committee for Quality Assurance (NCQA) and is the most widely used health plan quality tool in the United States. Health plans use HEDIS to measure performance across dozens of clinical domains including preventive care, chronic disease management, behavioral health, and maternal health. Results are used for NCQA accreditation, public reporting through Quality Compass, and value-based contracting with employers, Medicaid agencies, and Medicare Advantage sponsors. As of the MY2023/2024 ratings cycle, approximately 227 million Americans are enrolled in health plans that report HEDIS results to NCQA — a scale that makes it unlike any other quality dataset in American healthcare.
HEDIS data is collected through three methods depending on the measure. Administrative data — claims and encounter records — is the most efficient source and sufficient for many measures. Supplemental data allows plans to incorporate information from provider EHRs and labs that does not appear in claims. The hybrid method combines administrative data with targeted medical record review for a random sample of eligible members, providing higher accuracy for measures where claims alone are insufficient. The MY 2024 State of Health Care Quality Report includes national averages for 90 quality measures covering clinical care and patient satisfaction, giving plans, purchasers, and regulators a comprehensive national benchmark.
NCQA's 2024 Health Plan Ratings are calculated as a weighted average of HEDIS clinical quality scores and CAHPS patient experience scores, plus bonus points for accreditation status. Plans use these ratings for marketing differentiation, member retention, and to satisfy contractual requirements from large employers and government programs. For Medicaid managed care plans and Medicare Advantage organizations, HEDIS performance can directly affect premium revenue through quality bonus payments, creating powerful financial incentives to invest in the care gaps HEDIS measures reveal. Vermont's Medicaid managed care and ACO programs rely on HEDIS as a core performance framework for their quality improvement portfolios.
227 million Americans are in plans that report HEDIS — making it the most widely used healthcare quality tool in the country.

How HEDIS Measurement Works
Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs)
Electronic Clinical Quality Measures (eCQMs) represent a fundamental shift in how quality data is collected. Traditional clinical quality measures (CQMs) required manual abstraction — a trained person reviewing paper charts or PDF-based records to find the information needed to calculate a rate. That process was expensive, slow, and prone to inter-rater variability. eCQMs are specified in a standard electronic format, with logic written using Health Quality Measure Format (HQMF) and expressed against standard clinical terminologies — SNOMED CT for clinical findings, LOINC for laboratory and clinical observations, ICD-10 for diagnoses, and RxNorm for medications. Data is extracted automatically from EHR systems, eliminating manual review for the bulk of reporting.
CMS uses eCQMs across multiple programs: the Medicaid Promoting Interoperability Program, the Medicare Promoting Interoperability Program (formerly Meaningful Use), the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS), and Alternative Payment Models (APMs). A critical operational advantage of eCQMs is coverage: because they run against structured EHR data for all applicable patients, eCQMs automatically meet MIPS's 75% reporting frequency threshold — a requirement that is administratively burdensome when using traditional chart-abstracted measures. This near-complete patient coverage also makes eCQM rates more statistically reliable than sample-based results, giving CMS and providers a more accurate picture of actual performance.
The next evolution of eCQMs is FHIR-based quality reporting. The HL7 FHIR standard — the same infrastructure driving patient access APIs and interoperability mandates — is now being applied to quality reporting. FHIR-based quality measures (sometimes called "digital quality measures" or dQMs) use FHIR resources and Clinical Quality Language (CQL) to define measure logic that can execute against FHIR-compliant EHR data. This approach promises to reduce the gap between care delivery and quality reporting, enabling near real-time feedback and making it feasible to expand measurement into clinical domains that were previously too complex or costly to abstract manually.
eCQMs extract data directly from EHRs in a standard electronic format — eliminating the manual chart abstraction that traditional CQMs required, reducing both cost and human error.
eCQMs depend on the quality of documentation in the EHR. Missing or inaccurate clinical data (wrong diagnosis codes, missing problem list entries) will cause patients to be excluded from denominators or counted incorrectly, distorting the measure rate.
Administrative Data Alone Is Not Enough

How an eCQM Gets Calculated
CMS Quality Reporting Programs: MIPS, IQR, and VBP
The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services operates the largest portfolio of quality reporting programs in American healthcare. For individual clinicians, the Merit-based Incentive Payment System (MIPS) is the primary vehicle. MIPS consolidates quality, improvement activities, promoting interoperability, and cost into a composite score that adjusts each clinician's Medicare Part B payments upward or downward. In 2024, the Quality performance category accounts for 30% of the MIPS final score — the single largest component. CMS finalized an inventory of 200 quality measures for the 2024 MIPS performance period, excluding Qualified Clinical Data Registry (QCDR) measures. Clinicians must report on a minimum of 6 quality measures, including at least one outcome or high-priority measure.
For acute care hospitals, the Hospital Inpatient Quality Reporting (IQR) Program is the foundational reporting vehicle. IQR is a pay-for-reporting program: hospitals that do not successfully report face a reduction in their annual payment update. But IQR data also feeds directly into programs with more direct payment consequences. The Hospital Value-Based Purchasing (VBP) Program uses IQR-reported measures to calculate a Total Performance Score that can either increase or decrease inpatient Medicare payments. The Hospital-Acquired Condition Reduction Program (HACRP) uses safety and infection measures to identify the worst-performing hospitals, which receive a 1% payment reduction on all Medicare discharges. Together these programs create a layered financial accountability structure for hospital quality.
The movement toward value-based payment has fundamentally changed how provider organizations think about quality measurement. When quality scores were used only for public reporting, the financial consequences of poor performance were reputational. Now they are direct and material. A large hospital system subject to HRRP penalties, HACRP reductions, and VBP adjustments simultaneously can see millions of dollars in annual payment impact from quality performance. This has driven significant investment in quality improvement infrastructure — care management teams, data analytics platforms, population health systems, and transitional care programs — all justified in part by the financial return on improving measure performance.

Quality Measurement and Health Equity
Aggregate quality scores can obscure profound inequities hidden within the average. A health system may achieve a respectable overall 30-day readmission rate while Black or Hispanic patients at the same institution face rates two to three times higher. A health plan may report strong HEDIS scores on diabetes care while patients with limited English proficiency receive far lower rates of A1C testing and retinal exams. When quality measurement programs report only aggregate rates, they cannot detect — and therefore cannot address — these disparities. Stratifying quality measures by race, ethnicity, preferred language, and socioeconomic status is the methodological prerequisite for an equitable quality improvement agenda.
Both CMS and NCQA have made explicit commitments to embed equity stratification into their quality measurement frameworks. NCQA has developed HEDIS equity measures and is expanding stratified reporting requirements. CMS's Universal Foundation for quality measurement, launched as part of its National Quality Strategy, includes health equity as a core domain and is incorporating race and ethnicity stratification into MIPS and Medicaid reporting. The practical challenge is data: stratified quality reporting requires that EHRs and health plans collect accurate, complete, and standardized race, ethnicity, and language data — a requirement that remains inconsistently met across the industry. Health information exchanges like Vermont's VITL play a growing role in aggregating this data across provider organizations to enable population-level equity analysis.
A hospital may have an excellent average 30-day readmission rate while having much higher rates for Black or Hispanic patients. Without stratification by race, ethnicity, and language, quality reporting programs can inadvertently reward systems that perform well for well-resourced patients while ignoring gaps for vulnerable populations.
Aggregate Quality Scores Can Hide Disparities
CMS and NCQA have both committed to adding equity stratification to quality measures. The goal is to make disparate performance visible — because you cannot improve what you cannot measure.
The Donabedian framework (structure → process → outcome) is the conceptual foundation of all modern quality measurement, first articulated in Donabedian's landmark 1966 article.
HEDIS, maintained by NCQA, covers approximately 227 million Americans and is the dominant quality measurement tool for health plans, used for accreditation, public reporting, and value-based contracting.
eCQMs automate quality reporting by extracting data directly from EHRs using standard terminologies, eliminating manual chart abstraction and achieving near-complete patient coverage.
In MIPS 2024, the Quality category accounts for 30% of the final score; clinicians report on at least 6 measures including one outcome or high-priority measure from an inventory of 200 measures.
Hospital quality programs — IQR, VBP, HACRP, and HRRP — create a layered financial incentive structure that ties Medicare payment directly to measured clinical performance.
Aggregate quality scores can mask significant disparities by race, ethnicity, and language; stratified reporting is essential to an equitable quality improvement strategy.
FHIR-based digital quality measures represent the next evolution of eCQMs, enabling near real-time quality feedback using the same interoperability infrastructure as patient access APIs.
HEDIS is maintained by NCQA — the National Committee for Quality Assurance. CMS runs its own quality reporting programs (MIPS, IQR, VBP) but does not own or maintain HEDIS. ONC oversees health IT policy and certification. The Joint Commission accredits hospitals but does not maintain HEDIS.

Health Disparities and Social Determinants of Health
What Are Health Disparities and Why Do They Persist?
Health disparities are preventable differences in the burden of disease, injury, violence, or opportunities to achieve optimal health experienced by socially disadvantaged groups. These differences are not random — they follow predictable patterns tied to race, ethnicity, income, geography, language, and disability status. Where a person is born, how they grow up, where they work and live, and how they age shape their health in ways that dwarf the influence of clinical care.
The data make the pattern unmistakable. In 2023, Black Americans had a life expectancy of 74.0 years — 4.4 years less than White Americans (78.4) and 7.3 years less than Hispanic Americans (81.3). Black infants died at a rate of 10.9 per 1,000 live births in 2023, more than twice the White rate of 4.5. Black maternal mortality reached 50.3 deaths per 100,000 live births — 3.5 times the White rate of 14.5 — and the gap is not closing.
These gaps persist not because of biological differences between groups, but because of cumulative structural disadvantages: income, neighborhood, education, environmental exposure, and unequal treatment within the healthcare system itself. Understanding their root causes is the first step to closing them.
Health disparities are differences in health outcomes between groups that are avoidable, unnecessary, and unjust. Health equity is the state in which every person has a fair and just opportunity to attain their highest possible level of health — regardless of race, income, zip code, or language.
