The Five Domains of Social Determinants of Health
Social determinants of health are the conditions in which people are born, grow, work, live, and age — and the broader forces shaping those conditions: economic policies, social norms, political systems, and community infrastructure. The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services' Healthy People 2030 framework organizes SDOH into five domains that interact and reinforce one another.
Economic stability is the most studied domain: poverty limits access to nutritious food, safe housing, and preventive care — driving chronic disease rates up and life expectancy down. Education shapes health literacy, employment options, and earning potential throughout life. Neighborhood and built environment determines whether people have access to grocery stores, safe places to exercise, clean air and water, and transportation to healthcare appointments. Social and community context — including discrimination, incarceration, and social cohesion — affects mental health, stress physiology, and health behaviors.
Health care access and quality is the fifth domain — and while it is what most people think of when they think of healthcare disparities, it is only one of five. Expanding coverage and reducing clinical bias matters enormously, but it cannot alone close gaps rooted in poverty, housing instability, or neighborhood disinvestment.
Income, employment, food security, and housing stability. Poverty is a primary driver of poor health across all age groups and conditions.
Economic Stability
Early childhood education, high school graduation rates, higher education, and language/literacy. Education predicts lifetime income, health behaviors, and health literacy.
Education Access and Quality
Health insurance coverage, proximity to providers, cultural competency, and quality of care received. Uninsured and underinsured populations delay and forgo care.
Health Care Access and Quality
Housing quality, air and water quality, access to healthy food, neighborhood safety, and transportation. ZIP code is a stronger predictor of health than genetic code.
Neighborhood and Built Environment
Discrimination, incarceration, civic participation, social support networks, and community cohesion. Chronic stress from racism and discrimination has measurable physiological effects.
Social and Community Context
Healthy People 2030 — Five SDOH Domains
Think of the five SDOH domains as the soil in which health grows. Clinical care is like adding fertilizer — it helps, but if the soil is toxic (poverty, unsafe housing, polluted water), no amount of fertilizer will produce a healthy harvest. You have to fix the soil.
Social Determinants of Health as Upstream Drivers
Racial and Ethnic Disparities: The Evidence
Racial and ethnic health disparities in the United States are among the most well-documented and persistent in the developed world. They exist across nearly every health condition — cardiovascular disease, diabetes, cancer, mental health, and maternal and infant health — and they exist even after controlling for income and insurance status, pointing to systemic and structural factors including discrimination in care delivery.
Black maternal mortality illustrates the depth of the problem. In 2023, Black women died from pregnancy-related causes at a rate of 50.3 per 100,000 live births — compared to 14.5 for White women. This 3.5-fold disparity persists across income levels and education levels: Black women with college degrees experience higher maternal mortality than White women without them. Research consistently identifies delayed or inadequate care, implicit bias among providers, and preterm birth driven by chronic stress as key mechanisms.
The Hispanic paradox — whereby Hispanic Americans have lower mortality than White Americans despite lower average income and insurance coverage — illustrates that SDOH operate differently across groups. Strong family cohesion, lower smoking rates, and immigration selection effects partially explain this pattern. Understanding the paradox is important: it demonstrates that SDOH are not simply about income, and that protective factors in culture and community can buffer against adverse exposures.
In 2023, the CDC reported that Black women died from pregnancy-related causes at 50.3 per 100,000 live births — 3.5 times the White rate of 14.5. The gap did not improve between 2022 and 2023 despite overall U.S. maternal mortality declining. Studies find that even among college-educated Black women, maternal mortality exceeds that of White women without college degrees. Causes include implicit bias in pain management, later diagnosis of complications, higher rates of preeclampsia driven by chronic stress (weathering hypothesis), and systemic underinvestment in maternal care in majority-Black communities. (Source: CDC NCHS Maternal Mortality Report, February 2025)

SDOH and Health IT: Screening, Data, and Action
Addressing SDOH requires knowing where individual patients stand — which means screening for food insecurity, housing instability, transportation barriers, social isolation, and financial strain during clinical encounters. Organizations like NACHC, PRAPARE (Protocol for Responding to and Assessing Patients' Assets, Risks, and Experiences), and AHC (Accountable Health Communities) have developed validated SDOH screening tools now used across thousands of clinical sites.
The challenge is what happens after screening. Identifying that a patient lacks stable housing is only useful if there is a referral pathway to a housing resource — and a closed-loop system to confirm whether the referral was acted on. Community-based organizations, 211 resource networks, and social care platforms like Unite Us and findhelp are working to build those closed-loop connections between clinical and social care.
CMS has prioritized SDOH data collection at the system level. Beginning in January 2023, CMS started collecting optional race and ethnicity data from Medicare Advantage enrollment forms. HHS has also moved to collect race and ethnicity data from ACA marketplace issuers through their EDGE server submissions. The goal is to stratify quality measures by race, ethnicity, and language — making disparities visible in reporting programs so health plans and providers are accountable for closing them.
Use a validated tool (PRAPARE, AHC HRSN screener, or Gravity Project Z-codes) to identify social needs during a clinical encounter.
Screen
Record social needs using standardized ICD-10-CM Z-codes (e.g., Z59.0 homelessness, Z59.4 food insecurity) so data is structured and reportable.
Document
Connect patients to community resources via a social care network (211, Unite Us, findhelp, local CBOs) with a warm handoff or electronic referral.
Refer
Receive confirmation from the community organization that the referral was received and acted on — avoiding referrals that vanish.
Close the Loop
Aggregate SDOH data across the population to identify patterns, target interventions, and measure whether social needs are being resolved.

CMS Strategy and the Road to Equity
CMS has made health equity a formal pillar of its strategic plan. The CMS Framework for Health Equity (2022–2032) set five priorities: expanding the collection, reporting, and analysis of standardized data; assessing the causes of disparities within CMS programs and addressing inequities in policies and operations; building the capacity of health care organizations and the workforce to reduce disparities; advancing language access, health literacy, and culturally tailored services; and increasing all forms of accessibility to health care services and coverage.
In quality reporting, CMS is moving toward requiring stratification of HEDIS, MIPS, and other measures by race, ethnicity, and language — making it impossible for plans and providers to submit aggregate scores that mask disparities. The logic is simple: if a health plan serves 100,000 members and reports a 90% diabetes control rate, but the rate is 95% for White members and 75% for Black members, the aggregate score obscures a 20-percentage-point gap that requires action.
Collecting race, ethnicity, and language data is necessary but not sufficient. The goal is not better reporting — it is closing the gaps the data reveals. Systems that collect demographic data but do not analyze it by subgroup, do not set disparity-reduction targets, and do not hold leaders accountable are performing equity theater, not achieving health equity.
Data Without Action Is Not Equity
CMS's long-term vision: every quality measure stratified by race, ethnicity, language, and geography — so that health plans, hospitals, and clinicians are held accountable not just for average performance, but for equitable performance across every population they serve.
Health disparities are preventable differences in health outcomes tied to race, income, geography, and other social factors — not random variation or biological fate.
In 2023, Black Americans had a life expectancy 4.4 years shorter than White Americans, Black maternal mortality was 3.5 times higher than White maternal mortality, and Black infant mortality was more than twice the White rate.
Social determinants of health — economic stability, education, neighborhood, social context, and health care access — drive 80–90% of health outcomes, dwarfing the 10–20% contribution of clinical care.
Healthy People 2030 organizes SDOH into five domains; addressing health disparities requires upstream interventions in all five, not just expanding insurance coverage.
SDOH screening tools (PRAPARE, AHC HRSN, Gravity Project Z-codes) allow clinicians to identify social needs, but closed-loop referral systems are essential to translate screening into actual resource connection.
CMS began collecting standardized race and ethnicity data from Medicare Advantage enrollment forms in January 2023 and is moving toward stratifying all quality measures by demographic group to make disparities measurable and accountable.
Health equity requires moving beyond data collection to disparity-reduction targets, accountability mechanisms, and sustained investment in the communities most affected by structural disadvantage.
The CDC's February 2025 report on 2023 maternal mortality data found that Black women died at a rate of 50.3 per 100,000 live births compared to 14.5 for White women — making Black women approximately 3.5 times more likely to die from pregnancy-related causes. This gap persists even among college-educated Black women, pointing to structural and systemic factors beyond income or access.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-workforce-roles | HIE Workforce & Roles
Workforce Roles in Health Information Exchange
The Ecosystem of Healthcare Roles
Modern healthcare delivery is not the work of any single profession. It is the result of a vast, interdisciplinary workforce spanning clinical care, data management, information technology infrastructure, and administrative leadership. Health Information Exchange (HIE) sits at the intersection of all of these domains, and making it function well requires each workforce category to do its part with precision and accountability.
Think of the healthcare workforce as an ecosystem. Clinicians — physicians, nurses, advanced practice providers, pharmacists, and allied health professionals — are the primary generators of health data. Every patient encounter they document becomes structured information that can flow through HIE networks. Health Information Management (HIM) professionals serve as stewards of that data, ensuring it is accurate, complete, coded correctly, and protected under HIPAA. Health IT and informatics roles build and maintain the pipelines that move data between systems. Population health analysts and care coordinators then consume that aggregated data to manage patient populations across care settings. Remove any one of these groups and the entire exchange ecosystem degrades.
The American Health Information Management Association (AHIMA) — the primary professional body for HIM practitioners — reflects this breadth: its members work in hospitals, physician practices, payers, vendors, public health agencies, and consulting firms, under a wide range of job titles. The Bureau of Labor Statistics projects 16% employment growth for health information technologists and medical registrars from 2025 to 2035, with about 3,000 job openings projected each year. Medical and health services managers are growing even faster, with BLS projecting 24% growth over the same decade. These are not niche specialties — they are among the fastest-growing occupational categories in the entire U.S. economy.
The Four Workforce Pillars of HIE: (1) Clinical — physicians, nurses, APPs, pharmacists who generate the data; (2) Health Information Management — HIM administrators and coders who steward the data; (3) Health IT / Informatics — engineers, analysts, and executives who exchange the data; (4) Population Health & Analytics — coordinators and analysts who use the data to improve care and close gaps across patient populations.

Clinical Roles — The Data Generators
Clinical professionals are the origin point of every piece of health data that flows through an HIE. Physicians (MDs and DOs), nurse practitioners (NPs), physician assistants (PAs), registered nurses (RNs), pharmacists, and allied health professionals — including physical therapists, respiratory therapists, social workers, and laboratory technicians — collectively create the clinical documentation that HIE systems are built to exchange.
Documentation is not a secondary function of clinical work — it is a core professional responsibility with direct downstream consequences for data quality. Every encounter note a physician writes, every discharge summary a hospitalist completes, every medication reconciliation a pharmacist performs, and every nursing assessment an RN documents becomes structured or semi-structured data in an EHR. When that EHR is connected to an HIE, that data becomes accessible across the care continuum — but only if it was documented correctly, with the right codes, the right patient identifiers, and the right level of clinical specificity. Clinicians who understand HIE are clinicians who understand that their documentation choices ripple outward to affect care coordination, billing, quality measurement, and population health analytics.
The context of clinical workforce shortages makes this even more critical. The Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC) projects a shortage of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036 (a range of 13,500 to 86,000), including 20,200 to 40,400 primary care physicians. AAMC analysis also finds that about one in five active physicians is already 65 or older, and more than a third will be within the next decade. These shortages mean that every remaining clinician must operate more efficiently — and HIE, with its ability to pre-populate records, surface relevant history, and eliminate redundant testing, is one of the most powerful tools available for extending clinical capacity.

Provider Types and Their HIE Touchpoints
Clinicians are not passive data sources. In modern HIE-enabled workflows, clinicians actively query patient records from the HIE at the point of care — pulling in prior imaging results, medication histories from other systems, and care summaries from recent hospitalizations. They are simultaneously contributors to and consumers of HIE data, making clinical HIE literacy a genuine professional competency, not a technical afterthought.
Common Misconception
Health Information Management (HIM) — The Data Stewards
If clinicians generate health data, HIM professionals are its custodians. This workforce category encompasses a range of specialties unified by a common mission: ensuring that health information is accurate, complete, accessible, and protected. In the HIE context, HIM professionals are the people who make raw clinical documentation usable as structured, exchangeable data.
At the management level, the Registered Health Information Administrator (RHIA) is AHIMA's flagship credential. RHIA-credentialed professionals oversee records systems, data quality programs, privacy and security compliance, release of information workflows, and information governance frameworks. In larger health systems, RHIAs often serve as directors of HIM departments, Chief Privacy Officers, or information governance leads — roles that place them at the table for HIE contract negotiations, consent policy design, and interoperability governance.
The Registered Health Information Technician (RHIT) operates at the technician level, handling day-to-day management of medical records, release of information requests, and data integrity checks. RHITs are often the first line of defense against data quality problems that could corrupt an HIE feed — catching mismatched patient identifiers, incomplete records, or unsigned clinical notes before they propagate across the network.
Medical coders — credentialed as Certified Coding Specialists (CCS) for inpatient or CCS-P for physician services — translate clinical encounter documentation into the standardized codes that drive billing, quality measurement, and aggregate data analysis. ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes, ICD-10-PCS procedure codes, and CPT codes are the lingua franca of healthcare data exchange. When those codes are wrong, every downstream system that depends on them — from payer claims to CMS quality measures to population health dashboards — is built on a flawed foundation.
The Certified Health Data Analyst (CHDA) credential represents the analytical tier of HIM practice. CHDA candidates must hold an RHIT or RHIA credential, or a bachelor's degree in a related field, before sitting for the exam. CHDAs mine claims data, clinical data, and operational data to generate performance insights for quality improvement, contract negotiation, and population health management. In an HIE-connected health system, CHDAs often function as the bridge between raw exchange data and actionable intelligence.
AHIMA's credentials form a deliberate career ladder. An entry-level HIM professional typically begins with the RHIT, gaining foundational competency in medical records management, data quality, and HIPAA compliance. With additional education and experience, the RHIT advances to the RHIA — taking on management responsibilities for departmental operations, information governance, and strategic data planning. Professionals who develop analytical expertise can layer in the CHDA credential, positioning themselves for roles in data analytics, interoperability consulting, and population health strategy. Each credential opens doors to higher-responsibility roles and, according to AHIMA, to materially higher compensation: in its 2019 salary survey, professionals holding four or more AHIMA credentials reported average earnings of $114,000 — a premium that reflects the market's recognition of specialized expertise in health information governance and data quality.
AHIMA Certification Ecosystem
Review flagged encounters from overnight admissions; assign ICD-10 codes to ensure clean claims submission and accurate diagnostic data for the HIE feed.
Morning Coding Review
Process patient and payer requests for medical records; verify authorizations and confirm HIPAA compliance before releasing records to external parties or HIE participants.
Release of Information Requests
Run EHR exception reports to catch missing diagnoses, unsigned notes, or mismatched patient identifiers that could compromise data integrity across HIE-connected systems.
Data Quality Audit
Confirm that inbound patient data arriving through the HIE matches the local record; flag potential duplicates for Master Patient Index (MPI) review and resolution.

A Day in the Life of an HIM Professional
Health IT and Informatics Roles — The Data Exchangers
Between the clinicians who generate health data and the analysts who consume it lies a critical layer of professionals who build, configure, and maintain the technical infrastructure that makes data exchange possible. Health IT and informatics roles are among the most specialized — and most consequential — in the HIE workforce.
The Chief Medical Information Officer (CMIO) is the physician executive who bridges clinical workflows and information technology strategy. Among the most senior physician-executive roles, the CMIO position demands both deep clinical expertise — most CMIOs hold an MD or DO degree with active board certification — and advanced training in health informatics, typically a master's degree or fellowship in clinical informatics. The CMIO leads EHR governance committees, designs clinical decision support (CDS) rules, shapes the organization's interoperability roadmap, and serves as the clinical voice in vendor negotiations. In an HIE context, the CMIO is often the executive sponsor who champions HIE participation and ensures that exchange workflows are clinically sensible.
Clinical Informatics Specialists and Analysts — classified in the Labor Department’s O*NET system as Health Informatics Specialists (15-1211.01) — analyze clinical workflows and translate them into data system requirements. They build data dictionaries, configure interface logic, design HL7 FHIR API endpoints, and document CDA (Clinical Document Architecture) templates. Many hold board certification in clinical informatics through the American Board of Preventive Medicine (ABPM) or the American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG), making clinical informatics one of the few formally board-certified health IT specialties.
HIE Project Managers and Directors oversee the onboarding of new participant organizations, manage interface engine configuration and testing schedules, coordinate governance committee operations, and ensure that data sharing agreements are executed and maintained. These roles require a hybrid skill set: enough technical knowledge to have meaningful conversations with interface engineers, combined with the project management discipline to coordinate across clinical, legal, compliance, and vendor teams simultaneously.
Interoperability Analysts are the specialists who configure the specific technical mappings that make data exchange work in practice. They write HL7 v2 message transformation rules in interface engines like Mirth Connect or Rhapsody, configure FHIR API endpoints for SMART on FHIR applications, and build CDA document transforms that convert clinical documentation from one EHR's proprietary format to a standard that another system can ingest. When an ADT alert fails to fire or a lab result arrives with the wrong patient identifier, it is the interoperability analyst who diagnoses and resolves the problem.
EHR Implementation Specialists occupy the intersection of technology and clinical adoption. They train clinical staff on new workflows, configure system settings to match clinical preferences, and serve as the ongoing liaison between vendor capabilities and clinical needs. In HIE projects, implementation specialists often lead the go-live support effort for new exchange workflows — ensuring that the moment a hospital begins receiving patient data from an HIE, the clinical staff knows how to find and act on it.
Think of the health IT workforce like a city's plumbing and electrical infrastructure. Clinicians are the residents using water and power — they care about the end result, not the pipes. HIM professionals manage the meters and billing systems, ensuring accurate records of consumption and delivery. IT specialists are the engineers who lay the pipes and run the wires — largely invisible when everything works, and catastrophic when something breaks. The CMIO is the city engineer who sets the standards and ensures that every new building connects to the grid correctly.
The invisible infrastructure workforce of healthcare
Population Health, Analytics, and Leadership Roles
The downstream beneficiaries of well-functioning HIE are the professionals who use aggregated, longitudinal patient data to manage health at the population level. These roles depend on HIE as their primary data source and would be severely constrained without reliable, timely exchange.
Population Health Analysts use aggregated HIE data to identify care gaps across patient panels, stratify patients by clinical risk, and design proactive outreach programs. A population health analyst at an Accountable Care Organization (ACO) might use HIE data to identify diabetic patients who have not had an HbA1c test in 12 months, then trigger an outreach campaign — all before those patients experience a preventable complication. This kind of proactive, data-driven care management is impossible without the comprehensive, cross-setting patient data that HIE provides.
Care Coordinators and Case Managers rely on real-time HIE alerts — specifically Admission/Discharge/Transfer (ADT) notification feeds — to track high-risk patients across care settings. When a high-risk patient with congestive heart failure is admitted to an emergency department, an ADT alert triggers an immediate notification to their care coordinator, who can begin discharge planning, schedule a follow-up appointment, and coordinate with the inpatient team — all before the patient leaves the hospital. Without HIE, care coordinators are blind to events happening outside their own organization's walls.
Quality Improvement Analysts translate HIE-derived clinical data into standardized performance metrics. They calculate HEDIS measures, build eCQM (electronic Clinical Quality Measure) reports, and prepare CMS quality submissions for value-based payment programs. Privacy Officers and Compliance Officers ensure that every data exchange operates within the boundaries of HIPAA's Privacy Rule and Security Rule, govern HIE consent policies, and manage breach notification processes. Chief Information Officers (CIOs) and Chief Data Officers provide executive oversight for technology strategy, data governance frameworks, and vendor relationship management.
A 2024 study in the Journal of General Internal Medicine (Bazemore, Petterson and McCulloch) projects a need for 57,559 additional primary care clinicians by 2040. This persistent, multi-decade shortage across primary care, behavioral health, and rural medicine creates compounding pressure on every support role to enable greater efficiency. Population health analysts, care coordinators, and quality improvement staff are not optional support functions — they are force multipliers that help a constrained clinical workforce deliver better outcomes across larger patient populations.

The Workforce Shortage and the Multiplier Effect
The United States is experiencing concurrent workforce shortages across multiple healthcare disciplines simultaneously — and those shortages are not isolated from one another. They compound. When there are fewer physicians, every supporting role in the care delivery ecosystem faces greater pressure to enable efficiency, close gaps, and prevent errors. HIE — and the workforce that makes it function — becomes not a nice-to-have enhancement but an essential piece of healthcare infrastructure.
The physician shortage is severe and accelerating. AAMC projects a shortfall of up to 86,000 physicians by 2036, with a primary care gap of 20,200 to 40,400 particularly acute. About one in five active physicians is already 65 or older, and more than a third will be within the next decade. As each departing physician is not fully replaced, the physicians who remain must manage larger patient panels — making HIE-enabled pre-populated records, automated care gap alerts, and clinical decision support tools critical labor-saving infrastructure rather than optional enhancements.
The nursing pipeline faces its own severe constraint. In 2023, U.S. nursing schools turned away 65,766 qualified applications (AACN) — from students who met admission standards but could not be accepted due to faculty shortages, clinical placement limitations, and classroom capacity constraints. The nursing workforce cannot grow fast enough to absorb this demand, meaning that informatics tools that reduce documentation burden, surface relevant patient information quickly, and automate routine communications must amplify the capacity of every nurse currently in practice.
HRSA's 2025 State of the Health Care Workforce report documents persistent shortfalls across primary care, behavioral health, and rural medicine through the late 2030s, and independent researchers project a need for 57,559 additional primary care clinicians by 2040 — a gap that cannot be filled by training alone. The policy and technology response to that gap must include enabling better team-based care, more effective care coordination, and smarter use of distributed clinical data — all of which depend on robust HIE and the professionals who manage it.
Every HIM professional, informaticist, and analyst who helps HIE data flow smoothly multiplies the impact of every clinician who sees a patient. In a constrained workforce, the return on investment in health information infrastructure is not marginal — it is the difference between a system that functions and one that collapses under demand.
HRSA's Bureau of Health Workforce publishes supply-and-demand projections across many health professions, summarized in its State of the U.S. Health Care Workforce report. The 2025 edition identified persistent shortfalls in primary care, behavioral health, oral health, and multiple nursing specialties, with rural and underserved communities bearing disproportionate shortages. Team-based, distributed care models — which depend on real-time patient data sharing — are among the most viable strategies for serving more patients with a constrained clinical workforce, so interoperable data systems are a structural intervention, not just a technology upgrade. For HIE stakeholders, these projections provide the public health rationale for sustaining investment in exchange infrastructure even when budgets are under pressure: the alternative is a healthcare system that cannot meet the demand it will face over the next two decades.

######## hie-health-reform-onboarding | hie-governance-consent-ethics | Governance, Consent & Data Ethics
HIE Governance, Consent, and Ethics
Why Governance Matters in Health Information Exchange
Health information exchange (HIE) is the electronic sharing of clinical data across organizations — hospitals, clinics, labs, pharmacies, insurers, and public health agencies — to improve care coordination and reduce redundancy. But technology alone cannot make exchange work. Without shared rules about who can access what data, when, and for what purpose, even the most sophisticated interoperability infrastructure collapses into a tangle of liability disputes, privacy violations, and clinical mistrust. Data governance is the backbone of every functioning HIE.
The core problem is fragmentation. Health data is generated and stored across thousands of unconnected systems, each with its own policies, data models, and access controls. When a patient sees a specialist, visits an emergency department in another state, or fills a prescription at a retail pharmacy, their data rarely follows them automatically. Without a governance framework — legal agreements, defined roles, audit trails, breach response plans — organizations have no basis for trusting that data received from another institution is accurate, appropriately de-identified, or used for legitimate purposes.
Effective HIE governance requires three interlocking frameworks to coexist: legal (what entities are permitted to share under which laws), technical (what standards and systems enable the exchange), and ethical (what uses are appropriate given patient expectations and societal values). Data sharing agreements (DSAs) are the primary legal instrument that ties these frameworks together for every participating organization.
Data Sharing Agreements (DSAs) are the legal foundation of any HIE. A DSA is a formal contract between participating organizations that codifies which entities are authorized to access the exchange, defines their roles and responsibilities, specifies what categories of data can be shared, establishes the conditions and permitted purposes for sharing, and assigns accountability for security, breach response, and compliance. Every organization that joins an HIE signs a DSA — no DSA, no access.
Centralized, Federated, and Hybrid — each with distinct governance and risk trade-offs

HIE Governance Models: Centralized, Federated, and Hybrid
There is no single governance architecture for HIEs. Organizations choose among three primary models — centralized, federated, and hybrid — each representing a different answer to the fundamental tension between data access speed and privacy risk. The model chosen shapes everything downstream: how quickly clinicians can retrieve records, how breaches are contained, how audits are conducted, and how much infrastructure investment is required upfront.
In a centralized model, a single governing organization stores and controls all data in a shared repository. This enables fast queries across all participants and simplifies auditing and compliance oversight, since there is one place to look. The trade-off is concentration of risk: a breach at the central repository exposes data for every patient in the network. Centralized HIEs also require significant upfront infrastructure investment and place substantial trust — and legal liability — in the governing entity. In a federated model, data stays at each provider site. When a query is sent, it travels to each node and data is returned on-demand. This distributes risk — a breach at one hospital does not expose records from others — and eliminates a single point of failure, but it makes cross-network queries slower and more complex, and demands strong interoperability standards at every node.
The hybrid model attempts to capture advantages of both. Common services — query routing, provider directories, consent management — are centralized, while clinical data remains at each provider. Many real-world HIEs have converged on hybrid architectures as governance complexity and privacy expectations have grown. Texas offers a prominent example of how a hybrid model can operate at a statewide scale.
Centralized
Single governing organization controls data
Fast query and data access
Easier auditing and compliance oversight
Higher breach impact if compromised
Significant upfront infrastructure cost
Federated
Data stays at each provider site
Distributed risk — breach limited to one node
Harder to query across the network
Requires strong interoperability standards
No single point of failure
HIE Architecture Models
The Texas Health Services Authority is a nonprofit corporation created by the Texas Legislature in 2007 to facilitate health information exchange across Texas. It uses a hybrid architecture, contracting with local HIEs for statewide shared services rather than building a single central repository. This model allows regional HIEs to retain data locally while THSA coordinates statewide governance standards, access policies, and technical frameworks — a practical compromise between centralized control and distributed autonomy.
Texas Health Services Authority (THSA)
TEFCA: A National Governance Framework
For decades, health information exchange in the United States was a patchwork of local and regional efforts — each with its own rules, technical standards, and participating organizations. A clinician in Boston could not easily retrieve records from a patient's prior care in Phoenix because the HIEs in those regions operated under incompatible governance frameworks. The 21st Century Cures Act of 2016 directed the Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology (ONC) to address this fragmentation by establishing a national framework for trusted exchange. The result was TEFCA — the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement.
ONC published version 1 of TEFCA on January 19, 2022. A subsequent Common Agreement v1.1 was published in November 2023. Version 2.0 was released on April 22, 2024, and added mandatory FHIR-based transaction support — marking a pivotal shift from older document-based exchange toward modern API-driven interoperability. TEFCA operates through Qualified Health Information Networks (QHINs): large-scale networks that sign the Common Agreement, agree to operate under shared technical and policy rules, and serve as the on-ramps for providers and health systems seeking nationwide exchange capability. Participation in TEFCA is voluntary, but any organization seeking TEFCA-based exchange must connect through a QHIN.
ONC does not administer the Common Agreement directly. Instead, ONC contracted with The Sequoia Project to serve as the Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE). The Sequoia Project develops and updates the Common Agreement, reviews and designates QHIN applicants, and monitors ongoing compliance. This structure — a public mandate executed through a nonprofit RCE — is a deliberate governance design that keeps the federal government at arm's length from day-to-day network operations while maintaining public accountability.
TEFCA's Common Agreement establishes the technical infrastructure model and governing rules for different health information networks to securely share clinical information — all under commonly agreed-to rules of the road. It sets baseline standards for privacy, security, patient matching, and exchange behaviors that all QHINs and their participants must follow, regardless of which QHIN they connect through.
ONC publishes the Trusted Exchange Framework and designates a Recognized Coordinating Entity (RCE) to manage it under the authority of the 21st Century Cures Act.
ONC Sets the Framework
The Sequoia Project (RCE) develops and updates the Common Agreement, reviews QHIN applications, and monitors compliance with technical and policy requirements.
RCE Administers Common Agreement
Qualified Health Information Networks voluntarily sign the Common Agreement and agree to operate under shared technical and policy rules, enabling cross-network data exchange.
QHINs Sign the Common Agreement
Hospitals, clinics, and health systems connect to a QHIN, gaining access to the broader TEFCA exchange network and the records of patients who received care through other participating organizations.
Providers Connect Through QHINs
Patient data flows across QHIN boundaries using FHIR APIs (required as of v2.0, April 2024) under the governance structure established by the Common Agreement — with consistent privacy, security, and audit standards.

Patient Consent: Opt-In, Opt-Out, and Everything In Between
One of the most consequential governance decisions any HIE must make is how to handle patient consent. Two primary models have emerged: opt-in and opt-out. In an opt-in model, a patient must affirmatively consent — sign a form, click a checkbox, or verbally agree — before their protected health information (PHI) is included in the HIE. In an opt-out model, patient data is included automatically upon enrollment with a participating provider, and the patient must take active steps — submitting an online form, calling a help line, or mailing a request — to have their records excluded.
HIPAA sets a federal floor for health information privacy but does not dictate which consent model HIEs must use. States have broad authority to impose stricter requirements, and consent models vary considerably across the country. Some states mandate opt-in; others permit opt-out; some allow community-wide consent — a single consent that covers all future sharing with all HIE participants in a community or state, reducing per-encounter administrative burden. The result is a patchwork that complicates cross-state exchange and creates compliance challenges for health systems operating in multiple jurisdictions.
The trade-offs between opt-in and opt-out are real and well-documented. Opt-out models produce more complete datasets: when participation is the default, a larger and more representative population of patients appears in the HIE, supporting more reliable quality measurement and population health analytics. Opt-in models give patients stronger control over their data, but the patients who engage are systematically different from those who do not — often more health-literate, more trusting of the healthcare system, and more likely to have established primary care relationships. This selection bias can distort clinical and quality data, making opt-in HIEs less useful for understanding outcomes across the full population.
Choosing between opt-in and opt-out is like choosing between a library that only lends books to people who fill out a membership form (opt-in) versus one that gives access to all residents automatically unless they specifically decline (opt-out) — the first is more respectful of individual choice; the second serves more people but requires residents to know the system exists and how to leave it.
Patient Consent Models in HIE

Substance use disorder (SUD) records governed by 42 CFR Part 2 carry protections far stricter than HIPAA. Even with an HIE opt-out consent in place, Part 2 records cannot be shared without specific patient consent — or a court order. Health IT teams must segment Part 2 records from general clinical data flows.
42 CFR Part 2 Is Not HIPAA
42 CFR Part 2: Special Protections for Substance Use Disorder Records
42 CFR Part 2 is a federal regulation that governs the confidentiality of substance use disorder (SUD) patient records held by federally assisted programs. It was enacted in an era when SUD stigma was — and in many contexts remains — so severe that patients refused to seek treatment if they believed their records could be used against them in employment, child custody, or criminal proceedings. Part 2's protections are intentionally stricter than HIPAA: they restrict disclosures that HIPAA would otherwise permit, and they apply a higher bar for consent before SUD treatment records can be shared with any external entity, including other treating providers.
The 2024 SAMHSA final rule, issued February 16, 2024 and effective April 16, 2024, made the most significant changes to Part 2 in decades. The most important change aligned Part 2 more closely with HIPAA's treatment, payment, and operations (TPO) framework: patients can now give a single consent covering all future TPO disclosures of their SUD records, eliminating the prior requirement to obtain consent for each individual disclosure. This change was designed to reduce the administrative friction that had made Part 2 records difficult to integrate into electronic health records and HIE data flows. SAMHSA provided a two-year implementation window; enforcement began February 16, 2026.
Despite the 2024 simplifications, several critical protections remain unchanged. SUD counseling notes — analogous to HIPAA's psychotherapy notes — still require a separate, distinct patient consent and cannot be shared under the general TPO consent. When a HIPAA-covered entity receives Part 2 records with TPO consent, it can redisclose that information under HIPAA rules for most purposes — but cannot use the information in any legal proceeding against the patient without a separate court order. And without any patient consent or court order, Part 2 programs cannot disclose any information identifying a person as having or having had a SUD, even in emergencies, with only narrow exceptions. HIEs and EHR vendors must implement technical segmentation to ensure Part 2 records do not travel with general clinical data under standard HIPAA-based consent.
The 2024 SAMHSA final rule (effective April 2024, enforcement February 2026) allows a single TPO consent for future SUD record sharing — eliminating the prior requirement to get consent for each individual disclosure — but SUD counseling notes still require a separate consent, and records can never be used in legal proceedings against the patient without separate authorization.
Patients can give one consent for all future treatment, payment, and operations disclosures — a major simplification from prior rules requiring per-disclosure consent.
Single TPO Consent Now Allowed
HIPAA-covered entities that receive Part 2 records with TPO consent can redisclose under standard HIPAA rules — no longer need to track and restrict each downstream sharing event.
Redisclosure Under HIPAA Permitted
SUD counseling notes require a distinct patient consent, analogous to HIPAA psychotherapy notes — these cannot travel with the TPO consent.
Counseling Notes Still Separately Protected
Part 2 records, even when shared under TPO consent, cannot be used in any criminal, civil, or administrative proceeding against the patient without a specific, separate court order.

Data Ethics and Secondary Use of Health Data
Secondary use refers to using EHR records, claims data, or HIE data for purposes beyond the direct care of the patient who generated that data — including clinical research, quality improvement, public health surveillance, and commercial analytics. Secondary use is not inherently unethical; it is, in fact, how most clinical knowledge is generated. But it raises persistent ethical tensions: the patient whose data is used in a research study did not consent to that specific study. The health system that shares data for a quality improvement initiative may not have disclosed that use to patients at the time of their care. The commercial analytics company that licenses claims data may use it in ways patients would find surprising or objectionable.
The ethical framework for secondary use rests on five stewardship principles that health information governance bodies, IRBs, and data custodians have converged on over the past two decades. These principles — purpose limitation, data minimization, transparency, accountability, and patient access and correction rights — do not eliminate the tension between research benefit and privacy protection, but they provide a structured basis for evaluating whether a proposed secondary use is justifiable. Studies consistently show that patients broadly support the use of their data for research and quality improvement, but they want to know who is using it, for what purpose, and with what safeguards. Trust is the currency of secondary use; when it is lost — through data breaches, opaque data sharing practices, or commercial uses patients did not anticipate — patients opt out, data completeness declines, and the system loses the population-level insights that motivated secondary use in the first place.
The ethical use of health data requires building and maintaining patient trust — not just technical safeguards. Patients broadly support research use of their data, but they want transparency about who uses it and for what.
Data collected for one purpose (e.g., treatment) should not be repurposed without patient knowledge or consent (e.g., sold to advertisers or used for employment screening).
Purpose Limitation
Only collect and share the minimum data necessary for the stated purpose; excess data collection increases breach risk and erodes trust.
Data Minimization
Patients and the public should know what data is held, who has access, and for what purposes — through clear notices, access logs, and governance disclosures.
Transparency
Designated data stewards must be responsible for compliance, breach response, and enforcing data sharing agreements across all participants.
Accountability
Patients have the right to access their data, correct errors, and in some contexts, request deletion — reinforced by HIPAA, 21st Century Cures Act, and state laws.
Patient Access and Correction Rights

######## five-pillars-one-imperative | why-single-pillar-thinking-fails | Why Single-Pillar Thinking Fails
Why Single-Pillar Thinking Fails
A fifteen-year natural experiment
In 2010, the Affordable Care Act created the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Innovation (CMMI) with a mandate to test new payment and delivery models and scale what worked. Over the next fifteen years, CMMI ran the largest natural experiment in American healthcare reform: dozens of models, billions of dollars, thousands of participating organizations, each testing a theory of what would fix the system.
The results are unusually well documented, because CMMI models are evaluated against the same statutory bar: does the model improve quality without increasing spending, reduce spending without reducing quality, or do both? A model that clears that bar is eligible for nationwide expansion. That is a clean, falsifiable test — and it produced a clear pattern.
That pattern is the subject of this lesson, and it holds up whether you look at the portfolio in aggregate or at any single model in detail. The next two sections do both: the aggregate scorecard, then two named models worth knowing by name, because you will hear them cited — correctly and incorrectly — for the rest of your career in this field.
Source: GAO
Models CMMI tested, 2011–2024
Source: GAO
Models that met the bar for nationwide expansion
Source: CBO, Sept. 2023
Spent by CMMI to operate its models
$7.9B
Source: CBO, Sept. 2023
Net increase in federal spending, 2011–2020
$5.4B
Not a failure of effort — a failure of scope
Read that scorecard carefully before drawing the wrong conclusion. It is not that payment reform doesn't work, or that CMMI wasted fifteen years. It's that the models were, almost without exception, narrow. Each one addressed a single part of the system while leaving the others unchanged — and the parts left unchanged determined the outcome.
Models that changed only what Medicare paid, without changing how care was delivered or whether providers had the infrastructure to respond, generated financial pressure with no behavioral change to show for it. Models that redesigned care coordination produced real clinical improvements — that the payment system then penalized, because better coordination usually means fewer billable services. Models that required new technology — EHRs, population health platforms, data exchange — ran into providers who had the tool but not the operational capacity to use it.
Each of these is a single-pillar intervention hitting a constraint created by a different pillar. That is the pattern this course exists to name and to fix.
Case study one: Comprehensive Primary Care Plus
CPC+ launched in 2017 as CMMI's largest primary care model to date — over 3,000 practices, more than 17 million patients, running five full years before ending in 2021. Its theory of change was squarely Clinical: pay primary care practices more, and enhance that payment specifically to fund care coordination, and practices will manage their populations well enough to keep patients out of the hospital.
The independent evaluation confirmed the clinical half of the theory. CPC+ practices reduced emergency department visits, hospitalizations, and hospitalization spending relative to comparison practices — a real, measured clinical effect, not a rounding error.
It did not reduce total Medicare spending. The enhanced payments CMS made to fund the care coordination, plus increases in spending elsewhere in the care continuum, more than offset the utilization reductions the model achieved. CPC+ is the cleanest available illustration of Clinical pillar success that never becomes Economics pillar success, because the payment model funding the intervention was never redesigned to capture the savings the intervention produced.
Case study two: the Medicare Diabetes Prevention Program
MDPP is the more uncomfortable example, because on paper it is one of CMMI's four unambiguous successes — its pilot met the statutory bar and CMS expanded it nationwide starting in 2018, the coverage decision that defines success in this framework's terms.
Expansion did not translate into reach. Only about 38% of primary care physicians were aware the program existed, and only 23% referred an eligible patient to it. The reimbursement structure paid so little, on such a delayed and performance-contingent schedule, that community organizations found it barely worth the administrative burden of becoming a supplier — producing a nationwide undersupply of physical sites offering the program. CMS's original design did not recognize telehealth delivery, which excluded exactly the rural beneficiaries who had the least access to an in-person site in the first place.
MDPP passed the evaluation CMMI uses to define success — the narrow Clinical-and-Economics question the statute asks. It failed on Policy (a reimbursement structure nobody wanted to operate under), on Operations (no supply of delivery sites), and on the Equity Imperative specifically (the access gap fell hardest on rural Medicare beneficiaries, the population with the fewest alternative options). A model can clear CMMI's bar and still fail the five-question test this course teaches — because the bar only asks two of the five questions.
The diagnostic test
For any transformation initiative — a CMMI model, a state Medicaid waiver, a hospital's own value-based care strategy — ask five questions: Is it permissible (Policy)? Is it possible (Technology)? Is it sustainable (Economics)? Is it effective (Clinical)? Is it executable (Operations)? An initiative that fails even one of these questions will underperform regardless of how well it answers the others.
The Equity Imperative is not a sixth question
There is a sixth question running underneath all five: is it just? Does the answer hold up the same way for a rural Medicaid patient as it does for an urban commercially-insured one? This is not a separate pillar competing for its own resources and its own success metric — it is a test applied to each of the five. A payment model can be permissible, possible, sustainable, effective, and executable, and still fail if it improves the average while widening the gap between the best-served and worst-served populations.
MDPP is the case study to hold onto here: a program CMS itself certified as a success produced an access pattern that concentrated its benefit in exactly the populations least likely to need it most, and left rural, lower-resource communities to figure out a program that had almost nowhere nearby to actually deliver it. You will see this Equity Imperative applied concretely, pillar by pillar, in Track 7 of this course and in Chapter 10 of the book.
What CMMI's pattern predicts
Economics only —
Payment changes, delivery doesn't → Financial pressure with no behavior change
Clinical only (CPC+) —
Care coordination improves, utilization falls → Payment model never redesigned to capture the savings — no net reduction in spending
Technology only —
New systems deployed → Providers lack operational capacity to use them
Clinical + Economics only (MDPP) —
Pilot meets the statutory bar, model expands nationwide → No Policy fix to reimbursement, no Operations base of delivery sites — reach collapses
Equity Imperative unapplied (MDPP) —
Program certified a national success → Access concentrated away from the rural beneficiaries who needed it most
All five, in sequence —
Mandate → data → incentive → care redesign → execution → Each stage removes the constraint blocking the next
Passing the evaluation is not the same as working
MDPP is proof that clearing CMMI's own statutory bar does not mean a model works at the scale and reach that matters to patients. Before you cite any pilot result — CMMI's or your own organization's — ask which of the five questions the evaluation actually measured, and which ones it silently assumed away.
How to use this pattern
The next time someone hands you a successful pilot result, don't ask 'did it work?' Ask 'which of the five questions did this evaluation answer, and which did it never ask?' CPC+ answered the Clinical question and never closed the Economics loop. MDPP answered the Clinical and Economics questions and never asked the Policy, Operations, or Equity ones. The gap between a pilot's finding and a program's real-world result is almost always one of the questions nobody thought to ask.

This lesson works the opening argument of Chapter 1 — the CMMI record and why interventions that address a single pillar keep running into the constraints of the ones they ignore.

Read it at /read/chapter-01.
Fifteen years of federal payment and delivery reform show the same pattern: interventions that touch only one part of the system run into constraints created by the parts they ignore. This lesson builds the case for treating transformation as a system problem.
######## five-pillars-one-imperative | five-pillars-diagnostic-questions | The Five Pillars and Their Diagnostic Questions
The Five Pillars and Their Diagnostic Questions
Five questions, asked in order
The framework's usefulness comes from precision. Each pillar is defined by a single diagnostic question, and the five questions are not interchangeable — they interrogate genuinely different things about the same initiative.
Policy asks: is it permissible? Technology asks: is it possible? Economics asks: is it sustainable? Clinical asks: is it effective? Operations asks: is it executable? An honest 'no' to any one of them predicts underperformance regardless of the other four answers.
The five pillars
Policy —
Is it permissible? → The mandatory architecture — converts aspirational reform into binding requirements. Without it, the highest-cost actors opt out.
Technology —
Is it possible? → The data substrate — makes population health management, VBC execution, and equity measurement analytically feasible.
Economics —
Is it sustainable? → The incentive architecture — determines whether organizations have a financial reason to behave differently.
Clinical —
Is it effective? → The mechanism of change — payment changes incentives; clinical redesign changes behavior.
Operations —
Is it executable? → The execution layer — translates mandates, models, platforms and programs into organizational reality.
What each pillar produces when it works
A pillar is not an abstraction; it has outputs you can look for. Policy produces statutory mandates that eliminate voluntary opt-out, and accountability timelines that cannot be deferred. Technology produces attribution lists, total-cost-of-care measurement, HEDIS stratification, risk stratification and care-gap identification. Economics produces payment models in which population health management is financially rational, and accountability for total cost rather than encounter volume. Clinical produces primary care transformation that prevents hospitalizations, behavioral health integration that reduces crisis presentations, and care management that closes gaps before they become acute. Operations produces transformation plans that are implemented rather than filed, and project-management infrastructure that tracks progress against real deadlines.
If you cannot point to the output, the pillar is not working — whatever the org chart says.
Vermont in one line per pillar
Policy: Act 68 makes reference-based pricing binding on hospitals and requires global budgets — one or more non-critical-access hospitals from FY2028, all hospitals by FY2030, resources permitting. Technology: VHCURES, VITL/VHIE, and the AHS–GMCB analytics capability. Economics: mandatory RBP (method set by GMCB rule in 2027, prices effective hospital FY2028) and hospital global budgets beginning FY2028 (all hospitals by FY2030). Clinical: Blueprint PCMHs, the Collaborative Care Model, CCBHCs, and community health teams. Operations: the 14-hospital transformation planning process, RHRC technical assistance, the proposed HSA Coordinator model, and EMS regionalization.
Case study: Economics as the binding constraint — the Pioneer ACO exodus
CMS's Pioneer ACO Model, launched in 2012, tested what the most advanced accountable care organizations in the country could do under two-sided financial risk — sharing not just in savings but in losses. CMS did not select novices: the 32 founding Pioneer ACOs were chosen specifically because they already had the care-coordination infrastructure most ACOs were still building. On the Clinical question — is it effective? — these were, by CMS's own selection criteria, the strongest answers available in the program.
The Economics pillar is what broke. Thirteen of the 32 Pioneer ACOs left the model in 2013 or 2014, and CMS confirmed by name that Franciscan Alliance (Indianapolis), Genesys PHO (Flint, Michigan), and Renaissance Health Network (Wayne, Pennsylvania) were among them. Genesys PHO owed Medicare $1.9 million in repayment after failing to hold down spending in its second year under the downside-risk formula. By 2016, only 9 of the original 32 remained.
None of this reflects a Clinical failure — the organizations that left were not clinically weaker than the ones that stayed. The reason most commonly cited for leaving was that the two-sided risk model was unsustainable even for already-efficient organizations: an ACO that has already wrung out the easy savings has less room left to keep beating its own benchmark year after year. That is a pure Economics-pillar failure — 'is it sustainable?' answered no — while Policy, Technology, Clinical, and Operations were, comparatively, in reasonable shape. More care coordination would not have kept them in the program.
Case study: Technology as the binding constraint — before and after ProvenCare
Geisinger Health System's ProvenCare program, launched in 2006, bundled the entire cost of elective coronary artery bypass graft (CABG) surgery into a single warrantied price and built the protocol around 40 evidence-based best-practice steps — things like correct pre-admission documentation and correct post-operative beta-blocker dosing. None of these 40 steps were new medical knowledge; every one was already an established best practice before ProvenCare existed.
What was new was hardwiring all 40 steps into the electronic health record so it could prompt clinicians in real time, and so Geisinger could monitor compliance across every patient rather than audit a sample after the fact. The published results (Casale et al., Annals of Surgery, 2007) show why that mattered: at launch, only 59% of patients received all 40 components — the same gap between known best practice and actual bedside practice that shows up everywhere in medicine. Within three months of the EHR-based prompting and monitoring going live, full-bundle compliance reached 100% and, after one dip to 86%, stayed there for the rest of the study period. Patients treated under the completed protocol had a 16% shorter hospital stay than the conventional-care comparison group.
Policy allowed this — nothing barred Geisinger from doing it. Economics rewarded it — the bundled price gave Geisinger a direct financial reason to eliminate variation. Clinical knowledge was not the constraint — the 40 steps were already known and written down. What was missing until the EHR build was Technology: a way to make 'is it possible to do this reliably on every patient' actually true. That is the diagnostic signature of a Technology-pillar constraint — the incentive and the know-how both exist, but nothing enforces or verifies the behavior at the point of care.
Diagnosing the binding constraint
In practice you rarely find all five failing at once. You find one that is blocking the others — the binding constraint. The diagnostic move is to walk the five questions in order and stop at the first honest 'no.'
An organization with a signed value-based contract, a redesigned care model, and no real-time cost data has an Economics pillar that exists on paper and a Technology pillar that cannot support it. Adding clinical staff will not help. Renegotiating the contract will not help. The constraint is data, and until it is relieved, investment in the other pillars produces less than it should.
Reading the failure signature
Policy —
Signal → Participation is voluntary, and the organizations most likely to lose money opt out or never join at all
Technology —
Signal → The incentive and the clinical know-how both exist, but frontline compliance is inconsistent because nothing prompts or verifies it in real time
Economics —
Signal → Clinically strong, well-run organizations exit or underperform specifically once real financial risk is introduced
Clinical —
Signal → Data, mandate, and payment all line up, but the care team's actual practice at the bedside doesn't change
Operations —
Signal → A funded plan with a real deadline exists on paper but is never actually implemented or tracked
Using the failure signature in practice
When you're handed an initiative that isn't performing, resist the urge to add more of whatever it already has plenty of. The Pioneer ACO exits didn't need better clinical protocols — they had those. Pre-EHR ProvenCare didn't need a bigger financial incentive or a better-written protocol — it had both. In each case, the fix was in the pillar with the honest 'no,' not the pillar that was easiest to invest in further.

######## five-pillars-one-imperative | the-equity-imperative-is-it-just | The Equity Imperative: Is It Just?
The Equity Imperative: Is It Just?
Why not a sixth pillar
Making equity a sixth pillar sounds generous and is quietly destructive. A sixth pillar has its own budget line, its own staff, its own success metric, and its own place in the queue — which means it can be sequenced last, funded least, and reported separately from the work that actually determines whether disparities close.
Treating it as an Imperative changes the structure. There is no separate equity workstream to defer, because every pillar's own deliverable carries an equity condition it must satisfy. The question is not 'did we do the equity project?' It is 'does this mandate, this data platform, this payment model, this care model, this implementation plan hold up for the people the current system serves worst?'
The justice question, pillar by pillar
Policy —
Is it permissible? → …and does the mandate close disparities or widen them?
Technology —
Is it possible? → …and does the data make disparities visible, or bury them in averages?
Economics —
Is it sustainable? → …and do the incentives reward serving the hardest-to-reach, or penalize it?
Clinical —
Is it effective? → …and effective for whom?
Operations —
Is it executable? → …and executable everywhere, including the rural and under-resourced?
The average that hides the gap
Vermont's primary care access rate is roughly 91% — about four points above the Agency of Human Services' 87% benchmark, and a genuine achievement. It also conceals gaps: in the Health Department's 2023–2024 survey data, 78% of Hispanic adults have a personal health care provider, against 91% of white adults. Nothing in the aggregate number reveals that gap. It becomes visible only when the underlying data is stratified by race and ethnicity — which is a Technology pillar capability, not a good intention.
Case study: Economics as the equity failure — the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program
CMS's Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program, in effect since 2012, answers the Economics pillar's own question cleanly: it is sustainable, in the narrow sense that it gives hospitals a real financial reason to reduce 30-day readmissions, and it has moved behavior. What its original design never asked was the Imperative's question — does the incentive reward serving the hardest-to-reach, or penalize it?
The initial risk-adjustment formula did not account for patients' socioeconomic status or social risk factors, which are strongly associated with readmission regardless of the quality of care a hospital delivers. The predictable result: safety-net hospitals serving disproportionately low-income and dually eligible (Medicare and Medicaid) patients were penalized far more consistently than others — one multi-year analysis found 72% of safety-net hospitals penalized in every one of four post-HRRP years studied, versus 59% of non-safety-net hospitals.
Congress fixed this in the 21st Century Cures Act (2016), which required CMS to stop comparing every hospital against the same national benchmark and instead sort hospitals into five peer quintiles by their share of dual-eligible patients, comparing readmission performance only within each quintile — a change that took effect in FY2019, seven years after the program began penalizing hospitals under the original design. The Economics pillar had been 'sustainable' and functioning exactly as built the entire time; the equity failure was invisible to its own diagnostic question, and it took a separate act of Congress to retrofit the fix.
Case study: Technology as the equity failure — pulse oximetry
Pulse oximeters are about as close to invisible infrastructure as medical technology gets: a clip on a fingertip, a number on a monitor, deployed in essentially every hospital room and used to make real-time decisions about who needs supplemental oxygen. On average, across the population the devices were validated on, they are accurate. Average accuracy is exactly the kind of result that can look like the Technology question — is it possible? — has been answered yes.
A 2020 New England Journal of Medicine study (Sjoding et al.) stratified that same 'accurate on average' technology by patient race and found it was not equally accurate at all. Across a multicenter cohort of 37,308 paired measurements from 178 hospitals, occult hypoxemia — a true blood oxygen level below 88% that the pulse oximeter was still reading as a reassuring 92–96% — occurred in 17.0% of Black patients versus 6.2% of white patients: nearly three times the rate. Patients were being screened as fine by the device precisely when they most needed intervention, and the pattern fell almost entirely on one racial group.
Nothing about this required new medical knowledge to fix once it was found — it required looking. The device had been in near-universal use for years; the disparity was invisible until someone deliberately stratified the data by race instead of reading the aggregate accuracy number and calling the Technology question closed. That is the Imperative's Technology-pillar question in its starkest form: does the data make disparities visible, or bury them in an average that looks fine?
Designed in, not reviewed in
The most common way equity fails is not opposition — it is sequencing. An equity review that happens at the approval stage, after the payment methodology is designed, can flag a problem but cannot cheaply fix one. By then the rate structure, the risk model and the measurement approach are already built around assumptions that did not include social risk.
The alternative is an equity constraint embedded in the design process itself. A reference-based-pricing methodology that sets rates uniformly, without adjusting for the conditions facing hospitals in underserved communities, is technically correct and practically inequitable — and it is far cheaper to catch that while the methodology is being written than after it is adopted.
Same failure, two pillars
HRRP (Economics) —
Looked solved: incentive cut aggregate readmissions and paid for itself → Hidden: safety-net hospitals penalized far more, for who they treat, not care quality
Pulse oximetry (Technology) —
Looked solved: validated accurate on average, decades of routine use → Hidden: occult hypoxemia missed in Black patients at nearly 3x the white-patient rate
The equity test to run before calling something done
Both failures above passed their pillar's own question for years before anyone caught them — because nobody had stratified the result by the population most likely to be underserved. Before you call a payment model sustainable or a technology validated, ask the version of the question this lesson is built around: sustainable, accurate, effective for whom, specifically — not just on average? That one stratification step is usually cheap. Finding the gap after a statute or a published study forces the fix is not.
