Why each feed alone is insufficient
State the failure precisely, because the generic version — "we need better data" — produces generic procurement.
Claims data alone creates a financial lag. You can see total spend, but you see it after the performance year in which you could have changed it, and you see it stripped of the clinical detail that would tell you why. Under fee-for-service that lag is merely expensive. Under a global budget it is disqualifying, because a hospital inside a fixed revenue envelope has to eliminate low-value volume specifically, and cannot eliminate what it cannot identify.
Clinical data alone gives no total-spend visibility. An exchange solves the narrow problem — a clinician can see that the same test was run last week at another hospital and not repeat it. Duplicate-test avoidance is the smallest version of the value question. The larger question is which of everything delivered to this population improved outcomes and which consumed resources without changing anything, and answering it requires knowing what a service cost, what it was meant to accomplish, and what happened afterward. Those three facts live in three systems.
Integration is therefore not a refinement of either asset. It is the capability, and neither asset delivers a usable fraction of it on its own.
The UHDS and the decision to lead with the faster feed
Vermont's answer is the Unified Health Data Space — not a second health information exchange but an implementation of the health data utility model, in which the combined clinical, claims, social and public health asset is treated as public infrastructure rather than any one participant's property.
Two statutory changes made it possible. Act 68 of 2025, section 10, directed AHS and the HIE Steering Committee to develop the Unified Health Data Space and decide whether and how to integrate clinical, claims and social-needs data — with no clinical–claims integration before January 1, 2027, and only on a Steering Committee majority vote. The quieter and more important change came in Act 167, which repealed 18 V.S.A. section 9410(e) — the provision that had barred the use of direct patient identifiers for record matching. Until that repeal Vermont's own statute forbade the technique its integration mandate requires.
The operational decision worth studying is which claims feed the state built on. Vermont routes integration primarily through the Medicaid Data Warehouse and Analytics Solution, which went live in early January 2026, rather than through VHCURES. MDWAS links Medicaid members' clinical data from the exchange with Medicaid claims inside the State's own system; VHCURES is collected quarterly with about six months of claims run-out, and its published measures run older still. For research, the lag is tolerable; for management, a timely feed on one payer beats a lagging feed on all of them. That is the correct trade, and it comes with an obligation: Medicaid is roughly a quarter of Vermont's primary coverage, so multi-payer scaling through 2029-2030 is not an enhancement to the plan, it is the plan.
Two claims feeds, two different jobs
Refresh cadence —
VHCURES: quarterly, with ~6 months of claims run-out → MDWAS: linked Medicaid claims and clinical data in the State's own system
Population —
All payers, but only 60% of commercial → Medicaid only, adding Medicare 2028-2029
Consent model —
No patient opt-out mechanism → Integrated opt-out, compliant with Act 53
Fit for purpose —
Retrospective analysis, rate review, price transparency → Care management, risk stratification, global budget monitoring
Beyond Vermont: Maryland made the exchange a utility by statute
Maryland runs hospital global budgets through the HSCRC and needed the same substrate. In 2022 the General Assembly passed House Bill 1127, requiring the state-designated exchange, CRISP, to operate as a health data utility effective October 1, 2022. It obliges the Maryland Department of Health, nursing homes, electronic health networks and prescription drug dispensers to supply data to the exchange, and obliges the exchange to deliver data in real time for treatment, care coordination and public health. The instructive point is the direction of travel: Maryland did not fund the exchange harder. It changed what the exchange was legally required to be. That is a Policy-pillar action taken in service of the Technology pillar, and it is the pattern any state should examine before writing another check.
The Equity Imperative at the gate
The sixth question — is it just? — is not a separate workstream. It is a test the Technology pillar has to pass on its own terms, and at the data layer it fails silently.
Vermont's own architecture documentation flags that race and ethnicity data is incomplete in commercial claims. That single gap propagates upward through every layer above it. Stratified quality reporting inherits it. Risk models inherit it. Equity monitoring under Act 68 inherits it. A state can hold a documented 13-point gap between white and Hispanic Vermonters on a 91% overall access measure, commit to closing it, and still be unable to demonstrate progress, because the denominator it needs is missing from the database it is measuring with.
This is what it means to say equity is a cross-cutting test rather than a pillar. Nobody has to oppose equity for the measurement to fail. The gap closes only if demographic completeness is a design requirement of the data layer itself — specified in the analytics procurement, not added as a reporting request afterward.
The diagnostic question
For any data asset, the question is not "do we have one?" It is: can an operator act on this inside the decision window that matters? A claims database refreshed quarterly with months of run-out and an exchange that most community providers have not joined can both be technically operational and jointly useless for managing risk. Ask what decision the data is supposed to support, then ask whether it arrives before that decision is made. If it does not, the asset is a research tool and the organization is not ready for downside risk.
What follows for sequencing
Vermont's Rural Health Transformation portfolio makes the dependency concrete. Shared-EMR incentives, the interfacility transfer tool, statewide e-consult, closed-loop referral and remote patient monitoring are each, in isolation, a vendor point solution. What converts any of them into measurable transformation is the data layer beneath. A closed-loop referral closes only if every provider and service agency can see the same correctly matched patient record.
Strip the substrate out and a large capital award becomes a set of disconnected purchases that cannot be attributed to a patient, linked to cost, or reported to CMS as evidence the investment worked. Capital arriving ahead of the data capability meant to carry it does not buy transformation.
That is the gate. Technology does not outrank Economics in importance — it precedes it in order, because the financial model cannot be operated without the visibility the data layer provides.

Technology is the gate Economics waits on: no organization can manage total-cost-of-care risk it cannot see. This lesson works through Vermont's three-layer data architecture, the documented limits of its all-payer claims database, and the managing-blind failure mode that took down OneCare Vermont.
######## five-pillars-one-imperative | fhir-interoperability-compliance-path | FHIR, Interoperability, and the Compliance Path
FHIR, Interoperability, and the Compliance Path
What FHIR actually is
FHIR — Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources — is an HL7 standard for representing and moving health data. It does two things. It defines a set of discrete resources, each a structured representation of one clinical or administrative concept: Patient, Observation, Condition, MedicationRequest, Coverage, Claim. And it defines a web API convention for requesting and writing those resources, so that a client asks for a patient's lab observations the same way it would ask any modern web service for a record.
That is genuinely important. Before FHIR, connecting two systems meant negotiating a point-to-point interface: a bespoke message format, a bespoke transport, a bespoke mapping, rebuilt for every new pair of endpoints. FHIR R4, the version CMS regulation is written against, replaced most of that with a published contract.
What FHIR is not is a product. It specifies a framework that compliant systems operate within. It does not specify which optional elements a given implementation populates, what local codes get mapped to, what business rules gate a request, or what an organization will agree to share. A hospital running Epic and a critical access hospital running TruBridge can both be accurately described as FHIR R4 compliant while exchanging documents with different content, triggering different workflows, and requiring custom integration work to interoperate at all.
The four things a standard cannot do
Optionality. FHIR resources carry many optional elements. Two conformant servers can populate different subsets, and a receiving system that expected a field it does not get has a data problem the standard does not consider an error. Implementation guides — US Core, the Da Vinci guides for prior authorization and coverage — exist precisely to narrow this, and adoption of the guides is a separate question from adoption of the standard.
Semantics. FHIR moves a coded value; it does not guarantee both ends mean the same thing by it. Vocabulary alignment across ICD-10, SNOMED CT, LOINC and RxNorm is terminology work, which is why Vermont's UHDS architecture puts terminology services in the foundational layer next to identity rather than treating them as a downstream cleanup.
Identity. FHIR assumes you know which patient you are asking about. Establishing that the record at one organization and the record at another belong to the same person is the matching problem, and the standard has nothing to say about it.
Trust and consent. Who may request what, under which authority, with what patient consent, and with what recourse when it is abused — none of that is in the specification. It lives in network agreements, state law, and 42 CFR Part 2 for substance use records.
Functional interoperability is FHIR compliance plus matching plus terminology plus event notification plus a workflow that puts the result in front of a person who can act on it. The standard supplies one of those five.
Compliant and non-interoperable at the same time
The most expensive mistake in a technology roadmap is treating FHIR compliance as a milestone rather than a precondition. A board can be shown a slide saying every hospital in the network is FHIR R4 certified and conclude the interoperability problem is closed. The operational test is different and much harder: can a care coordinator at one hospital see, today, that their patient was discharged from an emergency department at another organization last night, and act on it before the care gap opens? That requires identity resolution, an event notification subscription, a trust agreement, and a workflow. Certification gets you none of them.
The rules that made it mandatory
Two CMS rules did most of the work, and they are frequently conflated.
The CMS Interoperability and Patient Access final rule, CMS-9115-F, was published May 1, 2020. It required Medicare Advantage organizations, Medicaid and CHIP fee-for-service and managed care programs, and qualified health plan issuers on the federally facilitated exchanges to stand up two FHIR APIs: a Patient Access API letting enrollees pull their claims, encounter and clinical data into a third-party app of their choosing, and a Provider Directory API. Both were required from January 1, 2021, with CMS exercising enforcement discretion until July 1, 2021.
The CMS Interoperability and Prior Authorization final rule, CMS-0057-F, was issued January 17, 2024 and is the more operationally disruptive of the two. It applies to the same payer set and arrives in two phases. From January 1, 2026, impacted payers must decide standard prior authorization requests within 7 calendar days and expedited requests within 72 hours, must give a specific reason for every denial regardless of how the request arrived, and must publicly report prior authorization metrics. From January 1, 2027, they must operate four FHIR APIs: a Prior Authorization API, a Provider Access API, a Payer-to-Payer API, and an expanded Patient Access API that now carries prior authorization information.
Read in sequence, the two rules describe a deliberate escalation. The 2020 rule gave patients a pipe. The 2024 rule puts a payer's most contested administrative process — prior authorization — onto that pipe, with a clock attached and the metrics published.
The two CMS interoperability rules
Rule —

Information blocking — the obligation that runs the other way
The CMS rules compel payers to build pipes. The 21st Century Cures Act runs in the opposite direction: it prohibits withholding data through the pipes that exist. The information blocking provisions apply to three categories of actor — health care providers, developers of certified health IT, and health information exchanges and networks — and prohibit a practice the actor knows is likely to interfere with access, exchange or use of electronic health information and knows to be unreasonable.
The regime is structured as a broad prohibition with a defined set of safe harbors. HHS has finalized nine exceptions covering situations such as preventing harm, protecting privacy, infeasibility, and the manner in which a request is fulfilled. A later addition, the TEFCA Manner Exception finalized in the HTI-2 rule, lets an actor satisfy a request via TEFCA when both parties are TEFCA participants. The exceptions are not vague principles; each carries specific conditions that must be met, and an actor either meets them or does not.
For most of the rule's life the prohibition had no teeth on the provider side. That changed. The HHS Office of Inspector General's civil monetary penalty rule took effect September 1, 2023, authorizing penalties of up to $1 million per violation against developers of certified health IT, entities offering certified health IT, and health information exchanges and networks. Then on June 24, 2024, HHS finalized the provider disincentives rule, effective July 31, 2024, which routes consequences through Medicare payment programs instead of fines.
Source: HHS information blocking disincentives final rule, June 24, 2024

75%

Why the disincentives changed the calculus
Before mid-2024, a provider organization weighing whether to share data with a competitor faced an enforceable-in-theory prohibition and no defined consequence. The disincentives rule converted that into arithmetic a CFO can run. Three quarters of a hospital's annual market basket update is a material number on any operating budget, and Shared Savings Program ineligibility for at least a year is existential for an ACO. Note also who reports: the Cures Act channels complaints through a public portal, and the actors most likely to file are the competitors and vendors on the other side of the refused request.
The unsolved problem: knowing who the patient is
Every use case that crosses an organizational boundary depends on matching — establishing that the John Smith born March 14, 1952 at one hospital is the same person as the John Smith born March 14, 1952 at another, and the Jonathan Smith with that date of birth in the Medicaid enrollment file.
The United States has no national patient identifier. A congressional appropriations rider has barred HHS from spending federal funds to promulgate one since 1999, which means matching is done probabilistically on demographic attributes: name, date of birth, address, sex, sometimes phone. Those attributes are entered by humans under time pressure, stored in inconsistent formats, and change over a lifetime.
The measured consequences are worse than most executives assume. Research published by The Pew Charitable Trusts in 2018 found match rates between organizations as low as 50% — including, per work by the ONC contractor Audacious Inquiry, between organizations running the same EHR vendor, because the variability is in process and configuration rather than in the software. Measured duplicate record creation rates within organizations ranged from 0.77% to 6%. Pew also found that standardizing addresses to USPS formatting raised match rates by roughly three percentage points, which is both a real gain and a measure of how far three percentage points leaves you from solved.
A master patient index is the infrastructure that manages this. It is the least demo-able thing in a health IT portfolio — it produces no screen a board wants to look at — which is precisely why organizations buy the portal and the dashboard first and discover afterward that every care coordination feature they wanted depends on the piece they deferred.
Treat the MPI as a go/no-go gate
Before approving any multi-organization care coordination initiative, ask one question: what is our measured match rate against the organizations we intend to coordinate with, and who measured it? Not whether an MPI exists — what rate it achieves, on real records, across the boundary that matters. If nobody can answer, the initiative is being planned on an assumption, and the pattern holds in any state and any network structure, not just Vermont's.
Vermont's version of the problem
Vermont carried a self-inflicted version of the matching constraint until recently. Under 18 V.S.A. section 9410(e), state law prohibited the use of direct patient identifiers for record matching — a privacy provision that had the effect of forbidding the technique that accurate identity resolution requires. Act 167 repealed it, which is why the UHDS architecture can now place a master patient index, supplied by Verato, in its foundational layer alongside terminology services and the integration engine.
The operational picture the state is matching across is genuinely fragmented. Vermont's 14 hospitals do not share an EHR — UVM Health Network's hospitals run Epic, the independent hospitals a mix of other vendors' systems — before accounting for community mental health agencies, skilled nursing facilities, home health agencies and independent practices, many of which have no FHIR-capable system at all. Oliver Wyman's community engagement surfaced the everyday version: one participant described having to call up to 31 EMS agencies to arrange a single transfer.
That fragmentation is the substance of the statewide EHR question Vermont has under active feasibility assessment. The analytical question is not whether one platform would be tidier. It is whether FHIR-based exchange across four existing platforms can deliver real-time bidirectional data sharing at an acceptable cost — because if it can, the case for a migration that would cost hundreds of millions and disrupt clinical workflow for years weakens considerably.
Three FHIR use cases, ranked by transformation value
Patient Access API —
Patients pull records into a third-party app of their choosing → Mandatory compliance. The gate is smaller hospitals without the IT capacity to maintain an endpoint.
Provider Access API —
A care coordinator queries clinical records held by another organization for a shared patient → Highest value for a clinically integrated network — and the use case most dependent on a working master patient index and a trust framework.
Payer-to-provider API —
Electronic prior authorization and formulary exchange via the Da Vinci CRD and DTR implementation guides → Administrative simplification. Requires both the EHR and the payer to implement complementary guides, which is why it lags the others.
TEFCA — the trust layer the standard does not supply
FHIR tells two systems how to talk. It does not tell them whether they are permitted to, or give either one recourse if the other misuses what it receives. That is the gap the Trusted Exchange Framework and Common Agreement fills: a single set of legal terms that participants sign once, rather than negotiating bilateral agreements with every counterparty.
Exchange runs through Qualified Health Information Networks designated by the Sequoia Project, which holds the Recognized Coordinating Entity contract. Eleven networks had QHIN status as of November 2025, including eHealth Exchange, Epic Nexus, CommonWell, Health Gorilla, KONZA and MedAllies, with Oracle Health subsequently designated. More than 23,000 organizations are live on TEFCA as QHINs, participants or subparticipants.
For a state network the practical implication is that national connectivity is now a membership decision rather than an engineering project — which matters most for exactly the encounters a state exchange cannot see. A Vermont patient treated at Dartmouth Hitchcock in New Hampshire generates a record that no Vermont-only infrastructure will ever hold.
The compliance path, in order
Sequence the work the way the dependencies run, not the way the deadlines are dated.
Identity first: measure the current match rate across the boundaries that matter and stand up or fix the master patient index. Terminology second: agree the code systems and map local vocabularies, because every downstream analysis inherits whatever is done here. Then the APIs and the implementation guides, which is where most roadmaps mistakenly begin. Then the trust and consent layer — network membership, participation agreements, and the segregated handling that 42 CFR Part 2 requires for substance use records. Then, last, the workflow integration that puts an exchanged record in front of someone at the moment they are making a decision.
An organization that reverses this order arrives at a defensible compliance posture and an unusable system. It will hold certifications, satisfy auditors, and still not be able to tell a care coordinator that their patient was in another hospital's emergency department last night.

Chapter 5 covers the FHIR compliance landscape and the interoperability rules this lesson works through in practice.

FHIR is a standard, not a product, and two systems can both be certified and still fail to exchange anything useful. This lesson covers what the standard actually specifies, the CMS rules and information blocking penalties that made it mandatory, and the patient matching problem none of it solves.
######## five-pillars-one-imperative | ai-governance-clinical-decision-support | AI Governance and Clinical Decision Support
AI Governance and Clinical Decision Support
Governance is not a document
Most organizations that say they govern clinical AI mean they have a committee and a policy. Neither catches the failures that actually occur, because the failures are not policy violations. They are models that work — that do exactly what they were built to do — deployed against a question they were never built to answer.
The two cases below are the best-documented examples in the literature. Both involved widely deployed commercial software. Both passed whatever review the deploying organizations applied. Both were found by outside researchers with access to the deploying institution's own data, which is the single most important operational fact in this lesson.
Case one: the cost proxy
In October 2019, Ziad Obermeyer and colleagues published "Dissecting racial bias in an algorithm used to manage the health of populations" in Science. The subject was a commercial population health risk algorithm — Optum's, applied to roughly 200 million people a year nationally — used to identify patients who should be enrolled in high-risk care management. The researchers studied about 50,000 patients at a large academic hospital: roughly 6,000 self-identified Black and roughly 44,000 self-identified White.
The algorithm contained no race variable. It predicted future health care costs and used that prediction as a stand-in for future health need. That single substitution was the defect. Because less is spent caring for Black patients than for White patients with the same conditions — a consequence of unequal access, not of lesser need — the model read lower spending as lower need.
The measured effect was large. Among patients the algorithm flagged as highest risk, Black patients had 26.3% more chronic conditions than White patients at the same risk score. Only 17.7% of patients the algorithm selected for extra care were Black; the researchers calculated that an unbiased algorithm would have selected 46.5%. Working with the vendor to predict health outcomes rather than costs reduced the disparity by 84%.
No clinician chose this. No policy was violated. A label was chosen because it was convenient and available, and the label carried the structure of the disparity into every downstream referral decision.
Source: Obermeyer et al., Science, October 2019
Share of patients flagged for extra care who were Black: observed vs. unbiased
17.7% → 46.5%
Source: Obermeyer et al., Science, 2019

Race variables in the algorithm
Case two: the sepsis model that was never externally validated
The Epic Sepsis Model was deployed at hundreds of US hospitals as a proprietary early-warning tool. In June 2021, Wong and colleagues published an external validation in JAMA Internal Medicine covering 27,697 patients across 38,455 hospitalizations at Michigan Medicine between December 6, 2018 and October 20, 2019.
The model's area under the curve was 0.63, against the 0.76 to 0.83 range cited in the vendor's own documentation. Sensitivity was 33%, specificity 83%, positive predictive value 12%. In plain operational terms: the model alerted on 18% of all hospitalized patients, missed 1,709 sepsis cases — 67% of all sepsis in the cohort — and a clinician would have to work up 109 alerts to detect one case of sepsis earlier than they would have without it.
That is both failure modes in one system. It missed two thirds of the condition it was sold to detect, and the alerts it did generate were numerous and unspecific enough to guarantee alert fatigue among the clinicians receiving them. Epic subsequently released a revised model in 2022, a gradient-boosted tree that addressed several of the methodological criticisms and, importantly, came with a recommendation that hospitals train it on their own data before clinical use — a substantial departure from the one-size-fits-all model that preceded it.
The governance lesson is the one the accompanying JAMA editorial made directly: nothing about this was discoverable from vendor materials. It required an external validation against local data.
Source: Wong et al., JAMA Internal Medicine, June 2021
Epic Sepsis Model AUC on external validation, vs. 0.76-0.83 in vendor documentation

Both of these passed review
Neither case involved a reckless organization. The population health algorithm was a mainstream commercial product used by health systems and payers across the country. The sepsis model shipped inside the dominant EHR and was switched on by hundreds of hospitals. What both deployments lacked was the same thing: an independent look at how the model performed on local patients, stratified by subgroup, against a clinically meaningful outcome. Governance that consists of approving a vendor and reviewing a policy will reproduce both outcomes exactly.
The four-stage lifecycle
Pre-deployment evaluation. Establish regulatory status — is this software as a medical device, and what clearance does it hold? Establish what the model actually predicts, which for risk tools is frequently not what its name implies. Establish training data provenance and whether the training population resembles yours. Demand published performance stratified by race, ethnicity, age, sex and disability. And establish whether it has been validated in a setting comparable to yours rather than only at academic medical centers.
Implementation and training. Decide where the output appears in the clinical workflow and what the clinician is expected to do with it. Train staff on what the tool does not know and how to recognize an unreliable output, not only on how to click it. Document override protocols. And measure baseline performance before go-live, because without a baseline there is nothing to detect drift against.
Active monitoring. Track performance against that baseline on a fixed cadence. Track it separately for priority populations, because an average conceals exactly the differential the Obermeyer case describes. Maintain a route for clinicians to report cases where an output contributed to harm or delay. And watch override rates: a systematically high override rate is clinicians telling you the tool is not trustworthy, in the only channel available to them.
Vendor management. Performance commitments with specific thresholds and actual remedies, not best-efforts language. Advance notice of model updates with the opportunity to re-evaluate before the update is deployed. Contractual disclosure of demographic performance data. And explicit terms on what patient data the vendor collects and whether it is used to train future versions.
Which stage would have caught each failure
Pre-deployment: what does the model actually predict? —
Optum algorithm: would have surfaced that the label was cost, not health → Epic Sepsis Model: would have surfaced that vendor AUC was self-reported and never externally validated
Pre-deployment: stratified performance disclosure —
Would have exposed differential performance by race before go-live → Less decisive — the model's failure was overall discrimination, not subgroup gap
Implementation: baseline measurement —
Would have established referral rates by subgroup to compare against → Would have established the pre-deployment sepsis detection rate the model had to beat
Monitoring: stratified performance tracking —
The primary control — the disparity was visible in the deploying institution's own data → Would have shown a 12% positive predictive value within weeks of go-live
Monitoring: override rate tracking —
Not applicable — the tool made referrals, not point-of-care alerts → 109 alerts per true case would have produced an unmistakable override signal
Drift, and why monitoring cannot be one-time
A validated model is validated against a population and a practice pattern at a point in time. Both move. Coding practice changes, a new service line opens, a payer mix shifts, a referral pattern reorganizes after a hospital closes a unit — and the relationship the model learned degrades without any change to the model itself. This is drift, and it is invisible unless something is watching for it.
Drift is also the reason the local-validation requirement is recurring rather than a gate passed once. Epic's own revised guidance — train the model on your hospital's data before clinical use — is an acknowledgment that the relationship between inputs and outcomes is local. If it is local, it is also temporal, and a model correct for your population in 2026 is an empirical claim about 2027, not a settled fact.
The regulatory floor is rising
Governance is no longer purely voluntary. The ONC HTI-1 final rule created a certification criterion for decision support interventions that took effect January 1, 2025. Certified health IT must support 13 source attributes for evidence-based interventions and 31 for predictive ones — covering the model's purpose, training data, validation, fairness assessment and maintenance — plus intervention risk management practices for predictive tools the developer supplies as part of its module. It is a transparency regime rather than a performance standard: it does not tell a hospital which models are good, it forces the information a hospital needs to judge that into the open.
The FDA route is separate. Clinical software that diagnoses, treats, mitigates or prevents disease falls under the software as a medical device framework. The FDA had authorized 1,451 AI-enabled medical devices through the end of December 2025, of which 1,104 — 76% — were radiology devices. That concentration matters for rural systems specifically: imaging is both the most mature category of clinical AI and the capability a small hospital with one radiologist covering every modality is least able to staff to volume.
Neither regime relieves the deploying organization of anything. FDA clearance addresses the device as submitted. HTI-1 addresses disclosure. How the tool performs on your patients remains yours to measure.
Two developments since then pull in opposite directions. ASTP/ONC's HTI-5 proposed rule, published December 29, 2025, would remove most of HTI-1's source-attribute and risk-management requirements for predictive decision support; it was not final as of October 2026. Meanwhile a different federal rule reaches the hospital directly: since May 1, 2025, the Section 1557 nondiscrimination rule (45 CFR § 92.210) has required covered health programs to make reasonable efforts to identify patient care decision support tools that use race, color, national origin, sex, age, or disability as inputs, and to mitigate the risk of discrimination from each. That provision was not among those a federal court vacated in October 2025.
Vermont has begun legislating as well. Act 156 of 2026 makes it unprofessional conduct for a mental health professional to deliver therapy through AI systems alone, and Act 101 of 2026 directs the State's Artificial Intelligence Advisory Council to recommend statutory changes — including on generative AI in the regulated professions and AI in insurance utilization review — by January 15, 2027.

The Equity Imperative applied to Technology
The sixth question — is it just? — is not a sixth pillar and not a separate program. It is a test each of the five pillars has to pass on its own terms. For Technology, the Obermeyer case is the clearest statement of what that means in practice, and of why a separate equity workstream would not have helped.
The algorithm had no race variable. An equity review that examined inputs would have found nothing. An equity office reading a model card would have found nothing. The disparity was only visible in stratified output performance against the deploying institution's own patients — which is to say, it was visible only to someone doing ordinary technical validation, correctly, with subgroups broken out.
So the Technology pillar's equity obligation is specific and technical: stratify every performance metric before you report an average, specify demographic completeness in the data layer that feeds the model, and make stratified performance disclosure a contractual term rather than a request. Chapter 4's warning about incomplete race and ethnicity data in commercial claims connects directly here — a model trained or monitored on a dataset that cannot identify subgroups cannot be audited for differential performance, regardless of anyone's intent. The fairness of the model is bounded by the completeness of the substrate.
Stratify before you average
The single highest-yield governance practice is cheap: never accept an aggregate performance number for a clinical AI tool without the same number broken out by race, ethnicity, age, sex, payer and geography. Averages are where differential performance hides, and the Obermeyer finding was recoverable from data the deploying institution already held. If a vendor will not supply stratified performance, that refusal is itself the finding.
Small hospitals cannot do this alone — and should not try
A critical access hospital with one IT staff member cannot run drift monitoring, subgroup audits and adverse event review for every AI tool it deploys. This is the strongest argument for governing clinical AI at the network level: one shared governance function, staffed with analysts no single small hospital could fund, monitoring every deployment across the network under one set of standards. Vermont's clinically integrated network is the intended vehicle, and the same logic applies to any regional network. The alternative is fourteen separate technology decisions, made at fourteen different levels of sophistication, with the weakest setting the network's real floor.
The capability gap nobody budgets for
One more failure mode deserves naming because it is specific to how rural systems buy AI. Ambient documentation tools transcribe clinical conversations, and they are trained predominantly on English. A health system with a growing multilingual population — immigrant communities, seasonal agricultural workers — that deploys a scribe without multilingual capability has introduced a documentation quality gap that falls entirely on the patients least able to absorb it, and has done so through a purchase nobody would have classified as an equity decision.
That is why the Equity Imperative belongs inside the procurement rather than beside it. Multilingual capability documentation, training data provenance, and stratified performance disclosure are evaluation criteria for a technology purchase. Written as grant conditions, they cost nothing. Discovered after deployment, they are a rebuild.
From the Book — Chapter 5
Chapter 5 covers AI governance and clinical decision support as part of the Technology substrate a transformed system depends on.

Read it at /read/chapter-05.
Two documented failures — a population health algorithm that systematically under-referred Black patients, and a sepsis model that missed two thirds of cases while alerting on 18% of admissions — show what ungoverned clinical AI produces. This lesson builds the validation, drift monitoring and bias auditing regime that would have caught both.
######## five-pillars-one-imperative | global-budgets-reference-based-pricing | Global Budgets and Reference-Based Pricing
Global Budgets and Reference-Based Pricing
Fee-for-Service Pays for the Wrong Thing
Fee-for-service payment is the foundational economic structure of American healthcare: providers are paid for each service delivered, at rates set by negotiated contracts or government schedules. The logic is simple and, transaction by transaction, entirely rational: more services delivered means more revenue.
That rationality at the individual transaction level produces irrational outcomes at the system level. Under fee-for-service, a hospital that prevents a hospitalization loses revenue. A hospital that prevents a readmission loses revenue. A hospital that manages a chronic condition well enough that a patient never reaches the emergency department loses revenue. This is not a criticism of individual clinicians or managers, who are generally motivated by genuine commitment to patient care -- it is an observation about the incentive built into the payment architecture itself. When the financial incentive and the clinical incentive point in opposite directions, the financial incentive wins systematically, at scale, even if not in every individual case.
This is also why fifteen years of voluntary value-based care programs have moved the needle on payment reform without fundamentally changing hospital behavior: as long as the underlying chassis is still fee-for-service, volume remains the path of least resistance to revenue.
Vermont's Price Extraction Problem, in Numbers
Fee-for-service creates a second structural problem distinct from the volume incentive: in concentrated hospital markets -- which describes the majority of U.S. hospital markets, and all of Vermont's -- it lets hospitals with market power charge commercial payers far above their actual cost of care. Vermont's data, documented in the Green Mountain Care Board's February 2026 report, sits well above the national average: UVMMC's commercial prices ran 358% of Medicare in RAND's 2020 study, the average Vermont hospital charges commercial payers 250-300% of Medicare, and the approximate break-even point is roughly 136% of Medicare.
The consequence for insurance premiums is direct and arithmetically straightforward. Vermont's lowest-cost silver marketplace premium rose from $456 a month in 2018 to $948 in 2024 -- a 108% increase in six years -- and GMCB reports 169% growth from 2018 to 2025, tracking hospital charge growth closely (Oliver Wyman Act 167 Report; GMCB, January 2026). These are not coincidental trends; they are the mathematical output of a price structure with no regulatory discipline.
Oliver Wyman's analysis found no relationship between price and quality across Vermont's hospital system. The gap between break-even and actual commercial charges is not explained by complexity or outcomes. It is market power -- the ability of a dominant provider to demand above-cost prices from payers with no viable network alternative.
What Reference-Based Pricing Actually Does, Mechanically
Reference-based pricing (RBP) addresses the price extraction problem directly. Rather than letting hospitals and payers negotiate bilaterally -- where hospital market power determines the outcome -- RBP establishes a transparent external benchmark, typically a percentage of Medicare reimbursement, as the maximum a hospital may accept as payment in full. Vermont's Act 68 directs the GMCB to implement mandatory RBP for commercial payers no later than hospital fiscal year 2027. The statute sets no single multiplier; Oliver Wyman's Act 167 study recommended 200% of Medicare or less for PPS hospitals as a level that moves the system toward a sustainable trajectory while still covering hospitals' actual costs.
Act 68's architecture rests on four design principles: mandatory, not voluntary, for every hospital and every commercial payer; a binding ceiling, not advisory guidance, meaning hospitals cannot charge or collect more than the established rate; a transparent, nationally comparable Medicare benchmark; and premium passthrough monitoring, so GMCB and Vermont's Department of Financial Regulation can verify that price reductions actually reach premiums rather than being absorbed as insurer margin.
GMCB's February 2026 report added a refinement reflecting Vermont's varied 14-hospital system: rather than one statewide multiplier, GMCB will weigh each hospital's payer mix, labor costs, social risk factors, and role in the system -- a critical access hospital serving a largely Medicaid and Medicare rural population has different cost economics than a large academic medical center, even under one binding ceiling principle.
The Cross-State Evidence Behind Vermont's 200%
Vermont is not designing RBP in a vacuum. Oregon implemented RBP for its state employee health plans in 2019, capping in-network payments at 200% of Medicare and out-of-network at 185%, covering roughly 300,000 lives. A Health Affairs study found the program saved an estimated $107.5 million over its first 27 months -- and, critically, all 24 hospitals affected by the cap remained in-network. That finding directly answers the most common objection to RBP: that hospitals will simply walk away from a regulated rate. At 200% of Medicare, they did not, because 200% of Medicare is still substantially above their actual cost of care.
Montana's 2016 state-employee-plan RBP program produced roughly $48 million in initial savings but proved politically fragile without a statutory mandate behind it -- a cautionary data point that helps explain why Vermont chose to legislate RBP rather than negotiate a smaller demonstration. Washington's 'Cascade Care' public option caps participating network payments at 160% of Medicare and is expanding toward state employee plans.
None of these programs, however, is a full statewide, all-hospital, all-commercial-payer mandate. Vermont's Act 68 is.
What RBP Fixes -- and What It Leaves Standing
GMCB's February 2026 report was precise about scope. RBP reduces hospital leverage to demand excessive commercial prices, narrows unjustified price variation for the same service, protects affordability with a binding ceiling, and incentivizes operational efficiency over price increases as the remaining margin lever. It also establishes the price denominator that a global budget needs to function.
RBP does not control total hospital spending -- it caps price, not volume. It does not guarantee that savings reach consumers without explicit passthrough monitoring. It does not restructure incentives around prevention or population health. And it does not solve the cross-subsidy collapse driven by Vermont's aging demographics, in which a shrinking commercially insured base must bear a growing share of below-cost Medicare and Medicaid patients.
This is why Act 68 sequences RBP first and global budgets second. RBP is a necessary but insufficient tool; global budgets are built to address what RBP leaves unresolved.
What a Global Budget Actually Is, Mechanically
A hospital global budget is a prospectively set annual revenue cap: an amount fixed before the fiscal year begins, based on population health needs and past performance, not on the volume of services a hospital happens to deliver during the year. Under a global budget, the hospital receives that fixed total regardless of how many patients it sees or procedures it performs.
This is a different lever than RBP. RBP caps the price of each unit of care; a global budget caps total revenue across all units combined, for the year, in advance. A Vermont hospital operating under a global budget knows its annual revenue before the year starts -- something fee-for-service, with its dependence on volume, acuity mix, and billing accuracy, can never provide.
That predictability is not a secondary benefit. For Vermont's financially distressed rural hospitals, knowing next year's revenue today is what makes multi-year capital planning and workforce investment possible at all.
The Incentive Flip: Why an Avoided Admission Becomes a Margin Gain
Under fee-for-service, revenue equals price times volume: the only way to grow revenue is to deliver more services or charge more per service. Under a global budget, revenue is fixed by construction. The only lever left to improve financial performance is reducing cost -- which means managing population health better, preventing hospitalizations, cutting avoidable readmissions, and delivering care in less expensive settings.
This flips the admission-avoidance calculus completely. Under fee-for-service, an avoided admission is lost revenue. Under a global budget, the same avoided admission reduces the cost side of a fixed-revenue equation -- which is, arithmetically, improved margin. The clinical success and the financial success point the same direction for the first time.
A Maryland state regulator, quoted in a JAMA Network Open study of the state's all-payer model, described the effect directly: the global budget "flipped the incentives for hospitals in the right direction. It was such a monumental change, a sea change, in the way that hospitals thought about raising revenue." This is not a theoretical claim -- it is a documented behavioral shift, from strategies that chase volume to strategies built around population health management.
Maryland: A Decade of Global Budget Evidence
Maryland's Health Services Cost Review Commission (HSCRC) was created by the Maryland General Assembly in 1971 with a unique statutory authority to set hospital rates for all commercial payers, and received a Medicare demonstration waiver in 1977 to extend that authority to Medicare as well. The current Global Budget Revenue (GBR) methodology, operating under a renegotiated federal waiver since 2014, fixes each hospital's total annual revenue before the year begins; prices for individual services then adjust during the year to hit that fixed target.
Maryland is the only U.S. state to have run mandatory all-payer hospital global budgets for more than a decade, and its results are the closest empirical evidence available for what Vermont is attempting: per the CMS-commissioned evaluation (RTI, 2019), $975 million less total Medicare spending over the first 4.5 years (2.8% slower growth), $796 million of it in hospital spending, and 6.7% fewer admissions for ambulatory-care-sensitive conditions; Maryland's regulator, measuring against the national trend, reports roughly $1.4 billion in Medicare hospital savings.
The model's accountability structure extends beyond the budget cap itself: a Medicare Performance Adjustment worth 1% of Medicare revenue tied to total cost of care, and a Quality Based Reimbursement program worth 2% of all-payer revenue tied to patient experience, safety, and outcomes. The budget constraint is non-negotiable; the quality components are calibrated to reward the population-health behavior the fixed budget is designed to produce.
What Maryland Also Proves: A Global Budget Alone Doesn't Fix Population Health
The Milbank Memorial Fund's evaluation of Maryland's model is not uniformly positive, and intellectual honesty requires presenting the limits alongside the achievements: it found mixed results on quality metrics and no improvement in population-level measures like smoking rates or obesity prevalence.
The reason is analytically important. A global budget creates a powerful incentive to reduce hospital utilization, but it does not automatically create the community infrastructure -- primary care capacity, behavioral health access, housing, transportation -- that addresses what drives that utilization in the first place. When Maryland's avoidable admissions fell, the reduction was concentrated among healthier patients who, with adequate primary care, would not have needed hospitalization. The sickest patients kept arriving at emergency departments, and hospitals spent more time treating them once there.
Vermont built this lesson into its design from the start rather than adding it years later, as Maryland did. The AHEAD State Agreement linked hospital global budgets to the Equity, Access, and Statewide Transformation (EAST) Fund for primary care, mental health, home health, and long-term care investment -- a plan undone when CMS capped the expected EAST Fund near $10 million and Vermont withdrew from AHEAD in July 2026 (see below). The Rural Health Transformation Program separately provides transformation capital -- a $195 million FY2026 award, an annual amount rather than a five-year total -- for workforce, telehealth, and community infrastructure.
Vermont's Four Attempts, and the One Lesson
Vermont has tried some version of hospital global budgeting for over a decade, and the pattern across the attempts is instructive. GMCB's net patient revenue cap, in place since 2012, partially constrained individual hospital revenue growth but did not align incentives across payers or address volume gaming. A 2014 pilot proposed for Rutland Regional Medical Center -- payments based on historical revenue plus inflation, adjusted for demographics -- was never implemented; hospital opposition and implementation complexity stopped it before launch.
The Vermont All-Payer ACO Model (2017-2025) went further: a voluntary arrangement aligning hospital global payments across Medicare, Medicaid, and commercial payers based on historical spend. But because participation was voluntary, the state's highest-cost commercial payers opted out, and OneCare Vermont -- the ACO administering the model -- could not compel them to join. The model produced modest results but never achieved the all-payer alignment that makes global budgets work, and it expired at the end of 2025.
The lesson across all three attempts is unambiguous: a global budget that is optional for the highest-price hospital or the highest-leverage payer in a market is not a global budget -- it is a demonstration project. Act 68's statutory mandate, requiring global budgets for one or more non-CAH hospitals by FY2028 and all Vermont hospitals by FY2030, resources permitting, removes the opt-out. That is the design difference that matters, and it is the reason Act 68 looks structurally different from everything that came before it.
The AHEAD Episode: A Model Vermont Signed, Then Left
In January 2025, Vermont signed the AHEAD (Achieving Healthcare Efficiency through Accountable Design) State Agreement with CMS, a federal model intended to bring Medicare fee-for-service hospitals under global budgets alongside Act 68's commercial reforms. Vermont expected roughly $138 million in additional federal funds to reinvest in primary care and community services as part of the deal.
A subsequent CMS renegotiation, imposed to align Vermont's terms with those of other AHEAD states, cut that expectation to a cap of about $10 million. With most of the money that had justified joining gone, but the model's administrative complexity and downside risk unchanged, Vermont formally notified CMS of its withdrawal in July 2026.
Because the performance period had not yet begun, the withdrawal changed nothing operationally for Vermont hospitals or providers: Act 68's global budget mandate rests on state statutory authority, not the federal AHEAD agreement, and Vermont's near-term transformation capital comes from the Rural Health Transformation Program, which does not depend on AHEAD either. The episode is a concrete illustration of a risk this course takes seriously -- because Vermont anchored its reform in state authority rather than a federal model, it could exit a bad federal deal without derailing the reform itself.
Before Your Next Contract Cycle
For a hospital executive, the practical task is to model your cost structure under a fixed-revenue scenario now, not after FY2028 arrives: what does cost per adjusted discharge look like at current volume, at 5% lower volume, at 10% lower volume? What administrative cost-reduction opportunities exist that are simply invisible under a volume-growth financial model?
The transition window is short. GMCB sets the RBP method by rule in 2027, and reference prices take effect for commercial payers in hospital FY2028 -- the same year the first non-CAH global budgets are due, one budget cycle away. Contracts negotiated today should already assume the fixed-revenue environment that is coming, not the volume-driven environment that is ending.
Payment reform is the master variable the rest of this course's framework depends on financially -- but a global budget only produces the incentive flip this lesson describes if the organization can actually measure and manage a fixed budget in practice. That is the subject of the next lesson.

Voluntary Models Fail
Vermont's own All-Payer ACO Model (2017-2025) proves this concretely: OneCare Vermont could not compel the state's highest-cost commercial payers to participate, so the model never achieved the all-payer alignment that makes global budgets work, and it expired at the end of 2025. This is why Act 68 made participation mandatory rather than trying to improve the voluntary model.
Maryland's Global Budget Results, and Their Limits
Maryland's decade-plus track record gives Vermont something no other state can offer: a mandatory, all-payer, statewide global budget program old enough to show both what it achieves and where it needs help. The savings and utilization results are real and independently evaluated by CMS, HSCRC, and outside researchers.
The population-health limits are equally real, and Vermont's planned response -- pairing the budget with the EAST Fund and Rural Health Transformation Program from day one -- was a direct answer to the specific gap Maryland's evaluators identified, though the EAST Fund half fell away when Vermont withdrew from AHEAD in July 2026.

The Oregon Counter-Evidence
The most common objection to reference-based pricing is that hospitals will simply refuse the regulated rate and exit commercial networks, cutting off patient access. Oregon's experience directly refutes this at 200% of Medicare: all 24 hospitals affected by the state's 2019 employee-plan RBP program remained in-network, because 200% of Medicare is still well above their actual cost of care.
A Global Budget Without Primary Care Is Half a Reform
Maryland's Milbank Fund evaluation found the global budget model reduced hospital utilization but did not, by itself, improve population health measures like smoking or obesity rates -- the reduction in admissions was concentrated among healthier patients. Vermont tried to build the lesson into its design from day one: the EAST Fund and Rural Health Transformation Program were to pair the fixed-revenue budget with community investment, rather than adding it years later as Maryland did. The EAST Fund fell away when Vermont withdrew from AHEAD in July 2026.
Reference-Based Pricing and Rate Regulation: Cross-State Comparison
Oregon (2019) —
200% of Medicare in-network / 185% out-of-network; state employee plan, ~300,000 covered lives → $107.5M saved in 27 months (Health Affairs); all 24 affected hospitals stayed in-network
Montana (2016) —
Direct contracting at a percentage of Medicare for the state employee plan → $48M initial savings; politically fragile without a statutory mandate behind it
Washington (2021) —
'Cascade Care' public option at 160% of Medicare → Voluntary; expanding to state employee plans and growing commercial adoption
Maryland (2014-present) —
All-payer rate setting; fixed annual global budget revenue; Medicare waiver → $975M lower Medicare spending in 4.5 years ($796M hospital); 6.7% fewer avoidable admissions (CMS/RTI)
Vermont Act 68 (FY2027) —
Mandatory statewide RBP, hospital-specific prices set by GMCB rule (Oliver Wyman recommended 200% of Medicare or less) → Implementation underway; FY2027 commercial hospital rates cut 2.9% statewide (GMCB, September 2026) as a transition step
Fee-for-Service vs. Global Budget: What Changes When Revenue Is Fixed
Revenue formula —
Price x volume -- more services delivered means more revenue → A fixed annual amount set before the year begins, independent of volume
An avoided admission —
Lost revenue -- the hospital is paid for services it no longer delivers → Reduced cost against a fixed revenue base -- in other words, improved margin
Planning horizon —
Revenue depends on volume, acuity, and billing accuracy -- variable and partly outside the hospital's control → Annual revenue is known before the year starts, enabling capital and workforce planning
What improves financial performance —
More services, higher-acuity coding, higher prices → Lower cost of care: prevention, fewer readmissions, efficient length of stay

Reference-based pricing caps what a hospital may charge; a global budget caps what a hospital may collect in total, regardless of volume. Together they are the two mechanisms Vermont uses to break the fee-for-service incentive, and Maryland's decade of results shows what each does and does not achieve on its own.
######## five-pillars-one-imperative | apm-readiness-vbc-financial-modeling | APM Readiness and VBC Financial Modeling
APM Readiness and VBC Financial Modeling
From Revenue Optimization to Population Cost Management
Chapter 6 established the payment architecture -- reference-based pricing and global budgets. This lesson turns from architecture to practice: how do organizations actually model the financial impact of alternative payment models before they sign one?
Under fee-for-service, the financial questions are about revenue optimization: how do we maximize reimbursement for the volume we deliver? Under value-based care, the questions are fundamentally different: what is our total cost of care for our attributed population, where is it higher than the benchmark and why, and what investment reduces it below the benchmark? These are population health economics questions, and they require different data infrastructure and different management skills than a revenue cycle department was built to provide.
Attribution: Defining Your Denominator Before the Year Starts
Attribution is the process of assigning patients to an organization for purposes of measuring shared savings or shared losses. It can be prospective -- the organization knows its panel before the performance year begins -- or retrospective, where the panel is only known after the year is over based on where care was actually delivered.
The methodology matters as much as the concept: attribution based on plurality of primary care visits produces a different, and typically more stable, population than attribution based on which provider billed the most for a patient. Prospective attribution enables proactive care management, because the organization can act on its panel during the year it is being measured against; retrospective attribution creates genuine uncertainty, since the organization is managing a population it cannot fully identify until the year is already over.
In Vermont, the AHEAD Model was to track total cost of care for Medicare fee-for-service beneficiaries attributed to Vermont hospitals across all payer settings, using the state's VHCURES all-payer claims database as the underlying data source, until Vermont withdrew from AHEAD in July 2026. Having the database is not the same as having the internal analytics capability to use it -- and many Vermont hospitals still lack that capability.
Benchmarking: The Number Everything Is Measured Against
Every alternative payment model is built around a benchmark: the expected cost of care against which actual performance is measured. Getting the benchmark methodology right -- or negotiating a favorable one -- is often the single most consequential financial decision in APM contract entry.
A historical spending baseline, the most common approach, sets the benchmark from the organization's own past cost, typically with a trend adjustment. This creates the 'efficient provider disadvantage': an organization that is already lean and efficient starts with a lower benchmark and less room to generate savings than a historically high-spending competitor entering the same model.
A regional benchmark uses area-wide average cost instead of an organization's own history, which eliminates the efficient-provider disadvantage but can penalize an organization operating in a genuinely high-cost region relative to its own trend. Vermont's reference-based pricing takes this approach at the price level: it anchors to Medicare rates rather than Vermont hospitals' own historical prices, directly addressing the problem of benchmarks built on historically inflated charges.
A prospective benchmark, used in global budgets and capitation, is set at the start of the year from projected population needs. It provides revenue certainty for planning, but its fairness depends entirely on the quality of the risk adjustment behind it -- which is the subject of the next section.
Risk Adjustment: The HCC Mechanism and Why It's a Financial Control
CMS's Hierarchical Condition Category (HCC) model translates a patient's diagnosis codes into a Risk Adjustment Factor (RAF) -- a multiplier applied to the benchmark to reflect that patient's expected cost of care. Accurate coding produces an accurate benchmark. RAF gaps -- diagnoses a patient actually has but that go uncoded -- understate the population's expected cost, producing apparent savings that disappear the moment coding is corrected. Every uncoded condition is real revenue and accuracy left on the table simply because documentation does not capture patients' actual complexity.
The opposite failure mode is worse. In January 2026, Kaiser Permanente affiliates agreed to pay $556 million -- the largest False Claims Act settlement to date involving Medicare Advantage -- to resolve Department of Justice allegations that employees in California and Colorado added diagnosis codes to patient charts after visits, codes the treating physicians had not identified or addressed at the visit itself, systematically inflating risk scores. The government alleged the practice drew roughly $1 billion in federal payments between 2009 and 2018.
The lesson for a CFO sits between these two cases. HCC coding accuracy is not a back-office administrative task; it is a financial control with legal exposure at one extreme and left-on-the-table accuracy at the other. Both point to the same underlying requirement: documentation that reflects real patient complexity, audited regularly against actual clinical records -- not managed as a number to be moved in either direction.
Shared Savings vs. Downside Risk: The Contract Mechanics
The core shared-savings calculation runs in steps. First, benchmark PMPM (per member per month) multiplied by attributed member-months sets the total benchmark -- the budget the organization is measured against. Second, actual total cost of care for the attributed population is measured, including out-of-network spending. Third, benchmark minus actual cost equals gross savings, or gross loss if actual spending exceeds the benchmark.
Before any payment changes hands, most models apply a minimum savings rate (MSR): under CMS's Medicare Shared Savings Program, this runs roughly 2% to 3.9% of the benchmark depending on the size of the attributed population, protecting against ordinary year-to-year cost variation triggering payments that do not reflect genuine performance change.
Once savings clear the MSR, a sharing rate applies. Under MSSP's one-sided track, with no downside risk, an organization can earn up to 50% of savings based on quality performance; under two-sided tracks that accept downside risk, sharing can reach 60%, and higher-risk tracks can share losses at 40% to 75%. The structural tradeoff is explicit: more upside sharing requires accepting more downside exposure.
The Care Management ROI Math
A care management program that prevents 50 hospitalizations in a population of 10,000 Medicare beneficiaries, at an average cost of $15,000 per hospitalization, avoids $750,000 in cost. If that program costs $200,000 a year to operate, the return is roughly 275%.
This math only works under value-based care. Under fee-for-service, the same prevented hospitalization is foregone revenue -- the identical clinical success becomes a financial loss. Vermont's data adds a second lever: 32.3% of Vermont emergency department visits are classified as potentially avoidable, at an average cost of $1,800 per visit.
This is not a hypothetical illustration -- it is the specific arithmetic reason population health management is financially rational under shared savings and financially irrational under fee-for-service, and it is why a CFO evaluating a transformation investment needs the avoided-event count and per-event cost, not a general sense that prevention 'should' pay off.
The Pioneer ACO Lesson: Benchmark Design Determines Survival
CMS's Pioneer ACO Model launched in 2012 with 32 participating health systems, selected specifically because they already had experience taking on financial risk. The benchmark combined each ACO's own historical spending with the national Medicare expenditure trend -- a design similar in spirit to today's historical-baseline approach.
Participation fell sharply over the model's life: down to 19 organizations by 2014, and to just 8 by the program's final performance year in 2016. Twenty-four organizations left over the model's life -- some for insufficient savings, some for outright losses, several moving to the less risky Medicare Shared Savings Program instead.
The lesson for any organization evaluating a new risk contract: a benchmark that looks reasonable on paper can still be the difference between an organization that thrives under risk and one that cannot sustain the model. A CFO's first question about any risk contract should be about benchmark mechanics, not the headline sharing rate.
Reading a Contract for the Risk That Isn't in the Headline Terms
A shared-savings contract's real financial risk often sits in provisions that don't appear in the summary terms: benchmark reset rules, attribution methodology, quality withholds, stop-loss thresholds, carve-outs, and reconciliation timing.
Work the math before you sign: a 30% quality withhold on 50% of gross savings means quality performance alone determines 15% of the total financial outcome. An organization that cannot yet reliably report the specific measures being withheld against is accepting risk on a number it cannot currently produce.
Carve-outs -- high-cost drugs, mental health, specialty services excluded from the shared-savings calculation -- reduce an organization's ability to manage total cost of care and shrink the addressable savings opportunity. Every carve-out is a place cost can shift without the organization being able to manage it.
The Readiness Domain That Actually Predicts Success
The VBC Transformation Readiness Assessment scores an organization across 30 dimensions in six domains -- strategic clarity, data and technology, care delivery capability, network and partnerships, revenue cycle, and workforce operations -- each rated 0 to 4. The platform reports an overall readiness percentage -- the average across all answered dimensions -- rather than a raw point total: 80%+ indicates Global Budget Readiness, 60-79% indicates Advanced stage (~6 months to readiness), and below 60% signals the organization is not ready for full downside risk.
For Vermont specifically, the book argues that Domain 2 (Data and Technology) is the binding constraint, while the Blueprint's patient-centered medical homes and Community Health Teams give Domain 3 (care delivery) a long head start. The gap is not clinical capability; it is the analytics infrastructure needed to act on what clinical teams already know how to do.
An organization should score itself against this framework, or an equivalent one, before signing a downside-risk contract -- not after the first year-end reconciliation reveals the gap the hard way.
Before Your Next Contract Cycle
The pre-signature checklist for a CFO: model your own benchmark under at least two methodologies (historical versus regional); run an HCC coding gap audit against actual clinical documentation; calculate minimum-savings-rate and sharing-rate outcomes at pessimistic, base, and optimistic total-cost-of-care performance; and list every carve-out in the contract and what it removes from your addressable savings.
Organizations that negotiate aligned VBC contracts ahead of Vermont's FY2028 global budget mandate will have a financial model that reinforces the transformation already underway. Organizations that wait will carry a commercial revenue model still built to reward volume -- in direct conflict with the fixed-budget environment the rest of their business is entering.

What Pioneer ACO's Attrition Actually Shows
CMS's Pioneer ACO Model began in 2012 with 32 organizations chosen for their risk experience; only 8 remained by the program's final performance year in 2016. Several exits were driven by benchmark design and financial losses, not clinical failure -- a reminder that a well-run clinical program can still fail financially under a poorly fitted benchmark.
Vermont's Binding Constraint Isn't Clinical
Vermont's Blueprint practices and Community Health Teams give it a head start on care delivery; data and technology is the weaker domain. Before assuming downside risk, close that gap first.
Benchmark Construction Methods
Historical baseline —
Advantage: high past spenders get more savings headroom to work with → Disadvantage: already-efficient organizations face the 'efficient provider disadvantage' -- a lower benchmark, less room to save
Regional benchmark —
Advantage: eliminates the efficient-provider disadvantage → Disadvantage: organizations in genuinely high-cost regions compete against a benchmark lower than their own cost history
Prospective benchmark —
Advantage: revenue certainty, set before the year begins → Disadvantage: fairness depends entirely on risk-adjustment quality -- poor adjustment rewards case mix, not care management
Shared Savings, Step by Step
1. Set the benchmark —
Benchmark PMPM x attributed member-months → = total benchmark spending -- the budget you are measured against
2. Measure performance —
Actual total cost of care for the attributed population → Includes all spending, even out-of-network care
3. Calculate gross savings/loss —
Benchmark minus actual total cost of care → Positive = gross savings; negative = gross loss
4. Apply the minimum savings rate —
Savings must clear roughly 2-3.9% before any payment → Filters out normal year-to-year variance from genuine performance
5. Apply the sharing rate —
Gross savings x sharing rate (50-60%+ depending on risk track) → = the organization's shared savings payment

Attribution, benchmarking, and risk adjustment determine an organization's financial exposure before it delivers a single service under a value-based contract.
